q: What is the largest animal on Earth?

q.e: Blue whales can reach lengths of roughly 100 feet (30 meters) and weigh up to 200 metric tons, making them the largest known animals ever to exist. African elephants are the largest living land animals, reaching around 6 metric tons.

q: How many legs does a spider have?

q.e: Spiders are arachnids rather than insects, which means they have eight walking legs instead of six. They also have a pair of pedipalps near their mouths that can look like extra mini-legs.

q: What is a baby dog called?

q.e: A young dog is called a puppy, or pup for short. A kitten is a baby cat, a calf is a young bovine, and a cub refers to the young of animals like bears, lions, or foxes.

q: Which animal has black and white stripes and lives in Africa?

q.e: Zebras are African equines known for their unique black-and-white striped coats. Although giant pandas are black and white, they are native to bamboo forests in China.

Caterpillars are the larval stage of insects in the order Lepidoptera, which undergo metamorphosis to become butterflies or moths. Insects like bees and beetles develop from different types of larvae, such as grubs.

q: What type of animal is a Komodo dragon?

q.e: The Komodo dragon is the largest living species of lizard, growing up to about 10 feet (3 meters) in length and weighing over 150 pounds (70 kg). They are members of the monitor lizard family Varanidae, native to several Indonesian islands.

q: What is the collective noun for a group of crows?

q.e: A group of crows is famously called a murder, a term originating from traditional English hunting poetry and folklore. A gaggle refers specifically to a flock of geese on the ground.

q: What is the fastest land animal?

q.e: The cheetah can sprint up to about 100-120 km/h (60-75 mph) in short bursts. It runs down prey in less than a minute before tiring.

q: What is Grumpy Cat's real name?

q.e: Grumpy Cat, whose real name was Tardar Sauce, became an internet star in 2012 for her permanently frowning face, caused by feline dwarfism and an underbite. She died in 2019.

q: What do you call a baby bat?

q.e: Baby bats are called pups, just like the young of dogs, seals, and otters. A group of bat pups is typically raised together in a nursery colony while their mothers forage.

q: What is the name of a rabbit's abode?

q.e: Rabbits live in underground tunnel networks called burrows, with interconnected systems known as warrens. A dray is the nest built by a squirrel, usually high up in tree branches.

q: Snakes and lizards are known to flick their tongue, this behavior is to?

q.e: Snakes and lizards flick their tongues to pick up scent particles from the air and ground. The tongue delivers them to the Jacobson's organ in the roof of the mouth.

q: What colour is the female blackbird?

q.e: The female blackbird is brown, with a streaked chest, while the male is glossy black with a yellow-orange bill. The difference helps females stay camouflaged on the nest.

q: The Kākāpō is a large, flightless, nocturnal parrot native to which country?

q.e: The kākāpō is a critically endangered, nocturnal parrot endemic to New Zealand. Weighing up to around 9 pounds (4 kg), it is the heaviest parrot species in the world and entirely flightless.

q: Wombats are native to which Country?

q.e: Wombats are marsupials native to Australia, including Tasmania. They have backward-facing pouches and make cube-shaped droppings.

q: Frogs and salamanders belong to which class of animals?

q.e: Frogs and salamanders are classified as amphibians, possessing permeable, glandular skin and typically undergoing metamorphosis from aquatic larvae to land-dwelling adults. Reptiles, by contrast, have dry scales and lay amniotic eggs.

q: Of the giant clam, giant crab and giant cockroach, which has the largest shell?

q.e: The giant clam (Tridacna gigas) can have a shell over a meter (4 feet) across, weighing hundreds of pounds. It is the largest living bivalve mollusc.

q: All of these animals have large ears (relative to their size) except one.

q.e: Polar bears have small, rounded ears, which reduce heat loss in the Arctic. Animals in hot places, such as fennec foxes and jackrabbits, have large ears to release heat.

q: Cobras are venomous snakes of family Elapidae, that generally inhabit regions of these two continents.

q.e: King cobras and true cobras live in Asia and Africa, in the family Elapidae. The family also includes mambas, coral snakes and sea snakes.

q: Name the rarest and most endangered of all wolves.

q.e: The red wolf (Canis rufus) of the southeastern US is one of the world's most endangered canids. Only about 20 live in the wild, in North Carolina.

q: Jack jumper ants, yellowish-orange carnivorous ants named after their characteristic jumpy motions, can be found only on which continent?

q.e: Jack jumper ants (Myrmecia pilosula) are found only in Australia, mostly in Tasmania and southern regions. Their sting can cause severe allergic reactions in some people.

q: Which word refers to the sound peacocks make?

q.e: Peacocks make a loud, piercing call that is often described as a scream or a "may-awe". The males also fan out their tails to attract peahens.

q: One of these is not a true breed of cat. Which one?

q.e: "French Twist" is a hairstyle, not a cat breed. Real breeds include the Siamese, Maine Coon and Persian.

q: Which of the following is not a type of spider?

q.e: "Glass spider" isn't a recognized spider type. Real spiders include the orb weaver, wolf spider and jumping spider (David Bowie had a "Glass Spider" tour).

q: All but one of the following are true types of bears. Which is the odd one?

q.e: The moon bear is another name for the Asiatic black bear, which is a real bear with a crescent-shaped white patch on its chest. The eight bear species include polar, brown, black, sun, sloth, spectacled and giant panda.

q: Which of these is not an actual breed of sheep?

q.e: Real sheep breeds include Merino, Suffolk and Dorset. The "Dakota" is not a standard breed, although there are Dakota-region sheep operations.

q: What is a group of lions called?

q.e: Lions are the only wild cats that live in stable social groups called prides, which typically consist of related females, their offspring, and a small coalition of defending males.

q: What is the average lifespan of a lion living in the wild?

q.e: A wild lion lives about 10-14 years, with males often dying earlier due to fights. In captivity, lions can reach 20 years.

q: If a cat pushes its face against your head, this means what?

q.e: When a cat bumps its head against you, it's called head bunting. It shows affection and trust, and it also leaves scent from glands on the cat's face.

q: Which statement about elephants is untrue?
Elephants do not have great memories
There are some pink elephants in India

q.e: Elephants do have excellent memories. They remember water sources, routes and other elephants for decades, and matriarchs lead herds with this knowledge.

q: What type of animal is a lamprey?

q.e: Lampreys are jawless fish with a round, sucker-like mouth. Some species attach to other fish and feed on their blood.

q: Chihuahuas are the only dogs to be born with what?

q.e: Chihuahuas are born with a soft spot (molera) in the skull, as human babies are, which may remain open into adulthood. They are the smallest dog breed.

q: What is the average lifespan of Chihuahuas?

q.e: Chihuahuas typically live 12-20 years, among the longest of any dog breed. Smaller dogs tend to outlive larger breeds.
"Hippopotamus" comes from Greek words meaning "river horse". Hippos are in fact more closely related to whales than horses.

q: Also called Sea Biscuit, this animal lives in deeper water half-buried in the sand.

q.e: A sand dollar is a flat, disc-shaped sea urchin that lives partially buried in sandy seafloors. The white "dollars" found on beaches are their skeletons, called tests.

q: The Komodo dragon, the largest living lizard on Earth, lives in which part of the world?

q.e: Komodo dragons are endemic to several Indonesian islands, including Komodo, Rinca, Flores, and Gili Motang, within Komodo National Park.

q: Chameleons are lizards that can change their colour. What does Chameleon mean in Greek?

q.e: "Chameleon" comes from the Greek "chamai leon", meaning "ground lion" or "earth lion". The lizards change color for communication and temperature control, not just camouflage.

q: This sharks white belly and grey back make it difficult for prey to spot.

q.e: The great white shark is dark on top and white below, a pattern called countershading. From above it blends with the deep water, and from below it blends with the bright surface.

q: Which of these sharks has a flat body like a stingray?

q.e: The angel shark has a flattened body and wide pectoral fins that look like a ray. It lies buried in the sand and ambushes fish.

q: What is the typical lifespan of the beagle?

q.e: Beagles typically live 12-15 years. They are scent hounds with a strong nose, bred for hunting rabbits.

q: What type of coat do beagles have?

q.e: Beagles have a short to medium-length, dense coat. It sheds regularly and comes in tricolor, lemon and other patterns.

q: In what country was the goldfish first domesticated?

q.e: Goldfish were first selectively bred from wild Prussian carp in ancient China during the Tang and Song dynasties, starting well over 1,000 years ago.

q: How long can a goldfish live in optimal conditions?

q.e: Goldfish can live 20 years or more in good conditions, and the record is over 40. In small bowls, they usually die much sooner.
Wild goldfish (relatives of carp) are olive-green or brownish. Orange and gold colors came from selective breeding in China.

q: The coyote lives in North America and also goes by this name.

q.e: The coyote (Canis latrans) is also called the prairie wolf or brush wolf. It's native to North America and has expanded into cities.

q: What type of animal is the cottonmouth?

q.e: The cottonmouth (water moccasin) is a venomous pit viper of the southeastern US. It gets its name from the white inside of its mouth when threatened.

q: Which of these coat colors is not found in wild Red Fox populations?

q.e: Red foxes come in several color forms, such as red, silver (black) and cross. The black and silver morph is a rarer variant of the same species.

q: Which of the following color of egg is incorrect for a chicken egg?

q.e: Chicken eggs can be white, brown, blue or green, depending on the breed, but not black. Shell color is determined by the hen's genetics.

q: What is the average lifespan of a lion in the wild?

q.e: Wild lions live about 10-14 years, though some live longer. Females in a pride tend to live longer than males.

q: Which of these is the largest species of penguins?

q.e: The Emperor Penguin is the tallest and heaviest living penguin species, standing about 45 inches (115 cm) tall and weighing up to around 88 pounds (40 kg).

q: What does the word penguin mean?

q.e: The word "penguin" may come from the Welsh "pen gwyn" (white head) or from Latin "pinguis", meaning fat. Its exact origin is debated.

q: Which of these animals is NOT a natural predator of penguins?

q.e: Polar bears and penguins live at opposite ends of the Earth, so polar bears don't hunt them. Penguin predators include leopard seals, orcas, skuas and sharks.

q: What color is a polar bears skin?

q.e: A polar bear's skin is black, which absorbs heat, and its hairs are transparent hollow tubes that look white. This helps it stay warm.

q: What is the estimated average lifespan of a crocodile?

q.e: Large crocodiles can live 70 years or more, and some may reach a century. Smaller species typically live 30-50 years.

q: On which of these continents can you find the Salt Water Crocodile?

q.e: Saltwater crocodiles live in northern Australia, Southeast Asia and eastern India. They're the largest living reptile, reaching 6 m (20 ft).

q: Butterflies taste their food through this organ.

q.e: Butterflies have chemoreceptors located on their feet (tarsi), allowing them to taste plants as soon as they land on them. The proboscis serves as a straw to drink nectar, but it is their legs that sense sugars to verify food sources.

q: Why does a cat bury his/ her waste?
To protect their trail from predators
Because they are very clean animals.

q.e: Cats bury their waste partly to hide their scent from predators and rivals. It is an instinct from wild ancestors.

q: Why do cats like to sleep in the sun?
To make up for the drop in body temperature when they sleep
To keep from shedding so much
It reminds them of being kittens
Because they can hear better when they are warm

q.e: Cats sleep in the sun to keep warm, because their body temperature drops during sleep. Their ideal ambient temperature is higher than ours.

q: Approximately how tall is a grizzly bear when standing on its hind legs?

q.e: Grizzly bears can stand 2.4 m (8 ft) tall on their hind legs, and weigh up to 360 kg (800 lb) or more. They stand to see and smell better.

q: In which country is the grizzly bear listed as a threatened species?

q.e: Grizzly bears are listed as threatened in the lower 48 states of the US under the Endangered Species Act. Alaska and Canada have larger populations.

q: Although the grizzly bear is on the flag of this state, the last grizzly was shot there in 1922.

q.e: The California grizzly bear is on the state flag, and the last one in the state was killed in 1922. The grizzly is the state animal.

q: Which of these things is something you should never feed your dog?

q.e: Chocolate contains theobromine and caffeine, methylxanthines that dogs metabolize far slower than humans, leading to potential cardiac and nervous system toxicity. Dark chocolate and baking cocoa carry the highest concentrations and are the most dangerous.

q: The does "cheetah" mean translated from Sanskrit?

q.e: "Cheetah" comes from the Hindi "chita", from Sanskrit "chitraka", meaning "spotted one". It's the fastest land animal.

q: Which of these is not a sound made by cheetahs?

q.e: Cheetahs can't roar. They chirp, purr, growl and hiss, because their larynx structure differs from lions and tigers.

q: What is the typical lifespan of the cheetah?

q.e: Wild cheetahs live about 10-12 years, while captive cheetahs can live up to 20 years. They are vulnerable to extinction.
The Brazilian gold frog (Brachycephalus didactylus) is about 1 cm long and among the smallest vertebrates. The tiny frog lives in leaf litter in Brazil's Atlantic forest.

q: This type of ant causes a lot of allergic reactions in the USA.

q.e: Fire ants have a painful, burning sting and cause many allergic reactions in the southern US. They were accidentally imported from South America in the 1930s.

q: This type of ant is considered the most venomous of all insects.

q.e: The jack jumper ant has a sting that is dangerous to allergic people in Australia. Some scientists rank harvester ants as having more toxic venom.

q: About how long have ants been around on Earth?

q.e: Ants evolved during the Cretaceous period, well over 100 million years ago. Fossil ants date back as far as 100-140 million years.

q: because of the stripes on their back
because of the vicious way in which they killed their prey

q.e: Thylacines (Tasmanian tigers) had dark stripes across their backs, giving them a tiger-like look. The last known one died in captivity in 1936.

q: What does the Malaysian word pangolin mean?

q.e: "Pangolin" comes from the Malay "pengguling", meaning "one who rolls up". When threatened, it curls into a ball.

q: Which of these statements concerning the way in which pangolins defend themselves is false?
They spray a noxious odor like a skunk.
They curl up in a ball.
They attack by slashing their long claws or whipping their tails.

q.e: Pangolins defend themselves by curling into a ball with their scales outward, not by outrunning predators. They are slow-moving and heavily trafficked.

q: If you happen to be near a big cat (e.g. lion, tiger, lynx) that seems to be about to attack you, which of the following shouldn't you do in any case?
Try to look larger than you really are

q.e: Running away from a big cat can trigger its chase instinct. Experts say to stay calm, face the cat, make yourself look large and back away slowly.

q: Although only a small percent of scorpions are venomous to people, 800 to 2000 human deaths each year are caused by scorpions. During which part of the day are these creatures most active?

q.e: Scorpions are mostly nocturnal, hiding during the day under rocks. They glow under ultraviolet light.

q: Which of the following statements about snakes is not true?
Snakes will attack almost always they sense the presence of a human.
Snakes can strike upto half their length.
A fully grown king cobra can rear up so it looks a human in the eyes.
Not all venomous snakes are capable of killing a man.

q.e: Most snakes avoid humans and bite only when threatened or stepped on. Snakes don't normally attack people on sight.

q: In which of these African environments are hyenas NOT found?

q.e: Hyenas live in savannas, grasslands, forests and mountains, and even semi-deserts such as the Namib. They are found throughout much of Africa.

q: Which of these is not a species of hyena?

q.e: There are four living hyena species: the spotted, striped, brown and aardwolf. There is no "golden" hyena, though the golden jackal exists.

q: What is a group of hyenas called?

q.e: A group of hyenas is called a clan. Spotted hyena clans are led by females.

q: What country was home to the Moa?

q.e: Moa were nine species of large, flightless birds endemic to New Zealand before becoming extinct around the year 1440, roughly 100 years after human arrival. Madagascar was instead home to the extinct elephant bird.

q: Which of these European countries is not home to any wild native reindeer?

q.e: Wild reindeer (caribou) live in the northern parts of Europe, such as Norway, Finland and Russia, but not Switzerland. They were in the Alps during the last Ice Age.

q: According to history/science/geology, dinosaurs became extinct approximately how many years ago?

q.e: The Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction event wiped out non-avian dinosaurs around 66 million years ago, traditionally approximated as 65 million years. It was triggered by a massive asteroid impact at the Chicxulub crater in modern-day Mexico.

q: How long is the average lifespan of an elephant?

q.e: Elephants live about 60-70 years in the wild. Their lifespan is similar to humans.

q: Through what body part can an elephant NOT hear?

q.e: Elephants hear through their large ears, and can also detect low-frequency vibrations through their feet and trunk. They communicate through infrasound.

q: The echidnas diet consists mainly of this group of animals.

q.e: Echidnas (spiny anteaters) eat mostly ants, termites and other insects, which they catch with a long sticky tongue. They are egg-laying mammals.

q: Where does the kookaburra, a common Australian bird, get its name from?

q.e: "Kookaburra" comes from Wiradjuri, an Aboriginal language (guuguubarra), imitating the bird's laughing call. It's the largest kingfisher.

q: How many cubs are usually in a tigers litter?

q.e: A tigress usually gives birth to two to four cubs. The cubs stay with their mother for about two years.

q: Which country does the Clydesdale horse originate from?

q.e: The Clydesdale horse originated in Clydesdale, Lanarkshire, in Scotland, in the 1700s. It's known for its feathered feet.

q: What class of horse breed does the Clydesdale horse belong to?

q.e: Clydesdales are draft horses, bred for farm work and heavy hauling. The Budweiser Clydesdales are well-known.

q: What common name does the dog breed New Guinea Highland Dog have?

q.e: The New Guinea Highland Dog is also called the "singer" for its distinctive howl. It's closely related to the New Guinea singing dog.

q: In what European country did the Rough Collie dog breed originate?

q.e: The Rough Collie originated in Scotland, as a herding dog. It's best known as Lassie.

q: In which European country did the Dalmatian dog breed originate?

q.e: The Dalmatian trace its historical roots to Dalmatia, a coastal region in modern-day Croatia, where early illustrations depict the spotted dogs as early as the 17th century. They later became famous in England and the United States as carriage and firehouse dogs.

q: What is the definition of the term hypercarnivore?
An animal whose diet consists exclusively of meat.
It is a synonym for apex carnivore.
A predator that feeds on carnivorous animals.
It is a term that refers to humans.

q.e: A hypercarnivore gets over 70% of its diet from meat. Examples include lions, wolves and orcas.
Whiteflies are tiny insects that feed on the sap of plant leaves, usually on the undersides. They can damage crops and spread plant viruses.

q: In what Latin American country did the Chihuahua dog breed originate?

q.e: The Chihuahua is named after the Mexican state of Chihuahua, where the breed was first discovered by travelers around the mid-19th century. They are believed to descend from the Techichi, a companion dog kept by the ancient Toltec civilization.

q: In what country did the American Akita dog breed originate?

q.e: The Akita originated in Japan, and the American Akita was developed later in the US. Hachiko is the famous Akita dog.

q: In what northern country did the Siberian Husky dog breed originate?

q.e: Siberian Huskies were developed by the Chukchi people of northeastern Siberia in modern-day Russia to pull sleds over long distances. They were brought to Nome, Alaska, in 1908 during the Klondike Gold Rush as racing sled dogs.

q: The nutria is native to which continent?

q.e: The nutria (coypu) is a rodent native to South America, introduced elsewhere for fur. It's now an invasive species in North America and Europe.

q: Which of the following is a characteristic of the nutria?

q.e: Nutria have large orange incisors, with a coating of iron. They also have webbed hind feet.

q: What do farmers raise nutrias for?
Their huge teeth can be sold as jewelry.
They can use their oil for shampoos and lotions.

q.e: Nutria were raised for fur on fur farms, and escapes created wild populations. Their fur is called "river mink".

q: What is the Yorkshire Terriers average lifespan?

q.e: Yorkshire Terriers typically live 11-15 years. They were bred in the 1800s to catch rats in textile mills.

q: The Northern Short-tailed Shrew is a small venomous mammal that populates this area.
Central America and the northern parts of South America

q.e: The northern short-tailed shrew has venomous saliva, and lives in the northeastern US and southeastern Canada. It uses it to subdue prey such as mice.

q: What is a group of jellyfish called?

q.e: A group of jellyfish is called a bloom, smack or swarm. Blooms can number in the thousands.

q: What is the largest fish in existence?

q.e: The whale shark is the largest fish, reaching 12 m (40 ft) or more. It's a filter feeder and harmless to people.

q: What is the largest living terrestrial organism on the planet?

q.e: The African bush elephant is the largest living land animal. The largest organism by area is a honey fungus (Armillaria) in Oregon, or by mass, the aspen grove called Pando.

q: Where are vampire bats mostly found?
Mexico, Central America and South America

q.e: Vampire bats live in Mexico, Central America and South America. They feed on blood from livestock and wild animals.

q: What is the largest wolf species on the planet as well as the largest wild representative of the Canidae family?

q.e: The gray wolf (Canis lupus) is the largest wild canid. Wolves in northern regions, such as Alaska and Canada, grow largest.

q: Wolf pups are usually born with irises of this color, which changes with time.

q.e: Wolf pups are born with blue eyes, which turn amber or yellow at around eight weeks old. They are born deaf and blind.

q: To what continent is the unique Maned Wolf endemic?

q.e: The maned wolf lives in South America, in grasslands of Brazil, Argentina, Paraguay and Bolivia. It is the largest canid there and has long legs.

q: What kind of animal is the Spotted wobbegong?

q.e: The spotted wobbegong is a carpet shark that lives on the seabed off eastern Australia. It uses its camouflage to ambush prey.

q: What is the common name of the Quoll, a carnivorous marsupial native to Australia and Papua New Guinea?

q.e: Quolls are carnivorous marsupials of Australia and New Guinea, sometimes called "native cats". They have spotted fur.

q: Which of these areas is the Black Salamander endemic to?

q.e: The black salamander (Aneides flavipunctatus) lives in northern California and southern Oregon. It's a lungless salamander.

q: How did the Black Mamba snake get its name?

q.e: The black mamba is named for the inside of its mouth, which is black, and displayed when threatened. Its skin is olive-gray to brown.

q: In nature, chinchillas can be found in only one color. Which one is it?

q.e: Wild chinchillas are gray. Selective breeding for the fur trade has produced many colors.

q: Which of the following should be avoided in the pet chinchillas diet?

q.e: Fresh vegetables and fruits can cause digestive upset (bloating, diarrhea) in chinchillas. Their diet should consist mainly of hay and pellets.

q: Which of these physiological features does the chinchilla lack?

q.e: Chinchillas can't sweat and overheat easily. They're best kept below 25 °C (77 °F).

q: Which breed group does the Chinese Crested dog belong to?

q.e: The Chinese Crested belongs to the Toy group. It comes in hairless and powderpuff varieties.

q: What notable feature does the Fennec Fox possess, that makes it easily recognizable?

q.e: The fennec fox has enormous ears, which help it hear prey underground and shed heat in the Sahara. It's the smallest fox.

q: To which of these geographical areas are hummingbirds indigenous?

q.e: Hummingbirds are native only to the Americas, from Alaska to Tierra del Fuego. There are more than 300 species.

q: How did the smallest bird in the world, the Bee Hummingbird, get its name?
Because it is approximately the size of a large bee
Because of the sound it make with its wings

q.e: The bee hummingbird is named because of its size, about 5-6 cm (2 in), no bigger than a large bee. It lives in Cuba.

q: What type of mammal is the Culpeo?

q.e: The culpeo is a South American fox, also called the Andean fox. It's the second largest canid there.

q: Which of the following is a characteristic of the tiger shark?
They give birth to live young.

q.e: Tiger sharks give birth to live young (ovoviviparous), with litters of 10-80 pups. They're named for stripes on their sides when young.

q: What does the Latin word omnivore stand for?

q.e: "Omnivore" comes from Latin "omnis" (all) and "vorare" (to devour). Humans, bears and pigs are omnivores.

q: What is the main food source for the sloth, an omnivorous mammal living in Central and South America?

q.e: Sloths eat mostly leaves, buds and twigs. They have a slow metabolism, so they digest food slowly.

q: What is the prevailing color of the fur of the Tasmanian devil?

q.e: Tasmanian devils have black fur, with a white patch on the chest. They have a powerful bite.

q: In what part of their body do Tasmanian devils store body fat?

q.e: Tasmanian devils store fat in their tails. A thick tail means a healthy devil.

q: At what time of the day are Tasmanian devils most active?

q.e: Tasmanian devils are mostly nocturnal. They scavenge at night.

q: In what geographical region can you find the Paradise Flying Snake, also called Paradise Tree Snake?

q.e: The paradise tree snake is found in Southeast Asia. It glides from tree to tree by flattening its body.

q: What body part of the giraffe can indicate its gender?

q.e: Giraffes' horns (ossicones) differ by sex: males have bald tops from sparring, and females have tufts of hair. Males use their necks in fights.

q: The family "delphinidae" include which kind of cetacean?

q.e: Delphinidae is the family of oceanic dolphins, including bottlenose dolphins and orcas. Porpoises belong to a different family.

q: The Microraptor, the smallest known non-avian dinosaur, inhabited this modern day area during the early Cretaceous Period 130-125.5 million years ago.

q.e: Microraptor lived in China in the early Cretaceous, and had four wings. It was about the size of a crow.

q: What type of animal is the smallest vertebrate?

q.e: The smallest known vertebrate is a frog, Paedophryne amauensis, at 7.7 mm, though small fish such as Paedocypris are also tiny. Both live in Southeast Asia/Papua New Guinea.

q: The smallest turtle in the world, the Speckled Padloper Tortoise, inhabits which of these areas?

q.e: The speckled padloper tortoise is the smallest tortoise in the world, native to South Africa and Namibia. It's only about 8-10 cm long.

q: What color is the crest on the head of the Southern Rockhopper Penguin, which is known for having red eyes?

q.e: The southern rockhopper penguin has a yellow crest above its red eyes. It breeds on sub-Antarctic islands.

q: Most penguin species are piscivorous, meaning what?
They have a tubular body shape

q.e: "Piscivorous" means fish-eating. Most penguins eat fish, krill and squid.

q: What is the special talent of the penguin Mumble from the 2006 animated movie Happy Feet?

q.e: Mumble, the main penguin in Happy Feet (2006), can't sing but is a great tap dancer. The dance steps were motion-captured from Savion Glover.

q: What is the weight range of normal mature platypuses?

q.e: Adult platypuses weigh 0.7-2.4 kg (1.5-5 lb). Males are larger and have a venomous spur.

q: To what geographic area is the ostrich native?

q.e: Ostriches are native to Africa. They are the largest living bird.

q: The feathers of adult male ostriches are primarily of this color.

q.e: Adult male ostriches have mostly black plumage with white wing and tail feathers. Females are brown-gray.

q: How many toes do ostriches have?

q.e: Ostriches have only two toes on each foot, unlike other birds. This helps them run fast.

q: How long does the gestation period of elephants last?

q.e: Elephants have the longest pregnancy of any living land mammal at about 22 months, allowing their large and complex brains to develop thoroughly before birth.

q: Which of these statements is true about the Jacksons Chameleon?
It gives birth to 8-30 live young.
It lays about 15-30 eggs that hatch in 10 days.
It lays about 5-10 eggs that hatch immediately.
It gives birth to 2-3 live young.

q.e: Jackson's chameleon gives birth to live young, 8-30 at a time. Males have three horns.

q: How many times per year is a healthy female guinea pig able to give birth?

q.e: Guinea pigs can have up to five litters a year. Each litter has two to four pups.

q: What geographic area did the guinea pig originate from?

q.e: Guinea pigs originated in the Andes of South America. They were domesticated for food over 3,000 years ago.

q: What type of food does the guinea pig naturally feed on?

q.e: Guinea pigs eat grass and hay. They also need vitamin C in their diet.

q: In this 2009 Walt Disney action comedy movie the main characters are guinea pigs.

q.e: G-Force (2009) is a Disney film about guinea pigs who are secret agents. It combined live action and CGI.

q: To what continent are raccoons native?

q.e: Raccoons are native to North America. They've also been introduced to Europe and Japan.

q: Raccoons are omnivorous animals but they have a preference for this type of food.

q.e: Raccoons are omnivorous and eat fruits, nuts, insects and small animals. They're opportunistic feeders.

q: What is the most important sense for raccoons?

q.e: Raccoons have a very sensitive sense of touch in their front paws. They "wash" food to feel it.

q: Why is it not recommended to be keep raccoons as pets?

q.e: Raccoons aren't recommended as pets, as they can be aggressive, destructive and carry diseases. It's also illegal in many places.

q: What have raccoons been mostly hunted for throughout history?

q.e: Raccoons have been hunted mostly for their fur. Their meat has also been eaten.

q: How did the glass lizard, also known as glass snake, get its interesting name?

q.e: Glass lizards (glass snakes) are legless lizards whose tails break off easily when caught. The tail then regrows.

q: What feature of the turtle species Dermochelys coriacea makes it easily distinguishable from all the other sea turtles?
It has a very long tail.
Its body has very vivid colors.
It has a horn on its head.

q.e: The leatherback sea turtle (Dermochelys coriacea) has no hard shell, but a leathery skin over bone. It's the largest sea turtle.

q: In what geographical area is the Rock monitor lizard, or Legavaan, found?

q.e: The rock monitor lizard is found in sub-Saharan Africa. "Legavaan" is the Afrikaans name.

q: Where is the natural habitat of sloths?
Australia and the island of Tasmania

q.e: Sloths live in the rainforests of Central and South America. They spend almost all their time in trees.

q: Sloths have this number of toes and fingers depending on the family they belong to.

q.e: Two-toed sloths have two fingers and three toes, and three-toed sloths have three on both. All have long claws.

q: How many hours of sleep do sloths normally need per day?

q.e: Wild sloths sleep only about 9-10 hours a day, not 15-20 as in captivity. They are active at night.

q: How many babies do female sloths give birth to per one pregnancy?

q.e: Sloths give birth to a single baby after a six-month pregnancy (three-toed) or longer (two-toed). The baby clings to its mother.

q: What term is used to refer to the young of the kangaroo?

q.e: A baby kangaroo is called a joey. It lives in its mother's pouch for months.

q: Male Western Grey Kangaroos were nicknamed Stinkers because they have this kind of odor.

q.e: Male Western Grey Kangaroos are nicknamed "stinkers" because of their curry-like smell. Both sexes have a distinct musk.

q: What is the meaning of the word kangaroo according to legend?

q.e: A popular legend says "kangaroo" means "I don't understand", but this is a myth. The word is from the Guugu Yimithirr language (gangurru), meaning a grey kangaroo.

q: What is the average lifespan of a mudpuppy?

q.e: Mudpuppies can live for 11 years or more in the wild and longer in captivity. They are fully aquatic salamanders.

q: In which of the following states will you not find the mudpuppy?

q.e: Mudpuppies live in eastern and central North America, from Canada to the southern US. They're found in Texas in the eastern half of the state, but not everywhere.

q: How long is the average mudpuppy?

q.e: Mudpuppies are about 20-33 cm (8-13 in) long, with some reaching 40 cm. They have red feathery gills.

q: How many babies does the female wombat give birth to every spring?

q.e: Wombats typically give birth to a single joey, which spends months in the pouch. The pouch faces backward to keep out dirt.

q: What should a person do to escape the attack of a wombat in the wild?

q.e: Wombats can be aggressive and powerful, and could injure people. Climbing a tree is a way to escape.

q: Which continent does the turtle-dove migrate to in the colder winter months?

q.e: European turtle-doves migrate to sub-Saharan Africa for the winter. Their numbers have declined sharply.

q: Which of the following statements is true about the turtle-dove?
They are viewed as a symbol of love.
They are not related to the pigeon.

q.e: Turtle-doves are seen as a symbol of love and fidelity, as in "The Twelve Days of Christmas". They mate for life.

q: What is the expected lifespan of a turtle-dove?

q.e: Turtle-doves live about 3-8 years in the wild, and can live up to 20 years in captivity.

q: What is the incubation period for turtle-dove eggs?

q.e: Turtle-dove eggs hatch after about 13-14 days. Both parents incubate them.

q: What are the main colors of turtle-doves?

q.e: European turtle-doves are mainly brown and gray, with striped patches on the neck. They are small doves.

q: What is the greatest depth the shell of a nautilus can withstand before imploding?

q.e: A nautilus shell can withstand pressure down to about 800 m (2,600 ft) before imploding. They live in deep water.

q: What is the average lifespan of a nautilus?

q.e: Nautiluses can live around 20 years, much longer than other cephalopods. They are "living fossils".

q: What is the color of the legs, bill and eye rims of the Green Magpie, a small Asian bird with bright green plumage?

q.e: The green magpie has a red bill and red legs, and bright green plumage. It lives in the forests of Southeast Asia.

q: To which Asian country is the Giant Panda native?

q.e: Giant pandas are native exclusively to south-central China, primarily residing in the temperate bamboo forests of Sichuan, Shaanxi, and Gansu provinces.

q: To what country is the Rhinoderma rufum, a species of frog from the family Rhinodermatidae, endemic?

q.e: Rhinoderma rufum, the Chile Darwin's frog, is endemic to Chile. The male carries tadpoles in his vocal sac.

q: What interesting characteristic do all amphibians called caecilians share?

q.e: Caecilians are legless, limbless amphibians that look like worms or snakes. They live underground in tropical areas.

q: What does the diet of the Eastern Tiger Salamander mainly consist of?

q.e: The eastern tiger salamander eats insects, worms and small animals. It's one of the largest land salamanders.

q: Where does the female Suriname Toad keep its eggs until they develop into young frogs?

q.e: The female Suriname toad carries her eggs embedded in the skin of her back until they develop into toadlets. The young emerge fully formed.

q: In what places does the nocturnal Aye-aye sleep during the daytime?
On a branch, covering its body with a big leaf

q.e: The aye-aye sleeps by day in nests built in trees. It's nocturnal and lives in Madagascar.

q: What is the Aye-aye traditionally associated with according to ancient Malagasy legends?

q.e: In Malagasy legends, the aye-aye is an omen of death, and some people kill it on sight. That superstition is a big threat to the species.

q: To what geographic area is the koala endemic?

q.e: Koalas live only in eastern Australia, in eucalyptus forests. They aren't bears; they are marsupials.

q: When anxious, the koala produces a loud sound similar to the cry made by this creature.

q.e: When distressed, koalas make loud sounds like a screaming human baby. Males also make deep bellows.

q: What is the literal meaning of the word giraffe considering its Arabic origin?

q.e: "Giraffe" comes from the Arabic "zarafa", and its exact meaning is debated, with suggestions such as "fast-walker" or "lovely one". Giraffes are the tallest land animals.

q: The horns of which giraffes are very often bald on top?

q.e: Male giraffes often have bald ossicones, because they use their heads in "necking" fights. Females' horns have tufts of hair.

q: Of all mammals, giraffes require the least amount of which of the following?

q.e: Giraffes sleep very little, often only 30 minutes to two hours a day in short naps. They sleep standing or lying with their neck curled back.

q: What does the name of the zebra literally mean?

q.e: The word "zebra" may come from a Portuguese word for wild ass. Zebras are in the horse family.

q: What animal is the number one predator of zebras?

q.e: Lions are the main predator of zebras, though hyenas, wild dogs and crocodiles also hunt them. Zebra stripes may help confuse predators.

q: What is the common length of a full grown male Komodo Dragon?

q.e: A male Komodo dragon is about 2.5 m (8-9 ft) long on average. It's the largest living lizard.

q: How heavy was the largest verified wild Komodo Dragon?

q.e: The largest verified wild Komodo dragon weighed about 166 kg (365 lb). Captive ones can be heavier.

q: What is the top speed that a Komodo Dragon can reach?

q.e: A Komodo dragon can run up to about 20 km/h (13 mph) in short bursts. It's usually an ambush hunter.

q: How fast can a black bear run?

q.e: A black bear can run about 48 km/h (30 mph), faster than any human. It can also climb trees and swim.

q: Which of the following is not a nickname for a polar bear?

q.e: Polar bears are known as "ice bears", "white bears" or "sea bears" (Ursus maritimus means "maritime bear"). "Great bear" is the meaning of "Ursa Major" instead.

q: How many years does a mother grizzly stay with her cubs?
1and a half to 3 and a half years

q.e: Grizzly cubs stay with their mother for about two to three years, learning to hunt and find food. Females then mate again.

q: What of these members of the bear family is the largest?

q.e: The polar bear is the largest bear and the largest land carnivore. Males weigh 350-700 kg (770-1,540 lb).

q: Where do orphaned grizzly cubs Grinder and Coola live?

q.e: Grinder and Coola are orphaned grizzly bears who live at Grouse Mountain near Vancouver, British Columbia. They became famous after their rescue.

q: How fast can a domestic cat sprint?

q.e: A domestic cat can sprint up to around 48 km/h (30 mph) for short distances. They're ambush predators.

q: Cats have 517 of these in their entire body.

q.e: Cats have about 517 muscles, which give them flexibility and speed. Humans have around 650 muscles.

q: On what continent can aardvarks be found?

q.e: Aardvarks live in sub-Saharan Africa. The name is Afrikaans for "earth pig".

q: Aardvark is a word coming from the Afrikaans/Dutch that literally translates as what?

q.e: In Afrikaans, aardvark translates directly to 'earth pig' (from Dutch aarde meaning earth and varken meaning pig), referring to its burrowing habits and snout.

q: How many young can an adult aardvark have at one time?

q.e: An aardvark usually has a single young after a gestation of about seven months. The baby stays in the burrow at first.

q: What is the gestation period for an aardvark?

q.e: The aardvark has a gestation period of about seven months. The newborn weighs about 2 kg.

q: What color was the aardvark from the Pink Panther cartoon?

q.e: In The Ant and the Aardvark (1969), the aardvark is blue. It was part of The Pink Panther Show.

q: What is the gestation period of a dolphin?

q.e: Dolphin gestation varies by species, from about 10 to 17 months. Bottlenose dolphins carry their young for about 12 months.

q: Where in the world can you find the dolphin known as the Boto?

q.e: The boto (Amazon river dolphin) lives in the rivers of South America, including the Amazon and Orinoco. Adults are often pink.

q: Which of these is not a part of the badgers diet?

q.e: Badgers are omnivores that eat earthworms, insects, small mammals, fruit and roots. Earthworms are a main food in Europe.

q: Which of the following best defines the octopus related word midden?
a burrow in the sand used as a den
a hole in the rock face or corral used as a den
a chemical in the ink sprayed from an octopus siphon

q.e: An octopus's midden is a pile of shells and debris outside its den, from the animal's meals. Researchers use it to see what it eats.

q: Octopuses have excellent vision. Which of the following statements about an octopuss vision is NOT true?
They can see well at night.
They can make out size and shape very well.

q.e: Octopuses have excellent eyesight but are thought to be colorblind, with only one type of photoreceptor. They use polarized light and skin sensors.

q: What two continents did Smilodon inhabit?

q.e: Smilodon (saber-toothed cat) lived in North and South America, from the Pleistocene. Famous fossils come from the La Brea Tar Pits in Los Angeles.

q: Approximately how long ago did Smilodon become extinct?

q.e: Smilodon went extinct about 10,000 years ago, at the end of the last Ice Age. The decline of large prey is one factor.

q: Tomato Frogs existence is threatened due to what reason?
Their legs are used for food in fine dining restaurants.
They are hunted for their oils that are used as a skin moisturizer.

q.e: Tomato frogs are endangered because of habitat loss in Madagascar. They are red-orange and secrete a sticky substance.

q: Due to the presence of a specific protein in the blood plasma octopuses have this unusual blood color.

q.e: Octopuses have blue blood because they use hemocyanin, a copper-based protein, to carry oxygen. Humans use iron-based hemoglobin, which looks red.

q: Cockroaches are among the most resilient creatures on our planet. But how long can they survive without air?

q.e: Cockroaches can hold their breath for up to about 40 minutes, and they close their spiracles. They also survive weeks without food.

q: The Flashlight fish, has a light-producing organ, which contains luminescent bacteria. Where is this organ located?
Below the eye of the fish
On the dorsal fin of the fish
Above the eye of the fish
Between the eyes of the fish

q.e: Flashlight fish have organs below their eyes that host glowing bacteria. They can "blink" the light by covering it.

q: The Giant Panda and which of the following serve as an Asian countrys national emblem?

q.e: The giant panda and the dragon are both symbols of China. The dragon is a mythical symbol of power.

q: This animal is the second most expensive for zoos to maintain after the Giant Panda.

q.e: Elephants are among the most expensive animals for zoos to keep after giant pandas, as they need space, food and care. An elephant can eat 150 kg of food daily.

q: When a panda is born, it is impossible to tell if it is male or female. How old is the panda before its gender is known?

q.e: Newborn pandas are tiny, about 100 g, which is a thousandth of their mother's weight. Sexing them can be hard at first.

q: How long does a panda usually live in captivity?

q.e: Giant pandas live about 20 years in the wild and up to 30 in captivity. The oldest known panda lived to 38.

q: In which country is the Gohongaze Starfish considered an edible delicacy?

q.e: Starfish are eaten in some Asian countries, where they are sold as snacks. In Japan, sea creatures are a big part of the cuisine.

q: What is located on the end of every arm of a starfish?

q.e: Starfish have an eyespot at the tip of each arm, which can detect light and dark. They have no brain.

q: What animal is the largest nocturnal prosimian on the planet?

q.e: The aye-aye is the world's largest nocturnal primate (prosimian). It taps trees to find grubs with its long middle finger.

q: How deep can a bottlenose dolphin dive?

q.e: Bottlenose dolphins typically dive to about 300 m, and have been recorded much deeper. They can hold their breath for 8-10 minutes.

q: Which continents does the natural habitat of the jaguar span upon?

q.e: The jaguar's range stretches from Mexico through Central America to South America. It's the largest cat in the Americas.

q: Which of the following statements is not true about the reproduction of jaguars?
Both males and females provide parenting of the cubs.
Female jaguars reach maturity earlier than males.
Jaguars mate throughout the whole year.

q.e: Jaguar cubs are raised only by their mother, and males provide no parental care. Cubs stay with her for up to two years.

q: What term is mainly used in literature to refer to a group of crows?

q.e: A group of crows is called a murder. The term is folklore and appears in old English texts.

q: What do the beetles from the genus Nicrophorus do after finding a carcass?
They remain right next to it and protect it violently.
They wait for it to decompose.
They tear it into small pieces.

q.e: Burying beetles (Nicrophorus) bury small animal carcasses, and lay eggs on them for larvae to feed on. They care for their young.

q: What is the color of the eggs of all parrot species?

q.e: All parrot eggs are white. Many cavity-nesting birds lay white eggs as they don't need camouflage.

q: Larger parrot species have longer life spans than smaller ones. What is the average life span of a large parrot?

q.e: Large parrots such as macaws and cockatoos can live 60-80 years in captivity. Smaller parrots live 15-20 years.

q: What is the predominant color in Amazon Parrots plumage?

q.e: Amazon parrots are mostly green. They have bright patches of color on the head and wings.

q: Where does the female scorpion raise its young?

q.e: A female scorpion carries her newborn young on her back for the first weeks of life, until they molt. They then disperse.

q: What kind of substance does the female redeye cicada prefer for laying eggs into?

q.e: Female periodical cicadas lay eggs in slits in the twigs of woody plants. After hatching, nymphs drop to the ground and burrow.

q: What part of their body do the insects from order Archaeognatha use to spring up into the air?

q.e: Jumping bristletails (Archaeognatha) spring into the air by flexing their abdomen. They are primitive wingless insects.

q: What is the main icon of the Animal Kingdom park?

q.e: The Tree of Life is the centerpiece of Disney's Animal Kingdom in Florida, a 145-foot tree with carvings of 325 animals. It opened in 1998.

q: You can see this animal around ant-hill. It is almost 6 feet long and it likes to eat ants.

q.e: The giant anteater is about 2 m (6 ft) long, including its tail. It eats ants and termites.

q: This is a repulsive insect either black or brown. It can live a couple of weeks with its head cut off.

q.e: Cockroaches can live for a week or more without their heads because they breathe through spiracles on their bodies. They die from lack of water.

q: This animal lives in Africa. It has a really long neck and eats leaves. It produces almost no sounds.

q.e: Giraffes are very quiet, but they can hum at night. They eat leaves from acacia trees.

q: This animal is similar to a mouse but it is bigger. It can give birth to more than 160 babies in a year.

q.e: Rats breed quickly, with females having up to 5-6 litters a year. Each litter can have 6-12 pups.

q: These animals live in the sea. They are very friendly to humans. Although they resemble fish, they will drown if kept underwater for too long.

q.e: Dolphins are mammals and breathe air through a blowhole. They sleep with half their brain at a time.

q: When this animal wants to defend itself, it throws a nasty smell toward its aggressor. This smell can be detected by a human a mile away.

q.e: A skunk sprays a foul-smelling liquid from glands near its tail. The smell can be detected from a long way away, up to a mile.

q: Harry Potter character Sirius Black was an Animagi meaning that he could take the form of an animal. What animal could he emulate?

q.e: In Harry Potter, Sirius Black is an Animagus who becomes a large black dog, nicknamed Padfoot. Peter Pettigrew becomes a rat and James Potter a stag.

q: What type of animal is the school superintendent on Webkinz?

q.e: Webkinz is a line of plush toys, each with a code for an online virtual world. Characters include various animals in "Webkinz World".

q: What type of insect is the Orange Tip?

q.e: The orange tip (Anthocharis cardamines) is a European butterfly. Males have bright orange wing tips.

q: Of what country is the kiwi bird a national symbol? It is also native to that country.

q.e: The flightless kiwi is native exclusively to New Zealand and has served as a cherished national emblem since the late 19th century. New Zealanders around the globe are colloquially known as 'Kiwis' after the bird.

q: Which insect would a myrmecophobic person want to stay away from?

q.e: Myrmecophobia is the fear of ants. The prefix comes from the Greek "myrmex", meaning ant.

q: A popular method of finding a vampires grave involved this animal that would supposedly balk at the grave.

q.e: In vampire folklore, a virgin boy riding a white horse was said to find a vampire's grave. The horse would refuse to walk over it.

q: Nabisco makes animal crackers in a plant located in this state.

q.e: Nabisco makes Barnum's Animal Crackers, and one of its major bakeries is in New Jersey. The cracker box with a string handle dates to 1902.

q: Chinese zodiac is not limited to just defining what animal you are. It also tells you this.

q.e: The Chinese zodiac assigns an animal sign for the year and an element (wood, fire, earth, metal, water). Together they form a 60-year cycle.

q: The slaughter of what animal is forbidden in almost all states in India by law?

q.e: Cow slaughter is banned in most Indian states, because cows are sacred in Hinduism. Laws differ by state.

q: What part of any animal is absolutely forbidden for consumption by Jewish laws?

q.e: Jewish dietary laws (kashrut) forbid eating blood. Meat is salted and soaked to remove it.

q: What is the common name for the rose species Rosa Chinensis?

q.e: Rosa chinensis is called the China rose, or Bengal rose. It was key in breeding modern roses.

q: The name of what animal is missing in the Chinese proverb, A ... father has no canine sons?

q.e: The proverb is "A tiger father has no dog sons", meaning a great parent will have great children. In Chinese, "虎父无犬子".

q: The second time Noah sent the dove from the Ark, the bird returned with this.

q.e: According to the Book of Genesis, the dove returned to Noah with a freshly plucked olive leaf in its beak, signaling that the floodwaters had receded. Olive branches have served as a universal symbol of peace ever since.

q: Two fish swim into a concrete wall. One turns to the other and says _________

q.e: The punch line is "Dam!" It's a pun, since a dam is a concrete wall, and "damn" is an exclamation.

q: The tiger is the national animal of which of the following countries?

q.e: The tiger is the national animal of India, as well as Bangladesh, Malaysia and South Korea. India has about 70% of the world's wild tigers.

q: In the animal world, what is a male cat called?

q.e: An uncastrated male domestic cat is called a tom or tomcat, while a female cat is called a molly or queen. A ram is an adult male sheep, and a bitch is a female canine.

q: Depending on the species, male deer are called all of these except one.

q.e: Male deer are called bucks, stags or harts, and females are called does or hinds. "Does" are female.

q: What animal are the Canary Islands named after?

q.e: The Canary Islands are named after dogs, from the Latin "Insula Canaria", meaning "island of dogs". The canary bird was named after the islands.

q: The first mammal sent into space was this.

q.e: Laika, a Soviet dog, was the first animal to orbit Earth, aboard Sputnik 2 in 1957. She did not survive the mission.

q: Humuhumu-nukunuku-a-pua'a is a word with Hawaiian origins, referring to what type of animal?

q.e: Humuhumunukunukuāpua'a is the reef triggerfish and Hawaii's state fish. The name means "triggerfish with a snout like a pig".

q: What animal has the broadest visual color spectrum?

q.e: Butterflies can see ultraviolet light, and some have many types of color receptors. Mantis shrimp have the most photoreceptor types.

q: Prometea, an example of successfully cloned mammal, was what type of animal?

q.e: Prometea, born in 2003 in Italy, was the first cloned horse. She was a Haflinger.

q: What is the weight of the smallest known bird egg on the planet?

q.e: The bee hummingbird's egg weighs about half a gram, and is the smallest bird egg. It's about the size of a pea.

q: What kind of animal is the primary host of the protozoan Toxoplasma gondii which causes toxoplasmosis?

q.e: Domestic cats and other felines are the definitive host of Toxoplasma gondii. Pregnant women are advised to avoid cleaning litter boxes.

q: What animal cell helped prove that membrane proteins drift?

q.e: In 1970, Frye and Edidin fused mouse and human cells to show membrane proteins can move. It supported the fluid mosaic model.

q: You should expect this, if fish jump out of the water while the weather is nice.

q.e: Fish often jump near the surface when insects are active, which may happen before rain. It's folk weather lore and not very reliable.

q: What is a baby kangaroo called?

q.e: Baby marsupials like kangaroos, wallabies, and koalas are known as joeys. They are born about the size of a jellybean and climb directly into their mother's pouch to finish developing.

q: Which bird is famous for copying human speech?

q.e: Parrots, particularly species like the African grey, use a specialized vocal organ called a syrinx along with their tongue and beak to precisely mimic human speech and complex sounds.

Bats are the only mammals capable of true, powered flight thanks to their elongated finger bones connected by a flexible membrane called a patagium. Gliding mammals like flying squirrels and sugar gliders can only glide downwards.

q: What is a group of lions called?

q.e: Lions are the only wild cats that live in stable social groups called prides, which typically consist of related females, their offspring, and a small coalition of defending males.

q: What does "hippopotamus" mean and in what langauge?

q.e: The word hippopotamus comes directly from ancient Greek, combining hippos, meaning horse, and potamos, meaning river.

q: What is the average lifespan of a domestic rabbit?

q.e: Domestic rabbits live about 8-12 years with good care. Wild rabbits have shorter lives.

q: What is the common term for bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE)?

q.e: Bovine spongiform encephalopathy is commonly called Mad Cow disease because the infectious prions deteriorate the animal's central nervous system, leading to aggressive behavior and loss of motor coordination.

q: The now extinct species "Thylacine" was native to where?

q.e: The thylacine, or Tasmanian tiger, lived in Tasmania and mainland Australia. The last known one died in a zoo in 1936.

q: What is the scientific name of the Common Chimpanzee?

q.e: The scientific name of the common chimpanzee is Pan troglodytes. The bonobo is Pan paniscus.
The peregrine falcon is the fastest animal, reaching over 320 km/h (200 mph) in a dive (stoop). The cheetah is the fastest on land.

q: What is the collective noun for bears?

q.e: A group of bears is called a sloth or sleuth. Bears are generally solitary.

q: What is the world's longest venomous snake?

q.e: The king cobra can reach lengths of over 18 feet (5.5 meters), making it the longest venomous snake in the world. The green anaconda is much heavier and longer overall, but it kills by constriction rather than venom.

q: What is the name for a male bee that comes from an unfertilized egg?

q.e: Male honeybees are called drones and hatch from unfertilized eggs through a process called arrhenotokous parthenogenesis. Worker bees and queen bees are female and develop from fertilized eggs.

q: "Decapods" are an order of ten-footed crustaceans. Which of these are NOT decapods?

q.e: Decapods are crustaceans with ten legs, such as crabs, lobsters and shrimp. Krill belong to a separate order (Euphausiacea).

q: What are rhino's horn made of?

q.e: Rhinoceros horns are made of dense keratin, the same fibrous structural protein found in human hair and fingernails. Unlike deer antlers or cattle horns, they contain no bony core.

q: Which of the following is true when alligators are behaving territorially?
They bellow while showing their tail and neck
Open their jaws while making a clicking noise
They run full force at the threat
Slap their tails on the ground

q.e: Alligators bellow, especially in the breeding season, to mark territory. Their bellow can make water dance on their backs.

q: Which of these species is not extinct?

q.e: Komodo dragons are still alive (endangered), while the dodo, the Tasmanian tiger and the moa are extinct. Komodo dragons live on Indonesian islands.

q: What color/colour is a polar bear's skin?

q.e: A polar bear's skin is black, which absorbs heat. Its fur looks white, but the hairs are clear and hollow.

q: What type of animal is a natterjack?

q.e: The natterjack is a toad found in Western Europe, with a yellow stripe down its back. It runs rather than hops.

q: What dog breed is one of the oldest breeds of dog and has flourished since before 400 BCE.

q.e: Pugs are one of the oldest dog breeds, dating back to around 400 BCE in China. They were pets of emperors.

q: What is the national bird of Bahrain?

q.e: The white-eared bulbul is Bahrain's national bird. Bahrain's name for it is "bulbul".

q: When you buy an ermine coat, you're actually buying the fur of which animal?

q.e: Ermine is the traditional trade name for the winter coat of the stoat, a species of short-tailed weasel. In cold regions, the animal's brown summer fur turns pure white except for a black tip on its tail.

q: Three of these animals hibernate. Which one does not?

q.e: Sloths don't hibernate, as they live in warm rainforests. Bears, bats and groundhogs do.

q: All of these animals are omnivorous except one.

q.e: Snails are mostly herbivores, eating leaves, though some species eat meat. Omnivores include bears, pigs and humans.

q: These are typical Australian animals except one.

q.e: Sloths live in Central and South America, not Australia. Typical Australian animals include kangaroos, koalas and wombats.

q: Representatives of three of these species produce venom of their own. Which is the odd species?

q.e: Mosquitoes don't produce venom, but inject saliva that stops blood from clotting. Venomous animals include snakes, spiders and some lizards.

q: Three of these species shed their skin. Which one does not?

q.e: Penguins molt their feathers, but don't shed skin like snakes, lizards and frogs. They replace feathers every year.

q: The cobras most recognizable feature is its hood, a flap of skin and muscle behind the head, believed to serve this purpose.

q.e: A cobra spreads its hood by stretching rib bones and loose skin to look bigger when threatened. It's a defensive display.

q: A baby cobra is fully able to defend itself in as little as this many hours after being born.

q.e: A baby cobra is venomous from birth, and can defend itself within hours. Its venom is as potent as an adult's, but in smaller quantities.

q: Which of these Presidents had the most pets?

q.e: Theodore Roosevelt had a large menagerie at the White House, including a badger, snakes and a pony. His kids kept many pets.

q: What breed is known as the favourite breed of Queen Elizabeth II?

q.e: Queen Elizabeth II owned more than 30 Pembroke Welsh Corgis throughout her reign, beginning with a corgi named Susan that she received as an 18th birthday gift in 1944.

q: What is the natural habitat of the snows leopard, that was hunted down for its beautiful fur, as a result of which its population went down to 1,000 animals in the 1960s?

q.e: The snow leopard lives in the mountains of Central Asia, such as the Himalayas. It's endangered and has thick fur.

q: This freshwater mammal, found only in the Yangtze River, is the most endangered (even possibly extinct) cetacean and one of the most endangered species in the world.

q.e: The baiji, or Yangtze River dolphin, was declared functionally extinct after a 2006 survey found none. It was a pale, nearly blind dolphin.

q: How many types of bats are there?

q.e: There are more than 1,400 bat species, making up about a fifth of all mammals. They are the only mammals that can fly.

q: This animal can clean its own ears with its 21-inch tongue.

q.e: A giraffe's prehensile tongue measures around 18 to 21 inches (45 to 53 cm) long and is dark purple to prevent sunburn. This length allows it to strip foliage from thorny acacia trees and even reach its own ears.

q: What is a female sheep called or known as?

q.e: An adult female sheep is called an ewe, while an adult male is a ram. A young female is often called an ewe lamb or gimmer until she gives birth.

q: Which of the following is not a type of chipmunk?

q.e: True chipmunks include the least, yellow-pine and eastern chipmunk. "Bushy-tailed" describes some squirrels and woodrats.

q: Which of the following is not a breed of dog?

q.e: A ferret terrier is not a recognized dog breed. Real terrier breeds include Jack Russell and Airedale.

q: Which of these is not a type of beetle?

q.e: Beetles are the largest order of insects, with 400,000 species. Examples include ladybugs, weevils and rhinoceros beetles.

q: One of these is not a true breed of chicken. Which one?

q.e: Real chicken breeds include the Rhode Island Red, Leghorn and Sussex. Many breeds are named for place names.

q: Generally, how many times in an interval of 5 hours do lions mate?

q.e: Lions mate frequently, up to every 20-30 minutes over several days. A pair can mate 20-40 times a day.

q: What do male lions have which females do not possess?

q.e: Male lions develop a prominent mane around age two, which protects their neck in territorial fights and signals vitality to females. Both male and female lions share the same teeth and claw structure.

q: Cats twitch the tips of their tails slightly when hunting or when angry, while stronger twitching indicates what?

q.e: A slight tail twitch means focus or irritation, while a strong swishing or lashing tail shows displeasure or agitation. Context matters.

q: Cats generally purr when they are happy, but they can also be heard purring in what other situation?
When they are distressed or in pain
When they are hunting or playing
When they are hungry or thirsty
When they are lonely or angry

q.e: Cats also purr when in pain, scared or ill, as a self-soothing mechanism. Purring vibrations may help healing.

q: How many different vocalization sounds does a cat make?

q.e: Cats can make about 100 different sounds, whereas dogs make about 10. Many are used to communicate with humans.

q: Pound for pound, humans are not the strongest animals. What is considered the strongest species, pound for pound?

q.e: The Hercules (rhinoceros) beetle can lift about 850 times its own weight. Ants and other beetles are also strong for their size.

q: Human beings have 23 pairs of chromosomes. Which animal has the most chromosomes?

q.e: Chromosome counts vary widely. Humans have 46, hermit crabs have over 250, and some butterflies have hundreds.

q: Which of these animals has the largest paws?

q.e: The lynx has large, furry paws that act like snowshoes. This helps it walk on snow.

q: How long in years is the life span of an average wild hippopotamus?

q.e: Wild hippos live about 40-50 years. They spend most of the day in water.

q: This is the basic food of the sea. Billions upon billions of these organisms live in the sea.

q.e: Plankton forms the foundation of marine food webs, comprising drifting microscopic algae (phytoplankton) and tiny animals (zooplankton) that sustain everything from small fish to massive baleen whales.

q: This is the result of the gravitational pull from the moon and sun.
Migration of certain species of whales

q.e: Tides result from the gravitational pull of the moon and, to a lesser degree, the sun on the oceans. Spring tides are strongest when they align.

q: This sea animal, widely considered the most valuable shellfish, is common in shallow, warmer waters of all oceans.

q.e: Oysters are valued for their meat and for pearls, produced by pearl oysters. They're found in shallow waters worldwide.

q: This crab is not really a crab, but an arthropod. Its closest relative is the spider.

q.e: Despite their name, horseshoe crabs are chelicerates rather than true decapod crustaceans, placing them phylogenetically closer to arachnids like spiders and scorpions.

q: The red kangaroo appears on the Coat of Arms of Australia together with what other endemic Australian animal?

q.e: The red kangaroo and the emu are the supporters on Australia's national coat of arms, chosen in part because neither animal can easily move backward, symbolizing national progress.

q: Which of these mammals was brought to Australia by humans?

q.e: The dingo was brought to Australia by humans, about 3,500-4,000 years ago, probably by seafarers from Asia. It's a wild dog.

q: The diet of the koala consists mainly of what plant species?

q.e: Koalas eat mostly eucalyptus leaves, which are toxic to most animals. They sleep up to 20 hours a day to save energy.

q: Qantas, Australias largest airline company, has what Australian animal on its red-and-white logo?

q.e: Qantas adopted its iconic 'Flying Kangaroo' insignia in 1944, originally modeled after the kangaroo depicted on the Australian one-penny coin.

q: Which lizard can squirt blood from the corners of its eyes in order to confuse and drive back its enemies?

q.e: Horned lizards can shoot blood from their eyes, to deter predators like coyotes. They're sometimes called "horned toads".

q: The venomous lizard Gila monster was named after what?

q.e: The Gila monster is named for the Gila River Basin in Arizona and New Mexico. It's one of the few venomous lizards.

q: Geckos have immovable eyelids and cant blink. How do they keep their eyes clean?
A tiny insect lives under their eyelids and cleans their eyes.
They dip their eyes in water.
They cover their eyes with their toes.

q.e: Geckos lick their eyes, since they have no moveable eyelids, and have transparent scales covering the eye. Their long tongues are long enough.

q: No lizard species live on which continent?

q.e: Antarctica is the only continent with no native reptiles or amphibians because its extreme sub-zero temperatures and ice-covered terrain cannot support cold-blooded ectotherms.

q: This shark is considered a filter- feeder. Its diet consists mainly of plankton, krill, and macro-algae.

q.e: The whale shark filter feeds on plankton, krill and small fish. It's the largest fish.

q: Which shark is the fastest swimmer?

q.e: The shortfin mako is the fastest shark, reaching up to about 74 km/h (46 mph). It can leap out of the water.

q: What is the common name for baby sharks?

q.e: Baby sharks are called pups. Some sharks lay eggs, while others give birth to live pups.

q: Which of these is not a subspecies of giraffe?

q.e: Giraffe subspecies (or species) include Masai, reticulated, Nubian, Rothschild's and Angolan. "East African giraffe" isn't a standard one.

q: The beagle was developed mainly for tracking what animal?

q.e: Beagles were developed to track rabbits and hares, in packs. They have a keen sense of smell.

q: About how many years have beagles been around?

q.e: Beagle-like dogs have existed for around 2,000 years, since the time of ancient Greece. The modern breed was developed in England in the 1800s.

q: Which of the following cartoon dogs was a beagle?

q.e: Snoopy, from Peanuts, is a beagle. He's Charlie Brown's pet.

q: The puggle is a mix between a beagle and what dog?

q.e: A puggle is a cross between a pug and a beagle. It's one of many "designer dogs".

q: This bird is the fastest animal on the planet in its hunting method, the stoop.

q.e: The peregrine falcon reaches over 320 km/h (200 mph) in its hunting dive (stoop). It's the fastest animal.

q: This animal is the largest of the deer family and can be found in the northern parts of North America.

q.e: Moose (Alces alces) are the largest members of the deer family (Cervidae), with adult males standing up to 7 feet (2.1 meters) tall at the shoulder and weighing over 1,500 pounds (680 kg).

q: Which of these animals cannot be found in North America?

q.e: The dingo lives in Australia and parts of Asia, and not in North America. Wolves, coyotes and bears are found in North America.

q: This mammal is known for its black fur with a white stripe and for its apparent odor.

q.e: Striped skunks feature distinct black fur with bold white stripes and defend themselves by accurately spraying a sulfur-containing chemical compound called thiol up to 10 feet (3 m).

q: How many species of skunk exist?

q.e: There are around 11-12 species of skunk, in the Americas. They include striped, spotted and hog-nosed skunks.

q: How many young skunks can be born in one litter?

q.e: A skunk litter usually has four to seven kits. Newborns are blind and deaf.

q: How many subspecies of Red Fox are found in India?
None. Red Fox are not native to India.

q.e: India has three subspecies of the red fox, including the Indian desert fox. They are found in different regions.

q: Which of the following is not a breed of chicken?

q.e: The Chinese Crested is a dog breed, not a chicken. Chicken breeds include the Silkie and the Orpington.

q: How many beats per minute does a chickens heart usually beat?

q.e: A chicken's heart beats about 250-300 times per minute. Resting humans average 60-100.

q: A crocodile bite strength is up to how many pounds psi (per square inch)?

q.e: A saltwater crocodile's bite force can reach about 3,700 psi, among the highest of any animal. Humans bite at about 160 psi.

q: Butterflies do not have lungs. They breathe trough this organ.

q.e: Butterflies breathe through tiny holes called spiracles along the thorax and abdomen. These connect to tubes (tracheae).

q: How many hearts does a typical earthworm have?

q.e: Earthworms have five pairs of "hearts" (aortic arches), so 10 in total. They pump blood around the body.

q: How many species of earthworm are native to Australia?

q.e: Australia has hundreds of native earthworm species, with about 650 described. Some are giant, such as the Gippsland earthworm.

q: How many arms do octopuses have?

q.e: Octopuses have eight arms lined with suckers. The name octopus comes from the ancient Greek 'októ', meaning eight, and 'pous', meaning foot.

q: How many fatal brown and grizzly bear attacks have been reported between 1900 and 2003 in North America?

q.e: Bear attacks on humans are rare but real. Staying alert, avoiding surprising a bear and carrying bear spray reduces risk.

q: Which of these is only a dog food brand?

q.e: Cesar is a dog food brand, and a Mars Petcare product. Cesar Millan is a dog trainer.

q: In what year did the dodo become extinct?

q.e: The last widely accepted sighting of a live dodo on Mauritius was in 1662, though statistical estimates by David Roberts and Andrew Solow place its extinction around 1681 or 1690.

q: What are cheetahs that have mutated patterning that creates blotches instead of spots called?

q.e: King cheetahs have blotchy stripes instead of spots, due to a recessive gene. They were thought to be a separate species.

q: In 2007 the amount of cheetahs left in the wild dropped to what number?

q.e: Cheetah numbers have declined greatly, from about 100,000 a century ago to around 7,000 now. Estimates in 2007 were around 12,000.

q: What frog is the most poisonous?

q.e: The golden poison frog (a dart frog) of Colombia is the most poisonous frog. One frog can kill several people.

q: Which of these types of frogs shares its name with an animal that is not a frog?

q.e: "Horned frog" shares a name with the "horned lizard" ("horned toad"), which is not a toad. Many common names mislead.

q: Which one of these is not a species of zebra?

q.e: The three true zebra species are the plains zebra, mountain zebra and Grévy's zebra. "Savanna zebra" is another name for the plains zebra.

q: Which of these are not a function of a zebras stripes?
A warning sign to other zebras

q.e: Zebra stripes may serve to deter biting flies, regulate temperature, confuse predators, and help recognition. They aren't warnings to other zebras.

q: The largest ant colony is located on the Ishikari coast of Hokkaido. Approximately how many ants are there in this colony?

q.e: The Ishikari supercolony in Hokkaido, Japan, has an estimated 300 million worker ants and a million queens. They are Formica yessensis.

q: What do we call the type of ants that plant seeds to grow food?

q.e: Harvester ants collect and store seeds as food. Leafcutter ants farm fungus.

q: In 1966 was found the first ant fossil. From which geological period did it come from?

q.e: The first ant fossil, found in New Jersey amber in 1966, was from the Cretaceous. It was named Sphecomyrma freyi.

q: Which of these flamingo species is not native to the Americas?

q.e: The lesser flamingo lives in Africa and India. The American flamingo and Chilean flamingo live in the Americas.

q: Why do flamingos often stand on one leg?
To keep their feet from becoming waterlogged.
To keep feet from getting tired.
To stir up as little silt from bottom as possible.

q.e: Flamingos stand on one leg, probably to conserve body heat. The exact reason is not settled.

q: When was the last reported killing of a Thylacine in Australia?

q.e: The last wild thylacine is thought to have been shot in 1930, in Tasmania. The last captive one died in 1936.

q: What was the fine for shooting a Thylacine?

q.e: Tasmania paid a bounty on thylacines, and only protected them in 1936, shortly before the last one died. Farmers blamed them for killing sheep.

q: Although not all bear subspecies are vicious, there is a tendency for increase in bear attacks due to this factor.

q.e: As humans take over habitats, bears come into contact with people more, causing more attacks. Food shortages also play a role.

q: Surprisingly, the number one killer among animals with about 2-3 million human fatalities a year is a tiny insect. Which is it?

q.e: Mosquitoes are the deadliest animals to humans, spreading malaria, dengue and other diseases. They cause hundreds of thousands to over a million deaths a year.

q: What is the #1 reason for the rhinos decline worldwide?

q.e: Poaching driven by the illegal trade in rhino horn, valued in traditional medicine and status symbols, remains the leading cause of the global decline in rhino populations.

q: Hyenas are most closely related to what creatures?

q.e: Hyenas are in the suborder Feliformia, closer to mongooses, civets and cats than to dogs. Many people think they're related to dogs.

q: How many species of Moa are known to have existed?

q.e: Scientists recognize nine moa species, all extinct. The giant moa stood up to 3.6 m tall.

q: What was the main reason for the extinction of the Moa?
It was hunted by man for food.
There was not enough room on the island for so many large birds
It could easily be caught by predators.
It got to large to support itself.

q.e: Moa were hunted to extinction by Māori settlers by around 1400, along with the loss of habitat. They were New Zealand's flightless giants.

q: In what year were the first Moa remains discovered by Europeans?

q.e: The first moa bone was brought to Richard Owen in 1839, who identified it as a giant bird. It was found in New Zealand.

q: Approximately how many miles per year can the North American caribou travel?

q.e: Caribou make one of the longest land migrations, up to about 5,000 km (3,000 miles) a year. Herds travel in thousands.

q: Which of these is not a species of reindeer?

q.e: In North America, reindeer and caribou are the same species (Rangifer tarandus). "Northern caribou" is a common name for a population.

q: How many species of pigeons and doves exist?

q.e: There are about 300-350 species of pigeons and doves in the family Columbidae. The "pigeon" and "dove" names are interchangeable and used for different species.

q: Why are pigeon nests or eggs rarely seen?
Pigeons are cliff dwellers and build their nests in high places.
Pigeons do their best to conceal nests.
Pigeons are picky and only build nests high up in certain types of trees.

q.e: Pigeons' nests are flimsy platforms of sticks, usually built in sheltered, high places such as cliffs, ledges and building tops. That is why we rarely see the nests or eggs.

q: What is the common name for the pigeon that we see in the city streets and in our backyards?
