q: Which American-owned brewery led the country in sales by volume in 2015?
D. G. Yuengling and Son, Inc

q.e: D. G. Yuengling & Son (Pottsville, Pennsylvania, founded 1829) has been called America's oldest brewery and a top US-owned brewer by volume.
Atari's arcade game Pong was released on 29 November 1972, sparking the video game industry.

q: How many cards are there in a standard deck of playing cards?

q.e: A standard deck has 52 cards in four suits, plus usually two jokers.

q: Which of the following card games revolves around numbers and basic math?

q.e: Uno is a card game of matching numbers and colors. Cards are numbered 0–9 with action cards.

q: What do the letters of the fast food chain KFC stand for?

q.e: KFC stands for Kentucky Fried Chicken, founded by Colonel Harland Sanders, who began selling his pressure-fried chicken with 11 herbs and spices during the Great Depression.

q: Waluigi's first appearance was in what game?

q.e: Waluigi debuted as Wario's partner in Mario Tennis for the N64 (2000).

q: Who triumphed over blindness and deafness and was granddaughter of Confederate Gen. Charles W. Adams?

q.e: Helen Keller, born in Tuscumbia, Alabama, in 1880, was deaf and blind from infancy. Her maternal grandfather was Confederate officer Charles W. Adams.

q: Which type of residence hall gets its name from the Latin for "sleeping quarters"?

q.e: "Dormitory" comes from the Latin noun "dormitorium," which derives from the verb "dormire," meaning "to sleep." In medieval monasteries, it originally referred to the common sleeping quarters of the monks.

q: Robert Duvall is known to be aligned with which political party?

q.e: Robert Duvall is a registered Republican, though he has supported candidates of both parties.

q: To which famous American can Robert Duvall trace his lineage?

q.e: Robert Duvall is a descendant of Confederate General Robert E. Lee through his mother's family and played Lee in Gods and Generals (2003).

q: Which of these characters was not portrayed by Robert Duvall?

q.e: Duvall played Tom Hagen, Colonel Kilgore and Stalin, but not Jimmy Carter.

q: What is the profession of Jack Blacks parents?

q.e: Jack Black's parents, Thomas and Judith, were satellite engineers, as the bank's "rocket scientists" suggests.

q: Following Jerry Garcias death in 1995, some of the remaining members of The Grateful Dead occasionally toured under what name?

q.e: After Jerry Garcia died in 1995, the surviving Grateful Dead members toured as The Other Ones.

q: Forest Whitaker was born in this state but was raised in South Central Los Angeles.

q.e: Forest Whitaker was born in Longview, Texas, in 1961 and raised in South Central Los Angeles.

q: Forest Whitaker attended California State Polytechnic University on what kind of scholarship?

q.e: Forest Whitaker attended Cal Poly Pomona on a football scholarship.

q: Where was American billionaire Mark Cuban born?

q.e: Mark Cuban was born in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, in 1958.

q: Which Australian state or territory would you be in if you visited Ayres Rock?

q.e: Uluru, historically known as Ayers Rock, is a massive sandstone monolith situated in Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park in the southern part of Australia's Northern Territory.

q: This giant Australian state takes up a third of Australias area.

q.e: Western Australia spans over 2.5 million square kilometers (about 976,000 square miles), making up roughly 33 percent of the Australian continent's total land area.
Mark Ruffalo has Italian ancestry on his father's side (Calabria and Sicily) and is also of French-Canadian descent.

q: In what show did Judd Hirsch voice a man who was building a nuclear bomb for the Keebler elves?

q.e: Judd Hirsch lent his voice to a "Family Guy" episode, among his many roles (Taxi).

q: Peter Riegert plays the crude detective Lt. Kellaway in this 1994 comedy.

q.e: Peter Riegert played Lt. Kellaway in "The Mask" (1994), with Jim Carrey.

q: Where did James Brown first become part of a singing group?

q.e: James Brown met bandmates in a juvenile detention center in Georgia; his later group, The Famous Flames, grew from a gospel quartet.

q: How long did James Brown serve in prison in 1986?

q.e: James Brown was jailed after a 1988 car chase and served about two years of a six-year sentence.

q: What is the name of Michael Jacksons third child?

q.e: Michael Jackson's third child, Prince Michael II, nicknamed "Blanket," was born in 2002.

q: Musician Steve Vai gave the name of this element to one of his children.

q.e: Guitarist Steve Vai named his daughter Fire Vai.

q: Which element is Taurus associated with?

q.e: Taurus is an Earth sign, along with Virgo and Capricorn.

q: Which part of the body does Taurus mostly govern?

q.e: Taurus rules the neck and throat in traditional astrology.

q: In 1991 Renée Zellweger graduated from the University of Texas at Austin. What was her major?

q.e: Renée Zellweger graduated from the University of Texas at Austin in 1991 with an English degree.

q: In 1965, Charles Lane played Uncle Abner in this program.

q.e: Charles Lane appeared in Get Smart (1965–70) and was a prolific character actor.

q: Which of these is one of Black Sabbaths former names?

q.e: Black Sabbath was originally called Earth, and then they changed it in 1969 to avoid confusion with another band.

q: Select the correct statement about Gregory Pecks life.
At about 23 he left California to become an actor in New York City.
His father ran a small theater outside of Los Angeles.
He never completed his college degree at U Cal Berkley.
He had a very stable childhood living in the suburbs of Los Angeles.

q.e: Gregory Peck studied at the Neighborhood Playhouse in New York and became a star in the 1940s.

q: What was Hank Williams Jr. first wifes name?

q.e: Hank Williams Jr.'s first wife was Gwen Yeargain (m. 1971), and the bank's "June" answer is questionable.

q: What is the official language of Austria?

q.e: German is Austria's official language, with regional Austrian variants.

q: Which of the following shows did Lou Ferrigno not appear in?

q.e: Lou Ferrigno, TV's Hulk, was in Seinfeld, King of Queens and others, but not Friends.

q: What is the official language of Argentina?

q.e: Spanish is the de facto official language of Argentina, spoken by the vast majority of its population of over 45 million people.

q: What flower did Cher have tattooed on her ankle?

q.e: Cher's tattoos include a rose on her bottom; the bank says ankle. Check other sources.

q: Which of the following did Beyonce have tattooed on her hips?

q.e: Beyoncé has an "IV" tattoo on her ring finger; the bank answer is a different tattoo claim.

q: A portrait of whom did Sylvester Stallone have tattooed on his right shoulder?

q.e: Sylvester Stallone had his wife Jennifer Flavin's portrait tattooed, then had it altered to a dog (Butkus) after they separated.

q: What king of tattoo did Gisele Bundchen get done on the inside of her left wrist?

q.e: Gisele Bündchen has a small star tattoo on her wrist, reportedly.

q: What number did Eva Longoria have tattooed in English on the back of her neck?

q.e: Eva Longoria's celebrity tattoo list is not well documented. Check other sources.

q: According to Duke Ellingtons autobiography, his childhood dream was what?

q.e: Duke Ellington wanted to be a baseball player as a boy and was nicknamed "Duke" for his manners.

q: How did Frank James Cooper become Gary Cooper?
His agent was born in Gary, Indiana.
He was given that name by Ron Howard.
His football coach at UCLA gave him the name.
Spencer Tracy said, He looks like a Gary.

q.e: Gary Cooper (born Frank James Cooper) took the name on the advice of his agent, who came from Gary, Indiana.

q: How many times was Gary Cooper married?
Once to a woman not in show business
Three times: to Marlene Dietrich, Patricia Neal, and Gloria Swanson
Four times: to Clara Bow, Evelyn Brent, Carole Lombard, and Ingrid Bergman

q.e: Gary Cooper married Veronica Balfe, a socialite, in 1933, and stayed married until his death in 1961.

q: Microsoft co-founder William Henry Gates III, a.k.a. Bill Gates, was born on October 28, 1955 in this US state.

q.e: Bill Gates was born in Seattle, Washington, on 28 October 1955.

q: Which Baldwin was born May 12, 1966, making him the youngest of the brothers?

q.e: Stephen Baldwin was born on 12 May 1966, the youngest of the Baldwin brothers.

q: In 1993 this Baldwin was cast in the Baltimore-based cop show Homicide: Life on the Street.

q.e: Daniel Baldwin played Detective Beau Felton in Homicide: Life on the Street from 1993.

q: Michael Jackson was born in this US state on August 29, 1958.

q.e: Michael Jackson was born on 29 August 1958 in Gary, Indiana.

q: Supermodel Cindy Crawford won an academic scholarship to major in this field at Northwestern University.

q.e: Cindy Crawford won a scholarship to study chemical engineering at Northwestern but left after a quarter to model.

q: What award did Fred Astaire receive from his long-time professional partner Ginger Rogers in 1950?

q.e: Fred Astaire received an honorary Academy Award in 1950, presented by Ginger Rogers.

q: How many children did Kirk Douglas father?

q.e: Kirk Douglas had four sons: Michael, Joel, Peter and Eric.

q: George Clooney tried to play this sport professionally when he was younger.

q.e: George Clooney tried out for the Cincinnati Reds and the Reds' team but didn't make it.

q: What member of Patrick Swayzes family was a dancer, choreographer and dance instructor?

q.e: Patrick Swayze's mother, Patsy Swayze, was a choreographer and dance teacher in Houston.

q: How did Audrey Hepburn like to kill time when she was a child?

q.e: Audrey Hepburn enjoyed drawing as a child, and she grew up partly in the Netherlands during WWII.

q: Where did Julia Roberts marry the father of her twins Hazel and Finn, cameraman Daniel Moder?

q.e: Julia Roberts and Danny Moder married on her ranch in Taos, New Mexico, in 2002.

q: When were Jennifer Lopez and Marc Anthonys twins Emme and Maximilian born?

q.e: Jennifer Lopez and Marc Anthony's twins Emme and Maximilian were born on 22 February 2008.

q: What two instruments can Terrence Howard play?

q.e: Terrence Howard plays piano and guitar and has recorded music.

q: What was Ben Stiller mostly interested in when he was a child?

q.e: Ben Stiller was drawn to filmmaking early, making short films as a kid.

q.e: John Quincy Adams, son of John Adams, served one term (1825–29).

q: I was the 39th President of the US. My wifes name is Rosalyn. Who Am I?

q.e: Jimmy Carter was the 39th president; Rosalynn was his wife.

q: I was responsible for the Louisiana Purchase and The Lewis and Clark Expedition. I also founded the University of Virginia. Who am I?

q.e: Jefferson arranged the Louisiana Purchase, backed Lewis and Clark and founded UVA.

q: I was the first President to be impeached and the first Vice President to become President due to assassination. Who am I?

q.e: Andrew Johnson assumed the presidency in April 1865 following Abraham Lincoln's assassination and was later impeached by the House in 1868 over his violation of the Tenure of Office Act. While John Tyler was the first vice president to become president upon a predecessor's death, William Henry Harrison died of illness rather than assassination.

q: Edvin van der Saar is famous as the goalie of Manchester United. What nationality is his name typical of?

q.e: Edwin van der Sar is Dutch; "van der" is a typical Dutch name pattern.

q: Zbigniew Brzezinski served as US National Security Advisor under President Jimmy Carter. Judging by his name, what was his native language?

q.e: Brzezinski was born in Poland, and Polish was his native language.

q: Naim Süleymanoğlu is a Bulgarian champion in weightlifting. What origin does his last name suggest?

q.e: Naim Süleymanoğlu, "Pocket Hercules," was an ethnic Turk from Bulgaria.

q: Which college did Helen Keller not attend?
The Cambridge School for Young Ladies

q.e: Helen Keller graduated from Radcliffe College in 1904, not Harvard College.

q: What president awarded Helen Keller the Presidential Medal of Freedom?

q.e: Lyndon Johnson gave Keller the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1964.

q: Which U.S. President studied nuclear physics but made a career in politics and farming?

q.e: Jimmy Carter studied nuclear physics in the Navy and later ran a peanut farm.

q: Which two U.S. Presidents were the first father and son to hold the office?
John Adams and John Quincy Adams
William Henry Harrison and Benjamin Harrison
George H.W. Bush and George Bush
Theodore Roosevelt and Franklin D. Roosevelt

q.e: John Adams served as the 2nd U.S. President (1797–1801), and his son John Quincy Adams served as the 6th U.S. President (1825–1829). George H.W. Bush and George W. Bush became the second father-son presidential pair in 2001.

q: Which U.S. President was the first to formally commit American military troops to the war between North and South Vietnam?

q.e: JFK sharply increased US advisers in Vietnam; combat troops came under Johnson in 1965. Check the source.

q: Under which U.S. President was the first atomic bomb developed?

q.e: The Manhattan Project began under FDR; the first bomb was tested in July 1945 under Truman.

q: Who was the first U.S. President to die in office?

q.e: William Henry Harrison died of pneumonia on April 4, 1841, just 31 days after his inauguration, making his the shortest presidency in U.S. history. Zachary Taylor was the second president to die in office, passing away in 1850.

q: Who was the first U.S. President to take office while unmarried?

q.e: Jefferson was a widower when he took office in 1801.

q: Who was the first U.S. President to serve non-consecutive terms?

q.e: Grover Cleveland served as both the 22nd president (1885–1889) and the 24th president (1893–1897), losing the 1888 election to Benjamin Harrison between terms. Donald Trump became the second president in U.S. history to achieve this by winning the 2024 election.

q: At the age of 14, this future general, born in Kefar Malal, Israel, joined the Haganah, an underground militia.

q.e: Ariel Sharon was born in Kfar Malal and joined the Haganah at 14.

q: What German scientist said: The difference between genius and stupidity is that genius has its limits.?

q.e: The "genius and stupidity" line is attributed to Einstein but unverified.

q: Who was the first first lady, wife of George Washington?

q.e: Martha Washington, born Martha Dandridge, was married to George Washington from 1759 until his death in 1799. Although the term 'First Lady' was not commonly used during her lifetime, she served as the nation's inaugural presidential spouse.

q: What were the first names of the U.S. presidential couple the Jeffersons?

q.e: Thomas Jefferson's wife was Martha, who died in 1782 before his presidency.

q: What was the last name of U.S. presidential couple John and Abigail?

q.e: John and Abigail Adams: the surname is Adams.

q: What were the first names of the U.S. presidential couple the Madisons?

q.e: James and Dolley Madison (often spelled "Dolly").

q: Which of the following was the first name of U.S. presidential wife Mrs. Roosevelt?

q.e: Eleanor Roosevelt was FDR's wife; Theodore's wife was Edith.

q: Saddam Hussein married Sajida Talfah in 1958. How were they related before the marriage?
She was a friend from school

q.e: Saddam married his cousin Sajida Talfah in 1958.

q: Why did Saddam Hussein leave Iraq in 1959?
He was involved in a failed attempt to overthrow the government.
He went to Syria to study.
He was called away to take care of family matters.

q.e: Saddam fled Iraq in 1959 after a failed attempt on Prime Minister Abd al-Karim Qasim.
Saddam Hussein was a Sunni Muslim.

q: In which direction do the Tigris and Euphrates Rivers flow?

q.e: Both rivers rise in the highlands of eastern Turkey and flow generally southeast through Syria and Iraq before merging to form the Shatt al-Arab, which empties into the Persian Gulf.

q: Who said: Dont be afraid to take a big step if one is indicated: You cant cross a chasm in two small jumps.?

q.e: David Lloyd George is credited with the "can't cross a chasm in two small jumps" line.

q: Which genius stated that, Insanity is doing the same thing over and over again and expecting a different result?

q.e: The "insanity" quote is widely credited to Einstein but is probably misattributed; early prints come from 1980s recovery literature.

q: What was the name of Richard Nixons wife?

q.e: Pat Nixon was Richard Nixon's wife.

q: Richard Nixon was raised in which of the following religions?

q.e: Richard Nixon was raised a Quaker.

q: Name the cult leader of the Peoples Temple who was responsible for the suicide/murder of over 900 members of the Peoples Temple on November 18th 1978.

q.e: Jim Jones led the Peoples Temple; over 900 died at Jonestown on November 18, 1978.

q: Which of the following U.S. presidents was not assassinated while in office?

q.e: FDR died of a stroke in 1945, not by assassination.

q: Which of these U.S. presidents was in office less than 1 year?

q.e: William Henry Harrison served the shortest presidency in U.S. history, dying of pneumonia on April 4, 1841, just 31 days after his inauguration.

q: How many terms can a U.S. president serve?

q.e: The 22nd Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, ratified in 1951, limits an individual to being elected president no more than twice. Franklin D. Roosevelt is the only president who served more, winning four consecutive elections between 1932 and 1944.

q: Who served as the 23rd President of the United States?

q.e: Benjamin Harrison was the 23rd president.

q: Who was the first U.S. president to serve over 12 years?

q.e: FDR served 12+ years (1933–45), the only president elected four times.

q: Who was the father of Nicholas II of Russia?

q.e: Nicholas II's father was Alexander III.

q: How many children did Nicholas II and his wife Alexandra have?

q.e: Nicholas and Alexandra had five children: Olga, Tatiana, Maria, Anastasia and Alexei.

q: What is the meaning of the name Amy according to popular beliefs?

q.e: Amy comes from Old French "Amée," meaning "beloved."

q: What does the Hawaiian female name Malia mean ?

q.e: Malia is the Hawaiian form of Mary; some sources translate it as "calm."

q: According to the 2007 statistics of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, what is the most common surname in Canada?

q.e: Name rankings vary by source; Smith is traditionally Canada's most common surname, Li is among the top. Check the source.

q: Which of the following surnames is not of German origin?

q.e: Roux is a French surname.

q: Which of these is the most widespread surname in the world by number of people bearing it?

q.e: Shared by over 100 million people across mainland China and the global diaspora, Li (along with Wang) consistently ranks as the most common surname on Earth.

q: Which state was admitted into the union during Theodore Roosevelts presidency?

q.e: Oklahoma became a state in 1907 under Theodore Roosevelt.

q: Who created the fictional character Big Brother?

q.e: George Orwell created Big Brother as the omnipresent symbol of the totalitarian regime of Oceania in his dystopian 1949 novel, 'Nineteen Eighty-Four'.

q: An atlas is a collection of maps. Where do we get the word atlas from?
The name of a Greek god

q.e: Atlas comes from the Titan Atlas; Mercator used the name for his map book.

q: Which president used to go skinny dipping on warm nights?

q.e: John Quincy Adams swam nude in the Potomac.

q: This U.S. president gave the longest inauguration speech ever to that date.

q.e: William Henry Harrison's 1841 inaugural speech ran nearly two hours; he died a month later.

q: Which U.S. president fathered 15 children: 8 with his first wife and 7 with his second wife?

q.e: John Tyler fathered 15 recognized children between 1815 and 1860, the most of any U.S. president. His last child, Pearl, was born when Tyler was 70 years old.

q: This U.S. president survived gall bladder surgery when he was 17 years of age.

q.e: Polk had surgery at 17 for urinary stones (1812), not the gall bladder.

q: Which of these U.S. presidents died of throat cancer?

q.e: Ulysses S. Grant died of throat cancer in 1885, soon after finishing his memoirs.

q: Which U.S. president had his jaw removed?

q.e: Grover Cleveland had a secret jaw operation on a yacht in 1893.

q: Which U.S. president published more than 16 books during his life?

q.e: Herbert Hoover wrote many books, before and after his presidency.

q: He was the first Roman Catholic US President and his father was a prominent businessman.

q.e: John F. Kennedy was elected in 1960 as the first Roman Catholic president of the United States. His father, Joseph P. Kennedy Sr., was an extraordinarily wealthy Wall Street financier and diplomat.

q: He was a peanut farmer from Plains Georgia, a governor of Georgia and a graduate of the US Naval Academy.

q.e: Jimmy Carter graduated from the United States Naval Academy in 1946 and managed his family's peanut farm before being elected governor of Georgia in 1970 and U.S. President in 1976.

q: Which US President was elected to four presidential terms?

q.e: FDR was elected four times (1932, 1936, 1940, 1944).

q: Which of the following US Presidents was NOT the governor of a state before becoming President?

q.e: Nixon never served as governor; he was a congressman, senator and VP.

q: Which US President was largely responsible for forming the international coalition that drove Saddam Hussein out of Kuwait in the Gulf War in the early 1990s?

q.e: George H. W. Bush built the coalition that liberated Kuwait in 1991.

q: This man was a famous inventor and an American founding father.

q.e: Benjamin Franklin was a key American Founding Father who also invented bifocal glasses, the Franklin stove, and the lightning rod. Thomas Jefferson and George Washington were also Founding Fathers, but both served as U.S. presidents, a role Franklin never held.

q: This man was a Confederate general but his loyalties almost always lied with the United States. He distinguished himself in the Mexican-American War and in the American Civil War.

q.e: The description doesn't fit Lee well, since he fought for the Confederacy. Check the source.

q: This man, who was a key figure in the Reagan administration, was involved in the Iran-Contra Affair.

q.e: Oliver North, a National Security Council aide, was a key figure in Iran-Contra.

q: This World War 2 general rushed to Belgium to rescue the 101st airborn.

q.e: Patton's Third Army relieved Bastogne and the 101st Airborne in December 1944.

q: This Civil War general led the march from Atlanta to Savannah.

q.e: Union General William Tecumseh Sherman led roughly 60,000 soldiers on his famous March to the Sea from Atlanta to Savannah between November and December 1864. Ulysses S. Grant was commanding all Union armies at the time from the Overland Campaign in Virginia.

q: This man served as U.S. President and was the primary writer of the Constitution.

q.e: James Madison was the main author of the Constitution and fourth president.

q: Who was the first person to set foot on the moon?

q.e: Neil Armstrong stepped onto the lunar surface on July 20, 1969, during the Apollo 11 mission, uttering his famous 'one small step' phrase. Fellow astronaut Buzz Aldrin stepped onto the Moon roughly 19 minutes later.

q: There is evidence that incestuous marriage was widespread at some point of Egyptian history. For example, Maatkare Hatshepsut, regarded as the earliest known queen regnant in history, married Thutmose II. What was her relationship to Thutmose II?

q.e: Hatshepsut was Thutmose II's half-sister and his wife.

q: Whose last words were: Thomas Jefferson survives.?

q.e: John Adams spoke these famous words on July 4, 1826, unaware that Thomas Jefferson had actually passed away roughly five hours earlier on the very same day.

q: Which witty prolific writer met death with these words: Either that wallpaper goes, or I go.?

q.e: Oscar Wilde reportedly uttered this famous quip shortly before his death in a modest Paris hotel room in November 1900.

q: The last words of what great 20th century writer were: Does nobody understand?

q.e: James Joyce's last words are reported as "Does nobody understand?"

q: Whose final words were..Nothing but death.

q.e: Jane Austen's reported last words were "Nothing but death," answering a request for anything she wanted.

q: Friends applaud - the comedy is over
I have lived like a philosopher, and died like a Christian.

q.e: Beethoven's reported last words are likely apocryphal.

q: Which Comedian made this quip: Boycott shampoo! Demand the REAL poo!?

q.e: The "demand the real poo" joke is a pun on shampoo; the attribution to Steven Wright is uncertain.

q: This chronically smoking comedian put his audience in place with this line Non-smokers die every day. Sleep tight!

q.e: Bill Hicks was a chain-smoker and used this line in his act.

q: This case allowed police officers to pat down people for weapons without violating the 4th Amendment of the U.S. constitution.

q.e: Terry v. Ohio (1968) allowed stop-and-frisk on reasonable suspicion.

q: All arrestees are read this warning before questioning due to the case with the same name.

q.e: The warning stems from the 1966 US Supreme Court case Miranda v. Arizona, which established that suspects must be informed of their Fifth and Sixth Amendment rights before interrogation.

q: Which of the following statements is true about the Life Imprisonment sentence in the U.S.?
You stay in prison for 25 years and are then eligible for a parole hearing.
You stay in prison until you die.
You are executed after all of your appeals have run out.
You are given a 100-year prison sentence

q.e: Life sentences vary by state. Parole eligibility after 25 years is common, but life without parole exists.

q: What Amendment of the U.S. Constitution guarantees the right to be presumed innocent until proven guilty?

q.e: The presumption of innocence isn't written in the Constitution; it comes from due process (5th and 14th Amendments).

q: How was the late Earl of Mountbatten related to Prince Philip.
He was Prince Philips great grandson.

q.e: Louis Mountbatten was Prince Philip's maternal uncle; the IRA killed him in 1979.

q: Queen Elizabeth II gave birth to how many children?

q.e: Elizabeth II had four children: Charles, Anne, Andrew and Edward.

q: A Thousand Clowns, Im Not Rappaport, Thieves, Conversations with My Father are plays by this dramatist.

q.e: Herb Gardner wrote A Thousand Clowns and I'm Not Rappaport.

q: This Richard played Jason Bourne in the original 1988 Bourne Identity.

q.e: Richard Chamberlain starred in the 1988 TV miniseries The Bourne Identity.

q: This Dick starred as Tom Bradford on Eight is Enough.

q.e: Dick Van Patten played Tom Bradford in Eight Is Enough.

q: What weapon did young David, the future king of Israel, use to defeat the giant Goliath?

q.e: According to 1 Samuel 17, David refused King Saul's heavy armor and instead chose five smooth stones from a stream, striking Goliath in the forehead with a single shot from his sling. He then used Goliath's own sword to cut off the giant's head.

q: John Adams was the second President of the United States. He was educated in the field of law at this Ivy League university.

q.e: John Adams graduated from Harvard in 1755 and then read law.

q: Which one of these British Prime Ministers studied chemistry at the University of Oxford?

q.e: Margaret Thatcher studied chemistry at Somerville College, Oxford.

q: The famous New York real estate developer, Donald Trump, earned his bachelors degree in economics from this university.

q.e: Trump graduated from Penn's Wharton School in 1968 with an economics degree.

q: In 1889, what professional education did Mahatma Gandhi receive at University College in London?

q.e: Mahatma Gandhi studied law at University College London and trained at the Inner Temple, being called to the bar in June 1891.

q: In 1894, the Natal Indian Congress was founded by Mahatma Gandhi in South Africa, for what purpose?
To fight with the discrimination against Indians.
To organize the Indian people in London.
To spread the teachings of Buddha.

q.e: Gandhi founded the Natal Indian Congress in 1894 to fight discrimination against Indians.

q: What was the main principle in Mahatma Gandhis philosophical teaching Satyagraha, which he employed in his fight against the apartheid in South Africa and the British Raj?
The war to end all wars

q.e: Satyagraha translates roughly from Sanskrit as insistence on truth or soul force, emphasizing determined non-violent resistance. Gandhi first developed the method while organizing Indian immigrants against discrimination in South Africa in the early 1900s.

q: On March 10, 1922 Mahatma Gandhi was sentenced to 6 years of prison for sedition but he served only two years. Why?
Because he needed urgent medical treatment.
Because the UN forced the British government to free him.
Because he was later found not guilty.
Because his followers helped him escape from prison.

q.e: Gandhi was sentenced to six years in 1922 but released in 1924 after an appendectomy.

q: What is the title of Mahatma Gandhis autobiography, originally written in the Gujarati language?
The Story of My Experiments with Truth

q.e: Gandhi's autobiography is The Story of My Experiments with Truth.

q: During World War II, Mahatma Gandhi organized this movement of civil disobedience, determined to achieve Indias total independence from the British.

q.e: Launched by Mahatma Gandhi and the All-India Congress Committee in August 1942, the Quit India Movement demanded an orderly British withdrawal from India amidst the turmoil of World War II.

q: On January 30, 1948 Mahatma Gandhi died on his way to a religious meeting in New Delhi. What was the cause of his death?
He was shot by a Hindu radical.
He was knocked down by a car.

q.e: Gandhi was shot on January 30, 1948 by Nathuram Godse, a Hindu nationalist.

q: Joan of Arc lived in this century.

q.e: Joan of Arc was born around 1412 and executed in 1431 during the Hundred Years' War, placing her entire life within the 15th century.

q: What can be inferred about Joans clothing?
Her clothing was more commonly worn by men.
Her clothing resembled very much the one worn by Popes.

q.e: Joan of Arc wore men's clothing, which was used against her at trial.

q: How many years after her execution was Joan of Arc declared innocent?

q.e: Joan was executed in 1431; a retrial cleared her in 1456, 25 years later.

q: Who was the twenty-third President of the United States?

q.e: Benjamin Harrison was the 23rd president.

q: Who was President of the United States when the atomic bombs were dropped in August 1945?

q.e: Harry S. Truman assumed the presidency following Franklin D. Roosevelt's death in April 1945 and authorized the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August of that year.

q: Which two U.S. Presidents died on the same day?

q.e: John Adams and Thomas Jefferson both died July 4, 1826.

q: Which U.S. President is considered the father of the Constitution?

q.e: James Madison is called the "Father of the Constitution."

q: What U.S. President used the words When in the course of human events?

q.e: Jefferson wrote "When in the course of human events" in the Declaration.

q: Christopher Columbus, one of the most successful explorers in the European Age of Discovery and among the first Europeans to explore the Americas (after the Vikings,) was of what nationality?

q.e: Columbus was from Genoa, Italy.

q: She received many honorary degrees before becoming First Lady.

q.e: Lou Hoover earned a geology degree from Stanford; the "honorary degrees" clue is unclear. Check the source.

q: Who was the first First Lady to receive a college degree?

q.e: Lucy Webb Hayes was the first First Lady with a college degree (1850).

q: This first lady was responsible for the Cherry Blossoms we can enjoy every spring.

q.e: First Lady Helen Herron Taft arranged the planting of the first Japanese cherry blossom trees along the Potomac River in 1912, after Tokyo gifted 3,020 trees to Washington, D.C.

q: In what year did Queen Beatrix of the Netherlands ascend the throne?

q.e: Beatrix became queen in 1980 when Juliana abdicated.

q: This German diplomat, who died on October 6, 2002 was the spouse of Queen Beatrix of the Netherlands.

q.e: Prince Claus, Beatrix's husband, died October 6, 2002.

q: Beatrix, Queen of the Netherlands, was born in what year?

q.e: Beatrix was born January 31, 1938.

q: What fictional character was James Bond first married to?

q.e: Bond married Teresa "Tracy" di Vicenzo; Draco was her father. She was killed in On Her Majesty's Secret Service.

q: In 1877, Spencer Gore was the first winner of what tournament?

q.e: Spencer Gore won the inaugural Wimbledon Gentlemen's Singles Championship in 1877, defeating William Marshall in the final on the grass courts of the All England Club.

q: Who was the inventor of dynamite?

q.e: Alfred Nobel patented dynamite in 1867.

q: Sigmund Freud was suffering from this type of cancer, which caused him to commit a suicide with the assistance of his doctor.

q.e: Freud had jaw cancer; in 1939 his doctor Max Schur gave him morphine, and he died.

q: How did Judas Iscariot choose to end his life according to the Gospel of Matthew?

q.e: Matthew says Judas hanged himself (27:5); Acts gives a different account.

q: Where was the first president of the United States of America, George Washington, buried?

q.e: After his death in December 1799, George Washington was interred in the family tomb at his Mount Vernon estate in Virginia, declining a planned crypt in the US Capitol building.

q: Who was the first vice president to succeed a president who had died before his term was over?

q.e: Vice President John Tyler assumed the presidency in April 1841 after William Henry Harrison died just a month into his term. By insisting on taking the presidential oath rather than acting as a caretaker, Tyler set the precedent for presidential succession that was formally codified in the 25th Amendment.

q: How many different presidential parties were there up to John Tyler?

q.e: Parties through Tyler: Federalist, Democratic-Republican, Democratic and Whig.

q: Which ruler of North Korea took over the rule from his father in 1994?

q.e: Kim Jong-il took over after his father Kim Il-sung died in 1994.

q: Which leaders rule of the Peoples Republic of China began in 2002?

q.e: Hu Jintao became Communist Party leader in 2002.

q: This US Senator of the 60-80s was known as Senator Wheat for his skill at raising wheat subsidies.

q.e: Milton Young of North Dakota was nicknamed "Senator Wheat."

q: This US Senator was born above a drug store in Wallace, SD.

q.e: Hubert Humphrey was born in Wallace, South Dakota, above his father's drugstore.

q: In 2006, this state reelected one of their liberal US Senators while continuing to maintain a Republican governorship and legislature.

q.e: North Dakota reelected Democrat Kent Conrad in 2006 under Republican governor John Hoeven.

q: 3rd century astronomer Aristarchus of Samos was ahead of his time in suggesting what?
That the earth revolves around the sun
That the earth revolves around its axis

q.e: Aristarchus of Samos proposed the first known heliocentric model in the 3rd century BCE, placing the Sun at the center nearly 1,800 years before Nicolaus Copernicus published his work.

q: Whom was Mary Ann Todd married to?

q.e: Mary Todd married Abraham Lincoln in 1842.

q: In 1687, what English scientist published Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica, which described the universal laws of mechanics?

q.e: Sir Isaac Newton's 1687 work Principia Mathematica formulated the three laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation, laying the foundation for classical mechanics.

q: According to the Bible, whom did King David speak his last words to?

q.e: On his deathbed, David gave Solomon his last charge (1 Kings 2).

q: Which great scientist said the following humorous statement about love: "Gravitation cannot be held responsible for people falling in love."?

q.e: Einstein is credited with the gravitation-and-love quip.

q: Fill in the missing word to get a quote on love by the great missionary Mother Teresa: If you _____ people, you have no time to love them.

q.e: Mother Teresa said, "If you judge people, you have no time to love them."

q: The controversial American photographer Diane Arbus defined love as a peculiar unfathomable combination of understanding and ______________.

q.e: Diane Arbus's love quote ends "understanding and misunderstanding."

q: How many US states contain the New adjective in their names?

q.e: The four states are New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, and New York. New York and New Hampshire were among the original Thirteen Colonies that declared independence in 1776.

q: Which of these is the correct official name of a Canadian province?

q.e: Nova Scotia is an official province name.

q: New Brunswick was named in honor of whom/what?
King George III of the House of Brunswick
HMS Brunswick, a ship of the British Royal Navy
A town in English West Midlands
Brunswick Corporation, an American manufacturing company

q.e: New Brunswick was named for the House of Brunswick, King George III's family.

q: Which US state is part of New England?

q.e: New England consists of six northeastern states: Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Rhode Island, and Vermont. Neighboring states like New York and Pennsylvania are part of the Mid-Atlantic region.

q: Which present day territory was NOT part of Nueva España (New Spain)?

q.e: Peru was a separate Spanish viceroyalty, not part of New Spain.

q: Which of the following athletes has the jock name closest to his real name?

q.e: Champ Bailey's real name is Roland; check the other options.

q: What US President was shot and later passed away only four months after his inauguration?

q.e: Garfield was inaugurated in March 1881, shot in July, and died in September 1881.

q: According to the Bible, Nebuchadrezzar I was king of what?

q.e: Nebuchadnezzar ruled Babylon (the Bible's Nebuchadrezzar).

q: To what comedy team did Graham Chapman belong?

q.e: Graham Chapman was a core member of Monty Python alongside John Cleese, Terry Gilliam, Eric Idle, Terry Jones, and Michael Palin, often playing the lead roles in Holy Grail and Life of Brian.

q: In 1985, who broke Ty Cobbs major league record for career hits?

q.e: On September 11, 1985, Pete Rose hit a single off San Diego Padres pitcher Eric Show to record hit number 4,192, surpassing Ty Cobb's longstanding record of 4,191. Rose retired with an MLB-record 4,256 career hits.

q: William, Duke of Normandy, married whom?

q.e: William the Conqueror married Matilda of Flanders.

q: What is the name of the decisive battle of the Conquest of Normandy?
Battle for the Throne of England

q.e: Hastings (1066) decided the Norman Conquest of England, not Normandy.

q: In what year did William the Conqueror die?

q.e: William the Conqueror died in 1087.

q: Name the famous Peter who played Frank Barone in Everybody Loves Raymond.

q.e: Peter Boyle played Frank Barone on Everybody Loves Raymond.

q: According to Christian tradition, St. Paul was beheaded in Rome during the reign of this emperor.

q.e: Tradition holds Paul was beheaded in Rome under Nero.

q: American entrepreneur Paul Allen, known as one of the wealthiest people in the world, is a co-founder of what corporation?

q.e: Paul Allen co-founded Microsoft with Bill Gates in 1975.

q: As head coach of this team, Paul Bear Bryant won six national championships and thirteen conference championships.

q.e: Bear Bryant won six national titles and 13 SEC titles at Alabama.

q: What was the birth name of Elizabeth Arden who built a cosmetics empire in the US?

q.e: Elizabeth Arden was born Florence Nightingale Graham in Canada.

q: Upon the death of her father King George VI in 1952, Elizabeth II ascended the thrones of seven countries. Which of the following is not one of them?

q.e: India wasn't one of Elizabeth II's realms at her 1952 accession; it was a republic from 1950.

q: Whose mother was Saint Elizabeth according to the New Testament?

q.e: Elizabeth was the mother of John the Baptist, and Mary's relative.

q: Where was Senator Barack Obama born?

q.e: Barack Obama was born at Kapiolani Maternity and Gynecological Hospital in Honolulu, Hawaii, on August 4, 1961, two years after Hawaii became the 50th US state.

q: When did Barack Obama's term as Senator in the United States Senate begin?

q.e: Obama began his Senate term on January 4, 2005.

q: Where was Senator Barack Obamas father born?

q.e: Barack Obama Sr. was born in Rachuonyo District in what was then British-ruled Kenya in 1936, later moving to Hawaii on a scholarship in 1959.

q: Whom did Barack Obama defeat to win his Senate seat in 2005?
Paul Simon and Richard Daily, Jr.

q.e: Obama defeated Alan Keyes in the 2004 Illinois Senate race.

q: Diane Downs was convicted in 1984 for shooting which of these?

q.e: Diane Downs shot her three children in 1983; one died, and she was convicted in 1984.

q: Who penned The Open Boat, The Snake, Four Men in a Cave and The Veteran?

q.e: Stephen Crane wrote "The Open Boat."

q: Which of these US Presidents was assassinated?

q.e: James Garfield was assassinated in 1881.

q: What US President served more than two terms?

Lust, Gluttony, Greed, Sloth, Wrath, Envy, Pride
Greed, Anger, Envy, Jealousy, Conciet, Lust, Gluttony
Greed, Anger, Envy, Jealousy, Dominance, Lust, Gluttony
Carelessness, Anger, Envy, Jealousy, Conciet, Lust, Gluttony

q.e: The seven deadly sins are lust, gluttony, greed, sloth, wrath, envy and pride; they are not exact opposites of this virtue list.

q: Apart from its culinary properties, sugar has many uses in science and manufacturing. It is used for all of the following, except one.
To increase ice creams freezing point
To tan leather, printer inks and dyes.

q.e: Sugar lowers ice cream's freezing point; it does not raise it.

q: In 2004 the United States elected their _____ President.

q.e: George W. Bush, elected in 2000 and re-elected in 2004, was the 43rd president.

q: All of these gadgets belong to James Bond except one. Can you spot it?

q.e: The Batarang is Batman's gadget, not Bond's.

q: Leather can bring out the best in some females. Which feline fatale said Youre the second man who killed me this week but Ive got seven lives left.?

q.e: Selina Kyle (Catwoman, in Batman Returns) says the line about having nine lives.

q: What is the last name of the man credited with inventing the modern bicycle?

q.e: Pierre Michaux and his family are often credited with the modern bicycle, though credit is disputed.

q: Which of these statements regarding the words imply and infer is correct?
The speaker implies, the listener infers
Imply and infer mean exactly the same thing
The speaker infers, the listener implies

q.e: The speaker implies; the listener infers.

q: You go into a diner and you hear the waitress yell out Cats Eyes. What has someone just ordered?
a breakfast of steak and two eggs

q.e: In diner slang, "cat's eyes" means tapioca pudding.

q: According to the Christian tradition there are 39 books in the Old Testament. How many books are there in the Old Testament according to the Jewish tradition?

q.e: The Jewish Tanakh counts 24 books, the same material as the Protestant 39.

q: Which if these is an area in Iraq, and a pilgrimage place for some Muslims?

q.e: Karbala in Iraq is a major Shia pilgrimage site, where Imam Hussein was killed.

q: What is the mathematical term for the shape of a footballs path, when thrown form one player to another?

q.e: Under the influence of gravity alone, any projectile travels along a parabolic trajectory. A catenary resembles a parabola but describes the natural curve formed by a hanging chain or cable supported at both ends.

q: Which of these is the odd one out?

q.e: A jonquil is a type of daffodil; check the other options.

q: Which Latin expression means actions speak louder than words?

q.e: "Facta non verba" means "deeds, not words."

q: John Howard Lawson, Herbert Biberman, Albert Maltz, Adrian Scott, Sam Ornitz, Dalton Trumbo, Ed Dmytryk, Ring Lardner Jr, Alvah Bessie, and Lester Cole made short speeches to denounce McCarthyism. All of them belonged to a group, known by what name?
The ten spies of the CIA
The ten players of Dr. James Naismith
The ten judges at the Nuremburg Trials

q.e: The Hollywood Ten were blacklisted after refusing to testify to HUAC in 1947.

q: This English shipbuilder, merchant and navigator, whose innovative measures made the new English ships fast and highly maneuverable, was one of the main commanders of the English fleet against the Spanish Armada in 1588.

q.e: John Hawkins reformed English warship design and served as an Armada commander in 1588.

q: In what year were pencils first mass-produced?

q.e: Mass production of pencils began in Nuremberg around 1662.

q: A great step forward in the world of pencils was made in 1858. What was it?
Hyman Lipman began putting an eraser on the end of pencils.
Sears-Roebuck began selling pencils in their catalog.
Sarah Teasdale Wallace patented the first indelible pencil.
Irving Kellogg Watson patented the first drawing pencils in different colors.

q.e: Hymen Lipman patented a pencil with an attached eraser in 1858.

q: What substance do South American Indians use on the tips of their poison darts?

q.e: Curare is a plant poison used on darts and arrows in South America.

q: Zoophobias are some of the most widespread abnormal fears. Which of the following is not a fear associated with animals?

q.e: Neophobia is fear of new things, not an animal phobia.

q: In 1867, Alfred Nobel introduced the first Pyrotechnic Fuse blasting cap, using what primary explosive to detonate dynamite?

q.e: Nobel used mercury fulminate in his blasting caps to detonate dynamite.

q: Who was the first guest on The Tonight Show when Johnny Carson was the host?

q.e: Groucho Marx was Johnny Carson's first Tonight Show guest (October 1, 1962).

q: Which famous writer introduced the term moron into everyday vocabulary?

q.e: American psychologist Henry Goddard coined "moron" in 1910; Molière had a character named Moron.

q: This person, who in 1919 became the General Manager of Radio Corporation of America (RCA), claimed that he was the first person to receive a signal from the sinking Titanic in 1912.

q.e: Sarnoff's claim to have heard the Titanic's distress signal is disputed by historians.

q: This artistic and architectural movement, formed by Vladimir Tatlin, dismissed pure art in favor of art used as an instrument for social purposes.

q.e: Vladimir Tatlin founded Constructivism in Russia in the 1910s.

q: All babies are born with a soft spot on the top of their heads. What is this called?

q.e: A fontanelle is an anatomical feature where skull plates have not yet fused, allowing the head to compress slightly during birth and giving space for brain growth.

q: This plantation located in Louisiana is said to be haunted by the vengeful ghost of a slave named Chloe, who supposedly murdered the wife and daughters of the owner.

q.e: The Myrtles Plantation's Chloe legend is folklore; historians find no records.

q: On this day in 1929, a massacre of mob members outside a warehouse on Clark Street in Chicago occurred. As people walk the street at night they claim to hear the sounds of machine guns and screams.

q.e: The St. Valentine's Day Massacre occurred February 14, 1929, in Chicago.

q: The ghost of this mobster is said to haunt two locations. One of them is a hotel in Las Vegas, the other - a private residence in Beverly Hills.

q.e: Bugsy Siegel is said to haunt the Flamingo in Las Vegas and a Beverly Hills home.

q: This monster, who is classified under the family, Homolycanth Ropus, really has a thing about silver bullets. By what other name do we know the character, Lawrence Talbort?

q.e: Larry Talbot is the Wolf Man.

q: She is a very rude monster. She sings with her mouth full. What is the name of the human flesh eating plant that sings Feed me Seymour. Feed me all night long.?

q.e: Audrey II is the man-eating plant in Little Shop of Horrors.

q: Lethality: He will not stop, EVER, until you are dead. What assassin from the year 2029 AD, had you better believe when he says Ill be back.?

q.e: The Terminator is a cyborg sent from 2029 in The Terminator.

q: The actresss father created The Today Show, The Wide World of Sports, Your Show of Shows(aka the Sid Caesar Show) and helped create The Tonight Show.

q.e: Sigourney Weaver's father, Pat Weaver, was an NBC executive who created Today and The Tonight Show.

q: Michael Jordan is often considered the best player the Chicago Bulls ever had but they did not start winning championships until they traded Charles Oakley for this other big man.

q.e: The Bulls traded Charles Oakley for Bill Cartwright in 1988 before their first title.

q: The first known use, in English, of the word orange in reference to a color was by this man.

q.e: "Orange" as a color word appears in English by the early 1500s; check the Henry VIII claim.

q: This law says that if things can go wrong, they jolly well will!

q.e: Murphy's Law is named after aerospace engineer Edward A. Murphy Jr., who popularized the adage following equipment calibration tests at Edwards Air Force Base in 1949. It famously states that if anything can go wrong, it will.

q: There is always an easy answer to every human problem - neat, plausible and wrong. What sharp and witty American writer made this observation?

q.e: H. L. Mencken wrote about the "neat, plausible and wrong" answer.

q: This is a ground-breaking law of linguistics first formulated in 1822. It highlights in a most intriguing way how European languages may have evolved since ancient times.

q.e: Grimm's Law (1822) describes systematic Germanic consonant shifts.

q: Work expands to fill the time available for its completion. Under what name is this law known?

q.e: Parkinson's Law: work expands to fill the time available.

q: Youve been working on a job for quite a while and achieved a lot. But now fatigue has set in and you find that despite your best efforts, youre no longer getting the same high level of results. This effect is neatly expressed in which law?

q.e: The law of diminishing returns describes shrinking gains from added effort.

q: Political leaders all too often engage in misguided undertakings in the hope of recapturing popular support. Not infrequently this backfires and popularity ratings tumble. This is a simple example of which of the following laws?

q.e: The law of unintended consequences fits backfiring policy; check the other options.

q: It was the largest rough diamond ever found, weighing in at 3 106 carats.

q.e: Discovered at the Premier No. 2 mine in South Africa in 1905, the Cullinan Diamond weighed 3,106.75 carats (about 1.37 pounds) before being cut into stones for the British Crown Jewels.

q: This is the famous quote from Rene Descartes that means I think, therefore I am.

q.e: Descartes introduced this foundational philosophical statement in French as 'Je pense, donc je suis' in 1637 before rendering it into Latin as 'Cogito, ergo sum' in 1644. 'Omnia vincit amor' is a separate Latin phrase from Virgil meaning 'love conquers all.'

q: I am suffering from poliosis. What is my problem?
Slowing of ones life due to age

q.e: Poliosis is a lack of pigment in hair, giving white or gray patches.

q: The Luddites were a social movement of English workers, who protested against industrial revolution, because they felt that their jobs were threatened. The movement, which was named after a mythical leader began in this year.

q.e: The Luddites began in 1811, named for the possibly mythical Ned Ludd.

q: Which of the following groups of mammals lay eggs?

q.e: Monotremes (platypus, echidnas) are the egg-laying mammals.

q: In the Middle Ages, the purple color was used only for royal clothing because the dye was much more expensive than gold. What was the purple dye made from?

q.e: Tyrian purple came from murex sea snails, a mollusk.

q: Which French phrase can mean tastes differ?

q.e: "Chacun à son goût" means "to each his own taste."

q: Plato won it twice. Aristotle, Socrates and Alexander the Great are all said to have been keen observers of it. Dioxippus was probably the most famous winner of it. What does this question refer to?

q.e: The question describes pankration, the ancient Greek combat sport.

q: Prior to his rise to power in Spain, what was Francos job?
He was in charge of Spains military bases in Morocco
He was an Associate Professor at Spains College for Infantry Officers
He was in charge of the last Cavalry division in the history of the Spanish Army
He was in charge of the Quartermaster Corps of the Spanish Army

q.e: Franco earned fame commanding the Spanish Foreign Legion in Morocco.

q: The Five Positions, which are the basis of ballet, as well as the starting and ending points for ballet movements, were finally established by Pierre Rameau in what year?

q.e: Pierre Rameau codified the five ballet positions in 1725.

q: Which of these statements about Albert Einstein is not true?
He wrote the Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica
He was awarded the 1921 Nobel Prize for Physics
He formulated the theory of relativity

q.e: Newton, not Einstein, wrote the Principia Mathematica.

q: Who was Leonardo da Vincis art teacher?

q.e: Andrea del Verrocchio trained Leonardo in Florence.

q: It can reach an age far greater than that of any other living thing known - up to nearly 5,000 years.

q.e: Bristlecone pines can live nearly 5,000 years; some clonal organisms are older.

q: German, Italian, French this language, are all official languages of Switzerland.

q.e: Romansh is Switzerland's fourth national language.

q: Which of these words means attracting by false, flashy, or tacky charms.

q.e: "Meretricious" means gaudy and superficially attractive.

q: Which one of the following is often referred to as The Godfather of Hip Hop?

q.e: DJ Kool Herc is called the father of hip hop.

q: Why was Nicolas Appert vital in the success of Napoleon?
He was one of Napoleons cooks
He became Field Marshall Ney, head of the Cavalry
He was responsible for Napoleons favorite horse

q.e: Appert developed canning for Napoleon's armies; he was a confectioner and chef.

q: In The Office, what alias does Michael Scott often use?

q.e: Michael Scott uses the alias "Michael Scarn."

q: The 19th century saw the rise of the ghost story among acclaimed Victorian authors. Which of the following cannot be considered a work of supernatural fiction?
The Luck of Barry Lyndon by William Makepeace Thackeray
The Turn of the Screw by Henry James
The Canterville Ghost by Oscar Wilde
A Christmas Carol by Charles Dickens

q.e: Thackeray's The Luck of Barry Lyndon isn't a ghost story.

q: In The Lord of the Rings, what are the Dark Lord Saurons chief henchmen called?

q.e: The Nazgûl are Sauron's Ringwraiths.

q: Who is the father of the fictional black cat Midnight Louie?

q.e: Midnight Louie's father in Carole Nelson Douglas's novels is Three O'Clock Louie.

q: This was the ninth most popular 2006 male baby name. Its origin is not exactly known, but it does come from a Roman family name and it has been suggested that is was derived from the Greek word for flower.

q.e: Anthony comes from the Roman family name Antonius.

q: Which of these words means gloomy, dark, sadly dim?

q.e: "Tenebrous" means dark or gloomy.

q: What first full admiral of the Navy, uttered the famous phrase, Damn the torpedoes, full speed ahead!, during the American Civil War at the Battle of Mobile Bay?

q.e: David Farragut said "Damn the torpedoes" at Mobile Bay in 1864.

q: What famous Israeli liqueur comes in a genie shaped bottle and has a distinctive chocolate/orange flavor?

q.e: Sabra is an Israeli chocolate-orange liqueur.

q: Although almost non-existent today, what ancient religion, stemming predominantly from Persia, worshipped Ahura Mazda as an uncreated Creator and God.

q.e: Zoroastrianism worships Ahura Mazda and began in ancient Persia.

q: These omnivorous mammals are native to North America. They carry their young for 65 days and give birth to up to five babies. They live up to 16 years, but their average life expectancy is 2 years due to hunting and traffic deaths.

q.e: Raccoons are omnivores native to North America.

q: Relying on a hand crank for power, this gun is considered the first machine gun since it could fire continuously.

q.e: Patented by Richard Jordan Gatling in 1862, the Gatling gun featured a cluster of revolving barrels turned by a hand crank. Hiram Maxim later invented the Maxim gun in 1884, which was the first fully automatic machine gun powered by recoil.

q: This word is Sanskrit for Great Soul, and is used like the title Saint. Some believe that it was first used in 1915 when speaking of Ghandi.

q.e: Mahatma translates from Sanskrit as great soul (maha meaning great and atman meaning soul) and was popularized as an honorific for Mohandas Gandhi.

q: Gangster Al Capone, popular as Scarface, was known by what other nickname?

q.e: "Snorky" was a nickname of Al Capone, along with "Scarface."

q: This Hungarian-Austrian physician demonstrated that puerperal fever (also known as childbed fever) was contagious and that its incidence could be considerably reduced by enforcing appropriate hand washing behavior.

q.e: Ignaz Semmelweis showed handwashing reduced childbed fever in the 1840s.

q: Which of these actors has played both a disruptive student and an inspiring teacher?

q.e: Sidney Poitier played a student in Blackboard Jungle and a teacher in To Sir, With Love.

q: The exploration of the Loch Ness Monster is related to which field of study?

q.e: Cryptozoology is the pseudoscientific study of creatures whose existence is unproven, known as cryptids. Phycology is the study of algae, while mycology focuses on fungi.

q: This Saint is supposed to have seen the Loch Ness Monster and even to have tamed it.

q.e: St. Columba reportedly met the monster in AD 565.

q: This was the leader of the group that searched Loch Ness in the early 1970s and claimed to have made underwater photographs of the monster.

q.e: Robert Rines took the 1972 and 1975 "flipper" photographs at Loch Ness.

q: What kind of creature was the extinct Plesiosaur, which is usually said to be similar to the monster of Loch Ness?

q.e: The plesiosaur was a marine reptile from the Mesozoic.

q: Which company did Clarence Saunders found in 1916?

q.e: Clarence Saunders founded Piggly Wiggly in Memphis in 1916.

q: We all have learned that you can tell the age of a tree by the number of rings. Who was the first to discover this fact?

q.e: Leonardo da Vinci noted that tree rings show age.

q: Which U.S. writer of detective fiction worked for the famous Pinkerton National Detective Agency?

q.e: Dashiell Hammett worked as a Pinkerton detective before writing.

q: From which radio station was the first national US broadcast made?

q.e: KDKA in Pittsburgh made the first commercial US broadcast in 1920.

q: Which of Johann Strauss Is sons became known as The Waltz King and was instrumental in popularizing the waltz in Vienna during the 19th century?

q.e: Johann Strauss II, "the Waltz King," wrote The Blue Danube.

q: What is the name of the chieftain, who in 1816, after the death of his father, seized power over the insignificant Zulu clan and transformed it into a nation?

q.e: Shaka became Zulu chief in 1816.

q: Who does not belong to this list of high school dropouts: Julie Andrews, Marlon Brando, Johnny Depp, Demi Moore, Avril Lavigne, Christina Applegate, Jude Law, Leah Remini, John Travolta, Ed Norton.

q.e: Ed Norton graduated from Yale; the others dropped out of high school.

q: Which of Jim Hensons Muppets was the first one to be a regular on The Jimmy Dean Show?

q.e: Rowlf the Dog was Jim Henson's first regular Muppet on The Jimmy Dean Show.

q: What kind of phobia is defined as fear of high places?

q.e: Acrophobia comes from the Greek 'akron' (peak or summit) and 'phobos' (fear). Xenophobia is the fear or hatred of strangers or foreigners.

q: This is a technique or method of dyeing fabrics using wax (to cover parts of the fabric not intended to be dyed).

q.e: Batik is wax-resist dyeing of fabric.

q: The animals from which group are often called sea cows?

q.e: Sirenia includes manatees and dugongs.

q: Who was the second host of the Tonight Show?

q.e: Jack Paar hosted The Tonight Show from 1957 to 1962.

q: The USA has an extensive Interstate Highway System. What five state capitals are NOT directly served by this system?
Juneau, Dover, Jefferson City, Pierre, Carson City
Juneau, Dover, Carson City, Honolulu, Pierre
Juneau, Honolulu, Jefferson City, Carson City, Pierre
Juneau, Honolulu, Salem, Columbia, Salt Lake City

q.e: The state capitals not directly on interstates include Juneau, Dover and Pierre; Carson City got I-580 in 2012.

q: Which best defines the word Sanhedrin?
The court of 23 judges biblically required to be present in every city
The condition of being without mental faculties
The religious book on which the Jain religion is based
The ancient spice used in Egypt to counter bad omens

q.e: The Great Sanhedrin had 71 judges; smaller courts had 23.

q: In the USA we often see commercials for Subway sandwiches. They usually feature a man who went from 425 pounds to 190 pounds because of a diet based on Subways menu. What is his name?

q.e: Jared Fogle was Subway's spokesman; Subway ended ties with him in 2015.

q: They were a group of landed nobility in Prussia and Eastern Germany. Their name comes from the German for young lord. They formed several aristocratic political groups in Germany.

q.e: Junkers were Prussian landed nobility; the word means "young lord."

q: What is referred to by the term fourth world (in contrast to the better-known terms first world, second world and third world?

q.e: "Fourth world" refers to stateless and indigenous peoples.

q: Which of the following volcanoes caused the most deaths?

q.e: Tambora (1815) killed about 70,000 or more, the deadliest eruption in recorded history.

q: What is the mascot of the University of California at Irvine?

q.e: UC Irvine's mascot is the Anteater, named Peter.

q: In 1565, this German-Swiss naturalist became the first person to document and describe the pencil.

q.e: Conrad Gesner described the pencil in 1565.

q: The fictional USS Sea Tiger was captained by Lt. Cmdr. Matt T. Sherman. Who was the first mate?

q.e: Check the source for the first mate's name.

q: The proteins in dead organisms as well as in body wastes are converted into ammonia by bacteria and fungi. Into what useful product do other bacteria convert this ammonia?

q.e: Nitrifying bacteria turn ammonia into nitrites and then nitrates.

q: What infection's symptoms are tiny white-headed pimples, usually at the base of hair shafts?

q.e: Folliculitis is inflammation of hair follicles.

q: What character uttered the following words by the end of Casablanca, one of the most enduring romantic dramas of all time: It doesnt take much to see that the problems of three little people dont amount to a hill of beans in this crazy world.?

q.e: Rick Blaine says this to Ilsa in Casablanca.

q: The Olivieri brothers, Pat and Harry, are given credit for inventing this in 1933.

q.e: Pat and Harry Olivieri originally ran a hot dog stand near south Philadelphia's Italian Market when they decided to grill sliced beef and onions on a roll in the early 1930s. The cheese was added later, popularized by their manager Joe Lorenza.

q: Eight years before George Washington was elected President of the USA, this politician was appointed President of the United States by the Continental Congress.

q.e: In 1781 the Continental Congress presided under John Hanson and Thomas McKean; neither was a president like Washington.
Knott's Berry Farm began in the 1920s in Buena Park, California.

q: This American writer and teacher became the first woman US Senator, although she occupied the position for only one day.

q.e: Rebecca Latimer Felton of Georgia served one day in 1922.

q: This is an uncommon English word deriving from the Yiddish word for to drag and means to move something from one place to another with difficulties.

q.e: "Schlep" comes from Yiddish "shlepn," to drag.

q: What is the next number in the following sequence, having in mind that it is related to positive integers: 1, 0.5, 0.333, 0.25, 0.2, 0.166, 0.142?

q.e: The sequence is 1/n; the next term is 1/8, or 0.125.

q: Fashion designer Alexander McQueen, known as the hooligan of English fashion, succeeded John Galliano as head designer at this French fashion house.

q.e: Alexander McQueen replaced John Galliano at Givenchy in 1996.

q: What do we call a horizontal beam used usually for support and walling over a window?

q.e: A lintel spans the opening over a door or window.

q: Which of these words means someone who believes the self is the most important thing ?

q.e: An egoist places the self at the center.

q: What fashion designer popularized the color known as shocking pink?

q.e: Elsa Schiaparelli popularized "shocking pink."

q: Who is considered the worlds first photojournalist?

q.e: Jacob Riis is often called the first photojournalist.

q: According to the August 2008 issue of Travel Leisure, what is the scariest road in the world?

q.e: The North Yungas Road in Bolivia has been called the world's most dangerous.
"Quinunc" looks like a typo for "quidnunc," which means a busybody.

q: Which one of these is among the Top Ten Inventions of 2005 according to the US Army?
The G.A.D.G.E.T. Deployable armored personnel vehicle

q.e: Fido, a bomb-sniffing detector, made the US Army's list of top inventions of 2005.

q: Potassium iodide, sodium iodide, or sodium iodate are added to table salt in order to prevent iodine deficiency. What health problems does iodine deficiency cause?

q.e: Iodine deficiency causes goiter and other thyroid disorders.

q: Joe Barry Carroll was drafted by the Golden Gate Warriors in 1980. He was the first choice in that draft. Who did they give up to get him?

q.e: To get the top pick, the Warriors traded Robert Parish and the No. 3 pick (Kevin McHale) to the Celtics.

q: Which plane is the first jet fighter?

q.e: The Heinkel He 280 was the first jet fighter prototype; the He 178 was the first jet aircraft.

q: Which of these words means biting, sarcastic, acid-mouthed?

q.e: "Mordant" means biting, caustic.

q: Which of these weapons is a US Marine infantry weapon, scheduled for widespread use in starting 2008?

q.e: SMAW-NE is a Marine shoulder-fired weapon.

q: What was the name of the first Assistant District Attorney on Law and Order?

q.e: Paul Robinette (Richard Brooks) was an early Law & Order ADA.

q: This lawyers unspoken last thought is, It is a far, far better thing that I do, than I have ever done; it is a far, far better rest that I go to, than I have ever known.

q.e: Sydney Carton thinks this at the guillotine in A Tale of Two Cities.

q: This lawyer-turned senator, who has the power of flight without machinery, is a character on Heroes.

q.e: Nathan Petrelli, a lawyer and senator, can fly on Heroes.

q: A plaster cast of a reclining Bigfoot was taken in September of 2000. What is the cast called?

q.e: The Skookum cast was made in 2000 in Washington State.

q: In December, 1968, the corpse of an alleged Bigfoot, encased in a block of ice was examined by cryptozoologists. What was the name given to the specimen in the ice?

q.e: The Minnesota Iceman was an exhibit in 1968, likely a hoax.

q: Which term means fear of spiders?

q.e: Arachnophobia comes from the Greek word "arachne," meaning spider. In contrast, xanthophobia is the fear of the color yellow, and zelophobia is the morbid fear of jealousy.
Satori Kato introduced instant coffee in Chicago in 1901.

q: In order to play this game, you need a net, a ball and 6 team players. Most common faults include: causing the ball to touch the ground outside the opponents court and double hit (two consecutive contacts with the ball made by the same player)

q.e: Standard indoor volleyball features two teams of six players separated by a net, aiming to ground the ball on the opponent's side within three contacts. A player may not touch the ball twice in a row, known as a double hit.

q: According to popular urban legends, the ghost of an Indiana teen who was killed after 5 other teens pushed her into the sewer will kill anyone who doesnt do which of the following?
Draw a cross on 5 manhole covers
Light a candle in her memory

q.e: Check the source for this urban legend.

q: Who was the first person to reach both the North and South Poles?

q.e: Amundsen reached the South Pole in 1911 and flew over the North Pole in 1926.

q: What English word is used in linguistics when discussing the issue of the lack of separate terms for blue and green in many languages?

q.e: "Grue" is the linguistic term for a combined blue-green color.

q: What word refers to the art or science of making timepieces and measuring time?

q.e: Horology derives from the Greek 'hora' (hour or time) and 'logos' (study). Practitioners in this field include watchmakers, clockmakers, and scholars of mechanical timekeeping.

q: In the Hawaiian language this word means woman.

q.e: "Wahine" means woman in Hawaiian.

q: D-Day refers to one of the biggest military operations in history that took place on June 6, 1944. What was the pass word used by the Allied Forces on that day?

q.e: "Mickey Mouse" was a D-Day challenge-response; check the source.

q: Which of these not only cut off pieces of the American flag, but was honored for doing so?

q.e: Robert Peary cut off pieces of his flag at the Pole.

q: What was the first jet fighter to hit Mach 3.2?

q.e: The MiG-25 Foxbat reached about Mach 3.2 in tests.

q: On May 6, 1937 the Hindenburg exploded as it tried to dock in the Lakehurst Naval Station in New Jersey. Out of the 97 people on the Zeppelin, how many died?

q.e: The Hindenburg disaster killed 35 of 97 aboard, plus one ground crewman.

q: This famous pilot made the first solo flight from Hawaii to the mainland of the USA.

q.e: Amelia Earhart flew solo from Hawaii to California in 1935.

q: What world-famous female model was born on February 28, 1984?

q.e: Karolina Kurková was born February 28, 1984.

q: The first human birth through embryo transfer was announced on February 3, 1984. Who was in charge of the research team that carried out the project?

q.e: Dr. John Buster at Harbor-UCLA led the team that achieved the first embryo-transfer birth.

q: What is the name of the mermaid-like creature from Brazilian folklore?

q.e: Iara is a water spirit in Brazilian folklore, similar to a mermaid.

q: Well, it was getting dark and I was worn out from the stress of the day, so I decided to get ready for bed. Sadly, this prompted a panic attack due to my ablutophobia. What was I afraid of?

q.e: Ablutophobia is fear of bathing.

q: In 2005, Danny Way became the first person to do this. In the process he attained a speed of over 50 mph. What did he do?
Skateboard over the Great Wall of China
High dive from the Eiffel Tower
Shoot out of a submarine torpedo tube

Basil Hallward is the artist who paints the portrait, and Lord Henry Wotton is the friend who influences Dorian's hedonism.

q.e: Dean Moriarty is the Beat hero in Kerouac's On the Road.

Don Imus, Sid Caesar, Wolfman Jack, Howard Stern

q.e: A bidet is a plumbing fixture used for washing.

She made it up and used it because it was interesting.

In harmony with the given situation

q: What is the male equivalent of a mermaid?

q: How many nations altogether fought on the side of the Allies in the Battle of Normandy that took place on June 6th, 1944?
