q: Which Star Wars character delivered the following words in his typical manner: Strong is Vader. Mind what you have learned. Save you it can�?

q.e: Yoda speaks these words to Luke Skywalker on the swamp planet Dagobah in The Empire Strikes Back, demonstrating his signature inverted object-subject-verb speech pattern.

q: This Star Wars character is an immense, fur-covered warrior of great strength and loyalty, and a sophisticated being with exceptional skills in starship piloting and repairing.

q.e: Chewbacca is the Wookiee co-pilot of the Millennium Falcon.

q: What National League pitcher threw a perfect game against the New York Mets on Fathers day in 1964?

q.e: Jim Bunning threw a perfect game against the Mets on Father's Day, June 21, 1964.

q: Her career started in the 50s when she was only 18. She joined Ike Turners touring show as an 18-year-old backup vocalist. Her real name is Annie Mae Bullock.

q.e: Tina Turner was born Anna Mae Bullock and joined Ike Turner's revue in the 1950s.

q: Ötzi the Iceman is a well-preserved natural mummy of a man who lived about 5300 years ago. It rivals an Egyptian mummy as the oldest known human mummy in the world. What is the name of the Egyptian mummy in question?

q.e: "Ginger" is a roughly 5,500-year-old Egyptian mummy at the British Museum.

q: Who was the monk and scientist, who laid the foundation for the study of genetics?

q.e: Gregor Mendel was an Austrian Augustinian friar who crossbred roughly 28,000 pea plants between 1856 and 1863, uncovering the basic principles of dominant and recessive inheritance.
A mohel performs the Jewish circumcision ceremony.

q: Counting those of Guam, Puerto Rico, Washington D.C. and the U.S. Virgin Islands , how many senators are there in the U.S. Senate?

q.e: The US Senate has 100 members; territories and DC have no senators.

q: One of these statements concerning giraffes is wrong.
Giraffes have only seven vertebrae in their neck.
Giraffes can run at speeds of up to 50kph.

q.e: Giraffes sleep very little and sometimes lie down; "always upright" is false.

q: This Michael is a member of the Monty Python comedy group. He was named a Commander of the Order of British Empire by Queen Elizabeth II.

q.e: Michael Palin was made a CBE in 2000.

q: Which is the correct spelling for an adjective meaning grossly irreverent toward what is or is held to be sacred?

q.e: "Sacrilegious" is the correct spelling.

q: This word is defined as a stone coffin, often inscribed or decorated with sculpture.

q.e: The term sarcophagus comes from Greek roots meaning flesh-eating, reflecting the belief that the limestone used in ancient coffins consumed the body.

q: Name the word which refers to any of a group of green pigments that are found in the chloroplasts of plants and in other photosynthetic organisms.

q.e: Chlorophyll comes from the Greek words chloros (pale green) and phyllon (leaf). The correct English spelling ends in '-phyll', distinguishing it from misspelled variants.

q: This adjective means capable of being understood or comprehended.

q.e: Intelligible means capable of being understood.

q: This word is defined as a medication that reduces fever.

q.e: An antipyretic reduces fever.

q: This siren, known for wearing mens clothes, studied to be a violinist until a wrist injury caused her to switch to acting.

q.e: Marlene Dietrich studied violin before an injury moved her to acting.

q: Lion's lips, rabbit's mouth and calves' snouts are alternative names of these flowers.

q.e: Snapdragons are nicknamed "lion's lips" and "rabbit's mouth."

q: One of the following pairs (flower - what it is a symbol of) is wrong.

q.e: Daisies symbolize innocence, not sin.

q: William Faulkner had great trouble early in his career -- he could not get published. What did he do to earn a living?

q.e: Faulkner held odd jobs, including postmaster; the rum-running story is a legend.

q: Frederick Dannay and Manfred B. Lee are the real names of two cousins, who published their detective fiction under this pseudonym.

q.e: Dannay and Lee wrote as Ellery Queen.

q: Why is the date April 23, 1616 important in World history?
The Pilgrims landed at Plymouth Rock

q.e: Although traditionally recorded as dying on the same date, they actually passed away about ten days apart because England still used the Julian calendar while Spain had adopted the Gregorian calendar. UNESCO later chose April 23 as World Book and Copyright Day in their honor.

q: Jim Brown, the great Syracuse University back made the number 44 famous. Which great Syracuse back wore 44 after Jim Brown?

q.e: Ernie Davis wore #44 after Jim Brown and won the 1961 Heisman.

q: If you are a coffee drinker, this is the recommended maximum number of cups you should have per day.

q.e: Health agencies say up to about 400 mg of caffeine, around four cups, is generally safe; limits vary.

q: Qui-Gon Jinn was former Padwan of who?

q.e: Qui-Gon Jinn was Count Dooku's Padawan.

q: During the 80s, British politics were dominated by a system of political views called Thatcherism. Which of the following statements is wrong about Thatcherism?
Britains economy fell into stagnation as a result of it.
It may be compared with Reaganomics.
Keith Joseph and Milton Friedman are thinkers, commonly associated with it.
It is characterized by a free market economy.

q.e: Thatcherism involved privatization and tough economic reforms; check the "stagnation" claim.

q: These wars lasted from 1804 to 1815 and removed France from the position of a dominant European power. At the same time they triggered a new political movement - nationalism.

q.e: The Napoleonic Wars ran from 1803 to 1815 and helped spark nationalism.

q: The reason for this war was the successful and unhampered traffic of opium from India to China. The war started in 1839.

q.e: The First Opium War began in 1839.

q: This event was initiated in Great Britain with the appearance of the first factories. Steam-powered ships, boats and railways were also introduced then. However, it is most famous for applying steam power and powered automated machinery in production.

q.e: The First Industrial Revolution began in Britain in the late 1700s.

q: This war was fought from 1861 until 1865 between the United States and the newly-formed Confederate States of America. 3 million soldiers fought in its battles and 600,000 of them died. One of the main causes for it was slavery.

q.e: The American Civil War (1861–65) killed at least 620,000 soldiers.

q: This drug was first produced in 1853 by German chemists. The name of this medicine comes from a plant, called spirea, that releases salicylic acid.

q.e: Chemist Charles Gerhardt first made acetylsalicylic acid in 1853; Bayer marketed aspirin in 1899.

q: What is the official name for a resident of the state of Utah?

q.e: A resident of Utah is a Utahn.

q: Which animals sees more daylight than any other creature on the planet, thanks to its 19,000 km (12,000 mile) journey to winter in the Antarctic?

q.e: Arctic terns complete an annual pole-to-pole migration, breeding during the northern summer and spending the southern summer in Antarctica. Because both habitats experience continuous polar daylight, they witness more sunlight than any other creature.

q: After 10 315 days in existence, the symbol of the Cold War came down. On 9 November 1989 East Germans could once again visit their relatives and beloved ones in West Berlin. But when was the Brandenburg Gate opened?

q.e: The Brandenburg Gate crossing opened on December 22, 1989.

q: How many bags of wool did the black sheep have in the nursery rhyme Baa Baa Black Sheep?

q.e: In the traditional 18th-century English nursery rhyme, the sheep has three bags full: one for the master, one for the dame, and one for the little boy who lives down the lane.

q: Who were the three men in the nursery rhyme Rub a Dud Dub?
Rich man, Poor man and Baker

q.e: "Rub-a-dub-dub, three men in a tub" are the butcher, the baker and the candlestick maker.

q: What does Jack jump over in the nursery rhyme Jack Be Nimble?

q.e: The traditional 19th-century nursery rhyme goes: 'Jack be nimble, Jack be quick, Jack jump over the candlestick.' Jumping over candles was historically linked to fortune-telling games where clearing the flame without putting it out brought good luck.

q: In the nursery rhyme Mary, Mary, Quite Contrary, what type of shells help Marys garden grow?

q.e: "Silver bells and cockle shells" help Mary's garden grow.

q: In 1881, this dentist and gunfighter of the Old West frontier took part in the Gunfight at the O.K. Corral in Tombstone, Arizona, along with Wyatt Earp, Virgil Earp, and Morgan Earp.

q.e: John Henry "Doc" Holliday was a dentist and gunfighter.

q: Which great Yankee was not elected to the Hall of Fame during his first year of eligibility?

q.e: Joe DiMaggio was elected in 1955, his fourth year on the ballot.

q: Between July 28, 1957, and May 10, 1959, this player set major league records by catching in 148 consecutive games and accepting 950 chances without making an error.

q.e: Yogi Berra set records for consecutive games and chances without an error.

q: Ive got an itch, because he ______ my watch. I am never going to find this thief.

q.e: "Snitched" here means stole.

q: This idiom was initiated by popular card games in the past. It was often used when a throw was out of play or not lying flat; in this case, the throw was considered not valid.
Not playing with a full deck

q.e: "No dice" comes from dice games in which a throw didn't count.

q: What did Stan Zbornak from The Golden Girls lose, while he was travelling to the girls house in his Corvette?

q.e: Stan Zbornak lost his toupee on The Golden Girls.

q: Which of these words were NOT said by Dory, while she was talking in her sleep in Finding Nemo?
The sea monkey has my money...

q.e: The Wallaby Way address is Nemo's, which Dory repeats awake and asleep; check the options.

q: This theory began a revolution in science. Postulated by Einstein, its basis was the identification of gravity with inertia.

q.e: Albert Einstein formulated his equivalence principle in 1907, asserting that the gravitational force felt locally is indistinguishable from acceleration (inertia). This insight became the foundation for his general theory of relativity, published in 1915.

q: Humanity made the gigantic leap to the moon in 1969, when his rocket took off from Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Four days later, he was walking on the Moon.

q.e: Neil Armstrong walked on the Moon on July 20, 1969, four days after launch.

q: This event gathered more than 450 000 people at a pasture in Sullivan County in 1969. Love was free, drugs were freely distributed and people claimed to be open minded.

q.e: The Woodstock Music and Art Fair took place from August 15 to 18, 1969, on Max Yasgur's dairy farm in Bethel, New York, within Sullivan County.

q: This war took place between 1964 and 1975. The average age of the soldiers who lost their lives was 23.11 years. Amputations and crippling wounds were 300 percent higher compared to previous wars.

q.e: The average age of US dead in Vietnam was about 22–23, not 19.

q: Do you mean to tell me, Katie Scarlett OHara, that Tara, that land doesnt mean anything to you? Why, land is the only thing in the world worth workin for, worth fightin for, worth dyin for, because its the only thing that lasts. (1939)

q.e: Gerald O'Hara says this to Scarlett in Gone with the Wind.

q: Im not looking forward to jumping in after you. But like I said, I dont see a choice. I guess Im kinda hoping youll come back over the rail and get me off the hook here. (1997)

q.e: Jack says this to Rose in Titanic (1997).

One Flew Over the Cuckoos Nest

q.e: The Captain says this in Cool Hand Luke (1967).

q: I coulda had class. I coulda been a contender. I coulda been somebody, instead of a bum, which is what I am, lets face it. (1954)

q.e: Marlon Brando delivered this famous line as washed-up boxer Terry Malloy speaking to his brother Charley in the back of a taxi in the 1954 classic On the Waterfront.

The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance

q.e: Hannibal Lecter says this in The Silence of the Lambs.

q.e: Marsellus Wallace says this in Pulp Fiction (1994).

q: One of these Yoga terms means truth.

q.e: "Satya" is the yogic principle of truthfulness.

q.e: Henry VIII's marriage to Anne of Cleves lasted from January to July 1540.

q.e: Hammurabi's code is famous, but Ur-Nammu's code is older.

q: This Roman emperor divided the Roman Empire in two parts, Eastern and Western.

q.e: Diocletian split rule among tetrarchs; the permanent east-west division was in 395.

q.e: Born Gabrielle Bonheur Chanel in 1883, the iconic French fashion designer adopted the nickname Coco while singing in cabarets in the early 1900s.

q: This is one of the oldest designer brands. Its founder opened a luggage store in Paris in 1854, but did not get fame and fortune until just after his death.

q.e: Louis Vuitton founded his luxury trunk-making shop in Paris in 1854, introducing flat-topped canvas trunks that were easily stackable. Prada and Gucci were founded later in Italy, in 1913 and 1921 respectively.

q: This designer is particularly noted for his menswear, but he also introduced a ladies wear line in 1975. The brand was much popularized by Richard Gere in the title role of American Gigolo.

q.e: Giorgio Armani rose to fame with American Gigolo (1980).

q.e: Opossums have natural resistance to snake venom.

q: Who was the first woman to serve on the U.S. Supreme Court?

q.e: Sandra Day O'Connor joined the court in 1981.

q: This Yorkshire Terrier became a hero in World War II. He participated in battles for 18 months. During that time he flew on 12 combat missions of 22 hours nonstop.

q.e: Smoky, a Yorkshire terrier, served in the Pacific in WWII.

q: This german shepherd was Adolf Hitlers favorite dog. Before Hitler committed suicide using cyanide he tested it on the dog.

q.e: Blondi was Hitler's German shepherd, used to test cyanide in April 1945.

q.e: Pizza boomed in America after WWII, especially in the 1950s.

q: One of the largest breeds of these animals is the Maine Coon. Males weigh twelve to twenty pounds (5.4 to 13.6 kg), with females weighing ten to fifteen pounds (4.5 to 6.8 kg).

q.e: The Maine Coon is one of the largest domesticated cat breeds, with adult males frequently reaching 18 pounds (about 8 kg) or more. Known for their dense, water-resistant coats and tufted paws, they are the official state cat of Maine.

q: Words beginning with a double letter are generally very rare in English language, and most of them start with oo. One such word is oomph, which has what basic meaning?

q.e: Oomph means energy or enthusiasm.

q: Aa is one of the few words in the English language which consist entirely of vowels. The word is used in geology to refer to what natural formation?

q.e: Aa is a Hawaiian term for rough, blocky lava.

q: According to Aristotle (Politics) and Diodorus Siculus (Diodorus), Philip II of Macedon (the father of Alexander the Great) was killed as a result of this.

q.e: Apollo was the god at Delphi.

q.e: Check the source for this African creation myth.

q: Although these famous dolls are presented as intimate friends, they are named after a brother and sister - who are the children of the dolls creator - Ruth Handler.

q.e: Mattel co-founder Ruth Handler introduced Barbie in 1959 and Ken in 1961, naming them after her real-life children, Barbara and Kenneth.

q: This couple, created by Robert Louis Stevenson, is like getting 2 for 1. Two personalities are hidden in one, one of them being his normal identity, and the other is his dark side.

q.e: Robert Louis Stevenson published 'Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde' in 1886. The novella popularized the concept of a dual personality representing the perpetual conflict between good and evil.

q: In the 16th century, the Roman Catholic Church allowed the consumption of what meat during Lent?

q.e: South American clergy ruled the capybara a fish, so it was allowed in Lent.

q: Keeping what rodent as a pet is illegal in the state of California?

q.e: Gerbils are illegal as pets in California.

q: Which rodent can be trained to sniff out land mines?

q.e: Gambian pouched rats are trained to detect landmines.

q: Complete the following wise sentence which belongs to Martin Fisher: Knowledge is a process of piling up facts; wisdom lies in their ...

q.e: Martin H. Fischer wrote about wisdom as simplification.

q: Finish this observation about wisdom, made by the scientist who discovered the theory of relativity: Wisdom is not a product of schooling but of the life-long attempt to ...

q.e: Einstein is credited with this line about wisdom and lifelong effort.

q: Complete this philosophical observation, made by Socrates: True knowledge exists in knowing that you know nothing. And in knowing that you know nothing, that makes you the ...

q.e: Socrates is credited with "I know that I know nothing."

q: Many soft drinks contain caffeine. Your body absorbs caffeine more readily from soft drinks than coffee, due to this.

q.e: Carbonation may speed caffeine uptake, though evidence is mixed.

q.e: Tigger is bouncy; Owl is the intellectual friend.

q.e: Check the source for this odd geography question.

Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery

q: Youll meet someone. Someone very special. Someone who wont press charges.
Star Wars: Episode V - The Empire Strikes Back
Dr. Strangelove or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb

q.e: Wednesday says this in Addams Family Values.

q: One mans compost is another mans potpourri. (2000)
The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring

q.e: The Grinch says this in How the Grinch Stole Christmas (2000).

q: This railroad, built between 1891 and 1916, is 9,288 kilometres (5,772 miles) long and spans 8 time zones.

q.e: The Trans-Siberian Railway runs from Moscow to Vladivostok, connecting western Russia with the Pacific coast. Spanning roughly 5,772 miles (9,289 km), it remains the longest continuous rail line in the world.

q: In 1982, a Worlds Fair-type exposition, named Energy Turns the World, was held in which of the following U.S. cities?

q.e: Knoxville hosted the 1982 World's Fair, "Energy Turns the World."

q: Which strategic part of Egypt was so important to the Italians, that they started the North African Campaign in 1940?

q.e: Italy invaded Egypt in 1940 aiming for the Suez Canal.

q.e: The Yalta Conference met in February 1945.

q.e: Check the source for Susan Banks's plot on Days of Our Lives.

q.e: Dr. Marlena Evans is Salem's psychiatrist.

q.e: Check the source for the Days of Our Lives ruby plot.

q: Which event provoked the Second Sino-Japanese War?

q.e: The 1937 Marco Polo Bridge Incident started the full war; Manchuria was taken in 1931.

q: What is the name of the German invasion of the Soviet Union, which began on 22 June 1941?

q.e: Operation Barbarossa began on June 22, 1941.

q: Name the most lethal outbreak in human history with an estimated 50 to 100 million people killed worldwide between 1918 and 1919. As many as 25 million may have been killed in the first 25 weeks!

q.e: The 1918 influenza killed an estimated 50–100 million people.

q: Which of these expressions will you use to thank somebody in French?

q.e: Merci is French for thank you, commonly paired with beaucoup to mean thank you very much. The other options are chat (cat), pour (for), and oui (yes).

q: According to the New Testament, who obtained permission to take Jesus Christs body down from the cross and place it in the tomb?

q.e: Joseph of Arimathea asked Pilate for Jesus's body.

q: This is a deck of 78 cards with pictures and inscriptions on them. They are divided into several suits and the person extracts cards that the reader interprets.

q.e: A standard occult tarot deck consists of 78 cards divided into the 22 Major Arcana trump cards and the 56 Minor Arcana suit cards.

q: This method of divination uses a set of 24 alphabet letters that are usually carved on small tiles, so that the person could extract one of all 24 and to interpret its meaning. They were also carved and drawn building walls for protection.

q.e: The Elder Futhark runic alphabet has 24 letters.

q: This is the careful screening of your palm, its shapes and lines in order to guess some events from the past and see events in the future.

q.e: Palmistry, or chiromancy, involves interpreting the lines, mounts, and shapes of the hand to divine personal traits and future fortunes. Tasseomancy, by contrast, is the practice of reading tea leaves or coffee grounds.

q: In ancient times people thought that illnesses were caused by demons, possessing the soul of a person. So they cured those illnesses with exorcism. Exorcism is derived from the Greek word exorkizein. What does this word mean?

q.e: "Exorkizein" meant to bind by oath.

q: Jesus Christ is considered to be an exorcist. One of the legends tells of Jesus casting out multiple demons from a madman. The spirits then entered the bodies of some animals. What kind of animals were they?

q.e: In the Gospels, the demons entered a herd of pigs.

q: This is one of the most widely used religious symbols. It is generally used for protection. Even though it is often associated with witchcraft, it was also used in Christianity, symbolizing the five wounds of Christ.

q.e: The pentagram is an ancient five-pointed star symbol.

q: This is when the spell casting powers are at their fullest. It is the hour of midnight on a full moon.

q: This tradition was founded in England in the 1960s by Alex Sanders, who referred to himself as the King of his Witches.

q.e: Alexandrian Wicca was founded by Alex Sanders in the 1960s.

q: The French rulers persecuted Voodoo priests and practitioners. In 1791 a revolution exploded, which was led by the Voodoo priests. It ended in the year of Napoleons crowning.

q.e: The Haitian Revolution began in 1791 and ended in 1804.

q: Voodoos equivalent in Cuba is Santeria. Do you know which the equivalent of Voodoo in Brazil is?

q.e: Macumba is a Brazilian Afro-religious term; Candomblé and Umbanda are related.

q: At Passover, Jews eat a special meal done in a special order. What is that meal called?
A festavus for the rest of us

q.e: The word seder literally translates to order in Hebrew, referring to the 15 distinct steps followed during the ritual meal. A shidduch is a match or arranged courtship in traditional Jewish communities.

q: Which Hebrew phrase is most commonly associated with the English expression Good Luck and/or Congratulations?

q.e: Mazel tov translates literally from Hebrew to 'good constellation' or good fortune, and is widely used to celebrate weddings, bar mitzvahs, and other milestones. Oy vey is an expression of dismay or frustration.

q: What tribe of Israel was Moses born into?

q.e: Moses was born into the tribe of Levi.

q: She held me spellbound in the night Dancing shadows and firelight Crazy laughter in another room And she drove herself to madness with a silver spoon. What group sings about a Witchy Woman with the moon in her eyes?

q.e: "Witchy Woman" is a 1972 Eagles hit.

q: The works of this Jewish thinker formed the basis of the writings of Thomas Aquinas.

q.e: Maimonides strongly influenced Thomas Aquinas.

q: What is prayer shawl worn by Jews in the morning Jewish services, during the Torah service, on Yom Kippur, and other holidays called?

q.e: A tallit is the Jewish prayer shawl.

q: The night before Yom Kippur, called this, is the most important night service in Judaism.

q.e: Kol Nidre opens the Yom Kippur evening service.

q: What was the birth name of the historic figure known as Buddha, the founder of the Buddhist religion?

q.e: Buddha was born Siddhartha Gautama.

q: What is the formula to end or reduce suffering according to the principles of Buddhism?

q.e: The Noble Eightfold Path is the Buddhist path to end suffering.

q: Son of a Jewish immigrant from Breslau, Prussia, Lucius Nathan Littauer was born in Gloversville, Upstate New York, in 1859. Being a politician wasnt his only occupation; what is Lucius Littauers other achievement with which he remained in history?
The first Jewish football coach at Harvard

The first professional Jewish baseball player
The first Jewish professional football coach

q: Isachar Zacharie, an English born Jew, who was related to important American politicians, worked as what?

q: Why was Rabbi David Einhorn, a German rabbi and later leader of the Jewish reform movement in the United States, forced to leave Baltimore in 1861, during the Civil War?
He insulted the Governor of Maryland,Thomas Hicks
He insulted the Mayor of Baltimore, George Williams

q: In Buddhism the cycle of rebirths is known as what?

q.e: Samsara is the Buddhist cycle of rebirth.

q: Who was the first Italian-American woman to be canonized as a saint of the Catholic Church?

q.e: Frances Cabrini was canonized in 1946 and was the first US citizen saint.

q: Who is the founder of the International Society for Krishna Consciousness, known as the Hare Krishna?

q.e: A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada founded ISKCON in 1966.

q: According to the Bible, King David saw this beautiful woman bathing, and immediately desired her, but she was married.

q: In the Bible, this woman gave birth to male twins and as she was in labor the twins jostled each other, one babys hand grasping the heel of the other infants foot.

q.e: Rebekah gave birth to Esau and Jacob (Genesis 25).

q: The Temple of Vespasian was begun by Titus after whose death?

q.e: Titus started the Temple of Vespasian after his father died in AD 79.

q: Jews build temporary huts for this holy day.

q.e: The Sahara covers roughly 3.5 million square miles (9 million square km) across North Africa, making it the largest hot desert on Earth.

q: Which of the following countries has a flag featuring a yellow lion wielding a sword on a dark red background?

q.e: Sri Lanka's flag shows a golden lion holding a sword on a maroon field, with green and orange stripes for its minorities. The lion stands for the Sinhalese people.

q: How many countries does the United States share a land border with?

q.e: The United States shares international land borders with only two nations: Canada to the north and Mexico to the south. Canada's border spans 5,525 miles, making it the longest international land border in the world.

q: How many federal states does Germany have?

q.e: Germany is composed of 16 federal states (Bundeslaender), which include three city-states: Berlin, Hamburg, and Bremen.

q: Which of these is NOT an Australian state or territory?

q.e: Alberta is a province of Canada. Australia has six states (e.g. Victoria, Queensland) and territories (e.g. the Northern Territory).

q: Which country does Austria not border?

q.e: Austria borders Germany, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Hungary, Slovenia, Italy, Switzerland and Liechtenstein, but not France.

q: Vatican City, the smallest country in the world, is fully enclosed by which country?

q.e: Covering just 0.49 square kilometers (about 121 acres), Vatican City is an independent enclave completely surrounded by the Italian capital of Rome.

q: In which ocean is the Réunion island?

q.e: Réunion is a French island in the Indian Ocean, east of Madagascar. It's an overseas department of France, so part of the EU.

q: Which Borough is the farthest in the north of New York City?

q.e: The Bronx is New York City's northernmost borough, and the only one on the US mainland. The others are Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens and Staten Island.

q: What is the largest country in the world?

q.e: Russia is the largest country by area, at about 17 million km², covering 11 time zones. Canada is second.

q: How many US states start with the letter K?

q.e: Kansas and Kentucky are the only two US states whose names begin with the letter K. Kansas gained statehood in 1861, while Kentucky joined the Union much earlier in 1792.

q: What is the name of the ocean that Hawaii is located in?

q.e: The Hawaiian archipelago lies in the North Pacific Ocean, roughly 2,400 miles (3,800 km) southwest of the continental United States.

q: What is the capital of Romania?

q.e: Bucuresti (Bucharest) has been the capital of Romania since 1862. It is often confused with Budapest, which is the capital of neighboring Hungary, while Belgrade is the capital of Serbia.

q: Which city is the biggest in Canada?

q.e: Toronto is Canada's largest city, with about 2.8 million people (6+ million in its metro area). Ottawa is the capital.

q: Which state capital sits on the Kentucky River?

q.e: Frankfort, the capital of Kentucky, sits on the Kentucky River. Louisville is the state's largest city.

q: Which country does Denmark share a land border with?

q.e: Denmark shares its sole primary land border of about 42 miles (68 km) with Germany along the Jutland Peninsula. It connects to Sweden via the Øresund Bridge rather than a natural land border.

q: On what continent is Argentina located?

q.e: Argentina is situated in southern South America. It is the second-largest country on the continent by area, after Brazil.

q: This country is located down under between the Pacific and Indian Oceans. Its capital is Canberra.

q.e: Australia's capital is Canberra, not Sydney or Melbourne. It was a planned city chosen as a compromise between those two rivals.

q: This continent is where Canada, The United States of America, and Mexico are located.

q.e: North America is the third-largest continent by area, covering roughly 9.5 million square miles (24.7 million square kilometers), with Canada, the United States, and Mexico making up its largest contiguous landmass.

q: This ocean is bordered by North and South America on the west and Europe and Africa on the east.

q.e: The Atlantic Ocean is the second-largest ocean in the world, covering about 106.5 million square kilometers (roughly 41.1 million square miles). It is divided into the North and South Atlantic by the Equator.

q: The Yellow River is the second largest river after the Yangtze in what country?

q.e: The Yellow River (Huang He) is China's second-longest river, after the Yangtze. It's nicknamed China's "mother river" and is yellow with silt.

q: The Yellow Sea is connected to what ocean?

q.e: The Yellow Sea is an arm of the Pacific, between China and the Korean Peninsula. It gets its color from sediment.

q: Once occupied by the Romans and then later the Vikings, which Yorkshire city is said to be the most haunted in Europe if not the world?

q.e: York, founded by the Romans as Eboracum and later Viking Jorvik, claims to be one of the most haunted cities in Europe. Ghost walks are a big tourist draw.

q: This small agricultural town, whose motto is solidarity in work, is located in Quebec, Canada, near the St. Lawrence River.

q.e: Saint-Louis-du-Ha! Ha! in Quebec has the world's only town name with two exclamation marks. "Ha! Ha!" is an old French word for an obstacle, here a bay.

q: The Orange River is the longest river in which country?

q.e: The Orange River is the longest river in South Africa, at about 2,200 km. It rises in Lesotho and flows west to the Atlantic.

q: What city, nicknamed The Mile-High City, is located on the plains east of the Rocky Mountains?

q.e: Denver earned its nickname because its official elevation is exactly 5,280 feet (1,609 meters), or one mile, above sea level on the steps of the Colorado State Capitol building.

q: What is the largest city in California?

q.e: Los Angeles is California's largest city, with nearly 4 million people. The state capital is Sacramento.

q: In which country would you find the worlds largest underground lake?

q.e: The Lost Sea in Tennessee is billed as America's largest underground lake. The world's largest known one may be in Namibia (Dragon's Breath Cave).

q: What is the largest country by area in Africa?

q.e: Since South Sudan split from Sudan in 2011, Algeria has been Africa's largest country by area. Sudan was largest before that.

q: In which US state is the city of Truth or Consequences located?

q.e: Truth or Consequences, New Mexico, renamed itself in 1950 after the radio game show Truth or Consequences. It was previously called Hot Springs.

q: What was the name of Ghana before the country gained its independence?

q.e: Ghana was known as the Gold Coast during its era as a British crown colony, named for its abundant gold resources. Upon achieving independence in March 1957 under Kwame Nkrumah, it adopted the name Ghana after an ancient West African empire.

q: There is no country in the world whose name begins with this letter of the alphabet.

q.e: No country's name begins with X. No sovereign state starts with X in English.

q: Which of these US states is not named after a river?

q.e: Iowa is named after the Ioway people, not a river. Many states, like Mississippi and Missouri, are named after rivers.

q: What country has a plain green flag?

q.e: Libya's flag was plain green from 1977 to 2011 under Gaddafi, the only country with a single-color flag. It has since reverted to its earlier flag.

q: In which of the New York City boroughs is Rockefeller Center situated?

q.e: Rockefeller Center is in Midtown Manhattan. It's known for the Christmas tree and ice rink.

q: Which of these is the nickname of New York City?

q.e: Sports writer John J. Fitz Gerald popularized 'The Big Apple' in the 1920s to describe New York's horse-racing prizes, and the city officially adopted it for tourism campaigns in 1971.

q: What is the capital and largest city of Austria?

q.e: Vienna is both the capital and largest city of Austria. It has a population of about 2 million.

q: Where can the Orange River be found ?

q.e: The Orange River flows through South Africa, Lesotho, Namibia and Botswana, mostly in South Africa.

q: In which European city is the headquarters of Interpol located?

q.e: Interpol, the International Criminal Police Organization, has its headquarters in Lyon, France. It moved there from Paris in 1989.

q: Which continent is the island of Madagascar part of?

q.e: Madagascar sits in the southwestern Indian Ocean about 250 miles (400 km) off the coast of Mozambique, making it geographically part of the African continent.

q: In what US city is the Lincoln Memorial located?

q.e: Dedicated in 1922, the neoclassical monument stands at the western end of the National Mall in Washington, D.C., directly across from the Washington Monument.

q: Located in the Northwest Territories, what lake empties into the Mackenzie River and is considered the largest lake that is entirely within Canada?

q.e: Great Bear Lake in the Northwest Territories is the largest lake entirely within Canada and the fourth largest in North America.

q: Which country had the largest prison population for 2006?

q.e: In 2006, the US had the world's largest prison population (over 2 million), ahead of China (about 1.5 million sentenced). Counts vary by source.

q: What is the state motto of Rhode Island?

q.e: Rhode Island's state motto is "Hope". The anchor on its flag also symbolizes hope.

q: In what body of water is the island of Malta located?

q.e: Malta is an island nation in the central Mediterranean Sea, south of Sicily.

q: Where is the city of Bahia Blanca located?

q.e: Bahía Blanca is a port city in southern Buenos Aires Province, Argentina.

q: Which lake is NOT one of the Great Lakes?

q.e: The Great Lakes are Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie and Ontario (remember HOMES). The Great Salt Lake is in Utah.

q: This was the first country that starts with the letter J to join the United Nations.

q.e: Jordan joined the UN in 1955. Japan joined in 1956 and Jamaica in 1962.

q: The largest consumption of cigarettes belongs to this country.

q.e: China consumes more cigarettes than any other country, about 40% of the global total. It has over 300 million smokers.

q: This country has the highest income tax rate.

q.e: Denmark's top tax rates are among the world's highest, topping 50% with local taxes. Rates vary by year and source.

q: Which river in China caused a flood of mammoth proportions in 1931?

q.e: The 1931 China floods, from the Yangtze, Huai and Yellow rivers, are among the deadliest natural disasters in history. The Yellow River is also known as "China's Sorrow".

q: What European country was affected the worst by the European Heat Wave of 2003?

q.e: France was hit hardest by the 2003 European heat wave, with about 15,000 deaths. Total deaths in Europe passed 70,000.

q: In which South American country can the Nazca Lines be found?

q.e: The Nazca Lines are ancient geoglyphs created between roughly 500 BC and 500 AD in the coastal plains of southern Peru by the Nazca culture.

q: What is the southernmost capital city?

q.e: Wellington, the capital of New Zealand, sits at approximately 41 degrees South latitude, making it the southernmost national capital on Earth. Sydney and Perth are state capitals in Australia, not national capitals.

q: In terms of population of the city proper, which is the first capital city with over 10,000,000 people?

q.e: Moscow was the first capital with over 10 million people, in recent decades, with Tokyo, Beijing and others later. Moscow is Europe's biggest city.

q: What is the street in New York City, famous for jewels and jewelry?

q.e: West 47th Street in Manhattan is the Diamond District, where much of the US diamond trade takes place.

q: Which city has a Pink Line rail service?

q.e: Chicago's "L" has a Pink Line, along with the Red, Blue, Brown, Green, Orange, Purple and Yellow lines.

q: In square miles, what is the largest country in the world?

q.e: Russia is the biggest country by area: about 6.6 million square miles (17 million km²). Canada, the US and China follow.

q: Which country has the highest population density according to 2009 estimates?

q.e: Monaco is the most densely populated country, and China isn't near the top. Bangladesh and Singapore also have high densities.

q: When was the Earths second highest mountain, K2, first climbed?

q.e: K2, the world's second-highest peak (8,611 m), was first climbed on 31 July 1954 by Italians Lino Lacedelli and Achille Compagnoni.

q: Rhode Island, the smallest US State, also has the shortest state motto. What is this one-word motto?

q.e: Adopted officially in 1875, Rhode Island's state motto is 'Hope', which appears beneath a golden anchor on both the state seal and the state flag.

q: In 1871 what major Midwest city burned down in a fire that was deemed one of the largest disasters in the United States?

q.e: The Great Chicago Fire raged from October 8 to 10, 1871, destroying more than three square miles of the city and leaving around 100,000 residents homeless.

q: Sarah Jessica Parkers popular character Carrie Bradshaw writes a weekly column called Sex and the City for this newspaper.

q.e: Carrie Bradshaw writes the "Sex and the City" column for the fictional New York Star in the show.

q: In which New York City borough is Central Park located?

q.e: Central Park spans 843 acres across the center of Manhattan, between 59th Street and 110th Street. It opened in 1858 based on a design by Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux.

q: Which of these is an existing country, recognized by the United Nations?

q.e: North Korea (DPRK) joined the United Nations in 1991 along with South Korea. Taiwan and Kosovo are not UN members.

q: What island is often referred to as the Emerald Isle, the green color being its symbol?

q.e: Ireland is known as the Emerald Isle due to its lush green landscape, a nickname first popularized in print by poet William Drennan in his 1795 poem 'When Erin First Rose'.

q: What country employs the blue color as its national sports color, as it denotes secularism?

q.e: Blue is considered India's sports color, as it's the color of the Indian cricket team. The reason given here is a claim of the quiz source.

q: In what country is the presidential residence called The Blue House?

q.e: The Blue House (Cheong Wa Dae) was the South Korean presidential residence until 2022, when the president moved to a new office. It is named for its blue roof tiles.

q: What country are the priciest emeralds in the world found?

q.e: Colombia's Muzo mines produce the world's most valued emeralds. Colombia supplies a large share of the global market.

q: Which city used to be called Lutetia?

q.e: Lutetia was the Roman name for Paris, from a Gaulish settlement of the Parisii tribe on the Île de la Cité.

q: In what country is a cake called Pink Panther very popular?

q.e: Pantera Rosa (Pink Panther) is a Spanish brand of cakes (Bimbo). Spanish bakeries make a popular pink-iced cake.

q: In which country was eyeball jewelry, or extraocular implantation, developed in 2002?

q.e: Eyeball jewelry (extraocular implants) was developed in the Netherlands in 2002 by Dr. Hendrik Peters, and is now used by some people in the US. It carries risks.

q: In 2007, where was a new record for the biggest country flag set?

q.e: In 2007, Israel unfurled a huge national flag at Masada in a Guinness record attempt. Records for the largest flag are often broken.

q: The worlds largest swimming pool in 2007 was in this country.

q.e: The San Alfonso del Mar resort in Chile has the world's largest swimming pool, at over 1 km long.

q: What was the destination of the Air France Flight 447 that crashed on June 1, 2009 in the Atlantic Ocean?

q.e: Air France Flight 447 was flying from Rio de Janeiro to Paris when it crashed in the Atlantic on 1 June 2009, killing all 228 aboard.

q: What country is the largest consumer of gold in the world?

q.e: India is one of the biggest gold consumers because of jewelry and weddings, and China is about the same. They compete for first place.

q: In this country one out of ten people owns a bicycle.

q.e: Denmark is one of the world's cycling nations, but ownership is higher than one in ten. Copenhagen has more bikes than cars.

q: The third largest landowner in New York City.

q.e: New York University is among the largest private landowners in New York City, with property in Greenwich Village and elsewhere.

q: New York Alki was a settlement which became part of which US city?

q.e: "New York Alki" was founded in 1851 at Alki Point, now part of West Seattle. The pioneers soon moved to Elliott Bay and named it Seattle.

q: This US city, whose original name was Terminus, is the county seat of Fulton County.

q.e: Atlanta, Georgia's capital, was called Terminus in 1837, then Marthasville, then Atlanta in 1845. It's the seat of Fulton County.

q: Of which major city was Tammany Hall the leading political power brokers?

q.e: Tammany Hall was the Democratic Party political machine that controlled New York City politics from the 1790s to the 1960s. Boss Tweed was its leader.

q: Tigers are native to what continent?

q.e: All wild tiger subspecies are native to Asia, ranging historically from Turkey and Russia down through India and Southeast Asia. Africa is home to lions and leopards, but not wild tigers.

q: This country has the largest number of gum producers, with over 60 gum factories.

q.e: Turkey has many chewing gum and confectionery producers, but this claim isn't widely documented. The US and Europe also have big gum industries.

q: The first European child, born in the Western Hemisphere, was born in what would become this country/state.

q.e: Snorri Thorfinnsson, born c. 1005 in Vinland (Newfoundland, Canada) to Norse settlers, is the first known European child born in the Americas.

q: The very advanced ocean liner, The Queen Mary II, was built in this country.

q.e: The Queen Mary 2 was built at the Chantiers de l'Atlantique shipyard in Saint-Nazaire, France, and launched in 2003.

q: Greenland is part of this country.

q.e: Greenland is an autonomous territory within the Kingdom of Denmark, which also includes the Faroe Islands and Denmark itself. Norway historically claimed parts of Greenland, but the Permanent Court of International Justice ruled in Denmark's favor in 1933.

q: Which of these is NOT a state capital?

q.e: Dallas is a city in Texas, but the capital of Texas is Austin.

q: The USA is divided into states. England is divided into counties. Which country is divided into departments?

q.e: France is divided into departments (about 100). England has counties, the US has states, and Canada has provinces.

q: Christianity is not the main religion in this country.

q.e: Sri Lanka's main religion is Buddhism, followed by about 70% of the population, with Hindus, Muslims and Christians as minorities.

q: About half of the 26,000 kg diamonds mined annually originate from which continent?

q.e: Africa has long been the major source of the world's diamonds (Botswana, DR Congo, South Africa), although Russia is the top producer by weight.

q: A major earthquake struck this city in 1906, killing almost 3,000 people.

q.e: The magnitude 7.9 earthquake struck San Francisco on April 18, 1906, igniting massive fires that burned for days and destroyed roughly 80% of the city.

q: This landlocked Alpine country, whose official Latin name is Confoederatio Helvetica, is a federation of relatively autonomous cantons.

q.e: Switzerland's official name is the Swiss Confederation, with "Confoederatio Helvetica" in Latin, shortened to CH on its car plates and internet domain.

q: In what city was the first , free, public high school opened?

q.e: Boston English High School, founded in 1821, was the first public high school in the US. Boston Latin School (1635) was the first public school.

q: The first professional sports organization in the USA was formed in this city.

q.e: The first professional sports team was the Cincinnati Red Stockings (1869) in baseball. Baltimore had early clubs, but the question's premise is debatable.

q: What is the correct formal name of the country known as the UK?
United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
United Kingdom of England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland
Union of Kingdoms of England and Scotland

q.e: The country's full official title has been the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland since 1927, reflecting the partition of Ireland in the early 1920s. Great Britain refers only to the island containing England, Scotland, and Wales.

q: What city is the capital of the European Union?
The EU has no official capital.

q.e: The EU has no official capital. Brussels hosts most institutions, Strasbourg the Parliament's plenary sessions and Luxembourg the Court of Justice.

q: In what country is the art of palm reading believed to have originated?

q.e: Palmistry (chiromancy) is believed to have originated in ancient India and spread to China, Persia and Greece.

q: What is the capital of Belgium?

q.e: Brussels serves as the capital of Belgium and also hosts the principal headquarters of the European Union and NATO.

q: What is the capital of Greece?

q.e: Athens is the capital of Greece. It's named after the goddess Athena.

q: What is the capital of Italy?

q.e: Rome is the capital of Italy, and surrounds Vatican City.

q: What is the capital of Israel?

q.e: Israel declares Jerusalem its capital, but many countries keep their embassies in Tel Aviv. The status is disputed.

q: What is the capital of Germany?

q.e: Berlin has been the capital of Germany since reunification in 1990 (the government moved from Bonn in 1999).

q: Which continents (landmasses, not peripheral islands) are entirely in the Northern Hemisphere?

q.e: North America, Europe and Asia are almost entirely in the Northern Hemisphere. Africa and South America straddle the equator, and Antarctica is in the south.

q: Which continents are entirely in the Western Hemisphere?

q.e: North and South America are almost wholly in the Western Hemisphere (west of the Prime Meridian), though a few islands cross it.

q: Which feature on a map helps determine direction?

q.e: A compass rose displays the cardinal directions (North, South, East, West) and intermediate points, whereas a map key or legend explains symbols, and a scale indicates distances.

q: Which of these continents is largest (by territory)?

q.e: Asia is the largest continent, at about 44.6 million km², followed by Africa, North America and South America.

q: Which of these US cities is largest (by population)?

q.e: Houston is the fourth-largest US city with over 2.3 million people. New York, LA and Chicago are bigger.

q: Which of these seas is largest?

q.e: The Mediterranean Sea, about 2.5 million km², is one of the world's biggest seas. The Sargasso and Caribbean are also large.

q: Which of these deserts is largest?

q.e: Of the world's deserts, Antarctica is the largest, then the Sahara (hot) and Arabian. The Syrian Desert is smaller (about 500,000 km²).

q: Which of these oceans has the greatest depth?

q.e: The Pacific Ocean contains Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench, the deepest known point on Earth at roughly 36,000 feet (11,000 meters) below sea level.

q: The rivers - the Tajo, the Ebro, the Duero, and the Guadiana, are located in this country.

q.e: The Tagus (Tajo), Ebro, Douro (Duero) and Guadiana are major rivers of the Iberian Peninsula. The Ebro is entirely in Spain.

q: The volcanoes - Akan, Aso, Mount Fuji and Rausu are located in this country.

q.e: Mount Fuji, Aso, Akan and Rausu are volcanoes in Japan, a country of over 100 active volcanoes.

q: Onega, Khanka and Chudskoye are three of the many lakes in this country.

q.e: Lake Onega, Lake Khanka and Lake Peipus (Chudskoye) are in Russia. Onega is Europe's second-largest lake.

q: The valleys of the Yellow River and the Pearl River are two of the seven main national valleys in this country.

q.e: The Yellow River and Pearl River valleys are among China's major river basins, along with the Yangtze, Huai, Liao, Hai and Songhua.

q: Pico da Bandeira, Pico do Cruzeiro and Pedra da Mina are three of the numerous mountains located in this South American country.

q.e: Pico da Bandeira, Pico do Cruzeiro and Pedra da Mina are Brazilian peaks. Pico da Neblina is the highest in Brazil.

q: Chauvet Cave and Meyrieres Cave are two caves located in this European state.

q.e: Chauvet Cave in southern France has some of the oldest known cave paintings, from about 30,000 years ago.

q: Kainji Lake and Lake Chad are considered lakes of this country.

q.e: Lake Chad and Kainji Lake are in Nigeria, with Kainji Lake formed by a dam on the Niger River.

q: Mitchell, Jardine, Staaten, Flinders, Leichhardt, and Nicholson are just few of the rivers in this country.

q.e: The Mitchell, Flinders, Leichhardt, Nicholson and Staaten rivers are all in Queensland, Australia.

q: Kaskaspakte, Akka and Sielmmacohkka are three mountains in this country.

q.e: Kebnekaise is Sweden's tallest mountain. Kaskasapakte and Akka (Akkamassivet) are peaks in Swedish Lapland.

q: Dasht-e Kavir and Kavir-e Lut are deserts located in this Asian country.

q.e: Dasht-e Kavir (the Great Salt Desert) and Dasht-e Lut are the large deserts of Iran. Lut is among the hottest places on Earth.

q: Which two countries border the Dead Sea?

q.e: The Dead Sea lies between Israel (and the West Bank) and Jordan.

q: Which statement about the emu and the kangaroo is not true?
Both are indigenous only to Australia.
Both are on the national emblem of Australia.
Both are incapable of walking backwards.

q.e: Emus and kangaroos are both native to Australia, and both appear on the coat of arms. The "not true" statement is the one that says they're only native elsewhere.

q: Where would you find the shortest river in the world?

q.e: The Roe River in Montana, near Great Falls, is claimed to be the world's shortest river at 201 feet (61 m). Oregon's D River also competes for the title.

q: Which would be found at 39 degrees 43 minutes North latitude?
The majority of the Mason-Dixon Line.
The border between Canada and Washington State.

q.e: The Mason-Dixon Line is the Maryland-Pennsylvania border at 39°43′N, and was surveyed in the 1760s.

q: Measuring at the Equator, what is the closest approximation of the Earths circumference?

q.e: Earth's equatorial circumference is about 24,901 miles (roughly 40,075 km). It is slightly larger around the Equator than around the poles because the planet's rotation creates an equatorial bulge.

q: The people of which country watched the most TV per week in 2005?

q.e: Surveys in the 2000s listed countries like the US, Japan and Thailand among top TV watchers. The figure was around 4 hours per day.

q: This country has more than 60% of worlds lakes due to its special drainage system.

q.e: Canada has over 60% of the world's lakes, more than 2 million, thanks to the glacial history of the Canadian Shield.

q: This is the lowest lake on Earth, situated at about 400 meters below sea level on the border between Israel and Jordan.

q.e: The Dead Sea's shore is about 430 m below sea level, the lowest land elevation on Earth. It's shrinking by about a meter a year.

q: Yellowstone Caldera is considered a supervolcano because within the past two million years it has erupted extremely violently three times . The most recent eruption occurred this long ago, and spread volcanic ash over most of the North American continent.

q.e: Yellowstone's last giant eruption, the Lava Creek eruption, was about 640,000 years ago. It spread ash across much of North America.

q: Which of the following states has an official motto In God we trust, which is also the official motto of the United States of America?

q.e: Florida's state motto is "In God We Trust" (adopted 1868), which is also the US national motto (1956).

q: Three of these US states have an official motto related to liberty. Spot the odd one.

q.e: Oklahoma's motto is "Labor omnia vincit" (Labor conquers all). New Hampshire ("Live free or die"), Illinois, Virginia and others refer to liberty.

q: North to the Future is the official motto of this US state, which is the largest in area.

q.e: Alaska's official state motto is "North to the Future," adopted in 1967. It's the largest US state by area.

q: The official motto of this state in the Pacific Northwest of the United States comes from Chinook Jargon.

q.e: Washington's motto is "Al-ki" (Chinook Jargon, "by and by"), meaning "eventually".

q: Which of these states has an official motto that doesnt include the word rights in it?

q.e: Indiana's motto is "The Crossroads of America", which doesn't have "rights". Several other states' mottos do mention rights.

q: Popocatépetl, a volcano whose name means Smoking Mountain, is 70 km away from the capital of which American country?

q.e: Popocatépetl ("Smoking Mountain") is an active volcano about 70 km southeast of Mexico City.

q: Where is the southernmost point in all 50 states?

q.e: Ka Lae, also known as South Point, is located on the Big Island of Hawaii at roughly 18.9 degrees North latitude, making it the southernmost point in all fifty US states. Key West, Florida, is the southernmost point in the contiguous United States.

q: And where is the lowest point in the USA, North America, and western hemisphere? I need the state and national park name.

q.e: Badwater Basin in Death Valley National Park, California, is the lowest point in North America, at 282 feet (86 m) below sea level.

q: The state with the largest area in the lower 48 is?

q.e: Covering approximately 268,596 square miles, Texas is the largest state in the contiguous United States, while Alaska is the largest state overall.

q: England, Norway, Belgium and Denmark all border this sea.

q.e: The North Sea touches England, Scotland, Norway, Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium and France.

q: Ireland, Germany and Austria are famous for the high consumption of this alcohol.

q.e: Ireland, Germany and Austria have some of the world's highest beer consumption, with the Czech Republic usually first.

q: All of these countries and commonwealth territories have a high divorce rate except one.

q.e: Sri Lanka has among the world's lowest divorce rates, while Western countries have much higher ones.

q: Barong is the embroidered formal garment of which country in South-East Asia?

q.e: The Barong Tagalog is the traditional embroidered shirt of the Philippines, worn at formal events. It's made of sheer fabric, such as piña.

q: The Badwater basin, the lowest point in North America, is located in which US valley?

q.e: Badwater Basin rests at 282 feet (86 meters) below sea level inside California's Death Valley National Park. Sun Valley is an alpine resort area located far to the north in Idaho.

q: The Grand Valley is an extended populated agricultural valley located along which US river?

q.e: Grand Valley in western Colorado, including the city of Grand Junction, lies along the Colorado River. It's known for peaches and wine.

q: This densely populated valley in the state of Utah is enclosed by steep mountains in every direction except the northwest.

q.e: Salt Lake Valley is enclosed by the Wasatch Range and Oquirrh Mountains and open to the northwest toward the Great Salt Lake.

q: The Shenandoah Valley in western Virginia derives its name from a Native American expression meaning what?

q.e: "Shenandoah" is of uncertain origin, and often translated as "Daughter of the Stars", although this is a legend. Some say it means "spruce river."

q: The Menomonee Valley along the Menomonee River in Milwaukee, Wisconsin has what peculiar shape?

q.e: The Menomonee Valley in Milwaukee, a former industrial area, has a U-shape, hence the name.

q: Owens Valley, the arid ranching valley of the Owens River, stretches for approximately 75 miles (120 km) on the territory of which US state?

q.e: Owens Valley lies in eastern California between the Sierra Nevada and the White-Inyo Mountains. Los Angeles takes its water via the aqueduct.

q: According to the 2000 Census, what is the approximate population of The Bronx, New York?

q.e: The Bronx had about 1.33 million people in the 2000 census, and about 1.4 million now.

q: Who was the first European to see The Bronx, NY?

q.e: Henry Hudson sailed past the area in 1609, but Verrazzano may have seen New York harbor first in 1524. Jonas Bronck settled the Bronx in 1639, giving it its name.

q: Which one of these statements is true about The Bronx, NY?
The only borough that is not an island
The only borough with a zoo
The only borough that has no colleges
The highest borough above sea level .

q.e: The Bronx is the only one of NYC's five boroughs on the North American mainland. The rest are on islands.

q: What are the colors on the flag of The Bronx, NY?

q.e: The flag of the Bronx has blue, white and orange stripes, the colors of the Dutch flag at the time of the Dutch settlers.

q: Little Rock is the capital and most populous city of this US state.

q.e: Little Rock became the territorial capital of Arkansas in 1821 and remained the state capital when Arkansas was admitted to the Union in 1836. Topeka and Wichita are cities in Kansas.

q: What US state borders the states of Virginia, Kentucky, Ohio, Pennsylvania and Maryland?

q.e: West Virginia borders Virginia, Kentucky, Ohio, Pennsylvania and Maryland. It separated from Virginia in 1863.

q: Which US state is nicknamed The Pine Tree State?

q.e: Maine is "The Pine Tree State", with the white pine on its flag. It's also called Vacationland.

q: The southern region of what US state is known as Little Egypt?

q.e: "Little Egypt" is southern Illinois, with towns named Cairo, Karnak, Thebes and Goshen.

q: The capital city of this US state is Trenton, and its largest city is Newark.

q.e: Trenton is the capital of New Jersey, and Newark is its largest city.

q: The name of which American state means red people in the Choctaw language?

q.e: "Oklahoma" comes from the Choctaw words okla (people) and humma (red), so "red people."

q: What US state is known as The Volunteer State?

q.e: Tennessee is "The Volunteer State" because of the many volunteer soldiers it provided in wars like the War of 1812.

q: The flag of what US state features a gold torch and nineteen stars on a blue rectangular field?

q.e: Indiana's flag has a torch surrounded by 19 stars on a blue field. The torch represents liberty and enlightenment.

q: What US state is known as the Peach State?

q.e: Georgia officially adopted 'The Peach State' as its state nickname in 1993, reflecting a rich agricultural reputation for growing high-quality peaches dating back to the 19th century.

q: Which country is known as Österreich in their native language?

q.e: Österreich is Austria in German, meaning "eastern realm."

q: Which country has the river Danube as most of its northern border?

q.e: The Danube forms most of the border between Bulgaria and Romania, and Bulgaria is on its southern bank.

q: Which EU member is divided into a Greek and a Turkish part?

q.e: Cyprus is divided between the Greek Cypriot south (EU member, Republic of Cyprus) and the Turkish-controlled north. The island has been split since 1974.

q: Which countrys first president was Václav Havel, a writer and dramatist?

q.e: Václav Havel was a prominent dissident playwright who led the peaceful Velvet Revolution in 1989. He served as the last president of Czechoslovakia and then as the first president of the independent Czech Republic from 1993 to 2003.

q: Which Nordic country was first to enter the European Union?

q.e: Denmark joined the European Communities in 1973, with the UK and Ireland. Sweden and Finland joined in 1995.

q: Which European Union member is home to Santa Claus?

q.e: In European folklore, Santa Claus's home and official workshop are located in the Lapland region of northern Finland, centered around the town of Rovaniemi.

q: Which of the EU founding members is the country of Liberté, Égalité, Fraternité?

q.e: France, a founding EU member, has the national motto "Liberté, Égalité, Fraternité" (liberty, equality, fraternity) from the Revolution.

q: Which European Union member has the greatest number of islands?

q.e: Greece has thousands of islands (about 6,000 islands and islets, 227 inhabited). Sweden also has a huge number.

q: Which country is the only member of the European Union that is partly located in Africa?

q.e: Spain is the only EU state with territory in Africa (Ceuta, Melilla and the Canary Islands). Portugal's Madeira is also in the Atlantic.

q: Which EU member has a significant part of its territory below sea level?

q.e: About 26% of the Netherlands lies below sea level, protected by a complex national system of dikes, canals, and pumping stations. The lowest point, near Rotterdam, is nearly 22 feet (6.7 meters) below sea level.

q: Which country is the biggest contributor to the European Union budget?

q.e: Germany is the largest net contributor to the EU budget in absolute terms, followed by France and others.

q: Which country has twice rejected European Union membership in national referendums?

q.e: Norwegians rejected EU membership in referendums in 1972 and 1994. The country is in the EEA.

q: Which country associated with banking is not a member of the European Union?

q.e: Switzerland is not an EU member but has bilateral treaties and is in the Schengen Area. Its banks are famous.

q: In which country is the European Union's biggest lake located?

q.e: Lake Vänern in Sweden is the largest lake in the European Union, at about 5,650 km².

q: Which member of the European Union completely surrounds two countries that are outside of the club?

q.e: Italy completely surrounds two non-EU states: San Marino and Vatican City.

q: The Shaolin temples are perhaps the Buddhist monasteries best known in the West. The word Shaolin means this.

q.e: "Shaolin" (少林) means "young forest". The Shaolin Temple in Henan is the birthplace of Chan (Zen) Buddhism and Shaolin kung fu.

q: Which EU country or US state is not entirely situated on (an) island(s)?

q.e: Rhode Island is mostly on the mainland, with some islands, including Aquidneck Island. Hawaii, Malta and Cyprus are entirely islands.

q: Which country or state was the first to be attacked in WWII?

q.e: Germany attacked Poland on 1 September 1939, starting WWII in Europe.

q: Where was the colonial settlement New Amsterdam located?

q.e: New Amsterdam, founded by the Dutch in 1625, was on the southern tip of Manhattan, and was renamed New York in 1664 when England took it over.

q: Which of these is the largest in terms of area?

q.e: Germany is about 357,000 km², larger than many European countries but small compared with the US or Russia.

q: Which of the following metropolitan areas is the largest in terms of population?

q.e: The New York metropolitan area has about 20 million people. Tokyo is larger worldwide, however.

q: Which of these cities was established first?

q.e: Madrid was founded as a Moorish fortress around the 9th century. Many cities were founded much earlier.

q: Which of the following flags doesnt include a cross?

q.e: Alaska's flag has the Big Dipper and North Star on blue, and no cross. Many flags in Scandinavia use a cross.

q: Birmingham is the most populous city of which country or US state?

q.e: Birmingham is the most populous city in Alabama (about 200,000) in older counts, but Huntsville has overtaken it in recent census figures.

q: What two colors are featured on the flag and coat of arms of Malta, a country consisting of seven Mediterranean islands?

q.e: Malta's flag is white and red, with the George Cross in the corner.

q: What motto do North Carolina license plates carry?

q.e: North Carolina introduced the slogan First in Flight on its license plates in 1982 to celebrate the Wright brothers' historic powered flights at Kitty Hawk in 1903.

q: What country gained independence from the British Mandate for Palestine in 1948?

q.e: Israel declared independence on 14 May 1948 as the British Mandate for Palestine ended.

q: What river encountered during the Lewis and Clark expedition (1804-1806) flows directly into the Pacific Ocean between Washington and Oregon?

q.e: The Columbia River forms much of the border between Washington and Oregon, and the Lewis and Clark Expedition reached the Pacific at its mouth in 1805.

q: What sea captain claimed British possession of the eastern part of Australia in 1770 naming it New South Wales?

q.e: Captain James Cook claimed the eastern coast of Australia for Britain in 1770, calling it New South Wales.

q: In what South American country was Che Ernesto Guevara born?

q.e: Ernesto "Che" Guevara was born in Rosario, Argentina, in 1928.

q: After World War II, this country was split into two states which were not reunited until 1990.

q.e: In 1949, Germany was divided into West Germany and the Soviet-controlled East Germany until formal reunification took place on October 3, 1990.

q: In what city in Switzerland is the headquarters of the World Trade Organization (WTO) located?

q.e: The World Trade Organization is based in Geneva, Switzerland, at the Centre William Rappard.

q: To which countrys territory does the Dead Sea belong?

q.e: The Dead Sea is shared by Israel, Jordan and the West Bank. Its borders are partly disputed.

q: What body of water feeds the Dead Sea?

q.e: The Jordan River is the primary freshwater tributary flowing southward into the landlocked Dead Sea, which loses water only through evaporation.

q: The Bible tells the story of a woman that was turned into a pillar of salt near the Dead Sea. Who was her famous husband?

q.e: Lot's wife was turned into a pillar of salt when she looked back at Sodom, per Genesis 19. Her husband was Lot, Abraham's nephew.

q: The Dead Sea, the lowest point on Earth, is how far below sea level?

q.e: The Dead Sea's surface is about 430 m (1,410 ft) below sea level, though older figures put it at 400-418 m. It's dropping.

q: The Dead Sea is part of the Great Rift Valley. How far does this valley extend in length?

q.e: The Great Rift Valley stretches about 6,000 km (3,700 miles) from Lebanon's Beqaa Valley through East Africa to Mozambique.

q: The Rosenbergs, who were convicted of conspiracy, were held at what prison?

q.e: Julius and Ethel Rosenberg were convicted of espionage conspiracy and executed at Sing Sing prison, Ossining, New York, in 1953.

q: The Kremlin, a historic fortified complex at the heart of Moscow, overlooks this square to the east.

q.e: Red Square borders the eastern walls of the Moscow Kremlin; its Russian name 'Krasnaya Ploshchad' originally meant 'beautiful square' before evolving to mean 'red'.

q: What is the name of the sea that borders the Netherlands?

q.e: The Netherlands borders the North Sea along its northern and western coasts, relying extensively on dikes and flood-control systems to manage sea levels.

q: What are the three colours of the national flag of the Netherlands from top to bottom?

q.e: The Dutch flag has red, white and blue horizontal stripes, red on top.

q: What is the capital city of the Netherlands?

q.e: Amsterdam is the capital of the Netherlands, though the government sits in The Hague.

q: What two countries border the Netherlands?

q.e: The Netherlands borders Belgium to the south and Germany to the east, and the North Sea to the north and west.

q: What European island is partially occupied by a neighbouring island nation, which has led to centuries of dispute?

q.e: Ireland is an island, with the six counties of Northern Ireland part of the UK (Great Britain). The partition dates from 1921.

q: What island is shared by the nations of Indonesia and Papua New Guinea?

q.e: New Guinea, the second-largest island in the world, is divided between Indonesia (west) and Papua New Guinea (east).

q: This tiny Caribbean island is shared by France and the Netherlands.

q.e: St. Martin/Sint Maarten is shared by France (north) and the Netherlands (south) and has been divided since 1648.

q: The island of Sebatik, located east of Borneo, is shared by Indonesia and what other nation?

q.e: Sebatik Island, off Borneo's east coast, is split between Indonesia (north) and Malaysia.
Covering roughly 5.4 million square miles (14 million square km), the Arctic Ocean is the smallest and shallowest of the world's five recognized oceans.

q: What portion of the Earth's surface do oceans cover?

q.e: Oceans cover approximately 71 percent of the Earth's surface, which is just over seven-tenths and therefore more than two-thirds.

q: The Marianas Trench, the deepest location on the surface of the Earths crust, lies in this ocean.

q.e: The Mariana Trench is located in the western Pacific Ocean east of the Mariana Islands. Its deepest spot, the Challenger Deep, plunges to nearly 36,000 feet (about 11,000 meters) below sea level.

q: The Bering Sea is a part of which ocean?

q.e: The Bering Sea is a marginal sea of the Pacific, between Alaska and Siberia.

q: The famous Île Notre-Dame, an artificial island built from earth excavated for a metropolitan railway, is located in which country?

q.e: Île Notre-Dame in Montreal, Canada, was built for Expo 67 using earth dug for the Metro. It hosts the Formula 1 Canadian Grand Prix circuit.

q: What is the popular name of the artificial island in Tokyo Bay, whose name is Yume No Shima in Japanese?

q.e: Yume no Shima ("Dream Island") in Tokyo Bay was built from landfill and houses a park. It has been used for the Olympic venues.

q: Rokko island, constructed between 1973 and 1992, is an artificial island situated in which country?

q.e: Rokkō Island, an artificial island in Kobe Bay, Japan, was built between 1973 and 1992. It was built with earth from mountains.

q: Which artificial island is situated in San Francisco Bay, between San Francisco and Oakland?

q.e: Treasure Island is a man-made island in San Francisco Bay, built in 1936-37 for the Golden Gate International Exposition. It connects to Yerba Buena Island, which carries the Bay Bridge.

q: Spiral Island, a small Mexican artificial floating island, was situated on the coast of which sea?

q.e: Spiral Island was a floating island made of plastic bottles by Richie Sowa near Puerto Aventuras, off Mexico's Caribbean coast. Hurricane Emily destroyed it in 2005.

q: Which country was not among the founding states of the European Economic Community (the European Union predecessor)?

q.e: The EEC's six founders (1957) were France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg. The UK joined in 1973.

q: The name of which US state means large creek in the Seneca language?

q.e: "Ohio" comes from the Seneca word ohi:yo', meaning "good river" or "large creek."

q: Montgomery is the capital city of this US state, and its largest city is Birmingham.

q.e: Montgomery is Alabama's capital, and Birmingham was historically its largest city (Huntsville has recently passed it).

q: Everglades National Park is located in this US state.

q.e: Established in 1947, Everglades National Park protects roughly 1.5 million acres of tropical wetlands across southern Florida. It is the largest subtropical wilderness in the United States and home to diverse species including the American alligator and Florida panther.

q: According to one theory, the name of this US state comes from the French word for hurricane.

q.e: Oregon's name is of uncertain origin. One theory ties it to the French "ouragan" (hurricane), after the Columbia River's wild water.

q: Baton Rouge is the capital of what US state?

q.e: Baton Rouge, which translates to red stick from French, was designated Louisiana's state capital in 1849, replacing New Orleans. It remains the second-largest city in the state after New Orleans.

q: The largest city in what US state hosts Summerfest, or The Worlds Largest Music Festival?

q.e: Summerfest, "The World's Largest Music Festival," is held every summer on the Milwaukee lakefront in Wisconsin.

q: The name of this US state means great river and its symbol is the magnolia tree.

q.e: "Mississippi" comes from the Ojibwe misi-ziibi, meaning "great river." Mississippi is "The Magnolia State."

q: The Ifugao Rice Terraces are located in Luzon, in the Philippines. If it were possible to place them end to end, how long would they extend?

q.e: The Ifugao terraces were carved by hand about 2,000 years ago and are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Claims about their total length run from thousands to tens of thousands of kilometers.

q: Which best describes the religious distribution of the populace of the Philippines?

q.e: About 80-85% of Filipinos are Catholic, making it Asia's largest Catholic nation, with Protestant, Muslim and other minorities.

q: This US President was born in South Carolina although he lived in Tennessee when he became president.

q.e: Andrew Jackson was born in 1767 in the Waxhaws region on the North Carolina/South Carolina border, and lived in Tennessee. He was elected in 1828.

q: Which of the following states borders South Carolina?

q.e: South Carolina borders Georgia to the southwest and North Carolina to the north. The Savannah River forms the Georgia border.

q: The city of Fargo is the largest city in which of these U.S. states?

q.e: Fargo is the largest city in North Dakota, on the Red River. Bismarck is the capital.

q: Which U.S. state has been nicknamed The Cornhusker State?

q.e: Nebraska is "The Cornhusker State" and also the "Beef State." The University of Nebraska teams are the Cornhuskers.

q: Topeka is the capital city of which U.S. state?

q.e: Topeka is the capital of Kansas. Wichita is the largest city.

q: Which of these nicknames refers to the U.S. state of Idaho?

q.e: Idaho is the "Gem State," for its many gemstones, and is also known for potatoes.

q: What does the name of the U.S. state of Utah mean in the Ute language?

q.e: "Utah" probably derives from a Ute word for "people of the mountains". The state's name is also linked to the Ute tribe.

q: The Himalayan range, part of which is Mount Everest, stretches across five different countries in Asia. Which of the following countries is not among them?

q.e: The Himalayas span India, Nepal, Bhutan, China (Tibet) and Pakistan. Israel is in the Middle East.

q: Edmund Hillary, the first mountaineer to reach mount Everest, was from what country?

q.e: Sir Edmund Hillary, a New Zealander, reached Everest's summit with Sherpa Tenzing Norgay on 29 May 1953.

q: What nationality was Junko Tabei - the first woman to reach the peak of Mount Everest?

q.e: Junko Tabei was a Japanese mountaineer who reached the summit of Mount Everest via the South Col route on May 16, 1975.

q: This island, located north of Australia, is the second-largest island on the planet.

q.e: Covering roughly 785,000 square kilometers, New Guinea is second in land area only to Greenland among the world's islands. It is divided between Indonesia in the west and Papua New Guinea in the east.

q: What is the most populous island in the world?

q.e: Java is home to more than 150 million people, making it by far the world's most populous island. Japan's main island of Honshu is second, with around 100 million residents.

q: This island is located in the Indian Ocean and is also known as Ceylon.

q.e: Sri Lanka, an island nation off India's south coast, was known as Ceylon until 1972.

q: The capital of this island country is Kingston.

q.e: Kingston is the capital and largest city of Jamaica, a Caribbean island.

q: Which nation claims ownership of the South Pole?

q.e: Under the Antarctic Treaty, signed in 1959 and entered into force in 1961, all territorial claims south of 60 degrees South latitude are suspended. Although countries like the United States operate research bases at the South Pole, no nation is legally recognized as owning it.

q: What happened at the North Pole on August 3, 1958?
A submarine travelled underwater under the Pole.
The northernmost US city, Naavetau, was founded.
The first airport in the Arctic was built.
The last Arctic Moa was killed.

q.e: On 3 August 1958, the US nuclear submarine USS Nautilus became the first vessel to reach the North Pole, traveling beneath the ice.

q: Which statement is true about the explorer and glaciologist Albert P. Crary?
He was the first person to reach both the North and South Poles.
He was the first person to set foot on Antarctica.
He was the first pilot to fly across the South Pole.
He was the first person to build a home above the Arctic Circle.

q.e: Albert Crary, a US geophysicist, was the first person to have set foot on both the North and South Poles (1952 and 1961).

q: Where are the origins of the Rhine?

q.e: The Rhine rises in the Swiss Alps in Graubünden (near Lake Toma), flowing to the North Sea at the Netherlands.

q: In what country does the River Po rise?

q.e: The Po rises on Monviso in the Cottian Alps of Piedmont, Italy, and flows 652 km east to the Adriatic. It's Italy's longest river.

q: What does the Filipino word lungsod mean in English?

q.e: "Lungsod" means "city" in Filipino (Tagalog). A larger metropolis is "kalakhang lungsod".

q: What does the Filipino word salita mean in English?

q.e: "Salita" means "word" in Filipino. The related "magsalita" means "to speak".

q: Wichita, the county seat of Sedgwick County, is nicknamed what?

q.e: Wichita, Kansas, is the "Air Capital of the World," as home to Cessna, Beechcraft, Learjet and Boeing plants.

q: What is the name of the European peninsula on which Italy is located?

q.e: Italy sits on the Italian Peninsula, bounded by the Tyrrhenian, Ionian and Adriatic seas. The Apennines run down its spine.

q: What is the capital and largest city of Italy?
