q.e: Rome has served as the capital of Italy since 1871, following the unification of the country. With a population of about 2.8 million residents within city limits, it is larger than Milan, which is Italy's second-largest city and primary financial center.

q: Which of these colors is not present on the national flag of the Italian Republic?

q.e: The Italian flag (il Tricolore) is green, white and red. There's no blue, but Italian national sports teams wear blue.

q: What is the meaning of the name of Italy according to scientists who have studied its origin?

q.e: "Italia" may come from "vitulus" (calf), so the "land of young cattle" (calves). It's one of several theories.

q: What is the shape of the Italian Peninsula?

q.e: Italy is often described as boot-shaped, with Sicily as a "ball" at the toe.

q: Maryland Day is celebrated every year on what date?
The first day of crab season

q.e: Maryland Day, 25 March, marks the 1634 landing of the first settlers on the Ark and the Dove.

q: Which was the seat of colonial government in Maryland until 1708?

q.e: St. Mary's City was Maryland's first capital (1634). The capital moved to Annapolis in 1695.

q: What are Maryland's two official state nicknames?
"The Old Line State" and "The Free State"
"The Crab State" and "The Old Line State"

q.e: Maryland is called the "Old Line State" (for Continental soldiers) and the "Free State" (a mid-1920s reference to the state's resistance to Prohibition).

q: Which is the state flower of Maryland?

q.e: The Black-eyed Susan is the state flower of Maryland, adopted in 1918. It's the "Preakness" flower.

q: The term Death Zone refers to what altitude?

q.e: The "Death Zone" is above 8,000 m (26,000 ft), where there's too little oxygen for humans to survive for long.

q: During Roman occupation, this city, popular nowadays as the Heaven of Romance, was called Lutetia.

q.e: Lutetia was the Roman name for Paris. The Parisii, a Gaulish tribe, lived there.

q: In what European city are Piazza San Marco and Canale Grande located?

q.e: Piazza San Marco and the Grand Canal (Canal Grande) are in Venice, Italy.

q: In what country will you find the impressive Neuschwanstein Castle, which was the inspiration for Sleeping Beauty Castle at Disneyland Park?

q.e: Bavaria's Neuschwanstein Castle, built for Ludwig II in the 1860s-80s, inspired Disney's Sleeping Beauty Castle.

q: What is the birthplace of Johann Strauss II, also known as The Waltz King?

q.e: Johann Strauss II was born in St. Ulrich near Vienna in 1825 and became world-famous for composing waltzes like 'The Blue Danube'. Salzburg is famous as the birthplace of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart.

q: What popular tourist destination stands at the foot of the Maritime Alps?

q.e: Monte Carlo, in Monaco, sits at the foot of the Maritime Alps on the French Riviera. The Monaco Grand Prix and casino are famous.

q: What city is home of Broadway Theatre?

q.e: Broadway theatre refers to commercial theatrical performances staged in 41 professional theatres, each with 500 or more seats, located along and around Broadway in Midtown Manhattan, New York City.

q: This island, also known as Formosa, is the largest island of the Republic of China.

q.e: Portuguese sailors named the island Ilha Formosa, meaning 'beautiful island', in the 16th century. Taiwan is the main and largest island governed by the Republic of China, covering roughly 35,800 square kilometers.

q: What island, located in the North Pacific Ocean, is also known as the Big Island?

q.e: Hawaii, the largest island in the state, is called the "Big Island". It has the active volcanoes Kīlauea and Mauna Loa.

q: This island country whose capital is Nicosia is the third-largest Mediterranean island.

q.e: Cyprus is the third-largest island in the Mediterranean (after Sicily and Sardinia). Its capital, Nicosia, is divided between Greek and Turkish sides.

q: This island is one of Indonesias 33 provinces.

q.e: Bali is an Indonesian province (the country now has 38). The capital is Denpasar.

q: What is the name of the capital and largest city of Spain?

q.e: Madrid became the capital of the Spanish Empire under King Philip II in 1561 and remains Spain's political and demographic center, home to more than 3.3 million people in the city proper.

q: Spain does not share a border with which one of these countries?

q.e: Spain borders Portugal, France, Andorra and Morocco (via Ceuta and Melilla), and Gibraltar, but not Germany.

q: When is the national holiday called Hispanic Day celebrated annually in Spain?

q.e: Spain's Hispanic Day (Fiesta Nacional de España) is on 12 October, marking Columbus's arrival in the Americas in 1492.

q: What is the title of the national anthem of Spain?

q.e: The "Marcha Real" (Royal March) is Spain's anthem. It's one of the few anthems without official lyrics.

q: What are the colors of the three vertical stripes on the national flag of Spain?

q.e: The Spanish flag has three horizontal stripes: red, yellow (double-wide), red. It isn't vertical.

q: What is the main ingredient of the traditional Spanish dish paella?

q.e: Originating in the Valencia region of Spain, paella traditionally features short-grain rice, such as Bomba rice, which absorbs the broth and develops a prized crispy bottom layer known as socarrat.

q: In which section of Israel is Eilat located?

q.e: Eilat is Israel's southernmost city, on the Red Sea at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba.

q: What best describes the climate of Eilat?
Humid and hot summers and humid and cool winters
Humid, hot summers and dry, cool winters
Hot, dry summers and humid, cool winters

q.e: Eilat has a hot desert climate with almost no rain, and mild winters.

q: Which city is a sister city to Eilat?

q.e: Eilat's sister cities include Los Angeles and other cities. (Sister city lists vary by source.)

q: Which is the major source of revenue for the Eilat area?

q.e: Tourism, with diving, resorts and beaches, is the main source of Eilat's income. The port also contributes.

q: Which four countries can be seen from Eilat?

q.e: From Eilat you can see Egypt (Taba), Jordan (Aqaba) and Saudi Arabia across the Gulf of Aqaba, and Israel itself.

q: The Peace Treaty between Jordan and Israel was signed near Eilat. In what year did this happen?

q.e: The Israel-Jordan peace treaty was signed on 26 October 1994 at the Arava crossing near Eilat and Aqaba. Clinton witnessed it.

q: How long is the crest of the American Falls if measured along the jagged lip of the falls?

q.e: The American Falls at Niagara are about 260-290 m wide at the crest and 21-30 m high. Measurements vary with the way the edge is counted.

q: Which U.S. state is nicknamed The Natural State?

q.e: Arkansas is "The Natural State" for its forests, rivers and mountains. It's also the "Razorback State."

q: What U.S. state is nicknamed Land of Infinite Variety?

q.e: South Dakota's nickname "Land of Infinite Variety" is on its tourism logo. Mount Rushmore is there.

q: Which of these nicknames has been given to the U.S. state of Illinois?

q.e: Illinois is "The Prairie State" and "Land of Lincoln." It's also a leading corn producer.

q: This U.S. state was nicknamed Vacationland, and the nickname is used on license plates.

q.e: Maine's license plates say "Vacationland". The state is famed for lobster and rocky coast.

q: The Independence State is one of the nicknames of this U.S. state.

q.e: Pennsylvania is the "Keystone State" and is also called the "Independence State" since the Declaration was signed in Philadelphia.

q: Which U.S. state is nicknamed The Cowboy State?

q.e: Wyoming is "The Cowboy State". Its license plate shows a bucking horse.

q: Which former empire were both Slovenia and Slovakia part of?

q.e: Both Slovenia and Slovakia were parts of the Austro-Hungarian Empire until 1918.

q: Which country borders both Slovenia and Slovakia?

q.e: Austria borders both Slovenia (south) and Slovakia (east).

q: What design is depicted on the national flag of Switzerland?

q.e: The Swiss flag displays an equilateral white cross on a square red field, adapted from the emblem of the Canton of Schwyz. The emblem of the International Red Cross was created in 1863 by reversing these national colors.

q: What is the unofficial national motto of Switzerland?
One for all, all for one

q.e: Switzerland's unofficial motto is "One for all, all for one" (Unus pro omnibus, omnes pro uno).

q: What is the main ingredient of the traditional Swiss dish Rosti?

q.e: Rösti is a Swiss dish of grated, fried potatoes. It's the national dish in German-speaking Switzerland.

q: What type of climate does North Korea have?

q.e: North Korea has a continental climate, with cold, dry winters and hot, humid summers.

q: Which of these events is regularly performed only in North Korea?

q.e: The Arirang Mass Games, with tens of thousands of performers, are a famous North Korean event.

q: What other name is commonly used to refer to the Colorado River in North America?

q.e: The Colorado River's name is Spanish for "colored red," from its silt. It is sometimes confused with the Red River.

q: What is the name of the longest river in the United States of America?

q.e: The Missouri River (about 2,340 miles) is the longest in the US. Together with the Mississippi, it forms the world's fourth-longest river system.

q: The Ohio River does not flow though the territory of this American state.

q.e: The Ohio River flows along the borders of Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Kentucky and West Virginia, and through Pennsylvania, but not through Virginia.

q: What is the meaning of the name of the Mississippi River, which originated from the Ojibwe word misi-ziibi?

q.e: "Mississippi" comes from the Ojibwe misi-ziibi: "misi" (great) + "ziibi" (river).

q: More than half of the Yukon River is located within this American state.

q.e: The Yukon River starts in Canada and flows through Alaska to the Bering Sea. About two-thirds of it is in Alaska.

q: According to some medieval texts, the name of Norway originated from the name of which of the following?

q.e: Norway's name comes from the Old Norse "Norðvegr," the "north way". Some sagas link it to a king named Nór.

q: What animal is depicted on the Coat of Arms of Norway?

q.e: Norway's coat of arms shows a golden lion with an axe, an emblem from the 13th century.

q: What is the official language adopted by the government of Norway?

q.e: Norway's official language is Norwegian, in two forms (Bokmål and Nynorsk). Sami is also official in some places.

q: What is the title of the national anthem of Norway?

q.e: "Ja, vi elsker dette landet" ("Yes, we love this country") is Norway's national anthem.
A bunad is traditional Norwegian folk costume, worn on 17 May (Constitution Day) and at weddings. Each region has its own design.

q: What is the popular Norwegian delicacy called Smalahove made from?

q.e: Smalahove is a Norwegian dish of a smoked and boiled sheep's head, traditionally from the west coast.

q: Which of the following is present on the national flag of Norway?

q.e: Norway's flag has a blue-bordered white cross on red (a Nordic cross).

q: What are the colors on the national flag of Madagascar, adopted on October 14, 1958?

q.e: Madagascar's flag (1958) has a white vertical stripe next to red and green horizontal stripes.

q: What kind of traditional ritual is the Famadihana, practiced by the Malagasy people in Madagascar?
Introducing boys into manhood by tattooing and scarring them

q.e: Famadihana, the "turning of the bones," is a Malagasy rite in which families exhume ancestors, rewrap them and dance with them.

q: According to the Shinsengumi rules, if the leader of a unit is mortally wounded in a fight, what should the rest of the group do?
All members of the unit must fight and die on the spot.
Take the body and run away

q.e: Shinsengumi (the Kyoto police force in the 1860s) had a strict code. If a unit leader was killed, the rest were to fight to the death.

q: This river is the longest in the United States, and it gave its name to one of the states.

q.e: Measuring roughly 2,341 miles (3,767 km), the Missouri River is the longest in the United States, slightly exceeding the main stem of the Mississippi River by about 100 miles before the two join near St. Louis.

q: What is the largest river on the planet by volume?

q.e: The Amazon River discharges an average of about 219,000 cubic meters of water per second into the Atlantic, roughly 20 percent of all global river flow. The Nile is traditionally considered the longest river, but its volume is far smaller.

q: What is the name of the river in which Jesus Christ was baptized by John the Baptist?

q.e: According to the New Testament gospels, John the Baptist conducted his baptisms in the Jordan River, which flows along the border of modern Jordan and Israel.

q: This North American river is also called Kaniatarowanenneh, which means big waterway in Mohawk.

q.e: The St. Lawrence River is "Kaniatarowanenneh" in Mohawk, meaning "big waterway." It drains the Great Lakes into the Atlantic.

q: A windspeed of 100 feet above the ground was observed in 1999 in what Oklahoma city?

q.e: On 3 May 1999, a Doppler on Wheels radar measured a wind speed of about 301 mph near Moore, Oklahoma, during an F5 tornado, the highest ever recorded.

q: The national motto of the Republic of Botswana is Pula. What does this mean in English?

q.e: "Pula" means "rain" in Setswana, and is also the name of Botswana's currency. Rain is precious in a dry country.

q: The national motto of what country is A Mari Usque Ad Mare, meaning From Sea to Sea in Latin?

q.e: Canada's motto "A mari usque ad mare" comes from Psalm 72 and means "from sea to sea."

q: The national motto of what country is Peace at Home, Peace in the World?

q.e: Turkey's motto, from Atatürk, is "Peace at home, peace in the world."

q: The national motto of the Republic of the Fiji Islands is Rerevaka na Kalou ka Doka na Tui. What does this mean?
Fear God and honor the Queen
We kneel before you, blessed land

q.e: Fiji's motto, "Rerevaka na Kalou ka Doka na Tui" means "Fear God and honour the Queen." It's from the colonial era.

q: The national motto of this Arabic country is God is the greatest.

q.e: Iraq's flag carries "Allahu Akbar" ("God is the greatest") in Arabic script, in green.

q: What is the meaning of the national motto of the Republic of Indonesia, Bhinneka Tunggal Ika?

q.e: Indonesia's motto "Bhinneka Tunggal Ika" is Old Javanese, meaning "Unity in Diversity."

q: In what country is the Angel Falls, the highest waterfall on the planet, located?

q.e: Angel Falls in Venezuela (Canaima National Park) is the world's tallest uninterrupted waterfall, at 979 m. It's named after Jimmie Angel.

q: In what U.S. state is the famous Bridalveil Fall located?

q.e: Bridalveil Fall is in Yosemite National Park, California, and is about 188 m (617 ft) high.

q: Jog Falls is the highest plunge waterfall in this Asian country.

q.e: Jog Falls in Karnataka, India, is India's second-highest plunge waterfall at 253 m, also known as Gersoppa Falls.

q: In what European country are the Rhine Falls located?

q.e: The Rhine Falls near Schaffhausen, Switzerland, is Europe's largest plain waterfall by volume.

q: In what U.S. state is the tallest waterfall in the country, Waihilau Falls, located?

q.e: Waihilau Falls on Hawaii's Big Island is a tall waterfall in Waipiʻo Valley, often listed as the tallest in the US.

q: In what country is Jurong Falls, the tallest artificial waterfall in the world, located?

q.e: Jurong Bird Park's Jurong Falls in Singapore is billed as the world's tallest man-made waterfall, at 30 m.

q: Madagascar is the worlds largest producer and exporter of what product?

q.e: Madagascar produces roughly 70 to 80 percent of the world's natural vanilla beans, primarily cultivated in its northeastern Sava region.

q: Where is New Guinea ranked in terms of size, among the islands of the world?
New Guinea is the second largest island in the world.
New Guinea is the third largest island in the world.
New Guinea is the fourth largest island in the world.
New Guinea is the largest island in the world.

q.e: New Guinea, at 786,000 km², is the world's second-largest island after Greenland.

q: The island of New Guinea was named after the country of Guinea. Which is Guinea located?

q.e: Spanish explorer Yñigo Ortiz de Retes named New Guinea in 1545 for resemblance to the African coast of Guinea.

q: The country of Papua New Guinea gained its independence from this country in 1975.

q.e: Papua New Guinea became independent from Australia on 16 September 1975, after being under Australian administration.

q: What is the literal translation of the title of the national anthem of Egypt, Bilady, Bilady, Bilady?
My country, my country, my country

q.e: "Bilady, Bilady, Bilady" means "My homeland, my homeland, my homeland." It was adopted in 1979.

q: What sea borders Egypt to the east?

q.e: Egypt is bordered by the Red Sea to the east and the Mediterranean Sea to the north, with the Suez Canal linking the two waterways.

q: What is the official language spoken in Egypt?

q.e: Modern Standard Arabic is the sole official language of Egypt, while Egyptian Arabic is the dominant spoken vernacular across the country.

q: Where was Omar Sharif, one of the most famous Egyptian actors, born?

q.e: Omar Sharif (Michel Shalhoub) was born in Alexandria, Egypt, in 1932. He starred in Lawrence of Arabia and Doctor Zhivago.

q: What sport is rated as the most popular sport among Egyptians?

q.e: Football (soccer) is by far Egypt's most popular sport, and Al Ahly and Zamalek are the biggest clubs.

q: The Egyptian territory is calculated to be roughly twice as large as the territory of this European country.

q.e: Egypt covers about one million km², almost twice the size of Spain (about 506,000 km²).

q: Luxembourg is bordered by all of the following nations except this one.

q.e: Luxembourg borders Belgium, France and Germany, but not the Netherlands.

q: Luxembourg has a population of approximately how many people?

q.e: Luxembourg's population is about 650,000 now, an increase from around 500,000 in the early 2000s.

q: How does Luxembourg, which is a member of NATO, contribute to NATO?
by maintaining the sixth largest NATO air force
by allowing extensive US and British military installations on its territory
by financially supporting a navy even though is has no coastline

q.e: Luxembourg is a founding member of NATO and contributes a small army, plus the NATO airborne radar (AWACS) program.

q: What is the predominant religion in Luxembourg?

q.e: Luxembourg is predominantly Roman Catholic (about 70% historically), although the share is declining.

q: In what country is Virginia Falls located?

q.e: Virginia Falls (Nailicho) is a 96 m waterfall on the Nahanni River in the Northwest Territories of Canada.

q: The Eas a Chual Aluinn is the highest waterfall in this country.

q.e: Eas a' Chùal Aluinn in Scotland is the tallest waterfall in the UK, at 200 m.

q: What is the English name of the Mosi-oa-Tunya waterfall located between Zambia and Zimbabwe?

q.e: Scottish explorer David Livingstone became the first European to view the massive waterfall in 1855, renaming it in honor of Britain's Queen Victoria. Its indigenous Lozi name, Mosi-oa-Tunya, translates to 'the smoke that thunders.'

q: In what country is Yumbilla Falls, the fifth-tallest waterfall on the planet, located?

q.e: Yumbilla Falls in the Amazonas region of Peru is about 896 m high, among the tallest in the world.

q: Where is the third-tallest waterfall on the planet, Ramnefjellsfossen, located?

q.e: Ramnefjellsfossen in Norway (818 m) is among the tallest waterfalls in the world, in Jostedalsbreen National Park.

q: What does the name of the Iguazu Falls, located in South America, mean in English?

q.e: "Iguazú" comes from Guaraní words "y" (water) and "guasu" (big). The falls are on the Argentina-Brazil border.

q: In what country is Gocta Waterfall located?

q.e: The Gocta Cataracts in the Amazonas region of Peru are 771 m high. They were publicized to the world only in 2006.

q: What is the name of the highest waterfall in North America?

q.e: James Bruce Falls, in British Columbia, Canada, is often cited as the tallest waterfall in North America, at 840 m.

q: In which U.S. state is the Multnomah Falls located?

q.e: Multnomah Falls, in the Columbia River Gorge in Oregon, is 189 m (620 ft) high and the state's tallest waterfall.

q: In what Asian country is the Mount Unzen volcanic group located?

q.e: Mount Unzen is a volcanic complex on Kyushu, Japan. A 1991 eruption killed 43 people, including volcanologists Maurice and Katia Krafft.

q: The Santorini volcanic islands are part of what European country?

q.e: Santorini is a volcanic island group located in the southern Aegean Sea, roughly 200 kilometers southeast of mainland Greece.

q: What is the name of the dangerous active volcano located in the Western Highlands of Guatemala?

q.e: Santa María, a stratovolcano near Quetzaltenango, Guatemala, erupted violently in 1902. Its Santiaguito dome is still active.

q: Who is the 16th president of the United States?

q.e: Abraham Lincoln served as the 16th U.S. president from March 1861 until his assassination in April 1865, leading the nation through the American Civil War.

q: The city of Saint Louis, nicknamed Gateway to the West, is located in which state?

q.e: Saint Louis is located on the eastern border of Missouri along the Mississippi River, marked by the 630-foot (192-meter) Gateway Arch built to honor westward expansion.

q: What is the capital of Illinois, the 21st US State?

q.e: Springfield is the capital of Illinois, Lincoln's home. Illinois became the 21st state in 1818.

q: Which one of these countries is largest in area?
Jordan and Japan are equal in size

q.e: Japan (378,000 km²) is bigger than countries such as Italy and Germany, but smaller than many others.

q: Which of the following oceans is the worlds largest?

q.e: The Pacific Ocean is the largest, covering about 165 million km², nearly a third of Earth.

q: Which of the following countries is the worlds smallest continent, and can also be considered an island since it is surrounded by water?

q.e: Australia is the smallest of the seven continents, and is surrounded by water (though also called an island continent).

q: Where was the late medieval kingdom of Aragon situated?
Eastern Spain, major islands on the Mediterranean Sea and southern Italy

q.e: The Crown of Aragon covered eastern Spain (Aragon, Catalonia, Valencia), the Balearic Islands, Sicily, Sardinia and southern Italy.

q: Where were the Boer Republics located?
They were early Puritan settlements in the eastern North America

q.e: The Boer Republics (Transvaal and the Orange Free State) were in what is now South Africa. Britain annexed them after the Boer War (1899-1902).

q: Finish this Irish saying: A tune is more lasting than the song of birds. And a word is more lasting than ________.

q.e: The Irish proverb says, "A tune is more lasting than the song of birds, and a word more lasting than the wealth of the world."

q: What is the missing word in this Irish saying: Every dog is _____ at his own house door.?

q.e: An Irish proverb says "Every dog is bold at his own door."

q: Complete this Irish saying: The whole world cannot make a ________ out of a donkey.

q.e: An Irish saying: "The whole world cannot make a racehorse out of a donkey."

q: Finish the following Irish saying: However long the day it ends with _______.

q.e: An Irish proverb says "However long the day, the evening will come".

q: Complete this Irish saying: Dont let your ______ cut your throat.

q.e: "Don't let your tongue cut your throat" is an Irish proverb warning against careless speech.

q: What is the missing word in this Irish saying: ______ is the poor mans doctor.?

q.e: "Death is the poor man's doctor" is an Irish proverb, meaning death ends suffering.

q: Complete the following Irish saying: If you want ______, always carry the back tooth of a horse with you.
to be the life of the party

q.e: An Irish superstition says "If you want money, always carry the back tooth of a horse." It is an old folk saying.

q: Finish this Irish saying: If someone is sick turn his bed so that it faces _________.

q.e: An Irish folk belief says a sick person's bed should be turned to face north. This is folklore, not medicine.

q: Finish this Irish saying: Often has the likely failed and the unlikely _________.
wrote a novel about the failure

q.e: The Irish proverb "Often has the likely failed and the unlikely succeeded" reminds us that outcomes are unpredictable.

q: What is the capital and largest city of Jamaica?

q.e: Kingston is Jamaica's capital and largest city, on the island's southeast coast.

q: What is the name of the capital city of India?

q.e: New Delhi, within the Delhi metropolitan area, is the capital of India. It was inaugurated as the capital in 1931.

q: Addis Ababa is the capital of what country?

q.e: Addis Ababa was founded in 1886 by Emperor Menelik II and serves as both the capital of Ethiopia and the headquarters of the African Union.

q: Kathmandu is the capital city of what country?

q.e: Kathmandu is the capital and largest metropolis of Nepal, situated in the Kathmandu Valley at an elevation of roughly 4,600 feet (1,400 meters).

q: Which U.S. state has been nicknamed The Silver State?

q.e: Nevada is the "Silver State," because of the Comstock Lode silver discovery in 1859.

q: Albuquerque is the largest city of which U.S. state?

q.e: Albuquerque is New Mexico's largest city, though Santa Fe is the capital.

q: What does the name of the U.S. state of Texas literally mean in Caddo?

q.e: "Texas" comes from the Caddo word táysha or teychas, meaning "friends" or "allies."

q: The first recorded Euroregion, Gronau, was founded in 1958. What countries established it?

q.e: The first Euroregion, EUREGIO, was set up in 1958 at Gronau on the German-Dutch border to encourage cooperation.

q: Which country is not a member of the Adriatic Euroregion?

q.e: The Adriatic Euroregion was set up in 2006 with members from Italy, Croatia, Slovenia, Albania, Bosnia and Montenegro. Serbia isn't a member.

q: Where would you find the Tornio River Valley Euroregion?

q.e: The Tornio River Valley (Tornedalen) Euroregion links Swedish and Finnish areas along the border river, the Torne.

q: The Cross Channel Euroregion includes France, the UK and what other country?

q.e: The Cross-Channel Euroregion (Transmanche) covers northern France, Kent in the UK and Belgium.

q: The TriRhena Euroregion is spans these three countries crossed by the Rhine River.

q.e: TriRhena links Alsace (France), Baden (Germany) and northwest Switzerland around Basel, along the Upper Rhine.

q: The Pyrenees-Mediterranean region is located along the border of which two countries?

q.e: The Pyrenees-Mediterranean Euroregion links Catalonia, the Balearic Islands, Languedoc-Roussillon and the Midi-Pyrénées of France and Spain.

q: Where would you find the Ore Mountains Euroregion?

q.e: The Ore Mountains (Erzgebirge) Euroregion is on the German-Czech border, in Saxony and northern Bohemia.

q: What U.S. interstate runs east and west through Colorado?

q.e: Interstate 70 runs east-west across Colorado, through Denver and over the Eisenhower Tunnel.

q: What does the word Colorado mean?

q.e: The name Colorado comes from Spanish, meaning colored red or ruddy, which Spanish explorers originally used to describe the silt-laden red waters of the Colorado River.

q: What city in Colorado is known as the Richest Square Mile on Earth?

q.e: Central City, Colorado, was dubbed "the richest square mile on earth" during the 1859 gold rush.

q: What city boasts the most parks in the US?

q.e: Denver has one of the largest city park systems in the US, with 200+ parks and a mountain parks network.

q: What legendary American frontiersman commanded a major fort in Colorado?

q.e: Kit Carson, a frontiersman, commanded Fort Garland in southern Colorado in 1866-67. He was also a guide and Indian agent.

q: On which continent is the famous active volcano Mount Nyiragongo located?

q.e: Mount Nyiragongo, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, holds one of the world's largest lava lakes. It erupted in 2002 and 2021.

q: On which of the islands of Papua New Guinea is the active volcano Ulawun located?

q.e: Ulawun is on New Britain, an island of Papua New Guinea, and is one of the country's most active volcanoes.

q: The Arabic name of Mount Etna, the second-largest active volcano in Europe, was Jebel Utlamat. What does this mean in English?

q.e: Etna's name may come from the Greek "aitho" (I burn). Its Arabic name Jebel Utlamat means "mountain of fire."

q: In what country is the active volcano Sakurajima located?

q.e: Sakurajima, near Kagoshima, Kyushu, Japan, erupts frequently, covering the city in ash.

q: What does the Indonesian name of the Mount Merapi volcano, Gunung Merapi, mean in English?

q.e: "Merapi" means "mountain of fire" in Javanese/Indonesian. It's the most active volcano in Indonesia, near Yogyakarta.

q: In what country is the active volcano Koryaksky located?

q.e: Koryaksky is an active stratovolcano near Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky on the Kamchatka Peninsula, in Russia.

q: In what US state is the Fourpeaked Volcano, also known as Fourpeaked Mountain, situated?

q.e: Fourpeaked Mountain is a volcano on the Alaska Peninsula that erupted in 2006.

q: Which of these European countries shares a land border with Sweden?

q.e: Sweden borders Norway (west) and Finland (northeast). It's connected to Denmark by a bridge.

q: What are the colors of the national flag of Sweden?

q.e: Sweden's national flag features a yellow Nordic cross extending to the edges on a field of blue, inspired by the Swedish coat of arms and in use since the 16th century.

q: What is the official language spoken by the citizens of Sweden?

q.e: Swedish is Sweden's official language. Five minority languages, such as Finnish and Sami, are also recognized.

q: What is the name of the largest city and capital of Sweden?

q.e: Stockholm is Sweden's capital and largest city, spread across 14 islands connected by more than 50 bridges. Gothenburg is Sweden's second-largest city, while Helsinki and Oslo are the capitals of Finland and Norway.

q: What type of food is the popular Swedish dish called Surstromming?

q.e: Surströmming is fermented Baltic herring, known for its strong smell. It's a traditional northern Swedish food.

q: What song is used as a de facto anthem of Sweden?

q.e: "Du gamla, Du fria" ("Thou ancient, thou free") is the de facto national anthem of Sweden, though not official.

q: What are the colors of the national flag of the Federative Republic of Brazil?

q.e: Brazil's flag is green with a yellow rhombus and a blue globe with a white banner. The colors are green, yellow, blue and white.

q: What is the official language of the Federative Republic of Brazil?

q.e: Portuguese is Brazil's official language, the largest Portuguese-speaking nation.

q: What is the most popular sport among the people living in Brazil?

q.e: Football (soccer) is by far Brazil's most popular sport, and the country has won five World Cups (1958-2002).

q: What is the national motto of the Federative Republic of Brazil, also featured in the national flag of the country?

q.e: "Ordem e Progresso" (Order and Progress) is on Brazil's flag, from Auguste Comte's positivism.

q: On what day of the week does the parade of the famous Rio Carnival traditionally start?

q.e: Rio's Carnival begins on the Friday before Ash Wednesday, but the main Sambadrome parades are Sunday and Monday nights.

q: Whisky is traditional for this country. The beverages color can give you a hint about its age.

q.e: Scotch whisky ages in oak casks. The color deepens with age and with cask type.

q: Vodka is traditional for this country. People there like to flavor vodka with lemon peel, pepper or herbs.

q.e: Vodka has been produced in Russia since at least the late 14th century, with traditional flavored varieties known as 'nastoiki' infused with ingredients like pepper (pertsóvka) or herbs.

q: Pastis is the most popular aperitif in this country. It is made with anise, licorice and additional aromatic plants.

q.e: Pastis is a French anise-flavored aperitif, drunk with water. Pernod and Ricard are two famous brands.

q: Caipirinha takes lime, caster sugar, and Cachaca, or Rum to chill out the citizens of this country.

q.e: Caipirinha is Brazil's national cocktail, made with cachaça (sugarcane spirit), lime and sugar.

q: Bratwurst is often consumed in this country. They are sausages made of pork and veal and seasoned with ginger, nutmeg, and coriander or caraway.

q.e: Bratwurst is a classic German sausage with regional varieties dating back centuries, with the earliest known documented mention in Thuringia in 1404.

q: Feijohada has been consumed for centuries in this country. It is a stew made of black beans and pork.

q.e: Feijoada is Brazil's national dish, a black bean stew with pork, usually served with rice, orange and farofa.

q: Tzatziki is a typical dip of this country. It is made with yogurt, olive oil, cucumbers and onions.

q.e: Tzatziki is a classic Greek salted strained yogurt dip typically flavored with grated cucumber, garlic, olive oil, and herbs such as dill or mint.

q: In which country does the typical breakfast consist of Caffè e latte and a pastry?

q.e: Italians usually have breakfast of caffè e latte (or cappuccino) and a pastry such as a cornetto.

q: Sesame is an annual plant , whose closest relatives originated in which continent?

q.e: Sesame's wild relatives are mainly found in Africa, although the cultivated crop may have originated in India. Sesame is among the oldest oilseed crops.

q: The European company Diesel, producing jeans and other clothing, was founded in which country?

q.e: Diesel, the jeans and fashion brand, was founded in 1978 by Renzo Rosso in Molvena, Italy.

q: In 1970, Elio Fiorucci showed designer jeans for the first time in which city?

q.e: Elio Fiorucci opened his Milan shop in 1967 and presented designer jeans in the 1970s, helping make denim fashionable.

q: The French fries are believed to have been invented in what country?

q.e: Belgian lore traces fried potatoes back to the late 1600s in the Meuse Valley, where locals supposedly fried potatoes when frozen rivers prevented fishing. American soldiers reportedly dubbed them French fries during World War I because the Belgian army spoke French.

q: Fry up is another name for the traditional breakfast of what country?

q.e: A "fry-up" is the traditional English breakfast: bacon, eggs, sausages, tomatoes, beans and toast. The "full English" is another name.

q: A Matryoshka is a wooden nested doll, whose name is derived from the female first name Matryona, which was popular among peasants in this country.

q.e: The first Russian nesting dolls were carved in 1890 by Vasily Zvyozdochkin in Abramtsevo, Russia. Matryona comes from the Latin root mater, meaning mother.

q: The carrot is thought to have originated from this country.

q.e: Carrots were first domesticated in Persia/Afghanistan around 1,000 years ago, and were originally purple or yellow. The orange carrot came later from the Netherlands.

q: Which country had the highest production of carrots in 2005?

q.e: China is by far the world's biggest carrot producer, with about 40% of the global total.

q: Absinthe was most popular in this country as it was the common beverage among artists and writers in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

q.e: Absinthe, the "Green Fairy," was hugely popular with Parisian artists like Van Gogh and Toulouse-Lautrec. France banned it in 1915.

q: In which U.S. city is the Blackjack Hall of Fame located?

q.e: The Blackjack Hall of Fame is at the Barona Resort & Casino in Lakeside, near San Diego, California.

q: The mall in this city has its own 400-meter ski slope.

q.e: Ski Dubai opened in 2005 inside the Mall of the Emirates, featuring an indoor ski mountain kept below freezing despite the desert climate outside.

q: In what Asian country did the Gado-gado salad originate?

q.e: Gado-gado is an Indonesian salad of vegetables with peanut sauce. The name means "mix-mix".

q: In what country did the popular Caesar salad originate?

q.e: The Caesar salad was invented in 1924 by Italian-American restaurateur Caesar Cardini at his restaurant in Tijuana, Mexico. He improvised the dish during a busy Fourth of July rush using leftover kitchen ingredients.

q: The Chonmage is a mans hairstyle traditional for this country.

q.e: The chonmage is a traditional Japanese topknot hairstyle once worn by samurai, and still worn by sumo wrestlers.

q: What continent did tomatoes originate from?

q.e: The tomato originated in western South America (the Andes) and was domesticated in Mexico. Spanish explorers took it to Europe.

q: What country was the largest producer of tomatoes in the world in 2008?

q.e: China is the world's largest tomato producer, growing roughly a third of the global crop.

q: Broccoli originated in this country about 2000 years ago.

q.e: Broccoli was developed in Italy from wild cabbage, perhaps by the Etruscans or Romans. The name is Italian for "little sprouts."

q: In what European country did the first modern perfume originate in 1370?

q.e: The first modern alcohol-based perfume, "Hungary Water," was made for Queen Elizabeth of Hungary around 1370.

q: Which of these cities is known as the Milk Capital of the World?

q.e: Harvard, Illinois, calls itself the "Milk Capital of the World" and holds Harvard Milk Days. It had a Borden condensed-milk plant.

q: In what country did the hat called ushanka originate?

q.e: The ushanka is a Russian fur hat with ear flaps, from "ukho" (ear). It's used across northern Europe and Asia.

q: What country did the Goulash soup originally come from?

q.e: Goulash originated as a meat stew cooked by 9th-century Hungarian cattle herders, known as gulyas. Paprika, which gives modern goulash its signature red color and flavor, was added centuries later in the 1700s.

q: Ajiaco is a popular soup that originated in this Latin American country.

q.e: Ajiaco is a chicken and potato soup from Bogotá, Colombia. It uses guascas, a local herb.

q: To what continent is the poisonous mushroom known as death cap indigenous?

q.e: The death cap (Amanita phalloides) is native to Europe, and now grows elsewhere. It causes most fatal mushroom poisonings worldwide.

q: What EU country first discovered the therapeutic powers of yogurt?

q.e: Yogurt is thought to have started in Central Asia or the Balkans with Turkic nomads. French king Francis I reputedly was cured with yogurt, thanks to the Ottoman sultan.

q: In what country is the yogurt Zabady produced?

q.e: Zabady is Egypt's word for yogurt, made in Egyptian dairies. In Arabic "zabadi" refers to yogurt.

q: In what country was the Garden strawberry first bred in 1740?

q.e: The modern garden strawberry came about in Brittany, France, around 1740, from a cross between a North American and a Chilean species.

q: What country is the largest producer of strawberries in the world?

q.e: The US was the biggest strawberry grower in the mid-2000s, mostly in California. China is now the largest.

q: On what continent is the watermelon plant believed to have originated?

q.e: Watermelon originated in Africa, likely the Kalahari region, and was cultivated in ancient Egypt about 4,000 years ago.

q: What country is the largest producer of strawberries in the world according to 2007 data?

q.e: In 2007 the US was the top strawberry producer. China overtook it afterward.

q: The traditional Arab cookies, called Kleicha, are considered the national cookies of this Arab country.

q.e: Kleicha is a date-filled cookie that is Iraq's national cookie, eaten at Eid.

q: The popular number placement puzzle Sudoku was invented in 1979 in which country?

q.e: The modern Sudoku was created by Howard Garns in the US in 1979 as "Number Place." It was named and popularized in Japan in the 1980s.

q: This country has the most full sized breweries:

q.e: Germany has long had the most breweries of any country, about 1,500 (and the US has overtaken it in total craft breweries).

q: In which country was coffee first roasted and brewed?

q.e: Coffee was first discovered in Ethiopia, where the legend of the goat herder Kaldi comes from. The first brewing was in Yemen's Sufi monasteries.

q: What city in the state of Oregon is known as The City of Roses?

q.e: Portland, Oregon, is "The City of Roses." The Portland Rose Festival has been held since 1907.

q: The peach tree belongs to the Prunus genus which is indigenous to this country.

q.e: The peach (Prunus persica) is native to northwest China and was cultivated there for thousands of years. The Latin name "persica" comes from Persia, an error.

q: A cuero is a mythical giant octopus of which continent?

q.e: The Cuero (Cuera) is a monster from Chilean and Argentine folklore, a giant octopus-like creature in lakes and rivers.

q: Which of these languages is not an official national language in a South American country?

q.e: Spanish, Portuguese, Dutch, French and English are official in South America. German isn't an official national language there.

q: It is estimated that this country has more English speakers than the United States.

q.e: China is estimated to have more English speakers than the US, with several hundred million learners. This counts those with limited ability.

q: In which country should you be careful with any objects labelled gift (when the word is used as a noun)?

q.e: "Gift" in German means "poison." The English word for a present is "Geschenk."

q: What is the country with the greatest number of official languages?

q.e: Zimbabwe has 16 official languages, more than any other country, and Bolivia has 37 official indigenous languages. India has 22 scheduled and 2 official national languages.
Yoga originated in ancient India more than 4,000 years ago, with its earliest written mentions found in the Rigveda and later systematized in Patanjali's Yoga Sutras.

q: The Afrikaans language is one of the official languages in this African country.

q.e: Afrikaans is one of the 12 official languages recognized in South Africa. Although it is also widely spoken across neighboring Namibia, it holds recognized regional language status there rather than official status.

q: On what continent is the Ga language spoken?

q.e: Ga is spoken by the Ga people of Accra, in Ghana, West Africa.

q: The Greek language has an official status on this Mediterranean island.

q.e: Greek is an official language of Cyprus, alongside Turkish. It's also official in Greece.

q: The Igbo language is one of the official languages in this African country.

q.e: Igbo is one of Nigeria's major languages, spoken mainly in the southeast. English is the country's official language.

q: The first legends about werewolves originated on this continent.

q.e: Werewolf legends originate in Europe, with ancient Greek (Lycaon) and Norse stories.

q: In what country is the Slavey language spoken?

q.e: Slavey is a Dene (Athabaskan) language spoken in northwestern Canada, in the Northwest Territories and nearby provinces.

q: On what continent is the Urdu language spoken?

q.e: Urdu is mainly spoken in Pakistan and India, in Asia. It's Pakistan's national language.

q: In what country did the Cha-cha-cha dance originate?

q.e: The Cha-cha-cha was created in the early 1950s by Cuban composer and violinist Enrique Jorrin. It evolved from the danzon-mambo and quickly became an internationally popular ballroom dance.

q: Which country is called Tyskland, Niemcy or Allemagne by some of its neighbors?

q.e: Germany is called Tyskland in Danish/Norwegian/Swedish, Niemcy in Polish and Allemagne in French.

q: The people of which Balkan country do not use a Cyrillic alphabet?

q.e: Greece uses the Greek alphabet. Serbian, Bulgarian and Macedonian use Cyrillic (Serbian uses both).

q: Esperanto is the official language of which country?
It is not a language of any country.

q.e: Esperanto, created by L. L. Zamenhof in 1887, isn't the official language of any country.

q: In which country is Flemish mostly spoken?

q.e: Flemish is the local variety of Dutch spoken in Flanders, the northern region of Belgium. Dutch is one of Belgium's three official languages, alongside French and German.

q: Sik Jo Fan Mei means have you eaten yet?. In which country it is used as a greeting?

q.e: "Sik jo fan mei?" is a Cantonese greeting meaning "Have you eaten yet?", used in Hong Kong and southern China.

q: Venetic is an extinct language from the Indo-European family that was spoken in what country?

q.e: Venetic was an Indo-European language spoken in northeast Italy (the Veneto) before the Roman era, and written in the Etruscan-derived alphabet.

q: What do you get when you cross the Atlantic Ocean with the Titanic?

q.e: It's a joke: "half-way" means you've gone halfway across the ocean, or the Titanic sank. Answer is "halfway."

q: On January 23 2012, the European Union adopted an oil embargo against this country.

q.e: On 23 January 2012 the EU imposed an oil embargo on Iran over its nuclear program, from 1 July.

q: What country launched operation Pillar of Defense on 14 November 2012?

q.e: Israel launched Operation Pillar of Defense on 14 November 2012 with the killing of Hamas commander Ahmed Jabari. An eight-day conflict followed.

q: The original Ferris Wheel was created for the 1893 Worlds Columbian Exposition, held in this city.

q.e: Engineered by George Washington Gale Ferris Jr. to rival the Eiffel Tower from the 1889 Paris Exposition, the wheel stood roughly 264 feet (80 meters) tall. It could carry over 2,000 passengers across its 36 spacious wooden cars.

q: Sachertorte, a specific type of chocolate cake, was invented by chance in this European city.

q.e: Sixteen-year-old apprentice Franz Sacher created the dense chocolate cake with apricot jam filling in Vienna in 1832 for Prince Klemens von Metternich. It became a famous culinary symbol of Austria, celebrated at the Hotel Sacher.

q: Angola won its independence in 1975, from what country?

q.e: Angola declared independence from Portugal on 11 November 1975, after a long colonial war and the Carnation Revolution.

q: The mixture of shaved ice and evaporated milk, known as Halo-halo, originated in this country.

q.e: Halo-halo ("mix-mix") is a Filipino dessert of shaved ice, evaporated milk, beans, fruit and ice cream.

q: What country began working on developing an atomic weapon before the United States and eventually joined with the US in its development?

q.e: Britain's "Tube Alloys" project began in 1940, before the US program, and merged with the Manhattan Project in 1943.

q: What is Ray Bradburys home city of Waukegan called in some of his novels?

q.e: Ray Bradbury, from Waukegan, Illinois, called it "Green Town" in Dandelion Wine and Something Wicked This Way Comes.

q: In what country is Carré Otiss character, Emily, when she awakens in her room and finds a bouquet of wild orchids?

q.e: In Wild Orchid (1989), Emily (Carré Otis) is working in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, during Carnival. The film was famous for its erotic content.

q: On January 24, 2011 an international airport in this European capital became the focus of a suicide bomber attack.

q.e: On 24 January 2011, a suicide bomber attacked Domodedovo Airport in Moscow, killing 37 people.

q: On March 11, 2011, a 9.1-magnitude earthquake and subsequent tsunami hit this country, killing 15,822 and leaving another 3,926 missing.

q.e: The Great East Japan Earthquake struck off the northeast coast of Honshu, triggering devastating tsunami waves that reached heights over 130 feet (40 m) and causing the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear disaster.

q: The capture of this city in the Mexican–American War was the final American victory that caused the Mexicans to surrender.

q.e: The US capture of Mexico City in September 1847 under Winfield Scott led to the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848).

q: The Beckoning Cat, also known as Welcoming Cat, is a common sculpture which originated in this country.

q.e: The beckoning cat figurine, known as maneki-neko, originated in Japan during the late Edo period and is traditionally believed to bring good fortune and customers to businesses.

q: In this country paan is a custom practised after dinner.

q.e: Paan is a betel leaf chew with areca nut and spices, eaten after meals in India. It aids digestion and freshens breath.

q: On what continent did anatomically modern humans evolve?

q.e: Fossil and genetic evidence shows that Homo sapiens evolved in Africa roughly 300,000 years ago, with the earliest known remains discovered at Jebel Irhoud in Morocco.

q: What current day continent was once part of Laurentia?

q.e: Laurentia was the ancient continent that formed the core of North America (and parts of Greenland and Scotland).

q: An extreme example of a fire whirl occurred in 1923 in this country.

q.e: The 1923 Great Kantō earthquake in Japan caused a firestorm in Tokyo. A fire whirl at the Hifukusho Atokyo killed ~38,000 in minutes.

q: Julius and Ethel Rosenberg were American Communists spying for this country.

q.e: The Rosenbergs were convicted of passing atomic secrets to the Soviet Union. They were executed in 1953.

q: Elizabeth Rosemond Taylor was born in 1932 in a wealthy district of this city.

q.e: Elizabeth Taylor was born on 27 February 1932 in Hampstead, London, to American parents.

q: What country conducted nuclear tests in 2006 and 2009, triggering widespread international condemnation?

q.e: North Korea tested nuclear devices in October 2006 and May 2009 (and again in 2013, 2016 and 2017), prompting UN sanctions.

q: In which of the following movies does the ancient city of Petra not appear?
Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade
Sinbad and the Eye of the Tiger

q.e: Petra appears in Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade (1989) and Transformers: Revenge of the Fallen. GoldenEye (1995) was not filmed there.

q: In what country was the Bilderberg conference first held?

q.e: The first Bilderberg meeting was held in May 1954 at the Hotel de Bilderberg in Oosterbeek, the Netherlands.

q: What country won the most gold medals at the 2010 Winter Olympics, held in Vancouver, Canada?

q.e: Canada won 14 gold medals at the 2010 Vancouver Winter Olympics, a record for most golds by a host nation at a Winter Games at that time.

q: Billy Wilder was born in what is now the territory of this country

q.e: Billy Wilder was born in Sucha, in Austria-Hungary, now Sucha Beskidzka, Poland.

q: What country does King Lear rule according to Shakespeares famous tragedy?

q.e: In Shakespeare's King Lear, the title character is the king of Britain, who divides his kingdom among his daughters.

q: In what country was Twiggy born?

q.e: Twiggy (Lesley Hornby), the 1960s supermodel, was born in London, England, in 1949.

q: Confucius was a thinker and social philosopher from this country.

q.e: Confucius lived during China's Spring and Autumn period (roughly 551–479 BC) in the State of Lu, modern-day Shandong province. His philosophical teachings became the foundation of Confucianism.

q: In what city did fictional character Paladin live?

q.e: Paladin, the gunfighter in Have Gun - Will Travel, lived at the Hotel Carlton in San Francisco.

q: What country awarded Gene Kelly the Legion of Honor in 1960?

q.e: Gene Kelly received the French Legion of Honor in 1960, due to his role in An American in Paris and his Paris ballet work.

q: In 2000, Bill Clinton became the first US President to visit this country.

q.e: Bill Clinton visited Vietnam in November 2000, the first US president to do so since the war ended.

q: David Livingstone is famous for exploring this continent.

q.e: Dr. David Livingstone was a Scottish missionary and explorer who mapped vast areas of central and southern Africa. In 1855, he became the first European to view Mosi-oa-Tunya, which he renamed Victoria Falls.

q: In what country was action star Bruce Lee born?

q.e: Bruce Lee was born in San Francisco in 1940 and grew up in Hong Kong.

q: The Pearl Islands are located near the coast of this country.

q.e: The Pearl Islands (Archipiélago de las Perlas) are in the Gulf of Panama. Survivor has filmed there.

q: In which U.S. state is the city called Pearl located?

q.e: Pearl is a city in Mississippi, near Jackson. Pearl River is nearby.

q: What is the name of the capital city of the U.S. state of South Dakota?

q.e: Pierre is South Dakota's capital. It's one of the smallest state capitals.

q: In what country were diamonds mined for the first time in human history?

q.e: India is believed to be the first source of diamonds, mined from about 4th century BC in the Golconda region. Brazil took over in the 18th century.

q: From what country did Winona Ryders grandparents emigrate to the United States?

q.e: Winona Ryder's grandparents were Russian-Jewish immigrants. Her birth name is Winona Laura Horowitz.

q: Which New York City borough is the largest in area?

q.e: Queens is the largest of the five boroughs by area, at about 109 square miles.

q: When was the territory of modern New York City first discovered by an European explorer?

q.e: Giovanni da Verrazzano sailed into New York harbor in 1524, the first European known to see the area.

q: In what country did Alicia Silverstone live before moving to the United States before she was born?

q.e: Alicia Silverstone's parents were British and moved to the US before she was born in 1976.

q: In which of these U.S. states is there a town called Iron City?

q.e: Iron City is a small town in Lawrence County, Tennessee. There are also towns with this name in Georgia.

q: In which river are the famous Thousand Islands located?

q.e: The Thousand Islands archipelago consists of 1,864 islands straddling the Canada-US border along the upper St. Lawrence River, as it flows out from Lake Ontario.

q: In what Italian city does the famous Uffizi Gallery located?

q.e: The Uffizi Gallery is in Florence, Italy. It has works by Botticelli, Leonardo and Michelangelo.

q: On what continent is the Great Sandy Desert located?

q.e: The Great Sandy Desert is in Western Australia, one of the country's biggest deserts.

q: In which city did Sandra Bullock open a restaurant in 2006?

q.e: Sandra Bullock opened Walton's Fancy and Staple, a restaurant-bakery, in Austin, Texas, in 2006.

q: Empress Alexandra Fyodorovna was from which country?

q.e: Alexandra Feodorovna, wife of Nicholas II, was born Princess Alix of Hesse and by Rhine in Germany. She was Queen Victoria's granddaughter.

q: Angela Merkel, a trained scientist, is the first woman to become Chancellor of this country.

q.e: Angela Merkel holds a doctorate in quantum chemistry and served as Chancellor of Germany from 2005 to 2021, leading the country for 16 years.

q: New Orleans is a city in southern US. Where is Orleans located?

q.e: New Orleans was founded in 1718 by French colonists and named in honor of Philippe II, Duke of Orléans, who served as Regent of France. The original city of Orléans is located on the Loire River southwest of Paris.

q: Which king of Israel captured Jerusalem and made it the capital of his kingdom?

q.e: King David captured Jerusalem from the Jebusites around 1000 BC and made it his capital ("City of David").

q: In 1953 Malcolm X went to what city to study to become a minister?

q.e: In 1953 Malcolm X moved to Chicago, where he studied at Elijah Muhammad's Temple. He became a minister in the Nation of Islam.

q: In what country was the vacuum cleaner created in the 19th century?

q.e: The first vacuum cleaners were invented in the US in the 19th century, with Daniel Hess's carpet sweeper (1860) and Ives McGaffey's "Whirlwind" (1869).

q: The graphite pencil in its early form was created in this country.

q.e: Graphite pencils started in Borrowdale, England, in the 1500s, after a graphite deposit was found there.

q: The prototype of the modern toothbrush was invented in this country.

q.e: The first bristle toothbrush was recorded in China in 1498, with hog hair set in bamboo or bone.

q: In 1972, Neil Armstrong was welcomed in this country where his ancestors were born.

q.e: In 1972, Neil Armstrong visited Langholm, Scotland, where his ancestors came from, and was named Freeman of the town.

q: Suzanne Mubarak was First Lady of this African country from 1981 until 2011.

q.e: Suzanne Mubarak was Egypt's First Lady for 30 years, while her husband Hosni Mubarak was president (1981-2011).

q: In what country was Isaac Newton born?

q.e: Sir Isaac Newton was born on Christmas Day 1642 in Woolsthorpe-by-Colsterworth, Lincolnshire, England. He spent much of his career at Trinity College, Cambridge, formulating the laws of motion and universal gravitation.

q: Pamela Anderson was born on July 1, 1967 in this country.

q.e: Pamela Anderson was born in Ladysmith, British Columbia, Canada, on 1 July 1967.

q: In which country was David Beckham born on May 2, 1975?

q.e: David Beckham was born in Leytonstone, London, England, on 2 May 1975.

q: What city do Doug and Carrie Heffernan live in on the show The King of Queens ?

q.e: The King of Queens is set in Queens, New York City, where Doug and Carrie live.

q: Writer J. R. R. Tolkien was born on January 3, 1892 in which country?

q.e: J. R. R. Tolkien was born in Bloemfontein, South Africa, on 3 January 1892, and moved to England at age three.

q: This US state is famous for Lake Okeechobee, the fourth largest lake completely within the United States.

q.e: Lake Okeechobee in Florida is the largest freshwater lake in the state and the 10th largest in the US by area (the question's ranking is another way of counting).

q: In which direction does the Nile river flow?

q.e: The Nile is one of the world's most famous north-flowing rivers, rising from headwaters near Lake Victoria in East Africa and emptying northward into the Mediterranean Sea through Egypt.

q: In which city was Whoopi Goldberg born?

q.e: Whoopi Goldberg was born Caryn Johnson in Manhattan, New York City, in 1955.

q: Which country was not part of the Tripartite Pact signed on 27 September 1940?

q.e: The Tripartite Pact (27 September 1940) was between Germany, Italy and Japan, with Hungary, Romania and Bulgaria joining. China was an Allied nation.
Fifth Avenue is the dividing line between Manhattan's East and West sides, where east-west street addresses start.

q: Which is the worlds third most populous country?

q.e: The US has the third-largest population, after India and China, with about 335 million people.

q: Which country tops the world in plastic surgery procedures?

q.e: The US ranks first in plastic surgery procedures overall, followed by Brazil, according to ISAPS surveys.

q: Operation Barbarossa was the largest invasion during World War II, whereby Germany attempted to occupy which country?

q.e: Operation Barbarossa (22 June 1941) was Germany's invasion of the Soviet Union, an attack on Russia and Ukraine and other republics.

q: The attack on Pearl Harbor, which took place in December 1941, was carried out by which Asian country?

q.e: Imperial Japan carried out the surprise strike on Pearl Harbor in Oahu, Hawaii, on December 7, 1941, prompting the United States to formally enter World War II.

q: Caledonii tradition comes from this country.

q.e: The Caledonii (Caledonians) were a Pictish tribe in what is now Scotland. "Caledonia" is the Roman name for Scotland.

q: The beginning of the Buddhist religion can be traced back to the fifth century BC in which country?

q.e: Siddhartha Gautama, who became the Buddha, lived and taught across ancient Magadha in northeastern India, attaining enlightenment under the Bodhi tree in Bodh Gaya.

q: What Biblical figure built an ark on top of a mountain?

q.e: Noah's ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat (in modern Turkey), according to Genesis.

q: It is considered that the Jewish Golden Age occurred in this country.

q.e: The Jewish Golden Age is dated to Muslim Spain (al-Andalus), roughly 900-1100, with scholars like Maimonides.

q: The Temple Mount, the Church of Holy Sepulchre and the Western Wall are landmarks found in this city.

q.e: All three sites are located within the walled Old City of Jerusalem, making it a sacred destination for Judaism, Christianity, and Islam.

q: To what kind of capital punishment was Joan of Arc condemned?

q.e: Joan of Arc was burned at the stake in Rouen on 30 May 1431 on charges of heresy. She was declared a saint in 1920.

q: In 1656 the first Jewish cemetery in the USA was founded in this city.

q.e: The first Jewish cemetery in North America was established in 1656 in New Amsterdam (New York City). The original burial ground was at Chatham Square.

q: He was a Christian saint from Egypt and a prominent leader among the Desert Fathers.

q.e: Anthony the Great (c. 251-356), an Egyptian monk, is the "Father of All Monks" and a leader of the Desert Fathers.

q: The largest lake in this state is Lake Okeechobee. The state is also home to one of the two naturally round lakes in the world.

q.e: Lake Okeechobee, Florida, is the biggest lake in the state. Florida has many round sinkhole lakes.

q: Francis Drake was 66 years old at his inauguration and the oldest governor of this state.

q.e: Francis Drake (1830-1903) was elected Governor of Iowa in 1896, aged 66.

q: What is the state capital of Oregon?

q.e: Salem is the capital of Oregon, in the Willamette Valley. Portland is the largest city.

q: What is the state capital of California?

q.e: Sacramento is California's capital, and is in the Central Valley.

q: What is the state capital of Nevada?

q.e: Carson City is the capital of Nevada, named after Kit Carson. Las Vegas is the largest city.

q: What is the state capital of Utah?

q.e: Salt Lake City was founded in 1847 by Mormon pioneers led by Brigham Young and became the capital of Utah Territory in the 1850s. It retained the title when Utah was admitted as the 45th U.S. state in 1896.

q: What is the state capital of Arizona?

q.e: Phoenix is the capital of Arizona and its largest city.

q: This country shares common boundaries with every South American country except Chile and Ecuador.

q.e: Covering roughly 3.3 million square miles (8.5 million square km), Brazil borders 10 of the other 12 nations in South America. Only Chile and Ecuador are geographically separated from it by other countries.

q: This country is home to the northernmost capital in mainland Europe?

q.e: Finland's capital Helsinki is the northernmost capital in mainland continental Europe (excluding Iceland's Reykjavik, which is on an island). It lies at about 60°N.

q: It is the sixth largest country and home of The Doctor breeze.

q.e: Australia is the sixth-largest country by area, at about 7.7 million km².

q: This country dominates the Aegian Sea and possesses an archipelago of about 2,000 islands.

q.e: Greece controls the vast majority of islands in the Aegean Sea, with Greek territory comprising several thousand islands and islets across archipelagos such as the Cyclades and Dodecanese.

q: The first American capital. It has a nick name coined by musicians - it means to play the big time.

q.e: New York was the first capital of the US (1789-90). The phrase "make it big in New York" comes from music and theater.

q: When broken down into kanji, the name of this capital city means "east" and "capital".

q.e: Tokyo is written with the kanji characters for east (to) and capital (kyo). The city was known as Edo until 1868, when Emperor Meiji moved the imperial seat there from Kyoto.

q: This city situated south of China is made up of 230 islands, Lantau Island being the largest.

q.e: Hong Kong has 260 islands according to some counts. Lantau Island is the largest, and the airport is built on a reclaimed area next to it.

q: This city is the only one located on two continents.

q.e: Istanbul straddles Europe and Asia across the Bosphorus. Some other cities, like Orenburg and Atyrau, also span both continents.

q: In the devilish year of 1666 a great fire occured in this European capital city. Half of it burned down.

q.e: The Great Fire of London (September 1666) destroyed about 13,000 houses and 87 churches, and killed relatively few people.

q: Which of these U.S. states is not a Four Corners state?

q.e: The Four Corners states are Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah. Wyoming isn't one of them.

q: The town of San Ysidro is located in what state, near what border?
California, near the border with Mexico.
Washington, near the border with Oregon
California, near the border with Arizona
Iowa, near the border with Missouri

q.e: San Ysidro is a neighborhood of San Diego, California, at the Mexican border crossing with Tijuana, the busiest land border crossing in the Western Hemisphere.

q: Mount Fuji is a nearly perfectly shaped volcano. It has been worshipped as a sacred mountain.

q.e: Mount Fuji is Japan's tallest peak (3,776 m) and an active volcano. It is a sacred mountain, a UNESCO site.

q: From forest to desert, the Grand Canyon has the most extreme nature climate.

q.e: The Grand Canyon in Arizona, USA, spans many ecological zones, from desert at the bottom to pine forest at the rim.

q: Through thousands of years in existence, Niagara Falls has been eroding at a rate of 4 feet (1.5 meters) per year.

q.e: Niagara Falls has retreated about 1 foot (0.3 m) per year recently, earlier it was about 3 feet. It sits on the Canada-US border.

q: The Great Barrier Reef consists of many colonies of corals. That is why it is sometimes referred to as the largest living animal in the world.

q.e: The Great Barrier Reef, off Queensland, Australia, is the world's biggest coral reef system, made of billions of tiny coral polyps.

q: The scientific name for the Northern Lights phenomenon is "Aurora Borealis. They are often mistaken for UFOs. Where do they happen?
In the northern part of our planet
In the southern part of our planet

q.e: The Aurora Borealis occurs in high-latitude regions of the Northern Hemisphere, caused by solar wind interacting with Earth's magnetosphere. Its southern counterpart is known as the Aurora Australis.

q: Nicknamed the Grand Canyon State, it entered the Union on Feb 14, 1912.

q.e: Arizona was admitted to the Union on Valentine's Day in 1912 as the 48th state, making it the last of the contiguous US states. Grand Canyon National Park was officially established there seven years later, in 1919.

q: This US state, nicknamed The Sunshine State, is famous with its beaches and theme parks.

q.e: Florida officially adopted The Sunshine State as its state nickname in 1970, reflecting its subtropical climate and major tourist attractions like Walt Disney World.

q: Nicknamed the Treasure State, this western US state is fourth largest in area.

q.e: Montana is nicknamed "The Treasure State" for its mineral wealth, and is the fourth-largest US state by area.

q: Nicknamed the Ocean State, it is the smallest US state.

q.e: Rhode Island is the "Ocean State" and the smallest state in the US, about 1,200 square miles.

q: Nicknamed The Buckeye State, it is the birthplace many former US presidents, including Ulysses S. Grant.

q.e: Ohio is the "Buckeye State" and the birthplace of seven presidents, including Grant, Hayes and Garfield.

q: Home on the Range is the state song of this US mid-western state, known as The Sunflower State.

q.e: "Home on the Range" is the state song of Kansas, "The Sunflower State."

q: This Bluegrass State hosts a famous horserace in Louisville, and is the birthplace of President Abraham Lincoln.

q.e: Kentucky's Churchill Downs in Louisville has hosted the Kentucky Derby annually since 1875. Abraham Lincoln was born in a one-room log cabin near Hodgenville, Kentucky, in 1809, though he later built his legal and political career in Illinois.

q: When I visited this lonely continent I was so moved by the spherical-sectioned shells of the opera house in this city.

q.e: The Sydney Opera House, with its sail-shaped shells, was designed by Jørn Utzon and opened in 1973. It's a UNESCO site.

q: Trenton is the capital of this eastern state.

q.e: Trenton is the capital of New Jersey, and the first Battle of Trenton was in 1776.

q: Juneau is the capital of this last frontier state.

q.e: Juneau is the capital of Alaska, "The Last Frontier," reachable only by air or sea.

q: Columbus discovered the Americas in 1492, and is rewarded with this midwestern state naming its capital after him.

q.e: Columbus, Ohio, is named after Christopher Columbus. It became the state capital in 1816.

q: Helena is this Rocky Mountain states capital.

q.e: Helena is the capital of Montana, founded during the gold rush in 1864.

q: Richmond is the capital of this state where many US presidents were born.

q.e: Richmond is the capital of Virginia, which is known as "Mother of Presidents" (8 presidents born there).

q: The capital of this diverse northwestern state is Salem.

q.e: Salem is the capital of Oregon, in the northwest.

q: This state, which houses one of the largest cities in the world, has Albany as its capital.

q.e: Albany is the capital of New York State, though New York City is the largest city.

q: Jefferson City serves as the capital of this Midwestern state.

q.e: Jefferson City is the capital of Missouri, on the Missouri River.

q: The capital of this southern state is also known as music city.

q.e: Nashville, Tennessee's capital, is called Music City because of country music's Grand Ole Opry.

q: Carson City is the capital of this Battle Born State.

q.e: Nevada is "The Battle Born State," because it was admitted in 1864 during the Civil War. Carson City is its capital.

q: Tallahassee is situated on the panhandle of this southern state and serves as its capital.

q.e: Tallahassee was designated the capital of the Florida Territory in 1824 because of its convenient midpoint location between the major settlements of Pensacola and St. Augustine.

q: Austin is the capital of this US state which once existed as an independent republic.

q.e: Austin is the capital of Texas, which was an independent republic from 1836 to 1845.

q: This northeast state has Augusta as its capital.

q.e: Augusta is the capital of Maine, on the Kennebec River.

q: This southern state has many beaches, an incredible fort from the revolutionary war, and Columbia as its capital.

q.e: South Carolina's capital is Columbia. Fort Moultrie in Charleston Harbor saw an important Revolutionary War victory in 1776.

q: This midwestern state has Madison as its capital.

q.e: Madison is the capital of Wisconsin, on an isthmus between Lakes Mendota and Monona.

q: This eastern state with rich history has Annapolis as its capital.

q.e: Annapolis has served as the capital of Maryland since 1694 and briefly served as the temporary capital of the United States from 1783 to 1784. Richmond is the capital of neighboring Virginia.

q: Springfield is the capital of this midwestern state.

q.e: Springfield became the capital of Illinois in 1837, largely through the lobbying efforts of local legislators including Abraham Lincoln. Kentucky's capital is Frankfort, Missouri's is Jefferson City, and Ohio's is Columbus.

q: In what century was the original version of the Seven Wonders of the World list created by Antipater of Sidon?

q.e: Antipater of Sidon, a Greek poet of the 2nd century BC, wrote the earliest known list of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

q: There is a vending machine for every 23 of the almost 130 million people that live in this country.

q.e: Japan has one of the highest densities of vending machines in the world, about one per 23 people (about 5 million).

q: This home to 144 million spans 11 time zones and its territory takes up 1/8th of the entire Earth surface.

q.e: Russia spans 11 time zones and about 17 million km². It has about 144 million people.

q: Islam, Christianity and Hinduism all coexist in this country of 160 million.

q.e: Pakistan has about 240 million people, mostly Muslim, with Christian and Hindu minorities. The question's 160 million is an older figure.

q: The first medical school, Ayurveda was founded in this populous country.

q.e: Ayurveda is India's ancient system of medicine. The ancient universities of Takshashila and Nalanda taught medicine.

q: This is the most populated country in the world - 1.3 billion people live there. The native language, Mandarin, is most widely spoken, with 885 million speakers.

q.e: China was the most populated country for centuries, with about 1.4 billion people, but India overtook it in 2023. Mandarin is spoken by nearly a billion people.

q: This American city used to be called El Pueblo de Nuestra Senora la Reina de (blank) de Porciuncula.

q.e: Founded in 1781 by Spanish settlers, the settlement's full original name was El Pueblo de Nuestra Señora la Reina de los Ángeles del Río Porciúncula.

q: The famous Forbidden City located in this Chinese city.

q.e: The Forbidden City served as the imperial palace for 24 emperors across the Ming and Qing dynasties from 1420 until 1924, and now operates as the Palace Museum in central Beijing.

q: This state, officially nicknamed The Golden State, is situated in the southern half of the west coast of the USA.

q.e: California officially adopted the moniker The Golden State in 1968, referencing both the 1848 California Gold Rush and its blooming golden poppies. Miami is a city in Florida, which holds the official nickname The Sunshine State.

q: Due to its natural beauty and relative wilderness, this Southern state is called The Natural State.

q.e: Arkansas is "The Natural State" for its forests, mountains and rivers.

q: This state, located in the mid-Atlantic region of the USA, has a capital called Trenton and is usually nicknamed The Garden State.

q.e: New Jersey is "The Garden State" and its capital is Trenton.

q: Nicknamed after the international park located in it, this state is often called The Peace Garden State.

q.e: North Dakota is the "Peace Garden State," named after the International Peace Garden on the Canadian border.

q: What is the real name of the Evergreen State, situated in the Pacific Northwest of the United States.

q.e: Washington was nicknamed the Evergreen State in the late 19th century by C.T. Conover due to its vast forests of firs, pines, and other conifers. The state officially adopted the nickname in 1953.

q: This small Mountain Sate is located in the region of Appalachia in the Eastern parts of the USA.

q.e: West Virginia, in Appalachia, is called the "Mountain State." It was created in 1863 during the Civil War.

q: This country, a victor in both World War I and World War II is the largest West European nation.

q.e: France is the largest country in Western Europe (about 640,000 km² with overseas territories, 550,000 in mainland Europe). It was an Allied victor in both world wars.

q: This powerful world empire of the 16th and 17th centuries borders Andorra, France, Gibraltar, Portugal and Morocco.

q.e: Spain was a 16th-17th-century world empire. It borders France, Portugal, Andorra, Morocco (at Ceuta/Melilla) and Gibraltar.

q: Which city, known as the City of Light, was originally called Lutetia in Latin?

q.e: The Romans founded Lutetia around the 1st century BC on the Île de la Cité and the banks of the Seine, eventually renaming it Paris after the local Celtic tribe, the Parisii.

q: What was the last state to join America?

q.e: Hawaii became the 50th U.S. state on August 21, 1959, just a few months after Alaska was admitted as the 49th state on January 3, 1959.

q: In 1776 America declared independence from what country?

q.e: The Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence on July 4, 1776, severing political ties with Great Britain and King George III.

q: Who was the first American on the moon?

q.e: Neil Armstrong was the commander of Apollo 11 and became the first human to step onto the lunar surface on July 20, 1969. Buzz Aldrin joined him on the surface about 19 minutes later, while Michael Collins remained in orbit.

q: What was the name of George Baileys fathers business in the movie "It's A Wonderful Life�?

q.e: In It's a Wonderful Life (1946), George Bailey's father ran the Bailey Building and Loan Association, a small savings and loan.

q: Lying near the equator, the Republic of Suriname is a country with a tropical climate, swampy coastal plains, broad savannas, and densely forested areas, located on what continent?

q.e: Suriname is on the northeastern coast of South America, between Guyana and French Guiana. It's the smallest independent country on the continent.

q: He likes it! Hey, Mikey!! was a popular phrase that advertised which product?

q.e: "He likes it! Hey Mikey!" was the famous 1972 Life cereal TV commercial, with the picky Mikey and his brothers.

q: Which city, founded in 1607, is the capital of New Mexico?

q.e: Santa Fe, the capital of New Mexico, was founded in 1607-1610 by the Spanish, and is the oldest state capital in the US.

q: Which city, located on the Cumberland River, is the capital of Tennessee?

q.e: Nashville, established on the Cumberland River in 1779, became the permanent capital of Tennessee in 1843. Atlanta and Richmond are also state capitals, but they serve Georgia and Virginia respectively.

q: This water basin contains the saltiest water on Earth. It is so salty, there is no life in it.

q.e: The Dead Sea, with about 34% salinity, is among the saltiest large bodies of water, although Antarctica's Don Juan Pond is saltier. Few organisms but some microbes live there.

q: At the end of How the Grinch Stole Christmas, how many times did the Grinchs heart grow?

q.e: In Dr. Seuss's 1957 holiday classic, the Whos' unbroken festive spirit prompts the famous line that the Grinch's small heart grew three sizes that day. This transformation allows him to return all the stolen toys and food to Whoville.

q: What does Frosty the Snowman, the character from an animated story produced by the Rankin-Bass company, say when he wakes up?

q.e: When Frosty is brought to life with a magic hat, he first says "Happy Birthday!" in the 1969 Rankin/Bass special.

q: From 1796 to 1806, Louisville, a city located on the Ogeechee River, was the capital of which state?

q.e: Louisville, Georgia, on the Ogeechee River, was the capital of Georgia from 1796 to 1806.

q: Vallejo, located in the Solano County, was the capital of which state in 1852 and 1853?

q.e: Vallejo served as California's capital briefly in 1852-53, before the capital moved to Benicia and then to Sacramento.

q: The city of Natchez, founded in 1716, was the capital of which state from 1817 to 1821?

q.e: Natchez was Mississippi's capital from 1817 to 1821, when Jackson became capital.

q: Wheeling was the capital of this state from 1863 to 1870 and again from 1875 to 1885.

q.e: Wheeling was West Virginia's capital from 1863-1870 and 1875-1885, then Charleston took over.

q: From 1819 to 1839, Vandalia, the county seat of Fayette County, was the capital of which state?

q.e: Vandalia was Illinois's second capital (1819-1839), before Springfield became the capital.

q: In 1862, during the American Civil War, Opelousas briefly served as capital of which state?
