q.e: Opelousas was Louisiana's Confederate capital briefly in 1862, after New Orleans fell. The capital later moved to Shreveport.

q: From 1810 to 1812, Zanesville, a city located in Muskingum County, was the capital of which state?

q.e: Zanesville was Ohio's capital from 1810 to 1812, before the capital moved to Chillicothe and then Columbus.

q: Until Jefferson City was build in 1826, Saint Charles served as capital of which state?

q.e: St. Charles, on the Missouri River, was the temporary capital of Missouri from 1821 to 1826, until Jefferson City was ready.

q: What country is called Polska in its native language?

q.e: Polska is the Polish name for Poland, derived from the Polans, a West Slavic tribe that inhabited the Warta River basin in the 8th century.

q: What country in West-central Europe is called Deutschland in its native language?

q.e: Deutschland derives from Old High German diutisc, which means of the people. Austria is known natively as Osterreich, meaning eastern realm.

q: What country is called Suomi in its native language?

q.e: Suomi is the native Finnish name for Finland, though the precise origins of the word remain debated among linguists. Sweden is known in Finnish as Ruotsi and in Swedish as Sverige.

q: What country is called Sverige in its native language?

q.e: Sverige is Sweden in Swedish, literally "the realm of the Svear."

q: What country is called Magyarorszag in its native language?

q.e: Magyarország is Hungary in Hungarian, meaning "land of the Magyars."

q: What country is called Eire in its native language?

q.e: Eire is the Irish-language name for Ireland, derived from the mythological goddess Eriu. It was formally adopted in the 1937 Constitution of Ireland.

q: This country on the Balkan Peninsula is called Ellada in its native language?

q.e: Greece calls itself Ellada (Hellas), after the Hellenes, rather than Greece.

q: What country is called Hrvatska in its native language?

q.e: Hrvatska is Croatia in Croatian, and gave the country the abbreviation HR.

q: The coupon is part of an airline ticket. This is what you do with it.
Keep it in order to prove that you have been on that flight.
Receive food on board in return for it.
It allows you to use the facilities of the airport free of charge.

q.e: An airline ticket is made of flight coupons, and each is taken from the ticket by the airline agent when you check in or board.

q: A window of convenience is generally considered to be this number of hours on either side of ideal departure or arrival time.

q.e: Air travel guidance often refers to a window of two hours on either side of the planned time for flights, when passengers should be ready.

q: Jonesboro (Arkansas), Fort Wayne (Indiana) and Louisville (Kentucky) are three cities whose other names contain these buildings.

q.e: Jonesboro, Arkansas (a "City of Churches" and Fort Wayne and Louisville have the same nickname, because of the many churches they've had.

q: One of the following pairs (city - what it is a capital of) is wrong.
Norman - Storm Capital of the World
New York City - The Capital of the World
Las Vegas - Entertainment Capital of the World
Binghamton - Carousel Capital of the World

q.e: Norman, Oklahoma, is home to the National Severe Storms Laboratory. The listed pair is the incorrect one in this quiz. Moore is also called "Tornado Alley" city.

q: Have it your way! was the advertising slogan of which company?

q.e: Burger King debuted the famous Have It Your Way slogan in 1974 to highlight that customers could customize their burgers, distinguishing themselves from competitors like McDonald's.

q: Which of these used the tagline The ultimate driving machine?

q.e: BMW introduced The Ultimate Driving Machine advertising slogan in North America in the 1970s through the Ammirati & Puris agency, cementing its performance identity.

q: On the Island of Misfit Toys in Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer, what makes the train a misfit?

q.e: On the Island of Misfit Toys in Rudolph (1964), the train has square wheels on its caboose, a misfit toy.

q: What did Hermie the elf do to subdue the snowmonster in Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer?
Shaved off all of its hair.

q.e: Hermey, the elf who wanted to be a dentist, pulled out the Abominable Snow Monster's teeth.

q: How many of the Seven Ancient World Wonders exist in the modern world?

q.e: Of the seven ancient wonders, only the Great Pyramid of Giza still stands.

q: What is the capital of South Dakota?

q.e: Pierre is the capital of South Dakota, with a population of fewer than 15,000.

q: This is how Santas helper, who judges which children were bad during the year, is called in the Netherlands.

q.e: In the Netherlands, Sinterklaas is helped by Zwarte Piet (Black Peter). The tradition has been criticized as racist and is being changed.

q: On December 24 and 25, 1974, tropical cyclone Tracy devastated Darwin, a city located on this countrys far north-western coastline.

q.e: Cyclone Tracy hit Darwin, Northern Territory, Australia, on Christmas Eve and Christmas Day 1974, destroying most of the city and killing 71 people.

q: What do the 13 red and white stripes on the US flag stand for?
The number of battles won for independence
The number of representatives that signed the Declaration of Independence

q.e: The 13 stripes on the US flag represent the original 13 colonies; the 50 stars stand for the states.

q: What do the stars on the flag of the United States of America represent?
The number of years to achieve freedom

q.e: The 50 white stars on the American flag represent the 50 current states of the Union, while the 13 alternating red and white stripes represent the original 13 colonies that declared independence.

q: When reciting the United States Pledge of Allegiance, what should you do?
Stand, face the flag and cover your heart with your right hand.

q.e: The US Flag Code says to stand, face the flag and place the right hand over the heart when saying the Pledge of Allegiance. Veterans may salute.

q: When is the United States Flag flown at half-mast?

q.e: The US flag is flown at half-staff to mourn the dead, and on certain days such as Memorial Day (until noon).

q: Who wrote the The Star-Spangled Banner, the national anthem of the United States of America?

q.e: Francis Scott Key wrote the poem Defence of Fort M'Henry after witnessing the British bombardment of the Baltimore fort in September 1814, which was later set to music as the national anthem.

q: In the USA, Flag Day, which commemorates the adoption of the flag, is observed on what date?

q.e: Flag Day, 14 June, marks the adoption of the Stars and Stripes in 1777. It's not a federal holiday.

q: A Mars a day helps you work, rest and ...

q.e: The old Mars bar slogan was "A Mars a day helps you work, rest and play."
"Between love and madness lies obsession" was the tagline for Calvin Klein's Obsession perfume (1985).

q: Melt in your mouth, not in your

q.e: M&M's slogan: "Melt in your mouth, not in your hand."

q: When a man youve never met before suddenly gives you ...

q.e: The line is from a perfume or chocolate ad where a stranger gives you flowers. The answer here is "flowers".

q: A mind is a terrible thing to ...

q.e: "A mind is a terrible thing to waste" is the United Negro College Fund slogan, since 1972.
"We bring good things to life" was General Electric's slogan from 1979 to 2003.

q: In early 1800s, marijuana was the number one crop in this American state.

q.e: In the early 1800s, hemp (a cannabis plant grown for rope and cloth, not drug use) was a major crop in Kentucky.

q: One of the first streetcars in this American city was made to resemble a horse.

q.e: San Francisco's early streetcars and cable cars were pulled by horses, so some designs imitated the animals. A horse-shaped car is an unusual claim.

q: In an ancient civilization, the cure for epilepcy was to spit on the person having a fit.

q.e: Roman writers (such as Pliny) record that spitting was thought to ward off epilepsy, the "sacred disease". Of course it doesn't work.

q: Oranges used to be popular in this European country as decorative items, much as gourds are today.

q.e: In Tudor and Stuart England, oranges, often studded with cloves (pomanders), were used as decorations at Christmas. They were a luxury.

q: In the 1500s translating the Bible was almost illegal. A strong public opinion was widespread that the Bible should not be translated into common languages. Where was that?

q.e: In 1408 the Constitutions of Oxford banned unlicensed English Bible translations in England. Tyndale was executed in 1536 for translating it.

q: Housewarming parties originated in this constituent country of the United Kingdom.

q.e: The housewarming party tradition is said to come from Scotland and Ireland, where neighbors brought fuel to light the first fire in a new home.

q: Where were eyeglasses known and worn 500 years before they became popular in Europe and America?

q.e: Eyeglasses are claimed to have existed in China earlier, but the first confirmed eyeglasses were made in Italy in the late 1200s.

q: During which of these wars was there an epidemic of opium addiction among American soldiers?

q.e: Many American soldiers in the Vietnam War used heroin and opium, which led to the 1971 military and policy response. Opium addiction also was seen in the Civil War (morphine).
Dublin is the capital of Ireland, on the River Liffey on the east coast.

q: Russia is the largest country in the world, located on which continent(s)?

q.e: Russia spans Eastern Europe and Northern Asia, covering over 17 million square kilometers. The Ural Mountains and the Ural River traditionally mark the geographic boundary dividing its European and Asian regions.

q: What currency is used in Japan?

q.e: Japan's currency is the yen (¥), one of the world's most traded currencies.

q: What currency is used in South Korea?

q.e: South Korea's currency is the won (₩).

q: Which of these is not an American movie with a character who is autistic?

q.e: Films with autistic characters include Rain Man (1988), Mercury Rising and Snow Cake. "My Very Wonderful Boy" isn't a known film.

q: In which US state would you find these cities: Alexis, Alhambra, Amboy, Argenta, Ashley, Zeigler, Zion, Wauconda?

q.e: Alexis, Alhambra, Amboy, Argenta, Ashley, Zeigler, Zion and Wauconda are all towns in Illinois.

q: How large is the largest United States flag and largest flag in the world, as designated by the Guinness Book of Records in 1998?

q.e: In 1998 Guinness certified a US flag 505 ft × 255 ft (the "Superflag") as the world's largest flag. It weighs over 3,000 lb.

q: In 2001, Dave Barlia set a world record for longest bungee jump. How long was the jump?

q.e: In 2001 Dave Barlia set a record for the longest bungee jump, jumping from a helicopter about 6,000 feet above the ground.

q: Which US state has an official piece of neckwear?

q.e: Arizona's official neckwear is the bolo tie, designated in 1973.

q: What is the main language of Brazil?

q.e: Portuguese became the dominant language of Brazil following Portuguese colonization beginning in 1500, making Brazil the only Portuguese-speaking nation in the Americas. Neighboring South American countries largely speak Spanish.

q: What is the main language of Austria?

q.e: Standard German is the official language of Austria, spoken natively by over 88% of the population, predominantly in Austrian German dialects. Austrian is a regional dialect group rather than an independent language.

q: What is the most widely spoken language in Hawaii?

q.e: English is the most widely spoken language in Hawaii. Hawaiian is also official, and Hawaiian Pidgin is common.

q: What is the most widely spoken language in Nigeria?

q.e: English is Nigeria's official language. Hausa, Yoruba and Igbo are the main native languages, with over 500 languages overall.

q: What is the main language of Tunisia?

q.e: Arabic is Tunisia's official language. Tunisian Arabic is the vernacular, and French is widely used.

q: Which US state ranks number ten in terms of area?

q.e: Wyoming is the 10th-largest state by area, at about 97,800 square miles, but the least populated.

q: What is the state flower of Alaska?

q.e: The forget-me-not is Alaska's state flower, adopted in 1917.
Echo Canyon is a canyon in northeastern Utah, along the old Mormon, Pony Express and Transcontinental Railroad routes.

q: What is the capital of the state of Nevada?

q.e: Carson City, named after Kit Carson, is Nevada's capital.

q: What is the state tree of Idaho?

q.e: The western white pine (Pinus monticola) is Idaho's state tree, adopted in 1935.

q: What was the 33rd US state admitted to the Union?

q.e: Oregon became the 33rd state on 14 February 1859.

q: According to the legend, leprechauns are unfriendly Irish fairies who live alone, possess hidden pots of gold and pass the time making what?

q.e: In traditional Irish folklore, leprechauns are solitary sprites often portrayed as cobblers or shoemakers, frequently detected by the tapping sound of their small hammers.

q: What are the two official national languages of Ireland?

q.e: Irish (Gaeilge) is Ireland's first official language, and English is the second.

q: Which of the following films did not star renowned Oscar-nominated Irish actor, Liam Neeson?

q.e: Liam Neeson was in Schindler's List, Taken and Michael Collins. Tom Hanks and Denzel Washington starred in Philadelphia.

q: Irish Fest, the largest celebration of Irish music and culture in the world, is held annually in which location?

q.e: Milwaukee Irish Fest, held every August in Wisconsin, is the world's largest celebration of Irish music and culture.

q: What is the motto of Republic of Sudan, the African country with the largest area?

q.e: Sudan's motto is "Victory is ours" (al-nasr lana). Since South Sudan's secession in 2011, Sudan is no longer Africa's largest country.

q: Legend has it that this European capital was founded by twins raised by a female wolf.

q.e: Rome was founded, according to legend, by the twins Romulus and Remus, who were raised by a she-wolf, in 753 BC.

q: Which capital is NOT situated on an island?

q.e: Amsterdam is on the mainland. Dublin, London, Valletta, Reykjavik, Nicosia and others are on islands.

q: The Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) is based in this European capital.

q.e: OPEC has its headquarters in Vienna, Austria, since 1965.

q: It is believed that the American Labor Day originates from a parade, organized on September 5, 1882 in this city.

q.e: The first Labor Day parade was held in New York City on 5 September 1882. It became a federal holiday in 1894.

q: Area code 213 is one of the original area codes in which major metropolitan area?

q.e: Area code 213 is for downtown Los Angeles, one of the original three California area codes created in 1947.

q: 312 is an area code in which major metro area?

q.e: 312 is a Chicago area code, one of the original area codes, assigned in 1947.

q: What geographic feature divides the 213 area code from the 818 area code?

q.e: The Santa Monica Mountains separate Los Angeles proper (213) from the San Fernando Valley (818).

q: What did Pericles call the School of Hellas?

q.e: Pericles called Athens "the school of Hellas" (Greece), in his funeral oration reported by Thucydides.

q: What is the capital of the Republic of Ireland?

q.e: Dublin is the capital of the Republic of Ireland.

q: The Irish are considered lucky because Ireland has none of what creature?

q.e: While folklore credits Saint Patrick with banishing snakes from Ireland, scientists note that post-glacial waters simply isolated the island before cold-blooded reptiles could migrate there from Britain or mainland Europe.

q: What is the most common religion in the Republic of Ireland?

q.e: Roman Catholicism is the largest religion in Ireland, followed by about 70-80% of the population.

q: What is the name of the national anthem of Ireland, adopted in 1926?

q.e: "Amhrán na bhFiann" ("The Soldier's Song") was adopted as Ireland's national anthem in 1926.

q: This state, that is home of Mount Whitney, is the third biggest state in the US.

q.e: California is the third-largest state by area (after Alaska and Texas) and has Mount Whitney (14,505 ft), the highest peak in the lower 48.
Augusta is the capital of Maine, on the Kennebec River.

q: Stone Mountain, one of the largest single masses of exposed granite in the world, is located in this state.

q.e: Stone Mountain, near Atlanta, is a granite dome with a huge Confederate carving. It's a state park in Georgia.

q: Dwight D. Eisenhowers family settled in this state in 1892. Its capital city is Topeka.

q.e: The Eisenhower family moved to Abilene, Kansas, in 1892. Topeka is the state capital.

q: In what state is the Space Needle located?

q.e: The 605-foot Space Needle is an iconic landmark in Seattle, Washington, originally built for the 1962 World's Fair.

q: Although the state is often called the Wolverine State there are no longer any wolverines in it.

q.e: Michigan is nicknamed the Wolverine State, historically linked to the 18th-century fur trade, though wild wolverines had disappeared from the state by the early 20th century.

q: It is known as the Lone Star State and is home to the Alamo.

q.e: Texas adopted the Lone Star State nickname from the single star on its 1839 national flag, and the historic Alamo mission is located in downtown San Antonio.

q: The capital of this eastern state is Hartford.

q.e: Hartford is the capital of Connecticut.

q: It is the only US state that starts with two vowels. Dubuque is the states oldest city.

q.e: Iowa is the only US state that begins with two vowels. Dubuque, on the Mississippi, was founded in 1833.

q: Which European country used to have Cracow (Kraków) as its capital?

q.e: Kraków was the capital of Poland from 1038 to 1596, before the capital moved to Warsaw.

q: In which Central European country will you find Munich (Muenchen)?

q.e: Munich is the capital and most populous city of Bavaria, the largest federal state by land area in Germany. It is situated roughly 50 kilometers (31 miles) north of the northern edge of the Alps.

q: Where is the city of Brno located?

q.e: Brno is the second-largest city in the Czech Republic, in Moravia.

q: In which German-speaking country will you find the city of Linz?

q.e: Linz is a city in Austria on the Danube, and Austria's third largest.

q: In what country is Lviv located?

q.e: Lviv is a city in western Ukraine, once part of Poland-Lithuania and Austria-Hungary.

q: In what country will you find the Adriatic town of Trieste (Trst, Triest)?

q.e: Trieste (Trst in Slovenian) is in northeast Italy on the Adriatic, near Slovenia.

q: Which countrys second largest port is Turku?

q.e: Turku is a port city in southwest Finland, and was its capital until 1812. It's an important ferry port to Sweden.

q: Is Geneva (Genève) located within the EU territory?
No, it is in Switzerland which is outside ot EU.
No, it is a self-governed city (like Monaco) which is outside of the EU.
Yes, it is an Italian city.

q.e: Geneva is in Switzerland, which isn't an EU member. It hosts the UN's European headquarters and the Red Cross.

q: In what country will you find the city of Narvik?

q.e: Narvik is a port in northern Norway, scene of fighting in 1940. It exports iron ore from Sweden.

q: The construction of the Titanic was fully completed on 31 March, 1912. Titanics maiden voyage commenced from Southampton, England on this memorable day.

q.e: The Titanic left Southampton on 10 April 1912, heading to New York via Cherbourg and Queenstown. It sank on 15 April.

q: Which country's name is derived from silver?

q.e: Argentina takes its name from 'argentum', the Latin word for silver. Early Spanish explorers named the Río de la Plata (River of Silver) based on rumors of rich silver deposits in the region.

q: What is the meaning of the name of China in the native language of the country?

q.e: The standard Chinese name for China is Zhōngguó, which combines the characters for 'middle' (zhōng) and 'state' or 'country' (guó), historically reflecting ancient concepts of the nation as the center of the civilized world.

q: Which country's name means rich harbour?

q.e: Puerto Rico means "rich port" in Spanish, a name given by Spanish explorers. The island was originally named San Juan Bautista.

q: Belarus is a country in Eastern Europe. The name relates to Russia. What is the proper translation?

q.e: Belarus means "White Rus'" or "White Russia", though the origin of the "white" is uncertain.

q: Which countrys name can be translated as God fights?

q.e: "Israel" is from Hebrew Yisra'el, which is often explained as "God contends" or "he who struggles with God," from Jacob's wrestling (Genesis 32).

q: Many Central Asian countries' names end with STAN. What does the suffix mean?

q.e: The suffix '-stan' comes from Persian and Proto-Indo-European roots meaning 'place of' or 'land'. For example, Kazakhstan translates directly to the 'land of the Kazakhs'.

q: Which country name does NOT contain a color?

q.e: Sri Lanka means "resplendent island" in Sanskrit; it has no color. Names with colors include Greenland, Red Sea (not a country) and Côte d'Ivoire (Ivory Coast, a color-ish name).

q: Many Caribbean nations are named after a saint. Which saint country is fictional?

q.e: Saint Lucia, Saint Kitts and Nevis, and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines are real Caribbean nations. Saint George is Grenada's capital, not a country.

q: Which African nation is country of the blacks?

q.e: "Sudan" comes from the Arabic bilad as-sudan, "land of the blacks," referring to the region south of the Sahara.

q: The song, Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas was introduced in which Broadway musical?

q.e: "Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas" was introduced by Judy Garland in the MGM musical Meet Me in St. Louis (1944), not on Broadway.

q: When listing all the U.S. states in alphabetical order, which state capital comes first?

q.e: Alabama is first in an alphabetical list of states, and its capital is Montgomery.

q: Which is the only state that has the word Saint (St.) in its state capital?

q.e: Saint Paul has served as Minnesota's state capital since the state was admitted to the Union in 1858. Together with neighboring Minneapolis, it forms the Core of the Twin Cities.

q: How many U.S. states that begin with the letter M, have state capitals that also start with the letter M?

q.e: Maine (Augusta), Maryland (Annapolis), Massachusetts (Boston), Michigan (Lansing), Minnesota (St. Paul), Mississippi (Jackson), Missouri (Jefferson City) and Montana (Helena). None match.

q: According to the myth, what do the children on Santas bad list often receive, instead of presents?
A book with proverbs and morals

q.e: Dating back to Victorian-era folklore, naughty children who end up on Santa Claus's naughty list wake up on Christmas morning to find a lump of coal in their stocking instead of toys.

q: The myth of Santa Claus was inspired by the story of which real person?

q.e: Saint Nicholas of Myra was a 4th-century Greek bishop in modern-day Turkey renowned for secret gift-giving, which later evolved into the Dutch figure Sinterklaas and modern Santa Claus.

q: What is the capital of the state of California?

q.e: Sacramento became California's capital in 1854.

q: Which of these states does not border California?

q.e: California borders Oregon, Nevada, Arizona and Mexico. Idaho doesn't touch it.

q: Which American building was the world's first building to have air conditioning installed for comfort?

q.e: Willis Carrier's air conditioning was installed in the New York Stock Exchange in 1903, an early use for comfort.

q: Which event happened for the first time on 3 April 1973 on Lexington Avenue in New York City?
The first cell phone call was made.
The first commercial sale of a microwave oven was done.
The first anabolic steroid was formed.
The first tablet computer was sold.

q.e: On 3 April 1973, Motorola's Martin Cooper made the first handheld cell phone call in New York City, to Joel Engel at Bell Labs.

q: What do the following US states have in common: Missouri, Wisconsin, Nebraska, and Mississippi.
Their capital cities are named after US Presidents.
Their largest cities are named after famous Americans.
Their state basketball teams have each won one national championship.
They have one and the same bird for state bird.

q.e: Jefferson City (MO), Madison (WI), Lincoln (NE) and Jackson (MS) are named after presidents Jefferson, Madison, Lincoln and Jackson.

q: In which US city was the childrens show Mr. Rogers Neighbourhood produced?

q.e: Mister Rogers' Neighborhood was produced by WQED in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, from 1968 to 2001.

q: Which are the colors of Purdue University?

q.e: Purdue University's colors are old gold and black, and its teams are the Boilermakers.

q: What is true about University of Pennsylvania, Cornell University and Brown University?
They are all members of the Ivy League
They all admit about 55% of their applicants
They all have filials in both Asia and Europe
They are all in one and the same state

q.e: Penn, Cornell, and Brown are three of the eight private research universities that make up the Ivy League collegiate athletic conference, founded in 1954.

q: Which of these schools is not famous for its Medicine Department?

q.e: The Rochester Institute of Technology is known for technology and design, not a medical school. The University of Rochester has a medical school.

q: Which ocean is the worlds largest body of water, covering nearly one third of the Earths surface?

q.e: Covering more than 60 million square miles (roughly 165 million square kilometers), the Pacific Ocean spans over 30% of Earth's total surface, making it larger than all landmasses combined. The second-largest ocean is the Atlantic, which is about half the Pacific's size.

q: On May 22, 1960, an earthquake with magnitude of 9.5 was recorded in which country?

q.e: The 1960 Valdivia earthquake in Chile (magnitude 9.5) is the strongest earthquake ever recorded.

q: This mega-city was originally a municipality, founded in 1521 by Fernán Cortés.

q.e: Hernán Cortés founded the Spanish city on the ruins of Tenochtitlan in 1521. It became Mexico City.

q: This sea, which is a basin of the Indian Ocean between Africa and Asia, is the worlds most northern tropical sea.

q.e: The Red Sea lies between Africa and Asia, linked to the Indian Ocean via the Gulf of Aden. It's the northernmost tropical sea.

q: Which one of the following countries borders Chile?

q.e: Chile shares a land border of roughly 3,300 miles (over 5,300 km) with Argentina along the Andes mountains, in addition to shorter borders with Peru and Bolivia.

q: Which one of these countries shares a border with Turkmenistan?

q.e: Turkmenistan borders Iran, Afghanistan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan, as well as the Caspian Sea.

q: Nepal is bordered by which of these countries?

q.e: Nepal is landlocked between China (Tibet) in the north and India to the south, east and west.

q: Which of the following countries borders Djibouti?

q.e: Djibouti borders Eritrea, Ethiopia and Somalia (Somaliland), and the Red Sea.

q: Which one of the following countries borders Uruguay?

q.e: Uruguay is bordered by Brazil to the north and Argentina to the west.

q: The Borobudur Temple is in what country?

q.e: Borobudur is a 9th-century Mahayana Buddhist temple located in Central Java, Indonesia, and is recognized as the largest Buddhist temple in the world.

q: Just one of these states has a minimum driving age of exactly sixteen.

q.e: In Texas, a driver aged 16 may get a license through a graduated license program. The minimum age varies by state, 14 to 18.

q: When a school bus is stopped and its red lights are flashing (or stop signs are extended), it means this.
You may pass if no children are on the road.
You may pass if you are facing the front of the bus.
You may pass if it is on the other side of a divided highway.

q.e: When a school bus has flashing red lights and a stop sign out, traffic must stop in both directions on undivided roads. Passing is illegal.

q: On long trips you can prevent drowsiness by performing this.
Stopping at regular intervals for a rest.
Moving your eyes from side to side as you drive.
Slowing down so you can react better.

q.e: Stopping every couple of hours to rest is the recommended way to avoid drowsy driving. Caffeine only helps briefly.

q: This is the only effective way to reduce your blood alcohol content (BAC).
Allow your body time to get rid of alcohol.

q.e: Only time lowers blood alcohol content, at around 0.015% per hour. Coffee, food and cold showers don't help.

q: Which one of these singers was not born in New Jersey?

q.e: Alice Cooper was born in Detroit, Michigan. Bruce Springsteen, Frank Sinatra and Whitney Houston were all born in New Jersey.

q: Which one of the following was not invented in New Jersey?

q.e: The sewing machine's inventor Elias Howe was from Massachusetts. Edison's work in Menlo Park, NJ, produced the phonograph and lightbulb.

q: Which of these firsts did not originate in New Jersey?

q.e: The first US iron works were in Saugus, Massachusetts, not New Jersey. New Jersey had the first brewery and first baseball game, in Hoboken.

q: New Jersey was settled first by this nation in the early 1630s.

q.e: The Dutch settled New Jersey in the 1620s-30s as part of New Netherland, followed by the Swedes and the English.

q: What is the capital of Texas?

q.e: Austin has served as the capital of Texas since 1839, during the era of the Republic of Texas. Houston and Dallas have larger populations, and Houston briefly served as the republic's capital earlier.
Geographically, Mexico forms the southern part of North America, bordering the United States to the north and Guatemala and Belize to the southeast.

q: Name the mountain chain that runs through British Columbia all the way down to New Mexico.

q.e: The Rocky Mountains stretch roughly 3,000 miles (4,800 km) from northern British Columbia in Canada down to northern New Mexico in the United States. The Appalachian range runs along the eastern side of North America.

q: Which state has the smallest area in North America?

q.e: Covering roughly 1,214 square miles (3,144 sq km), Rhode Island is the smallest US state by area, about one-third the size of the next smallest state, Delaware.

q: Which of the following is not a real ocean?

q.e: The five oceans are the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic. The Red Sea is a sea.

q: Which ocean does New York City border?

q.e: New York City sits along the Atlantic Ocean via the New York Bight, Upper and Lower New York Bay, and Long Island Sound. The East Coast of the United States borders the western rim of the North Atlantic.

q: On what continent is the highest mountain in the world located?

q.e: Mount Everest (8,849 m) is in the Himalayas, on the Nepal-Tibet border in Asia.

q: The name of the deepest lake in the world, Lake Baikal, derives from Tatar Bai-Kul, meaning this.

q.e: Baikal may derive from Turkic "Bay-Kul," meaning "rich lake," or Buryat "Baigal Nuur" (nature lake). It holds about 20% of Earth's fresh surface water.

q: The Bay of Pigs is located on the coast of this country.

q.e: The Bay of Pigs (Bahía de Cochinos) is on the southern coast of Cuba. The failed 1961 US-backed invasion happened there.

q: The Suez canal connects the Red Sea with this sea.

q.e: Opened in 1869 across the Isthmus of Suez in Egypt, the Suez Canal links the Mediterranean Sea to the northern end of the Red Sea at the Gulf of Suez.

q: The Bermuda Triangle is located in this ocean.

q.e: The Bermuda Triangle lies in the western part of the North Atlantic Ocean, roughly bounded by Miami, Bermuda, and San Juan, Puerto Rico.

q: Prior to 1989, this county was bordered by three countries that do not exist anymore.

q.e: Poland, before 1989, was bordered by the Soviet Union, East Germany and Czechoslovakia, none of which exist today.

q: Which country used to rule vast areas from South America through Africa to East Asia?

q.e: The Portuguese Empire stretched from Brazil through Africa (Angola, Mozambique) to Goa in India, Macau and Timor, from the 15th century.

q: Which country is divided by a canal connecting the Pacific and Atlantic Oceans?

q.e: The Panama Canal opened in 1914, cutting roughly 50 miles (80 km) across the Isthmus of Panama to link the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. It eliminated the need for ships to navigate the hazardous route around South America's Cape Horn.

q: The name of which country means Rich Harbour?

q.e: Puerto Rico means "rich port" in Spanish.

q: Which of these countries is inhabited by the largest number of Muslims?

q.e: Indonesia has the world's largest Muslim population, followed by Pakistan and India. Pakistan is largest among the options.
Lima is the capital of Peru. It was founded in 1535 by Francisco Pizarro.

q: Which is the only mostly Christian country in Asia?

q.e: The Philippines (about 90% Christian) is Asia's largest Christian nation. East Timor is also mostly Catholic.

q: Which of the following is not an independent nation?

q.e: Palestine is a UN observer state recognized by many countries but isn't a full UN member, so it's not generally considered independent by all.

q: What is the origin of the name 3M, the company that makes almost everything?
McGonagle, McKnight, McNemey were the founders
Me and My Mom (the company was established bu a mother and son duo)

q.e: 3M stands for Minnesota Mining and Manufacturing Company, founded in 1902 in Two Harbors. It makes Post-it Notes and Scotch Tape.

q: Which Far East company name can be translated as three stars?

q.e: In Korean, 'sam' means three and 'sung' means stars, chosen by founder Lee Byung-chull in 1938 to represent something big, numerous, and eternal.

q: The British Airways London Eye, which opened in 1999, is what type of structure?

q.e: Standing 443 feet (135 meters) tall on the South Bank of the River Thames, the London Eye is a cantilevered observation wheel that carries passengers in 32 sealed glass pods.

q: Designed by architect Norman Foster, this building has housed some of Londons most important authorities since 2002.

q.e: London's City Hall, designed by Norman Foster, opened in 2002 near Tower Bridge, and was home to the Greater London Authority.

q: This London building, sometimes referred to as Covent Garden, functions as a performing arts venue.

q.e: The Royal Opera House in Covent Garden is home to the Royal Opera and Royal Ballet.

q: This 183-meter skyscraper in London was originally built for the National Westminster Bank.

q.e: Tower 42 (formerly the NatWest Tower), 183 m, was completed in 1980. It was London's tallest building until 1990.

q: Apart from actions related to the Civil War, which two American states declared war on each other?

q.e: Ohio and Michigan nearly went to war in the 1835 Toledo War over a strip of land including Toledo. Michigan got the Upper Peninsula as compensation.

q: In 1915 the boll weevil devastated the cotton crop in this state.

q.e: The boll weevil devastated Alabama's cotton crop in 1915. Enterprise, Alabama, built a monument to the weevil for forcing farmers to diversify.

q: In which state would one see the House on the Rock?

q.e: The House on the Rock is a tourist attraction near Spring Green, Wisconsin, with odd collections and a huge carousel.

q: In which state was the first sales tax enacted?

q.e: West Virginia introduced a state sales tax in 1921, the first in the US (some say Mississippi in 1932).

q: Which was the 14th state admitted to the Union?

q.e: Vermont, admitted in 1791, was the 14th state and the first to join after the original 13.

q: Which US President occupied every major non-judicial elected office in the American political system?

q.e: Andrew Johnson held every major elected office: alderman, mayor, state legislator, governor, US representative, US senator, vice president and president.

q: When was Puerto Rico admitted to the Union?
It is not a US state

q.e: Puerto Rico has been an unincorporated US territory since the Spanish-American War in 1898, meaning its residents are US citizens but it is not a US state.

q: Which of these seas with color names doesnt exist?

q.e: There's a Red Sea, Black Sea, White Sea and Yellow Sea, but no "Blue Sea" proper.

q: Where is the White Sea located?

q.e: The White Sea is an inlet of the Barents Sea in northwestern Russia, near Arkhangelsk.

q: Between the Arctic and Atlantic oceans
West of Great Britain, its a nickname of Ireland

q.e: Greenland lies between the Arctic and Atlantic oceans, as an autonomous territory of Denmark. It's the world's largest island.

q: Belarus is a country containing a color in its name. Which color is it?

q.e: The name Belarus derives from the Slavic root bely, meaning white, paired with Rus, the historic East Slavic region. Historically, English speakers often referred to the country as White Russia or Belorussia.

q: Where is the Purple Mountain located?

q.e: Purple Mountain (Zijin Shan) is in Nanjing, China, with the Sun Yat-sen Mausoleum.

q: This city, famous for the Parthenon on the Acropolis, is the capital of Greece.

q.e: Athens has been the capital of Greece since 1834, following the Greek War of Independence. The Parthenon, dedicated to the goddess Athena, was completed there in 438 BC on the Acropolis hill.

q: Which city, founded in 1848, is the capital of the State of California, USA?

q.e: Sacramento, founded in 1848 after the Gold Rush began, has been the state capital since 1854.

q: When was Arnold Schwarzenegger sworn into office as the 38th Governor of California?

q.e: Arnold Schwarzenegger became California's 38th governor on 17 November 2003, after the recall of Gray Davis.

q: During the summer, what time is it in Los Angeles, CA, when it is 3 PM local time in Paris, France?

q.e: In summer, Paris (CEST, UTC+2) is 9 hours ahead of Los Angeles (PDT, UTC-7), so 3 PM in Paris is 6 AM in LA.

q: What is depicted on the back of the $10 bill?

q.e: The back of the $10 bill shows the US Treasury Building, the only US bill to depict a government building other than the White House.

q: What city coincides with the letter B on the Federal Reserve Seal?

q.e: Each Federal Reserve district has a letter: A is Boston and B is New York. The seal's letter B stands for the New York Fed.

q: What is the title of the signature in the lower right hand corner of the U.S. $10 bill?

q.e: The signature in the lower right of the $10 bill is the Secretary of the Treasury, and in the lower left the Treasurer of the United States.

q: Whose portrait appears on the face of the $20 bill?

q.e: Andrew Jackson, the 7th U.S. president, was placed on the front of the $20 bill in 1928, replacing Grover Cleveland.

q: Which of the following cities does not have a Federal Reserve Bank?

q.e: The Federal Reserve Banks are in Boston, New York, Philadelphia, Cleveland, Richmond, Atlanta, Chicago, St. Louis, Minneapolis, Kansas City, Dallas and San Francisco. Pittsburgh has none.

q: Which state name means the object towards which the action of the sea is directed?

q.e: "Alaska" comes from the Aleut "alaxsxaq," meaning "the object toward which the action of the sea is directed", i.e. the mainland.

q: Which state name doesnt refer to a king or a queen?

q.e: Virginia, Maryland, the Carolinas, Georgia and Louisiana honor monarchs. Vermont means "green mountain" (French).

q: What is the meaning of Indiana?

q.e: "Indiana" means "land of the Indians" and was named in 1800 for the Indian Territory.

q: Which state name is not color-related?

q.e: Colorado means "colored red" in Spanish and Florida means "flowery". California may come from a fictional island in a Spanish romance, so no color.

q: Which state name means great river?

q.e: "Mississippi" means "great river" (Ojibwe misi-ziibi).
"Nevada" means "snow-covered" or "snowy" in Spanish, after the Sierra Nevada.

q: Which state was named in honor of a non-English royalty?

q.e: Louisiana was named for King Louis XIV of France by René-Robert Cavelier de La Salle in 1682.

q: The name of which US state means beautiful?

q.e: "Oregon"'s meaning is uncertain; some say it comes from French "ouragan" or the Algonquian word for "beautiful water". Its origin is debated.
"Dakota" means "friends" or "allies" in the Dakota/Lakota language.

q: What word is missing? And laying his finger aside of his _____, And giving a nod, up the chimney he rose;

q.e: From "A Visit from St. Nicholas": "And laying his finger aside of his nose, / And giving a nod, up the chimney he rose."

q: When did Playboy photographers take the photo of Marilyn Monroe, which became the first centerfold?

q.e: Marilyn Monroe's nude photographs were taken by Tom Kelley in 1949 for a calendar, not by Playboy photographers. Hefner bought the rights for the first issue (Dec 1953).

q: Who was the first person interviewed for the "Playboy Interview, a monthly column famous for its confrontational style.

q.e: Miles Davis was the first person interviewed for the "Playboy Interview" series, in September 1962, by Alex Haley.

q: What designer created the famous Playboy logo, depicting a rabbit with a tuxedo bow tie?

q.e: Art Paul, Playboy's first art director, designed the Rabbit Head logo in 1953.

q: This issue of Playboy magazine sold 7,161,561 copies. A cropped image of the issues centerfold, featuring Swedish model Lena Soderberg, became a standard image for testing image processing algorithms.

q.e: The November 1972 issue sold more than seven million copies. Its Lena Forsén (Söderberg) centerfold gave the standard test image "Lenna" used in image processing.

q: From which country did Barbados gain its independence in 1966?

q.e: Barbados became independent from the United Kingdom on 30 November 1966, and became a republic in 2021.

q: Although the majority of the inhabitants speak a patois, or dialect, this is the official language of Barbados.

q.e: English is the official language of Barbados. Most people speak Bajan, an English-based creole.

q: What it the area of Barbados?

q.e: Barbados is about 166 square miles (430 km²), a small island in the Eastern Caribbean.

q: Most of the inhabitants of Barbados originate from where?

q.e: Most Barbadians are of African descent, descendants of enslaved people brought to work the sugar plantations.

q: The reputation of which league was hurt by Michael Vick?

q.e: Michael Vick's 2007 dogfighting conviction badly hurt his reputation and the NFL's image. He served 21 months in prison.

q: Napoleon Bonaparte I is entombed in Les Invalides, a former military hospital found in what European city/town?

q.e: Napoleon is entombed under the golden dome of Les Invalides in Paris, in a red quartzite sarcophagus.

q: In what European city is the Rembrandt House Museum located?

q.e: The Rembrandt House Museum is in the Jodenbreestraat in Amsterdam, the house where he lived from 1639 to 1658.

q: A museum dedicated to French sculptor Auguste Rodin is found in Philadelphia, USA and what European city?

q.e: The Rodin Museum is in Paris (Hôtel Biron) and Philadelphia (opened 1929). There are Rodin museums elsewhere too.

q: The Van Gogh Museum is found in what city?

q.e: Located on Museum Square in Amsterdam, the Van Gogh Museum opened in 1973 and houses the world's largest collection of paintings and drawings by Vincent van Gogh.

q: This west coast provincial capital is named after British Royalty.

q.e: Victoria, the provincial capital of British Columbia on Vancouver Island, was named in honor of Queen Victoria in 1843.

q: Which city is the capital of the province of Quebec?

q.e: Quebec City serves as the provincial capital of Quebec and was founded by Samuel de Champlain in 1608. Montreal is the province's largest city by population, but not its capital.

q: Name Canadas largest city which is also the capital of Ontario.

q.e: Toronto is Canada's most populous city with nearly 3 million residents and serves as the capital of Ontario, while Ottawa is the national capital of Canada.

q: What is the capital of Canada?

q.e: Queen Victoria selected Ottawa as Canada's capital in 1857, largely due to its defensible inland location near the border between Ontario and Quebec. Toronto is Canada's largest city.

q: Castles can be found in three of these countries. Which is the odd one?

q.e: Castles are plentiful in Europe, and Brazil, which has few castles, is the odd one out.

q: Titanics voyage across the Atlantic bound for New York City began where?

q.e: The Titanic's maiden voyage began at Southampton, England, on 10 April 1912, headed for New York.

q: Where is the biggest EU lake located?

q.e: Lake Vänern in Sweden is the largest lake in the EU.

q: Which country has the most EU neighbours?

q.e: Germany has nine neighbors (Denmark, Poland, Czechia, Austria, Switzerland, France, Luxembourg, Belgium, the Netherlands), more than any other EU state. Neighbors outside the EU are Switzerland.

q: Which EU capital city is elevated the highest above sea level?

q.e: Madrid, at about 650 m above sea level, is the highest capital in the EU. Andorra la Vella (not in the EU) is higher.

q: Where is the highest EU peak, Mont Blanc?

q.e: Mont Blanc stands at about 4,808 meters (15,774 ft) along the border between Haute-Savoie, France, and the Aosta Valley, Italy, though the exact border definition on the summit ridge has been historically contested.

q: How long is the Great Aletsch glacier, the mightiest of all Alpine ice-rivers?

q.e: The Great Aletsch Glacier in Switzerland is the longest in the Alps, at about 23 km today, and 27 km historically. It's shrinking with climate change.

q: The Moskstraumen strait, famous for its whirlpools, is located in which country?

q.e: The Moskstraumen (Maelstrom) is a powerful tidal current system near the Lofoten Islands in Norway.

q: In which of the following countries can you experience the midnight sun phenomenon?

q.e: The midnight sun occurs north of the Arctic Circle, in northern Norway, Sweden, Finland, Russia, Iceland, Greenland, Alaska and Canada.

q: It is the 72nd largest country of the world located in Southeast- Asia. Its capital is Manila.

q.e: The Philippines, an archipelago of over 7,000 islands in Southeast Asia, has Manila as its capital.

q: A transcontinental country that belongs to Asia and Africa. Its capital is Cairo

q.e: Egypt spans two continents: Africa, and the Sinai Peninsula in Asia. Cairo is its capital.

q: The first school in the United States, called King Williams, opened its doors in this state.

q.e: King William's School, founded in Annapolis, Maryland, in 1696, was the first public school in the colonies. It later became St. John's College.

q: What state was labor leader Ceasar Chavez born in?

q.e: César Chávez, the labor leader, was born near Yuma, Arizona, in 1927.

q: Two of the most famous outlaw brothers of yesteryear, Frank and Jesse, are from Kentucky. What was their last name?

q.e: Frank and Jesse James, famous outlaws, were from Missouri (born in Clay County), although the question places them in Kentucky, where their father was born.

q: The 16th president of the United States came from Kentucky. Who was he?

q.e: Abraham Lincoln was born in a one-room log cabin near Hodgenville, Kentucky, in 1809, before his family relocated to Indiana when he was seven years old.

q: The fourth Monday of every May

q.e: Established as a federal holiday in 1971 under the Uniform Monday Holiday Act, Memorial Day is observed on the last Monday in May to create a three-day weekend.

q: For which of these traits is Ebenezer Scrooge best known?

q.e: In Charles Dickens's 1843 novella 'A Christmas Carol', Ebenezer Scrooge is introduced as a bitter, covetous miser before undergoing a transformation following visits from four spirits.

q: Which of these is most important to Ebenezer Scrooge?

q.e: Ebenezer Scrooge, in Dickens's A Christmas Carol (1843), is obsessed with money until visited by three spirits.

q: What is the official currency of the European Union?

q.e: The euro was officially introduced on January 1, 1999, initially for electronic payments, and physical cash entered circulation in 2002. As of 2024, 20 of the 27 EU member states form the eurozone and use the euro as their legal tender.

q: Which country uses the yen as its national currency?

q.e: Japan's currency is the yen.

q: Rubles are used in which Eastern European country?

q.e: Russia's currency is the ruble (Belarus also has its own ruble).

q: Before switching to the euro, which of these countries used francs?

q.e: France used the French franc for centuries until transitioning to the euro for accounting in 1999 and cash in 2002. Finland previously used the markka, and Austria used the schilling.

q: Which of the following countries uses the pound as its currency?

q.e: The United Kingdom uses the pound sterling as its official currency, whereas France, Spain, and Germany all adopted the euro in 1999.

q: Which of these countries does not use the peso as its national currency?

q.e: Venezuela uses the bolívar. Mexico, Colombia, Argentina and others use pesos.

q: Which ancient empire used the denarius?

q.e: Introduced around 211 BC during the Second Punic War, the silver denarius served as the backbone of Roman currency for over four centuries.

q: Which of these countries used the lira before it switched to the euro?

q.e: Italy used the lira until adopting the euro in 2002. Spain used the peseta and France the franc.

q: Which of these countries use dollars?

q.e: Both Canada and Australia use their own official currencies named the dollar (the Canadian dollar and Australian dollar), whereas Great Britain uses the pound sterling.

q: Before it started using the euro, which country used marks?

q.e: Germany's currency before adopting the euro in 1999 was the Deutsche Mark, which had been introduced in 1948. Spain previously used the peseta, France used the franc, and Portugal used the escudo.

q: Which 102-storey Art Deco style building was officially opened in May, 1931?

q.e: The Empire State Building opened on 1 May 1931. It was the tallest building in the world for about 40 years.

q: Jumeirah Beach Hotel, one of Dubais most luxurious hotels, has a unique architectural structure, resembling what?

q.e: The Jumeirah Beach Hotel in Dubai is built in the shape of a wave. Next to it is the sail-shaped Burj Al Arab.

q: Until the reunification of Germany in 1990, this city was a West German enclave, completely surrounded by East Germany.

q.e: After World War II, the Allied sectors of Berlin formed West Berlin, which lay about 100 miles inside Soviet-controlled East Germany until reunification in 1990.

q: The towns of Ceuta and Melilla in northern Morocco are autonomous cities of what nation?

q.e: Ceuta and Melilla are Spanish autonomous cities on Morocco's northern coast, which Morocco claims.

q: Name the mythical figure, depicted as an old bearded man, dressed in a robe and usually carrying a scythe and an hourglass.

q.e: Father Time has personified time since antiquity, frequently paired with a scythe borrowed from the Greek titan Cronus and an hourglass representing the flow of moments. In modern tradition, he hands over duties to Baby New Year.

q: In the judicial system of England and Wales this court has two divisions - Civil Division and Criminal Division.

q.e: The Court of Appeal of England and Wales has Civil and Criminal Divisions. It hears appeals from the High Court and Crown Court.

q: Who had the dubious honor of being Alcatrazs very first inmate?

q.e: Alcatraz became a federal penitentiary in 1934. Its earliest prisoners arrived by train from Atlanta in August 1934.

q: When did the US Air Force officially become activated?

q.e: The US Air Force became a separate branch on 18 September 1947, following the National Security Act of 1947.

q: Before becoming a separate entity, the US Air Force existed under this name.

q.e: Before 1947 the USAF's predecessor was the US Army Air Forces (1941-47), and earlier the Army Air Corps.

q: On what date did the Korean War begin and when did it end?

q.e: The Korean War began on 25 June 1950, when North Korea invaded the South, and ended with an armistice on 27 July 1953. No peace treaty was signed.

q: When George Washington first won the Presidency, how many states did he carry?
10 - he did not carry three states
None - he was appointed, not voted in

q.e: In 1789 Washington was elected unanimously by the electors. New York didn't choose electors, and North Carolina and Rhode Island had not yet ratified the Constitution.

q: Who was the first US president with no natural children?

q.e: George Washington had no biological children, though he raised Martha's children from her first marriage.

q: Two streets in Jerusalem are named after US Presidents. Which two?

q.e: Jerusalem has streets named for Presidents Washington and Lincoln. Streets named after Truman are also in Israel.

q: This country, bordering the Arabian Sea on the south, also has land borders with Iran, Afghanistan, China and India.

q.e: Pakistan borders the Arabian Sea in the south, and has land borders with Iran, Afghanistan, China and India.

q: Take a good look, one of these US cities is as counterfeit as that fiver you spent on coffee this morning!

q.e: West Orange and South Orange are real towns in New Jersey. North Orange isn't one.

q: Help me with this list, one of these towns does not exist.

q.e: West Memphis is in Arkansas, across the Mississippi from Memphis, Tennessee. There is no W. Memphis, TN.

q: Which of these is a nickname of West Virginia?

q.e: West Virginia is "The Mountain State." The state is entirely in the Appalachian Mountains.

q: Which of these is an unofficial nickname of South Dakota?

q.e: South Dakota's best-known nicknames are "The Mount Rushmore State" and "Coyote State." "Sunshine State" is more associated with Florida.

q: Which of these states is called The Cactus State?

q.e: Arizona is called "The Grand Canyon State," and some also use "Cactus State." New Mexico is "Land of Enchantment".

q: Margaux Hemingway, who plays a fashion model in the movie Lipstick, died in the month of June. What did she die from?

q.e: Margaux Hemingway (1954-1996), granddaughter of Ernest Hemingway, was a model and actress. She starred in Lipstick (1976), and died in 1996.

q: What day is Flag Day celebrated on in the United States?

q.e: Flag Day in the US is on 14 June, the anniversary of the 1777 Flag Resolution.

q: Which of these statements about Seattle, Washington, is NOT true?
Seattle is the capital of the State of Washington.
The original settlement, later to become Seattle, was initially called New York.
In 2005 Seattle was proclaimed the most literate city in the USA.
Three people committed suicide jumping from the Space Needle in the 1970s.

q.e: Seattle is Washington State's largest city, but the capital is Olympia.

q: What mountain range is Mt. Rushmore located in?

q.e: Mount Rushmore is situated in the Black Hills mountain range near Keystone, South Dakota, rising to an elevation of roughly 5,725 feet (1,745 meters).

q: Which of these lakes is not part of the Great Lakes?

q.e: The Great Salt Lake is an endorheic saltwater lake located in northern Utah. The five Laurentian Great Lakes bordering the northern US and Canada are Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie, and Ontario.

q: What river connects Lake Ontario, one of the Great Lakes, to the Atlantic Ocean?

q.e: The St. Lawrence River drains Lake Ontario into the Gulf of St. Lawrence and the Atlantic Ocean, while the Niagara River flows upstream between Lake Erie and Lake Ontario.

q: The US shares water borders with all but one of these countries. Which is the odd one?

q.e: The US has maritime borders with Canada, Mexico, Cuba, The Bahamas and Russia, but Argentina is far away.

q: What US state is situated to the East of the Bering Strait?

q.e: The Bering Strait connects the Arctic Ocean to the Bering Sea, with Russia's Chukchi Peninsula on its western side and Alaska's Seward Peninsula to its east.

q: The Great Plains lie west of this river and east of the Rocky Mountains.

q.e: The Great Plains lie west of the Mississippi River (roughly) and east of the Rocky Mountains. They stretch from Canada to Texas.

q: What was special about Jacques-Yves Cousteaus ship Calypso, which was originally built for the British Royal Navy?
She was equipped as a mobile laboratory for field research
She sank mysteriously and was never seen again

q.e: Calypso was a former Royal Navy minesweeper converted by Cousteau into a floating research vessel in 1951. It sank in 1996 after a collision.

q: Which ship was named after the consort of George V of the United Kingdom and sailed the North Atlantic Ocean from 1936 to 1967?

q.e: RMS Queen Mary, named after Mary of Teck (George V's wife), sailed the North Atlantic from 1936 until 1967, and is now a hotel in Long Beach.

q: The highest waterfall on the planet, the Angel Falls, is located on this continent.

q.e: Angel Falls is in Venezuela, South America.

q: The Republic of Djibouti is a small country located in the northeastern part of this continent.

q.e: Djibouti is on the Horn of Africa, at the entrance to the Red Sea.

q: The most populous country in the world is in this continent.

q.e: Asia is home to the two most populous countries, India and China.

q: The Jutland Peninsula, a.k.a. the Cimbrian Peninsula in the past, is located in this continent.

q.e: The Jutland Peninsula (Denmark and northern Germany) is in Europe. "Cimbrian" comes from the Cimbri tribe.

q: On what continent is the Great Victoria Desert located?

q.e: The Great Victoria Desert, in Western and South Australia, is Australia's largest desert.

q: On what continent is the city of Puebla located?

q.e: Puebla, a city southeast of Mexico City, is in North America.

q: The capybara, the largest extant rodent species on the planet, is endemic to this continent.

q.e: Native to South America, capybaras inhabit savannas and dense forests near water bodies across every country on the continent except Chile. Adults can weigh up to around 140 pounds (65 kg).

q: The Amur River, the ninth longest river in the world, is located on this continent.

q.e: The Amur River forms part of the border between Russia and China, in Asia. It's about 2,800 miles long.

q: On what continent is the Yoruba language spoken as a native language of the indigenous people?

q.e: The Yoruba language is spoken in Nigeria, Benin and Togo, in West Africa.

q: One of the most notable civilizations of pre-Columbian America was the Inca Empire. The Incas referred to their king by what title?

q.e: The Inca ruler was the "Sapa Inca," considered a child of the sun god Inti.

q: What is the official language of the smallest sovereign state of South America, Suriname?

q.e: Suriname was a Dutch colony until gaining independence in 1975, making it the only independent nation in South America where Dutch is the official language.

q: The novelty song Monster Mash is narrated by whom?

q.e: "Monster Mash" (Bobby "Boris" Pickett, 1962) is sung from the perspective of a mad scientist whose creation does a new dance.

q: In which of these countries was the Monster Mash song eventually banned?

q.e: The BBC banned "Monster Mash" in 1962 as "too morbid." It wasn't played until 1973.

q: Which saint does not have his/her own island in the Caribbean?

q.e: Caribbean nations named after saints include Saint Lucia, Saint Kitts and Nevis, and Saint Vincent. There's no Saint Clara island.

q: To which country does the term Holy Land refer?

q.e: The term 'Holy Land' traditionally designates the historic region roughly situated between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea, encompassing modern-day Israel and the Palestinian territories.

q: Strasbourg is the main city of the Alsace region which is located in this country.

q.e: Strasbourg is the capital of Alsace in France, seat of the European Parliament. It sits on the Rhine, next to Germany.

q: Three of these movies are set in Pittsburgh. Which is the odd one?

q.e: Good Will Hunting (1997) is set in Boston. Pittsburgh is the setting for Flashdance, Dawn of the Dead and others.

q: Bangs, Gun Barrel City, Honey Island, Oatmeal, Chocolate Bayeau, Ben Franklin, Cut and Shoot, Ben Hur, Lollipop, Uncertain are cities in this state.

q.e: Bangs, Gun Barrel City, Oatmeal, Cut and Shoot, Ben Hur, Lollipop and Uncertain are towns in Texas.

q: Roscoe, Bonesteel, Box Elder, Eaglebutte, Red Butte, Crooks are the names of cities in this state.

q.e: Roscoe, Bonesteel, Box Elder and Crooks are towns in South Dakota.

q: Where are the cities Eros, Vixen, Waterproof, Ft. Necessity, Cutoff, Plain Dealer, Angie?

q.e: Eros, Vixen, Waterproof, Cutoff and Angie are Louisiana communities with odd names.

q: Which city was formerly known as Kaapstad?

q.e: "Kaapstad" is the Afrikaans name for Cape Town, meaning "Cape Town".

q: What is the modern name of Tenochtitlan, the capital of the Aztec civilization?

q.e: Tenochtitlan was founded around 1325 on an island in Lake Texcoco. After Spanish conquistadors under Hernan Cortes destroyed it in 1521, Mexico City was established on its ruins.

q: Edo was an important Japanese city and capital of the Togukawa shogunate. Under what name is it known nowadays?

q.e: Edo was renamed Tokyo ("eastern capital") in 1868, when the Meiji Emperor moved there.

q: Who gave the current title, The Star-Spangled Banner, to the US anthem?

q.e: Baltimore music publisher Thomas Carr published Francis Scott Key's poem to the tune "To Anacreon in Heaven" in 1814 under the name "The Star-Spangled Banner".

q: What country is this national anthem of?

q.e: "O Canada" is the national anthem of Canada, official since 1980.

q: Which of these cars was named after a girl?

q.e: The Mercedes brand was named after Mercédès Jellinek, the daughter of Austrian automobile entrepreneur Emil Jellinek, who marketed Daimler vehicles in the early 1900s.

q: The Ferrari Testarossa went into production in 1984. What does Testarossa mean?

q.e: "Testarossa" means "red head" in Italian, from the red-painted cylinder heads on the Ferrari's engine.
The RMS Titanic was constructed by the Harland and Wolff shipyard in Belfast, which was part of Ireland at the time of construction between 1909 and 1911.

The RMS Titanic was operated by the White Star Line, a British shipping company founded in 1845. Its chief rival, Cunard Line, operated famous liners like the Lusitania and later merged with White Star in 1934.
The Titanic was launched on 31 May 1911 in Belfast. It was fitted out for almost a year.

q: From what harbor did the Titanic set sail?

q.e: The Titanic left Southampton harbor on 10 April 1912.

q: Who was the Captain for the Titanics Maiden voyage?

q.e: Captain Edward John Smith was the commodore of the White Star Line who was chosen to command RMS Titanic on its doomed maiden voyage in April 1912.

q: What time did the Titanic strike the iceberg?

q.e: The Titanic struck an iceberg at 11:40 PM on 14 April 1912 and sank at 2:20 AM on 15 April.

q: Which one of the following was commonly referred to as El Caudillo?

q.e: "El Caudillo" ("the leader") was the title of Spain's dictator, Francisco Franco, who ruled from 1939 to 1975.

q: On what date is Festivus celebrated?

q.e: Festivus, the holiday from Seinfeld, is celebrated on 23 December, with the "airing of grievances" and "feats of strength."

q: What is used on Festivus instead of a tree?

q.e: Festivus uses an unadorned aluminum pole instead of a Christmas tree.

q: It is generally accepted that the April Fools Day tradition started in this country.

q.e: April Fools' Day is often linked to France's switch to the Gregorian calendar in 1582 (when New Year moved from April 1), which created "poisson d'avril."

q: According a legend all April Fools pranks must be perpetrated by this time on April 1st.

q.e: By tradition, April Fools' pranks must be played before noon. After noon, "the joke's on you."

q: In this European country April 1 is called April Gowk.

q.e: In Scotland, April Fools' Day is "Hunt-the-Gowk Day" (gowk = cuckoo or fool).

q: Which of these actors is not a Bronxite?

q.e: Nicolas Cage was born in Long Beach, California. He is not from the Bronx.

q: Which one of these famous personalities is a Bronxite?

q.e: Billy Joel was born in the Bronx in 1949 and raised on Long Island.

q: Which one of these political or military figures is a Broxnite?

q.e: Colin Powell, born in Harlem, was raised in the South Bronx. He was Chairman of the Joint Chiefs and Secretary of State.

q: Which one of these persons is not a Bronxite?

q.e: Spike Lee was born in Atlanta and grew up in Brooklyn, not the Bronx.

q: Which one of these famous people is not a Bronxite ?

q.e: Anne Rice, the Vampire Chronicles author, was born in New Orleans.

q: It is generally unknown that ten dollars are referred to as this.

q.e: A $10 gold coin was called an "eagle" in the US from 1792. A half eagle was $5, and a double eagle $20.

q: Until 1974 the value of the United States dollar was tied to and backed by ...

q.e: The US dollar was tied to gold under Bretton Woods until 1971. Americans couldn't own gold bullion until 1974.

q: Which is NOT one of the official eight Australian States or Territories?

q.e: Australia has six states and two main mainland territories (NT and ACT), plus external territories like the Coral Sea Islands. The latter isn't one of the eight.

q: What continent is the Gobi Desert in?

q.e: The Gobi Desert covers approximately 500,000 square miles across southern Mongolia and northern China in Asia. It is a rain-shadow desert formed because the Himalayas block rain-carrying clouds from the Indian Ocean.

q: In December 1981, General Leopoldo Galtieri seized power in this South American country.

q.e: General Leopoldo Galtieri took power in Argentina in December 1981 and launched the Falklands invasion in April 1982.

q: Vidkun Quisling was leader of this country during World War II.

q.e: Vidkun Quisling headed the Nazi puppet government of Norway during WWII. His name became a word for "traitor".

q: What is the capital of the Netherlands?

q.e: Amsterdam is the constitutional capital of the Netherlands, though the seat of government, parliament, and the Supreme Court are located in The Hague. Hungary is a European country, not a city.

q: Many European countries have a flag with three horizontal stripes, colored white, blue and red (in different orders or shades). Which country is not one of them?

q.e: France's flag is blue-white-red, with vertical bands. The Netherlands (red-white-blue), Russia (white-blue-red) and Luxembourg have horizontal bands.

q: All Nordic countries have a Scandinavian cross on their flags. Which statement is true about these flags?
The Swedish flag is the only one without any white.
The Finnish flag has the cross upside down.
Norway and Iceland have exactly the same flags.
Yellow is the dominant color of Scandinavian flags.

q.e: Sweden's flag is yellow on blue, the only Nordic flag with no white. All other Nordic cross flags use white.

q: Which country has the most colors on its flag that does not have any seal or brocade?

q.e: South Africa's flag has six colors (black, gold, green, white, red and blue), the most for a flag with no emblem.

q: Which of these nations has a flag not rectangular in shape?

q.e: Nepal's flag is the only national flag that isn't a rectangle, made of two stacked pennants.

q: Which countrys flag has the Latin motto Ordem e Progresso (Order and Progress) on it?

q.e: Brazil adopted its national flag in 1889 featuring the motto 'Ordem e Progresso' across a central blue disc, inspired by French philosopher Auguste Comte's positivist motto.

q: The Italian flag is green-white-red. What is the traditional color of Italian athletes in international competitions?

q.e: Italian national sports teams wear blue (azzurro), from the House of Savoy's color. They're called the Azzurri.

q: The Dutch are sometimes called Oranje, which means the orange colored. What is orange on the Dutch flag?
The thin stripe with the Dutch motto

q.e: The Dutch flag is red, white and blue. Orange comes from the House of Orange-Nassau, the royal family.

q: Which country has a plain green flag?
None, the green flag is the official symbol of Green Peace

q.e: Libya had a plain green flag from 1977 to 2011. Since then it uses the red-black-green flag with a crescent.

q: On which Sunday in May is Mothers Day celebrated in the USA and Canada?

q.e: In 1914, US President Woodrow Wilson signed a proclamation establishing Mother's Day as an official holiday on the second Sunday in May, an observance Canada adopted as well. By contrast, the UK celebrates Mothering Sunday on the fourth Sunday of Lent.

q: What is unique about the month of May?
No other month begins on the same day of the week as May.
It is the only month with no holidays.

q.e: May is the only month that starts on a different day of the week than every other month in the same year.

q: February is African American Heritage Month. What group is May associated with?

q.e: May is Asian American and Pacific Islander Heritage Month in the US. February is Black History Month.

q: May in the Northern Hemisphere is the seasonal equivalent to what month in the Southern Hemisphere?

q.e: May is late spring in the Northern Hemisphere and late autumn in the Southern Hemisphere, as November in the north is.

q: E. J. Smith, the captain of the RMS Titanic, served on which other ship of the White Star Line?

q.e: Captain Edward J. Smith commanded the Olympic, Titanic's sister ship, before the Titanic. It was his last voyage.

q: What was the name of the ship that nearly collided with the Titanic in Southampton?

q.e: As the Titanic left Southampton, its suction nearly pulled the SS New York free from its moorings, and they nearly collided.

q: What was the name of the daily newspaper on board the Titanic?

q.e: The "Atlantic Daily Bulletin" was printed aboard the Titanic, with news, stock quotes and the menu.

q: Where was the Carpathia headed when the distress call from Titanic was transmitted?

q.e: The Carpathia was bound for Fiume (Rijeka), on a Mediterranean route, when it heard the Titanic's distress call and rushed to help.

q: When did the Carpathia arrive in New York with the rescued survivors of the RMS Titanic?

q.e: The Carpathia arrived in New York on the evening of 18 April 1912, with 705 survivors.

q: Jock Hume, violinist with the orchestra on board the Titanic, perished when the ship sank. What did the agency that employed the musician send to his family after the disaster?

q.e: Jock Hume, the violinist, died on the Titanic. The agency that hired him reportedly billed his family for his uniform.

q: These countries are all republics except one. Which one is a kingdom?

q.e: Spain is a constitutional monarchy under King Felipe VI. France, Germany, Italy and Portugal are republics.

q: Three of these countries are kingdoms. One is a republic. Which one is it?

q.e: Italy has been a republic since 1946. Spain, Belgium and the Netherlands are kingdoms.

q: On 15 September, 1973 King Carl XVI Gustaf became the ruler of which of these modern kingdoms?

q.e: Carl XVI Gustaf became King of Sweden on 15 September 1973, after the death of his grandfather Gustaf VI Adolf.

q: What is the proper name of Queen Elizabeth IIs realm?
The Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
The Kingdom of Great Britain, Ireland and Scotland

q.e: Her realm is the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, plus the other Commonwealth realms she reigned over.

q: According to the Roman calendar, in which of these months did the day of ides fall on the same day as in March ?

q.e: The Ides fell on the 15th in March, May, July and October, and on the 13th in the other months.

q: In the Roman calendar, what did the day called ides mark each month?

q.e: The Ides originally fell on the full moon in the Roman lunar calendar. Later it was a fixed date.

q: This actress, who played on The Golden Girls, was born On January 17, 1922.

q.e: Betty White, who played Rose on The Golden Girls, was born on 17 January 1922 and died on 31 December 2021.

q: Two significant earthquakes occurred on January 17. The first was a 6.7 magnitude earthquake in Northbridge, California. The second was a 7.3 magnitude earthquake near Kobe, Japan. In what two consecutive years did they occur?

q.e: The Northridge, California earthquake (6.7) struck on 17 January 1994, and the Kobe earthquake (6.9-7.3) on 17 January 1995.

q: St. Patricks Day is traditionally a feast day celebrating the Patron Saint of what country?

q.e: Saint Patrick is the primary patron saint of Ireland, commemorated on March 17, the reputed date of his death in the fifth century. Despite becoming the symbol of Irish heritage, historical records show he was born in Roman Britain.

q: In what city does the largest St. Patricks Day Parade take place?

q.e: New York City's St. Patrick's Day Parade is the largest in the world, held annually since 1762. It runs up Fifth Avenue.

q: Out in the Mojave desert, Las Vegas is far from any other metropolitan areas. Which is the closest?

q.e: Las Vegas's nearest big metropolitan area is Los Angeles, about 270 miles away. Phoenix and Salt Lake City are also far.

q: Which of the following is the major interstate highway running through Las Vegas?

q.e: Interstate 15 runs through Las Vegas, from San Diego to the Canadian border.

q: Each year the celebrations of Independence Day in Coney Island, Brooklyn, New York City include this unusual contest.

q.e: Nathan's Famous Fourth of July Hot Dog Eating Contest has taken place annually at Coney Island since roughly 1972, drawing world-class competitive eaters from across the globe.

q: Which is the first day of the forty-day period of Lent in the Western Christian calendar?

q.e: Ash Wednesday marks the start of the 40-day penitential season leading up to Easter, excluding Sundays. On this day, worshippers often receive ashes in the shape of a cross on their foreheads.

q: Which of these famous Scots was not born in Edinburgh, Scotlands capital since 1437?

q.e: Adam Smith, the economist, was born in Kirkcaldy, Fife. Edinburgh-born figures include Alexander Graham Bell and Arthur Conan Doyle.

q: When did the independent Kingdom of Scotland become a part of the Kingdom of Great Britain?
With the Act of Union of 1707
With the Act of Union of August, 1800
With the Act of Union of 1814
With the Act of Union of 1840

q.e: The Acts of Union in 1707 united England and Scotland into the Kingdom of Great Britain.

q: Which is the patron saint of Scotland, celebrated on November 30?

q.e: St Andrew's Day is 30 November, and he's Scotland's patron saint. The saltire flag is a cross of St Andrew.

q: Which of the following statements about Scottish law is true?
In criminal cases, there is a third possible verdict - not proven.
Scottish law is not taught as a university subject.
Scottish law is not based on Roman law.
When Scotland joined Great Britain, the Scottish legal system was abolished.

q.e: Scottish courts can give a "not proven" verdict, besides guilty and not guilty. Not proven results in acquittal.

q: Which of these Scottish bands was named after a character from Wim Wenders movie Paris, Texas?

q.e: Travis, the Scottish band from Glasgow, took its name from Harry Dean Stanton's character, Travis Henderson, in Paris, Texas (1984).

q: The national flag of Scotland features what two colours?

q.e: Scotland's flag, the Saltire, is a white diagonal cross on a blue field.

q: The worlds first international football match was played in 1872 between the national teams of Scotland and which country?

q.e: The first official international football match was Scotland v England, held in Glasgow on 30 November 1872. It ended 0-0.

q: No Pants Day is when people celebrate the freedom associated with not wearing pants. When is it celebrated?

q.e: No Pants Day is celebrated on the first Friday in May. The "No Pants Subway Ride" started in New York in 2002.

q: This is what some people celebrate on April 20th.

q.e: "4/20" (April 20) is an informal holiday for cannabis users. The origin is a 1971 California high school group.

q: July 22 and April 26 are unofficial celebration days of the mathematical constant Pi. Which is the third day held in honor of Pi?

q.e: Pi Day is 14 March (3.14), Pi Approximation Day is 22 July (22/7), and 26 April is for 'Pi' as 6.28/2 = 3.14 in Tau terms.

q: International Talk Like a Pirate day, invented by two Americans, is celebrated on this date.

q.e: International Talk Like a Pirate Day is on 19 September, started in 1995 by John Baur and Mark Summers.

q: Who celebrates Ask a Stupid Question day?

q.e: Ask a Stupid Question Day is 28 September, which started with teachers who liked to encourage students to ask questions.

q: Sweetest Day, observed on the 3rd Saturday of October, originated in this city.

q.e: Sweetest Day, held on the third Saturday in October, started in Cleveland, Ohio, in 1921 as a candy promotion.

q: Labor Day in the United States falls on what Monday of the month?

q.e: President Grover Cleveland signed legislation in 1894 establishing Labor Day as a federal holiday celebrated annually on the first Monday in September.
Mexico's Independence Day is on 16 September, marking Father Hidalgo's "Grito de Dolores" in 1810.

q: Which Cabinet Officer first assumed his duties in the month of September?

q.e: The Department of Justice's Attorney General (Edmund Randolph) first took duty in September 1789, and Washington's Cabinet came into being that fall.

q: What was the currency unit in Germany until 2001?

q.e: Germany's currency was the Deutsche Mark until the euro replaced it in 2002 (notes and coins), after the euro was introduced in 1999.

q: What is the currency unit in Japan?

q.e: The yen was officially adopted during the Meiji Restoration by the New Currency Act of 1871. The word yen translates literally to round object or circle.

q: This famous skyscraper in Hong Kong, designed by the architect I. M. Pei, and is 315 meters high?

q.e: The Bank of China Tower in Hong Kong, designed by I. M. Pei and completed in 1990, is 315 m (367 m with spires).

q: Which famous 102-storey skyscraper was designed by Shreve, Lamb and Harmon and built in 1931?

q.e: The Empire State Building opened in New York City on May 1, 1931, standing at 1,250 feet tall (excluding the spire) and holding the title of world's tallest building for nearly 40 years.

q: This amazingly tall and slender 175-meter cylindrical building in London was used for different post and telecommunications services.

q.e: The BT Tower (formerly the Post Office Tower) in London, 177 m tall, opened in 1965 for telecommunications.

q: What is the name of the capital city of Scotland?

q.e: Edinburgh is the capital of Scotland, though Glasgow is bigger.

q: Khartoum is the capital city of this country.

q.e: Khartoum is the capital of Sudan, where the Blue Nile and White Nile meet.

q: Detroit, Michigan, aka Motown, is twinned with this city.

q.e: Detroit and Windsor, Ontario, face each other across the Detroit River and are sister cities.
