q: Kansas City, Kansas and Kansas City, Missouri are twin cities. Which of them had a larger population in 2006?

q.e: Kansas City, Missouri, has more people (about 460,000) than Kansas City, Kansas (about 150,000). They are separate cities in separate states.

q: In which South American country was the Nazi murderer Adolph Eichman captured?

q.e: Adolf Eichmann was captured by Israeli agents in Buenos Aires, Argentina, in May 1960, and was tried and hanged in Israel in 1962.

q: The famous soprano Yma Sumac is from which Latin American country?

q.e: Yma Sumac (1922-2008) was a Peruvian soprano known for her extraordinary vocal range.

q: On October 4, 1648, Dutch Director-General Peter Stuyvesant created Americas first volunteer fire department in which city?

q.e: In 1648 Peter Stuyvesant created a "Rattle Watch" in New Amsterdam, the first organized fire protection in what became New York.

q: What was the first European city to have a complex sewage disposal system?

q.e: Rome had the first major sewer system in Europe, the Cloaca Maxima, built in the 6th century BC.

q: Soccers home is Europe. Which two teams played the first official international game?

q.e: The first official international football match was between Scotland and England in 1872.

q: Who were the first Europeans allowed to trade with Japan?

q.e: The Dutch were the only Europeans allowed to trade with Japan from 1641 to 1853, on the island of Dejima in Nagasaki.

q: In 2005 three bombs exploded in the London Underground killing 52 and injuring 700. This first kamikaze attack in Western Europe took place in which month?

q.e: The 7 July 2005 London bombings, on the Underground and a bus, killed 52 people and injured about 700. They were suicide bombings.

q: What does the word kamikaze mean in Japanese?

q.e: Kamikaze combines kami (spirit or divine) and kaze (wind). It originally referred to the historic typhoons in 1274 and 1281 that saved Japan by dispersing invading Mongol fleets.

q: 192 people died and 2,050 were wounded in the Madrid train bombings in 2004. What part of the day was it, when the tragic event took place?

q.e: The Madrid train bombings happened on the morning of 11 March 2004, during the morning rush hour.

q: What is the state motto of Texas, also called The Lone Star State?

q.e: Texas's motto is "Friendship." The state name comes from the Caddo word táysha, "friends."

q: Which historical figure is referred to as the Father of Texas?

q.e: Stephen F. Austin brought the first 300 Anglo-American families, known as the 'Old Three Hundred', to Mexican Texas in the 1820s. Texas's state capital was named in his honor in 1839.

q: After gaining its independence from Mexico, the Republic of Texas existed for what period of time?

q.e: The Republic of Texas lasted from 1836, when it declared independence, until annexation by the US in 1845.

q: Which one of these American entertainers was not born in Texas?

q.e: Tommy Lee, Mötley Crüe's drummer, was born in Athens, Greece. Janis Joplin and Beyoncé were born in Texas.

q: Which song was selected in 1929 as the official state song of Texas?

q.e: "Texas, Our Texas" was adopted as the Texas state song in 1929.

q: The slogan Tippecanoe and Tyler Too was used by which presidential candidate?

q.e: "Tippecanoe and Tyler Too" was William Henry Harrison and John Tyler's 1840 campaign slogan. Harrison had won at Tippecanoe in 1811.

q: A Choice, Not an Echo was the slogan of Republicans opposed to what?

q.e: "A Choice, Not an Echo" is Phyllis Schlafly's 1964 book that backed Barry Goldwater and criticized the Republican establishment.

q: The RMS Titanic set sail from Southampton, England on what date?

q.e: The Titanic left Southampton on 10 April 1912 on its maiden voyage.
The Titanic was 882 feet 9 inches (269 m) long, and 92 feet wide.

q: How long did it take for the Titanic to sink?

q.e: The Titanic sank in about 2 hours and 40 minutes after striking the iceberg at 11:40 PM on 14 April 1912.

q: What state is Mount Rushmore in?

q.e: Mount Rushmore is located in the Black Hills region of Pennington County, South Dakota. Carved between 1927 and 1941, it depicts the 60-foot faces of four US presidents.

q: Which former US president won the Nobel Peace Prize on 11 October 2002?

q.e: Jimmy Carter won the 2002 Nobel Peace Prize, announced on 11 October 2002, for his work for peace and human rights after his presidency.

q: On 11 October 1942, the United States defeated this country in the Battle of Esperance.

q.e: The Battle of Cape Esperance (11-12 October 1942) was a US Navy victory over Japan near Guadalcanal.

q: Which former president and first lady got married on October 11th?

q.e: Bill and Hillary Clinton married on 11 October 1975 in Fayetteville, Arkansas.

q: What are the primary colors of the Philippine national flag?

q.e: The Philippine flag has blue and red bands, a white triangle, and a yellow sun with eight rays and three stars.

q: This constitutional monarchy is located in Western Asia, its capital is Amman, and its official language is Arabic.

q.e: Jordan is a constitutional monarchy in Western Asia, with Amman as the capital.

q: According to the Bureau of Engraving and Printing, the average life of a one dollar bill is this.

q.e: The Bureau of Engraving and Printing says a $1 bill lasts about 6.6 years today. Older figures said 18-22 months.

q: If you had $1 million in $1 bills then the million would weigh this much.

q.e: One US bill weighs about one gram, so a million $1 bills weighs about a metric ton, or 2,200 pounds.

q: This is the time on the Independence Hall clock on the back of the $100 bill.

q.e: The clock on Independence Hall on the back of the $100 bill reads 4:10.

q: On the back of the $50 bill you can see this building.

q.e: The back of the $50 bill shows the US Capitol.

q: Its a beautiful Saturday morning and you want to explore Central Park with your family. Which form of transportation should your family NOT plan on using?

q.e: Central Park's drives are closed to cars on weekends, so families can walk, cycle or take carriages.

q: Which of the following countries shares its independence day with the United States?

q.e: The Philippines marked 4 July (the date of US independence) as its own independence day from 1946 to 1962, before switching to 12 June. Puerto Rico isn't independent.

q: Which country elected Felipe Calderon President on September 6, 2006?

q.e: Felipe Calderón was declared winner of Mexico's 2006 presidential election by a narrow margin. The election result was contested.

q: Which of the following countries is located in Central America?

q.e: Costa Rica is in Central America. The other countries in the region are Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua and Panama.

q: This northern English city is noted for a Viking Centre, a street of mediaeval shops known as The Shambles, and a famous Minster.

q.e: York, in North Yorkshire, has the Jorvik Viking Centre, the medieval Shambles street and York Minster.

q: On November 18 in 1913, Lincoln Beachy became the first American to perform which one of the following?
Double inside one and one-hale dive

q.e: Lincoln Beachey was the first American to loop-the-loop in a plane, in 1913. He died in a crash in 1915.

q: Gotland, the largest island in the Baltic Sea, is also a province of this Baltic country.

q.e: Gotland, in the Baltic Sea, is Sweden's largest island and a province and county of Sweden.

q: He was the second U.S. President and was born on October 30, 1735.

q.e: John Adams served as the first U.S. Vice President under George Washington before becoming the second President in 1797. Thomas Jefferson, born in 1743, was his vice president and succeeded him as the third president.

q: What make was the official state limousine of many US Presidents, including Franklin D. Roosevelt and John F. Kennedy?

q.e: Lincoln Motor Company limousines were used by presidents, including FDR's "Sunshine Special" and JFK's Continental, in which he was shot.

q: Which of the following races is always held in July and lasts approximately 3 weeks?

q.e: The Tour de France is traditionally held each July over roughly 23 days with 21 stages. The Giro d'Italia is held in May, while the Vuelta a España takes place in late summer, typically August and September.

q: Which President assured the American people, I am not a crook.?

q.e: Richard Nixon uttered the famous phrase I am not a crook during a televised press conference at Walt Disney World on November 17, 1973, while addressing the Watergate scandal. He resigned from office the following year.

q: What President spoke of a kinder, gentler nation and a thousand points of light?

q.e: George H. W. Bush spoke of a "kinder, gentler nation" and "a thousand points of light" in his 1989 inaugural and 1988 convention speeches.

q: Which President said Ich bin ein Berliner.?

q.e: John F. Kennedy delivered his historic speech in West Berlin on June 26, 1963, to show American solidarity with West Germany following the construction of the Berlin Wall in 1961.

q: What city is the Walt Disney World Resort located in?

q.e: Walt Disney World is in Bay Lake and Lake Buena Vista, near Orlando, Florida. It opened in 1971.

q: The freedom of speech, religion, petition and assembly are outlined in this amendment of the United States Bill of Rights.

q.e: Ratified in 1791, the First Amendment protects five distinct freedoms: speech, religion, the press, peaceful assembly, and the right to petition the government for redress of grievances.

q: Who is the author of the United States Bill of Rights?

q.e: James Madison introduced the amendments to the First United States Congress in 1789, earning him the nickname Father of the Constitution. Thomas Jefferson was serving as minister to France at the time.

q: This politician did not originally want a Bill of Rights for the United States.

q.e: James Madison opposed a Bill of Rights at first, believing the Constitution already protected rights, and later drafted it. Jefferson supported one.

q: Which was the tenth state to approve the United States Bill of Rights?

q.e: Virginia ratified the Bill of Rights on 15 December 1791, which made it effective, as the 10th of 14 states.

q: Which amendment of the United States Bill of Rights prohibits cruel and unusual punishment?

q.e: The Eighth Amendment prohibits the federal government from imposing excessive bail, excessive fines, or cruel and unusual punishments. Ratified in 1791, its language was largely borrowed from the English Bill of Rights of 1689.

q: Which amendment of the United States Bill of Rights gives the defendant the right to be judged by jury?

q.e: The Sixth Amendment guarantees the right to a jury trial in criminal cases, and the Seventh in civil cases.

q: Which amendment of the United States Bill of Rights protects the individual from unreasonable search and seizures?

q.e: The Fourth Amendment safeguards citizens against unreasonable searches and seizures and establishes that warrants must be supported by probable cause. The First Amendment covers speech, religion, and assembly, while the Second covers the right to bear arms.

q: Which of these states does not border Pennsylvania?

q.e: Pennsylvania borders New York, New Jersey, Delaware, Maryland, West Virginia and Ohio (plus Lake Erie). Connecticut doesn't border it.

q: This king, born in Bethlehem, was the second King of Israel.

q.e: According to the Hebrew Bible, David succeeded Saul as the second king of the United Monarchy of Israel around 1000 BCE. Born in Bethlehem, he was anointed as a youth by the prophet Samuel.

q: Bethlehem is six miles south of what city?

q.e: Bethlehem is about six miles south of Jerusalem, in the West Bank, and the traditional birthplace of Jesus.

q: In what state was a person executed by lethal injection on December 14, 1982?

q.e: Charlie Brooks Jr. became the first person executed by lethal injection in the US, in Texas on 7 December 1982.

q: Which of the following countries gained its independence from Russia in December of 1917?

q.e: Finland declared independence from Russia on 6 December 1917, during the chaos of the Russian Revolution. Soviet Russia recognized it on 4 January 1918.

q: What state capital is also the county seat of Marion County, U.S.?

q.e: Indianapolis is both Indiana's capital and the seat of Marion County.

q: This U.S. state capital is located on a land that was once a Native American village called Standing Peachtree.

q.e: Atlanta's site was once the Creek village of Standing Peachtree on the Chattahoochee River.

q: Where did the production of the Mustang model of Ford first begin?

q.e: Ford began producing the Mustang in 1964 at its Dearborn, Michigan, plant before it went on sale on 17 April 1964.

q: Where is the Honda Motor Company headquarters located?

q.e: Honda was founded by Soichiro Honda in Hamamatsu in 1948 and is headquartered in the Minato ward of Tokyo, Japan.

q: In what Northeastern state did the first daily newspaper originate?

q.e: The Pennsylvania Packet and Daily Advertiser, launched in Philadelphia in 1784, was the first daily newspaper in the US.

q: Cumberland University, located in Lebanon, Tennessee, lost the most lopsided football game in history to what school?

q.e: Georgia Tech beat Cumberland College 222-0 on 5 October 1916, the most lopsided score in American football history.

q: Most European countries are divided into provinces, regions, federal subjects or municipalities. Which of the following is divided into states?

q.e: Germany is a federal republic of 16 states (Länder), like Bavaria and Berlin.

q: The first 3D movie presentation was done in this citys famous Astor Theater.

q.e: The first 3D movie shown to the public was in 1915 at the Astor Theatre in New York City. It used red-green anaglyph glasses.

q: What is the official state bird of Illinois?

q.e: The northern cardinal is the state bird of Illinois (and six other states).

q: What is the official nickname of Illinois?

q.e: Illinois was nicknamed the Prairie State in the 19th century because much of its original landscape was covered by vast, flat tallgrass prairies.

q: Complete the state motto of Pennsylvania: Virtue, Liberty and _________ .

q.e: Pennsylvania's motto is "Virtue, Liberty and Independence."

q: Which of the following was first created by Benjamin Franklin?

q.e: Benjamin Franklin founded the first public lending library, volunteer fire company and hospital in America, but not the first zoo.

q: Drivers Education classes were first offered in this Pennsylvania town.

q.e: Driver's education started in State College, Pennsylvania, in the 1930s, when Amos Neyhart taught the first high school course.

q: General Washington slept here during the winter of 1777 - 1778.

q.e: Washington and the Continental Army encamped at Valley Forge, Pennsylvania, from December 1777 to June 1778, enduring severe winter shortages while reorganizing their forces.

q: The name of Michigan is a French adaptation of the Ojibwe word meaning what?

q.e: "Michigan" comes from the Ojibwe "mishigami," meaning "large water". It is surrounded by four of the five Great Lakes.

q: How long is the Mackinac Bridge?

q.e: The Mackinac Bridge, which connects Michigan's two peninsulas, is about 5 miles long (8,614 ft between anchorages), one of the longest suspension bridges in the world.

q: What animal is the dominant object on the Michigan state flag?

q.e: Michigan's flag shows the state coat of arms with an elk and a moose supporting a shield, and a bald eagle above. A deer appears elsewhere on the state seal.

q: What city does Carl Sandburg call Hog Butcher for the World and City of the Big Shoulders?

q.e: Carl Sandburg introduced these iconic epithets in his 1914 poem Chicago, highlighting the city's booming Union Stock Yards meatpacking industry and industrial strength.

q: The term caliber in the field of firearms refers to which of the following?
Diameter of the barrel/bullet in inches
Length of the bullet in inches
Weight of the slug of a bullet

q.e: Caliber is the diameter of a gun's bore (or its bullet), usually in hundredths of an inch (.45) or in millimeters (9 mm).

q: Who is Deputy Sheriff Isaac Smith?
The first U.S. police officer to be killed in the line of duty
The man that shot Ronald Regan
The first police officer to become president of the U.S.
The first chief of police in NYC

q.e: Deputy Sheriff Isaac Smith of the New York City Sheriff's Office was killed in 1791 and is recorded as the first US police officer killed on duty.

q: City police in the U.S. gain their power and authority to arrest from which government body/person?

q.e: City police in the US get their authority to arrest from state law and local charters, usually through a city or state government.

q: What does the name Texas mean?

q.e: "Texas" comes from the Caddo word táysha, meaning "friends" or "allies."

q: Which port in Texas is the largest in the USA in terms of international commerce?

q.e: The Port of Houston is the busiest US port in international waterborne tonnage.

q: What river forms the Texas/Mexico border?

q.e: The Rio Grande, known in Mexico as the Rio Bravo, flows about 1,896 miles from Colorado to the Gulf of Mexico, forming over 1,250 miles of the US-Mexico border.

q: In which country does the Infant Jesus help Santa to give presents to children?

q.e: In the Czech Republic, Ježíšek (Baby Jesus) brings Christmas presents. Santa isn't part of the tradition.

q: How many reindeer pull the sleigh of Father Frost according to beliefs in Ukraine?

q.e: In Ukraine and Russia, Ded Moroz (Father Frost) traditionally rides a three-horse troika. The number of animals is a quiz-source detail.

q: In which country does Santa visit children twice, once on December 4th and once on December 6th?

q.e: In Belgium and the Netherlands, Sinterklaas (St. Nicholas) brings gifts on 6 December, and children receive treats on St. Nicholas's Eve.

q: In which country are presents brought to children by a camel instead of by Santa Claus?

q.e: In some Middle Eastern Christian traditions, the camel of one of the Three Wise Men brings children presents on Epiphany (6 January).

q: In terms of area, which US state is about the size of Israel?

q.e: New Jersey is about 8,700 square miles, similar to Israel at about 8,500 (within its pre-1967 borders).

q: Which ancient city was declared Israel's official capital with a law from January 1950?

q.e: Israel's Knesset declared Jerusalem its capital in January 1950, though most countries keep embassies in Tel Aviv.

q: What are the only two colors on the Israeli flag?

q.e: The flag of Israel, adopted five months after the country's declaration of independence in 1948, features a blue Star of David and two horizontal blue stripes on a white field.

q: What are the official languages in the linguistically and culturally diverse community of Israel?

q.e: Hebrew and Arabic were Israel's official languages; the 2018 Nation-State Law made Hebrew the sole official language and gave Arabic a special status.

q: This river, flowing through the Great Rift Valley into the Dead Sea, forms much of the border between Jordan and Israel.

q.e: The Jordan River flows roughly 156 miles (251 km) southward through the Jordan Rift Valley, connecting the Sea of Galilee to the Dead Sea.

q: What do you call a trade union that consists of employees of one company?

q.e: A union that covers workers at a single company is a "company union" or "enterprise union", as opposed to an industry-wide or craft union.

q: This movie centered on A. Phillip Randolphs efforts to organize the porters at the Pullman Rail Company.

q.e: 10,000 Black Men Named George (2002) is a TV film about A. Philip Randolph's effort to unionize Pullman porters, who were often called "George."

q: In 1936 the United Rubber Workers became the first unionists to use this tactic.

q.e: In 1936 Akron rubber workers staged one of the first sit-down strikes in the US, at Goodyear, where they stayed inside the factory.

q: What was the largest ancestry group in Hawaii according to 2000 estimates?

q.e: Asian Americans (Japanese, Filipino, Chinese) are Hawaii's largest ancestry group, with whites and Native Hawaiians behind.

q: The first recorded military submarine was designed to attach explosive charges to ships in harbor and was called Turtle. It was invented by David Bushnell in 1775 and was operated by this number of crewmen.

q.e: David Bushnell's Turtle (1775) was a one-man submersible, hand-cranked by its operator, Sergeant Ezra Lee.

q: SS submarines use diesel-electric propulsion. What kind of propulsion do SSN submarines utilize?

q.e: SSN means nuclear-powered attack submarine. SS is a diesel-electric attack submarine.

q: Peoples Republic of Kampuchea is a former name of what country?

q.e: The People's Republic of Kampuchea (1979-1989) was the Vietnamese-backed state that followed the Khmer Rouge regime in Cambodia.

q: What is the nickname of Australia?

q.e: Australia is nicknamed "The Lucky Country," from Donald Horne's 1964 book, which used it ironically.

q: Which of these is a nickname of New Zealand?

q.e: New Zealand's nicknames include "Land of the Long White Cloud" (Aotearoa) and "Godzone." "High Country" refers to a region of the South Island.

q: Mesopotamia is the former name of what country?

q.e: Mesopotamia comes from ancient Greek meaning 'land between rivers', referring to the Tigris and Euphrates river systems. The heartland of ancient Mesopotamia corresponds directly with modern-day Iraq.

Indonesia was colonized by the Netherlands and known as the Dutch East Indies until declaring independence in 1945. The Spanish East Indies referred instead to territories centered around the Philippines.

q: Spanish East Indies is the former name of what country?

q.e: The Spanish East Indies (1565-1899) included the Philippines, the Marianas, Guam and other Pacific islands.

q: What U.S. state capital was founded in 1868 near the Salt River?

q.e: Phoenix, Arizona, was founded in 1867-68 near the Salt River, by settlers who used old Hohokam canals.

q: What is the capital of the U.S. state in which the largest city is Omaha?

q.e: Omaha is Nebraska's largest city, and the capital is Lincoln.

q: What is the largest U.S. state capital that is not the largest city in its state?

q.e: Austin has a population of roughly 970,000 residents, but Houston is the largest city in Texas with over 2.2 million. Phoenix and Boston are both the largest cities in their respective states.

q: What U.S. state capital has served as a state capital for the longest period, without a break?

q.e: Boston has been the capital of Massachusetts since 1630, the longest continuous run of any US state capital.

q: What state capital in the United States is nicknamed "The City Different�?

q.e: Santa Fe adopted the nickname The City Different in the early 20th century to celebrate its distinctive Pueblo Revival architecture and blend of Native American, Hispanic, and Anglo cultures.

q: Which of the following U. S. presidents was born in Massachusetts?

q.e: George H. W. Bush was born in Milton, Massachusetts, in 1924. John Adams, J.Q. Adams, JFK and Calvin Coolidge (Vermont-born) are also tied to Massachusetts, but Coolidge was born in Vermont.

q: Who was the first female Governor of Massachusetts?

q.e: Jane Swift became Massachusetts's first female governor (acting) in 2001, succeeding Paul Cellucci, when she was just 36. She was also the first to give birth in office.

q: Which town is located at the southwestern corner of Massachusetts?

q.e: Mount Washington is a town in the southwestern corner of Massachusetts, with fewer than 200 residents.

q: What is the name of the highest court in Massachusetts?

q.e: The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court (SJC) is the state's highest court and the oldest continuously functioning appellate court in the Americas (1692).

q: Which one of the following distinctions does the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority (MBTA) hold?
oldest subway tunnel still in use in the United States
deepest subway station in use in the world
longest subway system in the world
most expensive subway fare in the United States

q.e: Boston's MBTA includes the Tremont Street Subway, which opened in 1897 and is the oldest subway tunnel in the US still in use.

q: Which other state was originally a part of Massachusetts?

q.e: Maine was administered as an exclave of Massachusetts until it separated and achieved statehood as the 23rd state under the Missouri Compromise of 1820.

q: This river, the longest in New England, runs north-south through western Massachusetts.

q.e: The Connecticut River (410 miles) is the longest river in New England, flowing from the Canadian border through NH, VT, MA and CT.

q: Amman is the capital of what country?

q.e: Amman has served as the capital of Jordan since 1921, when the Emirate of Transjordan was established.

q: How many emirates does the United Arab Emirates consist of?

q.e: The United Arab Emirates is a federation formed in 1971 that consists of Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Sharjah, Ajman, Umm Al Quwain, and Fujairah, with Ras Al Khaimah joining in early 1972.

q: Which European capital is home to major EU institutions?

q.e: Brussels serves as the de facto capital of the European Union, hosting the headquarters of the European Commission and the Council of the European Union.

q: What Asian capital was known as the "Venice of the East?�

q.e: Bangkok, with its canals (khlongs), was called the "Venice of the East".

q: The Thames river is a major geographical feature of what capital city?

q.e: The River Thames flows 215 miles (346 km) through southern England, directly bisecting central London before emptying into the North Sea.

q: The United Nations was founded as a successor of this organization.

q.e: The League of Nations was created after World War I in 1920 to prevent future conflicts, but its failure to stop World War II led to the creation of the United Nations in 1945.

q: When was the flag of the United Nations adopted?

q.e: The UN flag, with the world map in a laurel wreath on a blue field, was adopted on 20 October 1947.

q: The United Nations headquarters building was constructed in New York City between 1949 and 1950 beside this river.

q.e: The United Nations headquarters, built 1948-1952, stands on the East River in Manhattan, on land donated by the Rockefeller family.

q: Which of these is not an official language of the United Nations?

q.e: The UN's six official languages are Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Russian and Spanish. Dutch is not one.

q: What is the form of address to a king or queen?

q.e: A king or queen is addressed as "Your Majesty" and referred to as "His/Her Majesty."

q: Who is the Supreme Governor of the Church of England?

q.e: The British monarch is the Supreme Governor of the Church of England. The Archbishop of Canterbury is its spiritual leader.

q: What is the most senior civil servant of a British Government ministry?

q.e: The Permanent Secretary is the most senior civil servant in a UK government department, working under the minister.

q: During what event is the Speech from the Throne delivered in the UK?
The appointment of the Archbishop of Canterbury

q.e: The Speech from the Throne (King's/Queen's Speech) is delivered at the State Opening of Parliament, and lays out the government's agenda.

q: The House of Lords includes appointed members, hereditary peers and which of the following?
representatives of the Church of England
senior members of the Royal Family

q.e: The House of Lords includes life peers, hereditary peers and 26 Church of England bishops (the Lords Spiritual).

q: In terms of yearly undrgraduate tuition the most expensive college in the USA is in this state.

q.e: College costs vary by year and source. In many rankings, the most expensive US colleges are private schools in places like New York and Massachusetts.

q: Which college has the largest endowment?

q.e: Harvard University holds the world's largest academic endowment, valued at over 50 billion dollars. The University of Texas system and Yale follow with endowments usually exceeding 40 billion dollars.

q: Dixie State College is located in this state.

q.e: Dixie State College is in St. George, Utah. It became Dixie State University and, since 2022, Utah Tech University.

q: All of the 80 or so students at this college spend half their sophmore years in Rome,Italy. Which school is this?

q.e: Thomas More College of Liberal Arts in Merrimack, New Hampshire, sends sophomores to Rome for a semester.

q: In Ireland and Scotland the Féile na Marbh traditionally took place at Samhain. What does Féile na Marbh mean?

q.e: Féile na Marbh means "Festival of the Dead", an Irish and Scottish Samhain tradition that honors the dead on 31 October-1 November.

q: The official motto of this country is the French phrase Liberté, égalité, fraternité.

q.e: Liberté, égalité, fraternité (Liberty, Equality, Fraternity) emerged during the French Revolution in the late 18th century. It was officially written into the French constitution as the national motto in 1946 and reaffirmed in 1958.

q: Three of the following states dont have an official state motto. Guess the odd one.

q.e: Every US state has an official motto. Poland is a country, not a state.

q: What is first TV station in the Philippines?

q.e: The Philippines' first TV station was DZAQ-TV, started by Alto Broadcasting System (ABS) in 1953.

q: Who was Abrahams nephew according to the Bible?

q.e: In the Book of Genesis, Lot is the son of Haran, making him the nephew of Abraham. He famously accompanied Abraham on his travels into Canaan.

q: Name the black scary ship featured in the first movie of Pirates of the Caribbean?

q.e: The Black Pearl is Captain Jack Sparrow's (later Barbossa's) ghostly black ship in Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl (2003).

q: What is the name of Captain Larsons seal-hunting schooner from the novel The Sea Wolf by Jack London?

q.e: In Jack London's The Sea-Wolf (1904), Captain Wolf Larsen commands the sealing schooner Ghost.

q: What is the name of Captain Disko Troops ship from Rudyard Kiplings novel Captains Courageous.

q.e: In Kipling's Captains Courageous (1897), Disko Troop captains the fishing schooner We're Here.

q: Who was the first ancient ruler, who officially declared Jerusalem capital of the Kingdom of Israel?

q.e: According to biblical tradition, King David captured Jerusalem from the Jebusites around 1000 BC and established it as the political and religious center of the United Kingdom of Israel. His son King Solomon later built the First Temple there.

q: Most of Jerusalems workforce is employed in what field?

q.e: Most of Jerusalem's workforce is employed in services, such as government, education, tourism and health care.

q: Which of these animals is the ancient symbol of Jerusalem and the Jewish People?

q.e: The Lion of Judah is a symbol of Jerusalem, whose flag and coat of arms features a lion.

q: What code word is assigned to the letter N in the Military Alphabet?

q.e: In the NATO phonetic alphabet, N is "November."

q: What code word is assigned to the letter W in the Military Alphabet?

q.e: W is "Whiskey" in the NATO phonetic alphabet.

q: What does Lima Zulu stand for?
Lemonade stand run by Zulu warriors

q.e: "Lima Zulu" is the phonetic form of "LZ", a landing zone for helicopters.

q: What is the oldest toy in the Istanbul Toy Museum?

q.e: The Istanbul Toy Museum has toys from the 19th century to today, and some older objects. Its oldest piece is claimed to be a miniature violin.

q: In what state is the town of Monkeys Eyebrow located?

q.e: Monkey's Eyebrow is an unincorporated community in Ballard County, Kentucky.

q: If you end up spending the night in the town of Santa Clause, what state are you in?

q.e: Santa Claus is a town in Spencer County, Indiana, and gets thousands of letters to Santa each year.

q: In what state is the town of Diagonal located?

q.e: Diagonal is a small town in Ringgold County, Iowa, named for a railroad route.

q: In this state there are two towns, named Green Level.

q.e: North Carolina has two (and more) communities named Green Level, in Alamance and Wake Counties.

q: Which of these is the name of a small California town?

q.e: Weed is a city in Siskiyou County, California, near Mount Shasta. It was named after Abner Weed.

q: In which state will you find the town of Cementville?

q.e: Cementville is a community in Clark County, Indiana, near Louisville.

q: A spinner in the airline industry refers to this.
A last-minute passenger, unable to locate their seat once aboard the aircraft
A wet runway, which requires additional braking room
A late arriving aircraft, which is reassigned a gate position

q.e: An airline "spinner" is a passenger who gets lost on the plane, spinning around looking for their seat.

q: In the airline industry, the term PAX, most commonly refers to which of the following?
A popular cable channel available on certain flights
The baggage compartment on an aircraft

q.e: PAX is airline shorthand for "passengers". It's used in ticketing and flight manifests.

q: The Term FLIFO, in the airline industry refers to this.
Flight Factors (contingents such as weather and other potential delay factors)

q.e: FLIFO stands for Flight Information, the system that displays arrival and departure times at airports.

q: In the US airline industry, TSA stands for this.

q.e: TSA is the Transportation Security Administration, created after 9/11 in 2001.

q: Massachusetts and Roxboro Rapid Transit Authority
Middlesboro and Annapolis Rapid Transit Authority

q.e: MARTA is the Metropolitan Atlanta Rapid Transit Authority.

q: If youre on the Blue Line, heading to Clinton/ Congress Station, what city are you in?

q.e: Chicago's CTA Blue Line serves Clinton, Jackson and other stations from O'Hare to Forest Park.
PATH stands for Port Authority Trans-Hudson, a rapid transit system between Manhattan and New Jersey.
BART stands for Bay Area Rapid Transit, serving San Francisco and the East Bay.

q: The 88 Corbett is a Bus line serving which city?

q.e: The 88 Corbett was a Muni bus line in San Francisco serving the Twin Peaks area (in San Francisco).

q: This aircraft was originally built as a tank buster.

q.e: The Fairchild Republic A-10 Thunderbolt II ("Warthog") was designed in the 1970s to destroy Soviet tanks, with a 30 mm cannon.

q: In 1980, U.S. President Jimmy Carter tried to free American hostages via a helicopter attack. Where were these hostages held?

q.e: Operation Eagle Claw (April 1980) aimed to rescue the 52 American hostages held in Tehran, Iran, but the helicopters failed in the desert.

q: All military equipment is effected by weather. During the Vietnam War, the Americans expected their equipment to last an average of 8 years. On average, how long did the equipment last in reality?

q.e: The jungle climate wore out US equipment in Vietnam within a couple of years, much faster than planned.

q: Once there was a settlement called New Amsterdam (named after Amsterdam) that was sold to the British. Under what name is New Amsterdam now known?

q.e: New Amsterdam became New York in 1664 when the English took the Dutch colony and renamed it after the Duke of York.

q: In which of the following countries is Dutch not an official language?

q.e: Dutch is official in the Netherlands, Belgium, Suriname and Curaçao, but not in Indonesia, despite the colonial past.

q: South Carolina was the ___ state to join the Union after the end of the Revolutionary War.

q.e: South Carolina ratified the US Constitution on 23 May 1788, becoming the 8th state.

q: What is the name of the capital and largest city of South Carolina?

q.e: Columbia is both the capital and largest city of South Carolina (the city was planned as the capital in 1786).

q: In what midwestern U.S. state is it legal to protest naked in front of city hall?

q.e: Lists of "weird laws" are often exaggerated or false. Public nudity laws in Illinois vary by city, and a general right to protest naked at city hall isn't a thing.

q: In what U.S. state is it illegal to dye baby chicks or ducklings blue and offer them for sale?

q.e: Several states, including Kentucky, ban selling dyed chicks and ducklings as novelty pets. Check the specific state law.

q: Which southwestern U.S. state actually has a law on the books making it illegal to sell or manufacture imitation cocaine?

q.e: Some states ban sale of imitation controlled substances. This is a real category of law, aimed at look-alike drugs.

q: In what U.S. state is it illegal to catch fish using the bare hands?

q.e: Fishing by hand ("noodling") is banned in some states and permitted in others. Indiana has allowed it at certain times.

q: What Smoky Mountain U.S. state has made it illegal to bring a skunk into the state?

q.e: Tennessee has restrictions on keeping wild animals like skunks. Pet skunk rules differ widely by state.

q: What is the amount of turkey consumed by the typical American in 2003?

q.e: Americans eat about 16 pounds of turkey per person per year (about 17.5 lb in 2003). The 13.7 lb figure is for a specific category or year.

q: What was the value of turkeys shipped by U.S. turkey producers in 2002?

q.e: US turkey production is worth several billion dollars. Figures for 2002 were around $3-4 billion.
Euston Station is a major London railway terminus in the Euston Road area, serving the West Coast Main Line to the Midlands and northwest England.

q: What country was once called Abyssinia?

q.e: Abyssinia was the historical European name for the Ethiopian Empire, derived from the Arabic Habashat. The nation officially adopted Ethiopia internationally in the early 20th century.

q: What is the official language of India?

q.e: India's constitution makes Hindi (Devanagari) the official language of the Union, with English as a second official language. There are also 22 scheduled languages.

q: What is the largest country in South America in terms of territory?

q.e: Brazil covers about 3.28 million square miles (8.51 million square km), taking up nearly half of the South American continent. Argentina is the second-largest country on the continent, covering about 1.07 million square miles.

q: What is the largest US state in terms of area?

q.e: Alaska covers roughly 665,000 square miles (1.72 million square km), which is more than twice the size of second-place Texas at about 268,597 square miles.

q: What is the name of the capital city of the Peoples Republic of China?

q.e: Beijing became the capital of the People's Republic of China upon its founding in 1949. While Shanghai has a larger population, Beijing remains the political and cultural center.

q: What is the largest country in the Americas in terms of territory?

q.e: Canada spans roughly 3.85 million square miles (9.98 million square km), making it larger than the United States, which covers about 3.8 million square miles (9.83 million square km). It is the second-largest country in the world overall after Russia.

q: What is the largest country on the planet in terms of territory?

q.e: Russia is by far the largest country in the world by area.

q: During the Vietnam War, Thailand was allied with what country?
Thailand was neutral, but favored the South Vietnamese.

q.e: Thailand supported the US in the Vietnam War, hosting US air bases and sending troops to South Vietnam.

q: On what date was the US Marine Corps founded?

q.e: The US Marine Corps was established on 10 November 1775 at Tun Tavern in Philadelphia by the Continental Congress.

q: What was the location of the first US Marine amphibious assault?

q.e: The first Marine amphibious landing was on New Providence in the Bahamas in March 1776, to capture gunpowder.

q: Where are the Pitcairn Islands located?

q.e: The Pitcairn Islands are in the South Pacific, midway between New Zealand and Peru. Descendants of the Bounty mutineers live there.

q: Who is in charge of the Vatican City?

q.e: The Pope is the sovereign of Vatican City, the world's smallest state, and head of the Catholic Church.

q: For what period of time are Popes elected to be the head of the Vatican City?

q.e: Under Catholic canon law, the Pope serves as the Bishop of Rome and sovereign of Vatican City for life, though voluntary resignation is permitted, as seen with Pope Benedict XVI in 2013.

q: What is the official language of the Vatican City?

q.e: Italian is the official language of Vatican City State used for legislation and daily administration, whereas Latin serves as the official language of the Holy See.

q: According to Vatican jurisdiction, what happens to a person who loses his/her Vatican citizenship and has no other citizenship?
Vatican citizenship cannot be lost - it is granted for life
Becomes citizen of whatever country he/she decides

q.e: Under Vatican law, a person who loses Vatican citizenship but has no other becomes an Italian citizen, which stops statelessness.

q: Which of the following facilities is not present in the Vatican City?

q.e: Vatican City has a heliport but no airport. It does have a railway station, a radio station and a pharmacy.

q: What abbreviation is used for a member of the Welsh Assembly?

q.e: "AM" meant Assembly Member in Wales, and since 2020 the Welsh Parliament (Senedd) has "MS" for Member of the Senedd.

q: Under what name is Thomas Woodward better known?

q.e: Tom Jones, the Welsh singer ("It's Not Unusual"), was born Thomas John Woodward in Pontypridd in 1940.

q: In which South American country is there a small population that speaks only Spanish and Welsh?

q.e: In Chubut Province, Argentina, Welsh settlers arrived in 1865 and their language and culture survive in Patagonia. Spanish is dominant.

q: The Japanese call Mount Fuji Fuji-san. San refers to which of the following?
A reading of the Chinese character that means mountain
A suffix adopted from WWII American troops
The Japanese word for the number three
A term of respect, like the san that follows Japanese names

q.e: In Fuji-san, "san" is a reading of the Chinese character for "mountain" (山). The honorific "-san" is a different word.

q: The Japanese word baitoh (pronounced BUY-toe) means part time job and is adapted from which language?

q.e: "Baito" (バイト) comes from German "Arbeit" (work) through "arubaito". Japanese uses many loanwords from German.

q: Before money existed, people obtained goods this way.

q.e: Before standardized commodity or fiat money was widely adopted, early human societies relied on bartering, exchanging goods and services directly for other needed items. Commodity currencies like grain, livestock, and cowrie shells eventually paved the way for coinage.

q: The first European metal coins, which resembled modern currency were made of this.

q.e: The first coins were made in Lydia (Turkey) around 600 BC from electrum, a gold-silver alloy. Silver coins came soon after, as in Greece.

q: The first bills (banknotes) appeared in this country.

q.e: Paper money was first developed during China's Tang dynasty in the 7th century as merchant receipts, and true government-issued banknotes appeared under the Song dynasty around the 11th century.

q: The first banknotes were made of this.

q.e: Early paper money in China followed earlier "leather money", with white deerskin tokens in the Han Dynasty (118 BC).

q: Oyster shells were used as money until this time.
Until the middle of the 20th century

q.e: Shells such as cowries and some oyster shells were used as currency in various parts of the world well into modern times.

q: This successful Russian submarine, used during World War II, was responsible for the sinking of the German refugee transport Goya in April 1945.

q.e: The Soviet submarine L-3 torpedoed the German ship Goya on 16 April 1945, killing about 6,000-7,000 refugees and soldiers.

q: What is the official state animal of Connecticut?

q.e: Connecticut's state animal is the sperm whale, chosen in 1975 in reference to its whaling history.

q: Who established the colony of Connecticut in 1636?

q.e: Thomas Hooker led settlers to found Hartford in 1636, and wrote the Fundamental Orders of Connecticut (1639).

q: What is the oldest university in Connecticut?

q.e: Yale University, founded in 1701 in New Haven, is Connecticut's oldest university and the third-oldest in the US.

q: She was the first Queen to win Time magazines title Man of the Year.

q.e: Queen Elizabeth II was Time's Woman of the Year in 1952. In 1936, Wallis Simpson was the first woman to be named.

q: The name of which continent is believed to mean dust, cave, and sunny according to various theories on the origin of its name?

q.e: Africa's name may come from the Latin "aprica" (sunny), the Greek "aphrike" (without cold), or a Phoenician word for dust.

q: Valletta is the capital city of an island country belonging to the territory of this continent.

q.e: Valletta is the capital of Malta, an island nation in southern Europe and an EU member.

q: On what continent is the Quechua language spoken by its indigenous peoples?

q.e: Quechua is spoken by millions in the Andes, in Peru, Bolivia, Ecuador and other countries in South America.

q: The Emu, the second-largest bird living on the planet, is indigenous to this continent.

q.e: The emu is an endemic flightless bird of Australia, second only to the African ostrich in height, reaching up to roughly 6.2 feet (1.9 meters) tall.

q: What is the largest and most populous continent on the planet?

q.e: Covering roughly 17 million square miles (44 million square km), Asia accounts for about 30 percent of Earth's land area. It is home to roughly 4.7 billion people, which is around 60 percent of the global population.

q: Mount McKinley, or Denali, is the highest mountain peak on this continent.

q.e: Denali (6,190 m), formerly Mount McKinley, is North America's highest peak, in Alaska's Alaska Range.

q: The longest river in the world is located on this continent, which is the second largest on the planet.

q.e: The Nile River runs roughly 6,650 kilometers (4,130 miles) northward through northeastern Africa, flowing through 11 countries into the Mediterranean Sea.

q: On which two continents are there cities named Darwin?

q.e: Darwin is a city in the Northern Territory of Australia. Other places named Darwin are in the USA (California) and the UK.

q: The name Canada comes from the St. Lawrence Iroquoian word, kanata. What does it mean in English?

q.e: "Canada" comes from "kanata," a St. Lawrence Iroquoian word for "village" or "settlement," recorded by Jacques Cartier in 1535.

q: What government agency was Newsweek Magazines CW 2008 referring to when they wrote Asleep at the regulatory switch?

q.e: Newsweek's 2008 "Asleep at the Switch" criticism of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) was linked to the financial crisis, as regulators failed to spot the problems.

q: Which of the following countries is smaller (in terms of land area) than Poland?

q.e: Poland's area is 312,696 km². Italy is about 301,000 km², a bit smaller.

q: Poland was one of the first countries to have a constitution (1791). Which constitution/s was/were passed earlier than the Polish one?

q.e: The US Constitution (1787) preceded Poland's Constitution of 3 May 1791, which was Europe's first modern codified national constitution.

q: What are the national colors of Poland?

q.e: Poland's national colors are white and red, as on its flag.

q: What was the Darfur region of western Sudan named after?
A tribe of people called the Fur tribe
A British explorer named William Darfur
The Fur river running through the region
The arabic word darfur meaning stove or furnace

q.e: Darfur means "home of the Fur," the Fur people, who ruled the Sultanate of Darfur.

q: If there is a crowd of children in a Darfur camp screaming Kawaja, kawaja! what is there in the center of the crowd?

q.e: "Kawaja" (khawaja) means a foreigner or white person in Sudanese Arabic. Children crowd around aid workers who are outsiders.

q: What feast commemorating Jesus triumphal entry into Jerusalem marks the beginning of the Holy Week?

q.e: Palm Sunday commemorates Jesus's entry into Jerusalem, where crowds laid palm branches on the road before him. Holy Week concludes a week later on Easter Sunday.

q: What day and year did the famous Battle of Culloden near Culloden, Scotland occur?

q.e: The Battle of Culloden was fought on 16 April 1746, the last pitched battle on British soil. The Jacobites were defeated.

q: Who smuggled the Scottish Bonnie Prince Charlie out of Scotland?

q.e: Flora MacDonald helped smuggle Bonnie Prince Charlie "over the sea to Skye" in June 1746, disguising him as her maid.

q: Which is the patron saint of Scotland?

q.e: Saint Andrew has been venerated as the patron saint of Scotland since at least the 8th century, and the saltire cross on which he was said to be martyred forms the Scottish national flag.

q: What is the common name for Prudhoe Bay?

q.e: Prudhoe Bay, on Alaska's Arctic coast, is on the "North Slope," the site of North America's largest oil field.

q: When individuals file for bankruptcy in the USA they file under this section of the Uniform Commercial Code.

q.e: Individuals in the US file for bankruptcy under the US Bankruptcy Code: Chapter 7 (liquidation) or Chapter 13 (repayment plan), not the Uniform Commercial Code.

q: Día de los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, is celebrated in what country on November 1st and 2nd?

q.e: Día de los Muertos is celebrated across Mexico on 1-2 November, with altars (ofrendas), marigolds and sugar skulls.

q: What famous television host deemed Americas Oldest Teenager celebrates his birthday in November?

q.e: Dick Clark, "America's Oldest Teenager," was born on 30 November 1929, and hosted American Bandstand and New Year's Rockin' Eve. He died in 2012.

q: What major annual thoroughbred horse race is held in Australia during the first week of November?

q.e: The Melbourne Cup, "the race that stops a nation," is run on the first Tuesday of November.

q: What famous basketball players father was murdered on July 23, 1993?

q.e: Michael Jordan's father, James R. Jordan Sr., was murdered on 23 July 1993. Michael retired from basketball that October.

q: Which member of the RB group Destinys Child was born on July 23,1980?

q.e: Michelle Williams of Destiny's Child was born on 23 July 1979 or 1980 (sources differ) in Rockford, Illinois.

q: What do Chinese kids have for lunch on their birthday?

q.e: Chinese people traditionally eat long noodles ("longevity noodles") on birthdays, symbolizing long life.

q: In Hungary, kids celebrating their birthday give out what to their classmates?

q.e: In Hungary, schoolchildren give sweets to classmates on their birthday. It's a common treat tradition.

q: Danish kids mark their birthdays by which of the following activities?
putting a flag outside their house
giving their classmates chocolates one day before their birthday
putting a scarf around the neck

q.e: In Denmark, birthdays are marked by hanging out a flag, Dannebrog, at the home and having flag-decorated cakes.

q: This is one of the leading industries in Israel, as well as the most rapidly developing one.

q.e: High technology (software, cybersecurity, medical devices) is Israel's leading and fastest-growing sector, so it's "Startup Nation."

q: What is the political system of Israel?

q.e: Israel is a parliamentary democracy with a unicameral parliament, the Knesset, of 120 members. There is no written constitution, but Basic Laws.

q: Which group of countries includes Israel's major international trading partners?

q.e: Israel's major trading partners include the US, China, Germany, Belgium, the UK and Hong Kong.

q: In 1991, Israel was attacked and for the first time did not retaliate. Which country was the attacker?

q.e: In 1991 Iraq fired Scud missiles at Israel during the Gulf War. At the US's request, Israel did not retaliate.

q: What happened to the Arabs living in Israel, after the Declaration of the Establishment of the State of Israel was signed?
Some stayed in Israel, some sold their land and moved.
All of them remained in the country.
They all left because of Israeli threats.
They all moved to the Gaza Strip.

q.e: After 1948 some Palestinian Arabs stayed in Israel and became citizens, while about 700,000 fled or were expelled. This is called the Nakba.

q: Which was the second country after Egypt to normalize its relations with Israel with a peace treaty of 1994?

q.e: Jordan signed a peace treaty with Israel in 1994, the second Arab country after Egypt (1979).

q: El Al, which is of major importance in Israel, is actually what kind of organization?
The national airline company of Israel

q.e: El Al is Israel's national airline, founded in 1948. It has strict security.

q: What modern-day country includes most of ancient Mesopotamia?

q.e: Most of ancient Mesopotamia ("between the rivers", the Tigris and Euphrates) is in present-day Iraq.

q: What does the Greek word mesopotamia mean?

q.e: Mesopotamia comes from the Greek mesos (middle or between) and potamos (river). It refers to the fertile region situated between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers in modern-day Iraq and surrounding areas.

q: What two foods were the staples of the diet of the Sumerians?

q.e: The Sumerians' staples were bread and beer, which were both made from barley. Beer was an important source of nutrition.

q: The highest peak in North America is located in this mountain range.

q.e: Denali, North America's tallest peak, is in the Alaska Range in Denali National Park.

q: In the 1970s what caused U.S. customers to become interested in companies like Toyota, Honda and Datsun (Nissan)?
The end of the Vietnam War
The distrust of Richard M. Nixon

q.e: The 1973 oil embargo made American drivers turn to small, fuel-efficient Japanese cars like Toyota, Honda and Datsun.

q: Toyota's T100, which was introduced in the 1990s, is what type of car?

q.e: The Toyota T100 (1993-98) was Toyota's first full-size pickup truck. It was replaced by the Tundra.

q: As the second largest automobile producer of 2006 for the United States, Toyota surpassed which company in the third place?

q.e: By 2006, Toyota had overtaken Ford for second place in US sales by some measures. In 2007 it went past GM globally.

q: Which famous U.S. magazine chose Albert Einstein as Person of the Century in 1999?

q.e: Time chose Albert Einstein as its "Person of the Century" in 1999 (published Dec. 31, 1999). Churchill and Gandhi were runners-up.

q: Which American newspaper won the 2002 Pulitzer Award for the coverage of the September 11 terrorist attacks on New York City?

q.e: The Wall Street Journal won the 2002 Pulitzer Prize for Breaking News Reporting for its 9/11 coverage. The New York Times won six other Pulitzers that year.

q: Which CBS news show was the first to feature live simultaneous transmissions both from the East Coast and the West Coast?

q.e: CBS's "See It Now" with Edward R. Murrow showed live views of both the Brooklyn Bridge and the Golden Gate Bridge on 18 November 1951, the first coast-to-coast TV transmission.

q: What does the term outside mean in Alaskan jargon?

q.e: In Alaska, "the Outside" means anywhere in the lower 48 states and the rest of the world.

q: What does the Alaskan term break up mean?
End of winter, beginning of summer
An iceberg breaking into two pieces

q.e: In Alaska "breakup" is the spring thaw when rivers' ice breaks up and roads turn muddy.

q: In Alaskan terms, what is a snowbird?
A person who lives in Alaska in summer only

q.e: In Alaska, a "snowbird" can refer to those who spend winters elsewhere. Elsewhere, a snowbird is a northerner wintering in the South.

q: Cats eye, a piece of equipment invented in 1933 by Briton Percy Shaw and used in road construction, is used as what?
Pedestrian warning device in the United States

q.e: Percy Shaw invented "cat's eyes" in 1934 (patent 1935), reflective road studs that guide drivers at night.

q: Which of these types of bridge constructions allows for the greatest span range?

q.e: Suspension bridges can span the greatest distances, over 2,000 m, like Japan's Akashi Kaikyō Bridge (1,991 m).

q: What major U.S. interstate highway runs north and south through Minnesota?

q.e: Interstate 35 runs north-south through Minnesota, from Duluth to the Iowa border, via the Twin Cities.

q: Which of the following is the largest ethnic group to immigrate to Minnesota?

q.e: Germans are Minnesota's largest ancestry group, followed by Norwegians and Irish.

q: What object was chosen as Person of the Year by Time magazine?

q.e: In 1982, Time named "The Computer" as "Machine of the Year" instead of a Person of the Year.

q: Time magazines 2006 choice for Person of the Year caused a great stir and criticisms. Who won in 2006?

q.e: Time's 2006 Person of the Year was "You", recognizing everyone contributing to the web through blogs, YouTube and social sites. The cover had a mirror.

q: Why did David Ho win Time magazines Person of the Year Award in 1996?
for his research into finding an AIDS/HIV vaccine
for his work in bringing peace between Taiwan and China
for his work on behalf of the refugees of Darfur
for his work in bringing peace to the former Yugoslavia

q.e: Dr. David Ho was Time's 1996 Man of the Year for pioneering combination drug therapy against HIV/AIDS. He did not develop a vaccine.

q: The first abstract choice for Man of the Year was made by Time magazine in 1950. To whom was the award given?
The Members of the United Nations

q.e: In 1950 Time named "The American Fighting-Man" Man of the Year, the first time it honored a group of people rather than an individual.

q: What bugler first sounded the musical piece Tapson Memorial Day?

q.e: Oliver Willcox Norton, a Union bugler, first played "Taps" in July 1862, working with General Daniel Butterfield to compose it.

q: Arlington National Cemetery, in Virginia is a military cemetery established during which war?

q.e: Arlington National Cemetery was established in 1864 during the American Civil War on land confiscated from Confederate General Robert E. Lee's estate.

q: The National Moment of Remembrance, a moment of silence at 3pm on every Memorial Day, was initiated by which US President?

q.e: President Bill Clinton signed the National Moment of Remembrance Act in 2000. It asks Americans to pause on Memorial Day.

q: What is the duration of the National Moment of Remembrance on Memorial Day?

q.e: The National Moment of Remembrance lasts one minute, at 3:00 pm local time on Memorial Day.

q: Name the sculptor who created the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.

q.e: The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington was sculpted by Thomas Hudson Jones, with design by Lorimer Rich, from Colorado Yule marble.

q: Which of these statements best describes the United States Navy Memorial?
a 100-foot diameter granite map of the world

q.e: The US Navy Memorial in Washington, D.C., includes the Granite Sea, a 100-foot-diameter map of the world, and the "Lone Sailor" statue.

q: Which was the first organization of veterans to distribute the official Memorial Day flower?

q.e: The VFW (Veterans of Foreign Wars) distributed the first Buddy Poppies in 1922, as the official Memorial Day flower in the US.

q: Which of the following rituals is not part of Memorial Day observance?
changing guards at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
flying the US flag at half-staff until noon
the Presidents speech at Arlington National Cemetery

q.e: Memorial Day observances include flying flags at half-staff until noon, laying wreaths and the National Moment of Remembrance. The question's listed ritual is a daily one.

q: What is the motto of the city of Fargo?

q.e: Fargo's motto, "Gateway to the West," refers to its position as a stop on the way west along the Northern Pacific Railway.

q: Fargo is the crossroads of these two major interstate highway systems.

q.e: Fargo is where Interstate 94 (east-west) and Interstate 29 (north-south) meet.

q: Fargo is situated on the banks of this river.

q.e: Fargo lies on the Red River of the North, across from Moorhead, Minnesota. The river flows north into Canada.

q: What did early settlers often called the Fargo area?

q.e: Early promoters of the Red River Valley advertised the fertile region as a "garden" for settlers. The exact claim is a quiz-source detail.

q: Which one of these is not a sister city of Fargo?

q.e: Fargo's sister cities include Hamar (Norway), Kalmar? and others. The question lists one that's not one, such as Aberdeen, Scotland.

q: Where is most of the movie Fargo set?

q.e: The Coen brothers' Fargo (1996) is mostly set in Minnesota, with only the opening scene in Fargo, North Dakota.

q: To what nation do the Faroe Islands belong?

q.e: The Faroe Islands are a self-governing territory of the Kingdom of Denmark in the North Atlantic.

q: The Appalachian Trail, that runs from Georgia to Maine, crosses the Hudson River at what point?
The Bear Mountain Bridge below West Point
The Patroon Island Bridge at Albany
The Tappan Zee Bridge in Westchester County

q.e: The Appalachian Trail crosses the Hudson at the Bear Mountain Bridge, its lowest elevation point (124 ft).

q: Which of these is NOT a ski resort in the Catskill Mountains?

q.e: Greek Peak is in the Finger Lakes region (Cortland County), not the Catskills. Hunter, Windham and Belleayre are Catskills resorts.

q: What is the official language in India?

q.e: India's constitution designates Hindi (in Devanagari) as the official Union language, with English as an associate official language.

q: What are the colors of Indias flag?

q.e: The national flag of India, known as the Tiranga (tricolor), features horizontal bands of saffron (orange), white, and green, with the blue 24-spoke Ashoka Chakra wheel at its center.

q: The national anthem of which country contains the following lyrics: O say, can you see, by the dawns early light, What so proudly we hailed at the twilights last gleaming??

q.e: The "Star-Spangled Banner" is the US anthem, with lyrics by Francis Scott Key (1814) set to a British tune. Congress made it official in 1931.

q: The first bank with a drive through window was in this city.

q.e: Chicago's Exchange National Bank is credited with the first drive-up bank window, in 1946. Other early ones were in Grand Rapids and Chicago.

q: Who was the first person to have his face on a dollar bill?

q.e: Salmon P. Chase, Lincoln's Treasury Secretary, was the first person pictured on a US dollar bill (1862). Washington replaced him in 1869.

q: What was the first of the American colonies to put E Pluribus Unum on coins?

q.e: New Jersey's 1786 copper coins were among the first to bear "E Pluribus Unum." The motto appeared on Great Seal of the US in 1782.

q: Sears was founded in 1886 in Chicago, Illinois. Which of these Sears stores is the largest?

q.e: Sears was founded in Chicago in the 1880s (Sears Roebuck, 1886-93). The Toronto flagship is a large store, though Sears Canada has closed.

q: Which county is the biggest in Maryland?

q.e: Frederick County is Maryland's largest county by land area. Montgomery County has the most people.
The black-eyed Susan is Maryland's state flower, and the Preakness Stakes uses it.

q: Which of the following states does not border Maryland?

q.e: Maryland borders Pennsylvania, West Virginia, Virginia, Delaware and the District of Columbia, but not New Jersey.

q: Which of the following is not one of Marylands state nicknames?
Maryland does not have a state nickname.

q.e: New Jersey is "The Garden State." Maryland is "The Old Line State" and "The Free State."

q: What is the nickname of the U.S. state of Oklahoma?

q.e: Oklahoma's name means "red people" in Choctaw. Its nickname is "Sooner State," while "Land of the Red Man" is an older nickname.

q: Which U.S. state is known by the nickname The Gem State?

q.e: Idaho is "The Gem State," since nearly every gemstone is found there.

q: Which U.S. state has been nicknamed The Friendship State?

q.e: Texas's state motto is "Friendship," and the state is nicknamed "The Friendship State" and also "The Lone Star State."

q: What interesting nickname was given to the U.S. state of Florida?

q.e: Florida's nickname "God's Waiting Room" refers to its large retiree population.

q: What is the nickname of the U.S. state of New Jersey?

q.e: Abraham Browning popularized the phrase in an 1874 speech by comparing New Jersey to a huge barrel tapped at both ends by New York and Philadelphia. The moniker 'Garden State' officially appeared on New Jersey license plates starting in 1954.

q: Which U.S. state has been nicknamed The Mother of Presidents?

q.e: Virginia is the "Mother of Presidents," for eight presidents born there including Washington, Jefferson and Madison.

q: Who is known as a Beefeater?
a person who guards the Tower of London
someone who prepares the Queens food
someone who tastes the Queens food
a person who guards Buckingham Palace

q.e: Beefeaters is the traditional nickname for the Yeomen Warders of Her Majesty's Royal Palace and Fortress the Tower of London, who have guarded the landmark since 1485.

q: Who lives at 10 Downing Street, London, colloquially known in the United Kingdom as Number 10?
the Heir Apparent to the throne

q.e: Number 10 Downing Street has served as the official London residence and office of the British Prime Minister since Sir Robert Walpole moved in during 1735.

q: Who of the following wasnt granted the title Prince of Wales?

q.e: George VI was never Prince of Wales (he was Duke of York before becoming king). His brother Edward VIII was Prince of Wales.

q: The flag of which country incorporates a red dragon as well as the Tudor colours of green and white?

q.e: The national flag of Wales, 'Y Ddraig Goch' (The Red Dragon), depicts a red dragon passant on a field divided horizontally into green and white, the livery colors of the Welsh-descended House of Tudor.

q: Which of the following is nicknamed The Old Lady of Threadneedle Street?

q.e: The Bank of England is called "The Old Lady of Threadneedle Street," from its location and a 1797 cartoon by James Gillray.

q: Name the English captain who claimed California for Queen Elizabeth I in 1579.

q.e: Sir Francis Drake landed in 1579 near California's coast and claimed it as "Nova Albion" (New England) for Elizabeth I.

q: Name the man from New Haven who invented the cotton gin.

q.e: Eli Whitney patented the modern cotton gin in 1794, which automated the separation of cottonseed from short-staple cotton fiber. Fellow Connecticut native Samuel Colt later patented the revolving cylinder pistol in 1836.

q: In which Connecticut city was the first telephone exchange in the U.S. established?

q.e: The first commercial telephone exchange opened in New Haven, Connecticut, in January 1878 with 21 subscribers.

q: Which of the following was not invented in Connecticut?

q.e: Thomas Edison's electric light was developed in New Jersey. Connecticut inventions include the cotton gin's rival, the Colt revolver and the lollipop.

q: During Spanish times Philippine foreign trade with Spain was carried out through this country.

q.e: Manila galleons carried goods between the Philippines and Acapulco, Mexico. Mexico acted as a hub for Philippine-Spanish trade.

q: Which of these was the head of the Philippine government during the Spanish period?

q.e: The Spanish colonial Philippines was ruled by a governor-general, who answered to the Viceroy of New Spain, then to Madrid.

q: Who introduced duck breeding in the Philippines?

q.e: Duck-raising in the Philippines is often credited to Chinese traders, not the Japanese. The question gives the Japanese in its answer.

q: What are the colors of the Romanian flag?

q.e: Romania's flag is a vertical tricolor of blue, yellow and red. Chad's flag is almost identical.
Area 51 is a highly classified United States Air Force facility located on the southern shore of Groom Lake in southern Nevada, roughly 83 miles northwest of Las Vegas.

q: How large is Area 51 all buildings included?
More than 3,000 but less than 6,000 sq miles

q.e: Area 51, in Nevada, sits in the Nevada Test and Training Range, which covers a much larger area of restricted land. The base itself is small.

q: What is the airspace around Nellis Air Force Base called?

q.e: Nellis Air Force Base's military operating area is often called "the Box", restricted airspace that also includes the Nevada Test Site.

q: Which automaker is NOT based in Detroit?

q.e: Porsche is based in Stuttgart, Germany. GM, Ford and Stellantis (Chrysler) are based around Detroit.

q: What is the name of Detroits MLB team?

q.e: The Detroit Tigers were founded in 1894 and joined the American League as a charter member in 1901. Detroit's other major teams include the Pistons in the NBA, the Lions in the NFL, and the Red Wings in the NHL.

q: Which of the following religions has the least number of followers in Japan?

q.e: Christians and Muslims are small minorities in Japan, which is mostly Shinto and Buddhist. Muslims are among the smallest groups.

q: From which country was the Japanese writing system imported and adapted for the Japanese language?

q.e: Chinese characters, known as kanji in Japan, were introduced around the 5th century CE via continental trade and Buddhist texts, later evolving alongside native phonetic scripts (hiragana and katakana).

q: What political party started to dominate Japanese politics after the end of the US Occupation?

q.e: The Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) dominated Japanese politics almost continuously since 1955 after the end of the US occupation.

q: How many Japanese Emperors were there from the end of the feudal period in 1868 to 1989, when Akihito acceded to the throne?

q.e: From 1868 to 1989 Japan had three emperors: Meiji, Taishō and Shōwa (Hirohito). Akihito was the fourth, taking the throne in 1989.

q: The European Commission conducts its internal business in these three languages, sometimes called procedural languages.

q.e: The European Commission's working languages are English, French and German.

q: What day was proclaimed an European Day of Languages by the Council of Europe?

q.e: The European Day of Languages is 26 September, established by the Council of Europe in 2001.

q: An alphabet is a standardized set of letters or the basic written symbols of a language. How many official alphabetic writing systems are used in the European Union?

q.e: The EU uses three alphabets: Latin, Greek and Cyrillic (for Bulgarian).

q: What is the most widely spoken of the Slavic languages, and the largest native language in Europe?

q.e: Russian is the most widely spoken Slavic language, with about 150 million native speakers, and Europe's most spoken native language.

q: In 2005, of all American cities with a population of at least 450,000 people, which city had the biggest population density?

q.e: New York City is by far the densest large US city, with about 27,000 people per square mile.

q: What is the average life expectancy for an American as estimated in 2007?

q.e: In 2007, US life expectancy was about 78 years, lower than in many other rich countries.

q: Which state had the county with the lowest median family income for 2006?

q.e: Counties in South Dakota with large Native American reservations, like Buffalo County, have some of the lowest incomes in the US.

q: Which city had the highest median income of any city in the USA for 2005?

q.e: Fisher Island, a private island off Miami, has the highest per capita income of any US place in the 2000s.

q: The annual charity Becas Ball of Puerto Vallarta is held on what day of the year?
It is held on different days.

q.e: The Becas Ball is an annual charity fundraiser in Puerto Vallarta, Mexico. Its date varies from year to year.

q: Which is Puerto Ricos official currency?

q.e: Puerto Rico has used the U.S. dollar as its legal currency since becoming an American territory following the Spanish-American War in 1898. Locals colloquially refer to the dollar as the 'peso'.

q: Puerto Ricos flag consists of which of three colors?

q.e: Puerto Rico's flag has red and white stripes with a white star on a blue triangle, similar to Cuba's flag with colors inverted.

q: What does the name Irish Spring refer to?

q.e: Irish Spring is a brand of deodorant soap, introduced by Colgate-Palmolive in 1972, with a green-and-white look.

q: What is the capital of the Philippines?

q.e: Manila is the historic and designated capital of the Philippines, though neighboring Quezon City actually served as the official capital between 1948 and 1976 and remains the country's most populous city.

q: On what continent is the Philippines located?

q.e: The Philippines is an archipelago of over 7,000 islands located in Southeast Asia, bordered by the South China Sea and the Philippine Sea.

q: a group of students protesting against the Vietnam War

q.e: On 20 November 1969, a group called Indians of All Tribes occupied Alcatraz Island and held it until 1971.

q: What 1995 film follows a man who spends three years in solitary confinement at Alcatraz?

q.e: Murder in the First (1995), starring Christian Slater and Kevin Bacon, is based on the Alcatraz inmate Henri Young.

q: In 1918, after a revolution to overthrow an autocratic ruler, this country experienced a small civil war in which socialists defeated communists.

q.e: The German Revolution of 1918-19 overthrew the Kaiser. Moderate socialists defeated the Spartacist communists in the January 1919 uprising.

q: What is/are the color/colors of the socialist flag?

q.e: The socialist flag is red, the color of the workers' movement.

q: Which of these US Presidents did not attend Yale University?

q.e: John F. Kennedy went to Harvard. Taft, both Bushes, Ford, Clinton and Obama (Harvard Law) were at Yale or Harvard.

q: Academy Award-winning actress Jodie Foster graduated magna cum laude from Yale University, earning a B.A. in this subject.

q.e: Jodie Foster graduated from Yale in 1985 with a degree in literature, magna cum laude.

q: What does Cinco de Mayo (May 5th) commemorate in Mexican culture?
A Mexican battle victory over the French
A Mexican battle victory over the British

q.e: Cinco de Mayo commemorates the Mexican army's unexpected victory over French forces at the Battle of Puebla on May 5, 1862. It is often confused with Mexican Independence Day, which is celebrated on September 16.

q: What are the two animals featured on the Mexican flag?

q.e: Mexico's coat of arms depicts a golden eagle perched on a prickly pear cactus devouring a rattlesnake, originating from an Aztec founding legend.

q: What is the name of the capital and largest city of France?

q.e: Paris has been the political center of France since the late 10th century under King Hugh Capet. With over 2 million residents in the city proper and more than 12 million in its metropolitan area, it is France's largest city.

q: Which of these colors is not present on the national flag of the French Republic?

q.e: The French flag (tricolore) is blue, white and red. It has no green.

q: What is the official language spoken within the territory of the French Republic?

q.e: French is the official language of France, as set down in the constitution (1992).

q: From which group of Native Americans do we get the word tipi?

q.e: "Tipi" comes from the Dakota (Lakota) word thípi, meaning "dwelling."

q: In May, 2005 the Massachusetts state government repealed a law involving Native Americans. What did the original law ban?
Native Americans teaching their own languages
Native Americans voting in state elections

q.e: A 1675 Massachusetts law barred Native Americans from entering Boston, mostly due to King Philip's War. It was formally repealed in 2005.

q: What are Navajo rugs really made from?

q.e: Navajo rugs are woven from wool, mostly from Churro sheep. They are a famous Native American craft.

q: Which African country has the highest GDP (gross domestic product) according to 2008 estimates?

q.e: South Africa had the largest African GDP around 2008. Nigeria and Egypt compete for first now.

q: Where was the first parking meter installed?

q.e: The first parking meters (Park-O-Meters) were installed in Oklahoma City on 16 July 1935.

q: According to a census done in the 1990s, Oklahoma is 2nd to what state in total Native American population?

q.e: Oklahoma has the second-largest Native American population after California (and Arizona is also close).

q: Oklahoma has 6 distinct regions for tourism promotion purposes. Which of the following is not an official region?

q.e: Oklahoma's tourism regions include Green Country, Frontier Country and Red Carpet Country. "Red Hills Country" isn't one.

q: Which one of these provinces does not belong to Indonesia?

q.e: Indonesia's Java has West Java, Central Java and East Java provinces, plus Banten, but not "North Java."

q: What word was commonly used before the 16th century to refer to the autumn season?

q.e: "Harvest" was used for autumn until "fall" and "autumn" became common in the 16th century.

q: In the Northern Hemisphere, autumn begins in September. When does it begin in the Southern Hemisphere?

q.e: Due to the tilt of Earth's axis, the seasons are flipped between hemispheres, meaning the Southern Hemisphere's autumnal equinox falls around March 20–21.

q: What term refers to the full moon closest to the autumnal equinox?

q.e: The Harvest Moon is the full moon nearest the autumnal equinox, which usually falls in September in the Northern Hemisphere. A Blue Moon typically refers to a second full moon within a single calendar month.

q: In what autumn movie can you see Richard Gere and Winona Ryder walking through a beautiful fall foliage?

q.e: Autumn in New York (2000), starring Richard Gere and Winona Ryder, was set among the fall foliage in Central Park.

q: Brightly colored foliage is the image most commonly associated with autumn. What region in the US is a popular leaf peeping tourist destination?

q.e: New England attracts millions of autumn travelers each year because its high concentration of sugar maples produces vivid red, orange, and yellow fall foliage.

q: Which capital is not the largest city (by population) in its country?

q.e: Washington, D.C. is smaller than New York City. Canberra and Ottawa are also not the largest cities in their countries.

q: Which of these colors is not present in the national flag of Tanzania?

q.e: Tanzania's flag has green, yellow, black and blue, with no red.

q: What countrys national flag simply consists of a blue and a yellow horizontal bands?

q.e: Adopted in 1918 and restored in 1992 after independence from the Soviet Union, Ukraine's flag features a top blue stripe representing the sky and a bottom yellow stripe representing golden wheat fields.

q: The flag of what country is a red rectangle with a white crescent moon and a star in the center?

q.e: Turkey's national flag, known as the 'Al Bayrak' (Red Flag), features a white crescent moon and a five-pointed star on a red field. Tunisia's flag also features a crescent and star on red, but places them inside an enclosing white disc.

q: What are the colors on the national flag of Somalia?

q.e: Somalia's flag is light blue with a white five-pointed star in the center.

q: What tree is depicted on the national flag of Lebanon?
