The largest club in the world
The greatest population density among all islands in the world
The only underwater club in the world
The busiest highway in the world

q.e: Shanghai has an urban population exceeding 24 million residents, making it the most populous city proper in China. Beijing is the national capital, while Chongqing has a larger municipality boundary that includes vast rural areas.

q: In 1983 William H. Macy, Giancarlo Esposito, Camryn Manheim, and Kristen Johnston formed an acting school and working company in New York City. What is its name?

q.e: The Atlantic Theater Company was founded by David Mamet and William H. Macy in New York City in 1985, from an acting workshop.

q: In what country were Isabella Rossellini and her twin sister Ingrid Rossellini born on 18 June 1952?

q.e: Isabella and Ingrid Rossellini were born in Rome, Italy, in 1952, to Ingrid Bergman and Roberto Rossellini.

q: In 1964 Lenny Bruce was arrested for obscenity at what famous New York City club?

q.e: Lenny Bruce was arrested for obscenity at the Cafe Au Go Go in Greenwich Village in April 1964.

q: In what New York City borough was Mary J. Blige born on January 11, 1971?

q.e: Mary J. Blige was born in the Bronx, New York, in 1971, and grew up in Yonkers.

q: Red River College (RRC) is a large and very comprehensive institute of applied learning, located in this city.

q.e: Red River College in Winnipeg, Manitoba, is a big applied-learning institute and was renamed Red River College Polytechnic in 2021.

q: This country is a founding member of the European Union and the United Nations and one of the five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council. It is visited by over 75 millions tourists annually.

q.e: France is a founding EU and UN member and a permanent UN Security Council member. It's the world's most-visited country.

q: It has an unemployment rate of 15%. According to the 2000 Census it is the poorest of the 100 largest US Cities. Which city is it?

q.e: Detroit had the highest poverty rate among large US cities in the 2000 Census, with about 15% unemployment at that time.

q: The 1.5 million square mile area, known as the Bermuda Triangle, has its equivalent in the Pacific ocean. What is it called?

q.e: The "Devil's Sea" or "Dragon's Triangle" is the Pacific counterpart to the Bermuda Triangle, near Japan.

q: Excluding Englands cities, which city built the first subway in Europe?

q.e: The Budapest Metro's Line 1, opened in 1896, was the first underground railway on the European continent. London's Underground opened in 1863.

q: What is the longest river in Asia Minor?

q.e: The Euphrates is the longest river in Western Asia. The Kızılırmak is the longest entirely within Turkey.

q: Who were the legendary founders of the city of Rome?

q.e: According to Roman mythology, twin brothers Romulus and Remus were raised by a she-wolf; Romulus later founded Rome on the Palatine Hill in 753 BC after killing Remus.

q: This island, which is a French territory, is located in the Indian Ocean, east of Madagascar, about 200 km southwest of Mauritius.

q.e: Réunion is a French island in the Indian Ocean east of Madagascar, southwest of Mauritius, and an overseas department.

q: The dram is the monetary unit of this country whose capital city is Yerevan.

q.e: The dram is Armenia's currency, and Yerevan is the capital.

q: Edaphic deserts can be found on some volcanic islands, in parts of Iceland and on the Colorado plateau in the USA. Which of these most accurately defines an edaphic desert?
One that gets enough rain but still lacks plants
One that gets less than 2.5 cm of rain a year
One that is so cold that nothing can grow
One that has been a desert for at least 1 million years

q.e: An edaphic desert lacks plants because of soil conditions, not lack of rain. Soil can be too salty, rocky or sandy.

q: This US city is located at the confluence of the Mississippi River and the Ohio River.

q.e: Cairo, Illinois, sits where the Ohio River meets the Mississippi. It's pronounced "KAY-ro."

q: Purple is the official color of what Hawaiian Island?

q.e: Purple is Kauai's color and it's called "The Garden Isle." Each Hawaiian island has an official color.

q: Monticello, meaning small mountain in Italian, is the name of an estate near Charlottesville, Virginia, which belonged to which US President?

q.e: Thomas Jefferson began designing and building Monticello in 1768 on his plantation near Charlottesville, Virginia, and is buried on the estate grounds.

q: What is the official name of Rhode Island, the 13th US state?
The State of Rhode Island and Providence Plantations
The Commonwealth of Rhode Island and Narragansett Bay
The State of Rhode Island and Narragansett Bay

q.e: Rhode Island's full official name is "State of Rhode Island and Providence Plantations," though voters in 2020 removed "and Providence Plantations."

q: New York City is divided into 5 boroughs. One of these is not part of NYC?

q.e: New York City has five boroughs: Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx and Staten Island. Yonkers is in Westchester County.

q: Which city hosts the International Clown Hall of Fame?

q.e: The International Clown Hall of Fame was in West Allis, Wisconsin, before moving to Baraboo in 2011 and later closing.

q: Kurt Waldheims Nazi past was revealed as he ran for president of this country, but he still won.

q.e: Kurt Waldheim's Wehrmacht service was exposed in 1986 and he still won Austria's presidency, serving 1986–1992.

q: What country in Southeast Asia changed its name to Myanmar?

q.e: Burma changed its English name to Myanmar in 1989, under military rule. Some countries still use Burma.

q: Which one of the listed African countries does not border a sea or an ocean?

q.e: Malawi is landlocked, with Lake Malawi but no coast. Other options like Kenya and Tanzania have an Indian Ocean coast.

q: The original name of which city is translated as The Great City of Angels�?

q.e: Bangkok's full ceremonial name begins with Krung Thep Mahanakhon, which translates to 'City of Angels, Great City'. Los Angeles translates to 'The Angels' from Spanish, but Bangkok holds the Guinness World Record for the longest ceremonial place name.

q: Hammerfest, which is often referred to as the northernmost town in Europe, is located in this Scandinavian country.

q.e: Hammerfest, Norway, is often called the northernmost town in Europe, at about 70°N. Honningsvåg claims the title too.

q: This US National Park, famous for its mineral waters, is located in southeastern Oklahoma, near the city of Sulphur.

q.e: Platt National Park, in Sulphur, Oklahoma, was merged into Chickasaw National Recreation Area in 1976. It's known for mineral springs.

q: Which of these cities is not a capital of a country in the European Union?

q.e: Zurich is Switzerland's largest city but not its capital (Bern is), and Switzerland isn't in the EU.

q: The ancient Roman Empire stretched from modern day Great Britain to Egypt. Which present day country was not part of the Roman Empire?

q.e: Poland lay outside the Roman Empire. The Romans reached Britain, Egypt, Spain and the Danube.

q: What is the capital of Finland?

q.e: Helsinki was founded by King Gustav I of Sweden in 1550 and was made the capital of the Grand Duchy of Finland by Czar Alexander I of Russia in 1812, replacing Turku.

q: What is the capital city of Iceland?

q.e: Reykjavik, Iceland's capital, is the northernmost capital of a sovereign state.

q: In April 2009, Gjorge Ivanov was elected the 4th President of what country?

q.e: Gjorge Ivanov was elected President of North Macedonia (then Republic of Macedonia) in 2009 and served until 2019.

q: The U.S. Supreme Court ruled in 1972, that capital punishment was unconstitutional. What was the name of the case?

q.e: Furman v. Georgia (1972) suspended the death penalty. Gregg v. Georgia (1976) reinstated it.

q: Which of these islands is the largest island in the Mediterranean Sea?

q.e: Sicily is the largest island in the Mediterranean, followed by Sardinia, then Cyprus.

q: Which country has the highest population density in the world as of 2008?

q.e: Monaco spans just over 0.8 square miles (about 2 square km) and has a density exceeding 19,000 people per square kilometer, making it the most densely populated sovereign state in the world. Singapore ranks second among sovereign nations.

q: This is the 3rd largest city in Germany and the capital of its largest state, Bavaria.

q.e: With about 1.5 million residents, Munich is Germany's third most populous city after Berlin and Hamburg. Although Nuremberg is also a major Bavarian city, it has only around 520,000 residents.

q: It is generally accepted that the name of these islands of volcanic origin derives from a Latin term, meaning Island of the Dogs.

q.e: The Canary Islands may derive from the Latin "Canariae Insulae," Island of the Dogs. The canary bird was named after the islands.

q: 1919 saw the first general, city-wide strike in the USA. It involved about 35,000 workers. In which city did this strike occur?

q.e: The Seattle General Strike of February 1919 involved around 65,000 workers in sympathy with shipyard strikers.

q: The Victoria Falls are situated on the Zambezi River, on the border between which two countries?

q.e: Victoria Falls forms a natural border between southern Zambia and northern Zimbabwe along the Zambezi River. Known locally as Mosi-oa-Tunya, it spans roughly 5,600 feet (1,700 m) across.

q: Who was the first guest star to step off the plane on Fantasy Island?

q.e: Fantasy Island aired from 1977 to 1984 on ABC. Its host was Mr. Roarke (Ricardo Montalbán) with Tattoo.

q: Which was the first country in the world to constitutionally abolish its army?

q.e: Costa Rica abolished its army in 1948, written into its 1949 constitution.

q: What is the fourth largest city in Canada (after Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver), as measured by metropolitan area according to 2006 estimates?

q.e: Ottawa is Canada's capital, and in 2006 was the fourth-largest metro area. Calgary has since overtaken it.

q: The town of Juarez, Mexico is located next to what U.S. city?

q.e: Ciudad Juárez, Mexico, lies across the Rio Grande from El Paso, Texas.

q: This tiny sovereign state, with a territory of about 0.44 square kilometres, is the smallest country in the world.

q.e: Vatican City, about 0.44 km² (110 acres), is the world's smallest sovereign state.

q: Which of the three classical types of columns has its capital ornately decorated to look like acanthus leaves?

q.e: The Corinthian column has an ornate capital decorated with acanthus leaves. Doric is plain, Ionic has scrolls.

q: What is the capital city of Bahrain?

q.e: Manama is the capital of Bahrain, an island nation in the Persian Gulf.

q: Almaty, or Alma-Ata as formerly known, is the largest city and capital of which country?

q.e: Almaty was the capital of Kazakhstan until 1997, when it moved to Astana, now Astana again.

q: Under whose rule was the island of Cyprus when it was conquered by the Ottoman Empire in 1571?

q.e: Venice ruled Cyprus when the Ottomans took it in 1571, after the siege of Famagusta.

q: Which Canadian city is the site of the haunted Carleton County Jail, said to be the home of the ghost of Patrick Whelen, hanged for the murder of Thomas DArcy McGee?

q.e: The Carleton County Jail in Ottawa is a haunted hostel. Patrick Whelan was hanged in 1869 for assassinating Thomas D'Arcy McGee.

q: This European country is divided into three districts, 12 cantons, and 116 communes.

q.e: Luxembourg is divided into 3 districts, 12 cantons and (as of 2018) 102 communes.

q: Audrey Hepburn, Jean-Claude Van Damme, Django Reinhardt, Toots Thielemans, and Adolphe Sax were all born in this country.

q.e: Belgium is the birthplace of Audrey Hepburn, Jean-Claude Van Damme, Django Reinhardt, Toots Thielemans and Adolphe Sax, saxophone inventor.

q: Measured from base to peak, what is the worlds highest mountain?

q.e: Mauna Kea in Hawaii measures roughly 33,500 feet (about 10,210 m) from its oceanic base to its summit, though only 13,796 feet (4,205 m) sit above sea level. Mount Everest is the highest mountain above sea level, reaching 29,032 feet (8,849 m).

q: During the Cold War, which city was the capital of West Germany?

q.e: Bonn was the capital of West Germany from 1949 to 1990. Berlin became the capital after reunification.

q: Which is an existing country, recognized by United Nations?

q.e: East Timor (Timor-Leste) gained independence in 2002 and is a UN member.

q: Which US city is nicknamed The Venice of America?

q.e: Fort Lauderdale is "The Venice of America" because of its canals.

q: A fire killed over 1600 people in 1845 in what Chinese city?

q.e: A theater fire killed over 1,600 in Guangzhou (Canton) in 1845, one of the deadliest fires in history.

q: What Oklahoma city saw a race riot that triggered a fire in 1921?

q.e: The Tulsa race massacre of 31 May–1 June 1921 destroyed the Greenwood district, "Black Wall Street."

q: The Don Paz passenger ferry was on its way to what island in 1987 when it collided with an oil tanker?

q.e: MV Doña Paz collided with the tanker Vector on 20 December 1987 in the Philippines, killing more than 4,000.

q: The worlds oldest lake is also the worlds deepest lake. Where would it be found?

q.e: Lake Baikal in Siberia is the world's oldest and deepest lake, at about 25 million years and 1,642 m.

q: This modern-day European country, once ruled by Khan Asparuh, was acknowledged by the Byzantine Empire in 681.

q.e: Khan Asparuh founded the First Bulgarian Empire, which Byzantium recognized in 681.

q: According to urban legends that spread in 1997, people in this country began pumping air from a bicycle pump into their rectum resulting in their explosion.

q.e: A 1997 urban legend said Thai people were exploding after pumping air into themselves. It was a hoax.

q: The flag of what country consists of a simple green field with no other features?

q.e: Libya's flag was plain green from 1977 to 2011. The current flag is the pre-Gaddafi red, black and green with a crescent.

q: The Mississippi is the longest North American river. The Missouri is the second. What is the third longest?

q.e: The Rio Grande is the fourth or so longest river in the US, at about 3,034 km. The Yukon is longer in North America.

q: Which country has Bratislava as its capital city, and the koruna as its unit of currency?

q.e: Bratislava is Slovakia's capital. Slovakia replaced the koruna with the euro in 2009.

q: The national flag of what country consists of a light blue field with a single white star in the center?

q.e: Somalia's flag is light blue with a white five-pointed star in the center, adopted in 1954.

q: A mermaid is the symbol of this European city; depicted on its coat of arms, it can be seen on statues throughout the city.

q.e: The Warsaw Mermaid, known in Polish as Syrenka, features on the city's coat of arms carrying a sword and shield to protect the Polish capital.

q: In what city a principal of an elementary school got a pink Mohawk haircut on 6 September 2007, as he had promised to do if the students raised the school's Academic Performance Index by at least 55 points?

q.e: In 2007, the principal of Bayview elementary school in San Francisco kept a promise to get a pink Mohawk after test scores rose.

q: In which of these New York City neighborhoods did the American Airlines Flight 587 crash on November 12, 2001?

q.e: American Airlines Flight 587 crashed in Belle Harbor, Queens, on 12 November 2001, killing 265 people.

q: This country, whose capital city is Tegucigalpa, uses the lempira as its currency.

q.e: Honduras uses the lempira, named for a 16th-century Lenca chief. The capital is Tegucigalpa.

q: The capital city of this country was once known as The Little Paris of Eastern Europe.

q.e: Bucharest, Romania, was called "Little Paris" or "Paris of the East" for its architecture and boulevards.

q: The Krahule hill , known as the geographic center of Europe, is it located in this country.

q.e: Krahule in Slovakia is claimed to be the geographic center of Europe, as are other sites in several countries.

q: What is the deepest lake in the world?

q.e: Lake Baikal in southern Russia plunges to a maximum depth of 5,387 feet (about 1,642 m). It is not only the deepest lake on Earth, but also the world's largest freshwater lake by volume, holding about 20% of the planet's unfrozen surface fresh water.

q: What country is generally regarded as the oldest republic in the world?

q.e: San Marino claims to be the world's oldest republic, founded in 301 AD.

q: What was the first American city to fluoridate its water system?

q.e: Grand Rapids, Michigan, became the first city in the world to add fluoride to its drinking water, on 25 January 1945.

q: In three of these countries corruption is widely spread. Which is the odd country?

q.e: Iceland ranks among the least corrupt countries in international indexes.

q: Ireland and Nigeria are considered to be among the countries with most adults, regularly attending church services. The citizens of one of this country also go to church regularly.

q.e: Poland is one of the most church-going countries in Europe, which is mostly Catholic, along with Ireland and Nigeria.

q: This country is not a federal republic.

q.e: Laos is a one-party socialist republic and is not federal. Federal republics include Germany and Mexico.

q: This island was originally called Van Diemens Land in honor of Anthony van Diemen.

q.e: Dutch explorer Abel Tasman reached the island in 1642 and named it after Anthony van Diemen, the Governor-General of the Dutch East Indies who financed his voyage. The British renamed it Tasmania in 1856 to honor Tasman himself.

q: Spanish is an official language of this African country.

q.e: Equatorial Guinea is the only African country with Spanish as an official language, alongside French and Portuguese.

q: In the 14th Century, Moscow replaced this city as the cultural center of Russia.

q.e: Moscow replaced Kiev (Kyiv) as Russia's cultural and political center in the 14th century after the Mongol invasion.

q: Ellis Island was the location of the entry facility used by many immigrants to enter the USA. When did the facility operate?

q.e: Ellis Island was an immigration station from 1892 to 1954, processing about 12 million immigrants.

q: In the Crimean war, which lasted from 28 March 1854 until 1856, an alliance of the United Kingdom, France, the Ottoman Empire and Piedmont-Sardinia fought against which country?

q.e: The Crimean War (1853–1856) saw Britain, France, the Ottoman Empire and Piedmont-Sardinia against Russia.

q: This city, known also as Anvil City, is situated in Northwest Alaska.

q.e: Nome, Alaska, is nicknamed "Anvil City" and is the end of the Iditarod Trail. Its gold rush was in 1899.

q: What city is the capital of the United Arab Emirates?

q.e: Abu Dhabi is the capital and the second-most populous city of the UAE, as well as the capital of the federation's largest emirate. Dubai is the country's most populous city.

q: In which country was Carlos Mencia born?

q.e: Carlos Mencia was born in San Pedro Sula, Honduras, in 1967, and moved to the US as a child.

q: If the world were a village of 1000 people, how many would be from the African continent?

q.e: In the "world as a village of 1,000" model, Africa has about 150 people, Asia about 600, Europe about 100.

q: If the world were a village of 1000 people, how many would be from the North American continent?

q.e: North America has around 79 per 1,000 in that model (including Central America and the Caribbean it is around 80).

q: What is the capital of Afghanistan?

q.e: Kabul, situated over 5,800 feet (1,790 m) above sea level in the Hindu Kush mountains, has been the capital of Afghanistan since 1776. Dushanbe and Tashkent are the capitals of Tajikistan and Uzbekistan, respectively.

q: What is the capital of Norway?

q.e: Oslo is the capital of Norway and its largest city.

q: What is the capital and largest city of Hawaii, the 50th US state?

q.e: Located on the southeast coast of Oahu, Honolulu became the capital of the Kingdom of Hawaii under King Kamehameha III in 1845 and remained the capital when Hawaii achieved statehood in 1959. Frankfort, Little Rock, and Dover are the capitals of Kentucky, Arkansas, and Delaware, respectively.

q: Name the line, which is the same distance from the North Pole and South Pole and runs horizontally around the world.

q.e: The Equator sits at 0 degrees latitude, precisely halfway between the North and South Poles. The Prime Meridian runs vertically between the poles at 0 degrees longitude, dividing East and West.

q: Which continents are entirely in the Southern Hemisphere?

q.e: Only Australia and Antarctica lie completely south of the Equator. South America and Africa are intersected by the Equator, meaning parts of both landmasses sit in the Northern Hemisphere.

q: Which of these is not a type of map projection?

q.e: Mercator and Robinson are map projections, but "Crusoe" is not.

q: Which of these countries is smallest (by territory)?

q.e: San Marino (61 km²) is smaller than the other choices, but Monaco and Vatican City are smaller still.

q: Which of these mountains is highest?

q.e: Mount McKinley (Denali), 6,190 m, is North America's highest peak. Alaska's official name has been Denali since 2015, but it was renamed McKinley again in 2025 in US federal usage.

q: Which of these lakes is deepest?

q.e: Lake Tanganyika is Africa's deepest lake, at 1,470 m, and the second deepest in the world, after Baikal.

q: Which of these rivers is longest?

q.e: The Yellow River (Huang He), about 5,464 km, is China's second longest after the Yangtze. Check the other options in the question.

q: What are the three Benelux countries?

q.e: The name Benelux is an acronym coined in 1944 combining the first letters of Belgium, the Netherlands, and Luxembourg for an economic union.

q: What was the former name of the city of Istanbul ?

q.e: The city was known as Byzantium in antiquity, renamed Constantinople in 330 CE after Roman Emperor Constantine the Great, and officially renamed Istanbul in 1930.

q: What major geographical feature is located at 23.5 degrees North latitude?

q.e: The Tropic of Cancer marks the northernmost latitude where the Sun can appear directly overhead at noon, which happens annually around June 21. Its southern counterpart at 23.5° S is the Tropic of Capricorn.

q: Which country held the record for the highest birth rate in the 2005 world statistics?

q.e: Niger has one of the world's highest birth rates, about 7 children per woman.

q: How many US states border the Gulf of Mexico?

q.e: Five US states border the Gulf of Mexico: Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama and Florida.

q: How many US states border the Pacific Ocean?

q.e: The five US states with coastlines on the Pacific Ocean are California, Oregon, Washington, Alaska, and Hawaii. Alaska has by far the longest Pacific coastline of any state.

q: The tallest mountain peak in the US is Mount McKinley. This is the second tallest.

q.e: Mount Saint Elias, 5,489 m, is the second highest peak in the US and on the Alaska–Canada border.

q: Which one of these mountains is not a volcano?

q.e: Mount Aspiring (Tititea) in New Zealand is not a volcano; it is a glaciated peak made of schist.

q: The highest mountain peak on our planet is Mount Everest. It was first climbed by Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay on May 29, 1953. What is the home country of Sir Edmund Hillary?

q.e: Sir Edmund Hillary was born in Auckland, New Zealand, in 1919. He was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II shortly after he and Sherpa mountaineer Tenzing Norgay completed the first confirmed ascent of Mount Everest in 1953.

q: This country, situated in North Europe, has almost 200 000 lakes - more than any other country in the world.

q.e: Finland has about 188,000 lakes and is called the "Land of a Thousand Lakes."

q: With a surface area of about 82,000 km², this lake between Ontario and Minnesota is the largest single freshwater lake in the world.

q.e: Lake Superior is the world's largest freshwater lake by surface area, at about 82,100 km².

q: Which of the following states of America is an inland one and has an official motto that does not come from Latin?

q.e: Montana's motto "Oro y Plata" is Spanish ("gold and silver"), and it's an inland state.

q: Three of the following US states have a motto consisting of one single word in English. Which one does not belong to the group?

q.e: West Virginia's motto "Montani Semper Liberi" is Latin. The others have one-word English mottoes such as "Equality" (Wyoming).

q: This famous exclamation, which has been attributed to ancient scientist Archimedes, is the official state motto of California.

q.e: Eureka, meaning 'I have found it' in Greek, was adopted as California's official state motto in 1963, referencing the California Gold Rush that began in 1848.

q: Mount Vesuvius, that is notorious for the destruction of two Roman cities in the year 79, was linked most closely to which hero and demigod?

q.e: Mount Vesuvius, which buried Pompeii and Herculaneum, was tied to Hercules, who legend said founded Herculaneum.

q: Towards the beginning of the new millennium, three of these four countries had a population of approximately 32 million people. Which is the odd one?

q.e: Colombia's population (around 40 million in 2000) differs from the other three, which had about 32 million.

q: USA is considered to be one of the most popular destinations, where thousands of immigrants come to seek asylum. Just one of these four states is similar in to USA in this respect.

q.e: France is, like the US, a major destination for immigrants and asylum seekers.

q: Because of its spectacular nature forms, one of this insular countrys islands has been a set for the filming of many movie productions, including the highly successful, Lord of the Rings and The Chronicles of Narnia.

q.e: New Zealand's South Island and North Island have been used to film The Lord of the Rings and The Chronicles of Narnia.

q: Despite being the largest in the world, this island is sparsely populated, due to its unfavourable climate.

q.e: Greenland is the world's largest island, with only about 56,000 people because of its ice and arctic climate.

q: This is the largest island in the Mediterranean Sea, famous for one of the worlds most active volcanoes - Etna.

q.e: Sicily is the largest Mediterranean island and home of Mount Etna, Europe's most active volcano.

q: The gowni is a typical national costume in which African country?

q.e: The "gonile" or "gown" is a national dress; the question links it with Tanzania. Check the spelling in other sources.

q: Hijab, which is also a term meaning barrier, is worn as a traditional clothing in which countries?

q.e: Hijab is an Arabic word meaning "barrier" or "cover" and is worn in many Muslim countries.

q: Which of these national costumes is closely related to Sikhism - a religion that comes from 16th-century northern India?

q.e: The turban (dastar) is a Sikh articleof faith, worn to cover uncut hair.

q: Which of these pieces of clothing is worn on the head?

q.e: The fez is a felt hat worn on the head, associated with Morocco and the Ottoman Empire.

q: While driving or walking down Kings Cross Road and Farringdon Road in London few people are aware that unseen beneath them runs which river?

q.e: The River Fleet is London's largest "lost" river, now running through sewers beneath Farringdon Road and King's Cross.

q: The Great Pavement, a hidden, unknown to most tourists and seldom-displayed treasure, is located in which building in London?

q.e: The Cosmati Pavement, from 1268, is in front of the high altar in Westminster Abbey.

q: The Old Royal Observatory, which is a part of the National Maritime Museum in London, was built in what year?

q.e: The Royal Observatory in Greenwich was built in 1675–76, designed by Christopher Wren, for Charles II.

q: This famous writer, whose house was at 17 Gough Square in London, said: When a man is tired of London, he is tired of life, for there is in London all life can afford.

q.e: Samuel Johnson lived at 17 Gough Square and compiled his Dictionary of the English Language there (1755). The house is now a museum.

q: The Big Smoky Valley, that runs between the Toiyabe Range and the Toquima Range, is located in which US state?

q.e: The Big Smoky Valley lies in central Nevada, between the Toiyabe and Toquima ranges.

q: In 1643, a Native American uprising killed this unauthorized Puritan preacher of a dissident church discussion group, and pioneer in Rhode Island and the Bronx.

q.e: Anne Hutchinson was killed in 1643 with most of her household in a Siwanoy attack in the Bronx, in what is now Pelham Bay Park.

q: The first college in The Bronx, known as this today, was built in 1884.

q.e: Fordham University in the Bronx was founded in 1841 as St. John's College. Other Bronx colleges were later.

q: Edgar Allen Poe wrote this famous poem in The Bronx in 1846.

q.e: Edgar Allan Poe lived in a cottage in the Bronx (Fordham) from 1846, and "Annabel Lee" was written there in 1849.

q: In 1899, this world famous institution was opened in The Bronx.
The U.S. Olympic Hall of Fame

q.e: The Bronx Zoo opened in 1899 and is the largest metropolitan zoo in the US.

q: This world famous building opened in The Bronx in 1923.

q.e: Yankee Stadium opened in 1923, "the House That Ruth Built."

q: The name of this US state means flat water and is derived from the name of the Platte River that flows through the state.

q.e: Nebraska comes from the Chiwere (Otoe) word nÃ­bthaska, meaning flat water, which was their name for the broad, shallow Platte River. French fur traders later translated the concept into the French word platte, meaning flat.

q: This European Union member was once known for huge migration of its people, mainly to the US and UK. Nowadays, however, it attracts many immigrants from new EU members.

q.e: Ireland had huge emigration to the US and UK and is now a destination for immigrants, including from newer EU states.

q: Which EU member was the largest country in Europe in XIV century, but now has land area of just 65 000 sq. km?

q.e: Lithuania was the largest country in Europe in the 14th century. Its territory is now about 65,300 km².

q: Which mini country was among the European Union founding members?

q.e: Luxembourg was a founding member of the EU (in the 1957 Treaty of Rome) and is one of the smallest.

q: In which European Union member the native people make up only 60% of the total population?

q.e: Latvia's population is about 60% ethnic Latvians, with a large Russian minority.

q: Which former British colony joined the European Union in 2004?

q.e: Malta was a British colony until 1964 and joined the EU in 2004.

q: Which European Union member was the first country to reject communist rule and thus sparkle the liberation of so called Eastern Block?

q.e: Poland was the first Eastern Bloc country to reject communism, in the 1989 elections won by Solidarity.

q: Which EU member state was known to the ancient Greeks and Romans as Dacia?

q.e: Dacia was an ancient kingdom conquered by Emperor Trajan between 101 and 106 AD, after which it became a Roman province located primarily in modern-day Romania.

q: Which country is the youngest independent state to be a member of the European Union? (It has been an independent country only since 1993.)

q.e: Slovakia became independent on 1 January 1993 after Czechoslovakia broke up peacefully, and joined the EU in 2004.

q: In May 2004 the European Union accepted 10 new countries. Which of them was first to adopt the Euro as its national currency?

q.e: Slovenia was the first of the 2004 entrants to adopt the euro, on 1 January 2007.

q: Which Muslim country was recognized as a candidate for accession in the EU on December 12th, 1999 at the Helsinki summit of the European Council?

q.e: Turkey was formally recognized as an EU candidate at the Helsinki summit in December 1999.

q: All but three European Union official languages are from the Indo-European family. They are Finnish, Estonian and which other language?

q.e: Finnish, Estonian and Hungarian are the three Uralic official EU languages. Maltese is Semitic, and Basque isn't official.

q: Most of the European Union members are also part of a Schengen Agreement that allows their citizens to travel without passports across the member states. Which EU member is outside of the Schengen group?

q.e: The UK (no longer in the EU after 2020) and Ireland stayed outside the Schengen Area. Several EU members like Bulgaria and Romania recently joined.

q: Wat Chiang Man is a temple in Thailand. In it, fifteen of these animals represent a sea of unformed matter upon which the cosmos of the Chedi floats.

q.e: At Wat Chiang Man, Chiang Mai, the Chedi Chang Lom is supported by 15 elephants sculptures around its base.

q: Which of these peaks is the highest?

q.e: Mount McKinley (Denali) in Alaska is the highest peak in North America, at 6,190 m.

q: Which of the following countries and states shares its name with its capital city?

q.e: Luxembourg (country and city) shares its name with its capital. Others include Singapore, Monaco and Kuwait.

q: Which one of these Mediterranean islands is the smallest in area?

q.e: Corfu is a large Greek island; the question's other options are bigger, so treat this as the smallest one.

q: Which one of these Mediterranean islands, belonging to Italy, is the largest in area?

q.e: Sardinia is Italy's second-largest island and the second largest in the Mediterranean, after Sicily (which is Italian too).

q: This island, on which the volcano Etna is situated, is the largest Mediterranean island.

q.e: Sicily has Mount Etna and is the largest island of the Mediterranean.

q: Which French Mediterranean island is the birthplace of Napoléon Bonaparte?

q.e: Napoleon Bonaparte was born in Ajaccio on the island of Corsica in 1769, just a year after the Republic of Genoa ceded the island to France.

q: Which one of these Mediterranean islands does not belong to the group of the Balearic Islands?

q.e: Capri is in Italy's Bay of Naples; the Balearics are Mallorca, Menorca, Ibiza and Formentera.

q: Riga is the capital of which Baltic country?

q.e: Riga is the capital of Latvia, one of the three Baltic states.

q: Which explorer was the first to reach the South Pole?

q.e: Roald Amundsen reached the South Pole on 14 December 1911, ahead of Scott's team.

q: Near what sea was the ancient city of Troy located ?

q.e: Troy was in Anatolia near the Dardanelles, close to the Aegean Sea (northwest Turkey).

q: Which of these rivers runs through the Czech Republic and Germany?

q.e: The Elbe rises in the Czech Republic and flows through Germany to the North Sea at Hamburg.

q: Mount Erebus is a volcano located on this continent.

q.e: Mount Erebus, on Ross Island, is the southernmost active volcano on Earth, in Antarctica.

q: Rastafarianism is a religion that venerates Haile Selassie as a god. Haile Selassie was the emperor of the third most populous country in Africa. Name that country.

q.e: Haile Selassie was Ethiopia's emperor (1930–1974). Rastafari consider him divine, and Ethiopia is Africa's second most populous country.

q: Name Asias most densely populated country which has about three million people and an area of less than 250 square miles (402 km²).

q.e: Singapore is among the most densely populated countries, at about 8,000 people per km² and 5.9 million people now.

q: What is the average salinity of the Dead Sea?

q.e: Dead Sea salinity is about 34%, almost ten times that of the ocean. The bank answer is approximate.

q: What famous California prison was home to Charles Manson?

q.e: Charles Manson was held at several prisons, including San Quentin, Folsom and Corcoran, and died in 2017.

q: Tiananmen Square, which has been the site of a number of political events and student protests, is located in what Chinese city?

q.e: Tiananmen Square sits at the center of Beijing, directly south of the Forbidden City. Covering around 109 acres, it is one of the largest public squares in the world.

q: What famous square is located in Vatican City, the papal enclave within Rome?

q.e: St. Peter's Square, designed by Gian Lorenzo Bernini and built between 1656 and 1667, sits directly in front of St. Peter's Basilica in Vatican City.

q: Grand Place, which is known for its large flower carpet, is the main square of this capital European city.

q.e: The Grand Place in Brussels hosts a flower carpet every other year and is a UNESCO site.

q: Piazza San Marco (St Marks Square), which Napoleon allegedly called The drawing room of Europe, is the principal square of this Italian city.

q.e: Piazza San Marco is the primary public square of Venice, dominated by St. Mark's Basilica and the Doge's Palace. Florence's main historic square is Piazza della Signoria, while Rome features Piazza Navona.

q: What former president has addressed more than a million people on many occasions on Plaza de la Revolución in Havana?

q.e: Fidel Castro spoke to large crowds in Havana's Plaza de la Revolución, sometimes for hours.

q: What Mediterranean island is divided between a Greek community and a Turkish community (although the latter is not internationally recognized as a separate entity)?

q.e: Cyprus has been divided since 1974, between the Republic of Cyprus and the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (recognized only by Turkey).

q: What South American island is shared by Chile and Argentina?

q.e: Isla Grande de Tierra del Fuego is partitioned between Chile in the west and Argentina in the east, separated from the South American mainland by the Strait of Magellan.

q: What island is shared by Indonesia and the nation of East Timor?

q.e: Timor is divided between Indonesia (West Timor) and East Timor (Timor-Leste).

q: Which of these islands is shared by three countries?

q.e: Borneo is shared by Indonesia, Malaysia and Brunei, which makes it the only island with three countries.

q: The tiny island of Märket / Märketin in the Baltic Sea is shared by these two nations.

q.e: Märket is a tiny island shared by Finland and Sweden, with a famously wiggly border.

q: Which one of these Asian rivers does not flow into the Indian Ocean?

q.e: The Saigon River flows into the South China Sea, which is part of the Pacific, not the Indian Ocean.

q: The Mediterranean Sea is connected to the Atlantic Ocean by this strait.

q.e: The Strait of Gibraltar connects the Atlantic Ocean to the Mediterranean Sea and separates Europe from Africa, narrowing to just about 14 kilometers (8.9 miles) wide.

q: The history of EU began on 25th of March 1957 when the European Economic Community was formed. What is the founding act called?

q.e: The Treaty of Rome (25 March 1957) created the European Economic Community.

q: When did Ireland join the European Union?

q.e: Ireland, the UK and Denmark joined the European Communities in 1973.

q: The citizens of which country rejected the idea of joining the EU in 1972 and again in 1994?

q.e: Norway rejected EU membership in referendums in 1972 and 1994.

q: The EU has been a western club for most of its history. But which of these western countries has stayed out of the EU?

q.e: Switzerland has stayed out of the EU, though it's in Schengen and the single market via treaties.

q: Which former Yugoslavian republic was the first to be admitted to the European Union?

q.e: Slovenia joined the EU in 2004 and is the first former Yugoslav republic to do so.

q: The 6th European Union enlargement took place on May 1 2004. How many countries were admitted then?

q.e: Ten countries joined the EU on 1 May 2004, the largest enlargement.

q: Many countries held national referenda before joining the European Union. Which of the following nations showed the highest support for joining (92% in favour)?

q.e: In 2003, 92.5% of Slovak voters backed joining the EU.

q: What kind of agreement is the Schengen Agreement?
It allows EU citizens to travel without passports within the EU borders.
It is a visionary chapter about a further EU enlargement.
It regulates the relationships with non-EU countries, especially Russia.
It introduced a common currency - the Euro.

q.e: Signed in 1985 in Schengen, Luxembourg, the Schengen Agreement led to the creation of Europe's border-free Schengen Area, abolishing internal border checks across most participating nations.

q: When did the euro become the official currency of the Eurozone?

q.e: The euro became legal tender in cash on 1 January 2002 (it was an accounting currency from 1999).

q: The flag of which US state features a white American Bison on a blue field?

q.e: Wyoming's flag has a white bison with the state seal on a blue field, with a red border.

q: The state drink of this US state is milk, its state bird is the Western Meadowlark, its state flower is the Wild Prairie Rose, and its state slogan is Legendary.

q.e: North Dakota's state beverage is milk, its flower the wild prairie rose, its bird the western meadowlark and slogan "Legendary."

q: Which US state has been nicknamed The First State, The Small Wonder, Blue Hen State, and The Diamond State?

q.e: Delaware is "The First State" because it ratified the Constitution first, on 7 December 1787.

q: From 1888-1889, American traders Simon and Thomas Metcalfe brought some men from Manila to the Western Hemisphere. Which state did they bring them to?

q.e: The Metcalfe brothers brought Filipino "Manilamen" to the US; the bank says Alaska. Louisiana had earlier Filipino settlement from the 1760s.

q: Who was the first female President of the Philippines?

q.e: Corazon Aquino became the Philippines' first female president in 1986 after the People Power Revolution toppled Marcos.

q: The Grand Strand is a long stretch of sandy beach situated near which of the following?

q.e: The Grand Strand is a 60-mile stretch of beaches along South Carolina's coast, centered on Myrtle Beach.

q: Name the capital city of the U.S. state of Washington.

q.e: Olympia is Washington State's capital. Seattle is the largest city.

q: Six countries are located along the Black Sea border. Which one among them has the longest Black Sea coast line (not including the Sea of Azov coast line)?

q.e: Turkey has the longest Black Sea coastline, about 1,700 km. The others are Bulgaria, Romania, Ukraine, Russia and Georgia.

q: The Black Sea, whose waters are known to be meromictic, is the largest water basin in the world where water layers do not intermix, and, thus, lack the dissolved form of what?

q.e: The Black Sea's deep water is anoxic and rich in hydrogen sulfide, so it lacks dissolved oxygen below about 150 m.

q: The Crimean peninsula has been under the control of multiple powers over the centuries. Although it is considered to be an autonomous republic, it is a part of this nation.

q.e: Crimea is internationally recognized as part of Ukraine, though Russia annexed it in 2014.

q: All these entities are located around the Black Sea except for one. Name the exception.

q.e: The Ural Mountains are far to the east, between Europe and Asia, not near the Black Sea.

q: The summit ridge of Mount Everest marks the border between which two Asian countries?

q.e: Everest's summit ridge marks the China (Tibet) and Nepal border.

q: The locals of Nepal call the highest mount in the world - Mount Everest - Sagarmatha. What is the meaning of this name in Sanskrit?

q.e: Sagarmatha is Nepali for "Forehead of the Sky" or "Head of the Sky." The Tibetan name is Chomolungma.

q: What nationality was mathematician and surveyor Radhanath Sikdar, who was the first person to measure the height of Everest?

q.e: Radhanath Sikdar, a Bengali mathematician in the Great Trigonometrical Survey, calculated Peak XV (Everest) as the world's highest in 1852.

q: Which of the following paths is one of the two most popular climbing routes to Mount Everest?

q.e: The two main routes are the southeast ridge from Nepal and the northeast ridge from Tibet.

q: What is the largest island on the planet in terms of territory?

q.e: Greenland is the world's largest island, at about 2.17 million km² (Australia counts as a continent).

q: This is the third-largest island on the planet, and it is also known as Kalimantan.

q.e: Borneo is the third-largest island, behind Greenland and New Guinea. Its Indonesian part is Kalimantan.

q: This is the fourth-largest island in the world, and it is home to 5% of the plant and animal species on the planet.

q.e: Spanning roughly 587,000 square kilometers, Madagascar is the world's fourth-largest island, behind Greenland, New Guinea, and Borneo. Because it split from the Indian subcontinent roughly 88 million years ago, over 90% of its wildlife is found nowhere else.

q: What is the largest island in the Mediterranean Sea?

q.e: Sicily covers roughly 9,927 square miles (25,711 square km) at the tip of Italy's boot, edging out Sardinia, which covers around 9,300 square miles. Cyprus is the third-largest island in the Mediterranean Sea.

q: The first time Antarctica was officially visited is a subject of controversy. Three people have claimed to have achieved this feat. Which of these is not one them?

q.e: Cook crossed the Antarctic Circle but never sighted the continent. Bellingshausen, Bransfield and Palmer are the first sighting claimants.

q: Who was the first person to reach the South Pole?

q.e: Norwegian explorer Roald Amundsen and his team reached the South Pole on December 14, 1911, using skis and sled dogs. British explorer Robert Falcon Scott reached the pole 34 days later, tragically perishing along with his team on the return journey.

q: Few animals inhabit the North Pole. Which of these types of animals can never be seen there?

q.e: Penguins are native almost exclusively to the Southern Hemisphere, primarily Antarctica and surrounding subantarctic islands, so none live in the wild at the North Pole.

q: What river, draining into the Caspian Sea, is the longest in Europe?

q.e: The Volga is Europe's longest river at roughly 2,194 miles (3,530 km). The Danube is Europe's second-longest river, flowing about 1,770 miles (2,850 km) into the Black Sea.

q: What is the longest river in France?

q.e: The Loire stretches approximately 1,006 kilometers (625 miles) from the Massif Central to the Atlantic Ocean, making it the longest river entirely within France. The Erdre and Maine are much smaller tributaries within the Loire basin.

q: What river named after a mythological figure is the longest river of Great Britain?

q.e: The Severn, 354 km, is Britain's longest river, named for Sabrina (Habren), a figure of Welsh legend.

q: What river flows through ten European countries and is the longest in the European Union?

q.e: The Danube flows through ten countries, more than any other river. It is the EU's longest river.

q: This bridge, that spans the Tagus River, is the longest bridge in Europe.

q.e: The Vasco da Gama Bridge in Lisbon is about 17 km long and spans the Tagus.

q: The Filipino word pangalan means name in English. What does the word pangngalan mean?

q.e: Pangalan means "name" in Filipino, while pangngalan means "noun".

q: What Filipino word means money in English?

q.e: "Pera" means "money" in Filipino, from Spanish "perra" (a coin).

q: How will you say I Love You in Filipino?

q.e: "Mahal kita" is "I love you" in Filipino. "Mahal" also means "expensive."

q: Who is considered the Father of Filipino Language?

q.e: Manuel Quezon, the Commonwealth president, is called the Father of the National Language for promoting a Tagalog-based national language in 1937.

q: What is the meaning of the Italian word riavvolgere, from which the name of the popular Italian dish ravioli originated?

q.e: Ravioli has a disputed origin. One popular theory links it to the Italian word for "to wrap", but it is not settled.

q: What is the title of the national anthem of the Italian Republic?

q.e: "Il Canto degli Italiani" (Song of the Italians), also "Inno di Mameli," is Italy's anthem.

q: Maryland is well known as a colony of religious tolerance. It was the first American colony to fully accept practitioners of which religion?

q.e: Maryland, founded in 1634 by Lord Baltimore (Cecil Calvert), was a refuge for English Catholics.

q: The Mason Dixon Line is a demarcation line surveyed between 1763 and 1767 by Charles Mason and Jeremiah Dixon to determine what?
The boundary between Maryland and Pennsylvania
The boundary between the confederacy and the union
The boundary between the slave states and free states
The boundary between southern colonies and northern colonies

q.e: The Mason-Dixon Line resolved a border dispute between the Penn and Calvert families, between Pennsylvania and Maryland.

q: Maryland derives its name from its Catholic founders, who named the state after which historic person?

q.e: Maryland was named for Queen Henrietta Maria, wife of Charles I.

q: What is the state sport of Maryland?

q.e: Jousting is Maryland's official state sport (1962), and the first state sport in the US.

q: What is considered to be the final major hurdle before reaching the summit of Mt. Everest from the South Col Route?
First Step, Second Step and Third Step

q.e: The Hillary Step, a rock wall near Everest's summit on the southeast ridge, appears to have collapsed in 2016-17.

q: This city, situated on the River Vltava, is sometimes called the mother of cities, the city of a hundred spires and the golden city.

q.e: Prague, on the Vltava, is called "the mother of cities", "city of a hundred spires" and "the golden city."

q: This island in the Pacific Ocean is surrounded by a lagoon and a barrier reef.

q.e: Bora Bora in French Polynesia is ringed by a lagoon and barrier reef.

q: The city of Casablanca, which is the setting of the classic 1942 movie, starring Humphrey Bogart and Ingrid Bergman, is located in what African country?

q.e: Casablanca is the largest city and primary port of Morocco, situated along the Atlantic coast, although the country's political capital is Rabat.

q: What islands are knows as "The beautiful garland in the Indian Ocean"?

q.e: The Maldives are called "the beautiful garland in the Indian Ocean", a chain of about 1,200 islands.

q: This island, located in the Caribbean Sea, is the largest island of an archipelago called Greater Antilles. The city of Havana is located on it.

q.e: Spanning over 100,000 square kilometers, Cuba is by far the largest island in the Caribbean and the Greater Antilles. Hispaniola ranks second in area and is divided between Haiti and the Dominican Republic.

q: This is the sixth largest island in the world, and the largest island that is entirely in Indonesia.

q.e: Sumatra is the sixth-largest island, and the largest entirely in Indonesia.

q: This island, sometimes called island of inspiration, is part of a very large country, and has a unique fauna.

q.e: Tasmania is called "the island of inspiration" and has unique fauna such as the Tasmanian devil.

q: Valletta is the capital city of this island country in the Mediterranean.

q.e: Valletta is the capital of Malta, an archipelago nation in the central Mediterranean. It was founded in 1566 by the Order of St. John following the Great Siege of Malta.

q: Name the largest of the Canary Islands.

q.e: Tenerife covers about 2,034 square kilometers (785 sq mi), making it the largest and most populous of the Canary Islands. It is also home to Mount Teide, Spain's highest peak at 3,715 meters (12,188 ft).

q: Which of these popular musicians was not born in Spain?

q.e: Shakira is Colombian. Enrique Iglesias (born in Madrid) and Julio Iglesias are Spanish.

q: When was the city of Eilat founded?

q.e: Eilat was founded in 1949 as a village and became a town in 1951, at the northern end of the Red Sea.

q: What is the population of Eilat according to the Israel Central Bureau of Statistics end of 2004 census?

q.e: Eilat's population is ~50,000 today (the bank figure is its 2004 count).

q: Where does the Freedom Trail begin and end?
Boston Public Gardens, Old North Church

q.e: The Freedom Trail runs 2.5 miles in Boston from Boston Common to the Bunker Hill Monument in Charlestown.

q: What is the famous Niagara boat called?

q.e: The Maid of the Mist tour boats have ferried passengers directly into the spray of the Horseshoe Falls since 1846, originally starting as a steam-powered ferry service.

q: Name the smallest of the three waterfalls that make up the Niagara Falls.
There are only two waterfalls that make up the Niagara Falls.

q.e: Bridal Veil Falls is the smallest of the three Niagara falls, beside the American Falls and Horseshoe (Canadian) Falls.

q: Approximately what percentage of the water of the Niagara River flows over the Horseshoe Falls?

q.e: About 90% of the Niagara River's water flows over the Horseshoe Falls.

q: The flow of the water over the American Falls was completely blocked from June to November in what year?

q.e: In 1969 the Army Corps of Engineers diverted the river from the American Falls for months to remove rock debris.

q: Which country, Slovakia or Slovenia, used to be part of Yugoslavia?

q.e: Slovenia was a Yugoslav republic until 1991. Slovakia was part of Czechoslovakia.

q: Slovakia and Slovenia joined the European Union on the same day (May 1, 2004). Which of them was first to accept the euro currency?
None of them has accepted the EURO currency.
Both did on the day of their accession to the EU.

q.e: Slovenia adopted the euro in 2007 and Slovakia in 2009.

q: What is the capital of Slovakia?

q.e: Bratislava became the capital of an independent Slovakia in 1993 following the dissolution of Czechoslovakia. Prague is the capital of the Czech Republic, and Ljubljana is the capital of Slovenia.

q: What is the capital of Slovenia?

q.e: Ljubljana has been the capital of Slovenia since the country declared independence in 1991. Zagreb is the capital of neighboring Croatia, while Bratislava is Slovakia's capital.

q: Which statement concerning Slovakia and Slovenia is true?
Slovenia has access to the Adriatic Sea.
Both countries have access to the Black Sea.
Slovakia has access to the Baltic Sea.

q.e: Slovenia has a short Adriatic coast. Slovakia is landlocked.

q: Which of these statements regarding Slovakia and Slovenia is true?
Only Slovenia is an Alpine country.
Only Slovakia is an Alpine country.
None of them is an Alpine country.

q.e: Slovenia lies in the Alps, home of Triglav. Slovakia is in the Carpathians, and the High Tatras.

q: What is the capital city of Switzerland?

q.e: Bern is Switzerland's capital, called the "federal city," while Zurich is the largest city.

q: What mountain covers about 65% of the territory of Switzerland?

q.e: The Swiss Alps cover roughly 60% to 65% of Switzerland's total area, forming a major geographic and cultural landmark of the country.

q: What is the title of the national anthem of Switzerland?

q.e: The "Swiss Psalm" (Schweizerpsalm) became the official anthem in 1981.

q: What is the largest city in Switzerland?

q.e: Zurich is Switzerland's financial center and largest city, with over 400,000 residents in the municipality. Bern serves as the federal seat of government, while Munich is actually located across the border in Germany.

q: Which of these famous philosophers was of Swiss descent?

q.e: Jean-Jacques Rousseau was born in Geneva in 1712.

q: Which of these is the capital and the largest city in North Korea?

q.e: Located on the Taedong River, Pyongyang has been the capital of North Korea since the country's founding in 1948 and has a population of roughly 3 million residents.

q: The establishment of the Democratic Peoples Republic of Korea in this year set the official beginning of North Koreas history.

q.e: The Democratic People's Republic of Korea was proclaimed on 9 September 1948 under Kim Il Sung.

q: Which of these musicians became the first US musical group ever to perform in North Korea?
The Helen Henderson Choir of Victory Baptist Church

q.e: The New York Philharmonic played in Pyongyang in 2008, the first major US orchestra to perform in North Korea.

q: What is the longest river located entirely within the territory of the state of California?

q.e: The Sacramento River, about 640 miles, is California's longest river entirely within the state.

q: What does the Mohawk name of the Saint Lawrence River, Kaniatarowanenneh, mean?

q.e: Kaniatarowanenneh means "big waterway" in Mohawk. It is the St. Lawrence River.

q: What is the name of the capital and largest city of Norway?

q.e: Oslo was founded around 1040 and was called Christiania (later Kristiania) from 1624 until 1925, when its historical Norse name was officially restored.

q: What type of government does Norway have?

q.e: Norway is a constitutional monarchy with a parliamentary system.

q: What is the predominant form of Christianity in Norway?

q.e: Protestantism, mostly Lutheran (Church of Norway), is the main form of Christianity in Norway.

q: What is the largest carnivorous mammal endemic to the island of Madagascar?

q.e: The fossa (Cryptoprocta ferox) can grow up to 6 feet (1.8 m) long from snout to tail tip and weigh up to 19 pounds (8.6 kg). Though it resembles a slender cougar, it is closely related to the mongoose family.

q: What is the title of the national anthem of Madagascar, written by Norbert Raharisoa and composed by Rahajason?

q.e: "Ry Tanindrazanay malala ô!" is Madagascar's anthem, "Oh, Our Beloved Fatherland."

q: What are the official languages spoken in Madagascar?

q.e: Malagasy and French are Madagascar's official languages. English was official from 2007 to 2010.

q: What type of meal is the godro-godro, which is very popular in the Madagascar cuisine?

q.e: Godro-godro is a sweet rice pudding or milk pudding in Madagascan cuisine.

q: How many new species of animals and plants were discovered on Borneo between July 2005 and September 2006?

q.e: WWF reported 52 new species on Borneo between July 2005 and September 2006.

q: From the 1600s to the 1800s, the British and Dutch were interested in Borneo because they wanted control of this resource.

q.e: Borneo's pepper and spices attracted the British and Dutch traders.

q: Which of the characteristics below is typical for the buildings on the Greek archipelago of Santorini?

q.e: Santorini's Cycladic architecture is renowned for its whitewashed walls and vibrant blue-domed churches, originally designed to reflect intense summer heat and repel insects using limestone wash.

q: What is the biggest Greek island ?

q.e: Covering roughly 3,200 square miles (about 8,300 square kilometers), Crete is Greece's largest island and the fifth-largest in the Mediterranean. Euboea is the second-largest Greek island, while Cyprus is an independent nation.

q: Halkidiki, one of the Greek peninsulas, has a peculiar form which resembles what?

q.e: Halkidiki looks like a trident (a hand with three fingers), with Kassandra, Sithonia and Mount Athos.

q: At its peak, how many members did the Shinsengumi group have?

q.e: The Shinsengumi, a samurai police force in Kyoto, had up to 300 members at its peak in the 1860s.

q: In which city was the Shinsengumi group founded?

q.e: The Shinsengumi was founded in 1863 in Kyoto, to protect the shogunate.

q: What was the favorite weapon of Harada Sanosuke, the 10th unit captain of the Shinsengumi?

q.e: Harada Sanosuke was known for his skill with the spear. He led the 10th unit of the Shinsengumi.

q: What river is considered the longest river on the planet?

q.e: The Nile (about 6,650 km) is traditionally the longest river, though the Amazon is sometimes claimed.

q: What is the name of the holy river of the Hindu people?

q.e: The Ganges, called Ganga, is the holy river of Hindus.

q: What river flows through the central part of the French capital, Paris?

q.e: The Seine flows through Paris, past Notre-Dame.

q: What is the name of the longest river in Asia, and the third-longest in the world?

q.e: The Yangtze (6,300 km) is Asia's longest river and the third longest in the world.

q: In what Oklahoma city was the shopping cart invented?

q.e: The shopping cart was invented by Sylvan Goldman in Oklahoma City in 1937. The bank says Ardmore, which is doubtful.

q: How many of the astronauts who have flown in space between 1959 and 2009 were from Oklahoma?

q.e: Oklahoma has produced several astronauts, including Thomas Stafford and Owen Garriott.

q: Will Rogers World Airport and the Wiley Post Airport were named after people who died in 1935. How did they meet their demise?
as a result of a boat accident

q.e: Will Rogers and Wiley Post died in a plane crash near Point Barrow, Alaska, in August 1935.

q: Which of the following is NOT an Oklahoma city?

q.e: Toledo is in Ohio. Oklahoma has Tulsa, Norman, Enid and Lawton.

q: What does the national motto of India, Satyameva Jayate, mean in Sanskrit?

q.e: "Satyameva Jayate" means "Truth alone triumphs" and comes from the Mundaka Upanishad.

q: The national motto of this South American country is Libertad o muerte, Spanish for Liberty or Death.

q.e: Uruguay's motto is "Libertad o Muerte." Its flag also carries the Sun of May.

q: The slogan Sub Umbra Floreo, or Under the Shade I Flourish is the national motto of what Central American country?

q.e: Belize's motto "Sub umbra floreo" means "Under the shade I flourish", from its mahogany trade.

q: The national motto of what island country is Ever Conscious of God We Aspire, Build and Advance as One People?

q.e: Grenada's motto is "Ever conscious of God we aspire, build and advance as one people."

q: Which of these is a section of the famous Niagara Falls?

q.e: Niagara Falls consists of three distinct waterfalls: Horseshoe Falls (the largest, on the Canadian side), American Falls, and Bridal Veil Falls.

q: What is the name of the tallest waterfall in eastern North America?

q.e: Pissing Mare Falls in Virginia is a nearby claim; the state's highest is not the tallest in eastern North America. Check other sources.

q: What is the old name of the country of Madagascar?

q.e: The Malagasy Republic (1958–1975) was Madagascar's earlier name after independence from France.

q: What are the 2 main languages spoken in Madagascar?

q.e: Malagasy and French are Madagascar's main languages.

q: Of the 10,000 plants native to Madagascar, what percent are found nowhere else in the world?

q.e: About 90% of Madagascar's plants (and nearly all lemurs) live nowhere else on Earth.

q: On what island is the country of Madagascar located?

q.e: Madagascar is on Madagascar island, the fourth-largest island in the world.

q: What Portuguese explorer was the first to sight the island of Madagascar?

q.e: Diogo Dias sighted Madagascar in 1500 after being blown off course on the way to India.

q: New Guinea is the most linguistically diverse area in the world. Approximately how many separate languages are spoken there?

q.e: New Guinea has about 1,000 languages, with over 800 in Papua New Guinea alone.

q: The west half of the island of New Guinea is part of Indonesia, which comprises how many islands?

q.e: Indonesia has about 17,000 islands.

q: Approximately what percentage of the population of the country of Papua New Guinea lives in rural areas?

q.e: About 86 percent of Papua New Guinea's people live in rural areas.

q: What is the capital city of the country of Papua New Guinea?

q.e: Port Moresby is the capital of Papua New Guinea, on the Coral Sea.

q: What Egyptian city is the largest city not only in Africa, but also in the whole Middle East?

q.e: With a metropolitan area population exceeding 20 million people, Greater Cairo is the largest urban agglomeration in both Africa and the Middle East.

q: What animal is depicted on Egypts national emblem, which is featured on the national flag of Egypt, adopted in 1984?

q.e: Egypt's emblem is the Eagle of Saladin, in gold, on the white band of the flag.

q: What expression is commonly used in Egypt to refer to the annual flooding of the river Nile, the longest river in the world?

q.e: Herodotus called Egypt the "gift of the Nile" because the flood made farming possible.

q: What is the official name of Luxembourg?

q.e: Luxembourg's official name is the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg, the world's only sovereign grand duchy.

q: What is the name of the largest volcano on Earth in terms of area?

q.e: Mauna Loa in Hawaii is the largest active volcano on Earth by area and volume.

q: On which of the Canary Islands is the Mount Teide volcano located?

q.e: Mount Teide is on Tenerife, the highest mountain in Spain, at 3,715 m.

q: What is the highest point in the state of Illinois?

q.e: Charles Mound, at 376 m (1,235 ft), is the highest natural point in Illinois.

q: The Kalahari Desert, meaning great thirst translated from the local language, is a vast area of red-brown sands, taking up a considerable area of which of these regions?

q.e: The Kalahari lies mostly in Botswana, and also spreads into Namibia and South Africa.

q: Rangipo Desert in the central part of New Zealands North Island, does not have its barren and lifeless appearance because of the lack of rain, but rather, due to which of these?

q.e: Rangipo Desert is dry because of porous volcanic soil and wind, even though it gets lots of rain.

q: The Atacama Desert of Chile and Peru is one of the driest and most lifeless places on Earth. This virtually rainless plateau is made up of sand, lava flows, and what other substance?

q.e: The Atacama is one of the driest places on Earth. Salt flats, sand and lava flows cover it.

q: This is the worlds smallest independent state with a population in 2007 of approximately 821.

q.e: Vatican City, with fewer than 1,000 residents, is the world's smallest state.

q: Which central European countrys all pre-1989 neighbors do not exist any more? The country is now bordered by 7 states.

q.e: Poland lost all pre-1989 neighbors (USSR, East Germany, Czechoslovakia). It now borders seven states.

q: The African kingdom of Dahomey was powerful in the XVIII century. Which modern day country did it cover?

q.e: The Kingdom of Dahomey covered the area of Benin, a West African slave-trading power until French conquest in the 1890s.

q: When Yugoslavia collapsed, one of its republics became an independent state known as FYROM. To which country does the acronym refer?

q.e: FYROM stood for Former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia, now North Macedonia since 2019.

q: Myanmar is a south-eastern Asian country. Under which name was it known before a military junta took over?

q.e: Burma was renamed Myanmar by the military junta in 1989.

q: The Ottoman Empire used to rule over North Africa, the Middle East and south-eastern Europe. Which modern day country is the successor of the empire?

q.e: Turkey is the successor state of the Ottoman Empire, founded in 1923 by Atatürk.

q: Which independent country was not a Soviet republic?

q.e: Albania was an independent communist country, not a Soviet republic.

q: Finish this Irish saying: The far off hills are _______.
alive with the sound of music

q.e: The Irish saying is "Far-off hills are green", which means that things far away look better.

q: Tegucigalpa is the capital and largest city of this country.

q.e: Tegucigalpa became the capital of Honduras in 1880, succeeding Comayagua, and sits nestled in a valley roughly 3,200 feet above sea level.

q: What is the capital and largest city of Romania?

q.e: Bucharest is Romania's capital and largest city.

q: What is the capital and largest city of Lebanon?

q.e: Beirut is positioned on a peninsula extending into the Mediterranean Sea and has been inhabited for over 5,000 years. Bujumbura was the former capital of Burundi, Dhaka is the capital of Bangladesh, and Baghdad is the capital of Iraq.

q: What is the name of the capital city of Latvia?

q.e: Riga, founded in 1201 on the Gulf of Riga, is the capital of Latvia and the largest city in the Baltic states. Reykjavik is the capital of Iceland, Port Vila is in Vanuatu, and Porto-Novo is in Benin.

q: This city is the capital of the Kingdom of Morocco.

q.e: Rabat is Morocco's capital. Casablanca is the largest city.

q: The capital city of what country is called Quito?

q.e: Quito sits at an elevation of 9,350 feet (2,850 meters), making it the second-highest official capital city in the world after La Paz, Bolivia.

q: Name Zimbabwes capital which is an independent city equivalent to a province.

q.e: Harare is the capital and largest city of Zimbabwe, operating as an independent metropolitan province. It was founded in 1890 and originally named Salisbury before being renamed Harare in 1982.

q: Name Moroccos capital that is also the capital of the Rabat-Salé-Zemmour-Zaer region.

q.e: Rabat has served as Morocco's capital since 1912; although Casablanca is the country's largest city and economic hub, Rabat is the political center.

q: What is the capital and largest commercial city of Libya?

q.e: Tripoli is located in northwestern Libya along the Mediterranean coast and houses over 1 million residents. Ethiopia is an East African country, Windhoek is the capital of Namibia, and Nouakchott is the capital of Mauritania.

q: This city is Kenyas capital and the most populous city in East Africa.

q.e: Founded in 1899 as a rail depot on the Uganda Railway, Nairobi grew into Kenya's capital and is now home to well over 4 million residents.

q: What is the currency of Russia?

q.e: The Russian ruble is the national currency.

q: Who is the first President of the Russian Federation?

q.e: Boris Yeltsin won the June 1991 popular election and served as president through the collapse of the Soviet Union until resigning on December 31, 1999, when Vladimir Putin succeeded him.

q: Name the capital city of the U.S. state of Wyoming.

q.e: Cheyenne is the capital of Wyoming.

q: The U.S. state of Oregon has been nicknamed after this animal, which is the official state animal.

q.e: Oregon is the "Beaver State", and the beaver is its state animal.

q: Name the capital city of the U.S. state of Montana.

q.e: Helena is Montana's capital.

q: The state of Louisiana is bordered by the Gulf of Mexico on the south and three states. Which state does NOT border Louisiana?

q.e: Louisiana borders Texas, Arkansas and Mississippi. It doesn't border Oklahoma.

q: The Beskidy (Beskydy) Euroregion is located in the west part of the Carpathian mountain range. Which three countries does it span?

q.e: The Beskids Euroregion spans the Czech Republic, Poland and Slovakia.

q: The ore and coal rich region of Silesia (pol.: Ślask, ger.: Schliesien, cz.: Slezsko) was ruled by Germans, Poles, Czechs and Austrians. To which country does it mostly belong today?

q.e: Most of Silesia is today in Poland, with parts in Czechia and Germany.

q: What is the state animal of Colorado and the symbol of Rocky Mountain National Park?

q.e: The bighorn sheep is Colorado's state animal and symbol of Rocky Mountain National Park.

q: Mesa Verde National Park in southern Colorado is best known for which of the following?
The best-preserved cliff dwellings in the U.S.
A very rare flower that only grows in the mountains

q.e: Mesa Verde National Park has well-preserved Ancestral Puebloan cliff dwellings, including Cliff Palace.

q: What is the state motto of Colorado?

q.e: Colorado's motto is "Nil sine Numine," "Nothing without Providence (the Deity)."

q: What is the state fish of Colorado?

q.e: The greenback cutthroat trout is Colorado's state fish.

q: What was the popular slogan of the Colorado Gold Rush?

q.e: "Pikes Peak or Bust" was the slogan of the 1859 Colorado Gold Rush.

q: What year did Colorado become a state?

q.e: Colorado became the 38th state on 1 August 1876, the "Centennial State."

q: The self-governed region of the Holy Mountain is considered part of the Greek state according to a decree passed in what year?

q.e: Mount Athos, a self-governed monastic state, was made part of Greece by the 1913 Treaty of London and other agreements.

q: The Swedish name of Sweden is Sverige. What does this word literally mean?

q.e: Sverige means "Kingdom of the Svear" or "Swedes' realm".

q: Which of these celebrities is not Swedish?

q.e: Lars Ulrich of Metallica is Danish. ABBA and Max Martin are Swedish.

q: What is the capital city of the Federative Republic of Brazil?

q.e: Brasília is Brazil's capital, built in the 1950s and inaugurated in 1960.

q: What is the meaning of the Portuguese word brasa from which the name of Brazil possibly originated?

q.e: "Brasa" means "ember" in Portuguese, and the name may come from brazilwood, a red dye wood.

q: What is the largest and richest city in Brazil?

q.e: Sao Paulo has over 12 million residents in the city proper and generates more than 10 percent of Brazil's total GDP. Brasilia serves as the political capital, while Rio de Janeiro is the country's second-largest financial hub.

q: What type of food is the traditional Brazilian dish called Moqueca?

q.e: Moqueca is a Brazilian fish stew, cooked with coconut milk or dendê oil.

q: Boza is a thick, fermented beverage with a sweet and sour taste. It is made from millet seed and various astringent substances and was invented in which country?

q.e: Boza is a fermented drink from the Balkans and Turkey. Its origins are disputed.

q: Popcorn is flavored with salt, butter, sugar, dried spices and many other condiments. In this country they even serve it with vinegar.

q.e: Popcorn with vinegar is a snack in some countries, with several countries claiming it.

q: Lego Group, best known for the manufacture of Lego-brand toys, was founded in 1932 in this country.

q.e: The Lego Group was founded in 1932 by carpenter Ole Kirk Christiansen in Billund, Denmark. The company name was derived from the Danish phrase leg godt, meaning play well.

q: The city of Stoke-on-Trent, Staffordshire, England is known as the home of what popular craft and hobby?

q.e: Stoke-on-Trent is famed for pottery, "The Potteries," with Wedgwood and Spode.

q: This plant has a long and colorful history and its legal status varies from country to country.

q.e: Cannabis has a long history, and its legal status varies by country.

q: The legendary creature Peryton, that was said to come from the lost continent Atlantis, is a hybrid of what two animals?

q.e: The peryton is a mythical beast with a stag's body and the wings of a bird, from Borges's Book of Imaginary Beings.

q: Which is the only South American country that uses English as its official language?

q.e: Guyana is the only South American country with English as its official language.

q: In what country in Africa is Spanish the official language?

q.e: Equatorial Guinea is the only African country where Spanish is an official language, a legacy of its history as a Spanish colony until gaining independence in 1968.

q: The term Quizling, which means a traitor, is derived from the name of Vidkun Quisling, who assisted Nazi Germany while serving as Minister-President of this country.

q.e: Vidkun Quisling led Norway's pro-Nazi government during the German occupation and was executed in 1945.

q: What is the official language of Andorra, a small country in southwestern Europe bordered by Spain and France?

q.e: Catalan is the sole official language of Andorra under its 1993 constitution, making it the only country where Catalan holds this exclusive status.

q: Which country is not correctly paired with its national dance?

q.e: Salsa is not Brazil's dance. Brazil is known for samba.

q: In what country did the Bachata dance originate?

q.e: Bachata began in the rural Dominican Republic in the 1960s.

q: A supposed unicorn skeleton was found in a cave in Europe. The skeleton was found to be a hoax but the cave retained the name Unicorn Cave. In which European country is Unicorn Cave located?

q.e: The Einhornhöhle (Unicorn Cave) in the Harz Mountains, Germany, gave "unicorn" bones that were actually mammoth fossils.

q: Any country that obeys seat belt laws is an object of my _____________.

q.e: This is a pun on "fastening," as in "fasten your seat belt".

q: The name of which legendary island comes from a word meaning apple?

q.e: Avalon is the legendary isle of King Arthur, whose name may derive from a word meaning "apple."

q: Which of these was NOT reelected president of his country in 2012?

q.e: Nicolas Sarkozy lost the 2012 French election to François Hollande.

q: The town of Kemi, which in 1996 became the home of the worlds largest snow castle, is located in this European country.

q.e: Kemi, in Finnish Lapland, has had the SnowCastle since 1996.

q: The translation of this soaps title is Tiny Angels and 4 of the characters are; Marcela Ferradas, Lidia Catalano, Adriana Salonia and, Mariana Briski. Which country had this soap?

q.e: "Los pequeños ángeles" is a soap from Argentina, but check original sources for details.

q: This soap operas original title included the words the need but in 2001 it dropped those words and is called by one name only. Cast characters include: Owen Meyer, Judy Ditchfield, Jo da Silva and, Bianca Amato. What country produced this soap?

q.e: "Isidingo: The Need" was a South African soap that dropped the subtitle in 2001.

q: Good Times, Bad Times is the translation of this soap that has the following characters: Lucas Sanders, Mike Brandt, Lorena Gonzalez and, Nuran Baydar. What country owns it?

q.e: "Goede Tijden, Slechte Tijden" (Good Times, Bad Times) is a Dutch soap running since 1990.

q: This soap claimed to be the answer to the popular American soap Melrose Place. Its characters included Angela Kostapas, Bronwyn Kellett, Gideon Miller and Wiki Taylor. In what country was it produced?

q.e: "Shortland Street," New Zealand's soap, premiered in 1992; the bank says another NZ show, so check.

q: I Hope Youre The One is the title of this soap that ran from 2001-2003. The characters were Frances Peron, Raul Gaston, Don Ramon Altamonte and Amadeus. Which country produced it?

q.e: A Filipino soap. The question is obscure, so check other sources.

q: Hotel Caesar has been around since 1998 and past characters on the show have been: Ragnar Lunde, Rolv Espevoll, Thomas Hildring and, Bob Affe. Which country owns it.

q.e: "Hotel Cæsar" is a Norwegian soap, running since 1998 on TV 2.

q: This country, famous for its fjords, has an extensive coastline, facing the North Atlantic Ocean and the Barents Sea.

q.e: Norway's jagged coastline measures over 15,000 miles (25,000 km) when including its famous glacial fjords like Geirangerfjord. It stretches all the way into the Arctic to border the Barents Sea.

q: How many dancers traditionally perform the Danse des petits cygnes (Dance of the Little Swans) in Swan Lake?

q.e: The Dance of the Little Swans in Swan Lake is danced by four dancers, arms linked.

q: In February 2011, the president of this country resigned after widespread protests calling for his departure and transferred authority to the Armed Forces.

q.e: Hosni Mubarak resigned on 11 February 2011 after the Egyptian uprising, handing power to the military.

q: In May, 2011, American President Barack Obama announced that Osama bin Laden had been killed during an American military operation in this country.
