q.e: Osama bin Laden was killed on May 2, 2011, during Operation Neptune Spear, carried out by US Navy SEALs in Abbottabad, Pakistan. The compound was located less than a mile from the Pakistan Military Academy.

q: An uprising which started in February 2011 led to a civil war in this Arab country.

q.e: The 2011 Libyan uprising became a civil war and led to Gaddafi's fall.

q: This character, known for roaming the depths of the sea in his submarine, the Nautilus, dies saying God and my country!

q.e: Captain Nemo, who first appeared in Jules Verne's 1870 novel Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea, meets his end in the 1875 sequel The Mysterious Island.

q: The Cincinnati Reds were once called the Cincinnati Red Stockings. The Red Sox, with a name (Sox) thats a plural of sock, is from what U.S. city?

q.e: The Boston Red Sox were named in 1908 and use "Sox" as short for "stockings".

q: This city, located north of the Dead Sea, is the lowest permanently inhabited site in the world.

q.e: Jericho, about 258 m below sea level, is often called the lowest city in the world.

q: What European city was named Philippopolis or the city of Philip?

q.e: Plovdiv in Bulgaria was Philippopolis, named for Philip II of Macedon.

q: In this country it is believed that a white elephant may contain the soul of a dead person, perhaps a Buddha.

q.e: In Thailand white elephants are sacred and a royal symbol, and have been believed to hold a soul.

q: At the beginning of the Spanish-American War a modern American fleet quickly and decisively defeated a somewhat antiquated Spanish fleet. Near what city was this early American victory?

q.e: Commodore Dewey defeated the Spanish fleet at the Battle of Manila Bay on 1 May 1898.

q: Under what rule did the historical city of Petra decline quickly as a result of which many of the tombs was damaged by thieves and many treasures were stolen?

q.e: Petra declined under Roman rule after 106 AD, and an earthquake in 363 AD did more damage.

q: In January, 2010 a 7.0-magnitude earthquake devastated the capital of this country and caused the death of 230,000 people.

q.e: On January 12, 2010, a magnitude 7.0 earthquake struck roughly 16 miles west of Port-au-Prince, Haiti. The catastrophic tremor destroyed vital infrastructure and displaced over 1.5 million people.

q: The 2010 eruption of the Eyjafjallajökull volcano, located in this country, caused extensive air travel disruption.

q.e: Eyjafjallajökull is an ice-capped volcano in southern Iceland. Its April 2010 eruption created an enormous ash cloud that grounded more than 100,000 commercial flights across northern and western Europe.

q: Which state capital did Gary Cooper grow up in?

q.e: Gary Cooper was raised in Helena, Montana, and attended school there and in England.

q: One of Enid Blytons first books, The Secret Island, had four sequels. Which of the following is not one of them?

q.e: The Secret Island sequels are The Secret of Spiggy Holes, The Secret Mountain, The Secret of Killimooin and The Secret Valley.

q: After many years of reporting on lands around the globe, this renowned travel writer turned to fiction and created the European city and state of Hav.

q.e: Jan Morris wrote the travel writer's novel "Hav" (2006), set in a fictional Mediterranean city-state.

q: On January 1, 1984, the Southeast Asian country Brunei proclaimed to be a fully independent state after it regained independence from the United Kingdom. What is the state religion of Brunei?

q.e: Islam is Brunei's state religion, and the Sultan is head of religion.

q: In September 1984, Western Australia became the last Australian state to abolish capital punishment. When was it last used in the country?

q.e: Ronald Ryan's 1967 hanging in Victoria was the last judicial execution in Australia.

q: In 1984, Joseph Kettinger became the first person to cross an ocean alone, in a hot air balloon. Which ocean did he cross?

q.e: Joe Kittinger completed the first solo transatlantic balloon flight in 1984, in the Rosie O'Grady's.

q: What is the tallest mountain in North America?

q.e: Denali (formerly Mount McKinley), 6,190 m, is the highest mountain in North America.

q: What is the tallest mountain in the North American Rockies?

q.e: Mount Elbert, Colorado (4,401 m), is the highest peak in the Rocky Mountains. Grand Teton (4,199 m) is in Wyoming.

q: Which is the second highest mountain in terms of above sea level elevation?

q.e: K2, located on the China-Pakistan border in the Karakoram range, reaches an elevation of 28,251 feet (8,611 m) above sea level, second only to Mount Everest's 29,032 feet (8,849 m).

q: The first mountain scaling to be recorded was done by this Roman Emperor.

q.e: The Roman emperor Hadrian is said to have climbed Mount Etna to see the sunrise.

q: What is the state capital of the U.S. state of Delaware?

q.e: Dover has served as Delaware's capital since 1777, when it replaced New Castle during the American Revolutionary War. Wilmington is the state's most populous city, but it has never been the capital.

q: What former capital of Japan lends its name to a famous Protocol aimed at combating global warming?

q.e: Kyoto served as Japan's imperial capital from 794 until 1868, when the court moved to Tokyo. The Kyoto Protocol was adopted there in December 1997 to commit industrialized countries to limiting greenhouse gas emissions.

q: Which British Prime Minister is considered to have saved his country during WW2?

q.e: Winston Churchill served as British Prime Minister from 1940 to 1945, rallying the nation and Allied forces with speeches during Britain's darkest hours after Neville Chamberlain resigned.

q: This George was the first president of the USA. Although the American capital city was named after him, he never lived there.

q.e: George Washington served as president from 1789 to 1797 while the national capital was located in New York City and then Philadelphia, before the federal government relocated to Washington, D.C. in 1800.

q: This John is the one who said Ask not what your country can do for you, ask what you can do for your country.

q.e: John F. Kennedy said this in his inaugural address on 20 January 1961.

q: Along with his brother, this famous explorer reached Kaifeng, the capital of Kublai Khans Mongol Empire in 1265.

q.e: Niccolò and Maffeo Polo, Marco's father and uncle, traveled to Kublai Khan around 1260-1266. Marco joined them in 1271.

q: This great explorer found a new continent thinking he had found a new way to India.

q.e: Christopher Columbus landed in the Bahamas in October 1492, believing he had reached the East Indies, which is why he called the Indigenous inhabitants 'Indians'.

q: Ask not what your country can do for you, ask what you can do for your country. These words were delivered by which US President?

q.e: JFK's 1961 inaugural address contained the line.

q: The Mafia was actually formed in Sicily in the Middle Ages as a secret society to resist the Turk and Norman invaders. Later, it spread to the United States and this was the first American city where it became influential.

q.e: New York was the first American city where the Mafia took hold, among Italian immigrants in the 1800s.

q: In 1967, John Lennon of the Beatles bought an island called Dorinish which was located in what part of the world?

q.e: John Lennon bought Dorinish in Clew Bay, County Mayo, Ireland, in 1967.

q: Pope John Paul II, the first non-Italian Pope since 1522, was born in which European country?

q.e: Born Karol Józef Wojtyła in Wadowice, Poland, in 1920, he was elected pope in 1978, ending a 455-year streak of Italian popes that dated back to Pope Adrian VI of the Netherlands in 1522.

q: She was the first recorded female leader. She ruled the Mesopotamian City-State of Ur around 2500 BCE.

q.e: Ku-Baba was a Sumerian queen of Kish, the only woman on the Sumerian King List.

q: Formula 1 driver Kimi Raikonnen is called The Iceman. Judging by his surname, what northern country is he from?

q.e: Kimi Räikkönen is Finnish. "Iceman" refers to his calm demeanor.

q: Judging by his name, Kim Jong-il became the ruler of this axis of evil country in 1994.

q.e: Kim Jong-il led North Korea from 1994 to 2011, after the death of Kim Il Sung.

q: Miss World 2005 was Unnur Birna Vilhjalmsdottir. Judging by her last name, what country is she from?

q.e: Unnur Birna Vilhjálmsdóttir is Icelandic. Icelandic surnames are patronymic.

q: Kazuyoshi Funaki was a champion in ski-jumping. You dont have to be a ski-jumping expert to know that he represented this country.

q.e: Kazuyoshi Funaki is Japanese. He won Olympic gold in 1998.
Rocky Mountain oysters are bull calf testicles, breaded and fried, a ranch delicacy in the American West.

q: The surname Eriksson is in the top 5 of the most common names in which European country?

q.e: Eriksson (son of Erik) is one of Sweden's most common surnames, alongside Andersson, Johansson and Karlsson.

q: If your surname was De Jong, your home country would most probably be this one.

q.e: "De Jong" ("the young") is one of the most common surnames in the Netherlands.

q: In which present day country was Vlad the Impaler born?

q.e: Vlad III, widely known as Vlad the Impaler or Vlad Dracula, was born around 1431 in the town of Sighisoara, located in the Transylvania region of modern-day Romania.

q: St. David, who is commemorated with a feast day falling on March 1 each year, is the national patron saint of this country.

q.e: Saint David, or Dewi Sant in Welsh, is the patron saint of Wales, celebrated annually on March 1 with traditional symbols like the leek and daffodil. Scotland's patron saint is Saint Andrew, celebrated on November 30.

q: New York City was originally established as which other New city?

q.e: New York City was first New Amsterdam, a Dutch settlement. The English renamed it in 1664 after the Duke of York.

q: To which country did Barack Obama's family move when he was six?

q.e: Barack Obama moved to Jakarta, Indonesia, in 1967 with his mother and stepfather, Lolo Soetoro.

q: At the start of World War II, Joseph P. Kennedy, Sr., the patriarch of the prominent political clan, served as the United States Ambassador to this country.

q.e: Joseph P. Kennedy Sr. was US Ambassador to the United Kingdom from 1938 to 1940.

q: George W. Bush, who became U.S. President in 2001, was born in which city?

q.e: George W. Bush was born in New Haven, Connecticut, in 1946 while his father was at Yale, and grew up in Texas.

q: In which middle eastern country did terrorists attack an American marine barracks during the Ronald Reagan administration?

q.e: Hezbollah-linked bombers killed 241 US service members at the Beirut barracks in October 1983 under Reagan.

q: Henry the Navigator, who initiated European worldwide expansion, was king of this country.

q.e: Prince Henry the Navigator was never king. He was a Portuguese prince who sponsored exploration in the 1400s.

q: After being overthrown Idi Amin first went to this country.

q.e: After the 1979 overthrow Idi Amin fled to Libya, then settled in Saudi Arabia.

q: In 1972 Idi Amin expelled these people from his country.

q.e: In 1972 Amin expelled about 50,000 Asians, mostly of Indian origin, from Uganda.

q: The city of Port Royal, known for Gallows Point where many pirates were executed, is located on what Caribbean Island?

q.e: Port Royal, Jamaica, was a notorious pirate haven, and much of it sank in an earthquake in 1692.

q: This Canadian explorer was the first North American to cross the Sahara desert alone on a camel in 1990.

q.e: Frank Cole's claim is obscure; check other sources.

q: What celebrity was murdered by Mark David Chapman on 8 December, 1980 in New York City?

q.e: Mark David Chapman shot John Lennon outside the Dakota in New York on 8 December 1980.

q: In what country were the first ocean-going vessels developed during the 15th century?

q.e: Portuguese caravels pioneered ocean-going sailing in the 15th century under Henry the Navigator.

q: The rise of what country limited the possibilities of European overland trade during the 14th and 15th century?

q.e: The rise of the Ottoman Empire blocked land routes to Asia, pushing Europeans to seek sea routes.

q: Madeira, discovered by Portuguese sailors between 1418 and 1420, is an archipelago located in this ocean.

q.e: Madeira is a Portuguese archipelago in the Atlantic Ocean, about 400 km north of the Canary Islands.

q: Mary I, usually remembered as Bloody Mary, was Queen of England and Ireland and Queen consort of this country.

q.e: Mary I was queen consort of Spain by marriage to Philip II (1554).

q: The first lady of this European country died in a plane crash on 10 April 2010.

q.e: Maria Kaczyńska, wife of President Lech Kaczyński, died in the Smolensk plane crash on 10 April 2010.

q: On 8 December 1980 he was shot in New York City.

q.e: Former Beatle John Lennon was tragically shot and killed outside the Dakota apartment building in New York City by Mark David Chapman on December 8, 1980.

q: Amerigo Vespuccis third voyage was commanded by Goncalo Coelho in the service of which country?

q.e: Gonçalo Coelho commanded the Portuguese expedition of 1501-02 that Amerigo Vespucci joined.

q: In what country was Che Guevara born?

q.e: Che Guevara was born in Rosario, Argentina, in 1928.

q: To what island did Mata Hari and her husband Rudolph MecLeod move?

q.e: Mata Hari moved to Java (Dutch East Indies) in 1897 with her husband, Captain Rudolf MacLeod.

q: In what country was Mata Hari born?

q.e: Mata Hari was born in Leeuwarden, the Netherlands, in 1876 as Margaretha Zelle. She was executed in France in 1917 for spying.

q: Somali pirates were known for getting their weaponry from this country.

q.e: Somali pirates' weapons arrived through trafficking, often through Yemen. Check other sources for details.

q: Where did Aristotle Onassis go after leaving his home country in 1923.

q.e: Aristotle Onassis left Turkey (Smyrna) in 1923 and went to Buenos Aires, where he started in the tobacco business.

q: Which President delivered the famous words, Ask not what your country can do for you--ask what you can do for your country.?

q.e: JFK said this in his inaugural address, on 20 January 1961.

q: What Genoese explorer sailed off Spain on 3 August 1492 across the Atlantic Ocean and discovered the Americas?

q.e: Columbus set sail from Palos, Spain, on 3 August 1492 on the Niña, Pinta and Santa María, and reached the Bahamas on 12 October.

q: This British captain explored the Pacific Ocean and was the first to reach New Zealand, Australia and Hawaii.

q.e: Captain James Cook was first European to reach Hawaii (1778) and the east coast of Australia, and he circled New Zealand. Tasman sighted NZ first.

q: What country sent its fleet to England with the intention to invade the country and overthrow Queen Elizabeth I of England, but was defeated in 1588?

q.e: King Philip II of Spain launched the Spanish Armada of around 130 ships in 1588, but English naval tactics and severe storms resulted in a decisive Spanish defeat.

q: I was a New York City sewer worker and Ralph and Alice Kramdens upstairs neighbor on The Honeymooners.

q.e: Ed Norton (Art Carney) was the sewer worker neighbor of Ralph Kramden on The Honeymooners.

q: I played the good-hearted, but dim-witted 1st mate on Gilligans Island.

q.e: Bob Denver played Gilligan, the first mate of the SS Minnow, on Gilligan's Island (1964–67).

q: The Drummond family, featured on Diffrent Strokes, lived on what street n New York City?

q.e: The Drummond family in Diff'rent Strokes lived in a Park Avenue penthouse in Manhattan.

q: Morehead State University is in the city of Morehead that is located in which state?

q.e: Morehead State University is in Morehead, Kentucky.

q: Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil, Absolute Power, Mystic River

q.e: Clint Eastwood directed Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil, and directed and starred in Absolute Power and Mystic River (directed only).

q: This country is famous for its lager beers, especially Amstel, Heineken and Grolsch.

q.e: The Netherlands is the home of brewing giants Heineken (founded in Amsterdam in 1864), Amstel, and Grolsch (founded in Groenlo in 1615). Belgium is also famed for beer, but primarily for specialty ales and lambics rather than these international pale lagers.

q: Which country did Germany invade on September 1, 1939?

q.e: Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939, starting WWII in Europe.

q: An estimated 62 million people lost their lives during World War II. Which country gave the most casualties?

q.e: The Soviet Union lost about 27 million people in WWII, the most of any country.

q: In 2007, what city was the most populous state capital in the United States?

q.e: Phoenix is the most populous US state capital. Arizona's capital since 1889.

q: What is the capital of New York State?

q.e: Albany is the capital of New York State, not New York City.

q: Which city serves as the state capital of California?

q.e: Sacramento became the permanent state capital of California in 1854, succeeding earlier short-lived capitals including Monterey, San Jose, Vallejo, and Benicia.

q: Which state capital also served as a capital of the Confederate States of America?

q.e: Richmond served as the capital of the Confederacy from May 1861 until April 1865, replacing Montgomery, Alabama, before returning to its role as the capital of Virginia.

q: Augusta is the capital of which state?

q.e: Augusta became the capital of Maine in 1827, replacing Portland. It is the easternmost state capital in the United States and has a population of fewer than 20,000 residents.

q: This Central-African country is named after a lake, located within its territories.

q.e: Chad is named after Lake Chad, a shallow lake it shares with Niger, Nigeria and Cameroon.

q: This country is a Caribbean communist state that is famous for both its ruler and its cigars.

q.e: Cuba became a socialist republic under Fidel Castro following the 1959 revolution and is globally famous for its hand-rolled Habano cigars made from Vuelta Abajo tobacco.

q: This is an island nation that has been divided into two parts under Greek and Turkish authority.

q.e: Cyprus has been divided since 1974 into the Republic of Cyprus in the south and the self-declared Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, separated by a United Nations buffer zone. The other options are not split island nations: Cuba is an undivided island nation, while Cambodia and Chad are continental countries.

q: How many major islands does the African island nation of Comoros consist of?

q.e: Comoros has four main islands: Grande Comore, Mohéli, Anjouan and Mayotte (the last claimed but administered by France).

q: Before Mount Everest was discovered, this was the highest mountain in the world.

q.e: Before Everest was surveyed in 1852, Kangchenjunga was thought the world's highest.

q: The outbreak of World War II began with the German invasion of which European country?

q.e: Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939.

q: What city did the Baltimore Orioles play in before moving to Baltimore?

q.e: The Baltimore Orioles were the St. Louis Browns until moving to Baltimore in 1954.

q: With its 3,287,590 sq. km. (1,269,346 sq. miles) this country ranks 7th largest in the world. Numbers were invented here, even though Europeans learned them from the Arabs.

q.e: India ranks seventh in area. The decimal number system we use developed in India and was transmitted by Arab scholars.

q: With a territory of 7,686,850 sq. km. (2,967,909 sq. miles), it the the smallest continent, the largest island, and the 6th biggest country in the world.

q.e: Australia is the smallest continent and largest island, sixth in country size.

q: Stretching over 8,511,965 sq. km. (3,286,488 sq. miles), this South American country ranks 5th largest. It has the worlds widest expressways, the Monumental Axis.

q.e: Brazil is the world's fifth-largest nation by land area, surpassed only by Russia, Canada, China, and the United States. Its capital, Brasília, features the Monumental Axis, designed by urban planner Lúcio Costa.

q: 9,596,960 sq. km. (3,705,407 sq. miles) position this Asian country as 4th largest in the world. Porcelain, gunpowder, paper and money were all invented here.

q.e: China is about 9.6 million km² and ranks third or fourth in area. It invented paper, gunpowder, printing and the compass.

q: This country ranks 3rd largest weighing in at 9,629,091sq. km. (3,717,813 sq. miles). One of the symbols of this North American country is a gift from France.

q.e: The US ranks third or fourth in size. The Statue of Liberty was a gift from France in 1886.

q: This immigrant friendly North American country is the second largest in the world with a total area of 9,976,140 sq. km (3,851,809 sq. miles). There are two official languages there: English and French.

q.e: Canada spans six time zones and encompasses nearly 10 million square kilometers, making it second only to Russia in total area. English and French were given equal official status by the Official Languages Act of 1969.

q: The largest country in the world, almost doubling the area of USA. It lies on 17,075,200 sq. km. (6,592,772 sq. miles) of terrain, even though it sold Alaska to the USA in 1867 for $7.2 million.

q.e: Spanning eleven time zones across Eastern Europe and northern Asia, Russia covers over 17 million square kilometers, making it roughly 1.7 times larger than Canada or the United States.

q: Peter Deunov is the founder of the Danovism movement and the Universal White Brotherhood. He was born in Bulgaria, but from 1888 to 1895 he studied medicine and theology in this US city.

q.e: Peter Deunov (Beinsa Douno), Bulgarian spiritual teacher, studied in the US at Boston University and Drew Seminary.

q: The Etruscan civilization, one of the most mysterious ancient civilizations, existed in the territory of this modern country.

q.e: The Etruscans lived in Etruria, now Tuscany, Lazio and Umbria in Italy, and influenced Rome.

q: The Great Depression in the US inspired these two to start travelling the Southwestern part of the country, robbing banks.

q.e: Bonnie Parker and Clyde Barrow committed robberies in the central and southwestern US in 1932–1934 and were killed in an ambush in Louisiana.

q: Which is the only country in South America, whose official language is English?

q.e: Guyana gained independence from the United Kingdom in 1966 and remains South America's only officially English-speaking country. Neighboring Suriname officially speaks Dutch.

q: How many islands does the country of Indonesia have?

q.e: Indonesia has about 17,000 islands, though counts vary from 13,000 to 18,000.

q: This country, which used to be known as Ceylon, was referred to as The Pearl of the East .

q.e: The island nation was known as Ceylon during British colonial rule until it adopted the name Sri Lanka in 1972. Because of its teardrop shape and location off India's southern coast, it is often called the 'Pearl of the Indian Ocean'.

q: Which of these animals did the Israelites worship while Moses was on the mountain?

q.e: According to the Book of Exodus, Aaron collected gold ornaments to craft the Golden Calf while Moses was atop Mount Sinai receiving the Ten Commandments.

q: According to Matthew and Luke, in what city was Jesus born?

q.e: Matthew and Luke place Jesus's birth in Bethlehem.

q: According to the Bibles interpretation of Moses life, who ran along the bank to make sure that Moses was alright in his basket after he was set adrift on the Nile river?

q.e: Moses's sister (Miriam) watched over the basket in the reeds of the Nile, per Exodus 2.

q: In every synagogue, in every country in the world, there are the same number of statues. How many?

q.e: Jewish law forbids graven images in houses of worship, so synagogues have no statues.

q: This is the holiest city in Judaism and the spiritual center of the Jewish people. It also plays an important role in Christianity and Islam.

q.e: Jerusalem is the holiest city in Judaism, and also sacred to Christians and Muslims.

q: Which Israeli city is a sister city of New York City?

q.e: Tel Aviv and Jerusalem are Israeli cities tied to New York. Check sources for the official sister city.

q: What city is called The capital of the Negev (desert)?

q.e: Beersheba is called the capital of the Negev, with Abraham's well nearby.

q: You can go snow skiing in the area of which Israeli mountain?

q.e: Mount Hermon, on the Golan Heights, has Israel's ski resort.

q: He was a Supreme Pontiff of the Roman Catholic Church and Sovereign of Vatican City from 1978 until his death in 2005.

q.e: John Paul II was pope from 1978 to 2005, the first non-Italian pope in 455 years. He was canonized in 2014.

q: This Coptic Orthodox monastery is located in an oasis in the Eastern Desert of Egypt.

q.e: The Monastery of St. Anthony near the Red Sea is one of the oldest Christian monasteries in the world, founded in the 4th century.

q: Burning women who were supposedly witches was a common practice on the European continent. In England, however, they punished witches in this way.
Stabbed them with a silver lance

q.e: In England witches were generally hanged, not burned. Burning was for treason or heresy.

q: One of the remnants of this states former status as a possession of France is the fact that it was named after a French king.

q.e: Louisiana is named for Louis XIV of France by René-Robert Cavelier de La Salle in 1682.

q: No state has as many different species of mammals as this one. The average square mile of land contains 1.4 elk, 1.4 pronghorn antelope, and 3.3 deer.

q.e: Montana has a wide variety of wildlife, with big herds of elk, pronghorn and deer.

q: One of the following pairs (state - its capital) is wrong.

q.e: The capital of North Dakota is Bismarck, not Fargo, which is the largest city.

q: What is the state capital of Washington?

q.e: Olympia was chosen as the territorial capital in 1853 and remained the seat of government when Washington attained statehood in 1889. While Seattle is the state's largest city and economic center, it is not the capital.

q: What is the state capital of Idaho?

q.e: Boise became the capital of the Idaho Territory in 1864, replacing Lewiston, and remained the capital when Idaho achieved statehood in 1890. It is also the most populous city in the state.

q: What is the state capital of Alaska?

q.e: Juneau is Alaska's capital. It is only reachable by boat or air.

q: After gaining its independence in 1991, it has retained closer political and economic ties to Russia than any of the other former Soviet republics.

q.e: Belarus has kept close ties with Russia since 1991, as part of the Union State.

q: It was once the center of power for an empire. Occupied by the allies in 1945, a state treaty ended its occupation in 1955 and recognized its independence.

q.e: Austria's Allied occupation ended with the Austrian State Treaty of 1955.

q: Its three-year-old Socialist government was overthrown in 1973 by a dictatorial military regime led by Augusto Pinochet.

q.e: Salvador Allende's government fell in Pinochet's coup on 11 September 1973.

q: This country controls the Sinai Peninsula. Following the completion of the Suez Canal in 1869, it became an important world transportation hub.

q.e: Egypt regained full sovereignty over the Sinai Peninsula in 1982 under the terms of the 1979 Egypt-Israel peace treaty. The Suez Canal, which slices through northeastern Egypt, connects the Mediterranean Sea directly to the Red Sea.

q: The Seine river divides this city into the Rive Droite (French for Right Bank) north of the river and the Rive Gauche (French for Left Bank) south of the river.

q.e: The Seine separates Paris's Right Bank (north) from the Left Bank (south).

q: One of this citys most prominent landmarks is the Brandenburger Tor (Brandenburg Gate). It once marked the boundary between East and West Germany.

q.e: Commissioned by King Frederick William II of Prussia and finished in 1791, the Brandenburg Gate stood within the exclusion zone of the Berlin Wall from 1961 to 1989. When the wall fell in November 1989, it became the central symbol of German reunification.

q: This city is famous for its water-channel traffic. It has been designated a World Heritage Site.

q.e: Venice is built across 118 small islands separated by canals and linked by more than 400 bridges, earning UNESCO World Heritage status in 1987.

q: This Peruvian city is stuck between the desert and the sea. It is also known as "The City of the Kings".

q.e: Lima, founded by Pizarro in 1535 as "City of the Kings," is in a desert on the Pacific.

q: The Appalachian Trail divides two states as it makes its trek through Great Smoky Mountains National Park. Name the states it divides.

q.e: The Appalachian Trail follows the North Carolina–Tennessee border through the Great Smoky Mountains.

q: Sullivan street (in Sullivan County) serves as the state line, running east and west, effectively bi-locating this town in two states. Name the city and the two states.

q.e: Bristol straddles the Tennessee–Virginia state line on State Street.

q: Although Angel Falls bear the notion of something angelic, the phenomenon is named after Jimmy Angel, a barnstorming pilot from Missouri, who has become a modern legend.

q.e: Angel Falls in Venezuela, 979 m, is the world's tallest uninterrupted waterfall, named for pilot Jimmie Angel.

q: The name of mount Kilimanjaro comes from Swahili and means the mountain that glitters.

q.e: Kilimanjaro, in Tanzania, is Africa's highest mountain. The origin of its name is uncertain.

q: Krakatoa volcano caused the most violent volcanic eruption recorded in worlds history. In 1883, it destroyed 75 % of the territory of its island.

q.e: Krakatoa erupted in 1883, in Indonesia, and the explosion was heard 4,800 km away.

q: Local Batonga people had named Victoria Falls Mosi-Oa-Tunya, which stands for "the smoke that thunders".

q.e: Mosi-oa-Tunya ("the smoke that thunders") is Victoria Falls, on the Zambia–Zimbabwe border.

q: The Beehive State requested admission to the Union in 1849 under the name Deseret. After polygamous marriage practices were discontinued, it was finally admitted in 1896, under what name?

q.e: Utah was admitted as the 45th US state on January 4, 1896, following the 1890 Mormon Manifesto that renounced the practice of plural marriage.

q: Nicknamed the Green Mountain State, this eastern US state was admitted to the Union on March 4, 1791.

q.e: Vermont, "The Green Mountain State," joined the Union on 4 March 1791, the 14th state.

q: Located in Tanzania, it is Africas highest mountain.

q.e: Kilimanjaro (5,895 m) is Africa's highest peak and the world's tallest free-standing mountain.

q: One of the most intriguing attractions of Venice is Ponte dei Sospiri, which means this in English.

q.e: Ponte dei Sospiri translates directly to the Bridge of Sighs, an enclosed white limestone bridge built in 1600 across the Rio di Palazzo. Lord Byron popularized the romantic notion that prisoners sighed at their final view of Venice while being led into the adjacent prison cells.

q: Madrid is the largest city and capital of this country, whose the most valuable natural resource is the soil - nearly one-third of the land is suitable for cultivation.

q.e: Madrid is Spain's capital and largest city.

q: Bern is the capital of this country, where most rivers are not suitable for navigation due to their great falls and swift currents.

q.e: Bern is the capital of Switzerland, which has few navigable rivers.

q: Ulaan Baator is the capital of this sparsely populated country, where domesticated animals outnumber people.

q.e: Ulaanbaatar is the capital of Mongolia, where livestock outnumber people.

q: This country's capital, Sucre, is nicknamed "the white city� because most of the colonial buildings in the city centre are white.

q.e: Sucre is the constitutional capital of Bolivia, called the "White City". La Paz is the seat of government.

q: This country is about the size of California but has about one -sixth of its population. Its capital city is Asunción.

q.e: Paraguay is about the size of California, with a capital in Asunción.

q: Vientiane is the capital of this country, which has more than 50 ethnic groups, divided into three broad categories.

q.e: Vientiane is the capital and largest city of Laos, situated along a bend in the Mekong River near the border with Thailand.

q: Phnom Penh is the capital of this country, whose official language is Khmer.

q.e: Phnom Penh is Cambodia's capital, and Khmer is the official language.

q: Vienna is the capital of this landlocked country, which became a member of the European Union in 1995.

q.e: Austria is landlocked and joined the EU in 1995, and Vienna is its capital.

q: Montevideo is the capital of this second smallest country in South America, after Suriname.

q.e: Covering about 176,000 square kilometers, Uruguay is South America's second-smallest independent nation after Suriname, with its capital located on the north bank of the Río de la Plata.

q: Caracas is the capital of this country, a Spanish colony for more than 300 years, before it declared its independence in the early 19th century.

q.e: Caracas is Venezuela's capital. Venezuela declared independence in 1811 and was under Spain for about 300 years.

q: In 1488, a bold captain named Bartholomew Diaz gave the name Cape of Storms to the most southern African tip. However, the Portuguese King altered the name to this.

q.e: King John II of Portugal renamed it the Cape of Good Hope (Cabo da Boa Esperança) to reflect optimism that a sea route to India had finally opened.

q: With the aid of Queen Isabella of Spain, Christopher Columbus set off in 1492 using three tiny ships. One of these ships was not part of the expedition.

q.e: The Victoria was Magellan's ship, not Columbus's. His were the Niña, Pinta and Santa María.

q: Which of the following pairs (explorer - region he discovered) is not correct?

q.e: Pedro Álvares Cabral reached Brazil in 1500, not Uruguay.

q: If you are in Sacramento, the capital of this western state, you are within a days drive to beautiful beaches, high mountains with famous national parks, and one of the deepest, most picturesque lakes in the world.

q.e: Sacramento is the capital of California, near the coast, the Sierra Nevada, Yosemite and Lake Tahoe.

q: Salt Lake City, known for the salty, barren desert lake to the west of the city, was founded by mormons and is the capital of this geographically diverse state.

q.e: Salt Lake City, Utah's capital, was founded by Mormons in 1847, next to the Great Salt Lake.

q: A wonder of the ancient world was built on the territory of all of these modern-day countries, but one. Which is the odd one?

q.e: Syria isn't a country where the Seven Wonders sites were. Check the sources for the question's countries.

q: According to legends, what was the purpose of the most mysterious of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World -- The Hanging Gardens of Babylon?
Provide a place of solace and recreation for the rulers

q.e: Legend says Nebuchadnezzar II built the Hanging Gardens for his wife Amytis, who missed her homeland's greenery.

q: Built in honor of the Greek goddess Artemis, the Temple of Artemis was an enormous architectural construction for its time. In Greek mythology, Artemis is the goddes of what?
Plague, beauty, light, healing, colonists, medicine

q.e: Artemis is the Greek goddess of the hunt, and the moon too in later tradition.

q: The Lighthouse of Alexandria, the only one of the Seven Wonders, which had a practical use in addition to architectural elegance, included this remarkable device that astonishes even modern researchers.

q.e: The Pharos of Alexandria supposedly had a mirror (or fire) reflecting light to sailors miles out.

q: Over 125 million people of more than 250 ethnic groups share the territory of this African country. This constitutes 1/5 of the population of the entire continent.

q.e: Nigeria is Africa's most populous country, with 250+ ethnic groups, roughly one in five Africans.

q: Dhaka, formerly Dacca, is the capital and largest city of this country with over 140 million citizens. Families there are large, unfortunately so is infant mortality.

q.e: Dhaka became the capital when Bangladesh gained independence from Pakistan in 1971. The country now has a population exceeding 170 million people.

q: About 75% of the 185 million citizens of this country live in the cities. The largest city is Sao Paulo with a population of 16 million.

q.e: Brazil is highly urbanized, with São Paulo as its largest city.

q: Constituted of 17,508 islands this country gives home to about 240 million. Its tropical rain forest accounts for 10% of the worlds rain forests.

q.e: Indonesia is the world's largest archipelagic state, spanning between the Indian and Pacific Oceans. Bali is merely one of Indonesia's 38 provinces, not an independent country.

q: It is home of almost 300 million. There were millions of buffaloes before the first settlers arrived, but urbanization has been a factor in their decrease.

q.e: The US has about 340 million people today, and the bison population dropped from tens of millions to hundreds in the 1880s.

q: The famous Bull Run is held in this Spanish city.

q.e: The Running of the Bulls takes place in Pamplona, Spain, during the San Fermín festival in July.

q: Indian city again. This one, founded in 1727 AD is known as The Pink City and is often visited by honeymooners.

q.e: Jaipur was founded in 1727 by Maharaja Jai Singh II. It earned the moniker 'The Pink City' after buildings were painted terracotta pink in 1876 to welcome Britain's Prince Albert.

q: The name of this 5th largest city in North America originates from a Mohawk word, meaning where there are trees standing in the water.

q.e: Toronto probably comes from a Mohawk word, "tkaronto," meaning "where there are trees standing in the water".

q: The name of this city means the capital in the native language. It is the capital of South Korea.

q.e: Seoul is derived from the archaic Korean word seobeol, which simply meant capital city. Unlike most city names in Korea, it has no native hanja (Chinese character) equivalent.

q: This mid-Atlantic state is called The First State due to the fact that it was the first to ratify the US Constitution.

q.e: Delaware, "The First State," ratified the Constitution on 7 December 1787.

q: Widely known for huge gambling and the legalization of gambling industry, this states official nickname is The Silver State.

q.e: Nevada is "The Silver State" because of silver mining (Comstock Lode), as well as "Battle Born."

q: This state of the New England region of the United States has the nicknames Pine Tree State and Vacationland.

q.e: Maine is the "Pine Tree State" and "Vacationland".

q: Which Southern state of the United States has a nickname The Magnolia State and a name that is the same as that of a big river?

q.e: Mississippi is "The Magnolia State", named after the Mississippi River.

q: After multiple agreements between 1772 and 1795, Russia, Prussia, and Austria divided this central European country among themselves. It finally regained its independence in 1918.

q.e: Poland was partitioned by Russia, Prussia and Austria in 1772, 1793 and 1795. It regained independence in 1918.

q: This Central America country, slightly smaller than South Carolina, withdrew from Colombia in 1903 with the help of US support.

q.e: Panama separated from Colombia in 1903 with US backing, which led to the Panama Canal.

q: In 1895, military defeat forced China to cede this country to Japan. China re-gained control after World War II.

q.e: China ceded Taiwan to Japan after the First Sino-Japanese War, by the Treaty of Shimonoseki (1895).

q: This kingdom was a founding member of NATO and the EU. It remained neutral during World War I, but was invaded and occupied by Germany during World War II.

q.e: The Netherlands was a NATO and EU founder, neutral in WWI and invaded by Germany in 1940.

q: Frances conquest of this country began in 1858 and was completed by 1884. Independence was declared after World War II, but the French continued to rule until 1954.

q.e: France conquered Vietnam (Indochina) from 1858 and was defeated at Dien Bien Phu in 1954.

q: Three of these names are of reindeers of Santa Claus. Which is the odd one?

q.e: Santa's reindeer are Dasher, Dancer, Prancer, Vixen, Comet, Cupid, Donner and Blitzen. Clement is not one of them.

q: Known as the Triumphant City, this place is one of the largest urban settlements which features both Christian and Islamic monuments.

q.e: Cairo's Arabic name, Al-Qahira, means "the Victorious." It has Coptic Christian and Islamic monuments.

q: The biggest mosque in India, called Jama Masjid, is situated in this city, which is considered the heart of the country.

q.e: Jama Masjid in Delhi, built by Shah Jahan (1656), is one of India's largest mosques.

q: What is the capital of the biggest Muslim-majority country, which is officially not a city but a province?

q.e: Jakarta is Indonesia's capital, with provincial status. A new capital, Nusantara, is being built.

q: This city originated from a Muslim settlement near the Pasig River in a country, which was a colony of Spain for almost three centuries.

q.e: Manila, on the Pasig River, was a Muslim settlement before Spain took it in 1571.

q: This city is located in the province Sindh in Pakistan, on the cost of the Arabian Sea.

q.e: Karachi, in Sindh, is Pakistan's largest city and main port.

q: This big city, originally named Naniwa, is famous for a huge aquarium called Kaiyukan.

q.e: Osaka was once Naniwa and its Kaiyukan aquarium is one of the largest in the world.

q: This Latin Amrican city, known also as the City of the Holy Trinity, is located on the southern shore of the Río de la Plata.

q.e: Buenos Aires, "Ciudad de la Santísima Trinidad y Puerto de Santa María del Buen Ayre," lies on the Río de la Plata.

q: Who was the first person to sign the the United States Declaration of Independence?

q.e: John Hancock, President of the Continental Congress, signed first and largest.

q: What is the highest mountain peak in the United States?

q.e: Denali (Mount McKinley), at 6,190 m, is the tallest in the US.

q: What was the first state to ratify the US Constitution and therefore the first state of the United States of America?

q.e: Delaware was first to ratify the Constitution, on 7 December 1787.

q: In the classic movie "It's A Wonderful Life,� George and Mary were at the gym dancing in a contest. What kind of contest was it?

q.e: In It's a Wonderful Life, George and Mary dance the Charleston, and fall into a pool under the gym floor.

q: In the classic movie Its A Wonderful Life, George Bailey is deaf in one ear. How did he become deaf?
He jumped into a pond saving his brother.
He was born deaf in one ear

q.e: George became deaf in one ear after saving his younger brother Harry, who fell through ice.

q: At the end of "It's A Wonderful Life, Harry Bailey made a toast to the richest man in town. Who was he referring to when he made this toast?

q.e: Harry Bailey toasts "my big brother George, the richest man in town."

q: Brunei is a small country (about 5,700 km² in area,) situated on the island of Borneo, in Southeast Asia. Brunei borders only one country, which one?

q.e: Brunei's only neighbor is Malaysia (Sarawak, on Borneo) and the South China Sea.

q: Geographically, Azerbaijan is a country situated at the crossroads of Europe and Southwest Asia, between what two major water basins?
The Persian Gulf and Caspian Sea
Red Sea and the Indian Ocean

q.e: Azerbaijan lies between the Caspian Sea and the Caucasus mountains, and doesn't border the Black Sea.

q: This southern African constitutional monarchy is entirely surrounded by the Republic of South Africa.

q.e: Lesotho is an enclave entirely surrounded by South Africa.

q: Leave the driving to us! was a phrase advertising which company?

q.e: "Leave the driving to us" was a Greyhound Lines slogan.

q: Which beverage was advertised with the phrase Its the real thing?

q.e: The Coca-Cola Company first adopted the slogan It's the Real Thing in 1942 and revived it in 1969 for a major advertising campaign that produced the famous 1971 I'd Like to Buy the World a Coke commercial.

q: Theyre GRR-eat!! was a slogan advertising which product?

q.e: Tony the Tiger has voiced the catchphrase Theyre Gr-r-reat! for Kelloggs Frosted Flakes since the cereal debuted in 1952.

q: Your kind of place, You deserve a break today and We do it all for you were advertising slogans used by which company?

q.e: McDonald's used all three slogans: "You deserve a break today," "We do it all for you," and "Your kind of place".

q: Its not nice to fool Mother Nature! was the advertising slogan for which product?
I Cant Believe Its Not Butter

q.e: "It's not nice to fool Mother Nature!" was a Chiffon margarine slogan.

q: Which is the worlds highest mountain system?

q.e: The Himalayas contain all 14 of the world's peaks over 8,000 meters (about 26,247 feet), including Mount Everest, making it Earth's highest mountain system. The Andes is the longest continental mountain range.

q: Excluding continents, which island is considered to be the largest island on Earth?

q.e: Covering roughly 2.16 million square kilometers (about 836,000 square miles), Greenland is the world's largest island. Australia is classified by geographers as a continental landmass rather than an island.

q: This mountain range, spanning seven countries, is the worlds longest.

q.e: The Andes, about 7,000 km, passes through seven South American countries.

q: Alhough not freshwater, it is the largest lake in the world, covering an area of 371,800 sq km.

q.e: The Caspian Sea (about 371,000 km²) is the world's largest inland body of water, and is a salt lake.

q: The highest recorded surface temperature of 136°F (about 58°C) was measured in this African country.

q.e: The 136°F reading at El Azizia, Libya, in 1922 was invalidated by the WMO in 2012. Death Valley's 134°F (1913) is the record.

q: This is the longest river on Earth.

q.e: The Nile (about 6,650 km) is usually listed as the longest river, but the Amazon is a rival claimant.

q: Paricutín is the youngest mountain on Earth. It is an active volcano and was formed from lava and ash as early as February 20, 1943. It is located in this country.

q.e: Parícutin volcano appeared in a Mexican cornfield (Michoacán) on 20 February 1943.

q: Arica, a place in this country, gets the least rainfall - only 0.03 inches (0.76 millimeters) per year.

q.e: Arica, Chile, in the Atacama region, is among the driest cities on Earth.

q: The lowest temperature on earth was recorded on this continent in 1983, when the termometer locked at -129F (- 88 C).

q.e: Vostok Station, Antarctica, recorded -89.2°C (-128.6°F) on 21 July 1983.

q: Santa Claus is a mispronunciation of the word Sinterklaas, by the English settlers of New York. The word Sinterklaas traces its origins to which country?

q.e: "Santa Claus" comes from Sinterklaas (St. Nicholas) from Dutch settlers in New Amsterdam.

q: From 1819 to 1826, Murfreesboro, famous for the Battle of Murfreesboro of 1862, was the capital of which state?

q.e: Murfreesboro was the capital of Tennessee from 1819 to 1826, before Nashville.

q: Founded in 1861, Lewiston was the territorial capital of this future state from 1863 to 1864.

q.e: Lewiston, Idaho, was the first capital of Idaho Territory (1863–1864) before Boise.

q: What former Yugoslavian republic is called Crna Gora in its native language?

q.e: Crna Gora means "Black Mountain," i.e. Montenegro.

q: This country is called Österreich in its native language, which is literally translated as the eastern state?

q.e: The name Osterreich traces back to the Old High German word Ostarrichi, first documented in 996 AD, which meant eastern realm. Austria shares a border with Germany, whose native name is Deutschland.

q: What Balkan country is called Shqiperia in its native language?

q.e: Shqipëria is the Albanian name for Albania, meaning "land of the eagles".

q: What country is called Slovensko in its native language?

q.e: Slovensko is the Slovak name for Slovakia.

q: The personal identification that must be attached to luggage checked by an airline is called this.

q.e: A baggage tag identifies checked luggage and its owner and destination.

q: One of these types of rates does not exist.

q.e: "Standby rate" is not a real type of airline fare; the real ones include coach and first class.

q: The U.S. city of Flagstaff is referred to as three of these nicknames. Which is the odd one?

q.e: Flagstaff is "City of Seven Wonders" and other names; the "Old Pueblo" is Tucson.

q: Three of these California cities have two popular nicknames each. Which city has just one?

q.e: Gilroy is just the "Garlic Capital of the World."

q: City of the Plains, Convention City, and Gateway to the Rockies are just three of the alternative names of this city.

q.e: Denver is the "Mile High City" and "Queen City of the Plains."

q: Look, Ma, no cavities! was the advertising slogan of which product?

q.e: Crest toothpaste's slogan "Look, Ma, no cavities!" started in the 1950s.

q: Which of these was advertised with the words Think small?

q.e: Volkswagen's "Think small" 1959 ad for the Beetle is considered one of the best ads ever.

q: We try harder was the motto of which company?

q.e: Avis's slogan, "We try harder", began in 1962 as it was number two behind Hertz.

q: Which company used the advertising slogan Reach out and touch someone?

q.e: AT&T's slogan was "Reach out and touch someone" (1979).

q: In what year did Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer first run on American television?

q.e: Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer premiered on NBC on 6 December 1964 and is the longest-running Christmas TV special.

q: Which of Santas eight famous Reindeer was the coach of the Reindeer Games in Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer?

q.e: Comet was the coach of the Reindeer Games in the 1964 special.

q: What kind of animal did the cowboy from The Island of Misfit Toys ride in Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer?

q.e: Cornelius, the Island of Misfit Toys cowboy, rides an ostrich in Rudolph.

q: Which of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World is the oldest?

q.e: Built around 2560 BC for the Pharaoh Khufu, the Great Pyramid of Giza is both the oldest of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World and the only one still largely intact.

q: Which of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World was built on the island of Rhodes?

q.e: The Colossus of Rhodes was a giant statue of the sun god Helios, finished about 280 BC and toppled by an earthquake in 226 BC.

q: To which Greek goddess was the Temple at Ephesus dedicated?

q.e: The Temple at Ephesus was dedicated to Artemis. It was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

q: Which of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World was built on the banks of the Euphrates River in present-day Iraq?

q.e: Ancient accounts place the Hanging Gardens in the city of Babylon, located along the Euphrates River near modern-day Hillah, Iraq. The Lighthouse of Alexandria stood in Egypt, and the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus was in modern-day Turkey.

q: Which of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World was inlaid with ivory, gold, ebony, and precious stones?

q.e: The Statue of Zeus at Olympia, by Phidias, was made of ivory and gold plates over a wooden frame, with ebony and precious stones.

q: What is the capital of Vermont?

q.e: Montpelier is the capital of Vermont and the smallest state capital by population.

q: What is the largest city and capital of Wyoming?

q.e: Cheyenne is Wyoming's capital and largest city.

q: What is the capital of New Hampshire?

q.e: Concord was designated the capital of New Hampshire in 1808. Manchester is the state's largest city by population.

q: What city, located on the Connecticut River, is the capital of Connecticut?

q.e: Hartford is Connecticut's capital, on the Connecticut River.

q: This city, known as the City of Oaks, is the capital of North Carolina?

q.e: Raleigh was established as North Carolina's planned capital in 1792 and earned the nickname City of Oaks due to its vast oak forests. While Charlotte is the state's most populous city, it has never served as the capital.

q: According to the Bible, this man was the king of Judea, when Jesus Christ was born.

q.e: Herod the Great was the Roman-appointed King of Judea who ruled until his death around 4 BCE, the ruler associated in Matthew with the decree known as the Massacre of the Innocents.

q: He is the French equivalent of Santa Claus.

q.e: Pere Noel is the traditional French gift-bringer who visits homes on Christmas Eve. Olentzero is a Basque Christmas figure, while Zwarte Piet is a companion to Sinterklaas in Dutch folklore.

q: Florida became this number state to enter the union on March 3, 1845.

q.e: Florida became the 27th state on 3 March 1845.

q: Florida is a Spanish adjective which means this.

q.e: Spanish explorer Juan Ponce de León named the region 'La Florida' when he arrived in April 1513, referencing its lush vegetation and Spain's Easter celebration, 'Pascua Florida' (Feast of Flowers).

q: This city is the oldest one in the US and is located in Florida.

q.e: St. Augustine, Florida, founded by Spain in 1565, is the oldest continuously inhabited European-founded city in the US.

q: The worlds first scheduled commercial airline flight occurred in Florida on January 1 of this year.

q.e: The St. Petersburg–Tampa Airboat Line made the first scheduled commercial airline flight on 1 January 1914.

q: Id walk a mile for a ...

q.e: "I'd walk a mile for a Camel" was an ad slogan for Camel cigarettes.

q: Until recent years this strange custom was practiced: when a husband died, his wife would walk into the funeral pyre and burn to death. Where did they perform it?

q.e: Sati, the burning of widows on their husbands' funeral pyres, was practiced in India and was banned in 1829.

q: About 1,400 years ago, a British girl named Bathilde was sold to King Clovis II as a slave. The king fell in love with her and they got married. He made her queen. This is how slavery ended in this country.

q.e: Bathilde was an Anglo-Saxon slave who became queen of the Franks and banned enslaving Christians, ending slavery in France according to tradition.

q: Which one of these countries is smallest in area?

q.e: Azerbaijan (86,600 km²) is likely smaller than other options, but check the options in your question.

q: What currency is used in India?

q.e: India's currency is the Indian rupee (₹).

q: What currency is used in Pakistan?

q.e: Pakistan's currency is the Pakistani rupee.

q: What currency is used in Libya?

q.e: Libya's currency is the Libyan dinar.

q: What currency is used in Kuwait?

q.e: Kuwait's currency is the Kuwaiti dinar, the world's highest-valued currency unit.

q: What currency is used in Norway?

q.e: Norway introduced the krone (meaning crown) in 1875 when it joined the Scandinavian Monetary Union alongside Denmark and Sweden.

q: This actress, whose career spanned almost 70 years, has won an Emmy, a Grammy, an Oscar and a Tony Award.

q.e: Helen Hayes won Emmy, Grammy, Oscar and Tony awards, making her an EGOT winner in 1977.

q: How many American made movies did Marlon Brando direct?

q.e: Marlon Brando directed only one film, One-Eyed Jacks (1961), in which he also starred.

q: What is the main language of Haiti?

q.e: Haitian Creole (Kreyòl) is Haiti's most widely spoken language. French is also official.

q: What is the main language of Bangladesh?

q.e: Bengali, also known as Bangla, is the official and national language of Bangladesh, spoken by roughly 98% of its citizens. The 1952 Bengali Language Movement played a crucial role in the nation's eventual independence.

q: What is the deepest lake in the United States?

q.e: Crater Lake in Oregon reaches a maximum depth of 1,943 feet (about 592 m), making it the deepest lake in the US. Lake Tahoe is the second deepest at roughly 1,645 feet (501 m).

q: What is the state tree of California?

q.e: California officially designated the California redwood as its state tree in 1937, which encompasses both the coastal redwood (Sequoia sempervirens) and the giant sequoia (Sequoiadendron giganteum). Coastal redwoods are the tallest living trees on Earth.

q: What is the state motto of Arizona?
The Welfare of the People Shall Be The Supreme Law

q.e: Arizona's motto "Ditat Deus" is Latin for "God enriches."

q: What is the state bird of Colorado?

q.e: The lark bunting is Colorado's state bird, adopted in 1931.

q: In Ireland, the shamrock, a three-leaved white clover, is a sacred plant which symbolizes what?

q.e: St. Patrick is said to have used the three-leaved shamrock to explain the Trinity. It also symbolizes spring and rebirth.

q: According to legends, St. Patrick, the patron saint and national apostle of Ireland, is most well known for doing what?
Driving all the snakes away from Ireland
Helping Pope Celestine deal with infidels
Setting on fire all statues of pagan gods

q.e: Legend says St. Patrick drove the snakes out of Ireland. Ireland never had snakes after the Ice Age.

q: Which ancient Celtic custom, once practiced in Ireland, involved tying the brides and grooms wrists together?

q.e: "Handfasting" was an old Celtic custom of tying a couple's hands together, which gave us the phrase "tying the knot."

q: What cape is the northernmost point of the second largest continent in the world, Africa?

q.e: Africa's northernmost point is in Tunisia. Cape Blanc (Ras al-Abyad) and Ras ben Sakka (Cape Angela) both claim it.

q: Which city used to serve as the capital of West Germany?

q.e: Bonn was West Germany's capital from 1949 to 1990.

q: Belgrade was the capital of former Yugoslavia. Which country has the city as its capital today?

q.e: Belgrade is now the capital of Serbia, and was the capital of Yugoslavia.

q: Prague is the capital of the Czech Republic. Bratislava is the capital of the Slovak Republic. Which city used to be the capital of Czechoslovakia?

q.e: Prague was the capital of Czechoslovakia, which split peacefully in 1993.

q: Which of these cities is NOT located on the shore of the Baltic sea?

q.e: Warsaw is inland on the Vistula, not on the Baltic coast. Gdańsk is on it.

q: Which city is the worlds most northern capital?

q.e: Reykjavik, Iceland, is situated at roughly 64°08' N latitude, making it the northernmost capital of any sovereign nation. Nuuk, Greenland is further north, but it is a territory rather than a sovereign capital.

q: Which capital was supposedly founded by Ulysses, after he left Troy escaping the Greeks?

q.e: Legend says Odysseus (Ulysses) founded Lisbon, called Olisipo. The Portuguese capital's name is said to come from this.

q: Which river flows through four European capitals?

q.e: The Danube flows through Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest, and Belgrade on its roughly 1,770-mile (2,850 km) journey from Germany's Black Forest to the Black Sea.

q: What is the capital of Switzerland?

q.e: Bern (often spelled Berne in French and English) was chosen as the federal seat of Switzerland in 1848. Although Switzerland legally has no single official capital, Bern acts as the de facto federal city.

q: Which country has Valletta as its capital?

q.e: Valletta is the capital of Malta, a UNESCO site and one of the smallest EU capitals.

q: The story in which Santa Claus Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer was first mentioned, was written in which year?

q.e: Rudolph first appeared in a 1939 booklet written by Robert L. May for Montgomery Ward.

q: Which of these is not a San Francisco area code?

q.e: San Francisco's area codes are 415 and 628. 931 is a Tennessee area code.

q: Which area code has been variously described as The Donut around Los Angeles?

q.e: Area codes around Los Angeles changed many times, with 323 and 626 among them. Check the question's other options.

q: If I make a call into the 718 area code, what general area am I calling into?
North of the Greater Miami area

q.e: 718 covers Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx and Staten Island, the boroughs outside Manhattan.

q: What were the two leading city-states of Ancient Greece?

q.e: Athens was known for its naval power, trade, and early democracy, while Sparta was renowned for its austere, land-based military culture. Their rivalry eventually culminated in the Peloponnesian War (431–404 BCE).

q: Which empire was the historical enemy of Ancient Greece?

q.e: Persia was the great enemy of the ancient Greeks, in the Persian Wars (499–449 BC).

q: He was killed during the war.

q.e: Convicted by an Athenian court in 399 BC for impiety and corrupting the youth, Socrates was sentenced to death and carried out the execution himself by drinking a liquid infusion of poison hemlock.

q: When did the Irish Civil War end?

q.e: The Irish Civil War ended on 24 May 1923, with the defeat of the anti-Treaty IRA.

q: How many counties are there in the Republic of Ireland?

q.e: The Republic of Ireland has 26 counties. Northern Ireland has six (UK).

q: It is the smallest state in size, and was also the last of the original thirteen colonies to become a state.

q.e: Rhode Island is the smallest US state and was the last of the original thirteen colonies to ratify the Constitution (1790).

q: In modern warfare, which alert level of DEFCON (DEFense CONditions) signifies maximum readiness of the US Army forces?

q.e: DEFCON 1 is the highest alert, meaning nuclear war is imminent. DEFCON 5 is normal readiness.

q: This South-Asian country has Dili as a capital and largest city. Its two official languages are Tetum and Portuguese.

q.e: Dili is the capital of East Timor (Timor-Leste), whose official languages are Tetum and Portuguese.

q: This country won its independence from France. Its currency is Gourde (HTG) and capital - Port-au-Prince.

q.e: Haiti declared independence from France on January 1, 1804, following the Haitian Revolution led by figures like Toussaint Louverture and Jean-Jacques Dessalines, making it the world's first independent Black republic.

q: Before the Spanish arrived, this country was home to various Pre-Inca cultures and later, to the Inca Empire. Francisco Pizarro landed on its coast in 1532.

q.e: Francisco Pizarro landed in Peru in 1532 and conquered the Inca Empire.

q: The name of this small African country means lioness mountains. Its written history begins in 1462 when Portuguese explorers first landed there.

q.e: Sierra Leone derives from Portuguese "Serra Leoa," meaning "lioness mountains", named by Pedro de Sintra in 1462.

q: Aalborg is the main city of the region of North Jutland which is located in this country.

q.e: Aalborg is in North Jutland, Denmark.

q: In which Baltic country will you find the city of Kaunas?

q.e: Kaunas is Lithuania's second-largest city, and the capital between the world wars.
Košice is Slovakia's second-largest city, in the east of the country.

q: The Titanic was the second of a trio of giant liners, designed to dominate the transatlantic travel business. It was owned by the White Star Line. Where was the Titanic built?

q.e: The Titanic was built by Harland and Wolff in Belfast, which is in Northern Ireland, part of the UK.

q: Which country has a lion in its name?

q.e: "Sierra Leone" means "lion mountains."

q: What is the origin of the name of Tanzania?
Its a combination of TANganyika and ZANzibar, the two main parts of the country.
It comes from Latin stanza, meaning poetry.
Tanzan, a Buddhist monk who was the legendary founder of the country
Land of the Proud in Swahili

q.e: Tanzania was formed in 1964 by merging Tanganyika and Zanzibar.

q: How many U.S. state capitals have the word city included in their name?

q.e: Four capitals have "City" in their name: Carson City, Jefferson City, Oklahoma City and Salt Lake City.

q: How many U.S. state capitals have two words in their name?

q.e: About eight or nine capitals have two words, such as Baton Rouge, Carson City, Des Moines, Little Rock, Santa Fe and Salt Lake City.

q: How many U.S. state capitals share the same first letter with their state?

q.e: Four capitals share their state's first letter: Dover (Delaware), Honolulu (Hawaii), Indianapolis (Indiana), Oklahoma City (Oklahoma).

q: You wouldnt want to be a bride in this country - the honey moon lasts three months and according to custom, the bride covers all expenses.

q.e: This is a folklore-style claim; real wedding customs in Thailand vary. Check other sources.

q: According to beliefs in Poland, swallowing a willow catkin from a branch consecrated by a priest would bring good health. When does this event take place?

q.e: In Poland, willow catkins are blessed on Palm Sunday, just before Easter, and are believed to protect health.

q: Russians have the strange custom of fighting these wild animals. After a hunt, the fighter combats this type of animal either with his bare hands or using a pitchfork.

q.e: Bear hunting is part of Russian folklore, though the "bare hands" tradition is mostly legend.

q: According to tradition, passengers of the train passing over the Jamuna river in India, should give tribute to the river by throwing this in it.

q.e: Travelers customarily throw coins into the Yamuna (Jamuna) River from the bridge as an offering.

q: Folk hero Santa Claus is a variant of a European folk tale based on the historical figure of Saint Nicholas, who lived on the territory of what present-day country?

q.e: St. Nicholas was bishop of Myra, in present-day Turkey, in the 4th century.

q: Which of Santa Clauss nine flying reindeer is known as The Red-Nosed Reindeer?

q.e: Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer was created in 1939 by Robert L. May for a Montgomery Ward Christmas promotional booklet. The original eight reindeer—including Cupid, Comet, and Blitzen—were introduced more than a century earlier in the 1823 poem A Visit from St. Nicholas.

q: According to the Christian Bible, where did Joseph and Mary live before Jesus was born?

q.e: According to Luke chapter 1 and 2, Mary and Joseph lived in the Galilean town of Nazareth before traveling south to Bethlehem to register for a Roman census.

q: According to popular belief, the angels first announced Jesus Christs birth to what group of people?

q.e: According to the Gospel of Luke chapter 2, an angel appeared to shepherds keeping watch over their flock by night in fields near Bethlehem to proclaim the birth of Jesus.

q: This celebration, observed on 26 December, is known as Boxing Day in in Britain, Australia, New Zealand and Canada.

q.e: 26 December is St. Stephen's Day, and Boxing Day in the UK and Commonwealth.

q: Which of these authors was not born in California?

q.e: Mark Twain was born in Missouri. Authors like John Steinbeck and Jack London were Californians.

q: In which subject would you come upon the word rhoticism?

q.e: Rhoticism is the pronunciation of the "r" sound, a term in linguistics.

q: What do these American movies have in common: "The Running Man�, "Predator�, and "Batman and Robin� (1997)?
They have two governors in their cast.
They have one and the same executive producer and director.
They have one and the same writers and director.
They each set box office records on their opening day.

q.e: Arnold Schwarzenegger (California) and Jesse Ventura (Minnesota) are both actors who became governors, and both were in these films.

q: Who won the Orteig Prize in 1927?

q.e: Charles Lindbergh won the $25,000 Orteig Prize for the first nonstop flight from New York to Paris in 1927.

q: What was South Carolinas nickname, before it was called the Palmetto State?

q.e: South Carolina was nicknamed the "Iodine State" for the iodine in its soils; the palmetto is its symbol.

q: 13 is the lucky number of which school?

q.e: Colgate's number 13 comes from the 13 founders, who started with $13 and 13 prayers in 1819.

q: Which university is prominent for its botanical garden, which is one of the biggest in the U.S.?

q.e: UC Berkeley's botanical garden has about 13,000 types of plants and is one of the largest in the US.

q: Which college/university is the first to own a dinosaur egg?

q.e: Colgate University holds a dinosaur egg and uses 13 as its lucky number.

q: On September 13, 1922 a temperature of 135.9°F (57.7°C) was recorded in Al Aziziyah, a city in which African country?

q.e: El Azizia, Libya, recorded 136°F (57.8°C) on 13 September 1922. The WMO invalidated it in 2012, so the record is Death Valley's 134°F.

q: What port on the Atlantic Ocean is the largest city and capital of Sierra Leone?

q.e: Freetown is Sierra Leone's capital and main port, on the Atlantic.

q: This state, with a capital of Jaipur, is the largest state in India.

q.e: Rajasthan, with Jaipur as capital, is India's largest state by area.

q: Which of these countries borders Belize?

q.e: Belize is bordered by Mexico to the north and Guatemala to the west and south. Honduras lies across the Gulf of Honduras but does not share a land border.

q: On a New York State highway where there is no posted speed limit, the fastest speed at which you may legally drive is this.

q.e: New York's maximum speed limit is 65 mph on some highways, and 55 mph on most roads.

q: If your car starts to skid on a slippery road, you should do this.
Steer in the direction you want the front wheels to go.
Lock your brakes until you come to a full stop.
Steer toward the side of the road to get off the wet pavement.
Brake quickly and keep the wheel straight.

q.e: In a skid, ease off the pedals and steer in the direction you want the front wheels to go.

q: A bicyclist differs from a motorist in that he is not required to do this.
Report accidents resulting in serious injury.

q.e: Cyclists need not insure their bikes, unlike motorists who must have car insurance.

q: What is the capital of New Jersey?

q.e: Trenton is New Jersey's capital.

q: This Nobel peace prize winner went from Governor of New Jersey to the President of the USA.

q.e: Woodrow Wilson was New Jersey's governor, then the 28th president, and won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1919.

q: This U.S. president, who served non-consecutive terms, was born in New Jersey.

q.e: Grover Cleveland (22nd and 24th president) was born in Caldwell, New Jersey.

q: Which of these people was not born in New Jersey?

q.e: Chuck Yeager was born in West Virginia. Others in the question are from New Jersey.

q: This famous singer from Hoboken became Chairman of the Board .

q.e: Frank Sinatra, born in Hoboken, New Jersey, in 1915, was nicknamed "Chairman of the Board."

q: The Great Lakes are a group of five large lakes on or near the United States-Canadian border. This is the largest of the Great Lakes.

q.e: Lake Superior is the largest of the Great Lakes by area, and the largest freshwater lake by surface area.

q: Which one of these rivers is not located in Asia?

q.e: The Segura River is in Spain, not Asia.

q: The city of Paris is built on an arc of this river.

q.e: The Seine flows roughly 483 miles (777 km) through northern France, dividing Paris into its traditional Left Bank and Right Bank before emptying into the English Channel.

q: Which of these countries doesnt exits anymore, but was very powerful in the XVIII and XIX centuries, dominating much of Central Europe?

q.e: Prussia, dominant in Central Europe, was formally abolished in 1947.

q: What style of hotel accommodation, developed in Japan by Kurokawa Kisho, features modular plastic quarters?

q.e: Kisho Kurokawa designed the Nakagin Capsule Tower, and the capsule hotel idea originated in Osaka.

q: The origin of this hotel dates back to the early twentieth century, when the first hotels along highways became popular.

q.e: A "motel" ("motor hotel") grew out of highway travel in the 1920s.

q: Which term refers to a small, usually sometimes ruined building in the middle of the woods?

q.e: Hut, cabin or shack may describe such a building. Check the question's other options.

q: What type of house was built using raw logs, particularly in the early years of United States and Canada?

q.e: Log cabins were typically built by early North American settlers using notched, interlocking round or hewn logs to form sturdy structures without needing manufactured nails.

q: McDonalds is named after its founders. Burger King is self-explanatory. Do you know what KFC stands for?
Kansas, Fort Cheenook (the place where it was established)

q.e: KFC originally stood for Kentucky Fried Chicken, founded by Colonel Harland Sanders who began selling fried chicken from his roadside restaurant in Corbin, Kentucky, during the 1930s. The company officially shortened its branding to the acronym KFC in 1991.

q: While surfing the Internet you may be using Cisco networking equipment without even knowing it. But do you know the origin of the name Cisco?
It was named for San FranCISCO
The founders where from Colorado, Indiana, South Carolina and Oregon
The founders were named Alain CISse and Erwin COfalka
It stands for Communication and Information Systems COrporation

q.e: Cisco comes from San Francisco. Its logo resembles the Golden Gate Bridge.

q: Iona is a small island from which Christianity was spread to Scotland and northern England. The island gave name to a company. What does Iona make?

q.e: IONA Technologies was an Irish software firm, named after the island.

q: You probably have heard of software and hardware. Can you tell what Compuware makes?
Software that ease the life of IT managers and practitioners

q.e: Compuware makes software for IT management, founded in 1973.

q: This amazing single-roofed structure, located on the Greenwich peninsula in south-east London, was engineered by Buro Happold.

q.e: The Millennium Dome (now The O2) in Greenwich was built for the Millennium celebrations.

q: Where is the National Civil Rights Museum?

q.e: The National Civil Rights Museum in Memphis is at the Lorraine Motel, where Martin Luther King Jr. was killed in 1968.

q: In which city were Malcolm X., Warren Buffett, Marlon Brando, and Gerald Ford born?

q.e: Malcolm X, Warren Buffett, Marlon Brando and Gerald Ford were all born in Omaha, Nebraska.

q: What distinction does Bailey Brown hold?
He was the first Union soldier killed by the Confederates in the Civil War.
He was the first American killed in the War of 1812.
He was the first American killed in the Spanish-American War.
He was he first American killed in World War I.
