q.e: Regis Philbin grew up in the Bronx, and went to Cardinal Hayes High School.

q: What is the title of the official in charge of running the The Bronx borough?

q.e: The Bronx Borough President is the elected head of the borough, with limited powers.

q: If you had $500 bill, up to what year could you have used it?

q.e: The US stopped printing $500 bills in 1945, and they were officially discontinued in 1969, but remain legal tender.

q: The dollar was chosen as the US monetary unit in this year.

q.e: The Continental Congress chose the dollar as the US monetary unit in 1785.

q: This famous Iowan became one of Hollywoods most popular actors. In the film Angel and The Badman he plays a man named Quirt Evans.

q.e: John Wayne, born in Winterset, Iowa, played Quirt Evans in Angel and the Badman (1947).

q: Iowa is named after the local Native American Iowa people. What is the states nickname?

q.e: Iowa is officially nicknamed 'The Hawkeye State', believed to be named in honor of the Sauk leader Black Hawk. 'The Dairy State' is Wisconsin's traditional nickname.

q: Parts of the 1996 disaster movie Twister were filmed in Iowa. Bill Paxton stars in the movie, partnered by this actress.

q.e: Helen Hunt co-starred with Bill Paxton in Twister (1996), partly filmed in Iowa.

q: Iowa is known for its unpredictable weather. What are the most frequent disasters that strike the state?

q.e: Tornadoes are Iowa's most frequent disaster, along with flooding.

q: The official colors of Iowa are red, white, and blue (appearing on the state's flag) and Iowas motto is, Our liberties we prize, our rights we will ____.

q.e: Iowa's motto is "Our liberties we prize and our rights we will maintain."

q: What is the capital and largest city of Peru?

q.e: Lima is Peru's capital and largest city.

q: Which two countries have flags with same patterns and colors, but in reversed order?

q.e: Monaco's and Poland's flags both have two horizontal bands (red/white versus white/red). Indonesia's matches Monaco's too.

q: How many stripes are there on the American flag?

q.e: The American flag has 13 stripes representing the original 13 colonies, while the 50 stars in the blue canton represent the 50 current US states.

q: The actual building of the Titanic took place at what shipyard?

q.e: The Titanic was built by Harland and Wolff in Belfast, Northern Ireland.

q: Passenger Michel Navratil, who boarded the Titanic at Southampton, sailed under the assumed name Louis Hoffman. Why?
He was hiding from his French wife and kidnapping their children.
He was trying to escape England after robbing a bank.
He was a spy sent on a mission to the US.
He was a famous actor from France.

q.e: Michel Navratil took his sons from his estranged wife and sailed as "Louis Hoffman." He died, but his sons survived.

q: How many women were among the crew on the Titanic?

q.e: 23 women were in the Titanic's crew (stewardesses and others). All but three survived.

q: How many honeymoon couples travelled on the Titanic?

q.e: Thirteen honeymoon couples were on the Titanic.

q: Three of these countries are kingdoms, which one is actually a sultanate?

q.e: Oman is a sultanate. Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Morocco are kingdoms.

q: Three of these countries are Islamic republics. Which one is a kingdom?

q.e: Bhutan is a kingdom. Pakistan, Iran and Mauritania are Islamic republics.

q: On what day in March was Julius Caesar assassinated?

q.e: Julius Caesar was assassinated on the Ides of March (15 March) in 44 BC.

q: In what year was Julius Caesar killed?

q.e: Caesar was assassinated in 44 BCE by senators including Brutus and Cassius.

q: Where did the assassination of Julius Caesar take place?

q.e: Caesar was assassinated in the Curia of Pompey, a building in the Theatre of Pompey complex.

q: Julius Caesar was struck down by his assassins while on his way to what location?

q.e: Caesar was killed while attending a Senate meeting at the Curia of Pompey.

q: During the battle of Belleau Wood, the U.S. Marines fierceness and toughness earned them the respect of the Germans, who rated them of storm-trooper quality. What nickname did the U.S. Marines reportedly earn in this battle?

q.e: The Marines at Belleau Wood (June 1918) reportedly earned "Teufelhunden" ("Devil Dogs") from the Germans, though that origin is debated.

q: Benjamin Franklin, famous statesman and inventor, was born on January 17 of what year?

q.e: Benjamin Franklin was born on 17 January 1706 (6 January in the old calendar) in Boston.

q: Which famous boxer, born on January 17, won a gold medal in the 1960 Olympics?

q.e: Competing as Cassius Clay before changing his name, he won gold in the light heavyweight division at the 1960 Rome Olympics. Joe Frazier also won Olympic gold, but in Tokyo in 1964 as a heavyweight.

q: On January 17, 2006, this person became the second oldest inmate to be executed in the United States since 1976.

q.e: Clarence Ray Allen, 76, was executed in California on 17 January 2006.

q: The first St. Patricks Day parade organized in the Irish Free State was held in 1931 in what city?

q.e: The first official St. Patrick's Day parade of the Irish Free State was in Dublin in 1931.

q: The players of which of these baseball teams do NOT wear green uniforms on St. Patricks Day?

q.e: Pittsburgh Pirates' colors are black and gold, but they have worn green uniforms on St. Patrick's Day sometimes. Check the question's options.

q: The European Economic Community, informally called the Common Market, was established by the Treaty of Rome in what year?

q.e: The Treaty of Rome in 1957 created the European Economic Community, or Common Market.

q: This country opted to stay out of the European Community during a referendum in 1972. On the next referendum, held in 1994, its people rejected the proposal to join the European Union.

q.e: Norway voted against joining the EU in 1972 and 1994.

q: The head office of the European Central Bank, established on June 1, 1998, is located in which city?

q.e: The European Central Bank is headquartered in Frankfurt, Germany, which serves as a major financial hub for the Eurozone. Brussels is the main seat of the European Union's political institutions, such as the European Commission.

q: The European Court of Justice, the Supreme Court of the European Union, is based in which country?

q.e: The Court of Justice of the European Union sits in Luxembourg City.

q: Las Vegas is situated in a high desert valley roughly 2,500 feet above sea level. What provides its main source of water?

q.e: Las Vegas gets most of its water from the Colorado River, via Lake Mead.

q: What Las Vegas building, completed in 1996, offers two observation decks, a revolving restaurant, and thrill rides?

q.e: The Stratosphere Tower in Las Vegas (1996), at 350 m, is the tallest freestanding observation tower in the US.

q: Nike started the Just Do It� campaign in this year.

q.e: Nike launched "Just Do It" in 1988, created by Dan Wieden.

q: Oklahoma means "Home of the Red Man� in which Native American language?

q.e: "Oklahoma" comes from the Choctaw "okla humma," meaning "red people."

q: What city was the first state capital of Oklahoma?

q.e: Guthrie was the first capital of Oklahoma, until Oklahoma City in 1910.

q: In what year did Oklahoma enter the union as the 46th state?

q.e: Oklahoma became the 46th state on 16 November 1907.

q: When did the Native Americans finally receive U.S. citizenship through The Indian Citizenship Act?

q.e: The Indian Citizenship Act of 1924 granted citizenship to Native Americans.

q: Which of the following was not taught to Native American children at Indian boarding schools during the 19th century and early 20th century?

q.e: Boarding schools banned Native languages, forcing English and assimilation.

q: According to a law, Native Americans were not allowed to enter Boston until which year?

q.e: Boston's 1675 ban on Native Americans was repealed in 2005.

q: The forced relocation of the Cherokee and the Choctaw to the western states, resulting in the death of 4,000 Native Americans, is known by what name?

q.e: Following the Indian Removal Act of 1830 signed by Andrew Jackson, tens of thousands of Native Americans were forcibly marched to present-day Oklahoma. Roughly 4,000 Cherokee alone died from exposure, disease, and starvation along the route.

q: Members of what Native American nation live on the Cheyenne River Indian Reservation?

q.e: The Cheyenne River Reservation in South Dakota is home to the Cheyenne River Sioux Tribe, who are Lakota.

q: Which of these names doesnt refer to the U.S. federal legislation that restored Native American self-government on a tribal basis in 1934?

q.e: The 1934 act is the Indian Reorganization Act (also Wheeler–Howard Act). The Curtis Act of 1898 is a different law.

q: What measures, related to Native American tribes, did the National Collegiate Athletic Association take in 2005?
They banned the abusive Native American imagery and nicknames in athletics.
They founded a scholarship for Native American athletes.
They allowed Native American teams to take part in tournaments.
They created the Native American Soccer League.

q.e: In 2005 the NCAA banned "hostile and abusive" Native American mascots from postseason play.

q: Although the whole Committee of Five participated in the drafting of the US Declaration of Independence, this man was the principal author of the Declaration.

q.e: Thomas Jefferson was chosen by the Committee of Five to draft the document in June 1776, after which John Adams and Benjamin Franklin suggested minor edits.

q: The final version of the Declaration of Independence was adopted by the Continental Congress on July 4, 1776. In which state did this happen?

q.e: The Declaration of Independence was adopted in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, on 4 July 1776.

q: The Declaration of Independence was signed by a total of 56 delegates, representing how many colonies?

q.e: The 56 signatories represented the Thirteen Colonies that declared independence from the Kingdom of Great Britain in July 1776.

q: The Syng inkstand used to sign the United States Declaration of Independence, was also used in the signing of what other important US document?

q.e: The Syng inkstand was used for both the Declaration of Independence and the US Constitution.

q: The US Declaration of Independence and a fictional treasure map on its back are the subject of what popular 2004 film?
Master and Commander: The Far Side of the World

q.e: The treasure map on the Declaration's back is in National Treasure (2004), with Nicolas Cage.

q: Which of these American cities got the nickname Americas Most Patriotic Town as a result of having the oldest Independence Day celebrations?

q.e: Bristol, Rhode Island, has held an Independence Day parade since 1785, the oldest in the US.

q: Pepsi 400 is the name of what major annual sports event held on July 4th, or the Saturday of the July 4th weekend?
A series of extreme sports events

q.e: The Pepsi 400 is a NASCAR race at Daytona International Speedway.

q: In the 1948 musical film, Easter Parade, Fred Astaire co-stars with which famous actress?

q.e: Fred Astaire co-starred with Judy Garland in Easter Parade (1948).

q: Which of these statements about the Scottish loch Loch Ness, the alleged home of the monster Nessie, is true?
It is located near the city of Inverness.
It is the largest Scottish loch by surface.
There are four islands on the loch.

q.e: Loch Ness is near Inverness in the Scottish Highlands, and is the largest lake in the UK by volume.

q: The Church of Scotland belongs to which branch of Protestantism?

q.e: The Church of Scotland is Presbyterian, with no bishops.

q: Who celebrates Mole Day on October 23?

q.e: Mole Day on October 23 (6:02, 10/23) honors Avogadro's number, 6.02 × 10²³.

q: The 1st Sunday after Labor Day in the United States and Canada is what special day?

q.e: Grandparents Day is on the first Sunday after Labor Day in the US.

q: What war began and ended in the month of September and lasted 6 years?

q.e: WWII ran from 1 September 1939 to 2 September 1945, six years and a day.

q: What is the currency unit in the Philippines?

q.e: The Philippine peso is the national currency.

q: What is the currency unit in Iraq?

q.e: Iraq uses the Iraqi dinar.

q: What is the currency unit in Thailand?

q.e: The Thai baht was originally a unit of mass used to measure silver before it became the official fiat currency unit. Thailand is the only country that uses the baht.

q: What is the currency unit in India?

q.e: The Indian rupee (symbol ₹, code INR) traces its name back to the rupiya, a silver coin introduced by Sultan Sher Shah Suri in the 16th century.

q: What is the currency unit in Russia?

q.e: The ruble has been used in Russia for centuries, dating back to the 13th century in the Novgorod Republic, making it one of the oldest national currencies still in use.

q: What is the currency unit in Costa Rica?

q.e: Costa Rica's currency is the colón, named after Columbus (Colón).

q: What was the currency unit in Italy prior to 2001?

q.e: The Italian lira was Italy's official currency from 1861 until the introduction of physical euro coins and banknotes in 2002.

q: What is the name of the 101-floor skyscraper, which is 509 meters high from the ground to the structural top?

q.e: Taipei 101 in Taiwan officially held the title of the world's tallest building from 2004 until the opening of Dubai's Burj Khalifa in 2010. Its design incorporates traditional Asian pagoda architecture with eight stepped sections representing prosperous growth.

q: Which 54-floor office building is situated in the city of Dubai in the United Arab Emirates?

q.e: Emirates Towers in Dubai has two towers, with the office Tower One at 355 m and 54 floors.

q: Which American skyscraper was the first building in the world to surpass the 1000 feet (305 m) threshold?

q.e: The Chrysler Building (1930) at 1,046 ft was the first building to top 1,000 feet, topped soon after by the Empire State.

q: What is the the name of the capital city of Chile?

q.e: Santiago was founded in 1541 by Spanish conquistador Pedro de Valdivia and serves as the capital and largest city of Chile. Sucre is the constitutional capital of Bolivia.

q: Port Moresby is the capital city of this country.

q.e: Port Moresby is the capital of Papua New Guinea.

q: What is the name of the official capital city of Malaysia?

q.e: Kuala Lumpur is Malaysia's constitutional and royal capital, home to the iconic Petronas Towers. Putrajaya serves as the country's administrative center and seat of the federal government.

q: Niamey is the capital city of what country?

q.e: Niamey is the capital of Niger, on the Niger River.

q: Freetown is the capital city of what country?

q.e: Freetown is the capital of Sierra Leone.

q: What is the name of the capital city of the Republic of Indonesia?

q.e: Jakarta is Indonesia's capital, on Java.

q: What city is the capital of Denmark?

q.e: Copenhagen spans the islands of Zealand and Amager and has served as Denmark's capital since the 15th century. Stockholm is the capital of neighboring Sweden.

q: There are many twin cities in the USA. Which of the following are twin cities in Minnesota?

q.e: Minneapolis and Saint Paul are neighboring cities built around the Mississippi, Minnesota, and St. Croix rivers, together forming the core of the Twin Cities metropolitan area.

q: Name the largest city in Israel and its neighboring port city, that are usually referred to as twin cities.

q.e: Tel Aviv–Yafo is Israel's second-largest city (after Jerusalem), merged with the old port of Jaffa in 1950.

q: This pair of twin cities includes the town in which Einstein was born in 1879.

q.e: Albert Einstein was born in Ulm, Germany, in 1879. Neu-Ulm lies across the Danube in Bavaria.

q: Buda, Pest and Óbuda united to form Budapest. What country is Budapest the capital of?

q.e: The cities of Buda and Óbuda on the west bank of the Danube officially merged with Pest on the east bank in November 1873 to establish Hungary's capital.

q: These two US cities are called The Twin Ports.
Laredo, Texas and Port Charles, Louisiana
Salford, California and San Diego, California

q.e: Duluth, Minnesota, and Superior, Wisconsin, are the Twin Ports on Lake Superior.

q: Manchester, UK is a hub of great soccer. Which city is the twin city to Manchester?

q.e: Salford borders Manchester and is its "twin" in Greater Manchester.

q: Ciudad Juarez in Chihuahua, Mexico is twined with this US city.

q.e: Ciudad Juárez and El Paso are on opposite banks of the Rio Grande.

q: Which word means a slum surrounding major Brazilian cities?

q.e: The term favela originated in the late 19th century in Rio de Janeiro, named after soldiers settled on Morro da Favela, a hill covered in a shrub called favela.

q: Which of these countries has two capital cities?

q.e: Bolivia has two capitals: Sucre (constitutional) and La Paz (seat of government).

q: Which two Latin American countries are landlocked?

q.e: Bolivia and Paraguay are South America's only landlocked countries.

q: Which two countries in Central and South America have English as their official language?

q.e: Belize (Central America) and Guyana (South America) are English-speaking.

q: Excluding the Falkland Islands, how many countries in Central and South America do not have Spanish listed as their official language?

q.e: Brazil (Portuguese), Suriname (Dutch), Guyana (English) and Belize (English) do not use Spanish officially.

q: Juan Santamaria, Franklin Chang-Diaz, Oscar Aria Sanchez, and Claudia Poll are famous people from which Latin American country?

q.e: Juan Santamaría, Franklin Chang-Díaz, Óscar Arias and Claudia Poll are Costa Rican.

q: Guarani is one of the official languages of which Latin American country?

q.e: Guaraní is an official language of Paraguay alongside Spanish.

q: Besides fighting off the indigenous nations, which European nation did Portugal have to fight off to control Brazil?

q.e: The Dutch invaded Brazil's northeast in the 1600s (Dutch Brazil), but Portugal expelled them in 1654.

q: On October 4, 1931, the comic strip Dick Tracy, debuted in the Detroit Daily Mirror. Who was the cartoonist who created Dick Tracy?

q.e: Chester Gould created Dick Tracy, which debuted in 1931.

q: The 70th single-season home run baseball hit by this man on October 4, 2001, was sold online for $52,500 by Charles Murphy, the man who caught the ball.

q.e: Barry Bonds hit his 70th home run on 4 October 2001 and ended with 73 that season.

q: The name of this sitcom, which debuted on October 4, 1957, on CBS, has become synonymous with the quintessential wholesome American family.

q.e: "Leave It to Beaver" debuted on CBS on 4 October 1957 with the Cleaver family.

q: The worlds first constitution was the American one. Which constitution was the second in the world and the first in Europe?

q.e: Poland's Constitution of 3 May 1791 was the world's second written national constitution and Europe's first.

q: Who made the first four-wheeled automobile powered by gasoline?

q.e: Karl Benz built a three-wheeled gasoline car in 1885–86. Gottlieb Daimler built the first four-wheeled one in 1886.

q: The calendar we use today is called Gregorian and was introduced in 1582. Which of these countries was among the first to implement it?

q.e: Catholic countries like Spain, Portugal, Italy and Poland–Lithuania adopted the Gregorian calendar in 1582.

q: When did the first large balloons replace real animals at the Macys Parade?

q.e: Macy's replaced live animals with giant helium balloons in 1927, starting with Felix the Cat.

q: What was the first balloon in the Macys parade to be modeled after a living person?

q.e: Macy's parade balloons depicted real people later, e.g., Eddie Cantor. The bank answer is doubtful.

q: Who was the perpetrator of the Oklahoma City bombing on April 19, 1995?

q.e: Timothy McVeigh bombed the Murrah Federal Building on 19 April 1995, killing 168 people. He was executed in 2001.

q: This play was shown at the Moscow theatre when Chechen terrorists took the audience hostage on October 23, 2002.

q.e: Chechen militants seized Moscow's Dubrovka theater during the musical "Nord-Ost" on 23 October 2002.

q: Which terrorist organization was responsible for the bombings of the U.S. embassy in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania and Nairobi, Kenya on August 7, 1998?

q.e: Al-Qaeda carried out the 1998 US embassy bombings in Nairobi and Dar es Salaam on 7 August.

q: What is the origin of the name al-Qaeda, the terrorist organization responsible for the 9/11 attacks in the USA?
A computer database of trained fighters
The name of an Islamic spiritual leader

q.e: "Al-Qaeda" means "the base." A popular theory is that it came from a computer database of Soviet-era mujahideen fighters.

q: The Beslan school siege in which 186 children were killed by Chechen terrorists took place in what year?

q.e: The Beslan school siege in September 2004 killed over 330 people, including 186 children.

q: On September 11, 2001 the four hijacked flights were United Airlines Flight 93, American Airlines Flight 77, American Airlines Flight 11 and which other flight?

q.e: The four flights were AA 11, UA 175, AA 77 and UA 93.

q: How many were The Old Three Hundred, the families which settled in south Texas and formed the first Anglo-American colony there?

q.e: Stephen F. Austin's "Old Three Hundred" settlers were actually 297 grantees (1821–24).

q: The population of which city in Texas does not exceed 1 million?

q.e: Pasadena, Texas has about 150,000 people, far below one million. Houston, San Antonio, Dallas, Austin are above.

q: Big Tex, the 16-meter tall icon of the State Fair of Texas, wears what brand of denim jeans?

q.e: Big Tex, the State Fair of Texas icon, wears size 70 boots and Wrangler jeans (earlier Lee).

q: Sam Houston, who was President of the Republic of Texas, Senator for the State of Texas and later its governor, was born in 1793 in which state?

q.e: Sam Houston was born in Rockbridge County, Virginia, in 1793.

q: On July 20, 1969, Houston was the first word ever spoken from the Moon by which member of the Appolo 11 mission?

q.e: Neil Armstrong's first words from the Moon's surface were "Houston, Tranquility Base here. The Eagle has landed."

q: In which region was Marquis de La Fayette born?

q.e: Lafayette was born in Chavaniac in the Auvergne region of France in 1757.

q: The phrase Vote Yourself a Farm was used in which US presidential election?

q.e: "Vote Yourself a Farm" was a land-reform slogan, used in the 1860 election, tied to the Republican homestead platform.

q: Finish this slogan used against the GOP presidential candidate in 1884: Blaine, Blaine, James G. Blaine ... .
... the continental liar from the state of Maine
... what have we done to deserve such pain?
... who first slew Abel and then murdered Cain
... who will sell all our possessions to the King of Spain

q.e: The 1884 Democratic chant was "Blaine, Blaine, James G. Blaine, the continental liar from the State of Maine."

q: Had Enough? was the slogan used against which president?

q.e: "Had enough?" was the 1946 Republican midterm slogan against Truman and the Democrats.

q: Democrats countered Barry Goldwaters 1964 slogan of In Your Heart You Know Hes Right with which of these rejoinders?
In Your Guts, You Know Hes Nuts
In Your Ear, He Speaks Only Fear
In Your Spleen, You Know Hes Mean
In Your Colon, You Know Hes Rollin

q.e: "In your guts you know he's nuts" was the Democratic reply to Goldwater's "In your heart you know he's right."

q: How many passengers were on the Titanic when she sank?

q.e: Titanic carried around 1,316 passengers (1,317 by some counts) and about 900 crew.

q: Which of these was one of the leaders of the expedition that discovered the wreck of the Titanic?

q.e: Robert Ballard's team found the Titanic wreck in September 1985.

q: What year was Mount Rushmore officially dedicated?

q.e: Mount Rushmore was completed in 1941. The 1991 date was a rededication by George H. W. Bush.

q: About how many people visited Mount Rushmore in 2004?

q.e: About 2 million people visit Mount Rushmore each year.

q: On 11 October 1968, the first staffed Apollo mission, Apollo 7, was launched. Which of the following was NOT an astronaut on that mission?

q.e: Apollo 7's crew was Walter Schirra, Donn Eisele and Walter Cunningham. Neil Armstrong flew on Apollo 11.

q: Who was the first guest host of Saturday Night Live on the shows premiere on October 11th, 1975?

q.e: George Carlin hosted the first Saturday Night Live on 11 October 1975.

q: This West African countrys capital is Conakry; it borders the Atlantic Ocean, and the official language is French.

q.e: Guinea's capital is Conakry. French is the official language.

q: This democratic parliamentary republics capital is Tallinn, and its national flag consists of three horizontal stripes of blue, black and white color.

q.e: Estonia's flag is blue, black and white, and the capital is Tallinn.

q: This country is located in Central America, its capital is San Jose, its official language is Spanish.

q.e: Costa Rica is situated on the Central American isthmus between Nicaragua and Panama, with San Jose serving as its capital since 1823. Panama's capital is Panama City, while El Salvador's capital is San Salvador.

q: This country, located in the South Pacific Ocean, comprises of about 322 larger islands, its capital is Suva, and one of the official languages is Hindi.

q.e: Fiji has about 330 islands and its capital is Suva; official languages are English, Fijian and Fiji Hindi.

q: This is the largest country both in Africa and in the Arab World in terms territory, and the tenth largest country in the world. Its capital is Khartoum.

q.e: Algeria has been Africa's largest country by area since South Sudan split from Sudan in 2011. Khartoum is Sudan's capital.

q: This republic is located in northwestern South America, it is named after a European explorer and its capital city is Bogota.

q.e: Colombia is named after Christopher Columbus. Its capital is Bogotá.

q: This is an island country consisting of almost one thousand islands, it is located east of Papua New Guinea and its capital is Honiara.

q.e: The Solomon Islands lie east of Papua New Guinea, with Honiara as the capital.

q: This island country is located east of the Caribbean Sea, it was a colony of the United Kingdom until 1966. Its flag features a trident.

q.e: Barbados has a trident on its flag and gained independence from the UK in 1966.

q: What was the original name of Mt. McKinley?

q.e: Denali is the traditional name given to the mountain by the indigenous Koyukon Athabascans, meaning 'the tall one'. It was named Mount McKinley in 1896 after politician William McKinley before its original name was officially restored federally in 2015.

q: In what year did Alaska become a state?

q.e: President Dwight D. Eisenhower signed the proclamation admitting Alaska as the 49th US state on January 3, 1959. Hawaii followed soon after as the 50th state in August of the same year.
The California Gold Rush (1848–55) came before the Klondike Gold Rush (1896–99).

q: In what year did the capital of Alaska move from Sitka to Juneau?

q.e: Alaska's capital moved from Sitka to Juneau in 1906.

q: In this year, the First Bank of the United States was chartered.

q.e: Congress chartered the First Bank of the United States in 1791, at Hamilton's urging.

q: The ridges on the sides of coins are called reedings or millings. The dime has this number of such ridges.

q.e: A US dime has 118 ridges (reeding) on its edge.

q: This is the percentage of bills in circulation, that are $1 notes.

q.e: $1 bills make up nearly half of all US notes in circulation (around 40% to 48% in various counts).

q: Which country was terribly devastated by Hurricane Mitch in 1998?

q.e: Hurricane Mitch (October 1998) devastated Honduras and Nicaragua and killed over 11,000.

q: Managua is the capital of this country whose currency is called cordoba.

q.e: Managua is Nicaragua's capital, and the currency is the córdoba.

q: The homeland of the Mayans stretched from Mexicos Yucatan peninsula southward into Belize and what other country?

q.e: The Maya homeland covered the Yucatán, Belize and Guatemala, and Honduras and El Salvador too.

q: The lost city of the Incas, Machu Picchu stands high above the gorges of the Urubamba, which is located in this country.

q.e: Machu Picchu stands above the Urubamba River in Peru.

q: What South American country borders Guyana to the east, Brazil to the south, and Columbia to the west?

q.e: Venezuela borders Guyana to the east, Brazil to the south and Colombia to the west.

q: Which South American country has two capitals, named La Paz and Sucre?

q.e: Bolivia has two capitals, Sucre and La Paz.

q: What is the capital of Iceland?

q.e: Reykjavik is the northernmost capital of a sovereign state, situated just below the Arctic Circle at roughly 64 degrees north latitude.

q: What is the capital of Poland?

q.e: Warsaw became the capital of Poland in 1596 when King Sigismund III Vasa moved the court from Krakow. Wroclaw is another major Polish city, while Wien is Vienna in German and Walsall is an English town.

q: On November 18 in 1820, US navigator Nathaniel Palmer became the first American to land on Antarctica. Why did he go there?
He wanted to hunt for seals.
There was no more meat on his ship and he was going after whale meat.
It was a total mistake - he was trying to get to Patagonia in Argentina.
His rudder was broken and his ship, the Hero, just sailed due South.

q.e: Nathaniel Palmer, a young sealer from Connecticut, sailed south in 1820 hunting seals.

q: According to legend, on November 18 in 1307 William Tell shot an arrow through an apple on top of his sons head. Tell is a national hero of which country?

q.e: William Tell is a legendary 14th-century Swiss hero who defied the Austrian bailiff Albrecht Gessler and was forced to shoot an apple off his son's head with a crossbow. His subsequent escape and assassination of Gessler became central to the Swiss struggle for independence.

q: On November 18 in 1978, Jim Jones and his followers committed mass suicide in Jonestown. Where was Jonestown?

q.e: Jonestown was Jim Jones's Peoples Temple settlement in Guyana. 918 died on 18 November 1978.

q: This Baltic country celebrates its Independence Day on November 18th. The people there speak an Indo-European language and its largest city is not Vilna.

q.e: Latvia declared independence on 18 November 1918. Its language, Latvian, is Indo-European (Baltic) and Riga is the capital.

q: Which comic strip, written and illustrated by Bill Watterson, began on November 18 in 1985?

q.e: "Calvin and Hobbes" debuted on 18 November 1985. Watterson ended it in 1995.

q: The first book printed on press was produced on November 18 in what year?

q.e: William Caxton printed "Dictes or Sayengis of the Philosophres," the first dated English printed book, on 18 November 1477.

q: Which was the second Western Hemisphere country (after the USA) to gain its independence after winning an important battle on November 18 in 1803?

q.e: Zac Efron, born 18 October 1987, starred in High School Musical.

q.e: Early automobiles (up to 1904) form the "Veteran era." Antiques follow the "Brass era."

q: The following are e-mails sent by a government official: If youll look at my lovely FEMA attire, youll really vomit., I am a fashion god., Can I quit now?, and I am trapped now, please rescue me. What FEMA Director wrote these e-mails?

q: Colorado, the 38th US state, attained statehood in what year?

q.e: Colorado has 58 peaks above 14,000 feet by the most common list. Some lists with stricter rules count 54.

q.e: Mount Elbert (4,401 m / 14,440 ft), in Lake County, is the highest peak in the Rockies and in Colorado.

q.e: The Gregory Lode, found in 1859 at Central City, led to gold rush riches and the nickname "the richest square mile on Earth."

q.e: Fort Garland, established in 1858, was commanded by Kit Carson in 1866–67 and is Colorado's oldest military post.

q: This road, which traverses Rocky Mountain National Park from Estes Park, Colorado in the east to Grand Lake in the west, is the highest paved-through highway in the United States.

Juan Ponce de León landed in Florida in 1513, naming it "La Florida" for the Easter season, "Pascua Florida".

q: In what city in Florida is the University of Miami located?

q.e: The University of Miami is in Coral Gables, Florida.

q: This amendment concerning the right to own and bear arms is considered by many the most contreversal one on the United States Bill of Rights.

q: How many Pennsylvania cities have served as capital of the USA?

q.e: Philadelphia, Lancaster and York all served as US capital, and Pennsylvania had three of them.

q.e: Oliver Hazard Perry built his fleet in Erie, Pennsylvania, and won the Battle of Lake Erie in 1813.

q: This is the capital city of the U.S. state in which Sioux Falls is the largest city.

q.e: Pierre is the capital of South Dakota, whose largest city is Sioux Falls.

q: What is the capital city of the U.S. state in which the largest city is Bridgeport?

q.e: New York City is the most populous city in the United States, but Albany has been New York State's official capital since 1797.

q: This city in Florida is considered to be the oldest European settlement in North America.

q.e: Illinois has 102 counties.

q: This animal, which is often hunted in the fall season, is the official state animal of Illinois.

q: What is the state flower for Pennsylvania?

q.e: The mountain laurel is Pennsylvania's state flower, adopted in 1933.

The first oil well was drilled there.

The first gas well was drilled there.
It hosted the first horse race in the state.

The strangest spelling of any town in PA

First police office to be killed in the line of duty
Designer of the first police car

Lean Your Head Back and Touch Your Nose

q.e: H is Hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet, the 8th letter.

q: The names of these two lovers are used in the Military Alphabet?

q.e: Romeo and Juliett (spelled that way) are in the NATO phonetic alphabet.
SEPTA is the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority (the question says "Transit").

q: This aircraft took the place of the Grumman Wildcat in World War II.

q.e: The Grumman F6F Hellcat replaced the F4F Wildcat in WWII.

q: What company manufactures the F-35 Joint Strike Fighter?

q.e: Lockheed Martin makes the F-35 Lightning II.

q: Which of these fighters was manufactured by North American Aviation in World War 2?

q.e: North American Aviation built the P-51 Mustang, a top WWII fighter.

q: This aircraft was one of the first jet fighters used by the United States military.

q.e: The F-86 Sabre was among the first US swept-wing jet fighters and flew in Korea, and the F-80 was the first operational jet.

q: For which flower is the Netherlands particularly famous?

q.e: The Netherlands is world-renowned for its tulips, a cultural staple ever since 'Tulip Mania' gripped the Dutch Republic in the 1630s. Today, the Keukenhof gardens display millions of bulbs annually.

q: Until 1890, the Dutch King was Head of State of this country.

q.e: Luxembourg split from the Dutch crown in 1890 when Wilhelmina became queen, since a woman couldn't inherit.

q: Which religion has the most followers in the Netherlands?

q.e: Catholicism is the largest religion in the Netherlands, but nonreligious people outnumber them.

q: What was the name of the city that served as South Carolinas capital until 1790?

q.e: Charleston was South Carolina's capital until 1786 (some say 1790), then Columbia.

q: What is the State Tree of South Carolina?

q.e: The cabbage palmetto is South Carolina's state tree, on the flag.

q: In what northwest U.S. state is it illegal for a motorist with criminal intentions to enter a city without first stopping to call the chief of police for the city?

q.e: Odd local "laws" like this one are often urban legends and unenforced. Check other sources.

q: The city of Gainsville has a law requiring chicken to be eaten only with the hands. What U.S. state is Gainsville located in?

q.e: Gainesville, Georgia, supposedly has an ordinance requiring that fried chicken be eaten with the fingers.
Tirana was founded in 1614 and officially designated as the capital of Albania in 1920 at the Congress of Lushnje.

q: On what continent are Queen Maud Land, Wilkes Land and Marie Byrd Land located?

q.e: Queen Maud Land, Wilkes Land and Marie Byrd Land are all in Antarctica.

q: What defines the border between North Korea and South Korea?

q.e: Established under the 1953 Korean Armistice Agreement, the Korean Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) is a buffer strip roughly 160 miles (250 km) long and 2.5 miles (4 km) wide. While the 38th parallel served as the original post-WWII division, the DMZ intersects it diagonally to form the modern border.

q: In what US city was Harry S. Truman born?

q.e: Harry Truman was born in Lamar, Missouri, in 1884.

q: Which of these South American countries has two official capitals?

q.e: Bolivia has two capitals: Sucre (constitutional) and La Paz (seat of government).

q: The Canadian sitcom Corner Gas is set in Dog River in this province.

q.e: Corner Gas (2004–09) is set in the fictional Dog River, Saskatchewan.

q: What is the largest country in Africa and in the Arab world in terms of area?

q.e: Algeria has been Africa's largest country since Sudan split in 2011.

q: What is the largest landlocked country in the world in terms of area?

q.e: Kazakhstan covers roughly 1.05 million square miles (2.72 million square km) in Central Asia, making it larger than Western Europe. Mongolia is the second-largest landlocked nation by area.

q: What is the capital and largest city of Argentina?

q.e: Buenos Aires is an autonomous federal district situated on the western shore of the Rio de la Plata estuary. Montevideo is just across the river, serving as the capital of Uruguay, while Bogota is the capital of Colombia.

q: What was Thailands previous official name?
It has always been called Thailand.

q.e: The country was officially known as Siam until 1939, when it was changed to Thailand, which translates roughly to Land of the Free.

q: In 1767, the ancient capital of Thailand was destroyed by an army from what country?

q.e: Burmese forces sacked Ayutthaya, the Siamese capital, in 1767.

q: What is the principal religion of Thailand?

q.e: Buddhism (Theravada) is Thailand's main religion, followed by about 90% of people.

q: What is the title of the King of Thailand, Bhumipol, who started reigning in 1946?

q.e: Bhumibol Adulyadej was King Rama IX of Thailand (1946–2016).

q: You are a US Ranger patrolling the whole Mexican border. What is the order of the American states you visit if your patrol starts at the Gulf of Mexico?

q.e: From the Gulf of Mexico heading west, the border states are Texas, New Mexico, Arizona and California.

q: You are sailing around Australia. In which order will you visit Australian seaports if you sail clockwise from Sydney?

q.e: Sailing clockwise around Australia from Sydney would pass Melbourne, Adelaide, Perth, Darwin and Brisbane.

q: If you fly from Amsterdam to Tokyo, what will you you be seeing below the plane during most of the trip, if the plane takes the shortest possible path?
The ice of the Arctic Ocean
Mountain ranges (flying over Turkey, Iran, Pakistan and China)
The waters of the Atlantic and Pacific oceans

q.e: The great-circle route from Amsterdam to Tokyo passes over northern Russia and sometimes the Arctic.

q: You get on your motorbike in Chicago and travel west down the famous Route 66. Which US state will you NOT visit?

q.e: Route 66 runs through Illinois, Missouri, Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas, New Mexico, Arizona and California, but not Colorado.

q: What European city has been known as the La Dominante, Queen of the Adriatic, City of Water, City of Masks?

q.e: Venice earned titles like Queen of the Adriatic and La Dominante due to its powerful maritime republic, as well as City of Water and Masks because of its canals and famous Carnival tradition.

q: What city, located in the Himalayas, is known as "The Land of Gods� .

q.e: Kathmandu is Nepal's capital in the Himalayas, in a valley with many temples.

q: Located in San Diego County, legally, La Jolla is recognized as what?

q.e: La Jolla is a community within the city of San Diego, so it's not a separate city.

q: What is the first line of the US Marine Corps hymn?

q.e: The first line of "The Marines' Hymn" is "From the Halls of Montezuma, to the shores of Tripoli."

q: This self-governing British overseas territory, located on the Iberian Peninsula, shares a border with Spain to the north.

q.e: Gibraltar covers just under 2.6 square miles at the southern tip of the Iberian Peninsula and has been a British territory since it was ceded by Spain under the 1713 Treaty of Utrecht.

q: Which of these British territories are located in North America?

q.e: The BVI and Anguilla are British territories in the Caribbean, part of North America.

q: How is the residence of the Bishtop of Rome, the Prope, referred to?

q.e: The Apostolic Palace is the pope's official residence in Vatican City, though Pope Francis lived in Casa Santa Marta.

q: The members of the Pontifical Guard, which reside in the Vatican City and serve as personal bodyguards of the Pope, are Catholic male citizens predominantly of this nationality.

q.e: Established in 1506 by Pope Julius II, the Swiss Guard requires all recruits to be unmarried Swiss Catholic males who have completed basic training with the Swiss Armed Forces.

q: In what year did Cardiff become the capital city of Wales?

q.e: Cardiff was proclaimed capital of Wales in 1955.

q: Who was the first Prime Minister of the UK to be born in Wales?

q.e: No UK prime minister was born in Wales. David Lloyd George, who grew up there, was born in Manchester.

q: In the America Bowl at Wembley stadium in 1987, the Welsh Full Back Paul Thorburn made a guest appearance for which NFL team?

q.e: Welsh kicker Paul Thorburn took part in the 1987 American Bowl at Wembley.

q: The Welsh are renowned for singing. One of their popular hymns is known in Welsh as Cwm Rhondda. By what name is it more commonly referred to in English?
When you come home again to Wales

q.e: "Cwm Rhondda" is usually sung to the English hymn "Guide Me, O Thou Great Redeemer" and "Bread of Heaven."

q: The first money appeared around 1,200 BC in the form of this.

q.e: Cowrie shells were used as money in China from about 1200 BC.

q: The first paper bills (banknotes) appeared in this year.

q.e: The first paper money (flying money) emerged in Tang dynasty China around 806 AD.

q: Paper money were very convenient and much used. This led to their devaluation and they disappeared around this year.

q.e: Chinese paper money was widely used under the Song and Yuan dynasties and ended around the 15th century in the Ming dynasty because of inflation.

q: In 1942, during World War II, RMS Laconia was sunk by what type of U-boat?

q.e: RMS Laconia was torpedoed by U-156 on 12 September 1942, leading to the "Laconia incident."

q: What is the capital city of Connecticut?

q.e: Hartford and New Haven shared the status of co-capitals of Connecticut until 1875, when Hartford became the sole capital. Bridgeport is actually the state's most populous city, but Hartford remains the political center.

q: One of the statesmen on the Committee that drafted the Declaration of Independence was the delegate from Connecticut. What was his name?

q.e: Roger Sherman of Connecticut was on the Committee of Five that drafted the Declaration of Independence.

q: Which of these was one of the early heroes of the American Revolution who was executed by the British?

q.e: Nathan Hale was hanged by the British in 1776 for spying. His last words are traditionally "I only regret that I have but one life to lose for my country."

q: What is the state song of Connecticut?
Long Live the Glories of Old Connecticut

q.e: "Yankee Doodle" is Connecticut's official state song (1978).

q: When did Time magazine begin selecting Man of the Year?

q.e: Time began naming the "Man of the Year" in 1927.

q: When was the title Man of the Year changed to Person of the Year?

q.e: Time changed the title to "Person of the Year" in 1999.

q: Who was selected as Time magazines first Man of the Year?

q.e: Charles Lindbergh was the first Time Man of the Year, in 1927.

q: Who was Time magazines first Man of the Year to be under 26 years old?

q.e: Charles Lindbergh was 25, the youngest Man of the Year.

q: Who was the first non-American to be granted Time magazines title Man of the Year?

q.e: Mahatma Gandhi was the first non-American Man of the Year, in 1930.

q: Who was the first person to be chosen Man (or Person) of the Year three times?

q.e: Franklin D. Roosevelt was chosen in 1932, 1934 and 1941.

q: He was the first person involved in the automobile industry to win Time magazines title Man (or Person) of the Year.

q.e: Walter P. Chrysler was Man of the Year for 1928, the first car industry figure.

q: He was the first person chosen for Time magazines Man of the Year award two years in a row.

q.e: Richard Nixon was Man of the Year in 1971 and 1972.

q: This two-time winner of Time magazines Man of the Year title came up with a plan to rebuild Europe after World War II.

q.e: George C. Marshall was Man of the Year in 1943 and 1947, and the Marshall Plan rebuilt Europe.

q: In 1956 the Freedom Fighters of this country won Time magazines Man of the Year award.

q.e: The Hungarian Freedom Fighter was Man of the Year for 1956, after the Hungarian Revolution.

q: Victoria Land is a region located on this continent.

q.e: Victoria Land is a region of East Antarctica, next to the Ross Sea.

q: Which is the highest peak in the Canadian Rockies?

q.e: Mount Robson, at 3,954 m, is the highest peak in the Canadian Rockies.

q: Which explorer sailed to the mouth of the Mississippi River and claimed it for France?

q.e: René-Robert Cavelier de La Salle reached the Mississippi's mouth in 1682 and claimed Louisiana for France.

q: Who set up the first permanent settlement in North America?

q.e: Samuel de Champlain founded Quebec City in 1608. Earlier European settlements include St. Augustine (1565).

q: This sea captain, who was second-in-command of the English fleet against the Spanish Armada, claimed for the Queen a North American territory called New Albion.

q.e: Sir Francis Drake claimed Nova Albion (New Albion) for Queen Elizabeth I in 1579 while circumnavigating the globe, landing along the coast of modern-day California.

q: How many provinces does Canada comprise?

q.e: Canada is made up of 10 provinces, such as Ontario, Quebec, and British Columbia, alongside 3 federal territories: Yukon, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut.

q: The arrow points up for this lady who, according to Newsweeks CW 2008, has brains, experience and a great work ethic. Who is Barack Obamas choice for U. S. Secretary of State?

q.e: Hillary Clinton was Barack Obama's pick for Secretary of State in 2008, serving 2009–2013.

q: Arrow down. Who according to Newsweeks CW 2008 is ill-informed, inarticulate shopaholic that has an ego bigger than Alaska?

q.e: Sarah Palin was John McCain's running mate in 2008 and governor of Alaska 2006–2009.

q: Which country does not have a land border with Poland?

q.e: Poland borders Germany, Czechia, Slovakia, Ukraine, Belarus, Lithuania and Russia (Kaliningrad). Latvia is not a neighbor.

q: In 1569 Poland united with this country to form a Commonwealth that covered an area of almost one million square kilometers.

q.e: The Union of Lublin (1569) created the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth.

q: When was Poland accepted into the European Union?

q.e: Poland joined the EU on 1 May 2004.

q: Which city did not serve as capital of Poland?

q.e: Poland's historical capitals were Gniezno, Kraków, Poznań and Warsaw. Gdańsk never was.

q: Which city lying on the Missouri River is the capital of North Dakota?

q.e: Bismarck was chosen as North Dakota's capital when the state was admitted to the Union in 1889. Fargo is the state's most populous city, while Pierre is the capital of neighboring South Dakota.

q: This park lies on the border between Canada and North Dakota. It could be why this border needs no fences.

q.e: The International Peace Garden straddles the US–Canada border between North Dakota and Manitoba and was dedicated in 1932.

q: Which U.S. president stated he would have never been president had it not been for his experiences in North Dakota as a cattle rancher?

q.e: Theodore Roosevelt said, "I never would have been President if it had not been for my experiences in North Dakota," where he ranched in the 1880s.

q: The North Dakota State Fair is held in which city each August?

q.e: The North Dakota State Fair is held in Minot every July.

q: This Police Woman was born and raised at Kulm, ND which also was the flax capital of North America!

q.e: Angie Dickinson, star of "Police Woman," was born in Kulm, North Dakota.

q: The best walleye fishing lake in North America, according to Field and Stream Magazine, is this lake in northeast central North Dakota.

q.e: Devils Lake is North Dakota's largest natural lake and a famous walleye and perch fishery.

q: Which US President signed the Treaty of Purchase between the United States and Russia, which brought about the formal transfer of Alaska from Russia to the US?

q.e: President Andrew Johnson signed the 1867 Alaska Purchase treaty (negotiated by Seward) for $7.2 million.

q: What does Maundy Thursday, also known as Holy Thursday, commemorate?
The Last Supper of Jesus Christ with the Apostles

q.e: Maundy Thursday commemorates the Last Supper, where Jesus instituted the Eucharist and washed the disciples' feet. Christ's crucifixion is observed on Good Friday, while Easter Sunday celebrates the resurrection.

q: What is another name for Golgotha, the site where Jesus was crucified?

q.e: Calvary comes from the Latin word 'Calvaria', which translates to 'place of the skull', matching the Aramaic name Golgotha. Gethsemane was the garden at the foot of the Mount of Olives where Jesus prayed before his arrest.

q: Who directed the 2004 movie The Passion of the Christ, which covers the final twelve hours of Jesus life?

q.e: Mel Gibson directed The Passion of the Christ (2004), in Aramaic, Latin and Hebrew.

q: Gamzigrad is an ancient Roman complex of palaces located in this European country.

q.e: Gamzigrad (Felix Romuliana), in eastern Serbia, was built by Emperor Galerius and is a UNESCO site.

q: The Trans-Alaska pipeline provided what percent of domestic oil for the US when completed?

q.e: The Trans-Alaska Pipeline System (1977) supplied about 20–25% of US domestic oil at its peak.

q: Although he never filed for bankruptcy, this very smart and very great American President left a $107,000 debt for his heirs.

q.e: Thomas Jefferson died in 1826 with about $107,000 in debt, and Monticello was sold.

q: She was a very popular singer with many corporate sponserships. Her open antagonism to homosexuals led to the loss of these sponsorships and singing success.

q.e: Anita Bryant lost sponsors, including the Florida Citrus Commission, after her 1977 anti-gay campaign.

q: This man (along with his half-brother) tried to corner the worlds silver market. His failure led to his bankruptcy.

q.e: Nelson Bunker Hunt and his brother William Herbert Hunt tried to corner the silver market in 1979–80. "Silver Thursday" followed in 1980.

q: In 1936 this founder of General Motors had a debt of $914,231 forcing bankruptcy.

q.e: William C. Durant, who founded General Motors in 1908, declared bankruptcy in 1936.

q: Wheaties is the Breakfast of Champions. At 18 appearances, which of these sports figures has graced the cover of the Wheaties box more than any other sports figure?

q.e: Michael Jordan has appeared on the Wheaties box more than any other athlete (18 times).

q: A series of riots, among the worst in US history, were started on July 23, 1967. Where did this event take place?

q.e: The 1967 Detroit riot began on 23 July 1967 and left 43 dead.

q: This famous royal couple were married on July 23, 1986. The marriage ended some years later in a highly publicized divorce.

q.e: Prince Andrew and Sarah Ferguson married at Westminster Abbey on 23 July 1986 and divorced in 1996.

q: Which eclectic pro marijuana actor was born on July 23, 1961?

q.e: Woody Harrelson was born on 23 July 1961, and he's an advocate for marijuana legalization.

q: What year was the first Boston Marathon run?

q.e: The first Boston Marathon was held on 19 April 1897, the oldest annual marathon.

q: Rocky Marciano is from which city in Massachusetts?

q.e: Rocky Marciano, undefeated heavyweight champion (49–0), was from Brockton, Massachusetts.

q: Birthday celebrants in Mexico gets blindfolded and have to hit a ____________.

q.e: A piñata, traditionally made of a clay pot or papier-mache covered in colorful crepe paper, is filled with candies and fruit and struck by blindfolded participants during Mexican celebrations.

q: About what percentage of Israels land of approximately 20,300 km² (7,849 mi²) is arable?

q.e: About 15–17% of Israel's land is arable.

q: What Gothic building, regarded as a haunted place, is the burial site of Karl Marx?

q.e: Highgate Cemetery in London is Gothic in style and holds Karl Marx's grave.

q: This extraordinary church in Whitby, North Yorkshire inspired Bram Stoker to write his famous book Drakula.

q.e: St Mary's Church in Whitby, with its 199 steps, appears in Bram Stoker's "Dracula" (1897).

q: What is the birth place of Queen Victoria?

q.e: Queen Victoria was born in Kensington Palace in 1819.

q: This coastal defence site was built on the Isle of Wight to protect Great Britain from French invasion.

q.e: The Needles Old Battery on the Isle of Wight was built in 1862 to guard against a French attack.

q: Where did the Tour de France start in 2007?

q.e: The 2007 Tour de France started in London, with a prologue past Trafalgar Square and Buckingham Palace.

q: A Gothic-styled memorial, which opened in 1872, included allegorical figures of Europe, Asia, Africa, and America and was made of granite and marble. It was erected in memory of this Royal person.
Prince Albert, husband of Queen Victoria

q.e: The Albert Memorial in London, opened in 1872, honors Prince Albert, Queen Victoria's husband.

q: Out of the four original counties of East Jersey, which countys seat is Hackensack?

q.e: Hackensack is the seat of Bergen County, one of East Jersey's four original counties.

q: Located in South Jersey, this county seat has a name related to a Hebrew word meaning peace.

q.e: Salem, New Jersey's county seat, shares its name from "shalom," the Hebrew word for peace.

q: This county seat, known as the Silk City, is the home city to famous American actor and comedian Lou Costello.

q.e: Paterson, New Jersey, is "Silk City." Lou Costello of Abbott and Costello was born there.

q: Bridgeton, which has the largest historic district of any incorporated town in New Jersey, is the seat of which county?

q.e: Bridgeton is the seat of Cumberland County, New Jersey.

q: Zoroastrianism is a religion which originated with which ancient civilization?

q.e: Founded by the prophet Zoroaster (Zarathustra) in ancient Iran around the early 1st millennium BCE, Zoroastrianism served as the state religion of major Persian empires, including the Achaemenid and Sasanian empires.

q: During the reigns of which 2 Persian kings were invasions of Greece attempted?

q.e: Darius I (490 BC, Marathon) and Xerxes I (480 BC) attempted invasions of Greece.

q: How many meals a day did ancient Mesopotamians customarily eat?

q.e: Ancient Mesopotamians customarily ate two meals a day.

q: This mountain contains the highest peak on the African continent.

q.e: Mount Kilimanjaro in Tanzania is a dormant stratovolcano whose highest peak, Uhuru Peak on the Kibo crater, stands 19,341 feet (5,895 m) above sea level. It is the tallest mountain in Africa and the world's highest free-standing mountain.

q: This mountain range is located in Eurasia between the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea.

q.e: The Caucasus Mountains stretch about 750 miles (1,200 km) between the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea, marking part of the traditional boundary between Europe and Asia. The range includes Mount Elbrus, Europe's highest peak at 18,510 feet (5,642 m).

q: This mountain range is the longest on the planet, and is located in South America.

q.e: The Andes stretch about 7,000 kilometers (4,350 miles) along the western coast of South America across seven countries. Its highest point is Mount Aconcagua in Argentina, which reaches 6,961 meters (22,838 feet).

q: This mountain range is located in Europe and its highest peak is Mont Blanc.

q.e: Mont Blanc stands at about 4,808 meters (15,774 feet) on the French-Italian border, making it the highest summit in the Alps. The Apennines run down the Italian peninsula, peaking much lower at Corno Grande.

q: In what mountain are the peaks Manaslu and Lhotse located?

q.e: Manaslu and Lhotse are in the Himalayas.

q: The Japanese multinational corporation Toyota Motor Corporation is the second largest automobile maker in the world for 2006 losing the first place to which company?

q.e: General Motors led global sales in 2006; Toyota overtook it in 2008.

q: Although it is a leading automobile maker, what else does Toyota Motor Corporation produce beside automobiles?
Television sets and medical X-ray equipment

q.e: Toyota started as a loom maker, Toyoda Automatic Loom Works, and has also produced sewing machines.

q: What is Toyotas luxury car line called?

q.e: Toyota launched the Lexus brand in 1989 with the release of the LS 400 sedan to compete directly with American and European luxury automakers.

q: The top selling hybrid car for the U.S. of 2006 was produced by Toyota. Which one is it?

q.e: The Toyota Prius dominated the hybrid market in 2006, selling over 100,000 units in the United States that year alone.

q: Which Emmy Award winner invented CBS news magazine 60 Minutes in 1968?

q.e: Don Hewitt created 60 Minutes at CBS in 1968.

q: In 1959, this journalist, author of the acclaimed book Black Like Me, darkened his skin in an attempt to experience the segregation in the American South.

q.e: John Howard Griffin darkened his skin in 1959 and wrote Black Like Me (1961).

q: This American journalist, awarded the 2003 Gerald R. Ford Prize for Distinguished Reporting on the Presidency, took part in the uncovering of the Watergate scandal.

q.e: Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein broke the Watergate story for the Washington Post.

q: Which is the United Kingdoms official newspaper first published on November 7, 1665?

q.e: The London Gazette, first published 7 November 1665 as the Oxford Gazette, is the UK's official journal of record.

q: Which weekly magazine, established in 1828 in London, had the same owner as The Daily Telegraph?

q.e: The Spectator, founded in 1828, shared an owner with the Daily Telegraph (the Barclay brothers) until 2023.

q: In what year did the first Iditarod Trail Sled Dog Race take place?

q.e: The first Iditarod Trail Sled Dog Race took place in 1973.

q: Helicopters are generally believed to excel most conventional fixed-wing aircraft in what aspect?

q.e: Helicopters excel at maneuverability: they can hover, fly backwards and land in tight spaces.

q: This canal, known as the largest man-made waterway in the world, with a total length of 1200 miles, is also one of the most ancient ones.

q.e: The Grand Canal stretches approximately 1,104 miles (1,776 km) between Beijing and Hangzhou, with parts of the waterway dating back as far as the 5th century BC.

q: The Great Manmade River is a tremendous transportation infrastructure, which is not a river as its name suggests, but what?

q.e: The Great Man-Made River in Libya is a network of underground pipes bringing fresh water from the Sahara aquifer to the coast.

q: Segway HT, a two-wheeled light-mode transportation device, invented by Dean Kamen and presented in December 2001, is the worlds first vehicle of what type?

q.e: The Segway is a self-balancing personal transporter, unveiled in 2001 by Dean Kamen.

q: Who created the modern image of the red-suited bearded, plump Santa Claus?

q.e: Thomas Nast's Harper's Weekly drawings in the 1860s–80s shaped Santa's modern look.

q: What happens to the eccentric shopping network executive, played by Whoopi Goldberg, in the 2001 TV special Call Me Claus?
She is chosen to become the next Santa Claus.
She is kidnapped by Santa Claus elves.
She meets the ghost of Santa Claus who was killed by her boss.
She founds out that her boss is the real Santa Claus.

q.e: In "Call Me Claus" (2001), Whoopi Goldberg's character is chosen to be the next Santa Claus.

q: In the comic strip Bloom County, Santa Claus tells the story of how his elves went on strike and were fired by this US President.

q.e: In Bloom County, Santa tells how the elves went on strike and Ronald Reagan fired them, as he did with air traffic controllers.

q: In many Christian countries the birth of this saint is celebrated on 24 June (Midsummer).

q.e: Christians celebrate the birth of St. John the Baptist on 24 June, close to the summer solstice.

q: This celebrity, who considered suntan a symbol denoting a life of privilege and leisure, made sunbathing fashionalble in the 1920s.

q.e: Coco Chanel popularized suntans in the 1920s after getting sunburned on a cruise.

q: This American-born author, who became a British subject in 1915 wrote, Summer afternoon—summer afternoon; to me those have always been the two most beautiful words in the English language.

q.e: Henry James, American-born, became a British subject in 1915, and wrote about "summer afternoon" as the most beautiful words.

q: Which popular island destination is not correctly matched with the country?

q.e: Bora Bora is in French Polynesia, not the Dominican Republic.

q: What is the correct title of Lee Hazlewoods song, which describes a man who awakens to find that his silver spurs a dollar and a dime had been stolen by a mysterious woman?

q.e: "Summer Wine" by Lee Hazlewood (1966) was a hit as a duet with Nancy Sinatra.

q: In what year was the Minnesota Vikings football team established?

q.e: The Minnesota Vikings were established in 1960 and began play in 1961.

q: This famous writer was born in St. Paul, MN in the month of September, but his family moved around a lot and he once lived on Summit Avenue.

q.e: F. Scott Fitzgerald was born on 24 September 1896 in St. Paul and lived on Summit Avenue.

q: He was the first winner of Times Person of the Year title to have a black belt in karate.

q.e: Vladimir Putin was Time's Person of the Year in 2007. He holds a black belt in judo and also practiced karate.

q: In December 1999, Time magazine announced its Person of the Century. Who was it?

q.e: Time named Albert Einstein its Person of the Century in its December 31, 1999 issue, with Mahatma Gandhi and Franklin D. Roosevelt named as the two runners-up.

q: In December 1949 this man was chosen Man of the Half-Century by Time magazine.

q.e: Winston Churchill was named "Man of the Half-Century" by Time on 3 January 1950.

q: Find the one who was never named Man (or Person) of the Year by Time magazine.

q.e: Mother Teresa was never named Time's Person of the Year (she was on its cover and in other lists).

q: Who was the first Pope named Man of the Year by Time magazine?

q.e: Pope John XXIII was Time's Man of the Year for 1962, the first pope so named.

q: How many times did President Harry S Truman win Time magazines Man of the Year award?

q.e: Harry Truman was Man of the Year in 1945 and 1948.

q: When did Dr. Martin L. King, Jr. win Time magazines Man of the Year award?

q.e: Martin Luther King Jr. was Time's Man of the Year in 1963.

q: Which of the following was never named Man (or Person) of the Year by Time magazine?

q.e: Albert Einstein was Time's Person of the Century (1999), but never Man of the Year.

q: Which city/village is the official birthplace of Memorial Day?

q.e: Waterloo, New York, was officially recognized as Memorial Day's birthplace in 1966 by Congress, and its first observance was in 1866.

q: The Uniform Holidays Bill according to which Memorial Day is celebrated on the last Monday of May, was passed in what year?

q.e: The Uniform Monday Holiday Act (1968) took effect in 1971, moving Memorial Day to the last Monday of May.

q: Which flower was adopted in 1922 as an official Memorial Day symbol?

q.e: The Veterans of Foreign Wars adopted the red poppy in 1922, inspired by John McCrae's 1915 poem 'In Flanders Fields'. The flower has long served as an international symbol of remembrance for fallen soldiers.

q: Which Congressman and later, US President, was the speaker at the first formal observance of Memorial Day?

q.e: James A. Garfield, then a congressman, spoke at Arlington's first big Decoration Day on 30 May 1868.

q: Who composed Taps, a famous musical piece played in the US military on Memorial Day?

q.e: Daniel Butterfield, a Union general, composed "Taps" in 1862.

q: In what year was Decoration Day renamed to Memorial Day?

q.e: "Memorial Day" was first used in 1882. It became the official name by federal law in 1967.

q: The Tomb of the Unknowns in Arlington National Cemetery, United States, is guarded by members of which military unit?

q.e: The 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment, "The Old Guard," guards the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.

q: Which statement about Memorial Day is true?
It commemorates US men and women who died in military service to their country
Memorial Day and Veterans Day coincide
It commemorates the contributions of those who served in the US military
Memorial Day is more recently established than Veterans Day

q.e: Memorial Day honors those who died serving in the US military. Veterans Day honors all who served.

q: Which US President presided over the funeral of the Vietnam Unknown, held at Arlington National Cemetery?

q.e: President Reagan presided over the burial of the Vietnam Unknown on Memorial Day 1984. He was identified in 1998 as Michael Blassie.

q: Womens Memorial is a site honoring all military women - past, present and future. Which cemetery is it located in?

q.e: The Women In Military Service For America Memorial is at the entrance to Arlington National Cemetery.

q: In what year was the city of Fargo founded?

q.e: Fargo, North Dakota, was founded in 1871 along the Northern Pacific Railway.

q: The museum honoring this professional baseball player is located in the West Acres Shopping Mall in Fargo, ND.

q.e: The Roger Maris Museum is in the West Acres Mall in Fargo. Maris hit 61 HRs in 1961.

q: In what country is Lake Nyos located?

q.e: Lake Nyos in Cameroon released a deadly cloud of carbon dioxide in 1986, killing about 1,700 people.

q: Iquitos, a major port city on the Amazon River, is located east of the Andes in what country?

q.e: Iquitos, Peru, is the world's largest city that cannot be reached by road.

q: Of the 46 peaks over 3800 in New York State, how many have a paved road going to, or near the summit?

q.e: Whiteface Mountain has a paved road to near its summit, the only one of the 46 High Peaks.

q: The Adirondack State Park, at 780,000 acres, is roughly equal in area to which of the following?

q.e: The Adirondack Park is about 6 million acres, larger than Yellowstone, Yosemite and others combined.

q: These verses are part of the national anthem of which country: Your history is an epic Of the most brilliant feats. And your valour, in faith steeped, Will protect our homes and our rights; Will protect our homes and our rights.?

q.e: These are verses of "O Canada," Canada's national anthem, adopted officially in 1980.

q: What was the first bank to manage over 2 trillion dollars?
Chase Manhattan Bank of New York

q.e: UBS was the first bank to manage over $2 trillion in client assets.

q: Checks were probably used by Dutch traders as early as the 1400s. In what year were the first printed checks made?

q.e: The first printed checks date to 1762 in Britain (some say the 1780s).

q: Prior to this year, all American paper money came in varying sizes.

q.e: From 1929, US paper money was reduced to a uniform smaller size.

q: Blagoevgrad BT is this countrys largest cigarette company. Kremikovtzi is its largest metalworking company. Mobiltel is one of its largest communications companies.

q.e: Blagoevgrad BT, Kremikovtzi and Mobiltel are all Bulgarian companies.

q: Which of these stores is the largest in terms of area?

q.e: Harrods in London covers about 1 million square feet. Macy's Herald Square and Shinsegae in Busan are among the biggest stores.

q: When did the Dow Jones Industrial Average first hit 1,000?

q.e: The Dow first closed above 1,000 on 14 November 1972.

q: The precursor of this company was founded by an employee of the US Census Bureau in 1896 in Broome County, New York.

q.e: IBM traces its roots to Herman Hollerith's Tabulating Machine Company (1896). Hollerith worked for the Census Bureau.

q: The highest point in Maryland is the Hoye Crest on Backbone Mountain, which is located in this county.

q.e: Hoye-Crest (3,360 ft) on Backbone Mountain is in Garrett County, Maryland.

q: Who is the first President of the independent Republic of the Philippines?

q.e: Manuel Roxas was the first president of the independent Philippines (1946–48).

q: Who is the Philippine President whose term ended up because of People Power?

q.e: Ferdinand Marcos was ousted in the 1986 People Power Revolution.

q: Who is the first female President of the Philippines?

q.e: Corazon Aquino was the first female president of the Philippines (1986–92).

q: Who is the thirteenth President of the Philippines?

q.e: Joseph Estrada was the 13th president (1998–2001).

q: The U.S. state of South Carolina used to be known by this nickname.

q.e: South Carolina was once nicknamed the "Iodine State," then the Palmetto State.

q: What nickname has been given to the U.S. state of Ohio?

q.e: Ohio is the "Birthplace of Aviation" (the Wright brothers, Dayton), and the "Buckeye State".

q: Vinegar valentines, ostensibly given on Valentines Day, became popular during the Victorian era. What type of message do they contain?

q.e: Vinegar valentines were insulting cards sent anonymously in the Victorian era.

q: During the prohibition era a conflict between two powerful criminal gangs resulted in what came to be known as the Saint Valentines Day massacre. In what US city did it occur?

q.e: The St. Valentine's Day Massacre took place in Chicago on 14 February 1929, ordered by Al Capone.

q: What is the occupation of Ashton Kutchers character, Reed Bennett, in Garry Marshalls 2010 romantic comedy Valentines Day?

q.e: Ashton Kutcher played Reed Bennett, a florist, in Valentine's Day (2010).

q: In modern times, the heart is the symbol representing love. What other organ was considered to be the seat of love and emotion in ancient times and in the Middle Ages?

q.e: The liver was considered the seat of love and emotion by the ancients and in the Middle Ages.

q: In Roman mythology, Cupid is the god of desire, affection and erotic love. Who is his Greek counterpart?

q.e: Eros is the Greek god of love and sexual passion, famously depicted carrying a bow and arrows, just like his Roman equivalent Cupid. Aphrodite is Eros's mother and the Greek goddess of love, whose Roman counterpart is Venus.

q: What species of bird does the term lovebird refer to?

q.e: Lovebirds belong to the genus Agapornis, a group of small, stocky parrots native to Africa, named for the intense pair-bonding and affectionate behavior they display toward their mates.

q: Name the longest river entirely in England, which flows through London, Oxford, Reading and Richmond.

q.e: The Thames is the longest river entirely in England (346 km), while the Severn is the longest in Britain.

q: What London department store was sold by Mohamed Al-Fayed to Qatar Holdings in 2010?

q.e: Mohamed Al-Fayed sold Harrods to Qatar Holdings in 2010 for about £1.5 billion.

q: Connecticut is called The Constitution State because the first written state constitution was penned there. What is the name of that constitution?

q.e: The Fundamental Orders of Connecticut (1639) are called the first written constitution.

q: Among the not so glorious firsts from Connecticut was the first traitor of the United States. What was his name?

q.e: Benedict Arnold, born in Norwich, Connecticut, was a celebrated Continental Army general before plotting to surrender the American fort at West Point to the British in 1780.

q: Connecticuts state hero is Nathan Hale. Who is the state heroine?

q.e: Prudence Crandall, who opened a school for Black girls in 1833, is Connecticut's state heroine.

q: Which of the following originated in Connecticut?

q.e: The hamburger is claimed to have been first served at Louis' Lunch in New Haven, Connecticut, around 1900.

q: The Danube river forms a natural border of Romania with how many countries?

q.e: The Danube forms Romania's border with Serbia, Bulgaria, Ukraine and, briefly, Moldova.

q: What year was the military base in Area 5 created?

q.e: Area 5 of the Nevada Test Site (Camp Mercury) dates to the early 1950s. Check other sources.
