q: If youre heading to Santa Barbara from LA Proper, its likely youll travel on the:

q.e: US 101 is the Ventura Freeway in LA, leading to Santa Barbara.
The I-710 is the Long Beach Freeway.
The I-105 is the Glenn Anderson Freeway (also the Century Freeway).

q: If Im having a Cholesterol Free snack (yeah, right) at Randys Donuts, at 805 Manchester Ave in Inglewood, Im closest in proximity to which Freeway?

q.e: Randy's Donuts in Inglewood is near the I-405 San Diego Freeway and the iconic giant doughnut.

q: Detroit is on the northern bank of the Detroit River. Which of the following is located on the southern bank?

q.e: Windsor, Ontario, Canada, lies on the south bank of the Detroit River, across from Detroit.

q: What is the name of the automated train that circles downtown Detroit?
SMART (Suburban Mobility Authority for Regional Transportation)

q.e: The Detroit People Mover is a 2.9-mile automated light rail loop downtown.

q: Detroit was established by French colonists. What does the name mean in French?

q.e: Detroit takes its name from the Detroit River, which French explorers called 'le détroit du lac Érié', meaning 'the strait of Lake Erie'. A strait is a narrow passage of water connecting two larger bodies.

q: Which of the Great Lakes is closest to Detroit?

q.e: Lake St. Clair and Lake Erie are the closest to Detroit.

q: What family ruled Japan for many years, using a feudal system, until overthrown in 1868?

q.e: The Tokugawa shogunate ruled Japan from 1603 to 1868 until the Meiji Restoration.

q: What sport has six major tournaments a year in Japan, three in Tokyo and three in other major cities?

q.e: Professional sumo holds six honbasho tournaments each year: three at the Ryogoku Kokugikan in Tokyo, and one each in Osaka, Nagoya, and Fukuoka.

q: The number of member states in the European Union exceeds the number of official languages, as several national languages are shared by two or more countries. Which official language is spoken in the greatest number of countries?

q.e: German is official in Germany, Austria, Belgium and Luxembourg.

q: Socrates was a classical Greek philosopher and Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian painter, sculptor, architect, mathematician and inventor. What do they have in common?
Some learning programmes of the European Commission are named after them.
They were both in love with Mona Lisa.
Leonardo da Vinci was one of Socrates students.

q.e: The EU's Erasmus+ programmes include Socrates, Leonardo da Vinci, Comenius and others, named after great thinkers.

q: From 1990 to 2001, what was the fastest growing religion in the USA?

q.e: Wicca and Buddhism were among the fastest-growing religions in the US between 1990 and 2001.

q: In 2003, what percentage of the Americans lived within 100 miles of an ocean?

q.e: About half of Americans live within 100 miles of an ocean or the Great Lakes coast.

q: When did the population of the USA hit the 100 million mark?

q.e: The US population passed 100 million around 1915.

q: In 2005, New York City, Chicago, and Los Angeles were respectively the first, second and third most populous cities in America. Which city was fourth?

q.e: Houston was the fourth most populous US city in 2005, after New York, Los Angeles and Chicago.

q: Which of these is not a golf course in the Puerto Vallarta area?

q.e: El Paso Golf is not a golf course in Puerto Vallarta.

q: What types of whales can often be seen visiting the Bay of Puerto Vallarta during wintertime?
There are no whales in the region.

q.e: Humpback whales visit Banderas Bay during the winter to breed and give birth.

q: What is Puerto Vallartas time zone?

q.e: Puerto Vallarta uses Central Time.

q: Which of the following movies, starring Richard Burton, was filmed in Puerto Vallarta?

q.e: The Night of the Iguana (1964), with Richard Burton and Ava Gardner, was filmed at Mismaloya near Puerto Vallarta.

q: This is the highest mountain in Puerto Rico; measuring 4,390 feet in elevation.

q.e: Cerro de Punta, 1,338 m (4,390 ft), is the highest peak in Puerto Rico.

q: Celebrities such as actress Roselyn Sanchez(Rush Hour 2) and Ricky Martin(musician) were born in this famous city in Puerto Rico.

q.e: Ricky Martin and Roselyn Sánchez were both born in San Juan, Puerto Rico.

q: What kind of animal is the Springbok?

q.e: The springbok is a medium-sized antelope native to southwestern Africa, famous for jumping up to 2 meters (6.6 feet) in the air, a display known as pronking.

q: What is the highest mountain in the Philippines?

q.e: Mount Apo (2,954 m) on Mindanao is the highest peak in the Philippines.

q: Who is the first woman president of the Philippines?

q.e: Corazon Aquino became the first female president of the Philippines in February 1986 following the nonviolent People Power Revolution. Gloria Macapagal Arroyo became the nation's second female president in 2001.

q: When did Alcatraz Island become a federal prison?

q.e: Alcatraz became a federal prison in 1934 and closed in 1963.

q: The first Spaniard to discover Alcatraz Island named it La Isla de los Alcatraces which translates as what?
The Island of the Lost Souls

q.e: Juan Manuel de Ayala named it "La Isla de los Alcatraces" ("Island of the Pelicans") in 1775.
The Triceratops is the state dinosaur of Wyoming.

q: What minor league baseball team moved to Casper, Wyoming in 2001?

q.e: The Casper Ghosts played in Wyoming from 2001 to 2007 in the Pioneer League.

q: Mikhail Bakunin, an 1800s socialist, was also the father of what other ideology?

q.e: Mikhail Bakunin, a Russian revolutionary, is a founder of collectivist anarchism.

q: Karl Marx, a teacher of socialism, said that a socialist state was possible because the lower classes were being brought together from distant farms into large cities. What revolution made this possible?

q.e: Karl Marx argued that the Industrial Revolution gathered workers into cities, creating the conditions for socialism.

q: What government, formed in 1871, was referred to by Marx and Engels as the first ever socialist state?

q.e: The Paris Commune (1871) is the first socialist government according to Marx.

q: What theory proposed socialism in one country?

q.e: "Socialism in one country" was Stalin's theory (with Bukharin) of the 1920s, against Trotsky's permanent revolution.

q: In 1930, this Yale graduate, author of It Cant Happen Here, became the first American to be awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature.

q.e: Sinclair Lewis (Yale 1908) won the 1930 Nobel Prize in Literature, the first American to do so.

q: This painter, telegraph pioneer and inventor graduated from Yale in 1810.

q.e: Samuel F. B. Morse (Yale 1810) was a painter and co-inventor of the telegraph and Morse code.

q: Juan Trippe was an airline entrepreneur and pioneer who graduated from Yale in 1921. Who portrayed him in Martin Scorseses movie The Aviator?

q.e: Alec Baldwin played Juan Trippe, Pan Am's founder, in The Aviator (2004).

q.e: Thornton Wilder won Pulitzer Prizes for "The Bridge of San Luis Rey" (1928) and "Our Town" (1938).

q.e: Felipe Calderón took office on 1 December 2006.

q: In 1879, which U.S. Supreme Court case invoked the famous dictum of Jefferson, calling for the erection of a wall of separation between church and state?

q.e: Reynolds v. United States (1879) upheld a ban on polygamy and used Jefferson's "wall of separation" phrase.

q: The case of Epperson v. State of Arkansas in 1968 dealt primarily with what?
Whether U.S. states could not forbid the teaching of evolution
Whether U.S. state tests may be given to home school children
Whether literacy tests are required for advancement into junior high school
Whether U.S. states must require a balance of creationism and evolution

q.e: Epperson v. Arkansas (1968) struck down a ban on teaching evolution in public schools.

q: The 1974 U.S. Supreme Court case in Iowa, Erb v. Iowa State Board of Education, dealt with what?
A teachers adultery is no reason to revoke license
Reduction in force must be in good faith

q.e: Erb v. Iowa State Board of Public Instruction (1974) concerned a teacher's license and adultery.

q: This court case dealt with a Title IX issue of the education amendments of 1972. It protects employees against gender discrimination in educational institutions.
North Haven v. Board of Education v. Bell

q.e: North Haven Board of Education v. Bell (1982) held that Title IX protects employees of educational institutions.

q: Which of these countries does not share a border with Metropolitan France, i.e. France in Western Europe?

q.e: Austria does not border France. France touches Belgium, Luxembourg, Germany, Switzerland, Italy, Spain, Andorra and Monaco.

q: What is the title of the national anthem of the French Republic?

q.e: France's national anthem is known in French as La Marseillaise, translating to The Song of Marseille. It was composed in 1792 by Claude Joseph Rouget de Lisle during the French Revolution.

q: What is the most popular religion in France according to official data from 2007?

q.e: Roman Catholicism is the most common religion in France, though many are unreligious.

q: What is the name of the woman that has been the symbol of France for centuries?

q.e: Marianne has been the national personification of the French Republic since the French Revolution of 1789, representing liberty, equality, and fraternity.

q: How many different tribal governments are recognized by the US government?

q.e: The US recognizes 574 tribes today. The bank figure of 563 is from earlier years.

q: Which Native American group lived in hogans?

q.e: The Navajo (Diné) traditionally lived in hogans.

q: What is the meaning of the Native American expression Dine'tah?

q.e: Diné Tah means "Navajo Land" or "among the people."

q: The first female Principal Chief of the Cherokee
The first Native American to be elected to the US Congress
The first female Native American to be director of UNESCO
The first female Native American to be a US Army General

q.e: Wilma Mankiller was the first female Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation (1985–95).

q: In the late 1800s, the European nations scrambled to acquire colonies in Africa. Which of the following did NOT become a colony of a European country?

q.e: Liberia (and Ethiopia) were never colonized by a European country, though Liberia was founded by freed Americans.

q: The African Union is a confederation of all African countries except one. Which is the only African country that is NOT a member of the African Union?

q.e: Seychelles has 115 islands and is counted as part of Africa.

q: How many African countries are there?

q.e: Africa has 54 UN-recognized countries (55 AU members counting Western Sahara).

q.e: The Central African Republic has a Christian majority. Egypt, Libya and Somalia are Muslim majority.

q: How many different languages are spoken in Africa?

q.e: Africa has around 2,000 languages, about a third of the world's total.

q: What year did the U.S. Supreme Court install its first photocopy machine?

q.e: The Supreme Court's first photocopier arrived around 1969. Check other sources.

q: What year was the U.S. Supreme Courts website created?

q.e: The Supreme Court launched its website in 2000.

q: Who was the second woman to be appointed to the U.S. Supreme Court?

q.e: Ruth Bader Ginsburg was the second woman on the Court (1993), after Sandra Day O'Connor (1981).

q: The Dred Scott case (Scott v. Sandford, 1857) is an infamous U.S. Supreme Court case involving which of the following?

q.e: Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857) ruled that Black people were not citizens and Congress couldn't ban slavery in the territories.

q: The Sixth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution does not guarantee the right to which of the following?

q.e: The Sixth Amendment guarantees a speedy public trial, impartial jury, counsel and confrontation of witnesses.

q: What is the original meaning of the term Slip Opinion as applied to the U.S. Supreme Court?
Opinions sent to the printer on the same day they are made
An opinion that has later been overturned after careful review
Opinions made by the justices for their own private records
The overall opinion of the garments that the justices wear under their robes

q: Stephen Hillenburg, the creator of Spongebob is from what Oklahoma city?

q.e: Stephen Hillenburg, SpongeBob's creator, was born in Lawton, Oklahoma, in 1961.

q: What is the capital of Indonesia?

q.e: Jakarta, located on the island of Java, has long served as Indonesia's capital. In 2019, the government announced plans to move the official capital to a newly built city named Nusantara in East Kalimantan.

q: Which of these birds do NOT migrate in autumn?

q.e: Ravens are residents who stay all year. Many other birds migrate in autumn.

q: What was the name of Americas first urban freeway?

q.e: The Davison Freeway in Detroit (1942) was the nation's first urban depressed freeway.

q: Which two Great Lakes are connected by the Detroit River?

q.e: The Detroit River links Lake St. Clair with Lake Erie. The St. Clair River links Lake Huron and Lake St. Clair.

q: The national flag of what country consists of three horizontal bands in red, black and white?

q.e: Yemen's flag has red, white and black horizontal bands.

q: The national flag of what country consists of a smaller white area and a larger purple section?

q.e: Qatar's flag is maroon with a white serrated band on the hoist.

q: What country has a red flag with a stylized eight-rayed yellow sun?

q.e: North Macedonia's flag has a yellow sun with eight rays on red (the Sun of Vergina was replaced in 1995).

q: How many U.S. Presidents of the 19th and 20th century were born in Ohio?

Ohio is known as the Buckeye State due to the prevalence of Ohio buckeye trees (Aesculus glabra). The Volunteer State is Tennessee, and the Hawkeye State is Iowa.
Ohio borders Pennsylvania, West Virginia, Kentucky, Indiana and Michigan.

q: Pristina is the capital of this country which gained its independence from Serbia on February 17 2008.

q.e: Kosovo declared independence from Serbia on 17 February 2008. Pristina is the capital.

q: This small country in Southeast Asia, also known as Timor-Leste, is located about 640 km (400 mi) northwest of Darwin, Australia.

q.e: East Timor (Timor-Leste) lies about 640 km northwest of Darwin, Australia.

q: What interesting reptile nickname has been given to the U.S. state of Alabama?

q: This spicy nickname has been given to the U.S. state of Connecticut.

q.e: Connecticut is the "Nutmeg State," from the claim that its peddlers sold wooden "nutmegs."

q: What interesting nickname was given to the U.S. state of Delaware?

q.e: Delaware is nicknamed "Uncle Sam's Pocket Handkerchief" for its small size, and also "The First State."

q: What fruity nickname has been given to the U.S. state of Hawaii?

q.e: Hawaii is nicknamed the "Pineapple State" for its former pineapple industry, and "Aloha State."

q: What Nicaraguan lake covers an amazing area of 3,255 square miles?

q: Lammas Day used to be observed in some English-speaking countries on 1 August. What was brought to church on that day?

q: Im as corny as Kansas in August is a line from the song Im in Love with a Wonderful Guy, which was performed in what Rodgers and Hammerstein musical?

q.e: "I'm in Love with a Wonderful Guy" is from South Pacific (1949), with the "corny as Kansas in August" line.

q: What WWII event that occurred on 6 August 1945 was code-named Little Boy?
the dropping of the atomic bomb on Hiroshima
the dropping of the atomic bomb on Nagasaki

q: What Nobel Prize and Pulitzer Prize-winning American author wrote the 1932 novel Light in August?

q: According to a popular weather saying, what will the winter be like if the first week of August is unusually warm?

q.e: This is folk weather lore without scientific basis. Check regional almanacs for variations.

q: This mountain, located in Siskiyou County, is the fifth highest in California.

q.e: The Missouri River is named for the Missouri (Missouria) tribe, whose name is said to mean "people with dugout canoes."

q: What is the state flower of the U.S. state of Missouri?

q.e: The white hawthorn blossom is Missouri's state flower.

q: Which of these sports teams is a baseball team from the U.S. state of Missouri?

q: In which of these countries is Fathers Day not celebrated on the third Sunday of June?

q: Which President was first to declare the third Sunday in June as Fathers Day?

q: What ghost allegedly appeared in Gibside Hall, Tyne and Wear, England?
The ghost of a servant- girl
The ghost of a white lady

q.e: An oblique aerial photo is taken at an angle, so the foreground is closer. Check the other options.

q: Which statement is true about the world famous carnival in Rio de Janeiro?
The costumes people wear are intended to hide differences among classes.
During the carnival salsa schools compete with rival salsa schools.

q.e: Rio's Carnival is held before Lent, ending on Ash Wednesday.

q: One of the Seven Wonders of the World was located on this Greek island.

q.e: The Colossus of Rhodes, a bronze statue of the sun god Helios standing roughly 108 feet (33 meters) high, was erected on Rhodes around 280 BC. It was toppled by a major earthquake in 226 BC and remained one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

q: This area in Slovenia within the Julian Alps, is a popular tourist destination.

q.e: Lake Bled in the Julian Alps is Slovenia's top tourist spot.

q: Which of the following animals spend the winter in the warm waters of the Mexican area Los Cabos?

q.e: Humpback whales visit Los Cabos from December to April to breed.

q: This resort was the setting of the movie And God Created Woman, starring Brigitte Bardot.

q.e: "And God Created Woman" (1956) was filmed in Saint-Tropez, which made Brigitte Bardot and the town famous.

q: When did banknotes over $100 stop being printed in the US?

q.e: The US ceased printing bills over $100 in 1945 and officially discontinued them in 1969.

q: When was the redeemable in gold clause removed from Federal Reserve Notes?

q.e: The gold redemption clause was removed in 1934, after the Gold Reserve Act.

q: Which of these US bills remains in circulation the least amount of time?

q.e: The $5 note has among the shortest lifespans, around 4.7 years. The $1 lasts about 6.6 years.

q: Which bill represents the majority of US money printed nowadays?

q.e: $1 bills make up the largest share of US currency printed.

q: Rio de Janeiro won its bid to host the 2016 Summer Olympics. What other cities were on the short list?

q.e: Chicago, Madrid, Rio and Tokyo were the 2016 finalists. Rio won in 2009.

q: The Lost City of the Incas, Machu Picchu, was featured prominently in what 21st century movie?

q.e: "The Motorcycle Diaries" (2004) features Che Guevara visiting Machu Picchu.

q: What is the official language of Malta?

q.e: Maltese and English are Malta's official languages.

q: What plant has been traditionally associated with Malta, and is featured on the national coat of arms of the country?

q.e: The olive branch appears on Malta's coat of arms, along with a palm branch.

q: In what year did Bolivia become an independent republic?

q.e: Bolivia declared independence on 6 August 1825 (Bolívar's name inspired its name).

q: During the colonial period, Bolivia was known as what?

q.e: Under Spanish rule, Bolivia was called Alto Perú (Upper Peru), part of the Viceroyalty of Peru, then La Plata.

q: Against which country did Bolivia fight in the Chaco War?

q.e: The Chaco War (1932–35) was fought between Bolivia and Paraguay over the Gran Chaco region, which Paraguay mostly won.

q: Which of these languages is not spoken in Bolivia?
All these languages are spoken in Bolivia.

q.e: Spanish, Quechua, Aymara and Guaraní are all spoken in Bolivia. The country recognizes 36 official languages.

q: Which of these movies ended in Bolivia?
Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid

q.e: "Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid" (1969) ends in San Vicente, Bolivia.

q: Which of the following is not a factor to be taken into account when selecting a marine pipeline route?

q.e: Pipeline routing considers seabed, depth and shipping lanes, not shark danger.

q: Which two countries had to reconcile in the 1980s before a gas pipeline route spanning the Strait of Gibraltar from Algeria to Spain was possible?

q.e: Algeria and Morocco had to resolve their dispute for the Maghreb–Europe pipeline across the Strait of Gibraltar, completed in 1996.

q: What President of the United States was Awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1906, mainly for his contribution to ending the Russo-Japanese war?

q.e: Theodore Roosevelt mediated the 1905 Treaty of Portsmouth in New Hampshire to end the Russo-Japanese War, making him the first American to win a Nobel Peace Prize.

q: Mother Teresa, the honorary winner of the 1979 Nobel Peace Prize, was of what descent?

q.e: Mother Teresa was born in Skopje to an ethnic Albanian family and won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979.

q: What United States Secretary of State received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1973?

q.e: Henry Kissinger shared the 1973 Nobel Peace Prize with Le Duc Tho, who declined it.

q: Which Dalai Lama was awarded a Nobel Peace Prize in 1989 for his struggle for the liberation of Tibet?

q.e: Tenzin Gyatso, the 14th Dalai Lama, won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1989.

q: How many of the men who signed the Declaration of Independence would later become US Presidents?

q.e: Two signers became presidents: John Adams and Thomas Jefferson.

q: This river flows through/past both Zagreb and Belgrade (Beograd).

q.e: The Sava river flows through Zagreb and joins the Danube at Belgrade.

q: Which of these pairs of lakes lie entirely within Italy?

q.e: Lakes Como and Garda lie entirely in Italy, while Maggiore and Lugano are shared with Switzerland.

q: These rivers empty into the Baltic Sea basin. Which discharges the greatest amount of water?

q.e: The Neva, which flows out of Lake Ladoga, is the largest river by discharge flowing into the Baltic.

q: What single act announced the Black Panther Partys presence to the people of Oakland in February of 1967?
They followed the police with shotguns and law books
They had two members elected to congress
They opened offices in every major city in America

q.e: In 1967 Black Panthers patrolled Oakland carrying law books and guns to monitor police, legally in California at the time.

q: What was the Black Panthers response when California passed the Mulford Act, a bill designed to ban the display of loaded weapons in 1967.
They held an armed march in Sacramento
They changed their name and ceased to function
They held a sit-in at the Capital building

q.e: In May 1967 about 30 Black Panthers armed marched to the California state capitol in Sacramento to protest the Mulford Act.

q: Who were the first Black Panther Members to run for political office?
Huey P. Newton and David Hilliard
Huey P. Newton and Bobby Seale

q.e: Bobby Seale ran for Oakland mayor and Elaine Brown for city council in 1973, among the first Panthers to run.

q: Which of these nicknames was given to the city of Chicago, Illinois, USA?

q.e: "Hog Butcher for the World" is from Carl Sandburg's poem "Chicago" (1914).

q: What type of government does Saudi Arabia have?

q.e: Saudi Arabia is an absolute monarchy ruled by the House of Saud.

q: What is the capital and largest city of Saudi Arabia?

q.e: Riyadh, located in the central Najd region, has a population exceeding 7 million people and serves as the political center of Saudi Arabia. Jeddah is the commercial hub, while Mecca and Medina are the holiest cities in Islam.

q: What is the capital and largest city in the Kingdom of Cambodia?

q.e: Phnom Penh has been the national capital since the French colonial era in the late 19th century, located at the confluence of the Mekong, Tonle Sap, and Bassac rivers. Over 2 million of Cambodia's roughly 17 million residents live in the metropolitan area.

q: What is the predominant religion among the population of Cambodia?

q.e: Theravada Buddhism is Cambodia's state religion, followed by about 97% of the population.

q: What type of the traditional Cambodian outfit is the krama?

q.e: The krama is a traditional checkered scarf worn by Cambodians.

q: What part of her clothing does a maiko, or an apprentice gaisha, change when she becomes a geisha in a ceremony called erikae?

q.e: When a maiko becomes a geisha (erikae), she changes her collar from red to white.

q: What is the name of the elegant, high-culture world that geisha are a part of in Japan?

q.e: Geisha live in the "karyūkai," the "flower and willow world."

q: What is the real name of Sayuki, the first Caucasian geisha in history, who was born in Melbourne, Australia?

q.e: Fiona Graham (Sayuki), born in Australia, became the first Western-born geisha in 2007.

q: Why were geisha trained to sleep with their necks on small supports called takamakura instead of on pillows?
Not to get wrinkles on their skin
To learn to keep balance even in their sleep

q.e: Takamakura, small pillow supports, kept elaborate hairstyles from being ruined.

q: It was traditional in the past for established geisha to have a danna. What does a danna mean?
A special and very expensive Japanese fan
A beautiful bird in a cage
A large chest to store her kimonos ans makeup

q.e: A danna is a geisha's wealthy patron, who funds her expenses.

q: The Latin motto of the US state of Kansas is Ad astra per aspera. What does this mean in English?
To the stars as we dream

q.e: "Ad astra per aspera" means "to the stars through difficulties."

q: What is the name of the capital city of the US state of Kansas?

q.e: Topeka became the capital of Kansas when the state was admitted to the Union in 1861. Wichita is Kansas's largest city by population, while Lincoln and Denver are the capitals of Nebraska and Colorado.

q: What is the state mammal of the US state of Kansas?

q.e: The American bison (buffalo) is Kansas's state animal.

q: What is the official state flower and symbol of the US state of Kansas?

q.e: Kansas officially designated the wild sunflower (Helianthus annuus) as its state floral emblem in 1903, earning Kansas the nickname 'The Sunflower State'.

q: According to 2007 estimates 99.66% of the population of Mozambique is of what ethnic group?

q.e: Mozambique's population is almost all African, including Makua, Tsonga and Sena groups, who are Bantu-speaking.

q: What is the capital city of Mozambique?

q.e: Maputo, situated on a large natural bay in southern Mozambique, was known as Lourenco Marques before the country gained independence from Portugal in 1975. Matola is an adjacent industrial center, while Beira and Nampula are other major Mozambican cities.

q: According to the World Health Organization, life expectancy in the United States is 67 years for males, 71 years for females. What is the life expectancy in Mozambique according to 2007 estimates?

q.e: Mozambique's life expectancy was low in 2007 (about 40–42), but is around 60 now.

q: What is the state flower of the U.S. state of Georgia?

q.e: The Cherokee rose is Georgia's state flower, adopted in 1916.

q: What is the official motto of the U.S. state of Georgia?

q.e: Georgia's motto is "Wisdom, Justice and Moderation."

q: What is the capital of Uganda?

q.e: Kampala was designated the capital of Uganda when the country gained independence in 1962. Kigali is the capital of Rwanda, Kinshasa is in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Khartoum is in Sudan.

q: Maseru is the capital of which African country?

q.e: Maseru is the capital of Lesotho.

q: What is the capital of the island African country Cape Verde?

q.e: Praia, on Santiago island, is the capital of Cape Verde.

q: Name the capital of DRC (Democratic Republic of Congo)?

q.e: Kinshasa is the capital and largest city of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It sits directly across the Congo River from Brazzaville, the capital of the Republic of the Congo.

q: Lusaka is the capital of which African country?

q.e: Lusaka was chosen to replace Livingstone as the capital of Northern Rhodesia in 1935 and remained the capital when the nation gained independence as Zambia in 1964.

q: The Sun of May is one of the national symbols of Argentina and what other South American country?

q.e: The Sun of May (Sol de Mayo) appears on both the Argentine and the Uruguayan flags.

q: During the War of the Triple Alliance the allied countries of Argentina, Brazil, and Uruguay fought against what country?

q.e: The War of the Triple Alliance (1864–70) saw Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay defeat Paraguay.

q: What is the capital city of Sudan?

q.e: Khartoum sits at the confluence of the White Nile and the Blue Nile. While neighboring Omdurman is Sudan's largest individual city by population, Khartoum serves as the political capital.

q: What kind of object is the jalabiya, which is an inseparable part of Sudanese culture?

q.e: The jalabiya (or jellabiya) is a long loose garment worn by men in Sudan and Egypt.

q: The Holy Mountain, which is located in Greece, is also known by this name.

q.e: Mount Athos is the Holy Mountain, a monastic republic in northern Greece.

q: In the 7th century, after the Islamic conquest of this territory many orthodox monks went to the Holy Mountain in Greece in an attempt to find another calm place.

q.e: Orthodox monks from Egypt, among others, sought refuge at Mount Athos after the Arab conquests.

q: Where does the name of Ecuador come from?

q.e: Ecuador is the Spanish word for equator, named because the Earth's equator passes directly through the country just north of its capital city, Quito.

q: What is the official language in Ecuador?

q.e: Spanish is Ecuador's official language. Quechua and Shuar are official in intercultural relations.

q: What is the capital city of the Socialist Republic of Vietnam?

q.e: Hanoi has served as the capital of unified Vietnam since 1976. Ho Chi Minh City, formerly Saigon, is the country's most populous metropolis and primary financial hub.

q: What type of animal is the Saola, an extremely rare species living only in Vietnam and Laos?

q.e: The saola, found in 1992 in the Annamite Mountains, is a rare bovine called the "Asian unicorn."

q: What is the largest religious group in Vietnam according to official data?

q.e: Buddhism is the largest religion in Vietnam, though many Vietnamese say they have no religion.

q: What part of traditional Vietnamese culture is the ao dai?

q.e: The ao dai is Vietnam's traditional long tunic worn over trousers.

q: Name the national anthem of Jamaica, written by Hugh Sherlock, composed by Robert Lightbourne and arranged by Mapletoft Poulle.

q.e: "Jamaica, Land We Love" is Jamaica's national anthem, adopted at independence in 1962.

q: This Jamaican athlete is a multiple Olympic medallist and the second woman in history to win two consecutive 200 m events at the Olympics.

q.e: Veronica Campbell-Brown won the 200 m at the 2004 and 2008 Olympics.

q: What kind of images of calligraphy will be appropriate as a decoration for a Japanese tea ceremony that is held at night?

q.e: Night tea ceremonies feature moon and rabbit imagery in Japanese tradition. Check sources.

q: What city houses the oldest university in Germany?

q.e: Heidelberg University, founded in 1386, is Germany's oldest.

q: What is the predominant religion among the population of Sri Lanka?

q.e: Theravada Buddhism is Sri Lanka's main religion, followed by about 70%.

q: Which of these statements is true about the Sri Lankan Elephant?
It is the largest subspecies of the Asian Elephant.
It is the largest elephant species on the planet.
It is the smallest elephant species on the planet.
It is the smallest subspecies of the Asian Elephant.

q.e: The Sri Lankan elephant is the largest of the three Asian elephant subspecies.

q: Belo Horizonte is the capital of which state of Brazil?

q.e: Belo Horizonte is the capital of Minas Gerais, Brazil.

q: Olinda is a historic city in which Brazilian state?

q.e: Olinda, a UNESCO site, is in Pernambuco, Brazil.

q: What city was the first colonial capital of Brazil?

q.e: Salvador da Bahia was Brazil's first colonial capital (1549–1763), before Rio.

q: What fictional character, described as valiant, found herself in a snowy wood at night- time with snow under her feet and snowflakes falling through the air?
Lucy in The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe

q.e: Lucy Pevensie finds the snowy wood beyond the wardrobe in C. S. Lewis's "The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe."

q: What poet, honored with four Pulitzer Prizes for Poetry, wrote the 1922 poem Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening?

q.e: Robert Frost published the poem in 1923 in his collection New Hampshire, concluding with the iconic line 'And miles to go before I sleep.'

q: In what fantasy novel do armored white bears live in the ice-and-snow-locked land Svalbard?
The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe

q.e: Armoured bears (panserbjørne) of Svalbard are in Philip Pullman's "Northern Lights" (The Golden Compass).

q: What rare findings have been made in the Hell Creek Formation in the U.S. state of Montana?

q.e: The Hell Creek Formation yields Tyrannosaurus, Triceratops and other dinosaur fossils.

q: What is the state animal of the U.S. state of Montana?

q.e: The grizzly bear is Montana's state animal.

q: What is the capital city of the U.S. state of Montana?

q.e: Helena was founded during the 1864 Montana gold rush along Last Chance Gulch and became the state capital when Montana was admitted to the Union in 1889. Billings is the state's most populous city.

q: What is the largest religious group on the island of Bali?

q.e: Balinese Hinduism is the main religion in Bali, while Indonesia is mostly Muslim.

q: When did the Arab Emirates gain independence from the UK?

q.e: The United Arab Emirates became independent from Britain on 2 December 1971.

q: What is the capital city of Algeria?

q.e: Algiers, nicknamed 'Algiers the White' due to its gleaming whitewashed buildings, overlooks a bay on the Mediterranean Sea. Bamako is the capital of Mali, Niamey is the capital of Niger, and Tripoli is the capital of Libya.

q: The title of the national anthem of Algeria is Kassaman or Qassaman. What does this mean in Arabic?

q.e: "Kassaman" means "We Pledge" in Arabic, the Algerian anthem.

q: Which of these African countries shares a border with Algeria?

q.e: Algeria borders Morocco, Niger, Mali, Mauritania, Libya, Tunisia and Western Sahara.

q: What is the largest city in the Republic of Colombia?

q.e: Bogota is Colombia's capital and biggest city, home to roughly 8 million residents in its urban area. Medellin is the country's second-largest city, with about 2.5 million residents.

q: What is the religion of the vast majority of the population of the Republic of Colombia?

q.e: Roman Catholicism is the main religion of Colombia, followed by around 80% of people.

q: What international pop star was born in Barranquilla, Colombia?

q.e: Shakira was born and raised in Barranquilla, Colombia, and has often referenced her coastal hometown in hits like Hips Don't Lie. Ricky Martin, by contrast, was born in San Juan, Puerto Rico.

q: What type of governmental control has been established in Malaysia?

q.e: Malaysia is a constitutional monarchy with an elected king (Yang di-Pertuan Agong) rotating among nine sultans.

q: What is the official language in Malaysia?

q.e: Malay (Bahasa Malaysia) is Malaysia's official language.

q: What popular Spanish resort city is the birth place of Pablo Picasso?

q.e: Pablo Picasso was born in Malaga in the Andalusia region in 1881, though he spent much of his youth studying art in Barcelona before settling in France.

q: The Torre del Oro is a site located in the Spanish port of Seville. What does the name torre del orro literally mean?

q.e: The Torre del Oro in Seville means "Tower of Gold."

q: What was the former name of Tokyo?

q.e: Tokyo was originally a small fishing village named Edo before becoming the seat of the Tokugawa shogunate in 1603. It was renamed Tokyo, meaning eastern capital, in 1868 when the imperial capital moved from Kyoto.

q: Situated very near Tokyo, this is the second largest city of Japan.

q.e: Yokohama, next to Tokyo, is Japan's second-largest city by population.

q: In what year were the Olympic Games held in Tokyo?

q.e: Tokyo hosted the Summer Olympic Games in October 1964, marking the first time the Games were held in Asia. Tokyo later hosted a second time in 2021 (delayed from 2020).

q: If you drew a line directly east from Tokyo, across the Pacific and through the United States you would pass very near this US city.

q.e: Tokyo and Raleigh, North Carolina, are at about 35.7° N latitude.

q: Which of these is NOT located in Tokyo?
the headquarters of the Sumo Wrestling Association
the Ginza shopping and entertainment district

q.e: Narita Airport is in Chiba Prefecture, not Tokyo. Haneda is in Tokyo.

q: What is the name of the capital and largest city of Venezuela?

q.e: Caracas has served as the capital of Venezuela since the country declared independence in 1811. Bogota and Lima are the capitals of Colombia and Peru, while Port of Spain is the capital of Trinidad and Tobago.

q: The melody of the national anthem of Venezuela, Gloria al Bravo Pueblo, is said to bear some resemblance to the melody of the national anthem of this European country.

q.e: "Gloria al Bravo Pueblo" has been compared to other anthems. Check sources for the claimed resemblance.

q: What is the national flower of Venezuela?

q.e: The orchid (Cattleya mossiae, the "Flor de Mayo") is Venezuela's national flower.

q: What is the state animal of the U.S. state of Maine?

q.e: The moose is Maine's state animal.

q: What is the nickname of the University of Arkansas at Monticello?

q.e: The University of Arkansas at Monticello teams are the Boll Weevils.

q: What conference does the University of Central Arkansas play in?

q.e: UCA played in the Southland Conference until 2021, then joined the ASUN.

q: Northwest Arkansas Community College is located in what northwest Arkansas city?

q.e: NorthWest Arkansas Community College is in Bentonville.

q: The first European settlers arrived in Phuket in the 16th century. What nationality were they?

q.e: Portuguese, French and Dutch traders reached Phuket in the 16th–17th centuries. Check the bank answer.

q: What small country is located entirely within the territory of the Republic of South Africa?

q.e: Lesotho is entirely surrounded by South Africa.

q: What is the largest city in the Republic of South Africa?

q.e: Johannesburg is home to nearly 5 million people in its municipal area and over 10 million in the wider urban agglomeration. Cape Town is South Africa's legislative capital and second-largest city, while Pretoria serves as the executive capital.

q: Which of these endangered rabbit species is not endemic to South Africa?

q.e: Several endangered hare/rabbit species live in South Africa, such as the riverine rabbit; scrub hare isn't endangered.

q: The adherents of what religion form the largest group in the Republic of South Africa according to the 2001 census?

q.e: In the 2001 census, Zion Christian churches were the largest group in South Africa.

q: What airport was originally known as Idlewild Airport?

q.e: The airport opened in 1948 as New York International Airport, commonly referred to as Idlewild. It was renamed John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) in December 1963, roughly a month after President Kennedy's assassination.

q: What airport was formerly a military installation known as Dow Air Force Base?

q.e: Bangor International Airport in Maine occupies the former Dow Air Force Base.

q: What is the capital and largest city of the Republic of Peru?

q.e: Lima was founded in 1535 by Spanish conquistador Francisco Pizarro as Ciudad de los Reyes ('City of the Kings'). Home to about a third of Peru's population, it is far larger than the secondary city of Arequipa.

q: Which of these statements is true about the demographics of Peru according to the 2007 census?
It is the fourth most populous country in South America.
It is the second most populous country in South America.
It is the seventh most populous country in the world.
It is the most populous country in South America.

q.e: Peru is the fourth most populous country in South America, after Brazil, Colombia and Argentina.

q: What religion has the largest number of followers in Peru according to the 2007 census?

q.e: Roman Catholicism is the largest religion in Peru.

q: Un peuple, un but, une foi, or One people, one goal, one faith, is the national motto of this African country.

q.e: "Un peuple, un but, une foi" is Mali's motto.

q: Тhe slogan The love of liberty brought us here is the national motto of what African country?

q.e: "The love of liberty brought us here" is Liberia's motto.

q: The Latin phrase Quo Fata Ferunt, or Whither the Fates Carry Us, is the national motto of this country.

q.e: "Quo fata ferunt" is Bermuda's motto, a British Overseas Territory, not a country.

q: The national motto of what South American country is One people, one nation, one destiny?

q.e: Guyana's motto is "One people, one nation, one destiny."

q: The national motto of what European country is The strength of the nation lies in unity?

q.e: Lithuania's motto "Vienybė težydi" means "May unity flourish."

q: What is the name of the capital and largest city of Iraq?

q.e: Baghdad was founded in 762 CE by the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur along the Tigris River and grew into one of the largest and most influential cultural centers of the Islamic Golden Age.

q: What language was adopted as official by the government of Iraq?

q.e: Iraq's official languages are Arabic and Kurdish.

q: When did Singapore become a British crown colony?

q.e: Singapore became a British crown colony in 1867, having been under the East India Company.

q: By 1900, Singapore had a population of nearly how many residents?

q.e: Singapore's population in 1901 was about 228,000.

q: What is the name of the capital and largest city of Taiwan?

q.e: Taipei is situated in northern Taiwan and serves as the seat of the Republic of China (Taiwan) government. While New Taipei City has more residents within its vast borders, Taipei forms the historical and core economic center.

q: What is the official language recognized by the government of Taiwan?

q.e: Mandarin Chinese is Taiwan's official language.

q: What religion has the largest number of followers among the population of Taiwan?

q.e: Buddhism and Taoism are the main religions in Taiwan.

q: Grass jelly is a popular desert in Taiwan and other countries in Southeast Asia. What is it made from?

q.e: Grass jelly is made from Mesona chinensis, a mint-family herb.

q: What type of governmental control has Morocco established?

q.e: Morocco is a constitutional monarchy led by a king.

q: What is the title of the national anthem of Morocco?

q.e: "Hymne Chérifien" (Hymn of the Sharif) is Morocco's anthem.

q: Name the only two African countries that share borders with Morocco.

q.e: Morocco borders Algeria, Mauritania (via Western Sahara) and Spain. Check the claimed borders.

q: Ibizas name dates back to 654 BC when Phoenician settlers founded a port called Ibossim. What is the meaning of this name?
It is a dedication to a god of music and dance
It is a dedication to a god of the fire

q.e: Ibiza derives from the Phoenician "Ibossim," meaning "island of Bes," the god of music and dance.

q: Which of these famous American actresses was born in the U.S. state of Virginia?

q.e: Sandra Bullock was born in Arlington, Virginia, in 1964.

q: What is the state mammal of the U.S. state of Arizona?

q.e: The ringtail is Arizona's state mammal.

q: Which of these celebrities was not born in the U.S. state of Arizona?

q.e: Steven Spielberg was born in Cincinnati, Ohio, though he grew up in Arizona.

q: What is the state gemstone of the U.S. state of Arizona?

q.e: Turquoise is Arizona's state gemstone.

q: What Hollywood actor starred in the 1993 movie Arizona Dream, filmed in Douglas, Arizona?

q.e: Johnny Depp starred in Emir Kusturica's Arizona Dream (1993).

q: What is the capital of the Dominican Republic?

q.e: Founded by Bartholomew Columbus in 1496, Santo Domingo is the oldest continuously inhabited European-established settlement in the Americas. San Juan is the capital of Puerto Rico.

q: What year did the Dominican Republic declare independence from Haiti?

q.e: The Dominican Republic declared independence from Haiti on 27 February 1844.

q: How does the dog get the pigeons off the antenna at Lake Minnewahwahs mountain in the game Dogs Life?
He gets a bird feeder to get them down.
He barks at them until they fly away.
He leaves them on and lets someone else do it.
He pees on the antenna to electrocute them.

q.e: This is a video game detail. Check the game guide.

q: In 1996 a movie called Independence Day (starring Will Smith) was released. What was it about?
Attempted alien takeover of the Earth
The act of signing the Declaration of Independence
Launching an expensive space shuttle, called July 4th

q.e: Independence Day (1996) is about an alien invasion of Earth.

q: Which of the following pairs is wrong? It is the representative who took part in writing the draft of the declaration and their state.

q.e: Roger Sherman represented Connecticut, not New York.

q: One of the most spectacular ways to celebrate July 4th is through colorful fireworks. Which of these types of fireworks is prohibited?

q.e: Cherry bombs are illegal federally (as M-80s).

q: It is generally considered that Santa Claus was a real person who lived in Myra in about 400 AD. In which present-day country is this place located?

q.e: Saint Nicholas served as Bishop of Myra in Lycia during the 4th century, an ancient city located in the Antalya Province of modern-day Turkey.

q: The story of Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer, that guides Santas sleigh, was written in what year?

q.e: "Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer" was written in 1939 by Robert L. May.

q: The 27th Amendment, which deals with congressional pay raises, was adopted in this year.

q.e: The 27th Amendment, ratified 1992, says Congress's pay raises take effect only after the next election. It was proposed in 1789.

q: Up to the beginning of the 20th century, this number of Amendments were ratified.

q.e: By 1900, 15 amendments had been ratified.

q: What year did congress approve the Declaration of Independence, making the 13 colonies a land of a sovereign nation?

q.e: The Continental Congress approved the Declaration on 4 July 1776.

q: One year after the Declaration was approved, the citizens of this city commemorated the event by setting off fireworks, ringing bells and firing their guns.

q.e: On 4 July 1777, Philadelphia held the first Independence Day celebration with bells, bonfires and fireworks.

q: How many towns in the USA have liberty in their names?

q.e: About 30 US places have "Liberty" in their name, by this question's count.

q: This prominent symbol associated with early American history and the battle for American independence summoned citizens for the reading of the Declaration of Independence on July 8, 1976.

q.e: The Liberty Bell was rung on 8 July 1776 for the first public reading of the Declaration.

q: In order to make the Declaration official, this President of the Continental Congress had to sign it.

q.e: As President of the Second Continental Congress, John Hancock was the first to sign the Declaration of Independence on August 2, 1776. His prominent signature in the center became so iconic that 'John Hancock' became an American idiom for an autograph.

q: He was the longest-serving Commandant of the Marine Corps, often referred to as the grand old man of the Marine Corps.

q.e: Archibald Henderson was the Marine Corps Commandant for 39 years (1820–1859), "the Grand Old Man of the Marine Corps."

q: These are the most elite Special Operation Forces of the US navy. They have fought in major conflicts, including Operation Enduring Freedom - the military response to the terrorist attacks on September 11, 2001.

q.e: United States Navy SEALs (Sea, Air, and Land) trace their roots to World War II underwater demolition units and were officially established by President John F. Kennedy in 1962.

q: This Special Operation Force of the US Army is officially referred to as the Combat Application Group. It was featured in Ridley Scot's movie, 'Black Hawk Down'.

q.e: Delta Force (1st SFOD-D, once known as Combat Applications Group) is portrayed in "Black Hawk Down."

q: This specialized paramilitary police unit in the USA, created in the city of Delano, California, in the 1960s, is often called upon for dangerous operations.

q.e: SWAT began in the 1960s with units in Delano and LAPD, which Daryl Gates formed in 1967.

q: This unit, formed in 1941, is part of the UK special forces. Its badge depicts a sword with an inscription: 'Who dares wins'.

q.e: The SAS, formed 1941 by David Stirling, has the motto "Who Dares Wins."

q: The Foreign Legion, founded in 1831, is an elite rapid deployment force which consists mainly of foreign volunteers. It is a military formation within the army of which country?

q.e: King Louis Philippe founded the French Foreign Legion (Légion étrangère) on March 10, 1831, to enlist foreign nationals into French military service while barring them from serving on mainland France during peacetime.

q: GEK Cobra, founded in 1972 to protect Jewish immigrants from Palestinian terrorists, is the counter-terrorist unit of this country.

q.e: Austria's GEK Cobra (EKO Cobra) was formed in 1978 after the Munich attacks.

q: The counter-terrorism unit, GSG-9, established on April 17, 1973 and considered to be among the best of such units in the world, is part of the federal police of which country?

q.e: GSG 9 is Germany's federal police counter-terrorist unit, formed after the 1972 Munich massacre.

q: In 2001, RB singer and actress Aaliyah was killed in a plane crash right after take-off in which part of the world?

q.e: Aaliyah died on 25 August 2001 when her plane crashed after takeoff in the Bahamas.

q: The mother of which popular American singer was killed in a plane crash in California on January 6, 1977?

q.e: Frank Sinatra's mother, Dolly, died in a plane crash in 1977 near Palm Springs.

q: How old was singer Otis Redding when he was killed in a plane crash into Lake Monona, Wisconsin, in 1967?

q.e: Otis Redding died at 26 on 10 December 1967 in a crash into Lake Monona, Madison, Wisconsin.

q: When did monarchs sit on the Stone of Scone in Scotland?

q.e: Scottish and later British monarchs sit on the Stone of Scone during the coronation chair ceremony.

q: The Scottish island Fair Isle is famous for what?

q.e: Fair Isle is famous for its multicolored, patterned knitting.
Berwick cockles are sweets, striped mint-flavored candies from Berwick-upon-Tweed.

q: Who was on the cover of the first issue of Rolling Stone magazine?

q.e: John Lennon was on the cover of Rolling Stone's first issue in November 1967.

q: Cupid, one of the major symbols in St. Valentines Day celebrations, is a mythological character, son of which goddess?

q.e: In Roman mythology, Cupid (meaning 'desire') is the son of Venus, the goddess of love, and Mars, the god of war. His Greek counterpart is Eros, son of Aphrodite.

q: In what song did Prince advise Baby Ure much 2 fast; U got to slow down.?

q.e: Prince sang "Life is just a bowl of fruit... Slow down" in "Little Red Corvette" (1983).

q: Everybody says that there is nobody meaner than this little old grandma from Pasadena. Shes the terror of Colorado Boulevard. What slick machine is hidden in her rickey old garage?

q.e: The Beach Boys-linked "Little Old Lady from Pasadena" (1964, Jan & Dean) drives a Super Stock Dodge.

q: This college hosts the Institute for Advanced Study, one of the worlds leading centers for theoretical research and intellectual inquiry.

q.e: The Institute for Advanced Study is in Princeton, New Jersey, but isn't part of the university.

q: Which of these institutions has the lowest reported level of alcohol drinking on campus ?

q.e: BYU, run by the LDS Church, has strict alcohol bans.

q: Elizabeth Swallow was the first woman professional chemist in America. From what school did she get her B.S. degree?

q.e: Ellen Swallow Richards was the first woman to graduate from MIT (1873) and America's first female professional chemist.

q: Which first class passenger on the Titanic was a famous dress designer known as Lucile?

q.e: Lucy, Lady Duff Gordon, a fashion designer known as Lucile, survived the Titanic.

q: Which of the Titanics officers is rumored to have killed himself?

q.e: Rumor says First Officer William Murdoch killed himself, though witnesses disagree.

q: What was the funnel color of the White Star shipping company?

q.e: White Star Line funnels were buff (yellow) with black tops.

q: What was the relationship between Thomas Andrews, Titanics chief designer and Lord Pirrie, chairman of Harland and Wolff, the shipyard that built Titanic?

q.e: Thomas Andrews was the nephew of Lord Pirrie of Harland & Wolff.

q: Pakistans flag has a star and what other symbol?

q.e: Pakistan's national flag, adopted in 1947, features a white crescent moon and a five-pointed star on a dark green field. The crescent represents progress, while the five-pointed star symbolizes light and knowledge.

q: What year was the GTO first offered as an option package for a Pontiac vehicle?

q.e: Pontiac made the GTO an option on the LeMans in 1964, starting the muscle car era.

q: It is common lore that the Jack olantern originated from the tale of a drunkard known as Stingy Jack or Jack the Smith. Who did Jack manage to trap?

q.e: In the Irish folktale, Stingy Jack tricked the Devil and was left carrying a carved turnip lantern.

q: Who was the last leader of the Soviet Union?

q.e: Mikhail Gorbachev was the last leader of the Soviet Union (1985–91).
Helmut Kohl served as Chancellor of West Germany from 1982 to 1990 and then led reunited Germany until 1998, earning the moniker the Chancellor of Unity.

q: Which former Soviet Republic was first to declare independence from the USSR?

q.e: Lithuania declared independence on 11 March 1990.

q: All revolutions of the 1989 Autumn of Nations in Europe were rather peaceful. Which country was the only one to overthrow their communist regime violently?

q.e: Romania's 1989 revolution toppled Ceaușescu violently. Others were largely peaceful.

q: After 1989, with the dissolution of the Soviet Union, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia, many new countries appeared on the map of Europe. Which is not one of them?

q.e: Hungary was independent before 1989; Slovakia, Czechia, Slovenia, Croatia and others emerged afterwards.

q: What is the meaning of the Latin word 'pelegrinus' from which the word 'pilgrim' originates?

q.e: "Peregrinus" meant "foreigner" or "traveler" in Latin, which became "pilgrim".

q: Benjamin Franklin considered the turkey a much more respectable bird than the Bald Eagle. He expressed his disapproval with the choice of the Bald Eagle as the national emblem in a letter to whom?
the editor of the Albany Gazette

q.e: Franklin wrote to his daughter Sarah Bache in 1784 about the turkey and the bald eagle.

q: What Academy Award and Grammy Award-winning song expresses the Native American belief that the earth is a living entity and people are connected to everything in nature?

q.e: Colors of the Wind, written by Alan Menken and lyricist Stephen Schwartz for Disney's 1995 film Pocahontas, won both the Oscar for Best Original Song and the Grammy for Best Song Written for a Motion Picture.

q: This Native American group often built homes that were 100 feet in length.

q.e: The Iroquois (Haudenosaunee) built bark longhouses, sometimes 100 feet long or more.

q: Which of these groups is the most populous in the USA?

q.e: The Navajo have the largest reservation, while Cherokee have the most enrolled members.

q: According to the 2003 US Census Bureau statistics, about how many Americans classify themselves as Native Americans?

q.e: The census counted about 2.8 million people identifying as American Indian or Alaska Native alone in 2003.

q: Who was the college football and track coach of Native American Jim Thorpe, one of the great athletes in world history?

q.e: Glenn "Pop" Warner coached Jim Thorpe at Carlisle Indian Industrial School.

q: How are nouns classified in Native American languages?

q.e: Many Native American languages classify nouns as animate or inanimate.

q: Which Article deals with Ratification of the U.S. Constitution?

q.e: Article VII of the Constitution sets the ratification procedure, which needed nine states.

q: Which section of the Legislative Branch gives U.S. Congress its powers?

q.e: Article I, Section 8 lists Congress's powers.

q: Which Amendment to the U.S. Constitution was ratified in 1992?

q.e: The 27th Amendment was ratified in 1992.

q: These two Oxford students were members of Monty Python.

q.e: Michael Palin and Terry Jones attended Oxford. Cleese, Chapman and Idle attended Cambridge.

q: This Oxford graduate wrote Lord of the Flies.

q.e: William Golding, an Oxford graduate, wrote "Lord of the Flies" (1954).

q: This Oxford graduate wrote The Leviathan, a classic work on legitimate government and society.

q.e: Thomas Hobbes studied at Oxford and wrote "Leviathan" (1651).

q: This neurologist was an Oxford grad who became famous for his athletic ability.

q.e: Roger Bannister, an Oxford-trained neurologist, ran the first sub-four-minute mile in 1954.

q: This Oxford scholar was a master of satire. He wrote A Modest Proposal, and An Argument Against Abolishing Christianity.

q.e: Jonathan Swift attended Trinity College Dublin and wrote "A Modest Proposal" (1729).

q: This Romantic poet lived 1788-1824. Among his best works are Don Juan and When We Two Parted.

q.e: Lord Byron (1788–1824) wrote "Don Juan" and "When We Two Parted."

q: This great scientist was able to show the equivalence of electricity, magnetism and light via a set of equations that carry his name.

q.e: James Clerk Maxwell's equations unified electricity, magnetism and light.

q: This Oxford scholar is the author of a series of books about a teddy bear .

q.e: A. A. Milne wrote "Winnie-the-Pooh," named for his son's teddy bear.

q: This Oxford scholar and Indian Prime Minister was assassinated in 1984.

q.e: Indira Gandhi attended Somerville College, Oxford, and was assassinated on 31 October 1984.

q: He was a great British explorer, an orientalist, and, probably, the first non-Muslim to visit Mecca and Medina.

q.e: Sir Richard Francis Burton, explorer and orientalist, entered Mecca in disguise in 1853.

q: On June 5 in the year 70, the Romans first broke through the walls of Jerusalem. Who was their leader?

q.e: Titus led the Roman siege of Jerusalem in AD 70 and destroyed the Second Temple.

q: Denmark became a constitutional monarchy on June 5 in what year?

q.e: Denmark's constitution was signed on 5 June 1849, ending absolute monarchy.

q: The USA began a program of Army registration day for World War I, on June 5 in what year?

q.e: The US held WWI draft registration on 5 June 1917.

q: The first fax across the Atlantic to Europe was sent on June 5 in what year?

q.e: The first transatlantic fax picture was sent in 1924 by radio. (June 5 is the date the question gives.)

q: On June 5 during World War II, Rome was liberated from the Fascists. In what year did this happen?

q.e: Allied forces entered Rome on 4 June 1944, and it was liberated by 5 June.

q: The Unknown Rebel halted an entire column of Chinese tanks in Tiananmen Square on June 5 in what year?

q.e: On 5 June 1989, an unknown man stood in front of tanks near Tiananmen Square, the day after the crackdown.

q: On October 12th, 1998, this University of Wyoming student was robbed, tortured and left for dead by two attackers outside of Laramie, Wyoming.

q.e: Matthew Shepard was attacked on 6-7 October 1998 near Laramie, Wyoming. He died on 12 October.

q: What did children attending American public schools do for the first time on October 12, 1892?
were released from classes by the ringing of a bell

q.e: The Pledge of Allegiance was first recited in schools on 12 October 1892, during Columbus Day celebrations.

q: What are the two countries referenced in the title of the Two Plus Four Treaty, which resulted in the first expansion of NATO after the Cold War?
East Germany and Federal Republic of Germany

q.e: The Two Plus Four Treaty (1990) allowed German reunification, between East and West Germany and the four WWII Allies.

q: The International Security Assistance Force (10), that started on 20 December 2001, is a NATO-led mission for security and development in what country?

q.e: ISAF was the NATO-led security mission in Afghanistan from 2001 to 2014.

q: Operation Essential Harvest, meant to disarm ethnic Albanian groups, was carried out in what country?

q.e: NATO's Operation Essential Harvest (2001) disarmed ethnic Albanian rebels in Macedonia.

q: What sounded the death knell for radio news on commercial radio stations?

q.e: In 1981 the FCC loosened rules for radio, ending requirements for news and public affairs programming. It was a deregulation decision, not an act.

q: What is the only country in the world whose national flag is not rectangular?

q.e: Nepal is the only sovereign country with a non-quadrilateral flag; its distinctive design consists of two stacked pennants symbolizing the Himalayas and the nation's two major religions.

q: What country has a crown depicted in the upper left corner of its flag?

q.e: Liechtenstein's flag has a gold crown in the upper-left of the blue field, added in 1937 after the Haiti flag clash at the Olympics.

q: What is the only country in the world whose flag features a building?

q.e: Cambodia's flag shows Angkor Wat, the only national flag with a building.

q: What is the name of the state capital of the Australian state of Tasmania?

q.e: Hobart, founded in 1804 as a penal colony on the Derwent River, is the state capital of Tasmania and Australia's second-oldest capital city after Sydney.

q: What animal became one of the symbols of the island and state of Tasmania?

q.e: The carnivorous marsupial became the official animal emblem of the Australian state of Tasmania in 2015, although it had served as a popular local symbol and badge insignia for decades.

q: The title of the national anthem of India is Jana Gana Mana. What does this mean?
Thou Art the Ruler of the Minds of All People
Thou Shall Listen to the Voice of the Prince

q.e: "Jana Gana Mana" is India's anthem. It means "Thou art the ruler of the minds of all people," written by Rabindranath Tagore.

q: Oh, Bright Dawn of May is the national anthem of this European country.

q.e: "Oj, svijetla majska zoro" ("Oh, Bright Dawn of May") is Montenegro's anthem, adopted in 2004.

q: My Fatherland, My Happiness and Joy is the title of the national anthem of this country.

q.e: "Mu isamaa, mu õnn ja rõõm" ("My Fatherland, My Happiness and Joy") is Estonia's anthem. Its tune is also Finland's.

q: God Is Great is the title of the national anthem of this African country.

q.e: Libya's anthem has changed. "Allahu Akbar" was a Gaddafi-era anthem, and "Libya, Libya, Libya" was reinstated in 2011.

q: What animal nickname was given to the U.S. state of Wisconsin?

q.e: Wisconsin is known as the Badger State not because of the animal, but because of 1820s lead miners who dug hillside shelters like badgers during harsh winters.

q: What is the capital of Brazil?

q.e: Brasília was inaugurated in 1960 as a planned city developed by Lúcio Costa and Oscar Niemeyer to shift the seat of government inland from Rio de Janeiro. São Paulo remains Brazil's most populous metropolis.

q: Mount Everest sits on the border of Nepal and which country?

q.e: The international border between Nepal and China's Tibet Autonomous Region runs directly across Mount Everest's summit point at 8,848.86 meters (29,031.7 ft).

q: Which country has the most natural lakes?

q.e: Canada is estimated to have over 879,000 lakes, which is more than half of all natural lakes on Earth. Finland is nicknamed the Land of a Thousand Lakes, but it only has about 188,000.

q: Which country has the largest population?

q.e: In 2023, United Nations demographic estimates showed India surpassing China to become the world's most populous nation, with each country home to more than 1.4 billion people.

q: What is the capital city of New Zealand?

q.e: Wellington replaced Auckland as New Zealand's capital in 1865 due to its central location on Cook Strait. It holds the title of the southernmost capital city of a sovereign state in the world.

q: What is the largest city and commercial capital of Sri Lanka?

q.e: Colombo is Sri Lanka's largest city and commercial capital. The legislative capital is Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte.

q: How many countries share a land border with Russia? (Not including disputed territories)

q.e: Russia borders 14 countries: Norway, Finland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Belarus, Ukraine, Georgia, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, China, Mongolia and North Korea.

q: Bir Tawil, an uninhabited track of land claimed by no country, is located along the border of which two countries?

q.e: Bir Tawil, a 2,060 km² patch between Egypt and Sudan, is terra nullius because each country claims the other's Hala'ib triangle instead.

q: What is the capital city of Bermuda?

q.e: Hamilton replaced the town of St. George as the capital of the British Overseas Territory of Bermuda in 1815. Havana is the capital of Cuba, San Juan is the capital of Puerto Rico, and Santo Domingo is the capital of the Dominican Republic.

q: What is the county seat of King County, Washington?

q.e: Seattle is the seat of King County, Washington.

q: How many islands does Kuwait have?

q.e: Kuwait has nine islands, including Failaka and Bubiyan, the largest.

q: Which of the following landlocked countries is entirely contained within another country?

q.e: The Kingdom of Lesotho is an enclave completely surrounded by South Africa, making it one of only three fully sovereign enclaves in the world alongside San Marino and Vatican City (both encircled by Italy).

q: Which is the largest freshwater lake in the world?

q.e: Lake Superior is the world's largest freshwater lake by surface area, covering approximately 31,700 square miles (82,100 square km). Lake Baikal in Russia holds the largest volume of freshwater, while the Caspian Sea is saline.

q: What is the official German name of the Swiss Federal Railways?

q.e: The Swiss Federal Railways is "Schweizerische Bundesbahnen" (SBB) in German, CFF in French, FFS in Italian.

q: What city is known as the Rose Capital of the World?

q.e: Tyler, Texas, is the "Rose Capital of the World," with a huge rose garden and festival.

q: The Andaman and Nicobar Islands in South East Asia are controlled by which country?

q.e: The Andaman and Nicobar Islands are an Indian union territory in the Bay of Bengal.

q: What was the original name of Ho Chi Minh City?

q.e: The city was officially renamed Ho Chi Minh City in 1976 after North Vietnam's revolutionary leader, though the historic name Saigon is still widely used today.

q: Bremen is the smallest state by area and population in which country?

q.e: Bremen is Germany's smallest state by area. Its population is also smaller than Saarland's.

q: Muscle Shoals is in which U.S. state?

q.e: Muscle Shoals, Alabama, is known for its recording studios, FAME and Muscle Shoals Sound.

q: Whilst appearing in the stage play, Cell Mates, in 1995 Stephen Fry suffered a nervous breakdown and disappeared for a number of days. In which country did he reappear in public?

q.e: Stephen Fry left the play "Cell Mates" in 1995 and fled to Belgium, where he was found.

q: I was born in 1956 on the island of Cuba and my family immigrated to the United States in 1961. Some of my co-stars on the big screen have been Meg Ryan, George Clooney and Ray Liotta. Who am I?

q.e: Andy García was born in Havana in 1956 and moved to the US in 1961. He co-starred with Meg Ryan, Clooney and Liotta.

q: In 1964, when this celebrity was just a 6-year-old boy, his famous father appeared on the cover of Time magazine because of his renown as a city planner.

q.e: Kevin Bacon's father, Edmund Bacon, a Philadelphia city planner, was on the cover of Time in 1964.

q: What job did Madonna hold, soon after her arrival in New York City?

q.e: Madonna worked at a Dunkin' Donuts in Times Square soon after arriving in New York in 1978.

q: On July 2nd 1986, Lindsay Morgan Lohan was born to Dina and Michael Lohan in New York City, New York. She was then raised in this town.

q.e: Lindsay Lohan was raised on Long Island, including in Cold Spring Harbor, New York.

q: This country, called Illyria by the Romans, is a republic located on the coast of the Adriatic Sea. Its capital is Tirana.

q.e: Albania was part of Illyria for the Romans, and Tirana is its capital.

q: This country was known to the Romans as Numidia. Today it is the second largest country in Africa. Its capital is Algiers.

q.e: Numidia was the Roman name of part of Algeria, now Africa's largest country by area.

q: This country and its capital have the same name. It is located between Spain and France in the Pyrenees Mountain Range.

q.e: Andorra's capital is Andorra la Vella, in the Pyrenees between Spain and France.

q: This country is located in the Caribbean Sea and has a capital named Saint Johns.

q.e: Antigua and Barbuda's capital is St. John's.

q: The capital of Mongolia is this city.

q.e: Ulaanbaatar is the capital of Mongolia, the coldest national capital in the world.

q: 3M Company was formed in 1902 in Two Harbors, Minnesota near Lake Superior with the intent of selling sandpaper. The company made $22.923 billion USD in 2006 and is famous for several inventions, including Scotch tape. What does 3M stand for?

q.e: 3M stands for Minnesota Mining and Manufacturing Company. It was founded in Two Harbors in 1902.

q: What is the largest mountain in the western hemisphere?

q.e: Aconcagua (6,961 m), in Argentina, is the highest peak in the Western and Southern hemispheres.

q: This country was formerly known as the Republic of Upper Volta. On August 4, 1984, President Thomas Sankara gave it a new name which means the land of upright people.

q.e: Burkina Faso's name combines Mooré and Dioula words meaning 'land of the upright people'. Thomas Sankara renamed the country on the first anniversary of his 1983 coup.

q: If I were to visit the wrist-wrestling capital of the world, where would I go?

q.e: Petaluma, California, hosts the World Wristwrestling Championships.

q: This Chinese city, the capital of Hubei province, lies at the confluence of the Yangtze River and Han River.

q.e: Wuhan, capital of Hubei, sits where the Han River meets the Yangtze.

q: The USA owns a territory in the Pacific called The Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands. What is its capital city?

q.e: Saipan is the largest island and administrative center of the Northern Mariana Islands, a US commonwealth.

q: This city state, also called Ragusa, was first to recognize the independence of the newly formed United States of America.

q.e: The Republic of Ragusa (Dubrovnik) is claimed to be one of the first states to recognize US independence in 1776.

q: The first Europeans to see this beautiful Caribbean island were on the boat of Alonzo Pinzon, who separated from Columbus to explore on his own, in 1492. It is the smallest of the Greater Antilles. What island is it ?

q.e: Puerto Rico is the smallest of the Greater Antilles. Columbus first visited it in 1493 on his second voyage.

q: He was first sail the length of the Amazon River and it was on this voyage that the Amazon got its name.

q.e: Francisco de Orellana sailed the length of the Amazon in 1541–42 and named it after warrior women he reported.

q: On August 20, 1968 five members of the Warsaw Pact invaded this country to quell the new reforms put in place by this countrys new leader. In what country did Alexander Dubcek try to bring freedom of the press and rights for workers?

q.e: On 20–21 August 1968 Warsaw Pact troops invaded Czechoslovakia to end Alexander Dubček's Prague Spring reforms.

q: Which of the following is an eponym meaning a traitor to his country?

q.e: The term quisling comes from Vidkun Quisling, a Norwegian army officer who headed a Nazi puppet government during World War II. In English, the word became an eponym for any traitor or collaborator.

q: We all know that New York, Los Angeles and Chicago are the three largest cities in the USA. What is the fourth largest city in the USA, as measured by metropolitan area (SMSA) according to 2006 US Census Bureau estimates?

q.e: In 2006, Dallas–Fort Worth was the fourth-largest US metro, after New York, Los Angeles and Chicago.

q: This city in the United States claims to house the largest ball of twine which was built by millionaire J. C. Payne.

q.e: J.C. Payne's ball of twine is in Branson, Missouri, but Darwin, Minnesota, and Cawker City, Kansas, also claim big balls.

q: Traditionally the people of the country of Georgia believe that they are descendants of this Biblical personality.

q.e: Georgian tradition traces their ancestry to Kartlos, great-grandson of Japheth, a son of Noah.

q: What do these places have in common: Wake Island, Johnston Atoll, Kingman Reef, Midway Island, Navassa, Baker Island and Jarvis Island?
They are a part of Nirvaau.
They are UN controlled islands in the Atlantic.
They are sites of famous WWII battles.

q.e: Wake, Johnston, Kingman, Midway, Navassa, Baker and Jarvis are US island territories with no permanent residents.

q: In every country in the world, except one, moving the head up and down means yes and moving the head side-to-side means no. In what one nation is that not the case?

q.e: Bulgarians shake their heads to say yes and nod for no.

q: According to modern geological theories, there was only one continent about 200 million years ago. What do geologists call it?

q.e: Pangaea, "all land," existed about 300-200 million years ago.

q: On the show Law and Order, Detective Lenny Briscoe was a New York City policeman for over 30 years. In that time, how many times did he shoot a person?

q.e: Detective Lennie Briscoe says he never fired his weapon at anybody on the job, according to the show. Check episodes for details.

q: Which country gained independence from the UK and France in 1980 and has a national anthem entitled Yumi, Yumi, Yumi?

q.e: Vanuatu's anthem is "Yumi, Yumi, Yumi" ("We, We, We") in Bislama. It became independent in 1980.

q: This Russian city, founded by Grand Duke George II of Russia in 1221, was called Gorky from 1932 to 1990.

q.e: Nizhny Novgorod was founded in 1221 and named Gorky (after Maxim Gorky) between 1932 and 1990.

q: What term refers to the horizontal line, 23.5 degrees S, which passes through South America, Africa, and Australia?

q.e: The Tropic of Capricorn sits at approximately 23.5 degrees south of the equator, marking the southernmost latitude where the sun can appear directly overhead at noon. The Tropic of Cancer is at 23.5 degrees north.

q: Which one of these ski resorts is not located in the Alps?

q.e: Mont-Tremblant is in the Laurentians of Quebec, Canada, not the Alps.

q: Which saltwater lake, bordered on the west by Azerbaijan and Russia, is the largest inland body of water in the world?

q.e: With a surface area of about 143,000 square miles (371,000 square kilometers), the Caspian Sea is the world's largest enclosed inland body of water. Lake Baikal is the deepest freshwater lake, not the largest.

q: Which body of water, situated in Southern Siberia, is the deepest and oldest freshwater lake on Earth?

q.e: Lake Baikal in Siberia is the deepest (1,642 m) and oldest (about 25 million years) freshwater lake.

q: This water body, which is South Americas largest freshwater lake, is the highest commercially navigable lake.

q.e: Sitting around 12,507 feet (3,812 m) above sea level in the Andes between Peru and Bolivia, Lake Titicaca is the world's highest commercially navigable body of water.

q: This freshwater-lake island, with a surface area of 2,766 km², is the biggest on Earth.

q.e: Manitoulin Island, in Lake Huron, is the largest freshwater lake island in the world.

q: The word volcano comes from the name of the Roman god of fire, Vulcan. Who is the analogue of Vulcan in Greek mythology?

q.e: Hephaestus was the Greek god of metalworking, carpentry, and fire, crafting divine weaponry on Mount Olympus. Helios was the personification of the Sun, while Hermes was the messenger god.

q: If magma contains more than 65% silica, the lava is called this.

q.e: Lava with over 65% silica is felsic (rhyolitic), highly viscous and explosive.

q: This famous Latin maxim, which is the official motto of South Carolina, means While I breathe, I hope.

q.e: "Dum spiro spero" is South Carolina's motto, meaning "While I breathe, I hope."

q: Which volcano, located on Ross Island, Antarctica, is the southernmost active volcano on Earth?

q.e: Mount Erebus on Ross Island is the southernmost active volcano.

q: This volcano, which is the largest in Europe, is located on the largest island in the Mediterranean Sea.

q.e: Mount Etna stands over 11,000 feet (about 3,357 meters) tall on the Italian island of Sicily, making it the highest and largest active volcano in Europe.

q: What is the biggest extinct volcano in Ecuador, situated in the Andes mountain.

q.e: Chimborazo (6,263 m) is Ecuador's highest peak and an inactive volcano. It's the farthest point from Earth's center.

q: This dormant volcano, which is 66 km northeast of Tehran, is the symbol of Iranian resistance against foreign rule.

q.e: Mount Damavand (5,610 m) is Iran's highest peak, dormant, about 66 km northeast of Tehran.

q: This active volcano, whose name means long mountain in Hawaiian, is one of the five peaks that form the Island of Hawaii.

q.e: Mauna Loa is the largest active volcano on Earth by volume and rises to an elevation of 13,678 feet (4,169 m). Its neighboring peak, Mauna Kea, is slightly taller but dormant.

q: What volcano located on the island of Tenerife represents the highest mountain on Spanish territories?

q.e: Mount Teide (3,715 m) on Tenerife is Spain's highest mountain.

q: Which is the volcanically active region that is situated in a famous national US park and has a territory of 55 kilometers by 72 kilometers?

q.e: The Yellowstone Caldera formed during a massive volcanic eruption roughly 631,000 years ago and measures approximately 45 miles by 30 miles (72 km by 55 km).

q: This island is well known in scientific fields for being home of five percent of the worlds plant and animal species, with 80% of them unique to it. The island is also the fourth biggest on Earth, with population of about 17,500,000 people.

q.e: Madagascar is the fourth-largest island and is a biodiversity hotspot. Its population is now about 30 million.

q: In Greek mythology, this island is the legendary birthplace of the goddess of beauty, love, and passion, the charming Aphrodite, where according to the legend, she emerged from the sea foam.
