q.e: Aphrodite was said to have risen from the sea foam near Petra tou Romiou, a sea stack off the coast of Paphos in Cyprus. The island became the foremost center of her worship in antiquity.

q: Al Nakheel Properties, one of the leading real estate developers in Dubai and creator of the worldwide famous Palm Islands, is also the initiator of another grand project of artificial islands, which resembles the shape of what?

q.e: Nakheel's "The World" in Dubai is an archipelago of artificial islands shaped like a world map.

q: These knee-breeches made of leather are a traditional Bavarian garment.

q.e: Lederhosen are traditional Bavarian leather breeches historically worn for rugged work, often accompanied by suspenders and paired with traditional checkered shirts.

q: Which of these national costumes does not belong to a European nation?

q.e: Hanfu is traditional Chinese clothing, so it's not European.

q: Which one of the following national costumes is not Chinese?

q.e: Kente cloth is Ghanaian (Ashanti), not Chinese.

q: According to the legend, which of these is a part of the Three Fortunate Concealments that protect Britain from any danger coming from the sea?
The head of Bran the Blessed
The bones of Gwerthefyr the Blessed

q.e: In Welsh legend, the head of Bran the Blessed, buried at the White Hill in London, protected Britain from invasion.

q: The famous department store Harrods that occupies an entire block is located on which road in London?

q.e: Harrods stands on Brompton Road in Knightsbridge.

q: Which scenic US valley was described by conservationist John Muir in the following way: (...) None can escape its charms. Its natural beauty cleans and warms like a fire, and you will be willing to stay forever in one place like a tree.?

q.e: John Muir wrote that about Yosemite Valley.

q: Where is the European Unions westernmost point not counting overseas territories?

q.e: The Azores are the EU's westernmost territory, Portuguese islands in the mid-Atlantic. Flores is the westernmost.

q: Which river, flowing entirely through a single country or state, is the longest?

q.e: The Vistula is Poland's longest river and the longest in the Baltic basin. Other answers may be longer; check the question's options.

q: Which one of these is not a Greek Mediterranean island?

q.e: Menorca (Minorca) is Spanish, not Greek.

q: On April 11, 2002, Al-Qaeda carried out a terrorist attack near a synagogue on which Tunisian island?

q.e: A truck bomb hit the Ghriba synagogue on Djerba on 11 April 2002, killing 21 people.

q: Which of these Mediterranean islands belongs to Croatia and is home of the endangered Griffon Vulture?

q.e: Cres, in Croatia's Kvarner Gulf, has a Eurasian griffon vulture colony.

q: North Carolina has been well represented on the American Idol TV series Which contestant from the state became Americas Idol in 2004?

q.e: Fantasia Barrino, from High Point, North Carolina, won American Idol season 3 in 2004.

q: This military complex in North Carolina is one of the largest in the world and home to the 82 Airborne, the Golden Knights, and U.S. Army Special Operations Command.

q.e: Fort Bragg (renamed Fort Liberty in 2023, then Bragg again in 2025) is home to the 82nd Airborne and Army Special Operations Command.

q: What city is the capital of Madagascar?

q.e: Antananarivo is Madagascar's capital, in the central highlands.

q: Name the European co-principality whose heads of state are the President of France and the Bishop of Urgel.

q.e: Andorra has been ruled under a joint arrangement established in 1278, meaning its co-princes are the Bishop of Urgell in Catalonia, Spain, and the head of state of France.

q: The Dead Sea Scrolls, found in caves at Qumran, are believed to have been made by a group of people called what?

q.e: The Dead Sea Scrolls are widely linked to the Essenes of Qumran, but this is debated.

q: What was the name of the great fortification built in 37-31 BC by Roman king Herod I on a high hill above the Dead Sea?

q.e: Masada is an ancient plateau fortress overlooking the Dead Sea where Jewish rebels made a famous last stand against Roman forces during the First Jewish-Roman War.

q: Which square is not correctly matched with the capital city in which it is located?

q.e: Azadi Square is in Tehran, Iran. Karachi's landmarks include Mazar-e-Quaid.

q: What city in Eastern Europe, often associated with the story of Dracula, is also famous for Revolution Square, which was the site of a 1989 revolt?

q.e: Bucharest's Revolution Square was the site of Ceaușescu's final speech in December 1989.

q: Dutch is the official language of the Netherlands. What is the second official language of the country?

q.e: Frisian (West Frisian) is the Netherlands' second official language, spoken in Friesland.

q: What is the name of the island shared by Haiti and the Dominican Republic?

q.e: Hispaniola is the second-largest island in the Caribbean by area (after Cuba), spanning roughly 76,000 square kilometers shared by Haiti in the west and the Dominican Republic in the east.

q: What sea is known to be the only sea without shores?

q.e: The Sargasso Sea is located entirely within the North Atlantic Gyre, bounded by ocean currents—such as the Gulf Stream—rather than any land borders.

q: What is the name of the Peruvian floating islands, located in Lake Titicaca?

q.e: The Uros people live on floating reed islands on Lake Titicaca.

q: Which man-made island, located to the southwest of Singapore, was created by joining several natural islands?

q.e: Jurong Island was formed by joining seven islands through land reclamation.

q: What is the name of the artificial island located in the Gatun Lake portion of the Panama Canal?

q.e: Barro Colorado Island in Gatun Lake was formed when the lake was created, a hilltop. It hosts a research station.

q: What are the largest cities in the Philippines in terms of land area?
Davao City and Puerto Princesa City

q.e: Davao City and Puerto Princesa are the largest Philippine cities by land area.

q: The Philippines has the worlds largest deposit of heavy water which can be used for atomic energy, in spectroscopy, and as an automobile fuel. What makes heavy water different from water?
One less hydrogen molecule making it HO not H2O

q.e: Heavy water contains deuterium (²H) instead of ordinary hydrogen. It's used in some nuclear reactors. The Philippines claim is not true.

q: Who is the first Filipino-American to become Governor of a US state?

q.e: Benjamin Cayetano, governor of Hawaii (1994–2002), was the first Filipino American governor.

q: On December 7, 1941 the Japanese launched a sneak attack on Pearl Harbor. On that day they also launched a similar attack on this American airbase in the Philippines.
Clark Air Force Base, Pampanga, Philippines

q.e: Japanese aircraft attacked Clark Field and other bases in the Philippines on 8 December 1941 (7 December in Hawaii).

q: What South Carolina Senator lived to be one hundred years old while still holding office?

q.e: Strom Thurmond retired in 2003 at age 100, after serving in the Senate for 48 years.

q: Francis Marion fought the British in the swamps of South Carolina during the Revolutionary War, using guerrilla tactics, that the communist Vietcong in Vietnam would have understood well. For this Marion was given the following nickname.

q.e: British officer Banastre Tarleton famously gave Francis Marion his moniker after pursuing him unsuccessfully through South Carolina marshes, complaining that the devil himself could not catch the Swamp Fox.

q: Not counting Istanbul, which of these cities is located on Bosphorus on the side of the Sea of Marmara and is the biggest city on the coast of the Black Sea?

q.e: Odessa is a major Ukrainian port on the Black Sea. Istanbul is on the Bosphorus.

q: The names of three large rivers flowing into the Black Sea begin with a letter D. Danube, the largest of the three, flows through ten European countries and enters the Black Sea in Romania. The other two end their flow in this country.

q.e: The Dnieper and Dniester flow through Ukraine into the Black Sea.

q: The Black Sea city of Sukhumi is the capital of this republic that proclaimed its independence from Georgia in the 90s.

q.e: Sukhumi is the capital of Abkhazia, which broke away from Georgia in the 1990s.

q: From the viewpoint of physical geography and ecology, the Ukrainian territories to the north of the Black Sea are known to contain what?

q.e: The area north of the Black Sea is Pontic steppe.

q: The Black Sea reaches the maximum depth of 2,210 m. Its neighbor, the Sea of Azov, is unique in terms of sea depth for what reason?
It is the shallowest sea in the world.
Its floor sinks constantly because it is located on a large basalt plate.
It has almost perfectly flat sea floor with a depth of 1370 m.
It has no established sea floor, it changes constantly with currents.

q.e: The Sea of Azov is the world's shallowest sea, with a maximum depth of about 14 m.

q: The highest mountain in the world is named after Sir George Everest, a famous Welshman. What was his profession?

q.e: Sir George Everest was a Welsh surveyor and geographer, Surveyor General of India.

q: This Italian climber, who was in the first expedition to reach Mount Everest without oxygen tanks, later became the first person to climb the summit alone.

q.e: Reinhold Messner (South Tyrol, Italy) climbed Everest without oxygen in 1978 with Peter Habeler, and solo in 1980.

q: What is the largest island of Canada, and the fifth-largest island in the world?

q.e: Baffin Island covers about 195,928 square miles (507,451 square km) in the northern territory of Nunavut. Victoria Island is Canada's second-largest island, ranking eighth in the world.

q: In 1728, he became the first person to sail into the Arctic Ocean and proved that Asia and North America are not joined by land.

q.e: Danish explorer Vitus Bering, sailing under the Russian flag, navigated the strait that now bears his name in 1728, confirming that Asia and North America were separated by water.

q: Who is given credit for being the first person to reach the North Pole?

q.e: Robert Peary claimed to have reached the North Pole on April 6, 1909, alongside Matthew Henson, though modern navigational analyses have raised doubts about whether his party actually reached the exact pole.

q: What river rises in the northwestern Czech Republic, flows through Germany and into the North Sea?

q.e: The Elbe rises in the Krkonoše mountains and enters the North Sea at Cuxhaven.

q: What river that flows through Spain and Portugal is the longest river on the Iberian Peninsula?

q.e: The Tagus (1,007 km) is the longest river on the Iberian Peninsula.

q: What is the longest river in Poland and the ninth longest in Europe?

q.e: The Vistula (1,047 km) is Poland's longest river.

q: How would you say What is your name? in Tagalog?

q.e: "Ano ang pangalan mo?" means "What is your name?" in Tagalog.

q: This western half of this island is part of Indonesia, while the eastern half is a nation which gained independence in 2002, following hundreds of years of European colonialism and 25 years of Indonesian occupation.

q.e: East Timor became independent in 2002 after centuries of Portuguese rule and 24 years of Indonesian occupation.

q: Which Indonesian island is shared by four Indonesian provinces and two other nations: the eastern half of Malaysia and the tiny oil-rich sultanate of Brunei?

q.e: Borneo is shared by Indonesia (Kalimantan), Malaysia and Brunei.

q: Which Indonesian island was in the news in 2003 when the remains of an extinct variety of small hominids (popularly referred to as Hobbits), measuring about 3 feet in height, were found there?

q.e: Homo floresiensis, "the Hobbit," was found on Flores, Indonesia, in 2003.

q: This island is the third largest in Indonesia, and is probably known for its coffee. It is also home to unique (and endangered) species of elephants, tigers, and rhinoceroses. It is also one of two islands which have indigenous orangutans.

q.e: Sumatra is a huge island that has unique wildlife and coffee (Mandheling), and orangutans live on it and Borneo.

q: Which of these describes best the location of the volcanic island of Krakatau (sometimes erroneously called Krakatoa), which had a well-known and devastating eruption on August 23, 1883?

q.e: Krakatau lies in the Sunda Strait between Java and Sumatra and erupted in 1883.

q: What large mountain range is located entirely within the territory of Italy?

q.e: The Apennines run down the length of Italy.

q: Which of the following famous people is NOT a Marylander?

q.e: Valerie Bertinelli was born in Wilmington, Delaware, not Maryland.

In December 2020, Nepal and China jointly announced the revised official height of Mount Everest as 8,848.86 meters, which rounds to 8,849 meters (29,032 feet). The earlier widely accepted survey was 8,848 meters.

q: Part of the Southeast Ridge Route for climbing Mt. Everest is the Lhotse Face in which Camp III is established. There are 14 peaks over 8,000 meters. Where does Lhotse rank?

q.e: Lhotse (8,516 m) is the fourth-highest mountain in the world.

q: Who is the first American to ascend all fourteen peaks over 8,000m without oxygen?

q.e: Ed Viesturs climbed all fourteen 8,000-meter peaks without supplemental oxygen, finishing in 2005.

q: Spanish painter and sculptor Pablo Picasso is known for co-founding what art movement?

q.e: Pablo Picasso co-founded Cubism in the early 20th century alongside French painter Georges Braque, pioneering a style that broke down subjects into geometric planes and multiple viewpoints.

q: In 1967, Egypt effectively blockaded Eilat by closing this area to Israel.

q.e: Egypt closed the Straits of Tiran to Israeli shipping in 1967, blocking Eilat, which helped trigger the Six-Day War.

q: On October 24, 1901, Annie Edson Taylor became the first person to go over the Niagara Falls in a barrel as a publicity stunt. How old was she at the time?

q.e: Annie Edson Taylor went over Niagara Falls in a barrel on her 63rd birthday in 1901 (she claimed to be younger).

q: The cities of Niagara Falls, Ontario and Niagara Falls, New York are connected by three bridges. Which of them is the oldest one?

q.e: The Whirlpool Rapids Bridge (1897) is the oldest of the three bridges between the Niagara Falls cities.

q: The Danube river flows through many Central European countries. Which of these statements concerning Slovakia and Slovenia is true?
Of the two countries, only Slovakia has Danubian banks.
The Danube does not flow through either of the 2 countries.
The Danube originates in Slovakia and then enters Slovenia.
The Danube originates in Slovenia and then flows through Slovakia.

q.e: Slovakia's Danube banks include Bratislava. Slovenia is in the Danube basin but has no Danube riverbank.

q: What river in North America provides food for the largest wintering Bald Eagle population in the continental United States?

q.e: The Skagit River in Washington hosts one of the largest wintering populations of bald eagles in the lower 48.

q: What city is the capital and largest city of Madagascar?

q.e: Antananarivo, often shortened to Tana, is situated in Madagascar's central highlands and has been the historical center of the Merina Kingdom as well as modern Madagascar.

q: The Navagio Bay (also known as the Shipwreck) is the most popular beach of which Greek island?

q.e: Navagio (Shipwreck) Beach is on the Greek island of Zakynthos.

q: Which island is NOT a part of Greece?

q.e: Gozo is part of Malta, not Greece.

q: The Corinth Canal separates this Greek peninsula from the mainland of Greece.

q.e: Completed in 1893, the Corinth Canal cuts across the narrow Isthmus of Corinth, turning the Peloponnese peninsula effectively into an island.

q: Which is the largest group of Greek islands?

q.e: The Cyclades are the largest group of Aegean islands, including Mykonos and Santorini.

q: Which of the following places in Greece is NOT an island?

q.e: Kavala is a port city on the Greek mainland, not an island.

q: What is the name of the leader of the first squad of Shinsengumi?

q.e: Okita Sōji led the 1st unit of the Shinsengumi, noted for swordsmanship.

q: Who was Shinsengumi Commander from 1863 to 1868?

q.e: Kondō Isami commanded the Shinsengumi (1863–68) and was executed in 1868.

q: What is the name of the second-tallest waterfall on the planet?

q.e: Tugela Falls in South Africa (948 m) is often listed as the second-tallest waterfall after Angel Falls, though this ranking is disputed.

q: Which of the following is NOT located in the country of Madagascar?

q.e: Bodrum is in Turkey. Madagascar has Antsirabe and Toliara.

q: I am a primate endemic to Madagascar. I have large, reflective eyes. I have a long tail. I have long toes, and opposable thumbs, useful for grasping tree branches. What am I?

q.e: Lemurs are native only to Madagascar and its neighboring Comoro Islands. Unlike apes and monkeys, they belong to the strepsirrhine suborder of primates, famous for their reflective tapetum lucidum layer behind the retina.

q: In the country of Papua New Guinea, how many children does the average woman give birth to during her lifetime according to 2006 estimates?

q.e: Papua New Guinea's fertility rate was about 4.6 children per woman in 2006.

q: This Andean stratovolcano in Colombia erupted in 1993, killing 9 people.

q.e: Galeras in Colombia erupted in January 1993, killing nine people, including scientists.

q: This city, located in Colorado, is the highest city in the United States.

q.e: Leadville, Colorado (3,094 m), is the highest incorporated city in the US.

q: Amelia Earhart, the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic, was born in what city and state?

q.e: Amelia Earhart was born in Atchison, Kansas, in 1897.

q: Arrange the following oceans by their total area, starting with the largest: 1)The Atlantic Ocean 2)The Pacific Ocean 3)The Indian Ocean 4)The Arctic Ocean 5)The Southern Ocean

q.e: By area: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern, Arctic.

q: In geography, the term desert is used to refer to a region that receives little or no precipitation. Approximately one-third of Earths land surface is desert, with the largest such region being which of these?

q.e: Covering roughly 5.4 million square miles (14 million sq km), the Antarctic polar desert is the largest on Earth. The Sahara is the largest hot desert, spanning around 3.5 million square miles.

q: This African desert, famous for its enormous sand dunes, is considered the oldest desert in the world, having endured its current arid conditions for at least 80 million years.

q.e: Extending along the coast of Namibia, the Namib Desert has experienced hyper-arid conditions for tens of millions of years and features dunes that can exceed 980 feet (300 m) in height.

q: This Australian desert of nearly 600,000 square kilometres is famous for its spectacular land and rock formations, such as Uluru and Kata Tjuta, its estimated 1,100 parallel dunes running north-south, and the fresh water lake, Rainbow Valley.

q.e: Uluru and Kata Tjuta are in the Northern Territory, in the Central Australian desert area. The Simpson Desert is known for parallel dunes.

q: The largest natural karst crater on Earth - Ramon Crater, with a length of 40 km (25 miles) and width of 2 to 10 km (1.5 to 6 miles), is situated in the heart of this Middle East desert.

q.e: Makhtesh Ramon, in the Negev desert in Israel, is the world's largest erosion crater.

q: Leonardo of Pisa or Leonardo Pisano, also known as Fibonacci, was an Italian mathematician and is best known for the discovery of the Fibonacci numbers, which form the following sequence. 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, ... Do you know what the next number is?

q.e: The Fibonacci sequence goes 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, and each number is the sum of the previous two.

q: The Holy Roman Empire of the German Nation was a loosely coupled union of mostly German speaking principalities. Which part of the union was the driver of the 19th century unification of Germany?

q.e: Prussia led German unification in 1871 under Bismarck.

q: By the end of the 16th century, a country called Commonwealth of Both Nations covered almost 1 million square kilometers of Europe. Which two countries formed it?

q.e: The Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth formed in 1569 at the Union of Lublin.

q: Phoenicia was an ancient civilization that spread maritime trade over the Mediterranean Sea. From where did the Phoenicians originate?
Greek islands on the Aegean Sea

q.e: The Phoenicians came from the coast of modern Lebanon, from cities like Tyre, Sidon and Byblos.

q: What is the capital and largest city of the Republic of the Congo?

q.e: Brazzaville sits on the northern bank of the Congo River, directly across from Kinshasa, the capital of the neighboring Democratic Republic of the Congo. Libreville is the capital of Gabon, and Lusaka is the capital of Zambia.

q: What port on the Atlantic Ocean is the capital and largest city of Guinea.

q.e: Conakry is the capital of Guinea, on the Atlantic Ocean.

q: When René-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle (Yikes!) claimed the territory he named it La Louisiane, which means....
Land of Louis or The Lousiana.
Land of Lords or Land of the Lords.
Land of France or Long Live France.
Land of Life or The Life.

q.e: La Salle named Louisiana in 1682 for King Louis XIV.

q: What is the closest definition of Santeria?
A Cuban based religion popular in Lousiana.
Another name for the Catholic Church in Lousiana.
Another name for the Protestant Baptists religion in Lousiana.
A Jewish based religion popular in Lousiana.

q.e: Santería is a Cuban religion of Yoruba origin, blended with Catholicism.

q: The region of Pomerania (ger.: Pomern, pol.: Pomorze) is located in north Germany and Poland. Which river divides the region into two parts?

q.e: The Oder (Odra) divides Pomerania into Western (Germany) and Eastern (Poland) parts.

q: Today people visit Colorado to go skiing, hiking, mountain biking and to enjoy the scenery. But 100 years ago, tourists more often went to the mountains to do what?

q.e: In the late 1800s, tourists came to Colorado for hot springs and mineral waters for health.

q: The huge grain industry in Colorado gives rise to breweries. Which of the following owns the biggest single site brewery located in Golden, Colorado?

q.e: Molson Coors operates the world's largest single-site brewery in Golden, Colorado.

q: On May 5, 1920 two Italian-Americans, Nicola Sacco and Bartolomeo Vanzetti, were arrested, tried, and executed for the April 15, 1920 murders of a South Braintree paymaster and security guard and theft of the payroll. What did Sacco give as his alibi?
He was at the Italian consulate in Boston.
He was in Plymouth peddling fish at the time.
He was visiting friends in West Bridgewater.
He was at work and had a time-card to prove it.

q.e: Nicola Sacco said he was in Boston on 15 April 1920, getting a passport at the Italian consulate.

q: Glenwood Springs, Colorado was known for its hot springs and hospital. What famous outlaw and gun slinger expired from Tuberculosis there?

q.e: Doc Holliday died of tuberculosis in Glenwood Springs, Colorado, in 1887.

q: What is the name of the most active volcano in Mexico, located mostly in the Mexican state of Jalisco?

q.e: Volcán de Colima, on the Jalisco–Colima border, is Mexico's most active volcano.

q: What is the name of the highest volcano in Asia, and the highest point in the Middle East?

q.e: Mount Damavand (5,610 m) is Asia's highest volcano and the highest peak in the Middle East.

q: What is the name of the active volcano situated in Skamania County, Washington, USA, 50 miles (80 km) northeast of Portland, Oregon?

q.e: Mount St. Helens is a composite volcano in the Cascade Range that famously experienced a cataclysmic eruption on May 18, 1980, which reduced its summit elevation from roughly 9,677 feet to 8,363 feet.

q: What is the prevailing religion in Sweden?

q.e: The Church of Sweden (Lutheran) was the state church until 2000, and still has most members.

q: The origin of the word denim is related to the name of which southern French city?

q.e: The word denim comes from the French phrase 'serge de Nîmes', referring to a sturdy twill fabric made in Nîmes. The word jeans also has a geographic origin, derived from the French word Gênes for Genoa, Italy.

q: This famous mountain flower, endangered in many countries, is the national flower of Switzerland and Austria.

q.e: Edelweiss is the national flower of Switzerland and Austria, and an alpine plant protected in many places.

q: This is the largest mall in the North American continent.

q.e: West Edmonton Mall in Alberta is the largest mall in North America.

q: This plant grows wild in the dry, desert ground of Texas and Mexico and is one of the very few spineless varieties among some two thousand different types of cacti growing in the world.

q.e: Peyote (Lophophora williamsii) is a spineless cactus containing mescaline, native to Texas and Mexico.

q: Probably the most famous and influential ballroom dance is Waltz. Its closed position became an example for many other dances and made it very fashionable. Waltz first became popular in this city and then spread all over the world.

q.e: Evolving from rural folk dances like the Ländler in the late 18th century, the waltz became fashionable in the grand ballrooms of Vienna, where composers like Johann Strauss II later cemented its worldwide renown.

q: In 1945 this man was given the Pulitzer Prize in News Photography for his famous photo of the raising the American flag on the Japanese island Iwo Jima.

q.e: Joe Rosenthal won the 1945 Pulitzer for "Raising the Flag on Iwo Jima."

q: What dance style, that evolved in the 1970s in New York City, involves moves known as Toprock and Downrock?

q.e: Breakdancing, or breaking, originated within the African American and Latino hip-hop culture of the Bronx in the 1970s, combining standing footwork called toprock with floor-based floorwork known as downrock.

q: Upon the death of her father, Elizabeth II was staying at the Treetops Hotel, built into the tops of the trees of the Aberdares National Park. In what country was Elizabeth II when she went up a princess and came down a queen?

q.e: Princess Elizabeth was staying at Kenya's Treetops Hotel on February 6, 1952, when King George VI died in his sleep, instantly making her Queen Elizabeth II.

q: What is the name the character in Swan Lake which is generally known as the Black Swan?

q.e: Odile is the Black Swan, the sorcerer's daughter who impersonates Odette in Swan Lake.

q: The New York Trilogy, which consists of the novels City of Glass, Ghosts, and The Locked Room, is this authors signature work.

q.e: Paul Auster wrote the New York Trilogy, published 1985–86.

q: The Soviets successful defense of this city and destruction of a German army in heavy, bloody fighting in 1942-43 is often called the turning point of WWII.

q.e: The Battle of Stalingrad ended in February 1943 when Soviet forces encircled and forced the surrender of General Friedrich Paulus and the German 6th Army, halting the Axis advance into the Soviet Union.

q: On and near what island in the Soloman Island group was the Japanese advance in the South Pacific stopped in 1943, after about six months of brutal fighting between the land and naval force of the US and Japan?

q.e: The Guadalcanal campaign (August 1942 to February 1943) ended Japanese expansion in the South Pacific.

q: In The Black Mountain, Nero Wolfe and his assistant Archie Goodwin are traveling in Europe and are almost arrested and taken to Titograd. By what name do we know Titograd?

q.e: Titograd is the old name of Podgorica, Montenegro's capital, renamed in 1992.

q: Calypso was a mythological nymph who lived by herself on an island. Once a hero came to her land by mistake, and she entertained him while he stayed there. Who was this hero?

q.e: In Homer's Odyssey, the nymph Calypso detained the Greek hero Odysseus on her island of Ogygia for roughly seven years before Hermes ordered her to let him build a raft and sail home.

q: The name of this super-continent means All land.

q.e: Pangaea means "all land" in Greek.

q: This early super-continent formed during the Mesoproterozoic era.

q.e: Rodinia formed about 1 billion years ago, in the Mesoproterozoic/Neoproterozoic era.

q: This is the Greek name of a city located about 40km from Beirut, Lebanon.

q.e: Byblos (Jbeil) is 40 km north of Beirut, among the oldest continuously inhabited cities.

q: Which Turkish city is a probable site of the Hellenistic city of Antiochia ad Taurum?

q.e: Gaziantep is thought to be the site of Antiochia ad Taurum, near ancient Zeugma.

q: Which explorer introduced the ruins of the city of Petra to the Western world?

q.e: Swiss explorer Johann Ludwig Burckhardt rediscovered Petra in 1812.

q: Which knight of the Round Table is raised by the Lady of the Lake after the death of his father?

q.e: Lancelot is known as Lancelot du Lac because the enchantress Viviane, the Lady of the Lake, fostered him after the death of his father, King Ban of Benwick.

q: What term used in diplomacy indicates a proscription against a person entering the country?

q.e: Persona non grata is Latin for an unwelcome person, codified in Article 9 of the 1961 Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations. A persona grata, by contrast, is an acceptable or welcomed representative.

q: What is the name of the river than runs through Nancy Drews fictional hometown?

q.e: Nancy Drew's fictional River Heights is on the Muskoka River in the books.

q: April 17, 1907 was the busiest day for new immigrants at Ellis Island. How many New Americans came through Ellis Island on that date?

q.e: On 17 April 1907, 11,747 immigrants were processed at Ellis Island, a one-day record.

q: What was the name of the character portrayed by Ricardo Montalban on Fantasy Island?

q.e: Ricardo Montalbán played Mr. Roarke on Fantasy Island, who grants guests' fantasies.

q: Which mountain is the highest in the Andes?

q.e: Located in western Argentina near the border with Chile, Mount Aconcagua rises to 22,838 feet (6,961 meters), making it the highest peak in both the Andes and the Western Hemisphere.

q: Mount Washington in New Hampshire, is the highest mountain in the Northeastern USA. It is known for its very high winds and bad weather. When was it first climbed?

q.e: Darby Field climbed Mount Washington in 1642, the first recorded ascent.

q: Which of these popular movies is not entirely or partially set in New York City?
One Flew Over the Cuckoos Nest

q.e: "One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest" is set in an Oregon mental hospital.

q: At 18,510 feet in height and located in the Caucasas mountain range, what is the highest peak in all of Europe?

q.e: Mount Elbrus, a dormant stratovolcano in Russia's Caucasus Mountains, stands at 18,510 feet (5,642 m). Mont Blanc is Western Europe's highest peak at 15,774 feet (4,808 m).

q: Held every year from July 7-14, the very dangerous, yet entertaining, Running of the Bulls event takes place in what Spanish city?

q.e: The Running of the Bulls takes place in Pamplona, Spain, during San Fermín, 6-14 July.

q: Gary Leon Rigway is known as the Green River Killer, responsible for at least 48 murders. What kind of people did he target?

q.e: Gary Ridgway, the Green River Killer, targeted sex workers and runaways. He pleaded guilty to 49 murders in 2003.

q: Which US President said the following words: Four score and seven years ago our fathers brought forth on this continent a new nation, conceived in Liberty, and dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal.?

q.e: Abraham Lincoln delivered the Gettysburg Address on 19 November 1863.

q: Princess Diana was buried on an island in the middle of the Round Oval lake in which country estate in England?

q.e: Diana is buried on an island in the Oval lake at Althorp, the Spencer family estate in Northamptonshire.

q: Pirates were squanderers and didnt have much money to bury. So the idea of a buried treasure is a romantic one, initiated by Treasure Island. However, this pirate was known for burying his money.

q.e: Captain William Kidd buried treasure on Gardiners Island, New York, in 1699, and most of it was recovered.

q: Prince Edward Island was the first Canadian province to prohibit alcohol in 1901. However, these two brothers were famous for smuggling alcohol on their rum running schooner.

q.e: Bootlegging in PEI is tied to local history. The bank's answer is obscure; check sources.

q: Tiberius Caesar Augustus is remembered as a depressed and unpopular ruler, whose reign was marked by terror. Tiberius was into a exile twice - once on the island of Rhodes and the second time on this island.

q.e: Tiberius retired to Rhodes and then to Capri, where he stayed from AD 26.

q: Which of these monarchs is not correctly matched to the country he ruled?

q.e: Harald V is the King of Norway, not Denmark (whose king is Frederik X).

q: Which Mediterranean country is the most probable place of birth of a person named Pablo Diego José Francisco de Paula Juan Nepomuceno María de los Remedios Cipriano de la Santísima Trinidad Clito Ruiz?

q.e: Pablo Picasso was born in Málaga, Spain, in 1881, and his full baptismal name was extremely long.

q: While this President was skinny dipping in the Potomac River a female journalist took his clothes and refused to give them to him until he gave an interview.

q.e: John Quincy Adams swam in the Potomac and journalist Anne Royall reportedly took his clothes until he gave an interview.

q: Which Spanish explorer was the first recorded European to reach the Mississippi River?

q.e: Hernando de Soto reached the Mississippi in 1541. Alonso Álvarez de Pineda had seen its mouth in 1519.

q: Which First Lady rescued the portrait of George Washington when the British burned the city during the war of 1812?

q.e: Dolley Madison famously refused to evacuate the White House in August 1814 until Gilbert Stuart's full-length Lansdowne portrait of George Washington was safely removed. British troops burned the mansion shortly after she fled.

q: Madeleine Albright, the first woman to become United States Secretary of State, was born Marie Jana Korbelová in this European country.

q.e: Madeleine Albright was born in Prague, Czechoslovakia, in 1937, and served as Secretary of State from 1997 to 2001.

q: What female politician is not correctly matched with the country of which she was Prime Minister?

q.e: Eva Perón was First Lady, never Prime Minister. Argentina has a president.

q: A self-proclaimed plain housewife, this lady was the first President of an Asian country.

q.e: Corazon Aquino called herself "just a plain housewife" and became president of the Philippines in 1986.

q: This leaders country has some oil resources but is very poor. Under his rule, we have the terrible genocide going on in Darfur. Who was dictator of the Sudan in 2007?

q.e: Omar al-Bashir led Sudan from 1989 until his ouster in 2019, and the ICC indicted him over Darfur.

q: Being the 8th Prime Minister of the country, this politician led Canada through World War I.

q.e: Sir Robert Borden was Canada's 8th Prime Minister (1911–1920), who led Canada through WWI.

q: The name of the largest ocean, the Pacific Ocean, is derived from the Latin name "Mare Pacificum�, which means peaceful sea. Who gave the ocean this name?

q.e: Ferdinand Magellan named the Pacific "Mar Pacífico" (peaceful sea) in 1520 after calm waters on his voyage.

q: What spiritual leader of his country made the following statement, We must be the change we wish to see in the world.?

q.e: Gandhi is widely quoted as saying "Be the change you wish to see in the world," but no exact record exists. It is a paraphrase.

q: What city was the capital of the ancient kingdom of Macedon when Alexander the Great was born?

q.e: Pella was the capital of Macedon when Alexander the Great was born in 356 BC.

q: Which one of the following is famous for running a school for mimes in New York City ?

q.e: This question refers to an obscure New York mime school. Check other sources.

q: What Spanish explorer became the first European to cross the Isthmus of Panama and see the Pacific ocean from the shores of America?

q.e: Vasco Nunez de Balboa marched across the Isthmus of Panama in September 1513, becoming the first recorded European to sight the eastern shore of the Pacific Ocean, which he named the South Sea.

q: Grigori Rasputin was murdered in December 1916. His body was recovered from this river flowing through the city of Saint Petersburg.

q.e: Rasputin's body was found in the Malaya Nevka, a branch of the Neva River, in December 1916.

q: Hal Holbrook toured the country in a one man show about this President. Raymond Massey, Henry Fonda and John Carradine won much fame for playing this great man.

q.e: Hal Holbrook is famous for his Mark Twain show; Raymond Massey, Henry Fonda and John Carradine played Abraham Lincoln.

q: With the exception of the Nobel Peace Prize, the Nobel Prizes are presented at an annual ceremony in Stockholm, Sweden. In what capital city ise the Nobel Peace Prize presented?

q.e: The Nobel Peace Prize is awarded in Oslo, Norway, while the other prizes are awarded in Stockholm.

q: According to Soviet records, Kim Jong-il was born on February 16, 1941 near this city.

q.e: Soviet records said Kim Jong-il was born in 1941 near Khabarovsk, while North Korea says Mount Paektu.

q: In 1974, this first lady of Argentina succeeded her husband as president of the country thus becoming the first non-royal female head of state in the Western Hemisphere.

q.e: Isabel Perón succeeded her husband Juan Perón in 1974, becoming the first woman president in the Americas.

q: This novelist depicted the fictional characters Doctor Daneeka, Snowden, Milo Minderbinder, who are stationed on an island off the coast of Italy during World War II.

q.e: Joseph Heller's "Catch-22" features Doc Daneeka, Snowden and Milo Minderbinder on the island of Pianosa.

q: The chemical element named after the creator of the first periodic table, Dmitri Mendeleev happens to be a US post office abbreviation of a state. Name the capital of the state.

q.e: Mendelevium's symbol is Md, which is Maryland's postal code. Annapolis is the capital.

q: This US President was forced to give an interview to Anne Royall, the first female professional journalist in the USA, after she learned that he liked skinny-dipping in the Potomac River.

q.e: President John Quincy Adams was interviewed by journalist Anne Royall after she sat on his clothes while he swam in the Potomac.

q: This company, founded in Long Island in 1972 by Hyman Golden, Arnold Greenberg and Leonard Marsh, initially offered only carbonated apple soda.

q.e: Snapple was founded in 1972 by Hyman Golden, Arnold Greenberg and Leonard Marsh as a natural juice and soda company.

q: This man is one of the greatest and most famous scientists of the 20th century. In 1921 he received the Nobel Prize in physics. He left his native country right after Hitler came to power and went to the US.

q.e: Albert Einstein won the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics and left Germany in 1933.

q: Which was the capital city of the Persian Empire?

q.e: Ecbatana was the capital of Media and later a Persian summer capital. Persepolis, Susa and Pasargadae were also capitals.

q: This archipelago country is located in the North Atlantic Ocean. It was not until the 15th century that the islands were colonized by the Portuguese.

q.e: Cape Verde, a Portuguese colony settled from the 1460s, has been independent since 1975.

q: During WW II, Italy invaded Greece on October 28th, 1940. The Italians attacked Greece through which country?

q.e: Italy invaded Greece on 28 October 1940 from Albania, which it had occupied in 1939.

q: What was the first attack in the Pacific Campaign, launched by the US forces on an island occupied by the Japanese?

q.e: The Guadalcanal campaign (August 1942) was the first major US land offensive in the Pacific.

q: Thetis, the mother of Achilles, tried to make her son immortal by holding him by the feet and dipping him in what river?

q.e: According to Roman-era myths such as Statius's Achilleid, dipping Achilles into the River Styx rendered his body invulnerable except for the heel by which Thetis held him.

q: This was the City and State where the family lived.

q.e: The Conners of "Roseanne" lived in fictional Lanford, Illinois.

q: James Jewell Osterberg, Jr. is famous as the father of punk rock. He appeared in The Crow: The City of Angels.

q.e: Iggy Pop (James Osterberg), the "Godfather of Punk" of the Stooges, appeared in The Crow: City of Angels (1996).

q: With its 2,505,810 sq. km (967,499 sq. miles) this is the largest country in Africa and the tenth largest in the world. Its ancient name was Nubia. Its contemporary name comes from an Arabic expression which means land of the blacks.

q.e: Algeria is now Africa's largest country since South Sudan's secession in 2011. "Sudan" comes from "bilad as-sudan," the land of the blacks.

q: This is the second largest country in South America and the 8th largest in the world, with a territory of 2,766,890 sq. km (1,068,302 sq. miles). More than one third of its population lives in or around Buenos Aires.

q.e: Argentina covers roughly 2.78 million square kilometers, making it second in South America only to Brazil, which spans over 8.5 million square kilometers. The Greater Buenos Aires metropolitan area accounts for well over 15 million of the nation's roughly 46 million residents.

q: This city is the capital of Armenia.

q.e: Founded in 782 BC as the fortress of Erebuni, Yerevan is one of the world's oldest continuously inhabited cities; Tbilisi is the capital of neighboring Georgia, and Baku is the capital of Azerbaijan.

q: According to legends, this was the home city of Helen - the woman whose beauty triggered the Trojan War.

q.e: Helen was the wife of Menelaus of Sparta. Her abduction by Paris triggered the Trojan War.

q: Hannibal, best known for his achievements in the Second Punic War, was a politician and military commander of this ancient city.

q.e: Hannibal was the Carthaginian general who crossed the Alps in the Second Punic War.

q: The sinking of which British ocean liner played a role in the United States entry into World War I?

q.e: The sinking of RMS Lusitania by a German U-boat in May 1915 killed 128 Americans and helped swing US opinion.

q: After the success of Operation Weserubun which began on 9 April 1940, this European country was occupied by German troops. Both the government and the king remained in the country during its occupation.

q.e: Germany invaded Denmark and Norway on 9 April 1940. Denmark's government and king stayed during the occupation.

q: This island, situated in central Mediterranean Sea, was most heavily bombed in the period 1940-1942 when Italy challenged the British supremacy of the Mediterranean.

q.e: Malta was bombed heavily from 1940 to 1942 and was awarded the George Cross.

q: What is the most sacred river for Hindus?

q.e: The Ganges (Ganga) is the most sacred river in Hinduism.

q: This Israeli city, which features many beautiful beaches and beautiful seashore views, is also the site of the first IKEA in Israel.

q.e: Netanya, on the Mediterranean coast of Israel, has Israel's first IKEA (opened 2000).

q: Morris Raphall, a Rabbi from New York City, was the first to open a session of Congress with a prayer. In what year did he do this?

q.e: Rabbi Morris Raphall delivered the first Jewish prayer opening the House of Representatives on 1 February 1860.

q: According to The Old Testament, the prophet Jonah was sent to which city to warn its inhabitants of the coming judgment on them?

q.e: The Book of Jonah recounts God commanding Jonah to travel to Nineveh, the capital of the Neo-Assyrian Empire, to preach repentance, though Jonah initially tried fleeing in the opposite direction toward Tarshish.

q: During World War II, this country was able to successfully defend its freedom and resist invasions by the Soviet Union - despite some loss of territory. It joined the European Union in 1995.

q.e: Finland resisted the USSR in the Winter War (1939–40) and Continuation War, and joined the EU in 1995.

q: Mount Everest was formed some 50 million years ago. It rises a few meters each year because of geological forces. On the border between which two countries is this mount situated?

q.e: Everest lies on the border between Nepal and China (Tibet).

q: This volcano, featured in a short 1933 Academy Award-winning movie, is located near the Indonesian island of Rakata, in the Sunda Strait.

q.e: Krakatoa (Krakatau) is in the Sunda Strait, whose island is named Rakata. It erupted in 1883.

q: How did the political life in England, Spain and France change as a result of the geographical discoveries?
They turned into strong monarchies with rich and autocratic monarchs
The political life did not change significantly
They were weakened because their armies were spread thin on other continents

q.e: The discoveries enriched the Spanish, English and French crowns and strengthened absolute monarchies.

q: Only this one of the seven wonders of the world survived the trials of time and is open to visitors.

q.e: The Great Pyramid of Giza is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still standing.

q: This East European capital city is famous for its wide, tree-lined boulevards and glorious Belle Epoque buildings. Some call it Little Paris because of these buildings.

q.e: Bucharest earned the nickname "Little Paris" for its Belle Époque architecture and boulevards.

q: In close proximity to this Italian city are the famous ruins of Pompeii, which once was a thriving town for wealthy Romans. The city of Pompeii was destroyed in the cataclysmic eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD.

q.e: Pompeii sits roughly 14 miles (23 km) southeast of Naples, near the foot of Mount Vesuvius, which buried the Roman city under pumice and ash in 79 AD.

q: This city is famous for the fact, that a living goddess dwells there. She is a young girl by the name of Kumari, believed to have appeared in the 18th century.

q.e: Kathmandu has the Kumari, a prepubescent girl worshipped as a living goddess.

q: This island country tried to gain its independence from Spain in 1821, but was conquered and ruled by the Haitians for 22 years. It finally became independent in 1844.

q.e: The Dominican Republic declared independence from Spain in 1821, was annexed by Haiti until 1844, then became independent.

q: This independent country, located in Southeastern Asia was first colonized by Portugal in the 16th century. Between 1976 and 1999 it was a provice of Indonesia.

q.e: Portugal colonized East Timor in the 16th century. Indonesia occupied it from 1975/76 until 1999.

q: This Southeast European country allied with the Axis powers and participated in the 1941 German invasion of the USSR. In 1947, overrun by the Soviets, it bacame a Communist peoples republic.

q.e: Romania joined the Axis and invaded the USSR in 1941, then became a communist people's republic in 1947.

q: In the movie "It's A Wonderful Life,� George gets beaten up by drugstore owner Mr. Gower, who happened to be drunk at the time. Ultimately, George saves Mr. Gower from putting poison in a drug prescription. What propelled Mr. Gower to getting drunk that day?
He just learnt about the death of his son.
He just turned 50 and was depressed.

q.e: Mr. Gower was drunk because he had just learned his son died of influenza, in It's a Wonderful Life.

q: The Lao Peoples Democratic Republic, a landlocked country in southeast Asia, neighbouring China, Vietnam, Cambodia, and Thailand, was previously known by the name of Lan Xang, which means what translated in English?

q.e: Lan Xang means "Land of a Million Elephants," the Lao kingdom founded in 1353.

q: The economy of the southern African republic of Botswana was formerly dependent on export of live cattle and meat, but since late 1960s, the mining industry has taken over. Which of these natural resources is Botswana a significant exporter of?

q.e: Botswana exports diamonds and is one of the biggest diamond producers in the world.

q: The State of Qatar, an emirate in the Middle East with substantial oil and natural gas deposits, is located on a small peninsula (The Qatari peninsula), in which of these bodies of water?

q.e: Qatar is a peninsula jutting into the Persian Gulf from Saudi Arabia.

q: Burma, the former name of this Southern Asian republic, was changed by the military government which took over political authority in 1988. Nevertheless, Burma is still often used to refer to this country.

q.e: The ruling military junta officially renamed Burma to Myanmar in 1989, also changing the capital's name from Rangoon to Yangon.

q: This island country, whose national motto is Te Mauri, Te Raoi ao Te Tabomoa (Health, Peace, and Prosperity), has its territory situated in both hemispheres.

q.e: Kiribati straddles the equator and the International Date Line, so it's in all four hemispheres.

q: 389 sq. km (150 sq. miles) is the entire territory of this country, situated in the Caribbean. Agriculture is the most important sector of its economy, more specifically, bananas.

q.e: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines (389 km²) has a banana-dependent economy.

q: This 316 sq. km (122 sq. miles) country is an island south of Italy. It has no mountains or rivers. Its university is one of the oldest in the world, founded in 1592.

q.e: Malta's university, founded in 1592, is among the oldest in the world.

q: This country is comprised of 1190 coral islands southwest of the southern tip of India. They constitute 300 sq. kilometers (115 sq. miles). The official language is Dhivehi, but English is also spoken.

q.e: The Republic of Maldives is an archipelago of 26 natural atolls spread across the Indian Ocean southwest of India and Sri Lanka. Dhivehi, an Indo-Aryan language closely related to Sinhala, is the country's official language.

q: This country, situated in the eastern Caribbean, stretches over 261 sq. km. (104 sq. miles). The two islands were first settled by the British in 1623 and gained their autonomy in 1967. Independence came in 1983.

q.e: Saint Kitts and Nevis gained independence from Britain in 1983.

q: Situated in central Europe, this country takes up 160 sq. km. (62 sq. miles). It is a famous winter resort, also known for its low tax rates.

q.e: Liechtenstein (160 km²) is a tax haven and winter resort between Switzerland and Austria.

q: This country is an enclave in central Italy. Its territory is 61.2 sq. km. (24 sq. miles). It claims to be the worlds oldest republic still in existence, founded in 301 A.D.

q.e: San Marino is an enclave surrounded by Italy and claims to be the oldest republic, founded in 301.

q: This Pacific country lies on 26 sq. km. (9 sq. miles). It stands between Hawaii and Australia, its name meaning Eight Standing Together in the local language.

q.e: Tuvalu means "eight standing together" in Tuvaluan, and has nine islands, eight of them populated.

q: The former name of this 21 sq. km. (8.5 sq. miles) country was Pleasant Island. This is the smallest republic in the World, situated in the Central Pacific west of Kiribati. A hundred years of phosphate mining has devastated four-fifths of the land area.

q.e: Nauru, formerly Pleasant Island, is the world's smallest republic.

q: This 1.95 sq. km. (0.7 sq. miles) country is a famous constitutional monarchy. It relies largely on foreign currency for an economic base. There are no farms and the main industry is tourism.

q.e: Covering roughly 2.08 square kilometers along the French Riviera, Monaco is the second-smallest independent state in the world after Vatican City.

q: This is the worlds smallest country with a territory of only 0.44 sq. km. (0.2 sq. miles) and population of 921 people. It is considered the capital of all Catholics and is ruled by the Pope.

q.e: Encircled entirely by Rome, Vatican City covers roughly 0.17 to 0.19 square miles (about 0.44 to 0.49 square kilometers) and is the smallest independent state by both area and population. Monaco is the second-smallest country, spanning about 2 square kilometers (0.78 square miles).

q: The catchphrase Does she or doesnt she...? was part of the advertising campaign of which of these?

q.e: Clairol's slogan "Does she... or doesn't she?" was used in hair color ads from 1956.

q: Which product was advertised with the slogan: Youve come a long way, baby!?

q.e: "You've come a long way, baby" was a Virginia Slims cigarette slogan starting in 1968.

q: Which product was advertised with the provocative words My wife, I think Ill keep her.?

q.e: "My wife, I think I'll keep her" was a Geritol ad slogan.

q: During a 1974 survey, it was discovered that this spot located in East Antarctica has the deepest ice cover on Earth.

q.e: Ice thickness in East Antarctica reaches over 4,700 m near Wilkes Land, and Vostok lies above Lake Vostok under about 3.7 km of ice.

q: The deepest lake in the world is also the third largest one in Asia. It located in Siberia, Russia.

q.e: Lake Baikal is the world's deepest lake at 1,642 m, in Siberia.

q: According to the Druidic religion of the Celts, this winter season began every year on the night of October 31.

q.e: The Celtic year began with Samhain, on the night of 31 October into 1 November. It became Halloween.

q: This country is located in Africa. Here you may get a hotel room for approximately $5/person, soft drinks are 20c, and dinner with drinks for $7. The worlds largest artifical lake, Lake Volta, is located here.

q.e: Ghana's Lake Volta (created in 1965) is the world's largest man-made lake by surface area.

q: This country has the Balboa as currency, which is the same as the Dollar. Actually the bills are US dollars and the coins are a mixture of Balboas and US coins.

q.e: Panama's balboa is pegged to the US dollar. Only coins are issued in balboas.

q: One of Detroits nicknames is The 313, one of Flints is That 810. The number in one of Lansing, Michigan nicknames is this.

q.e: Lansing's area code is 517, like Detroit's 313 and Flint's 810.

q: The slogan Is it true blondes have more fun was used by which company?

q.e: "Is it true blondes have more fun?" was a Clairol slogan.

q: Which of these used the advertising slogan, Ring around the collar!?

q.e: "Ring around the collar" was a Wisk laundry detergent ad.

q: The popular phrase Sorry, Charlie is associated with which product?

q.e: "Sorry, Charlie" was a StarKist tuna slogan featuring Charlie the Tuna.

q: On the Island of Misfit Toys there are many unusual toys in Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer. On that island, what does the water gun shoot that makes it a misfit?

q.e: In Rudolph, the misfit toy water pistol shoots jelly instead of water.

q: At the end of Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer, Yukon Cornelius and the snowmonster arrive at Christmastown. What job is the snowmonster given?
Puting the stars on top of trees

q.e: At the end, the Abominable Snowman is given the job of putting the star on top of the Christmas tree.

q: For which ruler was the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus built?

q.e: The Mausoleum at Halicarnassus was built for King Mausolus of Caria, hence the word "mausoleum."

q: What is the other name of the Lighthouse at Alexandria?

q.e: The Pharos of Alexandria was the great lighthouse of Alexandria.

q: Two of Wonders of the Ancient World were built as tombs. Of those listed below, which was one of these tombs?

q.e: The Great Pyramid of Giza and the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus were both tombs.

q: According to the Bible, after Christ was born in Bethlehem, three Magi visited him. They presented Jesus with all these treasures, but one. Can you spot it?

q.e: The Magi brought gold, frankincense and myrrh. Chrism (holy oil) was not one of them.

q: The 2004 movie The Polar Express starred this actor in five distinct roles. For example, he was the Boy, the Conductor and even Santa Claus.

q.e: Tom Hanks played five roles in The Polar Express (2004), including Santa Claus and the Conductor.

q: Sidney Poitier is a Bahamian-American actor, born in Miami, Florida. He won the Academy Award for Best Actor for his role in this movie.

q.e: Sidney Poitier won the Best Actor Oscar for Lilies of the Field (1963), the first Black man to win it.

q: What currency is used in Bermuda?

q.e: Bermuda uses the Bermudian dollar, pegged to the US dollar.

q: What is the most widely spoken language in Papua New Guinea?

q.e: Tok Pisin is the lingua franca of Papua New Guinea, an English-based creole.

q: What is the most widely spoken language in Ethiopia?

q.e: Amharic is Ethiopia's working language, though Oromo has more native speakers.

q: What famous female Irish pirate of the 1500s was condemned to death, but later pardoned by Queen Elizabeth?

q.e: Grace O'Malley (Gráinne Mhaol) was an Irish pirate queen who met Elizabeth I in 1593.

q: The Official Post Office of Santa Claus is situated in which city in Finland?

q.e: Santa Claus Village is located just north of Rovaniemi, right on the Arctic Circle in Finnish Lapland. Its official post office receives over half a million letters each year from children around the world.

q: Which term refers to a method of education based on inquiry and examination of key moral concepts?

q.e: Named after classical Greek philosopher Socrates, the Socratic method uses cooperative, question-and-answer dialogue to stimulate critical thinking and uncover underlying beliefs.

q: In the year 1620, this ship carried 102 Pilgrims from Plymouth, England to the shores of North America.

q.e: The Mayflower carried 102 passengers from Plymouth in 1620.

q: Jerusalem is of great importance to Jews, Christians and Muslims. It is closely linked to the lives of prophets such as David, Salomon and Jesus Christ. According to the Bible, which of the following is attributed to king Salomon?
Building the First Jewish Temple in Jerusalem
Declaring Jerusalem capital of the Kingdom of Israel
Defending the city against a Roman siege

q.e: According to the Bible, King Solomon built the First Temple in Jerusalem.

q: In 571 CE the Prophet Muhammad was born in Mecca. There, he started preaching Islam and gathered some followers. However, he was persecuted in Mecca and therefore he moved to the city of Yathrib. What is the present name of Yathrib?

q.e: Yathrib became Medina after Muhammad's Hijra in 622.

q: Many Judaic customs and festivals take place in the city of Jerusalem. Such are the festivals Pesach Seder and Yom Kippur as well as the saddest day for all Jews, the Ninth of Av. What do Jews mourn over on the Ninth of Av?
The destruction of the city and the loss of their holy temples

q.e: Tisha B'Av (9th of Av) mourns the destruction of the First and Second Temples in Jerusalem.

q: A pilgrimage to Mecca is required for every Muslim that can afford it. When a Muslim pilgrim visits the city, he has to circle the House of God (Kabah) seven times and then try to kiss or touch its cornerstone. What is the name of this cornerstone?

q.e: The Black Stone (Hajar al-Aswad) is set in the corner of the Kaaba.

q: This is another ritual, performed by Muslim pilgrims. It takes place in Mina (a city just outside Mecca). There, they collect a number of pebbles and throw them at the three pillars at Mina. This is what the ritual is called.

q.e: During Hajj, pilgrims throw pebbles at the Jamarat pillars in Mina in the "stoning of the devil."

q: After it became clear that the Titanic could not stay afloat, safety measures to save the crew and the passengers were taken. At 12:40 AM the first lifeboat, boat 7, was lowered. How many of these boats did Titanic have?

q.e: The Titanic had 20 lifeboats, enough for about 1,178 of its 2,200 people.

q: The Titanic broke into two sections and by 2:20 AM they had both sunk into the ocean. About two hours later, this ship arrived and began rescuing the survivors.

q.e: The RMS Carpathia arrived about 4 am to rescue survivors.

q: July 7th-14th is the time when youd better stay out of the streets in Pamplona, Spain. A herd of fighting bulls are let loose onto the streets, after a crowd of young men. A lot of injuries occur during this famous fiesta.

q.e: The Running of the Bulls, or encierro, takes place every morning during the festival of San Fermin in Pamplona, where runners race along an 875-meter course ahead of six fighting bulls.

q: The key to the notorious prison in France, the Bastille, is in the USA. Where is it kept?

q.e: The Bastille key was given to George Washington by Lafayette in 1790 and is at Mount Vernon.

q: What mountain, located in the Sentinel Range of the Ellesworth Mountains, is the highest mountain in Antarctica?

q.e: Vinson Massif (4,892 m) in the Sentinel Range is Antarctica's highest mountain.

q: Which of these was not born in New Jersey?

q.e: Ally Sheedy was born in New York City, not New Jersey.

q: The Adriatic Sea separates these two peninsulas.
The Apennine Peninsula from the Balkan Peninsula
The Scandinavian Peninsula from the Balkan Peninsula
The Iberian Peninsula from the Apennine Peninsula
The Balkan Peninsula from the Iberian Peninsula

q.e: The Adriatic Sea separates the Italian (Apennine) peninsula from the Balkan peninsula.

q: Which country, situated in todays Iraq and Iran, was a major enemy of the Roman Empire?

q.e: Parthia, in today's Iran and Iraq, was Rome's chief rival in the East.

q: What is the name of an English shelter, usually free for use by anyone, found in remote mountain areas?

q.e: A bothy is a simple shelter for walkers, found in remote areas of Scotland, England and Wales.

q: This is a traditional Japanese inn dating back to the 17th century, nowadays often situated along highways.

q.e: A ryokan is a traditional Japanese inn with tatami rooms, dating back centuries.

q: What kind of lodging, traditionally constructed in the northern hemisphere, is sometimes called a snow house?

q.e: An igloo, derived from the Inuit word 'iglu' for house, is a dome-shaped shelter constructed from blocks of compressed snow, which act as an excellent thermal insulator.

q: Name the portable dwelling structure used by nomads during their constant travels in Central Asia.

q.e: A yurt (or ger in Mongolian) is a circular, collapsible tent made of an expanding lattice frame covered in felt. A tipi is a conical tent traditionally used by Indigenous peoples of the Great Plains in North America.

q: What conical tent is constructed by Native Americans, using buffalo hide?

q.e: Tipis are portable, conical dwellings traditionally made of wooden poles wrapped with buffalo hides by nomadic Plains tribes. Wigwams are domed structures usually covered with bark or mats rather than hides.

q: Which dome-like Native American tent is made by the semi-nomadic tribes of the American West and Southwest?

q.e: A wickiup is a dome-shaped hut used by Apache and other tribes in the Southwest.

q: This temple, discovered in Walbrook in 1957, was built in the middle of the third century in worship of a popular mystic religion.

q.e: The Temple of Mithras in London was discovered in Walbrook in 1954, built around AD 240.

q: The Black Sea is almost a lake. How is it connected to other sea waters?

q.e: The Black Sea connects to the Mediterranean via the Bosphorus, the Sea of Marmara and the Dardanelles.

q: The faction of the Russian Social Democratic Workers Party, led by Lenin, succeeded in overthrowing the regime of Alexander Kerensky by revolution. When did it take place?

q.e: The Bolsheviks seized power in the October Revolution of 1917 (November in the Western calendar).

q: After the end of World War II many countries were overtaken by communist influence. Most of them were in Eastern European, but not all. Mao Zedong came to power in China and established the Peoples Republic of China in this year.

q.e: Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic of China on 1 October 1949.

q: What city, located on Upolu Island, is the capital of Samoa?

q.e: Apia, on Upolu, is the capital of Samoa.

q: What is the capital of the unincorporated territory of the United States, known as American Samoa?

q.e: Pago Pago is the main settlement of American Samoa, a US territory.

q: Which language is the source of most US states names?

q.e: Many US state names, like Michigan, Mississippi and Massachusetts, come from Algonquian languages.

q: Fill in the missing words: As dry leaves that before the wild hurricane fly, When they meet with an obstacle, mount to the sky, So up to the house-top the coursers they flew, With the sleigh full of toys, and _____ ________ ___.

q.e: In "A Visit from St. Nicholas" the line ends "...and St. Nicholas, too."

q: What is the missing word? And then, in a twinkling, I heard on the roof The prancing and pawing of each little hoof. As I drew in my hand, and was turning around, Down the _______ St. Nicholas came with a bound!

q.e: The missing word is "chimney."

q: Complete the line from the famous Christmas poem: His droll little mouth was drawn up like a bow, And the beard of his chin was __ _____ __ ___ ____; The stump of a pipe he held tight in his teeth, And the smoke it encircled his head like a wreath;

q.e: The line is "And the beard of his chin was as white as the snow."

q: What are the missing words? He had a broad face and a little round belly, That shook, when he laughed like _ ________ ___ _____.

q.e: The line is "That shook, when he laughed, like a bowlful of jelly."

q: In December 1998, this figure skater, winner of two Olympic gold medals appeared on the cover of Playboy magazine.

q.e: Katarina Witt, East German figure skating champion (1984, 1988), posed for Playboy in December 1998.

q: This person, who in 1979 established the Hugh M. Hefner First Amendment Award, became CEO of Playboy in 1988.

q.e: Christie Hefner became CEO of Playboy Enterprises in 1988, and she was Hugh Hefner's daughter.

q: This company launched a series of ads to combat its competitor. They show a young guy dressed in jeans and tee shirt on the right and an overweight dork, wearing a suit and glasses on the left. The guy in jeans was used as the image for what product?

q.e: In Apple's "Get a Mac" ads, Justin Long played the Mac and John Hodgman the PC.

q: This Canadian city of Stately Elms is located on the banks of the St. John River and was established as provincial capital on April 25, 1785.

q.e: Fredericton, "The City of Stately Elms," became New Brunswick's capital in 1785, on the Saint John River.

q: This city, which was an important supply centre during the Klondike Gold Rush, is the capital of the Canadian territory of Yukon.

q.e: Whitehorse was a Klondike Gold Rush supply stop and is the capital of Yukon.

q: What is the capital of Nunavut, Canada's newest and largest territory?

q.e: Iqaluit, situated on Baffin Island, became the capital of Nunavut when the territory was created in 1999. The community was known as Frobisher Bay until 1987, named after English explorer Martin Frobisher.

q: This bridge across the Rhine was an objective of the allied Operation Market Garden in 1944. A movie of the battle was later made.

q.e: Operation Market Garden (September 1944) aimed to take the bridge at Arnhem, as depicted in "A Bridge Too Far."

q: Lech Walesa, a former president of Poland, was the leader of an unofficial strike at the Lenin Shipyard in this town.

q.e: Lech Wałęsa led the 1980 strike at the Lenin Shipyard in Gdańsk, which led to Solidarity.

q: A suburb of Edinburgh, this is the seat of the Scottish Parliament, and the British Queens official residence in Scotland.

q.e: Holyrood in Edinburgh has the Scottish Parliament building and the Palace of Holyroodhouse.

q: The headquarters of a German car producer whose tag line is Vorsprung durch Technik are located in this city.

q.e: Audi is headquartered in Ingolstadt, Bavaria. Its slogan is "Vorsprung durch Technik."

q: Situated on the Baltic Sea, this city is linked to the North Sea via a canal of the same name.

q.e: The Kiel Canal links the Baltic Sea to the North Sea, and Kiel is on the Baltic.

q: Which river flowing entirely within the EU borders is the longest?

q.e: The Elbe (1,094 km) is the longest river wholly within EU territory.

q: This plant lives on the salty banks of lagoons and estuaries. It can exist in areas far from fresh water and has a prop roots that extend down from its branches and form a dense tangle.

q.e: Mangroves have prop roots and live in salty coastal waters.

q: Pisa reached its apex in the Middle Ages when it was one of the four Marine Republics of Italy, together with three of these cities. Which is the odd one?

q.e: Pisa was one of the four maritime republics, along with Amalfi, Genoa and Venice. Palermo wasn't one.

q: The creator of the Kentucky Fried Chicken franchise was also from the bluegrass state. He was known as Colonel Sanders, but what was his first name?

q.e: Colonel Harland Sanders, from Kentucky, founded KFC.

q: This college basketball coach won 875 games while coaching the University of Kentucky Wildcats basketball team for 41 years.

q.e: Adolph Rupp coached Kentucky for 41 years (1930–72) and won 876 games.

q: This host of many game shows, such as Love Connection and Lingo, was born in Ashland, KY.

q.e: Chuck Woolery, host of "Love Connection," was born in Ashland, Kentucky.

q: There are two countries in the world which are double-landlocked meaning they are surrounded by other landlocked countries. One is Uzbekistan. Name the other one which is a small principality in the European Alps.

q.e: Liechtenstein and Uzbekistan are the world's two doubly landlocked countries.

q: For a variety of reasons, mostly relating to ethnic conflict, the three landlocked nations in East Africa have been home to terrible atrocities and genocide. Which of the following is NOT one of these East African landlocked nations?

q.e: Burundi, Rwanda and Uganda are the landlocked East African nations of the Great Lakes region. Sudan has a Red Sea coast.

q: Thirteen countries, or almost a third of all landlocked countries in the world, have gained their independence in 1990, mostly due to the breakup of the Soviet Union and the breakup of Yugoslavia. Which of the following is NOT one of these thirteen countries?

q.e: Montenegro isn't landlocked; it has an Adriatic coast.

q: What is the name of Ebenezer Scrooges underpaid clerk?

q.e: Bob Cratchit is the father of Tiny Tim and works long hours for meager wages at Ebenezer Scrooge's counting house in Charles Dickens's 1843 novella A Christmas Carol.

q: Founded in 1899 by three brothers, this French vehicle company has produced models called Voiturette 1CV and Dauphine, but generally numbers its models. The company was first to patent the sedan car and the turbocharger.

q.e: Renault was founded in 1899 by Louis, Marcel and Fernand Renault.

q: This Italian motor company, originally called Anonima Lombarda Fabbrica Automobili, was founded in 1910 and was acquired by Fiat in 1986.

q.e: Alfa Romeo was founded in 1910 as A.L.F.A. and acquired by Fiat in 1986.

q: Name Nissans luxury car brand in the American, Canadian, Mexican, Middle Eastern, South Korean and Taiwanese markets. Models include G37, M, EX35 and QX56.

q.e: Infiniti is Nissan's luxury brand.

q: Which model of car, first released by Lotus in 1996, has a hand-finished fibreglass shell bonded to an extruded aluminium frame, is capable of speeds up to 150 mph (240 km/h) and at the time of its release weighed just over half of what a Porsche Boxter did?

q.e: The Lotus Elise (1996) has a lightweight fiberglass body on an aluminum chassis.

q: A small part of Russia lies just north of Poland on the Baltic Sea, separated from the rest of Russia by three nations. What is the current name of this exclave of Russia?

q.e: Kaliningrad, formerly Königsberg, is a Russian exclave between Poland and Lithuania.

q: This nation, which became independent in 2002, shares an island with Indonesia. Part of its territory, the district of Oecussi-Ambeno, is separated from the rest of the country by a part of the Indonesian province of East Nusa Tenggara.

q.e: East Timor (Timor-Leste) became independent in 2002; the exclave Oecusse is within Indonesian West Timor.

q: The exclave of Cabinda in Africa is separated from the rest of the country it is part of by the Atlantic coastal portion of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. What nation does Cabinda belong to?

q.e: Cabinda is an exclave province of Angola, separated by the DR Congo coastline.

q: The Musandam peninsula on the southern side of the entrance to the Persian Gulf is an exclave of what country, separated from the rest of the country by the United Arab Emirates?

q.e: Musandam is an exclave of Oman, cut off by the UAE.

q: This Roman god, usually depicted with two faces looking away from each other, gives the name of one of the months of the year and is a symbol of change and transition.

q.e: Janus was the Roman god of beginnings, gates, transitions, and endings, lending his name to the month of January (Ianuarius in Latin).

q: This English Poet Laureate, regarded as the chief representative of the Victorian age poetry, wrote the poem, 'The Death of the Old Year'.

q.e: Alfred, Lord Tennyson, Poet Laureate (1850–92), wrote "The Death of the Old Year."

q: This collection of laws, originating from Mesopotamia, is known as one of the earliest sets of laws.

q.e: The Code of Hammurabi (about 1754 BC), Babylonian king, is one of the oldest known legal codes, famous for "an eye for an eye."

q: This legal Latin term, which in English means obvious, denotes evidence that is sufficient to prove a particular fact.

q.e: "Prima facie" means "at first sight" and refers to evidence enough to establish a fact unless rebutted.

q: Clara Shortidge Foltz was the first woman to be admitted to practice law in the State of California. This happened in what year?

q.e: Clara Shortridge Foltz became California's first woman lawyer in 1878.

q: This person presided over the Federal Constitutional Court of Germany from 1987 to 1994, before being elected President of Germany.

q.e: Roman Herzog led the Federal Constitutional Court (1987–94) before being president of Germany (1994–99).

q: What was the nickname given to the group of Black pilots in WW II that excelled in aerial combat?

q.e: The Tuskegee Airmen trained at Tuskegee Army Airfield in Alabama and flew more than 1,500 missions during World War II, earning the nickname 'Red Tails' for the painted empennage on their fighters.

q: This ancient-Greek structure had a single path running to and from the center, in 7 concentric rings. It was burned to the ground in the 15th century.

q.e: The Labyrinth of Knossos is a Minoan myth tied to a palace on Crete. The palace was destroyed around 1400 BC.

q: This great marble temple was built in Ephesus. It is famous for being one of the biggest temples the ancient Greeks ever built. It was burned by a madman, who wanted to immortalize his name.

q.e: The Temple of Artemis at Ephesus, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, was destroyed by arson in 356 BC by Herostratus, who sought notoriety through the act.

q: This was the monumental marble tomb of the Anatolian king Mausolus. 140 feet high, it rivalled even the Egyptian pyramids.

q.e: The Mausoleum at Halicarnassus was built around 350 BC for Mausolus, the ruler of Caria, and gave rise to the generic term mausoleum.

q: These buildings were designed to be both tombs and temples. Mayan royalties carried out self-torture and mutilation rites on the roofs, as they believed that blood nourished gods.
Ggantija and the Megalithic Temples on Malta

q.e: Mayan pyramids were temples and tombs, where blood-letting rites were performed.

q: Who was the first incumbent, one-term President not to be even nominated for another term although he wanted the office?

q.e: Millard Fillmore wasn't nominated by the Whigs in 1852. Winfield Scott was.

q: Who actually built Monticello, the estate of Thomas Jefferson?
Jefferson built it with his own two hands.
Masons brought over from Europe by Jefferson

q.e: Monticello was built by enslaved laborers and hired craftsmen, to Jefferson's design.

q: This candy bar, produced by the Hershey Company, was created around 1928 by a former dairy farmer and shipping foreman for Milton S. Hershey.

q.e: Reese's Peanut Butter Cups were created by H.B. Reese, a former Hershey shipping foreman and dairy farmer, around 1928.

q: I am thinking of a US state. The capitals of the states bordering it are Sacramento, Salem, Boise, Salt Lake City and Phoenix. What is the capital of the state I am thinking of?

q.e: Nevada borders California, Oregon, Idaho, Utah and Arizona. Carson City is its capital.

q: Three of these US cities are real, the fourth is a fake.

q.e: West Illiad, Arkansas, appears to be fictional. Check the other options in your question.

q: One of these towns is about as fake as that clip - on tie youre wearing.

q.e: Carruthers, South Carolina, appears to be fictional.

q: Which town on this list is fake?

q.e: Proctors Corner, Virginia, appears to be fictional.

Nebraska was officially designated the Cornhusker State by its legislature in 1945, derived from the nickname for the University of Nebraska's athletic teams. The Sagebrush State is Nevada, and the Garden State is New Jersey.

q: Seattle was named after the Native American chief Seattle who belonged to what tribe?

q.e: Chief Seattle (Si'ahl) was a leader of the Suquamish and Duwamish peoples.

q: Christopher Columbus went on his first voyage across the Atlantic Ocean in 1492, using three famous ships. Which of the following was not among them?

q.e: Columbus's ships were the Niña, Pinta and Santa María, not the Doria.

q: Lusitania and Mauretania were sister ships, built to compete with fast German liners. Which one of them was torpedoed and sunk by a German submarine in 1915?

q.e: The Lusitania was torpedoed by U-20 on 7 May 1915. The Mauretania survived until 1935.

q: In 1620, this ship made a historical voyage from Plymouth, England to North Virginia, transporting the Pilgrims to America.

q.e: The Mayflower carried the Pilgrims to America in 1620.

q: This 8,600-ton transatlantic passenger steamship became famous after rescuing the survivors after the sinking of Titanic.

q.e: RMS Carpathia, Cunard's liner, rescued the 705 Titanic survivors.

q: All of these vessels except one are famous steam-powered ships crossing the Atlantic Ocean. Name the odd vessel.

q.e: The Cutty Sark was a sailing clipper, not a steamship.

q: The Amazon River is the largest river in the world by volume. Because of its dimensions it has been nicknamed The River Sea. What width does the Amazon River reach at its widest point during the dry season?

q.e: In the dry season the Amazon is about 11 km wide at its widest, and it can be much wider (40 km) in flood.

q: With the Louisiana Purchase of 1803 America was able to double the size of its territory, and for a bargain price to boot. Who was the generous salesman?

q.e: Napoleon Bonaparte, First Consul, sold Louisiana to the US in 1803 for $15 million.

q: The Monster Mash song was performed in an impersonation of which famous horror actor?

q.e: Bobby "Boris" Pickett imitated Boris Karloff on "Monster Mash" (1962).
