q: In what decade were the first commercial Valentines cards produced in the United States?

q.e: The first commercial valentines in the US were made by Esther Howland in the 1840s.

q: Which city houses the oldest Polish university, established in 1364?

q.e: Kraków's Jagiellonian University was founded in 1364 by Casimir III.

q: Legend has it that Martin Luther nailed a copy of his 95 Theses to the door of the Castle Church in this city, thus beginning the Reformation.

q.e: Martin Luther posted his Ninety-five Theses in Wittenberg on October 31, 1517, challenging church practices such as the sale of indulgences.

q: In which Danish city was Hans Christian Andersen born?

q.e: Fairy tale author Hans Christian Andersen was born in Odense on the Danish island of Funen in 1805. He later moved to Copenhagen at age 14 to pursue an artistic career.

q: This city, which is an administrative center of a Russian enclave, was once a Prussian city called Königsberg.

q.e: Kaliningrad, formerly Königsberg, is Prussia's old capital and Kant's hometown.

q: Stalingrad was the scene of an important battle during WW II. What is the name of the city today?

q.e: The city was originally named Tsaritsyn before being renamed Stalingrad in 1925 after Joseph Stalin. In 1961, during the Soviet de-Stalinization program led by Nikita Khrushchev, it was renamed Volgograd after the Volga River.

q: Communists liked to name cities after their leaders. Which German city was known as Karl Marx Stadt?

q.e: Chemnitz was named Karl-Marx-Stadt from 1953 to 1990.

q: Francis Scott Key wrote this poem in 1814, which later became the lyrics of the US national anthem.

q.e: Francis Scott Key wrote "Defence of Fort M'Henry" in 1814, which became "The Star-Spangled Banner."

q: This actress, writer, talk-show host and comedian performed The Star Spangled Banner before a baseball game in San Diego on July 25, 1990.

q.e: Roseanne Barr's screeching rendition of the anthem at a Padres game in San Diego was on 25 July 1990.

q: French automobile manufacturer Citroen is not very creative. C2, C3, C4.. are not interesting for us. However one of their models bears the name of a famous painter. Which one?

q.e: Citroën's Xsara Picasso and C3 Picasso honor Pablo Picasso.

q: SEAT, the subsidiary of the VW group, names car models after Spanish cities or regions. Which is not one of them?

q.e: SEAT names cars for Spanish places: Ibiza, León, Toledo, Córdoba, Marbella. Corsa is an Opel.
Renault's models are Clio, Twingo, Mégane and others. Check the question's pun.

q: The name of this car was also the name of a ship used for the exploration of the New World in the 15th century.

q.e: The Caravelle, a VW/Renault model, shares a name with the light ships used by Columbus.

q: Which of the following was not a passenger on the Titanic?

q.e: J. Pierpont Morgan cancelled his Titanic trip at the last minute.

q: What was the name of the ship that rescued the passengers from the sea after the Titanic hit the iceberg?

q.e: The RMS Carpathia, captained by Arthur Rostron, arrived roughly two hours after Titanic sank on April 15, 1912, rescuing 705 survivors from the lifeboats.

q: Which of the following had the nickname Papa Doc?

q.e: François "Papa Doc" Duvalier ruled Haiti from 1957 to 1971.
Festivus was created by Daniel O'Keefe, whose son Dan O'Keefe was a Seinfeld writer, in the 1960s.

q: How do the French call the first day of April?

q.e: The French call April 1 "poisson d'avril" (April fish).

q: McLaren and General Motors teamed up from 1989 to 1990 to build this factory turbocharged passenger car.

q.e: The 1989 Pontiac Turbo Grand Prix was built by McLaren with GM.

q: The state of Iowa borders Minnesota on the north, Missouri on the south, Nebraska and South Dakota on the west, and Wisconsin and Illinois on the east. Which river forms the eastern boundary of the state?

q.e: The Mississippi River forms Iowa's eastern border, and the Missouri River the western.

q: This company in Cedar Rapids, Iowa was founded in 1901, as a result of the merger of three separate companies. In 1969, they acquired Fisher-Price, a toy company.

q.e: Quaker Oats, Cedar Rapids' big employer, acquired Fisher-Price in 1969.

q: The Ohio, Monongahela and Allegheny Rivers merge in Piitsburgh, PA, at the location of this outpost, established during the Fench and Indian War (1755-1763).

q.e: The three rivers meet at the Forks of the Ohio, the site of Fort Duquesne, built by the French in 1754.

q: Which of these flags is the oldest still in use?

q.e: Denmark's Dannebrog (c. 1219) is the world's oldest continuously used national flag.

q: What is the shape of the Star of David, visible in the center of the Israeli flag?
It looks like a comet, with a head and tail

q.e: The Star of David on Israel's flag is a hexagram, a six-pointed star, between two blue stripes.

q: Who was the managing director of the White Star Line at the time the Titanic sailed?

q.e: J. Bruce Ismay, chairman and managing director of White Star Line, survived the Titanic.

q: From the Halls of Montezuma To the Shores of Tripoli, We fight our countrys battles In the air on land and sea. is the beginning of what song related to the United States Marine Corps?

q.e: "The Marines' Hymn" opens "From the Halls of Montezuma to the shores of Tripoli."

q: In this city, St. Patricks Day is celebrated in bars such as the Silver Dollar Saloon, the MM Cigar Store, The Irish Times Pub and the traditional parade is led by the Ancient Order of Hibernians.

q.e: Butte, Montana, with its Irish mining heritage, hosts a huge St. Patrick's Day party, with the Ancient Order of Hibernians leading the parade.

q: This treaty was signed on February 7, 1992 by the members of the European Community, resulting in the creation of the European Union.

q.e: The Maastricht Treaty (7 February 1992) established the European Union, effective in November 1993.

q: Which casino-hotel in Las Vegas opened on April 28, 2005 and at the time of its completion was the largest privately-funded construction project in the U.S.?

q.e: Wynn Las Vegas opened on 28 April 2005, costing about $2.7 billion.

q: If you travel southeast from Las Vegas, youre heading toward two tourist attractions. One is 35 miles away, the other is a couple hundred miles further. Name them.

q.e: Hoover Dam is about 35 miles southeast of Las Vegas, and the Grand Canyon is a few hours further.

q: The area code for Las Vegas is 702. This was the code for all of Nevada until 1996. What is now the area code for the rest of the state?

q.e: Las Vegas keeps area code 702, while the rest of Nevada has used 775 since 1998.

q: Which of these is the mountain that boasts a skiing area, a lodge complete with cabins, hiking trails, and alpine terrain all within 50 miles of the center of the Las Vegas valley?

q.e: Mount Charleston, in the Spring Mountains, has skiing and cabins within an hour of Las Vegas.

q: Adidas acquired the Salomon Group with the brands Salomon, TaylorMade, Mavic and Bonfire in December 1997. What is the name of the new company?

q.e: Adidas bought Salomon in 1997, creating Adidas-Salomon AG, later renamed Adidas AG.

q: A collaboration between Adidas and designer Yohji Yamamoto
The mechanism of a Nike watch
A new cushioning technology from Nike

q.e: Y-3 is a fashion line launched in 2002 by Adidas and Japanese designer Yohji Yamamoto.

q: Adidas was a company of two brothers. In 1948 one of them - Rudolf, left it and created his own brand. Which is it?

q.e: Brothers Adolf and Rudolf Dassler originally ran the Gebrüder Dassler Schuhfabrik together. Following a bitter feud in 1948, Adolf founded Adidas while Rudolf founded Puma.

q: Which one of these is not a group belonging to the Apache nation?

q.e: The Assiniboine are a Plains people (Nakoda), not Apache. The Apache include the Chiricahua, Mescalero and Jicarilla.

q: Who invented the writing system of the Cherokee language?

q.e: Sequoyah created the Cherokee syllabary in the 1820s.

q: Fifteen days after the signing of the Declaration, the Congress ordered a copy to be engrossed for the delegates of the colonies to sign. Who was the first person to sign this copy?

q.e: John Hancock signed first on the engrossed Declaration on 2 August 1776.

q: Almost half of the 56 delegates who signed the US Declaration of Independence were representatives of what profession?

q.e: About 25 of the 56 signers were lawyers or jurists.

q: The Liberty Bell, located in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, is an item of great historic significance for all Americans. On July 8, 1776 the bell was tolled for several hours, for what reason?
To summon the locals to hear the reading of the Declaration of Independence
To summon the locals for the first celebration of Independence Day
To celebrate the signing of the Lee Resolution

q.e: The Liberty Bell was rung on 8 July 1776 to call citizens to the Declaration's first public reading.

q: Which of these is not a brand of Scotch whisky?

q.e: Tullamore D.E.W. is an Irish whiskey, not a Scotch.

q: What was the monetary unit in Greece before it was replaced by the euro in the year 2001?

q.e: Greece used the drachma until the euro in 2001 (cash in 2002).

q: What is the currency unit in Indonesia?

q.e: Indonesia's currency is the rupiah, derived from the Sanskrit word rupyakam, meaning wrought silver. It was first issued in 1946 to replace the Japanese guilder.

q: What is the currency unit in Saudi Arabia?

q.e: The Saudi riyal has served as the kingdom's official currency since the country was unified in 1932. It is pegged to the US dollar at a fixed rate of 3.75 riyals per dollar.

q: Which twin towers, located in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, were worlds highest buildings from 1998 to 2004?

q.e: Standing at 1,483 feet (451.9 m), the 88-story Petronas Twin Towers held the title of the world's tallest buildings from 1998 until Taipei 101 surpassed them in 2004.

q: Name the first circular skyscraper, which is 216 meters tall, has 64 storeys and was built in Hong Kong.

q.e: Hopewell Centre in Hong Kong (1980) is 216 m tall, with 64 floors, a circular tower.

q: What is the name of this extremely tall luxury hotel in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, that stands in the sea on an artificial island?

q.e: Burj Al Arab in Dubai, on an artificial island, is a luxury hotel shaped like a sail.

q: What is the capital of Burkina Faso?

q.e: Ouagadougou, often shortened to Ouaga, has been the capital since the Mossi Kingdoms and became the official capital of modern Burkina Faso upon independence in 1960.

q: Brownsville, Texas is the twin city to this city.

q.e: Brownsville, Texas, and Matamoros, Tamaulipas, are sister cities on the Rio Grande.

q: Seoul, South Korea has a twin city that has declared itself an English-speaking city. Which city is Seouls twin city?

q.e: Seoul has several sister cities. Incheon is a neighboring city with a free economic zone. Check the question's other options.

q: Which word means a Mexican factory in which parts made in other countries are assembled?

q.e: A maquiladora is a factory in Mexico that assembles imported parts for export.

q: Which word means a simple farmer or a farmer on a subsistence farm?

q.e: "Campesino" is Spanish for peasant farmer.

q: Two Latin American countries are landlocked. Three Latin American countries are called the ABC countries. How many of the ABC countries are landlocked?

q.e: The ABC countries, Argentina, Brazil and Chile, all have coastlines. The landlocked Latin American ones are Bolivia and Paraguay.

q: On October 4, 1970 this singer was found dead of a heroin overdose in a Los Angeles motel room at the age of 27.

q.e: Janis Joplin died on 4 October 1970 at age 27 in Hollywood, Los Angeles, from an accidental heroin overdose.

q: Which two teams played in the first World Series of baseball to be held west of St. Louis, starting on October 1, 1959, with Game 3 being played on October 4?
LA Dodgers v Chicago White Sox
San Francisco Giants v Chicago Cubs
Oakland As v Boston Red Sox

q.e: The 1959 World Series: Los Angeles Dodgers beat the Chicago White Sox in 6 games. Game 3 was in LA, the first World Series game on the West Coast.

q: Which of these great European explorers was first to reach American soil?

q.e: Leif Erikson reached North America around 1000 AD, about 500 years before Columbus.

q: This was the first family to have two members who got the Nobel Prize in the same year.

q.e: Pierre and Marie Curie shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with Henri Becquerel.

q: Who made the first transatlantic radio transmission?

q.e: Guglielmo Marconi achieved the milestone in December 1901 by transmitting Morse code for the letter 'S' across roughly 2,100 miles (3,400 km) from Cornwall, England, to St. John's, Newfoundland.

q: Who was the first explorer to reach both the North and the South Poles?

q.e: Roald Amundsen led the first expedition to the South Pole (1911) and was on the 1926 Norge flight over the North Pole.

q: Tetris is a popular computer game with hundreds of versions. Who designed and programmed the original game?

q.e: Soviet software engineer Alexey Pajitnov created and coded the original version of Tetris in 1984 on an Electronika 60 terminal at the Soviet Academy of Sciences.

q: How many were the terrorists who hijacked the four airliners and carried out the September 11 attacks on the World Trade Center and the Pentagon?

q.e: Nineteen al-Qaeda hijackers carried out the 11 September 2001 attacks.

q: The following lines are from a poem written by this author who was part of the Harlem Renaissance: What happens to a dream deferred? Does it dry up Like a raisin in the sun?.

q.e: Langston Hughes's poem "Harlem" asks "What happens to a dream deferred?"

q: Chief Goyathlay, generally known as Geronimo, was a prominent leader of the last major independent Native American warriors, who refused to surrender to the U.S. government. Which tribe did he belong to?

q.e: Geronimo was a prominent leader and medicine man of the Bedonkohe band of the Ndendahe Apache. He led resistance campaigns against Mexican and US troops before his final surrender in September 1886.

q: Cheyenne Chief Black Kettle and his band were attacked by the U.S. Cavalry on November 27, 1868. This bloody massacre remained in history under what name?

q.e: The Battle of the Washita River (27 November 1868) saw Custer's 7th Cavalry attack Black Kettle's Cheyenne camp.

q: This warrior, who led the Seminole resistance in Florida during the Second Seminole War, was captured by deceit and died in 1838.

q.e: Osceola led the Seminoles in the Second Seminole War and was captured under a flag of truce in 1837, dying in 1838.

q: Which one of these Native American warriors did not participate in the Battle of Little Bighorn in June 1876?

q.e: Osceola died in 1838, well before the 1876 Battle of Little Bighorn.

q: This Native American chief of the Nez Perce tribe, called by the press the Red Napoleon, was a renowned peacemaker. He is famous for his words: I am tired of fighting.... From where the sun now stands I will fight no more forever.

q.e: Chief Joseph of the Nez Perce said his 1877 surrender speech: "From where the sun now stands, I will fight no more forever."

q: What was the maiden name of Jacqueline Kennedy who was of French descent?

q.e: Jacqueline Bouvier married John F. Kennedy in 1953.

q: Which French actress won the 1959 Academy Award for Best Actress in a Leading Role?

q.e: Simone Signoret won the 1959 Oscar for Best Actress for "Room at the Top".

q: Which French actress won the 1997 Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress?

q.e: Juliette Binoche won the Oscar for Best Supporting Actress for The English Patient, at the 1997 ceremony.

q: In which region was Marquis de Montcalm born?

q.e: The Marquis de Montcalm was born in Candiac, near Nîmes, in Languedoc, in 1712.

q: Dont Swap Horses in the Middle of the Stream was a slogan used in which presidents re-election campaign?

q.e: "Don't swap horses in the middle of the stream" was a slogan for Abraham Lincoln's 1864 re-election.

q: This author who wrote the novel Get Shorty, was born on 11 October 1925, in New Orleans.

q.e: Elmore Leonard, born in New Orleans on 11 October 1925, wrote "Get Shorty" (1990).

q: What country located in Southeastern Europe has the city Podgorica as a capital, and was part of a larger state until 2006?

q.e: Montenegro peacefully dissolved its federation with Serbia following a May 2006 independence referendum, establishing its capital at Podgorica.

q: The $100,000 is an odd bill, in that it was not generally issued, and printed only as a gold certificate of series of 1934. It featured the portrait of this great American.

q.e: The $100,000 gold certificate (1934) bore Woodrow Wilson's portrait and was only used between Federal Reserve Banks.

q: The Reservoir in Central Park was renamed in 1994 in honor of this former first lady who could often be seen strolling or jogging around the reservoir.

q.e: The Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis Reservoir in Central Park was renamed in 1994 after she died.

q: This port of Athens is the largest port in Europe in terms of passengers.

q.e: Piraeus is Athens's port and one of the busiest passenger ports in Europe.

q: Cobh, a town in Cork Harbour, Ireland , was known by this name until the founding of the Irish Free State in 1922.

q.e: Cobh was named Queenstown from 1850 to 1920/22, and it was the Titanic's last port of call.

q: This Italian town is famous for the Palio, which is a horse race around the Piazza del Campo held between 17 Contrade, or city neighbourhoods.

q.e: Siena's famous bareback horse race takes place twice every summer, on July 2 and August 16, in the shell-shaped Piazza del Campo. Ten of the city's 17 historical wards, known as contrade, compete in each event.

q: This river, over 1000 km in length, flows through Spain and Portugal.

q.e: The Tagus (Tajo/Tejo) is over 1,000 km long and flows through Spain and Portugal into the Atlantic at Lisbon.

q: What is the capital city of Malta, a small island nation in the Mediterranean?

q.e: Valletta (often spelled Valetta) was established in the 1560s by the Order of St. John and named after Grand Master Jean Parisot de Valette. Covering less than 0.4 square miles (under 1 square kilometer), it is the smallest national capital in the European Union.

q: The Brussels American School (US Department of Defense School) and Brussels Airport are located in this municipality in the Belgian province of Flemish Brabant.

q.e: Brussels Airport is in Zaventem, in Flemish Brabant.

q: What is the title of Mark Twains first story, which was printed in the New York Saturday Evening Post on November 18 in 1865?
The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County
A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthurs Court

q.e: Mark Twain's "The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County" appeared on 18 November 1865 in the New York Saturday Press.

q: Who directed Steamboat Willie, the first fully synchronized sound cartoon with Mickey Mouse, which was released on November 18 in 1928?

q.e: Walt Disney and Ub Iwerks made "Steamboat Willie" (18 November 1928), a Mickey Mouse short with synchronized sound.

q: There are nine countries that surround the Baltic Sea. Some of their capitals are port-cities located on the Baltic Sea, its gulfs, bays, or straits. Which Baltic capital has access to the sea only via a river system?

q.e: Vilnius is on the Neris River, inland, not on the Baltic coast.

q: Some countries around the Baltic Sea have very similar culture, history and language. The Prussian language that was a part of the Baltic language group is now extinct. What are the two remaining languages of the Baltic group?

q.e: Latvian and Lithuanian are the only two living Baltic languages. Old Prussian is extinct.

q: A disaster that took the lives of 852 people occurred in September of 1994 when the ferry ship named after this country sank in the Baltic Sea.

q.e: MS Estonia sank in the Baltic in September 1994, killing 852 people.

q: Born on October 26, 1947, this previous First Lady is also known for being Senator of New York.

q.e: Hillary Rodham Clinton was born on 26 October 1947, was First Lady, Senator and Secretary of State.

q: His birthdate is October 4, 1924. He was a heroic actor and president of the National Rifle Association for five years.

q.e: Charlton Heston, born 4 October 1924, was president of the NRA from 1998 to 2003.

q: The character Short Round drove a replica of this car in the opening scenes of Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom, a film released in 1984. It was a United States make of car. The company existed from 1930 to 1936.

q.e: In Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom, Short Round drives an Auburn 851 Speedster replica, built from 1930–36.

q: Each generation of BMW has been signified by an e-code - the letter E and a number. Which was the first generation of BMW cars?

q.e: The BMW E-code system began with the E3 (1968–77). Check other sources for E-code history.

q: Which of the following extraordinarily tall people died on July 15, 1940?

q.e: Robert Wadlow, the tallest man in history at 8 ft 11 in, died on 15 July 1940.

q: At the beginning of his show he says, At no point are actors or stooges used in this show or There were no actors or stooges used in this show?

q.e: Derren Brown says that actors or stooges aren't used in his shows.

q: What popular actor was born on December 17, 1953 and played characters named Dennis Alan (1988), Bob Hinson (1992), Ed Masterson (1994), President Thomas J. Whitmore (1996) and Peter Kirk (2004)?

q.e: Bill Pullman, born 17 December 1953, played Dennis Alan, Bob Hinson, Ed Masterson, President Whitmore and Peter Kirk.

q: Here, at what legend says Zeus called the navel of the world, Apollo killed a winged snake whose blood gave prophetic visions to those who inhaled its fumes. By what better name do we know the seer, Pythia?

q.e: The Oracle of Delphi operated at the sanctuary of Apollo on the slopes of Mount Parnassus, where the high priestess, known as the Pythia, delivered cryptic prophecies in trance states.

q: Which town saw the first privately owned Nuclear Power Plant in the United States?

q.e: Shippingport Atomic Power Station (1957) was the first full-scale US nuclear plant; Dresden 1 (1960) was the first privately financed one.

q: Bartletts Book of Anecdotes describes this poet and short story writer as a doyenne of light verse and wit. This line is from her most often quoted poem: Men seldom make passes At girls who wear glasses. Name the author of this poem.

q.e: Dorothy Parker wrote "Men seldom make passes at girls who wear glasses."

q: What was the profession of the man who first performed Grandma Got Run Over by a Reindeer, before he made it big as a singer of comedy songs?

q.e: Dr. Elmo Shropshire, a veterinarian, performs "Grandma Got Run Over by a Reindeer."

q: Which of these was the first oil well in Texas?

q.e: Spindletop (1901) was the gusher that began the Texas oil boom, though Corsicana (1894) was earlier.

q: Which desert is situated in the southern part of Israel and covers a large part of Israels official Southern District?

q.e: The Negev is a rocky desert covering more than half of Israel's land area, roughly 4,700 square miles (12,000 sq km), stretching down to the port city of Eilat.

q: The Dead Sea, the lowest exposed point on Earths surface, has an average depth of how many feet/meters below sea level?

q.e: The Dead Sea's surface is about 430 m below sea level, the lowest land elevation on Earth.

q: What was the capital of Hawaii before Honolulu?

q.e: Lahaina was the capital of the Kingdom of Hawaii from 1820 to 1845, before Honolulu.

q: Narcís Monturiol is credited for inventing the first mechanically powered submarine - Ictineu II. It used steam for propulsion and was originally designed to do this.

q.e: Narcís Monturiol built the Ictíneo, a Spanish submarine, designed to harvest coral.

q: The Trident II SSBNs are among the most dangerous and destructive submarines -- each one carries a destructive power more than nine times greater than all Allied ordnance dropped during World War II. What class of submarine is the Trident II?

q.e: Trident II missiles are carried by the Ohio-class ballistic missile submarines.

q: What is a former name of Malawi?

q.e: Malawi was Nyasaland until independence in 1964.

q: What is the longest of the eleven Finger Lakes, located in Upstate New York?

q.e: Cayuga Lake is the longest of the Finger Lakes (about 38 miles), while Seneca is the deepest.

q: Which beat generation writer, whose works include On the Road and Big Sur, hailed from Lowell, Massachusetts?

q.e: Jack Kerouac was born in Lowell, Massachusetts, in 1922. He wrote "On the Road" (1957).

q: Robert H. Goddard, a scientist born in Worcester, Massachusetts, is known as the father of what?

q.e: Robert H. Goddard launched the world's first liquid-fueled rocket in Auburn, Massachusetts, on March 16, 1926. His pioneering patents and mathematical theories earned him recognition as the father of modern rocketry.

q: Which of the following famous advocates of women suffrage was NOT born in Massachusetts?

q.e: Carrie Chapman Catt was born in Ripon, Wisconsin. Susan B. Anthony was born in Adams, Massachusetts.

q: What is the highest peak in Massachusetts?

q.e: Mount Greylock (1,064 m), in the Berkshires, is Massachusetts's highest peak.

q: The so-called afflicted children, whose actions gave rise to the infamous Salem Witch Trials lived in which modern-day Massachusetts town?

q.e: Salem Village, where the afflicted girls lived, is now Danvers, Massachusetts.

q: The Seven Sisters were a group of seven womens colleges in Massachusetts, Pennsylvania, and New York. Which of these Massachusetts womens colleges was not one of the Seven Sisters?

q.e: The original Seven Sisters were Barnard, Bryn Mawr, Mount Holyoke, Radcliffe, Smith, Vassar and Wellesley. Regis was not one.

q: What is the legislature in the UK?

q.e: The UK Parliament is bicameral: the House of Commons and the House of Lords.

q: A red Lockheed Vega 5B that this woman piloted from Newfoundland to Ireland to become the first woman to fly solo, nonstop trans-Atlantic can be seen in the Air and Space Museum. Who was this woman?

q.e: On May 20–21, 1932, Amelia Earhart completed the 2,026-mile flight in about 15 hours, landing in Culmore, Northern Ireland. She was the first woman and second person overall, after Charles Lindbergh, to complete a solo transatlantic flight.

q: Houston, the Eagle has landed., signaled to the world that man had reached the moon. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin were the first and second man to walk on the moon. Who was the third man on the Apollo 11 mission?

q.e: Michael Collins stayed in orbit in the command module while Armstrong and Aldrin walked on the Moon in 1969.

q: TV Guide named this man the greatest television character of all times. He lived with his wife Edith at 704 Hauser Street in Queens, New York. What television characters favorite chair can be seen in the National Museum of American History?

q.e: Archie Bunker's chair from "All in the Family" is in the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History.

q: Dawn Moore donated, at her Fathers request, an item worn by her fathers most famous character, John Reid. John Reid would be a combination of Zorro, Robin Hood and the Texas Rangers. By what name is John Reid better known?

q.e: John Reid is the Lone Ranger, played by Clayton Moore on TV (1949–57).

q: At this school, each student gets a full scholarship in return for doing about 15 hours of work each week on campus .

q.e: Berea College in Kentucky charges no tuition, and every student works at least 10 hours a week in its labor program.

q: This is a two year school that has a student body numbering under 30. It is over 40 miles from the nearest town. The school generates its own electricity from solar panels. Which college is this?

q.e: Deep Springs College is a tiny two-year school in the California desert with about 26 students.

q: This is a small engineering school that gives full scholarships to all of its students. Exams at this school are taken outside of class and students are allowed to use any source (other than other people) to answer test questions.

q.e: Olin College of Engineering (Massachusetts) gave full-tuition scholarships to all students, and it has an honor code.

q: In this school, undergraduates are allowed to design and teach their own courses. It was the first college to regularly admit women and to regularly admit African-American students.

q.e: Oberlin College was the first US college to admit women (1837) and Black students regularly.

q: About 85% of this schools students study abroad. It also has the largest percentage of students who serve in the Peace Corps.

q.e: Kalamazoo College in Michigan has a K-Plan with a heavy emphasis on study abroad.

q: In parts of Western Brittany, in France, cakes called kornigou are baked at Samhain. What natural shape are the cakes baked in?

q.e: In Brittany, "kornigou" are cakes baked in the shape of antlers or horns for Samhain.

q: Samhain was a time when the future was divined for the forthcoming year. Which of the following was not commonly used to divine the future at these times?

q.e: The Ouija board is a 19th-century invention. Samhain divination used apples, nuts and mirrors.

q: In New Orleans one of the biggest festivals of the year is the New Orleans Jazz and Heritage Festival. To locals it is known as Jazz Fest which celebrates the rich musical history of the city. In what year was Jazz Fest founded?

q.e: New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Festival began in 1970 in Congo Square.

q: A European country and an African one have one and the same motto - Virtus Unita Fortior. Name the countries.

q.e: "Virtus Unita Fortior" ("Virtue united is stronger") is Andorra's motto. Check the other country in the question.

q: Identify the language behind each of the given country mottoes: 1) Un isla feliz, 2) Odlar Yurdu, 3) Brunei darussalam.

q.e: Aruba's slogan is "Un isla feliz" in Papiamento, Azerbaijan is "Land of Fire" in Azeri, and "Brunei Darussalam" is Arabic-derived.

q: Which of the following phrases is the state motto of Switzerland as well as the motto of a famous book by Alexandre Dumas?
Unus pro omnibus, omnes pro uno

q.e: "Unus pro omnibus, omnes pro uno" ("One for all, all for one") is Switzerland's motto, popularized in Dumas's "The Three Musketeers."

q: Which of the following is Kenyas motto, that means Lets work together in Swahili?
Te mauri, te raoi ao te tabomoa

q.e: "Harambee" means "all pull together" in Swahili and is Kenya's motto.

q: Which phrase meaning God and my right is the official Royal motto of the UK?

q.e: Dieu et mon droit has served as the royal motto of the English and later British monarchy since King Henry V adopted it in the early 15th century.

q: Which French explorers are credited with bringing the Mardi Gras festivities to America?

q.e: Pierre Le Moyne d'Iberville and his brother Bienville celebrated Mardi Gras on the Mississippi in 1699.

q: In New Orleans, the Carnival Season is culminated with the Meeting of Courts, which is a meeting of the royal courts of which two Krewes?

q.e: On Mardi Gras evening, the courts of Rex and Comus meet at the Meeting of the Courts.

q: What is the name of the mythical ship on which Jason and the Argonauts sailed in quest for the Golden Fleece?

q.e: Constructed by the shipwright Argus with the guidance of the goddess Athena, the Argo carried Jason and his crew to Colchis to retrieve the Golden Fleece.

q: Which ship was described by Scottish author Robert Louis Stevenson in the novel The Treasure Island?

q.e: The Hispaniola was the ship in Robert Louis Stevenson's "Treasure Island."

q: What major body of water provided the citizens of Jerusalem with fresh water in later Biblical times?

q.e: The Pool of Siloam, fed by the Gihon spring through Hezekiah's Tunnel, supplied fresh water in Jerusalem.

q: Which of the following is not the name of a main street in Jerusalem?

q.e: Dizengoff Street is in Tel Aviv. Jerusalem's main streets include Jaffa Road and King George.

q: What is the Turkish word for hello?

q.e: Merhaba is the standard Turkish greeting for hello. Gunaydin means good morning, and Iyi aksamlar translates to good evening.

q: In the airline industry, a child travelling without an adult, is referred to as this.

q.e: An unaccompanied minor is abbreviated UM or UNMR in the airline industry.

q: If youre on the Blue Line, heading to Clinton/ Congress Station, which Tourist Attraction/ Area of Interest is nearby?

q.e: Greektown in Chicago is near the Blue Line's UIC–Halsted and Clinton stops.

q: The Blue Line has its Terminus at this major Airport, one of the busiest in the world.

q.e: The Chicago Blue Line's terminus is O'Hare International Airport.

q: In the early 18th century Charles XII of Sweden was undefeated until this happened. In 1812 Napoleons attempt to conquer Europe failed because of the same. Hitlers Operation Barbarossa was stopped by the same obstacle.
The lack of adequate water supplies in Northern Europe
The overabundance of muddy terrain in Northern Europe
The lack of grain in Eastern Europe

q.e: Charles XII (1709), Napoleon (1812) and Hitler (1941) were all defeated by the Russian winter and vast distances.

q: The Chinese army was able to invade South Korea in 1951 because what river froze?

q.e: The Chinese crossed the frozen Yalu River into Korea in late 1950, not 1951.

q: In 1954 the French were defeated at this very famous battle partly because their area of defense received 50% more rain than any other area of Vietnam, which badly effected their equipment.

q.e: The French lost at Dien Bien Phu on 7 May 1954. Heavy rain hampered the fortress.

q: The 1991 Ryder Cup matches, known as the War by the Shore, won by the US (or, more correctly lost by the Europeans) were played where in South Carolina?
The Dunes Golf and Beach Club, Dunes Course, in Myrtle Beach
Harbour Town Golf Links at Hilton Head

q.e: The 1991 Ryder Cup at Kiawah Island's Ocean Course in South Carolina was nicknamed "The War by the Shore."

q: Which of these South American capital cities is the farthest north?

q.e: Caracas and Bogotá are further north than Asunción (Paraguay), which is at about 25°S.

q: What was the name of the old capital of Thailand, founded in 1350?

q.e: The Ayutthaya Kingdom ruled from 1350 until 1767, when the city was sacked by the Burmese army, leading to the capital moving south to Thonburi and then Bangkok.

q: Name King Bhumipols wife whom he married on April 28, 1950.

q.e: Queen Sirikit married King Bhumibol Adulyadej on 28 April 1950.

q: If you rent a yacht in Monte Carlo and sail to Athens, which Mediterranean islands can you visit staying on the course?

q.e: From Monte Carlo toward Athens, one passes Corsica, Sardinia and Sicily, but Crete is further south-east.

q: You want to learn about the history of the Teutonic Knights, so you travel from Marienburg (present-day Malbork in Poland) to Reval (present-day Talinn) ALONG the Baltic shore. Which countries will you visit?

q.e: Along the Baltic shore from Malbork to Tallinn: Poland, Russia (Kaliningrad), Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia.

q: You are now the captain of a German boat and you take tourists down the river Danube. Which European capitals can you visit?

q.e: Flowing roughly 1,770 miles (2,850 km), the Danube passes through more countries than any other river and touches four European capital cities: Vienna (Austria), Bratislava (Slovakia), Budapest (Hungary), and Belgrade (Serbia).

q: If you were a Japanese fisherman sailing from north to south, in which order will you pass the main islands of your country?

q.e: From north to south, Japan's main islands are Hokkaido, Honshu, Shikoku and Kyushu.

q: What castle was the inspiration for Disneylands Sleeping Beauty Castle?

q.e: Walt Disney visited Bavaria's Neuschwanstein Castle, commissioned by King Ludwig II in 1869, which inspired the design for Disneyland's iconic 1955 Sleeping Beauty Castle.

q: Which Turkish town is home to the odd-looking rock formations called fairy chimneys?

q.e: Cappadocia, in central Turkey, is known for "fairy chimneys" (tuff pillars) around Göreme.

q: What Portuguese town inspired Lord Byron to write the "Wanderings of Childe Harold�?

q.e: Lord Byron praised Sintra as a "glorious Eden" in "Childe Harold's Pilgrimage."

q: Academicians have debated the origins of La Jollas name, but it is generally accepted that the name comes from a variation of the Spanish la joya which means what?

q.e: "La Jolla" probably derives from the Spanish "la joya," "the jewel."

q: What sword do US Marine Officers carry?

q.e: US Marine officers carry the Mameluke sword, after Lieutenant Presley O'Bannon's 1805 deeds in Tripoli.

q: What type of knot do US Marine officers wear atop their covers?

q.e: The quatrefoil is the cross-shaped braid on Marine officer covers (hats).

q: What is the capital of the group of four volcanic islands, known as the Pitcairn Islands?

q.e: Adamstown is the capital of the Pitcairn Islands, settled by Bounty mutineers.

q: The Vatican City has its own bank – Instituto per le Opere di Releigione or simply the Vatican Bank as it is more popular. This bank is owner of the only ATM in the country which is unique and famous with which of these features?
It is blessed by the Pope.

q.e: The Vatican's ATM offers instructions in Latin.

q: Rooms in Japanese houses and apartments are typically measured by which of the following?
The number of tatami mats in the room
The number of futons that will fit in the room

q.e: Japanese room sizes are measured in tatami mats, such as a six-mat room.

q: In America, it is not unusual to find buildings with no thirteenth floor. In Japan, which floor of a hotel might one find missing?

q.e: The number four in Japanese can be pronounced 'shi', which is a homophone for death (死). As a result, many Japanese hotels and hospitals omit the fourth floor.

q: This is when the first metal coins appeared.

q.e: The first metal coins appeared around 600 BC in Lydia (modern Turkey), though China had bronze imitations earlier.

q: American Indians used beaded shells as money. They called them this.

q.e: Wampum are beads made from shells, used by Native Americans of the Northeast.

q: Operation Deadlight was the code name for the scuttling of U-boats surrendered to the Allies after the defeat of Germany, near the end of World War II. How many U-boats were scuttled?

q.e: Operation Deadlight scuttled 121 U-boats in late 1945 and early 1946.

q: This British submarine, under the command of lieutenant-commander Malcolm David Wanklyn, completed 24 patrols, sinking around 120,000 tons of enemy shipping.

q.e: HMS Upholder under Malcolm Wanklyn sank about 120,000 tons in the Mediterranean in 1941–42 and earned a VC.

q: The Brook Farm area was a settlement of intellectuals on the outskirts of Hartford. Among its distinguished residents were Harriet Beecher Stowe and this author.

q.e: Harriet Beecher Stowe and Mark Twain lived in the Nook Farm community in Hartford, Connecticut. Brook Farm was near Boston.

q: Who was the first woman to win Time magazines title Man of the Year?

q.e: Wallis Simpson was Time's Woman of the Year (billed as "Man of the Year") for 1936.

q: He was the first European to be selected Man of the Year by Time magazine. He was also the first winner to be executed in his country for treason.

q.e: Pierre Laval, French politician, was Time's Man of the Year for 1931 and was executed in 1945 for treason.

q: In 1986 this brave woman won Time magazines Man of the Year award. Three years earlier she witnessed the assassination of her husband.

q.e: Corazon Aquino, whose husband Ninoy was assassinated in 1983, was Time's Woman of the Year 1986.

q: When he was voted Man of the Year his photograph was not put on the cover of Time magazine.

q.e: Adolf Hitler was Time's Man of the Year for 1938; the cover was an illustration, a painting of Hitler as organ-grinder.

q: In 1968 the Apollo astronauts were chosen for Time magazines Man of the Year award. Who were they ?

q.e: Frank Borman, Jim Lovell and Bill Anders of Apollo 8 were Time's Men of the Year for 1968.

q: This man, named Person of the Year by Time magazine in 2001, stood tall after the 9/11 and inspired his city to get through the terrible attack.

q.e: Rudy Giuliani, mayor of New York City, was Time's Person of the Year for 2001.

q: Cynthia Cooper, Coleen Rowley, and Sherron Watkins were granted Time magazines Person of the Year award. Under what title did they win?

q.e: Cynthia Cooper, Coleen Rowley and Sherron Watkins were "The Whistleblowers," Person of the Year 2002.

q: Which is the longest river flowing through Poland?

q.e: The Vistula (Wisla) is Poland's longest river, stretching roughly 651 miles (1,047 km) from the Barania Gora mountains to the Baltic Sea near Gdansk.

q: Poland has suffered many wars and has been occupied for many years. But Polish troops have been the attacking side as well. Which current European capital has never been occupied by the Polish army?

q.e: Polish forces took Moscow (1610) and Kyiv (1920), and Prague, but never Budapest.

q: What is the lower house of the Polish Parliament called?

q.e: The Sejm is the lower house of Poland's parliament. The Senate is the upper house.

q: This U.S. Senator from the 60s and 70s was known as Senator Wheat for his work at getting a higher price for wheat which during that time North Dakota was the leading producer.

q.e: Milton R. Young was a US Senator from North Dakota for 1945–1981.

q: This city and historical park in North Dakota boasts the rarity of having an albino buffalo. At the birth of White Cloud, Native American people from around the country came to view this creature, which is looked on spiritually by Native American Indians.

q.e: Jamestown, North Dakota, was home to the white buffalo calf "White Cloud," born in 1996.

q: General George Armstrong Custer left Fort Lincoln on the southern edge of this North Dakota town (named after the Native American tribes from that area) on his fateful trip to The Little Bighorn.

q.e: Custer left Fort Abraham Lincoln near Mandan, North Dakota, on 17 May 1876.

q: In 1953, television first came to Alaska. What were the call letters of the first broadcasting television station in Alaska?

q.e: KENI-TV in Anchorage became Alaska's first TV station in 1953.

q: Which United Nations representative was forced to leave Sudan in October, 2006 because of comments made about the Sudanese Army?

q.e: UN envoy Jan Pronk was expelled from Sudan in October 2006 after commenting on the army's defeats in Darfur.

q: There is much speculation as to how many people died as a direct result of the Darfur conflict. What figure do most Non-governmental organizations use when calculating the total number of deaths?

q.e: Estimates of deaths in Darfur range from 300,000 (UN) to 400,000 or more.

q: What is the name of the volcanic mountainous region in the center of Darfur, Sudan?

q.e: The Jebel Marra is a volcanic massif in Darfur, reaching 3,042 m.

q: Designed by Skidmore, Owings Merrill LLP, this building consists of 9 bundled square tubes, each 75 feet wide with no columns between the core and the perimeter.

q.e: The Sears Tower (now Willis Tower) in Chicago, designed by SOM, is a bundle of nine square tubes.

q: Name the Roman governor of Judaea who, according to the gospels, authorized the Crucifixion of Jesus.

q.e: Pontius Pilate served as the fifth prefect of the Roman province of Judaea from around 26 to 36 AD under Emperor Tiberius. Valerius Gratus was his direct predecessor in the role.

q: According to a tradition among followers of Eastern Christianity, this disciple of Jesus Christ brought cooked eggs at his tomb and they miraculously turned red.

q.e: In Orthodox tradition, Mary Magdalene brought a white egg to Emperor Tiberius, and it turned red.

q: What is the real first name of Screech Diamond of Saved by the Bell fame, who was forced to declare bankruptcy due to the loss of hundreds of thousands of dollars?

q.e: Screech actor Dustin Diamond filed for bankruptcy in 2015, after his Saved by the Bell tell-all.

q: Two Out of Three [one might say ] Aint Bad, but this singer/actor had a $1,600,000 debt in 1983.

q.e: Meat Loaf declared bankruptcy in 1983, with $1.6 million in debts. His song "Two Out of Three Ain't Bad" is from 1977.

q: Coppertone was born in the kitchen of Miami pharmacist, Benjamin Green. It became one of Americas leading sun care products through the strength of its advertising campaign featuring the Coppertone Girl. What actress got her start as the 1965 Coppertone Girl?

q.e: Jodie Foster, age 3, was the Coppertone girl in 1965 TV ads.

q: This Filipino-American serial killer went on a murder spree, killing five people, that ended with his suicide on July 23, 1997.

q.e: Andrew Cunanan shot Gianni Versace in July 1997, and died by suicide on 23 July 1997.

q: Nathaniel Hawthorne is said to have changed the spelling of his name for what reason?
He was a descendant of John Hathorne, a judge in the Salem witch trials.
He was a descendant of Nathan Hawthorne, accused of an Indian massacre.
It was the one he chose to write under.
He was a descendant of Nathaniel Hathorne, a judge in the Salem witch trials.

q.e: Nathaniel Hawthorne added a "w" to distance himself from his ancestor John Hathorne, a Salem witch trials judge.

q: In which form of Israeli cooperative agricultural system, several farms agree to buy and use large machinery commonly?

q.e: A moshav is a cooperative agricultural community of individual farms, which share machinery and marketing.

q: This is the year of the termination of the British mandate of Palestine and the signing of the Declaration of the Establishment of the State of Israel.

q.e: The British mandate ended and Israel declared independence on 14 May 1948.

q: In 1977, this Arab nation leader signed a peace agreement, known as the Camp David Accords with Israeli Prime Minister Menachem Begin.

q.e: Egyptian president Anwar Sadat signed the Camp David Accords with Menachem Begin in 1978, brokered by Jimmy Carter.

q: Only the little people pay taxes, declared the Queen of Mean. What lady faced charges of tax evasion, mail fraud, extortion and filing false tax returns for over 4 million dollars?

q.e: Leona Helmsley, the "Queen of Mean," was convicted of tax evasion in 1989.

q: This house, situated in Westerham, Kent was bought by Winston Churchill in 1922.

q.e: Winston Churchill bought Chartwell in Westerham, Kent, in 1922.

q: These Victorian gardens in Staffordshire represent China, Egypt and a Scottish glen.

q.e: Biddulph Grange in Staffordshire has a Chinese garden, an Egyptian garden and a Scottish glen.

q: What fountain, sculpted by Thomas Waldo Story, features female figures and cherubs dancing next to a giant shell?
Тhe Fountain of Love in Cliveden
Artemis Fountain in Hyde Park, London
The Victoria Fountain in Old Steine, Brighton

q.e: The Fountain of Love at Cliveden, by Thomas Waldo Story, shows dancing figures around a giant shell.

q: This county seat is known as The Military Capital of the Revolution, and contains sites like Fords Mansion and Jockey Hollow. It was where George Washington encamped in the brutal winter of 1777.

q.e: Morristown, New Jersey, was Washington's winter headquarters in 1777 and 1779–80, "Military Capital of the Revolution."

q: This county, formed in 1714, has Flemington as its county seat.

q.e: Hunterdon County, New Jersey, formed in 1714, has Flemington as its county seat.

q: Of the following 4 civilizations which occupied Mesopotamia, which came first?

q.e: The Sumerians came first, then the Akkadians (c. 2334 BC), Babylonians and Assyrians.

q: Which of the following pairings of ancient civilization and modern-day country is NOT CORRECT?

q.e: The Phoenicians came from what is now Lebanon, not Egypt.

q: Which king of the Akkadians conquered Sumeria to unite Mesopotamia under one ruler for the first time?

q.e: Sargon of Akkad conquered Sumer around 2334 BC and created the world's first empire.

q: This Babylonian ruler established written laws. His laws were one of the first written codes of law in recorded history.

q.e: Hammurabi ruled the First Babylonian Dynasty from roughly 1792 to 1750 BCE. His famous code, consisting of 282 laws carved onto a towering basalt stele, introduced the concept of lex talionis, commonly known as an eye for an eye.

q: This mountain contains the highest peak in Antarctica, and is located about 750 miles (1,200 km) from the South Pole.

q.e: Mount Vinson, situated within the Vinson Massif in the Sentinel Range, is the highest peak in Antarctica at 16,050 feet (4,892 m). It was first summited in December 1966 by an American Alpine Club expedition led by Nicholas Clinch.

q: This mountain range is located in Asia, its name means abode of snow, and it lies across the territory of six countries.

q.e: The name Himalaya comes from the Sanskrit words 'hima' (snow) and 'alaya' (dwelling or abode). The range spans about 1,500 miles (2,400 km) across India, Pakistan, Nepal, Bhutan, China, and Afghanistan.

q: This mountain range is located in North America and its highest peak is Mount Mitchell.

q.e: Mount Mitchell, in North Carolina (2,037 m), is the highest peak of the Appalachians.

q: What is the highest mountain on the Australian mainland?

q.e: Located in the Snowy Mountains of New South Wales, Mount Kosciuszko is mainland Australia's highest peak at 2,228 meters (7,310 feet). Mawson Peak on Heard Island is higher overall for Australian territory at 2,745 meters.

q: Where is the headquarters of the Toyota Motor Corporation located?

q.e: Toyota is headquartered in Toyota City, Aichi Prefecture, Japan.

q: This period, in which some newspapers and magazines built their reputations thanks to their use of photography, is known as the Golden Age of Photojournalism.

q.e: The Golden Age of Photojournalism is usually the 1930s to the 1950s, with Life and Look magazines.

q: Which journalist received the Pulitzer Prize in 1964 for his brilliant coverage of President John F. Kennedys assassination?

q.e: Merriman Smith of UPI won the 1964 Pulitzer for his coverage of Kennedy's assassination.

q: Which baleen whale that can be seen in Alaskan waters has a white band on each flipper?

q.e: The minke whale has a white band on each flipper and lives in Alaskan waters.

q: Plus 15, opened in 1970 and located in Calgary, Canada, is what type of modern transport infrastructure?

q.e: The +15 in Calgary is a network of enclosed pedestrian skywalks 15 feet above street level (opened 1970).

q: In his work History of New York (1809), this author Americanized Sinterklaas into Santa Claus and depicted him as a thick-bellied Dutch sailor with a pipe in a green winter coat.

q.e: Washington Irving's "A History of New York" (1809) described a Dutch Saint Nicholas and was echoed in later Santa images.

q: Summertime, which has become a popular jazz standard, was written by George Gershwin for this opera.

q.e: "Summertime" is from George Gershwin's opera "Porgy and Bess" (1935).

q: Saint-Tropez, France has been referred to as the playground to jetsetters, fashion models, and millionaires. What former fashion model and actress made the resort world-famous in the 1950s?

q.e: Brigitte Bardot made Saint-Tropez famous after "And God Created Woman" (1956).

q: Who originally recorded the 1966 song Summer in the City, which was later covered by B. B. King and Joe Cocker?

q.e: The Lovin' Spoonful recorded "Summer in the City" in 1966.

q: What actress wore the iconic white bikini in the 1962 James Bond film, Dr. No?

q.e: Ursula Andress wore the white bikini in Dr. No (1962) as Honey Ryder.

q: The Mall of America, one of the largest entertainment and retail complexes in the U.S., opened in 1992 on the site of the old Met Stadium. Which suburb of Minneapolis is it located in?

q.e: The Mall of America is in Bloomington, Minnesota, where Metropolitan Stadium once stood.

q: At the time of European contact, the Minnesota region was home to these two large tribal groups.

q.e: The Ojibwe (Anishinaabe) and Dakota were the large tribes in Minnesota at contact.

q: The famous cartoonist Charles Schulz, who was born in Minneapolis in 1922, developed a nationwide cartoon strip called Peanuts. What was the name of the dog in the cartoon strip?

q.e: Charles Schulz (1922–2000), born in Minneapolis, created "Peanuts" and Snoopy the beagle.

q: In the late 1880s and 1890s, two brothers, Dr. William and Dr. Charles Mayo, joined forces with an order of Catholic nuns to form one of the worlds best-known medical establishments. What town is it located in?

q.e: The Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota, grew out of the Mayo brothers' work with the Sisters of St. Francis.

q: Who was the first US President to be named Man (or Person) of the Year by Time magazine?

q.e: Franklin D. Roosevelt was Time's Man of the Year in 1932, the first US president to get the title.

q: Who was the first monarch chosen as Man of the Year by Time magazine?

q.e: Haile Selassie, Emperor of Ethiopia, was Time's Man of the Year for 1935, the first monarch.

q: They were the first couple to win Time magazines Man of the Year award?
King George VIII and Wallis Simpson

q.e: Chiang Kai-shek and Soong Mei-ling (Madame Chiang) were Time's Man and Wife of the Year in 1937, the first couple.

q: In 1998, Time magazine used an Internet poll to help them select Man of the Year. They rejected the person selected by this pole. Who was that person?

q.e: Time rejected the winner of its 1998 online poll, wrestler Mick Foley. It chose Bill Clinton and Ken Starr.

q: Time magazines 1993 Man of the Yearaward was given to four people. What were they referred to as?

q.e: Time's 1993 "The Peacemakers" were Nelson Mandela, F.W. de Klerk, Yasser Arafat and Yitzhak Rabin.

q: Indianapolis 500 is an automobile race held annually over Memorial Day weekend. What driver won the first edition of the race in 1911?

q.e: Ray Harroun won the first Indianapolis 500 in 1911 in a Marmon Wasp, averaging 74.6 mph.

q: The section of the Catskill Mountains famous for its Jewish resorts populated by comics like Rodney Dangerfield, Sid Caesar, Mel Brooks, Woody Allen, and dozens more was known as The ________ Belt.

q.e: The "Borscht Belt" resort area in the Catskills nurtured Jewish comedians.

q: What is the highest point in New York City?

q.e: Todt Hill on Staten Island (124 m) is the highest natural point in New York City.

q: How high is Mt. Marcy, the highest peak in New York State?

q.e: Mount Marcy, in the Adirondacks, is 5,344 ft (1,629 m).

q: What is done to many coins so that unscrupulous people can not clip off part of he coin to melt down?
Coins have special radioactive particles so that the pieced can be traced.
Coins are made of very malleable metals.

q.e: Coins have milled (reeded) edges so that metal can't be clipped off unnoticed.

q: Who is recognized as the first female millionaire?

q.e: Madam C. J. Walker (born Sarah Breedlove) is often cited as the first self-made female millionaire in America.

q: What did ATT announce in December, 2007?
It would eliminate all of its payphones by the end of 2008.
It would accept credit cards at payphones.
It would be called US SouthWestern Bell.
It would raise payphones rates to $1 for the first minute.

q.e: In December 2007, AT&T announced it would exit the payphone business by the end of 2008.

q: Which of these is considered the first supermarket in the USA?

q.e: King Kullen, opened in 1930 in Queens, New York, is often called America's first supermarket.

q: In 2004 this Russian company, founded in 1989, accounted for about 93% of Russian natural gas production.

q.e: Gazprom, Russia's state gas company, was formed in 1989.

q: Who is considered the first President of the Philippines?

q.e: Emilio Aguinaldo became the first president of the Philippines in 1899.

q: Who is the seventh President of the Philippines?

q.e: Ramon Magsaysay was the Philippines' 7th president (1953–57), who died in a plane crash.

q: The first recorded association of Valentines Day with romantic love is found in the poem Parlement of Foules (Parliament of Fowls), written by this medieval English author.

q.e: Chaucer's "Parlement of Foules" (c. 1382) links St. Valentine's Day with romantic love.

q: In Sleepless in Seattle, Meg Ryans character impulsively writes a letter to Sam Baldwin (Tom Hanks) suggesting that he meet her on top of the Empire State Building on Valentines Day. What classic romantic movie inspired Sleepless in Seattle?

q.e: "Sleepless in Seattle" references "An Affair to Remember" (1957), in which lovers agree to meet atop the Empire State Building.

q: The first woman to be elected governor, in her own right, was from Connecticut. Name her.

q.e: Ella Grasso (Connecticut, 1975) was the first woman elected US governor in her own right.

q: What Spanish navigator first used the name Las Islas Filipinas (The Philippine Islands)?

q.e: Ruy López de Villalobos named the islands "Las Islas Filipinas" in 1543, after Prince Philip (later Philip II).

q: What did Spanish invaders call Pygmies, the aborigines of the Philippines?

q.e: The Spaniards called the indigenous dark-skinned Aetas of the Philippines "Negritos."

q: What is the capital of Romania?

q.e: Bucuresti (Bucharest) has been the capital of Romania since 1862. It is often confused with Budapest, which is the capital of neighboring Hungary, while Belgrade is the capital of Serbia.

q: This Romanian city, which was the Axis main source of oil, was heavily bombed during WWII by the US Air Force.

q.e: Ploiești, Romania, supplied the Axis with oil, and it was bombed by US aircraft (Operation Tidal Wave, 1943).

q: Which of these IT companies has its headquarters in downtown Detroit?

q.e: Compuware's headquarters is in downtown Detroit.

q: Which district in downtown Detroit is famous for its restaurants and casino?

q.e: Greektown, Detroit, has restaurants and the Greektown Casino.

q: 8 Mile Road in Detroit was featured in a movie about rapper Eminem. The road is 8 miles away from which of these?

q.e: 8 Mile Road is 8 miles north of the city center in Detroit, near Campus Martius.

q: Which of the following is the largest and most populous of the four main islands of Japan?

q.e: Honshu is Japan's main island, accounting for roughly 60 percent of the country's total land area and home to major cities like Tokyo, Osaka, and Kyoto. Hokkaido is the second largest, while Kyushu and Shikoku are smaller southern islands.

q: During mid-summer many Japanese return to their ancestral homes to pay homage to their departed family members. What is this custom called?

q.e: Obon is a Buddhist festival honoring ancestral spirits, in mid-summer.

q: In the 1990s the site of the Tokyo Municipal government was moved to two tall twin towers located in which Tokyo municipality?

q.e: The Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building (1991) in Shinjuku has twin towers.

q: To get from Tokyo to Osaka on the Shinkansen (Bullet Train) one must pass through which of the following cities?

q.e: The Tokaido Shinkansen from Tokyo to Osaka stops in Nagoya, along with Yokohama and Kyoto.

q: The Common European Framework divides language learners into different levels based on what a learner is supposed to be able to do in reading, listening, speaking and writing. How many are the levels?

q.e: The Common European Framework (CEFR) has six levels, from A1 to C2.

q: What two languages are not official European Union languages, although they are official languages of some of the member states?

q.e: Luxembourgish and Turkish aren't official EU languages, though they're official languages in Luxembourg and Cyprus (Turkish).

q: According to Leonardo Orban, the first Romanian EU Commissioner, this language is the ideal solution for the language problems in the EU, as it is a neutral, logical, easy-to-learn and rich.

q.e: Leonard Orban, EU Commissioner for Multilingualism, praised Esperanto, a constructed language.

q: Although it is the most populous of all American cities, where did New York City rank in 2005 compared to other big cities in the world?

q.e: New York City ranked about 13th among the world's largest metropolitan areas around 2005.

q: What is the name of the main seaside strollway in the city of Puerto Vallarta?

q.e: Puerto Vallarta's Malecón is its seaside promenade.

q: Which of the following is a folkloric genre of music native to Puerto Rico? Essentially utilizing maracas and percussion instruments.

q.e: Plena is a Puerto Rican folk genre with panderetas and percussion.

q: Built on 1963 in Puerto Rico, this is one of worlds largest radio telescopes.

q.e: The Arecibo Observatory telescope (1963) in Puerto Rico collapsed in December 2020.

q: La primavera, or Spring, is Concerto No. 1, in E major which is part of The Four Seasons violin concertos. Who composed The Four Seasons?

q.e: Italian composer Antonio Vivaldi published The Four Seasons in 1725 as part of his Opus 8 collection, pioneering program music that depicted natural elements in sound.

q: What phrase means good morning in Filipino?

q.e: "Magandang umaga" means "good morning" in Filipino.

q: What volcano in the Philippines is famous for its perfectly-shaped cone?

q.e: Mayon Volcano in Albay is famed for its near-perfect cone.

q: Who is the first president of the 1st Philippine Republic?

q.e: Emilio Aguinaldo served as the inaugural president of the First Philippine Republic, established with the proclamation of the Malolos Constitution in January 1899. Manuel L. Quezon became the first president of the later Philippine Commonwealth in 1935.

q: Who made the following statement: I prefer a country run like hell by Filipinos to a country run like heaven by Americans. Because, however bad a Filipino government might be, we can always change it.?

q.e: Manuel Quezon said he'd rather have a "government run like hell by Filipinos than one run like heaven by Americans."

q: Which of the following was not among Alcatraz inmates?
Robert Franklin Stroud (the Birdman of Alcatraz)

q.e: Alcatraz inmates included Al Capone and Machine Gun Kelly. Mafalda Capone is not known to be one.

q: Which socialist theorist advocated permanent revolution, arguing that a socialist state could only prosper if the capitalist states that influenced it also became socialist.

q.e: Leon Trotsky advocated "permanent revolution," unlike Stalin's "socialism in one country."

q: Which of these notable Yale graduates is not correctly matched with the movie they directed?
Home for the Holidays - Jodie Foster

q.e: Gentleman's Agreement (1947) was directed by Elia Kazan, not George Roy Hill.

q: What Yale graduate is credited with creating the first time bomb and first submarine ever used in combat?

q.e: David Bushnell (Yale class of 1775) built the first submarine used in combat, the Turtle, and sea mines.

q: This actor, who earned an MFA from Yale School of Drama, is famous for his long-running roles on Law Order and Sex and the City.

q.e: Chris Noth, a Yale School of Drama MFA, played Mike Logan on Law & Order and Mr. Big on Sex and the City.

q: Although it was recognized on September 27, 1821, the Independence of Mexico from Spain was declared on September 16, 1810 by this priest.

q.e: Father Miguel Hidalgo's "Grito de Dolores" on 16 September 1810 started the Mexican War of Independence.

q: Vicente Fernandez, Pedro Infante, Javier Solis, and Lola Beltran are representatives of this traditional, Mexican genre of music.

q.e: Ranchera is traditional Mexican music, sung by Vicente Fernández, Pedro Infante and Lola Beltrán.

q: What do we call the dwellings built by the Pawnees?

q.e: The Pawnee built earth lodges, large domed homes of earth and timber.

q: In what year did the US Government pass a law making the government responsible for preserving the languages of indigenous peoples of the USA?

q.e: The Native American Languages Act of 1990 made it US policy to preserve indigenous languages.

q: Which famous Native American ballerina has been honored for her great achievements?

q.e: Maria Tallchief (Osage) was America's first major prima ballerina.

q: Which list includes the five native American tribes regarded by Early Europeans as "civilized?
Seminole, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Cherokee, and Creek
Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, and Iroquois
Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, and Cree
Cherokee, Choctaw, Creek, Chirokawa, and Cree

q.e: The Five Civilized Tribes were the Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek (Muscogee) and Seminole.

q: This landlocked African country is one of the 10 poorest countries in the world. Its capital, Bujumbura, is located on Lake Tanganyika.

q.e: Burundi's capital, Bujumbura, is on Lake Tanganyika.

q: This land-locked country is bordered on 3 sides by the Republic of South Africa, and on the east by Mozambique. It has the highest HIV/AIDS prevalence in the world at 39% according to 2006 estimates.

q.e: Eswatini (formerly Swaziland) is surrounded by South Africa and Mozambique. It had one of the highest HIV rates.

q: The click languages of Africa (also known as the Khoisan languages) are spoken in all of the following countries except one. In which of these countries is a click language NOT widely spoken?

q.e: Ethiopia has no Khoisan-type click languages. Southern African countries do.

q: Oklahoma is the birthplace of many famous astronauts, but this one was the first Native American in space.

q.e: John Herrington, a Chickasaw, was the first Native American in space in 2002.

q: What English Romantic poet wrote the poem To Autumn, which describes the season as a time of mellow fruitfulness but also evokes a sense of melancholy?

q.e: John Keats wrote "To Autumn" (1819) about "Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness."

q: What English novelist and poet, best known for her book Wuthering Heights, wrote a poem containing the verses Every leaf speaks bliss to me/ fluttering from the autumn tree?

q.e: Emily Brontë wrote those lines in a poem. Her only novel is Wuthering Heights (1847).

q: This nearly submerged continent or microcontinent, also known as Tasmantis, sank after breaking away from Antarctica between 85 and 130 million years ago.

q.e: Zealandia is an underwater continent roughly 4.9 million square kilometers in size, with approximately 94 percent submerged beneath the southwest Pacific Ocean. New Zealand and New Caledonia are its largest above-water landmasses.

q: A small portion of this underwater volcanic region breaks sea level, forming the Kerguelen Islands, Heard Island and the McDonald Islands.

q.e: The Kerguelen Plateau, a submarine plateau in the Indian Ocean, includes the Kerguelen and Heard Islands.

q: This autonomous region is located in the Horn of Africa and is part of the Somali Republic.

q.e: Somaliland declared independence from Somalia in 1991 but is unrecognized internationally.

q: Garowe is the capital of this region in northeastern Somalia.

q.e: Garowe is the capital of Puntland, an autonomous region in northeastern Somalia.

q: This supercontinent broke up into two continents, then into the seven continents existing today.

q.e: Pangea formed roughly 335 million years ago and began breaking apart around 175 million years ago. It initially split into Laurasia in the north and Gondwana in the south before further dividing into the modern continents.

q: Which historical figure became dictator of Nicaraguas government in 1937?

q.e: Anastasio Somoza García took power in Nicaragua in 1937, founding a family dynasty.

q: Which of the following is not an actual city in Nicaragua?

q.e: Tegucigalpa is the capital of Honduras, not Nicaragua.

q: Nicaraguas folk music predominantly implements this musical instrument.

q.e: The marimba is central to Nicaraguan folk music.

q: Which of the following is one of Nicaraguas boxing world champions?

q.e: Alexis Argüello was a Nicaraguan boxing champion in three weight classes.

q: This author, who graduated from Harvard summa cum laude in 1954, received the Pulitzer Prize for two of his Rabbit novels.

q.e: John Updike graduated summa cum laude from Harvard in 1954 and won Pulitzers for "Rabbit Is Rich" and "Rabbit at Rest."

q: Which Harvard graduate is not correctly matched with the literary work he created?
Norman Mailer - The Naked and the Dead

q.e: "Look Homeward, Angel" was by Thomas Wolfe, a UNC graduate (who also attended Harvard).

q: In 1988, this Harvard graduate became the first female Prime Minister of her country.

q.e: Benazir Bhutto (Harvard 1973) became prime minister of Pakistan in 1988, the first woman to lead a Muslim-majority country.

q: This Israeli American actress, who graduated from Harvard College with a bachelors degree in psychology, became popular when she was cast in the Star Wars prequel trilogy.

q.e: Natalie Portman graduated from Harvard in 2003 with a psychology degree and played Padmé Amidala.

q: This Harvard graduate, also known as the Unabomber, carried out a campaign of mail bombings.

q.e: Theodore Kaczynski, the Unabomber, graduated from Harvard in 1962.

q: In the 1989 movie Dad Ted Danson becomes his fathers caretaker as a result of which they become closer. Who played his father?

q.e: Jack Lemmon played Ted Danson's ailing father in "Dad" (1989).

q: Two agricultural crops, both cultivated by slave labor, were the primary reason that South Carolina was one of the wealthiest of the colonies before the American Revolution. What were the two crops?

q.e: Rice and indigo, grown with slave labor, made colonial South Carolina rich.

q: Lyme Park in Cheshire, England is believed to be haunted by which of the following?

q.e: Lyme Park (Cheshire) is said to be haunted by a phantom funeral procession and other ghosts.

q: What are the names of the two schools of higher education in Haifa?
Haifa University and Ben Gurion Universitry.
Haifa University and Bar Ilan University.
Bar Ilan University and the Weitzmann Institute.

q.e: Haifa has the University of Haifa and the Technion – Israel Institute of Technology.

q: What religion's headquarters is located in the city of Haifa?

q.e: The Bahá'í World Centre in Haifa includes the Shrine of the Báb.

q: What do the following cities have in common with Haifa: Portsmouth in UK, Marseille in France, Antwerp in Belgium?
They are some of the sister cites of Haifa.
They are approximately the same size as Haifa.
They have approximately the same population as Haifa.
The are all on the same latitude as Haifa.

q.e: Portsmouth, Marseille and Antwerp are sister cities of Haifa.

q: In which type of aircraft is the tailplane located ahead of the main lifting surfaces?

q.e: A canard aircraft has its small wings (foreplanes) ahead of the main wing.

q: What is the acronym for the small generator, used to start the main engines of an aircraft?

q.e: An APU (auxiliary power unit) starts the main engines and powers systems on the ground.

q: Which term refers to the angle between the wing of a plane and the local horizon?

q.e: Dihedral angle is the upward angle of wings relative to the horizontal, which gives roll stability.

q: Which American naval vessel disappeared in 1918 with 306 passengers on board?

q.e: USS Cyclops vanished in the Bermuda Triangle in March 1918 with 306 people.

q: This place in the Netherlands, known as the Garden of Europe, is famous for a large permanent display of tulips.

q.e: Keukenhof, in Lisse, Netherlands, is the "Garden of Europe," with millions of tulips.

q: On December 15, 1939 all eyes were on Atlanta as Clark Gable, Vivian Lee and many other Hollywood stars came out for the long-awaited premeir of Gone With the Wind. At what theater did the movie make its world debut?

q.e: "Gone with the Wind" premiered at Loew's Grand Theatre in Atlanta on 15 December 1939.

q: What traditional greeting is used by the Maori, the indigenous Polynesian people of New Zealand?

q.e: The hongi is a traditional Maori greeting where two people press their noses and foreheads together. This physical contact symbolizes the sharing of the breath of life, known as ha.

q: What is the official state sport of the U.S. state of Alaska?

q.e: Mushing (dogsled racing) is Alaska's state sport.

q: The United States Census Bureau defined the Ashtabula area as what?

q.e: The Census Bureau classifies Ashtabula, Ohio, as a micropolitan statistical area.

q: The Pentagon is controlled by the Secretary of Defense. Who was the first one to hold that position in 1947?

q.e: James Forrestal was the first Secretary of Defense (1947–49).

q: Where did the Titanic depart from en route to New York City?

q.e: RMS Titanic set sail on its ill-fated maiden voyage from Southampton, England, on April 10, 1912. It called at Cherbourg in France and Queenstown (now Cobh) in Ireland before heading into the open Atlantic toward New York.

q: If you are stationed in Germany, you will not be on a post, but most likely on which of the following?

q.e: US soldiers in Germany are stationed on a Kaserne (barracks), not a "post."

q: What did Howard Crater discover in 1922?

q.e: Howard Carter discovered Tutankhamun's tomb in the Valley of the Kings in November 1922.

q: Unthanksgiving Day is an annual event commemorating the survival of Native American peoples following the settlement of Europeans in the Western Hemisphere. Where is the event held?

q.e: The "Unthanksgiving Day" sunrise gathering is held on Alcatraz Island, since the 1970 occupation.

q: Which term collectively describes all parts of Earths surface where water is in frozen form?

q.e: The cryosphere includes ice sheets, glaciers, sea ice, snow and permafrost.

q: What popular actress portrayed Buffy Summers in the Buffy the Vampire Slayer TV series?

q.e: Sarah Michelle Gellar played Buffy Summers (1997–2003).

q: From which opera composed by George Gershwin is the famous aria Summertime?

q.e: Composed in 1934 for the folk opera Porgy and Bess, 'Summertime' features lyrics by DuBose Heyward and has gone on to become one of the most covered songs in music history.

q: Which treasure was discovered by Howard Carter in 1922?

q.e: Howard Carter discovered the intact tomb (KV62) of the boy Pharaoh Tutankhamun in Egypt's Valley of the Kings in November 1922, unearthing thousands of artifacts including the iconic gold burial mask.

q: What notable Portuguese novelist and playwright was honored with the 1998 Nobel Prize for literature?

q.e: José Saramago won the 1998 Nobel Prize in Literature. He wrote "Blindness."

q: What parrot is one of the national animals of Brazil?

q.e: The macaw (like the scarlet macaw) is a national animal of Brazil. The jaguar and rufous-bellied thrush are others.

q: In 1993, this large beverage production company, successfully mounted a massive PR campaign to restore customers confidence, after a syringe was found in a can of their products.

q.e: In 1993 PepsiCo faced a syringe-in-can hoax and responded with an effective PR campaign.

q: Who helped to establish the Missouri School of Journalism and the Columbia University Graduate School of Journalism, two of the most prestigious journalism schools in the US?

q.e: Joseph Pulitzer funded the Columbia School of Journalism and backed the Missouri School.

q: The name of this city means "Shelter under the tree�.

q.e: Kathmandu is derived from Kasthamandap, a wooden shelter ("wood pavilion").

q: Which resort town located near Rio de Janeiro is called The Saint Tropez of Brazil?

q.e: Búzios, a resort town near Rio, is called the "Saint-Tropez of Brazil" thanks to Brigitte Bardot's 1964 visit.

q: The life story of this man began in the central Iowa town of Winterset. He was born Marion Robert Morrison, the son of Clyde and Mary Brown Morrison. He went on to become a well-known actor who appeared in many western and war movies.

q.e: John Wayne was born Marion Robert Morrison in Winterset, Iowa, in 1907.

q: Glenn Miller, born March 1, 1904 in Clarinda, Iowa was a trombonist and leader of one of the most popular dance bands of the swing era. What was his real first name?

q.e: Glenn Miller's first name was Alton: Alton Glenn Miller, born in Clarinda, Iowa.

q: What is the national bird of Honduras?

q.e: The scarlet macaw is Honduras's national bird.

q: What is the currency of Honduras?

q.e: The Honduran lempira was introduced in 1931 and is named after Lempira, a 16th-century indigenous ruler of the Lenca people who led resistance against Spanish conquistadors.

q: What is the official language adopted by the government of Iceland?

q.e: Icelandic is Iceland's official language, and Icelandic Sign Language was recognized in 2011. Faroese isn't official.

q: What is the name of the traditional South Indian crepe made from rice and black lentils and eaten for breakfast or dinner?

q.e: Dosa is a fermented rice and urad dal crepe from South India.

q: What is the literal translation of the word pranahara, used commonly by some people to refer to the traditional Indian sweets called Sandesh?

q.e: "Pranahara" means "heart stealer" in Bengali and it's the old name for sandesh.

q: What traditional Indian beverage is made from female Cannabis?

q.e: Bhang is a cannabis preparation, eaten or drunk (often during Holi).

q: What is the official religion in England?

q.e: The Church of England (Anglican) is England's established church.

q: What place of historical importance in Constantinople is known nowadays as Sultan Ahmet Square?

q.e: The Hippodrome of Constantinople is now Istanbul's Sultanahmet Square.

q: Constantinople is located between the Golden Horn and this sea.

q.e: Constantinople (Istanbul) is between the Golden Horn and the Sea of Marmara.

q: This tradition of course camarguaise is anchored in several French departments. Which one is not among them?

q.e: Course camarguaise is in the Camargue region, in the Gard, Hérault and Bouches-du-Rhône. Lozère isn't one.

q: Music plays an important role in the French style of bullfighting, course camarguaise. What music is played every time something impressive happens in the arena?
Claude Debussy - En blanc et noir

q.e: At course camarguaise, the band plays the toreador song from Bizet's "Carmen" after an exciting moment.

q: What English rock band recorded the 1971 song July Morning?

q.e: Uriah Heep released "July Morning" on the album "Look at Yourself" (1971).

q: According to tradition, the weather on this saints feast day (15 July) will continue for forty days.

q.e: According to folklore, if it rains on St. Swithin's Day (15 July) it will rain for 40 days.

q: Horace Tabor contributed greatly to Denver, and Leadville, Colorado with Opera Houses, business buildings etc. but he is known best as the owner of which silver mine in Leadville?

q.e: Horace Tabor owned the Matchless Mine in Leadville, Colorado.

q: The highest sea cliffs in the world can be seen on this island.

q.e: Molokai's north-shore sea cliffs reach about 1,000 m, among the tallest on Earth.

q: What town is the largest settlement on the island of Hawaii and the the second largest settlement in the state of Hawaii?

q.e: Hilo is the largest town on the Big Island of Hawaii.

q: This landlocked province of the Philippines borders Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, Apayao, Kalinga and Moutain Province. Its capital is Bangued.
