q.e: Abra, a landlocked province in northern Luzon, has Bangued as its capital.

q: The Banaue Rice Terraces are located in what landlocked province of the Philippines?

q.e: The Banaue Rice Terraces are in Ifugao province.

q: This landlocked province, located in the Central Luzon region, is often referred to as the "Rice Granary of the Philippines�.

q.e: Nueva Ecija is the "Rice Granary of the Philippines."

q: In 1942, this province of the Philippines, which used to be a territory of the vast Cagayan Valley, was occupied by Japanese troops.

q.e: Nueva Vizcaya was part of the Cagayan Valley and was occupied by Japan in 1942.

q: This disputed area is a group of islands and reefs, located between the Macclesfield Bank and Luzon, Philippines in the South China Sea.

q.e: Scarborough Shoal is claimed by China and the Philippines in the South China Sea.

q: This extinct volcanic ridge is in the western Philippine Sea.

q.e: Benham Rise (Philippine Rise) is an undersea plateau east of Luzon in the Philippine Sea.

q: This Oscar-winning movie was set and filmed in the U.S. state of Oregon.
One Flew Over the Cuckoos Nest

q.e: "One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest" (1975) was filmed in Oregon and swept the Oscars.

q: What is the official musical instrument of the U.S. state of Louisiana?

q.e: The diatonic (Cajun) accordion is Louisiana's official state musical instrument (1990).

q: What is the name of the capital and largest city of Greenland?

q.e: Nuuk, founded by Danish-Norwegian missionary Hans Egede in 1728 under the name Godthåb, holds about a third of Greenland's total population with roughly 19,000 inhabitants.

q: What is the official language in Greenland?

q.e: Greenlandic (Kalaallisut) is the official language of Greenland, with Danish also used.

q: What is the religion of the majority of the population of Greenland?

q.e: Most Greenlanders are Evangelical Lutherans (Church of Greenland).

q: Which of these actresses was born in the US state of Alabama?

q.e: Courteney Cox was born in Birmingham, Alabama.

q: St Petersburgs most famous avenue, Nevsky Prospekt stretches from where to where?
From the Admiralty building to the Aleksander Nevsky Monastery
From St Isaacs Cathedral to the Kazan Cathedral
From the Moscow Station to the Finland Station
From the Winter Palace to the Moscow Station on Uprising Square

q.e: Nevsky Prospekt runs from the Admiralty building to the Alexander Nevsky Monastery.

q: This famous Greek complex of monasteries is located in the Pindus Mountains.

q.e: Meteora's monasteries stand on rock pillars in Thessaly, near the Pindus Mountains.

q: What mountain was regarded as the home of the gods in Greek mythology?

q.e: Mount Olympus was the home of the Greek gods. Mount Helicon was home of the Muses.

q: What Greek island is the home of the monastery of "Nea Moni�, which is a UNESCO World Heritage Site?

q.e: The Nea Moni monastery (11th century) on Chios is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

q: It is known as the "Pearl of the Adriatic� and is located at the southern tip of Croatia on the coast of Southern Dalmatia.

q.e: Dubrovnik earned the nickname Pearl of the Adriatic for its well-preserved medieval stone walls and coastal beauty, becoming a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1979.

q: Which one is not a nickname for the $10 US bill?

q.e: A $10 bill is a "sawbuck" or "ten-spot." A "double sawbuck" is a $20 bill.

q: In April, 2009, Bolivia and Paraguay ended something that began in the 1930s. What was it?

q.e: Bolivia and Paraguay signed a final border treaty in April 2009 ending the Chaco War's last dispute.

q: Bolivia is unusual in that the official capital is not the seat of government. What city is the official capital?

q.e: Sucre is the constitutional and judicial capital of Bolivia, while La Paz serves as the administrative capital where the executive and legislative branches meet.

q: What city is the seat of government of Bolivia?

q.e: La Paz is Bolivia's seat of government, while Sucre is the constitutional capital.

q: What is unusual about Bolivias navy?
Bolivia is landlocked and the navy patrols Lake Titicaca.
Its the second-largest navy in the world.
It is actually run by the Peruvian government.

q.e: Bolivia lost its coastline to Chile during the War of the Pacific (1879-1884), but it still maintains the Bolivian Navy (Armada Boliviana), which patrols Lake Titicaca and major inland rivers.

q: There are many users of the sea bed, including fishermen, the military, commercial shippers and mineral dredgers. What is the most common problem for pipeline designers when selecting a route?
Disturbance of nuclear and chemical waste

q.e: Crossing existing pipelines and cables is a frequent problem in pipeline routing.

q: Submarine landslides are prevalent in deltas such as North Americas Mississippi and Fraser deltas. When the sediment slides across a pipe it can cause significant movement, so that this type of force can actually break it.

q.e: A landslide moving sediment across a pipe produces large lateral forces and can cause rupture. Check the options for tensile, shear and so on.

q: What is the name of the first woman to be awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1905?

q.e: Bertha von Suttner won the 1905 Nobel Peace Prize, the first woman to win it.

q: The Second Continental Congress approved the Declaration of Independence on July 4, 1776. What politician had written a day earlier to his wife Abigail that The second day of July, 1776, will be the most memorable epoch in the history of America.?

q.e: John Adams wrote to Abigail on 3 July 1776 that July 2 would be the "most memorable epoch."

q: Who recorded the 1973 ballad 4th of July, Asbury Park (Sandy) which opens with the lyrics, Sandy, the fireworks are hailin over Little Eden tonight Forcin a light into all those stony faces left stranded on this warm July?

q.e: Bruce Springsteen recorded "4th of July, Asbury Park (Sandy)" on "The Wild, the Innocent & the E Street Shuffle" (1973).

q: The city of Koblenz is situated where the Rhine meets which river?

q.e: Koblenz is where the Moselle joins the Rhine, at the "Deutsches Eck."

q: What is the name of the largest lake (or loch / lough) in the British Isles (by surface area)?

q.e: Lough Neagh in Northern Ireland covers roughly 392 square kilometers (151 sq mi), making it the largest lake in the British Isles. Loch Lomond is the largest lake on the island of Great Britain at about 71 square kilometers.

q: Who are the founding members of the Black Panther Party for Self Defense?
Bobby Seale and Huey P. Newton
Heuy P. Newton and Che Guevera

q.e: Huey P. Newton and Bobby Seale founded the Black Panther Party in Oakland in 1966.

q: Who did the Black Panther Party draft as Field Marshall of the East Coast in June of 1967?

q.e: In 1967 the Panthers named Stokely Carmichael "Honorary Prime Minister." Other titles went to H. Rap Brown and others.

q: What is the name of the queen who tells the king the stories in the Arabian collection of fairy tales One Thousand and One Nights?

q.e: Scheherazade delays her execution by telling King Shahryar stories that end on cliffhangers each evening for 1,001 nights. Shahryar is the king listening to the tales, not the storyteller.

q: What is the mane of the flat-soled sandals that geisha wear outdoors?

q.e: Zori are flat sandals worn with kimono, and geisha wear geta or zori outdoors.

q: This explorer sailed around the Cape of Good Hope into the Indian Ocean and explored Mozambique in 1498. He was the first European to establish a trade route around the southern tip of Africa all the way to India.

q.e: Vasco da Gama rounded the Cape of Good Hope in 1497 and reached India (Calicut) in 1498, opening a sea route to Asia.

q: According to the World Health Organization, the top 3 causes of death in the USA are heart disease, stroke, and lung cancer. What are the top 3 causes of death in Mozambique?

q.e: In Mozambique, HIV/AIDS, malaria and diarrheal diseases are among the top causes of death.

q: According to the World Health Organization, in 2007 0.6% of American adults had HIV. What percentage of the population of Mozambique had HIV?

q.e: Mozambique's adult HIV prevalence was around 12% in 2007.

q: What is the capital and largest city of CAR (Central African Republic)?

q.e: Bangui is the capital and largest city of the Central African Republic.

q: What is the capital of Swaziland?

q.e: Mbabane is the administrative capital of Eswatini (Swaziland). Lobamba is the legislative capital.

q: What is the capital of Mauritania?

q.e: Nouakchott is the capital of Mauritania.

q: What is the capital of Côte dIvoire (Ivory Coast)?

q.e: Yamoussoukro became the political capital of Côte d'Ivoire in 1983, home to the Basilica of Our Lady of Peace. However, coastal Abidjan remains the de facto economic and administrative center.

q: According to an ancient story Virgin Mary and St. John were sailing to Cyprus to visit this Biblical figure, when their ship was blown off course to the then pagan Holy Mountain.

q.e: According to tradition, the Virgin Mary was sailing with St. John to visit Lazarus in Cyprus when her ship landed at Athos.

q: What is the largest monastery on the Holy Mountain in Greece?

q.e: The Great Lavra, founded in 963, is the largest and oldest monastery on Mount Athos.

q: What is the second-largest Cuban island?

q.e: Isla de la Juventud is Cuba's second-largest island and was once known as the Isle of Pines.

q: What is the name of the traditional Japanese way of sitting used on formal occasions such as the Japanese tea ceremony?

q.e: "Seiza" is the formal kneeling posture used in the Japanese tea ceremony.

q: Where are the Augustusburg and Falkenlust palaces located?

q.e: The Augustusburg and Falkenlust palaces are in Brühl, North Rhine–Westphalia, a UNESCO site.

q: What Brazilian architect designed public buildings in the city of Brasilia as well as the the United Nations Headquarters in New York City?

q.e: Oscar Niemeyer designed buildings in Brasília and was one of the designers of the UN Headquarters in New York.

q: This densely populated city is the capital of Ceara, one of the 27 states of Brazil.

q.e: Fortaleza is the capital of Ceará in northeastern Brazil.

q: What best-selling novel was written by American writer David Guterson in the early morning hours over a ten-year period?

q.e: David Guterson wrote "Snow Falling on Cedars" (1994), which won the PEN/Faulkner Award.

q: Who wrote the novel The Long Winter, which is set in South Dakota during the severe winter of 1880–1881?

q.e: Laura Ingalls Wilder wrote "The Long Winter" (1940) about South Dakota's winter of 1880–81.

q: The novel Miss Smillas Sense of Snow tells the story of Smilla Jaspersen who has developed an almost intuitive understanding of all types of snow. What nationality is author Peter Høeg who penned the novel?

q.e: Peter Høeg is a Danish author. "Miss Smilla's Feeling for Snow" is its UK title.

q: What is the name of the provincial capital of the island of Bali?

q.e: Denpasar is the provincial capital of Bali.

q: What is the height of the Burj Dubai skyscraper which comprises 162 floors?

q.e: The Burj Khalifa (formerly Burj Dubai) is 828 m tall, with 163 floors.

q: Many people think of a motorcycle when they hear this name but it is also the name of a city of over a million people that is a next door suburb of Tokyo. Name the city.

q.e: Kawasaki, a city of over 1.5 million between Tokyo and Yokohama, shares its name with the motorcycle brand.

q: What Chinese city, located in the northwest of Yunnan Province, is often called the Oriental Venice?

q.e: Lijiang in Yunnan, with canals, is called the "Venice of the Orient" and a UNESCO site.

q: The Wild Turkey, which is native to North America, belongs to what genus of birds?

q.e: The wild turkey's genus is Meleagris.

q: What was the name of the first Native American to make contact with the Pilgrims after their first winter in the New World?

q.e: Samoset, an Abenaki, greeted the Pilgrims in March 1621 in English, and introduced them to Squanto (Tisquantum).

q: What song, related to Thanksgiving, is a satirical musical monologue based on a true story that began on Thanksgiving Day in 1965?
Over the River and through the Woods

q.e: "Alice's Restaurant" (1967), by Arlo Guthrie, is based on a 1965 Thanksgiving arrest.

q: What is the University of Arkansas nickname?

q.e: The University of Arkansas teams are the Razorbacks.

q: On what river is Prague situated?

q.e: The Vltava is the longest river in the Czech Republic, flowing directly through Prague and spanned by historical landmarks like the Charles Bridge.

q: What river in Peru is considered to be the main headwater of the Amazon River?

q.e: The Apurímac is regarded as the Amazon's most distant source. The Ucayali is formed by the Apurímac and Urubamba.

q: This civilization, which is believed to be the oldest on the planet, flourished in the lands of modern Iraq.

q.e: The Sumerians of Mesopotamia built the first known civilization, around 4500–1900 BC.

q: Iraq is known for the musical instruments oud and rebab. What type of instruments are they?

q.e: The oud and rebab are stringed instruments of the Middle East.

q: What is the state flower and one of the symbols of the US state of Virginia?

q.e: The flowering dogwood is Virginia's state flower and tree.

q: Which of these is a soccer team from the U.S. state of Virginia?

q.e: The Hampton Roads Piranhas played in the USL Premier Development League. Check the other options.

q: The official state motto of the U.S. state of Arizona is Ditat Deus. What does this mean in English?

q.e: "Ditat Deus" means "God enriches."

q: Each year a Liberty Medal is given on July 4th to a prominent world leader in honor of Independence Day. Which award is the medal accompanied by?

q.e: The Liberty Medal, awarded by the National Constitution Center in Philadelphia, carries a $100,000 prize.

q: There was not a single signature appended to the Declaration of Independence until the 4th of July. Thomas McKean, one of the signers, did not sign the Declaration until this year.

q.e: Thomas McKean signed the Declaration later than 1776. Some accounts say 1777; others say 1781.

q: The fictional character John Rambo, portrayed on the big screen by actor Sylvester Stallone, belongs to what US special forces?

q.e: John Rambo is a Vietnam War veteran and former US Army Special Forces ("Green Beret") soldier in First Blood.

q: This Australian special force deals with reconnaissance and counter-terrorism. It played a significant role in providing security during the Sydney Olympic Games in 2000.

q.e: The Special Air Service Regiment (SASR) is Australia's special forces, which supported security at the Sydney Olympics.

q: Which of these members of rock band Lynyrd Skynyrd survived the plane crash in Mississippi on October 20, 1977?

q.e: Artimus Pyle, the drummer, survived the 1977 Lynyrd Skynyrd plane crash in Mississippi that killed Ronnie Van Zant.

q: This famous Norwegian explorer, the first man to reach the South Pole, died in a plane crash in the Barens Sea on June 18, 1928.

q.e: Amundsen reached the South Pole on December 14, 1911, and died in 1928 while flying a rescue mission for the Italian airship Italia over the Barents Sea.

q: Which musicians were killed in the crash on February 3, 1959, a day widely known as The Day The Music Died?
Buddy Holly, the Big Bopper, Ritchie Valens
The Big Bopper, Patsy Cline, Frank Sinatra
Buddy Holly, Elvis Presley, Stevie Ray Vaughan
Otis Redding, Ritchie Valens, Buddy Holly

q.e: Buddy Holly, J.P. Richardson (The Big Bopper), and Ritchie Valens were killed alongside pilot Roger Peterson when their chartered plane crashed near Clear Lake, Iowa, on February 3, 1959. Singer-songwriter Don McLean famously coined the phrase The Day the Music Died in his 1971 song American Pie.

q: American singer Patsy Cline died in a plane crash in Tennessee together with what other popular country singer?

q.e: Patsy Cline died in a plane crash on 5 March 1963 with Cowboy Copas, Hawkshaw Hawkins and her manager Randy Hughes.

q: This female character, depicted by Shakespeare, delivers the following line in her insane speech: Tomorrow is Saint Valentines Day.

q.e: Ophelia, in Hamlet, sings "Tomorrow is Saint Valentine's day" during her mad scene (Act 4, Scene 5).

q: The day of February 14, 1929 remained in history not with its romantic atmosphere, but with one of the most publicized murders in the United States. Which famous American gangster stood behind these murders?

q.e: Al Capone was blamed for the Saint Valentine's Day Massacre of 14 February 1929 in Chicago.

q: This little beauty had three deuces and a four speed and a 389. Ronnie and the Daytonas sang Cmon and turn it on, wind it up, blow it out, GTO. What make of car could really why-ee-eye-ine?

q.e: "G.T.O." by Ronny & the Daytonas (1964) praised the Pontiac GTO, with its 389 engine and four-speed.

q: What were the Titanics wireless call letters?

q.e: The Titanic's Marconi call letters were MGY, and "CQD" and "SOS" were distress calls.

q: During the mid-late 60s Royal Pontiac (a car dealer in Royal Oaks, Michigan) offered a special tune-up package for the GTO 389 engine. What was the name of that performance package?

q.e: Royal Pontiac's "Bobcat" package boosted the GTO's performance in the mid-1960s.

q: In what year did General Motors decide to drop the GTO as an option package and add it to their vehicle lineup as a separate model series?

q.e: The GTO started as an option on the Pontiac Tempest/LeMans in 1964 and became its own model in 1966.

q: In what year did General Motors decide to drop GTO as a separate model and reinstate the GTO as an option package for the LeMans and LeMans sport coupes?

q.e: In 1972 the GTO went back to being an option package on the LeMans, and in 1974 it was a Ventura trim.

q: What fictional character, created by Charles M. Schulz, believes in the Great Pumpkin and says, There are three things I have learned never to discuss with people: religion, politics, and the Great Pumpkin.?

q.e: Linus van Pelt is Charlie Brown's blanket-toting best friend in the Peanuts comic strip by Charles M. Schulz. He spends every Halloween waiting in a pumpkin patch for the Great Pumpkin to appear.

q: Who was the leader of the legendary Solidarność (Solidarity) labor union that led the efforts to end communist rule in Poland?

q.e: Lech Wałęsa led the Solidarity trade union (1980) and became Poland's president in 1990.

q: In his satirical book "The Devils Dictionary�, this American journalist and writer defined turkey as "a large bird whose flesh, when eaten on certain religious anniversaries has the peculiar property of attesting piety and gratitude�.

q.e: Ambrose Bierce wrote "The Devil's Dictionary" (1906), with satirical definitions.

q: What was the dominant type of Native American living structure in the Eastern United States and Canada?

q.e: The wigwam (domed bark or hide-covered hut) was typical in the Eastern Woodlands. The Iroquois used longhouses.

q: Non-Native Americans refer to this group as Delaware.

q.e: The Lenape (Lenni-Lenape) were called Delaware by Europeans, after Lord De La Warr.

q: Which native American tribe was lead by Sitting Bull?

q.e: Sitting Bull (Tatanka Iyotake) was a Hunkpapa Lakota leader, who helped defeat Custer at Little Bighorn.

q: Rock carvings made by the Anasazi
Rock carvings made by Iroquois people
Rock carvings made by Sioux and Cheyenne people
Rock carvings made by Navajo people

q.e: Petroglyphs are rock carvings, made by many peoples, including the ancestral Puebloans (Anasazi).

q: This English philosopher wrote Two Treatises on Government , a philosophical work that had a great influence on the writers of the US Declaration of Independence and the US Constitution.

q.e: John Locke's Two Treatises of Government (1689) inspired the Declaration of Independence.

q: This Oxford scholar dared to try spread freedom and was assassinated as a result.

q.e: Benazir Bhutto studied at Oxford and was assassinated on 27 December 2007 in Rawalpindi.

q: This Oxford scholar is credited with making the first mechanical computer.

q.e: Charles Babbage designed the Difference Engine and Analytical Engine, the first mechanical computers. He studied at Cambridge.

q: He was a great British mathematician, scientist, and philosopher. His attempt to give mathematics a complete axiomatic basis was foiled. In 1950 he won the Nobel Prize in Literature.

q.e: Bertrand Russell won the 1950 Nobel Prize in Literature. Russell's paradox undermined Frege's axiomatic basis for math.

q: Who wrote The Spy Who Came in From the Cold and The Constant Gardener?

q.e: John le Carré (David Cornwell) wrote "The Spy Who Came in from the Cold" (1963) and "The Constant Gardener" (2001).

q: This Oxford scholar is given credit for developing the World Wide Web.

q.e: Tim Berners-Lee, an Oxford graduate, invented the World Wide Web at CERN in 1989–91. Vannevar Bush proposed the "memex."

q: Ah, beauty and brains! This British beauty attended Oxford but left before graduation to become an actress. She was seen in Pearl Harbor, Laural Canyon, and Serendipidy.

q.e: Kate Beckinsale studied at Oxford, left to act, and appeared in Pearl Harbor, Laurel Canyon and Serendipity.

q: This English author depicts an Oxford scholar (Clerk) as one of the pilgrims in his most famous work.

q.e: Chaucer's "Canterbury Tales" has the Clerk of Oxenford, an Oxford student, among the pilgrims.

q: On June 5 in 1851 The Natonal Era began publishing a serial that took ten months to finish. The serial which treated slavery was made into a very popular book. Who was the author?

q.e: Harriet Beecher Stowe's "Uncle Tom's Cabin" began serialization in The National Era on 5 June 1851.

q: On June 5 in 1833 the first person acknowledged to be a computer programmer met the person considered the father of modern computing. Who met whom?

q.e: Ada Lovelace met Charles Babbage on 5 June 1833 at a party. She later wrote the first algorithm for his Analytical Engine.

q: On June 5 in 1956 young Elvis Presley introduced his version of Hound Dog during his third appearance on a TV show. What was the show?

q.e: Elvis Presley performed "Hound Dog" on The Milton Berle Show on 5 June 1956, causing controversy.

q: On 12 October in 1810, the first Oktoberfest was held to celebrate the marriage of then Bavarian Crown Prince Louis (Ludwig) and his bride, Princess Therese von Sachsen-Hildburghausen. Near what city were the festivities held?

q.e: The original 1810 celebration took place on the Theresienwiese, an open meadow located just outside Munich, which has remained the festival's permanent home ever since.

q: What is the capital of Mongolia?

q.e: Ulaanbaatar is the world's coldest national capital by annual average temperature, hovering around 31 degrees Fahrenheit (-0.4 C). It is home to roughly half of Mongolia's total population.

q: What is the deepest lake in the world?

q.e: Lake Baikal in southern Russia plunges to a maximum depth of 5,387 feet (about 1,642 m). It is not only the deepest lake on Earth, but also the world's largest freshwater lake by volume, holding about 20% of the planet's unfrozen surface fresh water.

q: The city of Timbuktu is in which country?

q.e: Timbuktu is situated just north of the Niger River in Mali and flourished as a major center of Islamic learning and trade starting in the 12th century.

q: Which African country has the most pyramids?

q.e: Sudan has around 200 to 255 known ancient pyramids, constructed primarily by the rulers of the Kingdom of Kush at sites like Meroe. Egypt, though home to larger and more famous pyramids like Giza, has roughly 120 to 140.

q: What is the capital and chief seaport of Trinidad and Tobago?

q.e: Port of Spain became the capital of Trinidad and Tobago in 1757, replacing the older capital of San Jose de Oruna. Kingston is the capital of Jamaica, and Bridgetown is the capital of Barbados.

q: More than half of Manitoba's people live in which city?

q.e: Winnipeg is home to roughly 750,000 residents, accounting for more than half of Manitoba's total provincial population of about 1.4 million. Regina and Saskatoon are in Saskatchewan.

q: Praia is the capital of which African island nation?

q.e: Praia is the capital and largest city of Cape Verde, located on Santiago Island in the Atlantic Ocean off the coast of West Africa. Antananarivo is the capital of Madagascar, and Victoria is the capital of Seychelles.

q: What is the largest city on the worlds largest island?

q.e: Nuuk (Godthåb) is the capital and largest city of Greenland, the world's largest island.

q: By what name did Marco Polo call the capital of China, present-day Beijing?

q.e: Marco Polo called Beijing "Cambaluc" (Khanbaliq, the Khan's city).

q: Victoria Falls is one of the most spectacular waterfalls in the world. The falls are named after Queen Victoria by David Livingstone, the explorer who visited them in 1855. The falls are 128 m (420 ft) high and are situated on this river.

q.e: Victoria Falls is located on the Zambezi River along the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe. Its indigenous name, Mosi-oa-Tunya, translates to 'The Smoke That Thunders.'

q: Which of these inhabited places is wettest?

q.e: Mawsynram (and nearby Cherrapunji) in India has the highest annual rainfall for inhabited places.

q: What Canadian lake is the largest in the world, located on an island?

q.e: Nettilling Lake, on Baffin Island, Nunavut, is the largest lake on an island in Canada.

q: Which tiny lake located in Tibet is the highest lake on Earth?

q.e: Lhagba Pool in Tibet is claimed as one of the world's highest lakes, at about 6,368 m.

q: This oldest house in The Bronx, build in 1748, is New York Citys first house museum, operated since 1897 as a public museum by The National Society of Colonial Dames in the State of New York.

q.e: The Van Cortlandt House (1748) in the Bronx is NYC's oldest house museum, run by the Colonial Dames.

q: Which countrys capital city is considered de facto capital of the European Union?

q.e: Brussels, Belgium, hosts most EU institutions, so it's the de facto capital.

q: It has been found that the black mineral soil from the Dead Sea area of Israel helps maintain a good, young complexion. What is the name of the Israeli company that exports beauty products from the Dead Sea area?

q.e: Ahava, an Israeli company, makes cosmetics from Dead Sea minerals and mud.

q: Which 20-kilometre artificial island, situated in the river Danube, was nicknamed the Copa Kagrana?

q.e: The Donauinsel in Vienna is a 21 km flood-control island. The "Copa Kagrana" is its beach strip.

q: This artificial island, whose name literally means Pepper Islet, is part of the Oresund Bridge, connecting Denmark with Sweden.

q.e: Peberholm ("Pepper Islet") is an artificial island next to the natural Saltholm, part of the Øresund Bridge.

q: The Black Sea drains into the Atlantic Ocean via the Sea of Marmara and the Mediterranean Sea on the South West. On the other, North East side of the Black Sea, there is a small sea which is connected to the Black Sea via the Strait of Kerch. Name this sea.

q.e: The Sea of Azov connects to the Black Sea via the Kerch Strait.

q: These islands were the original spice islands, which have drawn traders from all over the world for thousands of years, and were a major factor in causing the European age of exploration, as explorers set out to find the fabled East Indies.

q.e: The Maluku (Moluccas) islands of Ternate, Tidore and Banda were the original Spice Islands (cloves, nutmeg).

q: This volcano, located on the island of Sumbawa, erupted in 1815, generally regarded as the largest volcanic eruption in recorded history. The eruption killed thousands, and changed global climatic patterns.

q.e: Mount Tambora on Sumbawa erupted in April 1815, causing the "Year Without a Summer" in 1816.

q: What is the Tibetan name of Mt. Everest?

q.e: In Tibet, Mount Everest is known as Chomolungma, which translates roughly to 'Goddess Mother of the World'. In Nepal, the peak is called Sagarmatha, meaning 'Goddess of the Sky'.

q: The Cave of Melissani is among the most popular geological landmarks of which Greek island?

q.e: The Melissani Cave on Kefalonia is a lake cave open to the sky.

q: The code of Shinsengumi comprised five rules. What was the punishment for breaking these rules?

q.e: Breaking the Shinsengumi's code meant seppuku (ritual suicide).

q: Carl Albert High School was named after Carl Bert Albert, who was the Speaker of the House of Representatives from 1971 to 1977. What small Oklahoma town did he hail from?

q.e: Carl Albert, House Speaker 1971–77, was from Bugtussle, Oklahoma ("the Little Giant from Little Dixie").

q: What is the name of the tallest waterfall made by humans, which is located in Umbria, Italy?

q.e: Cascata delle Marmore, near Terni, Italy, is a man-made waterfall of 165 m built by the Romans in 271 BC.

q: What is the name of the tallest waterfall in Asia?

q.e: Hannoki Falls in Japan is often listed as the tallest waterfall in Japan. Check other sources for Asia.

q: This Russian volcano, located on the Kamchatka Peninsula, is one of the most active volcanoes on the planet.

q.e: Avachinsky is an active stratovolcano on the Kamchatka Peninsula, near Petropavlovsk.

q: How do you say hello in Russian?

q.e: "Zdravstvuyte" is the formal Russian greeting. "Privet" is informal.

q: What phrase means I love you in Russian?

q.e: "Ya lyublyu tebya" is "I love you" in Russian.

q: My brother lives in Mexico City. He wants to be a trainer. What would his job be called in Spanish?

q.e: "Entrenador" is Spanish for "trainer" or "coach".

q: After US forces captured this island, a major air base was built there because it was close enough to Japan. The plane that dropped the first atomic bomb on Japan flew from the base on this island.

q.e: Tinian, in the Northern Marianas, was the base for the Enola Gay, which dropped the Hiroshima bomb in 1945.

q: The volcano known as Eyjafjallajokull is closest to what Icelandic City?

q.e: Eyjafjallajökull is in southern Iceland, about 125 km from Reykjavik. Its 2010 eruption disrupted European air travel.

q: This ocean existed throughout the Paleozoic in the northern hemisphere and is now represented by the Pacific Ocean.

q.e: Panthalassa was the super-ocean around Pangaea, the ancestor of the Pacific.

q: This Catch-22 character buys and sells goods through black market channels and has no allegiance to any country, person or principle unless it pays him.

q.e: Milo Minderbinder is the profiteer of Joseph Heller's "Catch-22," who founded M&M Enterprises.

q: This Italian explored the east coast of South America much further south than any other European before and realized that this land was part of a new continent while many other European explorers crossing the Atlantic thought they were reaching Asia.

q.e: Amerigo Vespucci explored South America's coast and recognized it as a new continent. "America" is named after him.

q: What American city did Blackbeard successfully blockade in his most daring and famous act?

q.e: Blackbeard blockaded Charleston, South Carolina, in May 1718.

q: What Pope said of Queen Elizabeth I of England, She is only a woman, only mistress of half an island, and yet she makes herself feared by Spain, by France, by the Empire, by all?

q.e: Pope Sixtus V said this about Queen Elizabeth I.

q: This fictional character is a World War II flier, stationed on the island of Pianosa, in the Mediterranean. He thinks that everyone wants to kill him. He wants to go home, but he cannot get out of combat duty, because there is a 'catch'.

q.e: John Yossarian, bombardier of Catch-22 on Pianosa, is trapped by the "catch."

q: Because of its close economic relations with France this country has turned into one of the most prosperous tropical African states. Its name relates to the tusks of elephants.

q.e: Côte d'Ivoire ("Ivory Coast") is a prosperous French-linked West African state.

q: The eruption of this volcano in 1883 on Pulau island in Indonesia is one of the greatest so far. It threw ash up to 50 miles in the sky above in a tremendous explosion. The latter could be heard in Australia, which is 2,200 miles away.

q.e: Krakatoa's 1883 eruption was heard thousands of km away, including in Australia and Rodrigues Island.

q: Where did the first people on North America cross to get to America?

q.e: The first Americans likely crossed Beringia, the land bridge between Siberia and Alaska.

q: In the movie "It's A Wonderful Life,� what is the name of the guardian angel that looks after George in his time of need?

q.e: Clarence Odbody, Angel Second Class, is George Bailey's guardian angel in It's a Wonderful Life.

q: Which product was advertised with the phrase Take it off...take it all off!?

q.e: Noxzema shaving cream's 1970s ad had "Take it off, take it all off" with Swedish model Gunilla Knutson.

q: Angel Falls, located in this country, is the highest waterfall in the world.

q.e: Angel Falls (979 m) is in Venezuela's Canaima National Park.

q: Antarctica could be considered the wettest place on our planet, as 90 per cent of its surface is ice. However the ice isnt melted. So the wettest place on Earth is a small village in India, called this.

q.e: Cherrapunji and nearby Mawsynram in Meghalaya, India, are among the wettest places on Earth.

q: Which brand was advertised with this slogan: Id rather fight than switch.?

q.e: "I'd rather fight than switch" was a Tareyton cigarette slogan.
"A newspaper, not a snoozepaper" was a slogan for a newspaper. Check other sources.

q: In 1931, the Coca-Cola Company developed the picture of Santa Claus, based on a Swedish painting of what Nordic mythical creature?

q.e: Haddon Sundblom's Coca-Cola Santa (1931) was inspired by Clement Moore's poem and Swedish tomte images.

q: Buddhists have four pilgrimage sites, closely linked to the life of Siddhartha Guatama (known as Buddha). This was the city where he sat under a peepal tree, meditating for three days and three nights until he attained Enlightenment.

q.e: Bodh Gaya in Bihar is where Siddhartha Gautama attained enlightenment under the Bodhi tree.

q: On the fatal day of the disaster, the Titanic recieved many iceberg warnings. The last one was recieved at 9:40 PM from this ship.

q.e: SS Mesaba warned of heavy pack ice at 9:40 pm on April 14, 1912, but the message wasn't delivered to the bridge.

q: There is a strange tradition in this Spanish town which involves geese. During the fiesta men try to pull the neck off a goose while repeatedly plunging into the water.

q.e: Lekeitio's "Día del Ganso" (Goose Day) in the Basque Country involves hanging a goose, now a dead one.

q: The American continent was named after which Italian merchant and cartographer?

q.e: German cartographer Martin Waldseemüller produced a world map in 1507 naming the continent "America" in honor of Italian explorer Amerigo Vespucci, who first recognized the lands as a New World distinct from Asia.

q: This Tibetan lake is located at the highest altitude.

q.e: Lhagba Pool in Tibet is reported as among the highest lakes in the world.

q: He was the communist dictator of Romania from 1965 to 1989. On 25 December 1989 he and his wife were executed by a firing squad. They were charged with various crimes, such as unjust gathering of wealth at the expense of the people and even genocide.

q.e: Nicolae Ceaușescu ruled Romania from 1965 to 1989 and was executed with his wife Elena on 25 December 1989.

q: Which of these record-breaking trees is not situated in the State of California?
El �rbol del Tule, the tree with the largest diameter on Earth
General Sherman, the largest living tree on Earth
Stratosphere Giant, the tallest tree on Earth
Methuselah, the oldest tree on Earth

q.e: El Árbol del Tule, a Montezuma cypress with the widest trunk of any tree, is in Oaxaca, Mexico.

q: What is the name of MTM Productions mascot?

q.e: MTM Enterprises' mascot is Mimsie the Cat, a parody of MGM's Leo the Lion.

q: Which mountain range is located entirely within the EU borders?

q.e: The Sudetes mountain range is in the Czech Republic and Poland (also Germany).

q: Marasmius oreades are mushrooms that form dark, unnaturally lush, green rings, described by William Shakespeare as green-sour ringlets. What is the common name of this mushroom that grows in circles?

q.e: Marasmius oreades is the fairy ring champignon, which grows in rings.

q: This hotel located in the capital of the small African country of Rwanda is not only famous for its luxury, but also for the nearly 1,000 people it saved during the Rwandan Genocide in 1994.

q.e: The Hôtel des Mille Collines in Kigali sheltered about 1,200 people in the 1994 genocide ("Hotel Rwanda").

q: This town was a South African enclave, surrounded on three sides by the nation of Namibia (and by the Atlantic Ocean on the other side) until it was ceded to Namibia in 1994.

q.e: Walvis Bay was a South African enclave in Namibia until 1994.

q: This ancient legislation, which stood at the foundation of the Roman law, marked the beginning of the Roman legal history.

q.e: The Twelve Tables (451–450 BC) were the foundation of Roman law.

q: These temples were built on the islands of Malta and Gozo earlier than the Egyptian pyramids and Stonehenge. They date from the Bronze Age - 3,600 BC.

q.e: Ġgantija temples on Gozo date to around 3600 BC, in the Neolithic era, older than Stonehenge and the pyramids.

q: Drat, I hate when the phone rings so early! Got another list for ya. Who could imagine thered be so many fake towns out there!? Can you spot the fake one?

q.e: St. Albins, Missouri, doesn't seem to exist. Check the other options.

q: Before we go to lunch, lets knock out one more list. Ya get it right, I buy you lunch! Hows that for a deal? Here, youll probably need this list, so you can spot the fake town on it.

q.e: Eden Prarie (Prairie), Montana, appears to be a fake.

q: Here, have a go at this while we wait to order. These towns all look good to me, but what do I know? One of them is fake.

q.e: Kentfield, North Dakota, appears to be a fake.

q: Which of these is a sister city to Seattle, Washington?

q.e: Reykjavik is a sister city of Seattle, among others like Kobe and Galway.

q: Three of the following vessels are sister ships. Which one does not belong to the group?

q.e: This question compares ocean liners. The odd one isn't a Titanic sister. Check the other options.

q: This famous French ocean liner was launched in 1932 and received a lot of applause. It was the first liner to surpass 60,000 tons, the first ship with 1,000 feet of length and the first to make an Atlantic crossing with an average speed of over 30 knots.

q.e: SS Normandie (1932), a French liner, was the first ship over 1,000 feet and 60,000 tons. It burned in New York in 1942.

q: The former name of this city was Breslau and it used to be a major city of south-eastern Germany. It came under Polish administration in 1945. What is its present-day name?

q.e: Following the 1945 Potsdam Conference, the Silesian city of Breslau was transferred from Germany to Poland along the Oder-Neisse line and officially renamed Wrocław.

q: Which European capital was known as Reval?

q.e: Reval is the old name of Tallinn, Estonia's capital.

q: The capital of the Russian enclave located between Poland and Lithuania is called Kaliningrad. What was its former name?

q.e: Founded by the Teutonic Order in 1255, Königsberg was the historic capital of East Prussia before it was ceded to the Soviet Union and renamed after Mikhail Kalinin in 1946.

q: Finish these lyrics of the US national anthem. On the shore, dimly seen through the mists of the deep, Where the foes haughty host in dread silence reposes, What is that which the breeze, oer the towering steep, As it fitfully blows, half conceals, ...

q.e: The anthem line reads "As it fitfully blows, half conceals, half discloses?"

q: During the 2000 NFL Playoffs, this coach of the Baltimore Ravens banned his players from using the word playoffs and had them use the word Festivus instead.

q.e: Ravens coach Brian Billick banned the word "playoffs" and used "Festivus" in 2000, and they won the Super Bowl.

q: Located in the capital of Bosnia and Herzegovina - Sarajevo, this high building was the first skyscraper on the Balkans.

q.e: The first Balkan skyscraper claim is unclear. Check the sources.

q: Although these are twin cities, they are in different time zones.
Torino, Italy and Lake Cuomo, Switzerland
Sao Piemendau, Portugal and Slamonca, Spain

q.e: Haparanda (Sweden) is an hour behind Tornio (Finland), on the Torne River.

q: The 14ers are a coveted goal for many an aspiring hikesr. Colorado has over 30 of these, topping out with this Rocky Mountain monster elevated at 14,433 ft (4 399.m) Name this behemoth.

q.e: Mount Elbert, 14,433 ft (4,399 m), is the highest peak in Colorado.

q: This ancient Greek city is in present day Turkey, in a district called Kinik. Its name became synonymous with the Lycia region. It is also the name of a river running through it.

q.e: Xanthos, the ancient capital of Lycia, is near Kınık in Turkey.

q: The Baltic Sea connects to the North Sea via several natural straits of different sizes between Denmark on one side and Sweden and Norway on the other. Which of the following is NOT a strait between the two seas?

q.e: The Øresund, Great Belt and Little Belt connect the Baltic and North seas. Gotland is an island, not a strait.

q: One of the most, if not the most, quoted line from a Vice Presidential debate was delivered by a Senator from Texas. What senator spoke the lines I knew Jack Kennedy; Jack Kennedy was a friend of mine. Senator, youre no Jack Kennedy.?

q.e: Lloyd Bentsen told Dan Quayle "Senator, you're no Jack Kennedy" in the 1988 VP debate.

q: Children in Michigan are taught to remember this word in order to easily recall all of Michigans great lakes.

q.e: HOMES: Huron, Ontario, Michigan, Erie, Superior.

q: In 1965 this man called for a national boycott of grapes because grape pickers were being abused by their employers.

q.e: Cesar Chavez and the United Farm Workers called for a grape boycott in 1965 (Delano grape strike).

q: The design of modern submarines is called teardrop hull and is based on the hydrodynamic body of the whale. This was the first submarine to use a teardrop hull.

q.e: USS Albacore (1953) was the first submarine with a teardrop hull.

q: It was from this Dutch castle that philosopher, playwright, and poet Hugo Grotius made his famous escape in a book-chest in 1621.

q.e: Hugo Grotius escaped from Loevestein Castle in 1621 in a book chest.

q: What city is considered the holiest for Judish, Jewesh, Islamic people?

q.e: Jerusalem is holy to Jews, Christians and Muslims.

q: Who was the first UN Secretary-General?

q.e: Trygve Lie of Norway was the first UN Secretary-General (1946–52).

q: Name the writer of the Star Spangled Banner and the star of the movies Blazing Saddles, Smokey and the Bandit II and Loose Cannons who were both born on August 1.
Francis Scott Key and Dom Deluise
Francis Scott Key and Burt Reynolds
Katharine Lee Bates and Dom Deluise
Adolphe Basile Routhier and Burt Reynolds

q.e: Francis Scott Key (b. 1 August 1779) wrote the anthem's lyrics, and Dom DeLuise (b. 1 August 1933) acted in Blazing Saddles.

q: Aaay! Happy Days are here again. When the Smithsonian added this characters leather jacket to their collection, the Smithsonian became the epitome of Cool. What television character would probably have said Whoa! when told he would become a museum piece?

q.e: The Fonz's leather jacket (Happy Days) is in the Smithsonian.

q: Which of the following countries mottoes is in Latin?

q.e: "Sub umbra floreo" is Belize's Latin motto, "Under the shade I flourish."

q: These burning kerosene torches, carried by twirling and dancing white-robed figures, traditionally light the night parades in New Orleans

q.e: Flambeaux carriers light the night parades in New Orleans during Carnival.

q: A king cake is a type of cake associated with the Carnival Season, traditionally holding a trinket inside. Which of the following is not a traditional trinket, found inside a king cake?
a plastic king wearing a crown

q.e: King cakes hide a small plastic baby. Doubloons are tossed from floats, not baked in.

q: Where did the first mass in the Philippines take place?

q.e: The first Mass in the Philippines took place on Limasawa Island, Leyte, on 31 March 1521 (Butuan also claims it).

q: Who is the first Filipino priest?

q.e: The first Filipino priest is disputed. Check other sources.

q: What is the name of the mystic haunted ship in the 2002 horror movie Ghost Ship?

q.e: The "Antonia Graza" is the fictional Italian liner in "Ghost Ship" (2002), loosely based on the Andrea Doria.

q: Bill and Taffy Danoff, with the band Fat City, sang backup on Take Me Home, Country Roads and later went on to score their own hit Afternoon Delight with what band?

q.e: Bill and Taffy Danoff sang backup on "Take Me Home, Country Roads" and formed the Starland Vocal Band ("Afternoon Delight," 1976).

q: Your flight has been delayed due to bad weather. The airline representative at the gate gives prompt updates concerning the time your flight may depart. Behind the scenes, the technical term for the estimated time of departure is this one.

q.e: EDCT is Expect Departure Clearance Time, set by air traffic control when delays occur.

q: The bus line which primarily serves the San Francisco Peninsula is known as this.
Stanford Area Transit or SAT for short!

q.e: SamTrans (San Mateo County Transit District) runs buses on the San Francisco Peninsula.

q: Due to a police officer being sprayed by silly string, the sale of silly string was banned in the city of Southington. In what U.S. state is Southington located?

q.e: Southington, Connecticut, banned Silly String in the 2000s after a police officer was sprayed.

q: What is the capital of Micronesia?

q.e: Palikir is the capital of the Federated States of Micronesia, on Pohnpei.

q: We move 500 years back in time. You are on a ship with Ferdinand Magellan, and you are trying to find the Western passage to India. In which order will you pass the estuaries of South American rivers?

q.e: Magellan sailed south down the South American coast: the Amazon, then the Río de la Plata.

q: Take some warm clothes. You are traveling the Trans-Siberian railway. In which order will you pass the great Asian rivers, if you start in Moscow and travel to Vladyvostok?

q.e: On the Trans-Siberian, you cross the Irtysh, the Ob and the Yenisei going east from Moscow.

q: Imagine you travel with Vasco da Gama to find the sea route to India. In which order will you pass the capes of Africa?
Cape Verde, Cape of Good Hope, Ras Hafun
Ras ben Sakka, Cape of Good Hope, Cape Verde

q.e: Da Gama rounded Cape Verde, then the Cape of Good Hope, then went up to Ras Hafun (Somalia) on the east coast.

q: What is the capital of Montserrat?

q.e: Montserrat's capital Plymouth was abandoned after the 1995–97 Soufrière Hills eruption; Brades is the interim capital.

q: Which of these is not a class of American submarines, used during World War II?

q.e: The Kairyu was a Japanese midget submarine, not American.

q: This American jurist won Time magazines Man of the Year award in 1973 and was influential in getting rid of the man who won the award in 1971.

q.e: Judge John Sirica was Time's Man of the Year for 1973 for his Watergate role. Nixon was the 1971 winner.

q: Who was the first President of Poland?

q.e: Gabriel Narutowicz was Poland's first president, elected in 1922 and assassinated five days after taking office.

q: Between late XV and XVIII centuries, Polands kings were elected. Theoretically any noble man could become king. On many occasions a foreigner would be chosen. Which European ruling family did not have a member who was elected king of Poland?

q.e: Polish elective kings included Valois, Báthory, Vasa, Wettin and others. The Habsburgs never won the throne.

q: Cleveland Indians 1st baseman/DH, Travis Hafner was born and raised in this North Dakota town.

q.e: Travis Hafner, born in Jamestown and raised in Sykeston, North Dakota, played for Cleveland (2002–2012).

q: What jewellery company is famous for designing exquisite jewel-encrusted eggs for the Russian Imperial Court?

q.e: The House of Fabergé crafted 50 imperial Easter eggs for the Russian royal family between 1885 and 1916, starting with the Hen Egg created for Tsar Alexander III.

q: What musher and his dog relayed diphtheria vaccine via the Iditarod Trail to fight an epidemic in Nome in 1925 and became national heroes?
John Muir and Rin Tin Tin

q.e: Leonhard Seppala and his dogs, including Togo, ran the longest leg of the 1925 serum run. Gunnar Kaasen and Balto ran the last leg into Nome.

q: This blond beauty, born in Athens, Georgia in 1953, made millions as a movie star but went bankrupt due, in part, to her purchase of the entire town of Baselton, Georgia.

q.e: Kim Basinger, born in Athens, Georgia, bought Braselton, Georgia, in 1989 and went bankrupt in 1993.

q: She was an actress famous for her role in Moulin Rouge. She is even more famous for her marriages, her sisters, and for being arrested for battery. Who is this actress who was forced into bankruptcy in 1994?

q.e: Zsa Zsa Gabor appeared in Moulin Rouge (1952) and was married nine times.

q: It was on a hot summer day that the outside world descended on the small town of Dayton, Tennessee to see famed defense lawyer Clarence Darrow take on The Great Commoner William Jennings Bryan in what was known as The Monkey Trial. Who was the defendant?

q.e: John T. Scopes was tried in 1925 in Dayton, Tennessee, for teaching evolution. Clarence Darrow defended him.

q: The Behistun Inscription was carved into a cliff wall. It was deciphered by Henry Rawlinson. It contains the same text in 3 different languages. All 3 of the texts, however, are written in the same script. What is this script called?

q.e: The Behistun Inscription is in cuneiform, in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian.

q: What do Alaskan people call bunny boots?
Native boots crafted of rabbit fur

q.e: Bunny boots are heavily insulated vapor-barrier boots, popular in Alaska.

q: What traditional gift-bringer is NOT correctly matched with the country?

q.e: Svatý Mikuláš is St. Nicholas in the Czech lands. In Russia, Ded Moroz brings gifts.
Maryland's motto "Fatti maschii, parole femine" means "Manly deeds, womanly words."

q: What is the official residence of the President of the Philippines?

q.e: Malacañang Palace in Manila is the official residence of the president of the Philippines.

q: Who is the second female president of the Philippines?

q.e: Gloria Macapagal Arroyo was the second woman to be president of the Philippines (2001–2010).

q: What famous French author and WWII aviator made the following statement about love: Life has taught us that love does not consist in gazing at each other but in looking outward together in the same direction.?

q.e: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry, author of The Little Prince, wrote this in "Wind, Sand and Stars" (1939).

q: Name the oldest amusement park in the U.S. which is located in Bristol, Connecticut.

q.e: Lake Compounce in Bristol, Connecticut, opened in 1846 and is America's oldest amusement park.

q: What did ancient Filipinos call the supreme being in which they believed?

q.e: Bathala was the supreme god in the pre-Hispanic Tagalog religion.

q: Who was known as Prince of Filipino Printers?

q.e: Tomás Pinpin, called the "Prince of Filipino Printers," published the first Tagalog books in the 1600s.

q: What is the typical Visayan love song called?

q.e: The "balitaw" is a Visayan love song.

q: What is the typical Tagalog love song called?

q.e: The "kundiman" is a Tagalog love song.

q: Which of these groups in the Philippines had the most elaborate tattoos in ancient times?

q.e: The Visayans were called "Pintados" (the painted ones) by the Spanish for their tattoos.

q: Romania is famous for its achievements in womens gymnastics. At the 1976 Olympic Games in Montreal this Romanian gymnast obtained the first 10 ever awarded in modern gymnastics.

q.e: Nadia Comăneci scored the first perfect 10 in Olympic gymnastics in Montreal in 1976.

q: How do you say I love you in Romanian?

q.e: "Te iubesc" is "I love you" in Romanian.

q: Admiral Perry forced Japan to end its isolation policy in 1854 when his fleet sailed to Japan and made a show of force at this port city. A replica of one of Perrys steam powered black ships can be seen near the railroad station of the city.

q.e: Commodore Perry's 1854 treaty opened the port of Shimoda, and a Black Ship replica sails there.

q: What is Puerto Ricos national anthem?

q.e: "La Borinqueña" is Puerto Rico's anthem.

q: In 1982, justice William J. Brennan delivered the U.S. Supreme Courts opinion on this case that stated undocumented children of alien parents cannot be denied a public education. It stemmed from a case in Texas.

q.e: Plyler v. Doe (1982) held that Texas couldn't deny public education to undocumented children.

q: What do we call the houses built by the Piute people?

q.e: The Paiute built wickiups, dome-shaped huts of brush.

q: Who was the last Chief of the Comanches?

q.e: Quanah Parker was the last chief of the Comanches, and surrendered in 1875.

q: What is the Navajo word for non-Native Americans?

q.e: "Bilagáana" is the Navajo word for white people.

q: What famous TV character spoke the words, There is a time of year in New York when, even before the first leaf falls, you can feel the seasons click. The air is crisp, the summer is gone. And for the first night in a long time, you need a blanket on your bed.?

q.e: Carrie Bradshaw said this in a "Sex and the City" voiceover.

q: South Galcayo is the administrative capital of this secular, decentralized state in the central region of Somalia.

q.e: Galmudug is a state in central Somalia whose capital is Dhusamareb (and South Galkayo).

q: When he was Democratic Chairman, this future Postmaster General was instrumental in brokering the deal that put Truman on the ticket with FDR. He also was owner of the St. Louis Cardinals for a short time.

q.e: Robert E. Hannegan, Democratic National Committee chair, helped put Truman on the 1944 ticket. He was Postmaster General and part-owner of the Cardinals.

q: Which of the following navigation instruments is located in the cockpit of an airplane?

q.e: The omnibearing selector (OBS) tunes a VOR navigation receiver in the cockpit.

q: In 1918, these two engineers were first to introduce the co-axial design of helicopters, where rotors are at the top of the aircraft.
Theodore von Karman and Asboth Oszkar
Juan de la Cierva and Arthur Young

q.e: Theodore von Kármán and Oszkár Asbóth worked on helicopters in WWI.

q: What tragic event occurred in Atlanta on December 7, 1946?
A mid-air collision of two planes during an air show

q.e: The Winecoff Hotel fire on 7 December 1946 killed 119 people, the deadliest hotel fire in US history.

q: What Arabic word is for Muslim babies, and is also the name of a gesture used to greet people?

q.e: This question's Arabic term isn't clear. Check other sources.

q: Which European city is a sister city of Ashtabula?
Chernobyl, Ukraine until the nuclear meltdown of 1986

q.e: Ashtabula's sister city question is obscure. Check other sources.

q: What is the official name of Cairo?

q.e: Cairo's Arabic name is Al-Qāhirah ("the Victorious").

q: Which treasure was discovered by a boy shepherd who literally stumbled over a golden vessel?

q.e: The Pereshchepina treasure was found by a shepherd in Ukraine in 1912.

q: Whose life story was a source of inspiration for the lead character in Orson Welles classic film, Citizen Kane?

q.e: Citizen Kane (1941) is widely thought to be based on William Randolph Hearst's life.

q: The objective in course camarguaise is to snatch several attributes fixed on the bulls horns. Which one is not among them?

q.e: In course camarguaise, the raseteurs try to snatch the cocarde, glands (tassels) and ficelles (strings) from the bull's horns.

q: Which word refers to the men practicing course camarguaise?

q.e: The participants in the course camarguaise are called raseteurs, who wear white.

q: Which term refers to the people who help the young participants in course camarguaise to place correctly the bull in front of them?

q.e: "Tourneurs" are the helpers in course camarguaise.

q: This person contributed to the revival of the course camarguaise, as well as to the to improvement in breeding of the Camarguese bull and to the codifying of the rules of the game.

q.e: Marquis Folco de Baroncelli-Javon revived Camargue traditions and the course camarguaise in the early 1900s.

q: Which of these volcanoes is not located on the island of Hawaii?

q.e: Menengai is a volcano in Kenya, not Hawaii.

q: The Canal des Deux Mers (i.e. the Two Seas Canal) is the name of a route that allows shipping to pass across France from the Atlantic to the Mediterranean. Which river forms a significant part of the route, by linking the Atlantic with the Canal du Midi?

q.e: The Garonne river connects the Atlantic with the Canal du Midi, forming the Canal des Deux Mers.

q: If you wanted to go snorkeling or scuba diving off the coast of Mozambique, you might want to explore which of the following popular diving spots?

q.e: The Bazaruto Archipelago is a prime diving spot off Mozambique.

q: What animal is a national symbol of Argentina?

q.e: The rufous hornero is Argentina's national bird.

q: What is the capital city of Sri Lanka?

q.e: Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte is Sri Lanka's legislative capital. Colombo is the commercial capital.

q: What was Singapore renamed to during the Japanese occupation (1942-1945)?
Singapore was not renamed by the Japanese.

q.e: Singapore was renamed Syonan-to ("Light of the South") by Japan from 1942 to 1945.

q: What bird is featured on the national flag of Papua New Guinea?

q.e: Raggiana bird-of-paradise is on Papua New Guinea's flag.

q: Who was the first President of the United States?

q.e: George Washington served as the first U.S. president under the Constitution from 1789 to 1797, winning unanimous support from the Electoral College in both elections. John Adams served as his vice president before becoming the second president.

q: Which ancient people built the pyramids of Giza?

q.e: Constructed during Egypt's Fourth Dynasty in the Old Kingdom around 2500 BC, the Giza pyramid complex was built as royal tombs for the pharaohs Khufu, Khafre, and Menkaure.

q: Which ship sank after hitting an iceberg in 1912?

q.e: The RMS Titanic struck an iceberg on the night of April 14, 1912, and sank early the following morning, resulting in the loss of more than 1,500 lives. Its sister ship, the Britannic, sank in 1916 after hitting an underwater mine.

q: In what year did the September 11 attacks happen?

q.e: On September 11, 2001, hijackers crashed four commercial airliners into the World Trade Center towers, the Pentagon, and a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania.

q: Julius Caesar was a leader of which ancient city?

q.e: Julius Caesar was a Roman general and statesman whose appointment as dictator in perpetuity in 44 BC played a critical role in the demise of the Roman Republic.

q: Which great wall was built to protect China from invaders?

q.e: The Great Wall of China spans thousands of miles, built and reinforced across multiple dynasties—most notably under the Qin and Ming—to defend against northern nomadic invasions.

q: The collapse of the Soviet Union took place in which year?

q.e: The Soviet Union officially dissolved on December 26, 1991, following Mikhail Gorbachev's resignation as president the previous day.

q: How long did World War II last?

q.e: World War II officially began on September 1, 1939, with Nazi Germany's invasion of Poland, and concluded on September 2, 1945, with Japan's formal surrender, lasting one day over six years.

q: When is the Ides of March?

q.e: In the Roman calendar, the Ides fell on the 15th of March, May, July and October (13th in other months). Julius Caesar was assassinated on the Ides of March, 44 BC.

q: Who was among those killed in the 2010 Smolensk, Russia plane crash tragedy?

q.e: Polish President Lech Kaczyński and 95 others died when their plane crashed near Smolensk on 10 April 2010. They were traveling to a memorial for the Katyn massacre.

q: Which German field marshal was known as the `Desert Fox`?

q.e: Erwin Rommel earned the nickname "Desert Fox" leading the Afrika Korps in North Africa in 1941-43. He later died in 1944 after being implicated in a plot against Hitler.

q: What was William Frederick Cody better known as?

q.e: William F. Cody gained the moniker Buffalo Bill after reportedly hunting thousands of bison to feed Kansas Pacific Railroad construction workers. He later achieved worldwide fame through his touring show, Buffalo Bill's Wild West, which began in 1883.

q: Which famous military commander marched an army, which included war elephants, over the Alps during the Second Punic War?

q.e: Hannibal of Carthage crossed the Alps in 218 BC with about 37 war elephants at the start of the Second Punic War. Few survived the trip.

q: What is the historical name of Sri Lanka?

q.e: Sri Lanka was known as Ceylon during British colonial rule and retained the name as an independent dominion until officially becoming the Republic of Sri Lanka in 1972.

q: Who succeded Josef Stalin as the leader of the Soviet Union?

q.e: Following Stalin's death in March 1953, Georgy Malenkov briefly headed the government, but Nikita Khrushchev emerged as First Secretary of the Communist Party by September 1953 and consolidated power.

q: The idea of Socialism was articulated and advanced by whom?

q.e: Karl Marx, with Friedrich Engels, laid out the ideas of communism and scientific socialism in The Communist Manifesto (1848). Earlier thinkers like Saint-Simon and Owen had set socialist ideas in motion.

q: How old was Adolf Hitler when he died?

q.e: Hitler was born on 20 April 1889 and died on 30 April 1945 in his Berlin bunker, aged 56.

q: In the 990s, which son of Erik the Red brought Christianity to Greenland?

q.e: According to the Icelandic sagas, Leif Erikson visited Norway around the year 999, was converted by King Olaf Tryggvason, and was sent back to Greenland to introduce Christianity to the Norse settlers.

q: On October 20, 1803, the U.S. Senate ratified the treaty for which land acquisition?

q.e: The Louisiana Purchase added about 828,000 square miles (2.14 million sq km) of territory from France for 15 million dollars, nearly doubling the size of the United States. The Gadsden Purchase followed decades later in 1853.

q: Before plastic money, Native American "wampum" currency was strings of what, made from shells?

q.e: Wampum was made of beads cut from quahog and whelk shells, strung or woven into belts. They were used for records and treaties as well as trade.

q: Which aviator disappeared over the Pacific in 1937?

q.e: Amelia Earhart vanished near Howland Island on 2 July 1937, on her attempt to fly round the world. She was the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic (1932).

q: Henry Kissinger held this US post from 1974 to 1977.
Speaker of the House of Representatives

q.e: Henry Kissinger was Secretary of State under Nixon and Ford (1973-77), after serving as National Security Advisor. He won the 1973 Nobel Peace Prize.

q: How many landing beaches were there in the 1944 Normandy Invasion, known as Operation Overlord?

q.e: The Allied invasion of Normandy on June 6, 1944, targeted five codenamed beach sectors: Utah and Omaha, assaulted by US forces, and Gold, Juno, and Sword, assaulted by British and Canadian forces.

q: In 1962 Jamaica gained full independence from the United Kingdom, but before even becoming a British colony, Jamaica was possession of this country.

q.e: Spain colonized Jamaica after Columbus arrived in 1494. England captured it in 1655, and it became independent in 1962.

q: One of the results of the Second Anglo-Dutch War, between England and the United Netherlands, was that the city of New Amsterdam was renamed to this.

q.e: The English seized New Amsterdam in 1664 and renamed it New York in honor of the Duke of York (later King James II). The 1667 Treaty of Breda formally confirmed English control at the close of the Second Anglo-Dutch War.

q: What term did hippies use to refer to the institutions and structures they rejected?

q.e: The Establishment is the term for the mainstream power structures that the 1960s counterculture rejected. The phrase was popularised in Britain in the 1950s.

q: Shooting at anti-war demonstrators at this university on May 4, 1970, triggered a nationwide student strike across America.

q.e: On May 4, 1970, the Ohio National Guard fired into a crowd of student protesters at Kent State University, killing four students and injuring nine others.

q: After the death of this Confederate general on on May 10, 1863, General Lee remarked, I have lost my right arm.

q.e: Stonewall Jackson died on 10 May 1863 after being accidentally shot by his own men at Chancellorsville. Lee called him his "right arm."

q: What African American Regiment helped to assault Fort Wagner in South Carolina during the American Civil War?

q.e: The 54th Massachusetts, one of the first Black regiments in the Union Army, led the failed assault on Fort Wagner in July 1863. The 1989 film Glory tells their story.

q: Which general commanded the Confederate forces at the Battle of Gettysburg, that started on July 1, 1863?

q.e: Robert E. Lee led the Confederate Army of Northern Virginia at Gettysburg (1-3 July 1863). Union General George Meade won, ending Lee's invasion of the North.

q: What play was President Lincoln watching at Fords Theatre, when he was assassinated by a Southern sympathizer from Maryland?

q.e: Actor and Confederate sympathizer John Wilkes Booth shot Abraham Lincoln on April 14, 1865, timing the gunshot to laughter caused by a funny line in Tom Taylor's comedy Our American Cousin.

q: The Battle of Worcester, the Battle of Hopton Heath, and the Battle of Winceby are just three of the battles during this civil war.

q.e: The English Civil War (1642-1651) was fought between Royalists and Parliamentarians. Hopton Heath (1643), Winceby (1643) and Worcester (1651) were among the battles.

q: The allies of WW2 initially consisted of three countries, which were later joined by others. Which of these countries never joined the Allies?

q.e: The original Allies were the UK, France and Poland, later joined by the USSR, US and China. Japan was part of the Axis powers.

q: Which was the formal reason for the end of World War II, on September 2, 1945?
The number of civilians that had died
The usage of an increased number of atomic weapons

q.e: Japan formally surrendered aboard USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay on 2 September 1945, ending World War II. V-J Day is also marked on 15 August, when Japan announced surrender.

q: What two countries were invaded by Germany on 9 April 1940?

q.e: Germany attacked Denmark and Norway on 9 April 1940 (Operation Weserübung). Denmark fell within hours, while Norway fought on for two months.

q: In which month of 1940 did the Soviet Union occupy Latvia, Lithuania, and Estonia?

q.e: The Soviet Union occupied and annexed the Baltic states in June 1940, following the secret Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact.

q: On 28 October 1940, launching the invasion from bases in Albania, Italy invaded this country.

q.e: Mussolini's Italy invaded Greece on 28 October 1940 from Albania. The Greeks pushed the Italians back, and Germany had to step in in 1941.

q: Nazi Germanys attempt at invading the Soviet Union, known as Operation Barbarossa, started on what date?

q.e: Operation Barbarossa began on 22 June 1941, with more than three million German troops attacking the Soviet Union. It broke the Nazi-Soviet pact.

q: The date November 11, 1918 is famous with what event?
The first case of Asian flu was reported in the USA

q.e: The Armistice of Compiègne took effect on the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month in 1918, silencing the guns and concluding fighting on the Western Front.

q: Both Thomas Jefferson and John Adams died
Russia declared war on Turkey, starting the Crimean War
The Mexican army crossed into Texas

q.e: Both founding fathers died on July 4, 1826, exactly 50 years after the adoption of the Declaration of Independence. Adams's famous last words were reportedly about Jefferson, unaware that Jefferson had died hours earlier.

q: Which of the following events happened on March,1692?
The Salem witch trials began in New England
An earthquake in Mexico killed over 10,000
General Braddock was killed by the French
The Indians sold Manhattan Island to the Dutch

q.e: The Salem witch trials began in early 1692 in Massachusetts, with the first formal examinations in March. Twenty people were executed.

q: President Reagan was shot in 1981 as he left this hotel.

q.e: President Reagan was shot outside the Washington Hilton on 30 March 1981 by John Hinckley Jr. He recovered, and press secretary James Brady was seriously wounded.

q: The Battle of Gettysburg was fought on these dates.

q.e: Gettysburg was fought 1-3 July 1863 and left about 50,000 casualties. It's often seen as the Civil War's turning point.

q: WW II started on September 1, 1939 when Germany invaded which country?

q.e: Germany invaded Poland on September 1, 1939, using a staged border attack at Gleiwitz as a pretext, which prompted Britain and France to declare war two days later.

q: The spinning jenny is a multi-spool spinning wheel invented in 1764 in this country.

q.e: James Hargreaves invented the spinning jenny in England in about 1764. It spun many threads at once and sped up the Industrial Revolution.

q: Which of the following was referred to as the Gift of the Nile?

q.e: The ancient Greek historian Herodotus famously called Egypt the 'gift of the Nile' because its rich civilization depended entirely on the river's annual flooding to fertilize the arid desert soil.

q: Where is the Nile Delta located?
at the source of the river

q.e: The Nile Delta is in Lower Egypt, in the north, where the river meets the Mediterranean. Lower Egypt is "lower" because the Nile flows north.

q: How many distinct kingdoms were there in Ancient Egypt?

q.e: Ancient Egyptian history is divided into the Old, Middle and New Kingdoms, with intermediate periods between them.

q: Who was chosen to be the 2006 Time Magazines Person of the Year?

q.e: Time's 2006 Person of the Year was "You", for the user-generated content on the web (YouTube, Wikipedia, MySpace).

q: Who was the last Tsar of Russia, King of Poland and Grand Duke of Finland?

q.e: Nicholas II ruled the Russian Empire from 1894 until his abdication in March 1917 amid the Russian Revolution, ending more than three centuries of Romanov dynastic rule.

q: What was the title of Karl Marxs influential treatise on political economy, first published in 1867?

q.e: Karl Marx's Capital (Das Kapital) Volume I came out in 1867. Engels edited Volumes II and III after Marx died.

q: Bolshevik revolutionary and Marxist theorist Leon Trotsky was assassinated in which country?

q.e: Trotsky was assassinated in Coyoacán, Mexico City, in August 1940. Ramón Mercader killed him with an ice axe on Stalin's orders.

q: During the Russian Revolution of 1917, which city was capital of Russia?

q.e: In 1917 the capital was Petrograd, the Russified name for Saint Petersburg adopted in 1914. It later became Leningrad, and since 1991 Saint Petersburg again.

q: Which northern state was last to make slavery illegal?
They all made it illegal at the same time

q.e: New Jersey was the last northern state to abolish slavery, with a gradual abolition law in 1804 and full abolition by the 13th Amendment in 1865.

q: Approximately how long was The Spanish-American War?

q.e: The Spanish-American War lasted about three and a half months, from April to August 1898. The US gained Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines.

q: Which war, fought in the 20th century, is sometimes referred to as The Forgotten War?

q.e: The Korean War (1950–1953) is often called The Forgotten War because it was overshadowed in American public memory by the scale of World War II and the controversy of the Vietnam War.

q: Who was the father of Alexander the Great?

q.e: King Philip II of Macedon unified most of classical Greece before being assassinated in 336 BC, paving the way for his son Alexander to conquer the Persian Empire.

q: This vessel, one of the symbols of progress during the Victorian Era, was the first steam ship purposely built for Atlantic crossing.

q.e: Isambard Kingdom Brunel designed the SS Great Western, which crossed the Atlantic under steam power in 1838 in about 15 days.

q: In 1847 Veracruz, one of the most important Mexican seaports, was besieged for 20 days. The beginning of the siege was marked when this country conducted its first large-scale amphibious assault on it.

q.e: In March 1847 General Winfield Scott led the first large US amphibious landing, at Veracruz. The city fell after about 20 days, opening the way to Mexico City.

q: What device was invented in 1879 by James Ritty, the owner of a tavern in Dayton, Ohio?

q.e: James Ritty invented the cash register ("Ritty's Incorruptible Cashier") in 1879 to stop employees pocketing sales. National Cash Register later developed it.

q: What was the real name of General Stonewall Jackson?

q.e: Stonewall Jackson was born Thomas Jonathan Jackson in 1824. He got the famous nickname at the First Battle of Bull Run (Manassas).

q: Before the Civil War, Stonewall Jackson was a professor of artillery and natural philosophy at which institute of higher learning?

q.e: Jackson taught at the Virginia Military Institute in Lexington from 1851 until the Civil War. Students found him an odd, stiff instructor.

q: General Jackson acquired his nickname of Stonewall at which Civil War battle?

q.e: At First Bull Run (July 1861), General Bee reportedly said, "There stands Jackson like a stone wall." The name stuck.

q: Stonewall Jacksons mortal wound necessitated the amputation of which limb?

q.e: Jackson's left arm was amputated after he was accidentally shot at Chancellorsville, and he died of pneumonia eight days later.

q: Who started the movement of Protestant Reformation in Europe?

q.e: Martin Luther initiated the Protestant Reformation in 1517 when he published his Ninety-five Theses attacking the Roman Catholic practice of selling indulgences.

q: In what country did the Industrial Revolution start?

q.e: The Industrial Revolution began in Great Britain during the mid-18th century, driven by innovations such as James Watt's improved steam engine and abundant coal and iron ore reserves.

q: In the early 1950s, which of the following became the third country to have an atomic bomb?

q.e: Britain tested its first atomic bomb in October 1952 (Operation Hurricane), after the US (1945) and Soviet Union (1949).

q: Which event did not occur in the 1950s?
Bobby Fisher becomes the World Champion in chess.
The Frisbee is successfully marketed in the USA.
The first successful test of a hydrogen bomb was done at Enewetak

q.e: Bobby Fischer won the World Championship in 1972 by beating Boris Spassky in Reykjavik. That was not in the 1950s.

q: The Rosetta stone helped scientists to decipher the alphabet of this ancient civilization.

q.e: Discovered in 1799, the Rosetta Stone features the same decree inscribed in Ancient Greek, Demotic, and Egyptian hieroglyphs, enabling Jean-François Champollion to decipher Egyptian hieroglyphs in 1822.

q: What precipitated the 1969 six-day war between El Salvador and Honduras?
Import tariffs on Honduran goods exported into El Salvador
Import tariffs on Salvadoran goods exported into Honduras
Control over the oil reserves in the Gulf of Fonseca

q.e: The Football War (July 1969) was set off by riots at World Cup qualifying games between El Salvador and Honduras. The deeper causes were land and immigration disputes.

q: The Battle of Crécy, which took place on 26 August 1346, was one of the most important battles of a war conflict between which two countries?

q.e: Crécy (1346) was an early English victory over France in the Hundred Years' War, in which English longbowmen broke the French cavalry.

q: Which country occupied Vietnam from the end of WW II to 1954, setting the scene for a civil war between North and South Vietnam?

q.e: France ruled Vietnam as part of French Indochina and tried to retake it after WWII (Japan occupied it during the war). It lost at Dien Bien Phu in 1954.

q: Before its trans-Atlantic voyage the Mayflower was a merchant ship travelling between England and other European countries. What was its primary cargo?

q.e: Before 1620 the Mayflower was a merchant ship that carried cargo such as wine across the Channel and to France and Spain.

q: Where did the pilgrims aboard the Mayflower intend to settle?

q.e: The Pilgrims meant to settle near the Hudson River (northern Virginia territory) but ended up at Cape Cod after storms, and settled Plymouth.

q: Napoleon Bonaparte usually wore a uniform of the following rank.

q.e: Napoleon often wore the green uniform of a colonel of the Chasseurs à Cheval of the Imperial Guard, even though he was Emperor.

q: The roots of the word knight are connected to cniht, an Old English word meaning this.

q.e: "Knight" comes from Old English cniht, meaning boy or servant. Over time it came to mean a mounted warrior.

q: Ritter is a title similar to that of a Knight, used in this country.

q.e: Ritter is the German equivalent of knight, from "reiten" (to ride). Austria and other German states also used it.

q: What state succeeded the Austrian Empire in 1867?

q.e: After losing a war with Prussia, the Austrian Empire became Austria-Hungary in 1867 with the Compromise (Ausgleich). It lasted until 1918.

q: This organization, established in Paris, 1951, was the predecessor of the European Union.

q.e: The European Coal and Steel Community, set up by the 1951 Treaty of Paris (in force 1952), joined six countries' coal and steel industries and led to the EU.

q: What city became the capital after the unification of Germany in 1990?

q.e: The 1990 Unification Treaty restored Berlin as the capital of reunified Germany, taking over from Bonn, which had served as the provisional capital of West Germany since 1949.

q: Which country transferred sovereignty of Hong Kong to China in 1997?

q.e: On July 1, 1997, the United Kingdom ended more than 150 years of British colonial rule by handing sovereignty of Hong Kong over to China under the 'one country, two systems' framework.

q: In 1994, which political party won the majority in the US congress for the first time in 40 years?

q.e: The Republicans won both houses of Congress in the 1994 midterms, led by Newt Gingrich's "Contract with America". It was their first House majority in 40 years.

q: Who was a serf in the Middle Ages?
A farmer who was not free

q.e: A medieval serf was a peasant tied to the land of a lord and not free to leave. They owed labor and a share of crops.

q: Which language was NOT commonly spoken by inhabitants of the Holy Roman Empire during the Middle Ages?
