q.e: In the Holy Roman Empire people spoke German, Latin (for church and law), Czech, Italian and French. Spanish was not common.

q: Which language was the medieval lingua franca?

q.e: Latin was the lingua franca of medieval Europe in religion, scholarship and law. The term "lingua franca" itself came from a Mediterranean trade language.

q: Which entity was ruled by Frederic Barbarossa?

q.e: Frederick I "Barbarossa" (red beard) was Holy Roman Emperor (1155-1190), and drowned while on the Third Crusade.

q: What was the objective of Operation Sea Lion?
Mining of the Norwegian coast to avoid German invasion
Commando raid on Dieppe to test Atlantic Wall defenses

q.e: Operation Sea Lion was Germany's plan to invade Britain in 1940. It was shelved after the Luftwaffe lost the Battle of Britain.

q: Geographically, Mayan cities were mainly situated in which of these locations?
The central parts of South America
The West coast of North America

q.e: Mayan cities were in Mesoamerica: southern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize and parts of Honduras and El Salvador. Tikal and Chichén Itzá are well-known examples.

q: Maya ritual ceremonies were particularly noted for which one of these reasons?

q.e: Maya ritual included bloodletting and human sacrifice, which they believed fed the gods and kept the world in order.

q: Due to the lack of natural resources, the Mayans were not familiar with this material, which helped in the advancement of many other civilizations.

q.e: The Maya had no ironworking and used stone, obsidian and wood tools. Iron wasn't known in pre-Columbian Americas.

q: In the 4th century, the Mayas were among the first civilizations to use what in their counting system?

q.e: The Maya civilization developed a sophisticated vigesimal (base-20) positional numeral system that used a shell symbol to represent zero as a place holder and a number. This was one of the earliest independent inventions of zero in human history, alongside ancient Indian mathematics.

q: What countrys civilian airliner was shot down by a Russian fighter jet in 1983?

q.e: Korean Air Lines Flight 007 was shot down by a Soviet Su-15 on 1 September 1983 after straying into Soviet airspace. All 269 aboard died.

q: 1981 marked the launch of this first spaceworthy NASA shuttle.

q.e: Space Shuttle Columbia, the first orbital shuttle, launched on 12 April 1981 with John Young and Robert Crippen.

q: 1987 brought this black day for the US stock market.

q.e: Black Monday, 19 October 1987: the Dow Jones fell 22.6% in a single day, the largest one-day percentage drop in its history.

q: What were the nicknames of the two atomic bombs dropped over Japan on 6 August 1945 and 9 August 1945?

q.e: The uranium bomb Little Boy was dropped on Hiroshima on August 6, 1945, by the Enola Gay. Three days later, the plutonium implosion device Fat Man was dropped on Nagasaki by the B-29 Bockscar.

q: Which country was divided into East and West during the Cold War?

q.e: Following World War II, Germany was split into the democratic Federal Republic of Germany (West) and the communist German Democratic Republic (East) until reunification in 1990.

q: Which nation revolted against Soviet-imposed policies in 1956?

q.e: The Hungarian Revolution began in October 1956 as a nationwide revolt against the Soviet-backed communist government before being crushed by Soviet tanks weeks later. The comparable uprising in Czechoslovakia, known as the Prague Spring, did not occur until 1968.

q: In which country did the Solidarność (Solidarity) movement start?

q.e: Solidarność was founded in September 1980 at the Lenin Shipyard in Gdańsk, Poland, under the leadership of Lech Wałęsa. It became the first independent trade union in a Warsaw Pact country.

q: Which Pope was credited with igniting the freedom movement in Poland and eventually in the whole Eastern European region?

q.e: Pope John Paul II, born Karol Wojtyła in Poland, visited Poland in 1979. This inspired the Solidarity movement and helped bring down communism.

q: Which of these dictators was the last to die?

q.e: Francisco Franco died in November 1975. Hitler died in 1945, Mussolini in 1945 and Stalin in 1953.

q: Who was the first Russian tsar of the Romanov dynasty?

q.e: Michael Romanov was elected tsar in 1613, ending the Time of Troubles. The Romanovs ruled until Nicholas II abdicated in 1917.

q: What city was the Russian capital before Tsar Peter the Great founded St. Petersburg?

q.e: Peter the Great moved the Russian capital from Moscow to his newly constructed coastal city of St. Petersburg in 1712; the capital returned to Moscow in 1918 under Vladimir Lenin.

q: Which ruler was crowned the first Tsar of All the Russias?

q.e: Ivan IV ("the Terrible") was crowned the first Tsar of All the Russias in 1547. Before that, rulers were Grand Princes of Moscow.

q: Who was Empress of Russia from 1741 to 1762?

q.e: Elizabeth Petrovna, daughter of Peter the Great, ruled Russia from 1741 to 1762. She built the Winter Palace.

q: The residence of the imperial family south of St. Petersburg
The site of a famous Russian battle
The true last name of the members of the Romanov dynasty

q.e: Tsarskoye Selo ("Tsar's Village"), south of St. Petersburg, was the imperial family's residence, home to the Catherine Palace. It is now called Pushkin.

q: In 1956 Bette Nesmith Graham invented Mistake Out which later became known by what name?

q.e: Bette Nesmith Graham created the correction fluid in her kitchen blender to fix typing mistakes on electric typewriters, originally naming it Mistake Out before renaming it Liquid Paper. Interestingly, Graham was also the mother of The Monkees musician Michael Nesmith.

q: How long was the Hundred Years War?

q.e: The Hundred Years' War between England and France lasted 116 years, from 1337 to 1453. Joan of Arc fought in it.

q: You probably know the term Blitzkrieg (lightning war), which refers to a quick invasion. But what does Sitzkrieg mean?

q.e: "Sitzkrieg" (sitting war) describes the quiet "Phoney War" from September 1939 to May 1940, when little fighting took place in the west.

q: Which war was fought by El Salvador and Honduras in 1969?

q.e: The 1969 Football War between El Salvador and Honduras lasted about 100 hours. It's the only war linked to a soccer match.

q: Which wars were fought in XV century England?

q.e: The Wars of the Roses (1455-1487) were fought between the Houses of Lancaster and York. The Tudors came to the throne at the end.

q: Against which country were the two Gulf Wars fought?

q.e: The Gulf Wars of 1990–1991 and 2003 were both fought against Saddam Hussein's regime in Iraq, the first to liberate Kuwait and the second leading to Hussein's overthrow.

q: The Boer Wars were fought by the British Empire against which colonists?

q.e: The Boer Wars (1880-81, 1899-1902) were fought against the Boers (Afrikaners), Dutch-descended settlers in the Transvaal and Orange Free State.

q: Against which of the following were the medieval Crusades fought?
Against anybody the Pope would declare an enemy
Against Jewish communities across Europe only
Against Moors on the Iberian Peninsula only
Against Turks in the Holy Land only

q.e: The Crusades were launched by the Pope mostly against Muslim-held lands, but also against pagans and heretics. They ran from 1096 to the 1200s.

q: After the 80 Years War (XVI-XVII century) a new colonial power was born in Europe. Which one?

q.e: After the Eighty Years' War (1568-1648) against Spain, the Dutch Republic became a major trading and colonial power.

q: During which war did the Battle of Marathon take place?

q.e: Marathon (490 BC) was part of the Greco-Persian Wars. The Athenians beat Darius's Persian army.

q: What kind of government did Athens have during the Golden Age?

q.e: Athens in the 5th century BC practiced direct democracy: male citizens voted on laws themselves in the assembly.

q: The Soviet war in Afghanistan which started in 1979, continued for how many years?

q.e: The Soviet war in Afghanistan lasted almost ten years, from December 1979 to February 1989. The Soviets withdrew.

q: Which one of these countries was not one of the Allies during WW II?

q.e: Italy was an Axis power until it switched sides in 1943. The Allies included Britain, France, the USSR, the US and China.

q: Operation Barbarossa, which began on June 22, 1941, was the code name of the German invasion of which country?

q.e: Barbarossa was the code name for the German invasion of the Soviet Union. It was named after Emperor Frederick Barbarossa.

q: What does the German word Blitzkrieg mean?

q.e: Blitzkrieg combines the German words Blitz (lightning) and Krieg (war). It describes a rapid, concentrated military strike combining mechanized ground forces and air support.

q: According to statistics, approximately how many people lost their lives in World War II?

q.e: Estimates for WWII deaths vary from about 70 to 85 million, including civilians. Older figures put it near 60 million.

q: Which U.S. state saw the bloodiest fighting of the Civil War?

q.e: Virginia saw the most Civil War fighting, with roughly a quarter of all battles including Bull Run, Fredericksburg and Appomattox.

q: From 1847 to 1923, there were eight U. S. Presidents hailing from this state.

q.e: Ohio is nicknamed the "Mother of Presidents," with seven or eight presidents born there, including Grant, Hayes, Garfield, McKinley, Taft and Harding.

q: This Silk Road dynasty succeeded the Qin Dynasty.

q.e: The Han Dynasty (206 BC-220 AD) followed the Qin and expanded the Silk Road trade routes.

q: The Ming Dynasty established the Forbidden City in Beijing. Do you know what ming means in Chinese?

q.e: Ming (明) means "bright." The Ming Dynasty (1368-1644) built the Forbidden City in Beijing.

q: How long did the Battle of Gettysburg last?

q.e: The Battle of Gettysburg, widely considered the turning point of the American Civil War, was fought from July 1 through July 3, 1863, ending in a Union victory.

q: What state has the most soldiers buried at the Gettysburg National Cemetery?

q.e: Gettysburg National Cemetery holds more Union dead from New York than any other state, about 867 graves.

q: What was the first state to secede from the Union?

q.e: On December 20, 1860, following Abraham Lincoln's election, South Carolina became the first state to adopt an ordinance of secession from the United States.

q: What was the last state to secede from the Union?

q.e: Tennessee was the last state to secede, in June 1861, and the first to be readmitted to the Union after the war (1866).

q: How many Union soldiers were killed during the bombardment of Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor?

q.e: No Union soldiers died in the bombardment of Fort Sumter (12-13 April 1861). One soldier died later in a salute accident.

q: What nickname did Erwin Rommel get during World War II?

q.e: Rommel's British opponents called him the "Desert Fox" in the North African campaign.

q: In what month in 1945 did Japan surrender to the US?

q.e: Japan announced its surrender on 15 August 1945 and signed the formal document on 2 September 1945, in September.

q: What day in 1944 is referred to as D-Day?

q.e: D-Day, 6 June 1944, was the Allied invasion of Normandy, the largest amphibious invasion in history.

q: In what month of 1941 did Nazi Germanys invasion of the Soviet Union start?

q.e: Germany invaded the Soviet Union on 22 June 1941, ending the Nazi-Soviet pact.

q: Who is the first president of the U. S. in the 21st century?

q.e: Bill Clinton was in office until 20 January 2001, while George W. Bush took office after that. Strictly, the 21st century began on 1 January 2001.

q: How long did Hitlers Third Reich last?

q.e: The Third Reich lasted from 1933, when Hitler became Chancellor, to 1945, a total of about 12 years, and was meant to last a thousand.

q: Which of these countries was not neutral during WWII?

q.e: Greece was attacked by Italy (1940) and Germany (1941) and fought in the war. Sweden, Switzerland, Spain and Portugal stayed neutral.

q: Which of the following city states was not on the territory of present-day Greece?

q.e: Troy was in Anatolia in present-day Turkey. Athens, Sparta and Corinth were city-states in present-day Greece.

q: During Cleopatras reign it was believed that she was the re-incarnation and embodiment of this goddess of wisdom.

q.e: Cleopatra presented herself as the living incarnation of the goddess Isis, the Egyptian goddess of magic, motherhood and wisdom.

q: The word Calendar comes form Latin kalendae. What does this word mean?

q.e: "Calendar" comes from the Latin kalendae, the first day of each month, when debts were due. "Kalends" listed accounts.

q: Why is the 9th month of the Gregorian calendar called September?
September was the 7th month in Roman calendar
After Septimus Severus - a Roman Emperor

q.e: The original Roman calendar began in Martius (March), making September the seventh month, derived from the Latin word septem, meaning seven.

q: A week denotes 7 days. Where/when weeks were 10 days long?
During the October Revolution in Russia

q.e: During the French Revolution, the Republican calendar used a 10-day week (décade) from 1793 to 1805.

q: When did the Battle of Trenton take place?

q.e: Washington's Continental Army surprised Hessian troops at Trenton the day after Christmas (26 December 1776), after crossing the icy Delaware River.

q: What were Washingtons passwords for the crossing of the Delaware River and the attack on Trenton?

q.e: Washington's password for the Trenton attack is traditionally reported to have been "Victory or Death".

q: Holland means what in the ancient Dutch language?

q.e: "Holland" is often traced to the Old Dutch "holtlant" (wood land), though some link it to "holland" (hollow land).

q: Who or what destroyed the Great Spanish Armada in 1588?
A hurricane off the coast of Ireland
Francis Drakes attack in the English Channel

q.e: The 1588 Spanish Armada was beaten by English fireships and fighting at Gravelines, and then storms wrecked many ships off Scotland and Ireland.

q: What was the last successful foreign invasion of Britain?

q.e: William of Orange landed in 1688 and took the throne in the Glorious Revolution. It's the last successful invasion of England.

q: Where did Scotland unsuccessfully try to establish a colony?

q.e: Scotland tried to colonize the Isthmus of Darien in Panama (1698-1700). The failure drained the nation's fortunes and led to the 1707 Union with England.

q: What was the relationship between Attila and Bleda who ruled the Huns together until 445?

q.e: The Hun brothers Attila and Bleda ruled together until Bleda died in about 445, probably killed by Attila.

q: Where was the assault rifle invented?

q.e: The Italian Cei-Rigotti was an early automatic rifle (about 1900). Germany's StG 44 (1944) is generally considered the first true assault rifle.

q: The operational jet fighter was invented during this war.

q.e: The first operational jet fighter was Germany's Messerschmitt Me 262, in 1944. The British Gloster Meteor came shortly after.

q: Who did Soviet leader Joseph Stalin appoint as his successor before his death in 1953?

q.e: Stalin never named a successor. After his death in March 1953, a collective leadership including Malenkov, Beria and Khrushchev took over, and Khrushchev came out on top.

q: How long did the United States keep the monopoly on the atomic bomb?

q.e: The US had an atomic monopoly from 1945 until the Soviet Union tested its first bomb in August 1949.

q: What European nation received US aid to try to put down the communist insurgency in Indochina in the late 1940s and early 1950s?

q.e: France fought the communist Viet Minh in Indochina and got heavy US aid, before losing in 1954.

q: When did the Cuban Missile Crisis occur?

q.e: The Cuban Missile Crisis lasted 13 days, 16-28 October 1962. The USSR agreed to remove its missiles from Cuba.

q: The US became convinced that Soviet nuclear missiles were in Cuba by which of the following?
photos taken by a U-2 spy plane
a Cuban defectors report and pictures of missiles sites
Soviet announcement of the instillation of nuclear missiles in Cuba

q.e: On 14 October 1962, a U-2 spy plane photographed Soviet missile sites under construction in Cuba.

q: The US gained some legality for their blockade of Cuba during the Cuban Missile Crisis, when they received strong approval and support from this organization.

q.e: The Organization of American States voted to support the US naval "quarantine" of Cuba in October 1962, giving it legal footing.

q: More than seventy million people were killed in this war, which made it the deadliest conflict of all time.

q.e: World War II (1939-1945) was the deadliest war in history, with an estimated 70-85 million deaths, including about six million Jews in the Holocaust.

q: The participants in this war never came to the point of a direct military clash, but fought indirectly through espionage, propaganda and competition in various fields.

q.e: The Cold War spanned roughly from 1947 to 1991 between the Western Bloc (led by the United States) and the Eastern Bloc (led by the Soviet Union). Both superpowers avoided direct combat due to the threat of nuclear annihilation, fighting instead via proxy wars, the Space Race, and espionage.

q: This war took place between September 26, 1959 and April 30, 1975 as part of the Cold War conflict.

q.e: The Vietnam War concluded on April 30, 1975, with the fall of Saigon, after decades of conflict between North Vietnam and South Vietnam and its allies, including the United States.

q: What statement is true about the US Presidential election scheduled in the midst of the war for November 1944?
It was carried out without any significant changes.
It was canceled and Roosevelt allowed to continue as President.
It had five voting days instead of one to give people a better chance to vote.
It was delayed until the Japanese surrender.

q.e: The 1944 US election was held on schedule in the middle of the war, and Franklin Roosevelt won a fourth term. He died in April 1945.

q: Which country in Europe had the first large permanent military force in Europe?

q.e: Historians often cite France's standing army under Charles VII (1445) as the first in Europe. Spain's Tercios were also an early professional force.

q: To what period does the Terror refer to?
The rule of the Legislative Assembly - 1793 - 1794
The rule of the Legislative Assembly - 1791 - 1792
The rule of the National Constitutional Assembly - 1789 - 1791

q.e: The Reign of Terror (1793-94) was carried out by the Committee of Public Safety under Robespierre, working with the National Convention. Thousands were guillotined.

q: What did the name Caligula originally refer to?

q.e: Caligula was a childhood nickname meaning little boots, derived from caliga, the heavy-soled hobnailed military sandal. Roman soldiers gave it to the future emperor Gaius when he accompanied his father Germanicus on campaigns wearing miniature uniform boots.

q: The United States Supreme Court declared that this man invented the radio.

q.e: In 1943 the US Supreme Court ruled that Marconi's patent was invalid because of earlier work by others, including Tesla. Tesla died that same year.

q: Who made the first light bulb?

q.e: Joseph Swan in England and Thomas Edison in the US developed practical incandescent bulbs in 1878-79. They later formed Ediswan.

q: What did Ivan Getting and Bradford Parkinson develop?

q.e: Ivan Getting and Bradford Parkinson led the development of the Global Positioning System (GPS), which began in the 1970s.

q: The elograph, which was invented in 1971, was the basis of what device?

q.e: The elograph, invented by Sam Hurst in 1971, was the first resistive touch sensor and led to touchscreens.

q: What everyday item was invented by Will Mueller in 1935?

q.e: Will Muller invented the automatic telephone answering machine in 1935 (the "Electronic Secretary"?). Ansafone was a later version.

q: Before arriving at Gallipoli, the Anzacs trained in what country?

q.e: Australian and New Zealand troops (ANZACs) trained in Egypt before landing at Gallipoli on 25 April 1915. Anzac Day marks it.

q: Following the outbreak of the First World War in 1914, which army opened the Western Front by invading Belgium and Luxembourg?

q.e: Germany invaded Belgium and Luxembourg in August 1914, after the Schlieffen Plan, and opened the Western Front.

q: What memorial was dedicated on May 30, 1922?

q.e: The Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C., was dedicated on 30 May 1922. Lincoln's statue was carved by the Piccirilli brothers.

q: What state became the 32nd state of the Union on May 11, 1858?

q.e: Minnesota became the 32nd state on 11 May 1858.

q: On May 23, 1934, bank robbers Bonnie Parker and Clyde Barrow were gunned down in this state.

q.e: Bonnie and Clyde were ambushed and killed by lawmen near Gibsland, Louisiana, on 23 May 1934.

q: The U.S. acquired Spanish Florida on the 22th day of this month in 1819.

q.e: The Adams-Onís Treaty, signed 22 February 1819, transferred Florida from Spain to the US. It also fixed the border with Spanish territory.

q: Patriot Day is celebrated in this month in the USA, in memory of the casualties in the September 11 attacks.

q.e: Patriot Day is observed on 11 September, remembering those killed in the 2001 attacks.

q: In this month Martin Luther King, Jr. Day is celebrated in the United States and Australia Day is celebrated in Australia.

q.e: Martin Luther King Jr. Day is the third Monday of January, and Australia Day is 26 January.

q: In this month, Julius Caesar was killed, and International Womens Day and Saint Patricks Day are celebrated.

q.e: In March, Julius Caesar was killed (Ides, 15 March), and International Women's Day (8 March) and St Patrick's Day (17 March) are marked.

q: In this month the USA celebrates its Independence Day.

q.e: Independence Day in the United States is celebrated every year on the Fourth of July. The holiday marks the formal adoption of the Declaration of Independence by the Second Continental Congress on July 4, 1776.

q: Napoleon Bonaparte was born in this month, which marks the official end of the Second World War.

q.e: Napoleon was born on 15 August 1769. Japan's surrender was announced on 15 August 1945 and formally signed on 2 September.

q: Valentines Day is celebrated in this month, which is also Black History Month in Canada and the United States.

q.e: Valentine's Day is 14 February, and February is also Black History Month in the US and Canada.

q: In many countries Labor Day is observed in this month, which is also dedicated to the Blessed Virgin Mary in Roman Catholic tradition.

q.e: International Workers' Day (Labour Day) is 1 May in many countries, and May is dedicated to Mary in Catholic tradition.

q: Thermopylae, the site of the historic Battle of Thermopylae, was what type of area?
It was a wide open plain

q.e: Thermopylae ("hot gates") was a narrow coastal pass in central Greece, where 300 Spartans and their allies held back the Persians in 480 BC.

q: In the historic Battle of Thermopylae, who is Ephialtes?

q.e: Ephialtes betrayed the Greeks at Thermopylae by showing the Persians a mountain path around the pass. His name came to mean "nightmare" in Greek.

q: Which of these was the legal successor to the classical Roman Empire?

q.e: The Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire lasted until 1453 as the continuation of the Roman Empire, long after the West fell in 476.

q: What was the language of science in the ancient world?

q.e: Greek was the language of science and philosophy in the ancient world, used by Aristotle, Euclid and Ptolemy.

q: When did the Christianisation of Germanic tribes begin?

q.e: Germanic tribes began converting to Christianity in the 4th century, with Bishop Ulfilas translating the Bible into Gothic.

q: When did the great migration of the Slavs begin?

q.e: The Slavs spread across Central and Eastern Europe from the 5th to the 7th centuries, as the Western Empire collapsed.
"Paleozoic" comes from Greek for "ancient life." It covers 541 to 252 million years ago, from the Cambrian explosion to the Permian extinction.

q: In which country did the name Gustav originate?

q.e: Gustav (Gustaf) is a Swedish name linked to Swedish kings such as Gustavus Adolphus and Gustav Vasa.

q: Which of these are not characteristic of Gothic architecture?

q.e: Gothic architecture is known for pointed arches, rib vaults, flying buttresses and large stained-glass windows. Dark walls are not a defining feature.

q: In which of the following present-day countries was Gothic language spoken?

q.e: The Goths included Visigoths and Ostrogoths. The Ostrogoths ruled Italy from 493 to 553, and Gothic was spoken there.

q: Which of these countries fought on the side of Britain during the Battle of Britain?

q.e: Pilots from Canada, Poland, Czechoslovakia and other countries joined the RAF in the Battle of Britain (1940).

q: How was Catherine the Great of Russia related to Petar III?

q.e: Catherine the Great married Peter III in 1745. She took the throne in a 1762 coup, after which he died.

q: How were Napoleon Bonaparte and Napoleon III related?

q.e: Napoleon III (Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte), emperor of France 1852-70, was the nephew of Napoleon I.

q: This King of the Franks conquered Italy and was crowned Imperator Augustus on 25 December 800.

q.e: Charlemagne (Charles the Great), king of the Franks, was crowned emperor by Pope Leo III on Christmas Day, 800, in Rome.

q: What English Queen was daughter of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn?

q.e: Elizabeth I was born in September 1533 to King Henry VIII and his second wife, Anne Boleyn, ruling England and Ireland for 44 years from 1558 until 1603.

q: What monarch transformed the Tsardom of Russia into the Russian Empire?

q.e: Peter the Great officially proclaimed the Russian Empire in 1721 following Russia's victory over Sweden in the Great Northern War, replacing the Tsardom of Russia.

q: What song hit # 1 on the Billboard Charts on July 9, 1955?

q.e: "Rock Around the Clock" by Bill Haley & His Comets hit #1 on the Billboard charts in July 1955, one of the first rock and roll hits.

q: On July 11, 1804, V.P. Aaron Burr fatally wounded this famous founding father in a duel.

q.e: Vice President Aaron Burr and former Treasury Secretary Alexander Hamilton fought their duel in Weehawken, New Jersey, where Hamilton was shot and died the following day.

q: What city opened the first Worlds Fair in the United States on July 14, 1853?

q.e: The first US world's fair, the Exhibition of the Industry of All Nations, opened in New York City's Crystal Palace in July 1853.

q: What federal institution was founded on July 26, 1908?

q.e: The Bureau of Investigation, later the FBI, was created on 26 July 1908. It was renamed the FBI in 1935.

q: What does the term seppuku, connected with the culture of Japanese samurai, refer to?

q.e: Seppuku, often colloquially called harakiri, was a ritual suicide by disembowelment practiced by the samurai class to restore honor or avoid falling into enemy hands.

q: Who would arrange the marriage of the Japanese samurai by tradition?
Someone with the same or higher rank

q.e: In samurai society marriages were arranged, and typically needed the approval of the lord, with partners from families of equal or similar rank.

q: What English sailor is believed to be the first Caucasian to receive the honor of becoming a samurai?

q.e: English sailor William Adams (1564-1620) became a samurai under Tokugawa Ieyasu, taking the name Miura Anjin. He inspired the character in Shōgun.

q: When was the Battle of Antietam fought?

q.e: Antietam was fought on 17 September 1862, the bloodiest single day in American history, with about 22,000 casualties.

q: Who was the Confederate commander at the Battle of Antietam?

q.e: Robert E. Lee commanded the Confederates at Antietam, against George McClellan's Union army.

q: How long did the Battle of Antietam last?

q.e: Antietam was fought in a single day, 17 September 1862. The armies stayed in place the next day before Lee withdrew.

q: Which battle preceded the Battle of Antietam?
The Second Battle of Bull Run

q.e: The Second Battle of Bull Run (late August 1862) was a Confederate win, and led Lee to invade Maryland and fight at Antietam.

q: The Byzantine period began in this century which also saw the Valerians massacre of Christians.

q.e: In the 3rd century AD the Roman Emperor Valerian persecuted Christians (257-260). Byzantium's earlier history spans the 3rd-4th centuries.

q: Nostradamus, Martin Luther and Elizabeth I of England lived during what century?

q.e: Nostradamus (1503-66), Martin Luther (1483-1546) and Elizabeth I (1533-1603) all lived in the 16th century.

q: The first novel ever is believed to have been written in this century by the Japanese Lady Murasaki Shikibu.

q.e: Lady Murasaki Shikibu wrote The Tale of Genji in early 11th-century Japan. It's often called the world's first novel.

q: Julius Caesar, Marcus Antonius, and Cleopatra VII of Egypt all lived in this century.

q.e: Caesar, Mark Antony and Cleopatra VII all lived in the 1st century BC.

q: What century marked the fall of the Western Roman Empire?

q.e: The Western Roman Empire fell in 476 AD, when Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus, in the 5th century.

q: During this century, the condom, the land mine and the sandpaper were invented.

q.e: Sandpaper was reportedly invented in 13th-century China, using crushed shells glued to parchment. Land mines are first reported in 13th-century China too.

q: In what century were the fountain pen, shaving soap and street lamps invented?

q.e: Items like fountain pens and street lamps appear in 9th- and 10th-century records of the Islamic world. Dates are debated.

q: In this century, the decline of the Classical Maya civilization began, and Charlemagne was crowned the first Holy Roman Emperor by Pope Leo III.

q.e: In 800, Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne emperor, and the Classic Maya collapse started around the 8th and 9th centuries.

q: What does the term Mesozoic mean?

q.e: "Mesozoic" means "middle life", the age of dinosaurs, from 252 to 66 million years ago. It includes the Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous.

q: The first true Homo sapiens (human) appeared in Africa about how many years ago?

q.e: Early Homo sapiens fossils date to roughly 300,000 years ago (Jebel Irhoud, Morocco) and about 200,000 at Omo, Ethiopia. The ~250,000 figure is a rough middle.
Radiometric dating of the oldest known meteorites and Moon rocks indicates the Earth and the rest of the solar system formed roughly 4.54 billion years ago.

q: Which one happened to the U.S. in 1791?
Bill of Rights goes into effect
1st recorded UFO sighting by an American
Benedict Arnold found guilty of being a traitor

q.e: The Bill of Rights, the first ten amendments to the US Constitution, took effect on 15 December 1791 once Virginia ratified it.

q: In 1987 Nike introduced these trainers that enable the wearer to jump higher.

q.e: Nike's Air Max 1 (1987) introduced the visible air cushioning unit. It was designed to cushion impact, not to make people jump higher.

q: The Civil War produced a number of technical innovations. One of the following was not used in this war.

q.e: Tanks didn't appear until World War I (1916). The Civil War did see ironclad ships, submarines, railroads, telegraphs and repeating rifles.

q: This Union general earned the nickname The Rock of Chickamauga.

q.e: George H. Thomas held the Union line at Chickamauga (September 1863) after other units collapsed, earning the nickname "Rock of Chickamauga."

q: In what state did pope John Paul II and president Reagan meet in May, 1984?

q.e: Reagan and Pope John Paul II met in Fairbanks, Alaska, on 2 May 1984, when the Pope stopped to refuel on his way to Asia.

q: Name the Ohio senator who made an unsuccessful bid for presidency in 1984.

q.e: Senator John Glenn, the first American to orbit Earth, sought the 1984 Democratic nomination but dropped out. Walter Mondale won.

q: Who was the first man to ride the space shuttle into orbit twice?

q.e: John Young flew on the first shuttle mission, Columbia's STS-1 in 1981, and again on STS-9 in 1983. He had flown six times overall, including Gemini and Apollo.

q: Whose visit to South Korea in May of 1984 promoted the tightest security in that nations history?

q.e: Pope John Paul II visited South Korea in May 1984 to canonize 103 Korean martyrs, with heavy security.

q: Adolf Hitler was the leader of Nazi Germany and the head of which German party?

q.e: Hitler led the National Socialist German Workers' Party (NSDAP), the Nazi Party. He became Chancellor in 1933.

q: Until which event did the US remain neutral in the Second World War?

q.e: Japan's surprise strike on Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941, killed over 2,400 Americans and prompted Congress to declare war the following day.

q: Which countries were Israels enemies during the 1967 Arab-Israeli War, also known as the Six-Day War?

q.e: In the Six-Day War (June 1967) Israel fought Egypt, Syria and Jordan, with Iraq and others lending support. Israel took the Sinai, Golan Heights and West Bank.

q: Rosie the Riveter was a character that represented all the women joining the workforce during World War II, when the factories were empty and needed staff. The picture of Rosie could be seen on many posters and stamps all of which had what slogan?

q.e: The "We Can Do It!" poster (1943) was made by J. Howard Miller for Westinghouse. It wasn't called Rosie the Riveter until later.
World War I began in July-August 1914, after the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand on 28 June.

q: Who was Time Magazines Person of the Year for 2007?

q.e: Time chose Vladimir Putin as 2007 Person of the Year, "for taking a country in turmoil and making it a power."

q: Which Anglo-Saxon King of England died at the Battle of Hastings?

q.e: Harold Godwinson, crowned King Harold II in January 1066, was killed on October 14, 1066, during the Battle of Hastings against Duke William of Normandy. His death marked the end of Anglo-Saxon rule in England.

q: How many minutes did President Bush remain seated, reading My Pet Goat in a 3rd-grade classroom in Florida, after he was first told America is under attack on September 11, 2001?

q.e: President Bush stayed in the Florida classroom for about five to seven minutes after being told of the second tower strike. Accounts vary on the exact time.

q: What was the flight number of the hijacked plane that crashed in rural Pennsylvania on September 11, 2001?

q.e: United Airlines Flight 93 crashed in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers and crew fought back against hijackers to prevent an attack on Washington, D.C.

q: What does the Arabic term Al Qaeda mean?

q.e: In Arabic, al-qa'ida literally translates to 'the base' or 'the foundation'. The militant organization adopted the name in the late 1980s during the Soviet-Afghan War.

q: It takes this long after liftoff, before the orbiter starts circling Earth at 17,500mph (28,000km/h).

q.e: The shuttle reached orbit about 8½ minutes after liftoff, when the main engines cut off. Orbital speed is about 17,500 mph.

q: NASA selected this astronaut to command the first Columbia flight. He was a veteran of two Gemini and two Apollo missions and considered to be NASAs most experienced astronaut at the time.

q.e: John Young commanded Columbia's first flight (STS-1, April 1981). He had flown two Gemini and two Apollo missions and walked on the Moon (Apollo 16).

q: How many days before 9/11 did George W. Bush receive a Presidents Daily Brief intelligence report entitled Bin Laden Determined to Strike in U.S.?

q.e: The Presidential Daily Brief titled "Bin Ladin Determined to Strike in US" was delivered on 6 August 2001, roughly five weeks before the attacks.

q: In 1942 there was a terrible ammonium nitrate explosion that killed 20 people. Where did it occur?
in the Atlantic Ocean on a cargo ship

q.e: Ammonium nitrate is both a fertilizer and an explosive component, and has caused many industrial disasters. The worst US one was at Texas City in 1947.

q: Which of the following is NOT true about the Battle of Saratoga in 1777?
General George Washington was wounded while directing the American troops.
It was the first major victory for the Americans.
The American victory convinced the French to give the Americans substantial aid.
British General Burgoyne invading from Canada lost his entire army.

q.e: At Saratoga (1777), Benedict Arnold was wounded, not Washington. The American victory convinced France to ally with the US.

q: Where would you be if you heard Tattoo yell out, Ze plane! Ze plane!

q.e: Tattoo (Hervé Villechaize) greeted guests on Fantasy Island by shouting "Ze plane! Ze plane!" Mr. Roarke ran the island.

q: In 1853 the Crimean War began. Which country was not part of the coalition against Russia?

q.e: The Crimean War (1853-56) saw Britain, France, Sardinia and the Ottomans fight Russia. Austria stayed out, although it threatened Russia.

q: The United Islamic Front for the Salvation of Afghanistan is also known as?

q.e: The United Islamic Front for the Salvation of Afghanistan, called the Northern Alliance in the West, opposed the Taliban. Its leader Ahmad Shah Massoud was killed in 2001.

q: On September 27th, 1779 this politician was appointed by American Congress to start negotiating peace with the British.

q.e: On 27 September 1779 Congress appointed John Adams to negotiate peace and commercial treaties with Britain. The Treaty of Paris was signed in 1783.

q: What is the War of Laws?
The implementation of National legislation laws vs. Soviet Union laws
The Iraqis democratic government attempt to get an acceptable constitution
ANCs attempt to change the discrimination laws in South Africas Apartheid regime
The EU attempt to override local Member State law

q.e: The "War of Laws" (1988-91) was a clash in which Soviet republics passed laws that overrode the central Soviet laws. It helped bring about the USSR's collapse.

q: What cartoon character made his film debut on June 9, 1934?

q.e: Donald Duck made his debut in the Silly Symphony "The Wise Little Hen," released on 9 June 1934.

q: This corporation, initially known as the Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company, was incorporated on June 15, 1911.

q.e: The Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company was renamed International Business Machines (IBM) in 1924. Thomas Watson led it.

q: What president signed legislation providing for an 8-hour work-day applicable to federal employees on June 25, 1868?

q.e: President Andrew Johnson signed the eight-hour day law for federal workers on 25 June 1868.

q: How did the Greeks overtake the city of Troy during the Trojan War?
They used a wooden hollow horse.
They destroyed the walls of the city.

q.e: Concealing a strike force inside a colossal wooden horse left as a mock offering to Athena, the Greeks tricked the Trojans into wheeling it inside their city walls, leading to Troy's downfall that night.

q: What common feature do all of the entrances of the Pyramids in Giza share?
They all face the exact north.
They all face the exact west.
They all face the Nile River bank.
They are all oriented towards the Sphinx.

q.e: The entrances of the Giza pyramids face north, so the tombs could be reached with the pole stars as a guide to the afterlife.

q: Towards the end of the 14th century, vandalized by an angered Sufi Muslim, the Great Sphinx of Giza lost what essential piece.

q.e: Arab historian al-Maqrizi recorded in the 15th century that a Sufi named Muhammad Sa'im al-Dahr defaced the nose of the Sphinx around 1378 AD to deter local villagers from making offerings to it.

q: Who portrayed Davy Crockett in the 1960 movie The Alamo?

q.e: John Wayne played Davy Crockett in his 1960 film The Alamo, which he also directed. Richard Widmark played Jim Bowie.

q: During this century the French Revolution began, and the United States Declaration of Independence was signedd.

q.e: The French Revolution (1789) and the American Declaration of Independence (1776) both took place in the 18th century.

q: In this century paper was first produced by Chinese people, and the Silk Road between Europe and Asia was created.

q.e: Paper was first made in China, with the earliest finds dating to the 2nd century BC, and the Silk Road opened up in the same era under the Han Dynasty.

q: In this century, the Muslim conquests began, and the population on the planet was reduced to approximately 208 million people.

q.e: The Muslim conquests began in the 7th century after Muhammad's death in 632, spreading from Arabia across the Middle East and North Africa.

q: This century saw the discovery of the Americas and of a sea route along Cape of Good Hope to India.

q.e: Columbus reached the Americas in 1492, and Vasco da Gama sailed around Africa's Cape of Good Hope to India in 1498. Both fell in the 15th century.

q: In this century gunpowder was first used in a battle, and lions become extinct in Europe.

q.e: Gunpowder was invented in China earlier, but military use grew around the 10th century. Lions died out in Europe in about 100 AD.

q: Roman Emperors Caligula, Augustus, Claudius and Nero lived in this century.

q.e: Augustus (died 14 AD), Caligula, Claudius and Nero all ruled in the 1st century AD. Nero was the last of the Julio-Claudian dynasty.

q: The Great Fire of London and the Great Plague of London occurred in this century.

q.e: Both disasters struck London in the 1660s: the Great Plague devastated the population in 1665, and the Great Fire razed much of the city over four days in September 1666.

q: What century witnessed the reign of the so-called Five Good Emperors of Rome?

q.e: The Five Good Emperors (Nerva, Trajan, Hadrian, Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius) ruled from 96 to 180 AD, in the 2nd century.

q: What movie won the Academy Award for Best Picture at the 61st Academy Awards ceremony held on March 27, 1989?
My Left Foot: The Story of Christy Brown

q.e: Rain Man won Best Picture at the 61st Academy Awards (March 1989). Dustin Hoffman won Best Actor.

q: What notable event happened in New York City on November 7, 1989?
The first African American mayor of the city was elected.
The city was visited by the Pope.
A grizzly bear on the loose fell asleep on Times Square.

q.e: On 7 November 1989 David Dinkins was elected the first Black mayor of New York City.

q: What American rapper was born on October 4, 1989 in New York City?

q.e: Lil' Mama (Niatia Kirkland) is a New York rapper from Harlem, known for "Lipgloss" (2007). Her birthdate is generally given as 7 October 1989.

q: In what year did humans first walk on the Moon?

q.e: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin stepped onto the lunar surface on July 20, 1969, during NASA's Apollo 11 mission.

q: In what year did the United States declare independence?

q.e: The Second Continental Congress formally adopted the Declaration of Independence in Philadelphia on July 4, 1776.

q: In what year did Christopher Columbus first reach the Americas?

q.e: Columbus made landfall on an island in the Bahamas on October 12, 1492, having sailed across the Atlantic with his three ships: the Nina, the Pinta, and the Santa Maria.

q: In what year did World War II end?

q.e: World War II concluded in 1945 with the unconditional surrender of Germany in May and the formal surrender of Japan aboard the USS Missouri in September.

Machu Picchu was built as an estate for the Inca emperor Pachacuti around 1450 in the Andes Mountains of modern-day Peru. The Maya and Olmec civilisations developed earlier and were located in Mesoamerica.

q: Who gave the "I Have a Dream" speech?

q.e: Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his iconic 'I Have a Dream' speech from the steps of the Lincoln Memorial on August 28, 1963, during the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom.

q: Which war was fought between the northern and southern U.S. states?

q.e: The American Civil War lasted from 1861 to 1865, fought between 23 northern and border Union states and 11 southern Confederate states that attempted to secede.

q: Which French military leader crowned himself Emperor of the French in 1804?

q.e: Napoleon Bonaparte took the imperial crown from the hands of Pope Pius VII and placed it on his own head at Notre-Dame Cathedral on December 2, 1804. Charlemagne was crowned Emperor of the Romans in 800, centuries earlier.

q: In what year did the First World War end?

q.e: World War I ended on the 11th hour of the 11th day of the 11th month in 1918, when the armistice between the Allies and Germany took effect.

q: Who famously coined the phrase "I think, therefore I am"?

q.e: French philosopher René Descartes introduced the proposition 'Je pense, donc je suis' in his 1637 Discourse on the Method, later expressed in Latin as 'Cogito, ergo sum'.

q: In what year did Texas secede from Mexico?

q.e: Texas declared independence from Mexico in March 1836, following the Texas Revolution. Texas remained an independent republic until joining the United States in 1845.

q: Which Greek god was the god of the Sun?

q.e: Helios was the Titan god and personification of the Sun, driving a fiery four-horse chariot across the sky each day, though Apollo was also later conflated with the sun in classical literature.

q: The Panama Canal was finished under the administration of which U.S. president?

q.e: The Panama Canal opened on 15 August 1914, in Woodrow Wilson's presidency. Construction began under Theodore Roosevelt.

q: How old was Lyndon B. Johnson when he assumed the role of President of the United States?

q.e: Lyndon B. Johnson (born 27 August 1908) took the oath on 22 November 1963, after Kennedy's assassination, at 55.

q: Joseph Stalin had a criminal past doing what?

q.e: In his early revolutionary years Stalin organized bank robberies for the Bolsheviks. The 1907 Tiflis robbery was one.

q: What historical event was Tchaikovsky's 1812 Overture referencing?
The Charge of the Light Brigade (Crimean War)

q.e: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky composed the overture to commemorate Russia's successful defense against Napoleon Bonaparte's Grande Armée during the 1812 French invasion of Russia. It famously incorporates artillery fire and Russian church hymns.

q: Who was the first wife of King Henry VIII?

q.e: Catherine of Aragon was King Henry VIII's first wife; their marriage lasted nearly 24 years from 1509 to 1533 and produced Queen Mary I. Henry's desire to annul this marriage to wed Anne Boleyn prompted the English Reformation.

q: Against which country did the Dutch Republic fight the Eighty Years' War?

q.e: The Dutch Republic fought Spain in the Eighty Years' War (1568-1648) for independence from Spanish rule.

q: When did the Battle of the Bulge end?

q.e: The Battle of the Bulge (16 December 1944 to 25 January 1945) was Germany's last big offensive on the Western Front.

q: Who was the leader of Sweden in the Great Northern War?

q.e: Charles XII of Sweden led his country in the Great Northern War (1700-1721) against Russia and its allies. Peter the Great beat him at Poltava in 1709.

q: Which Louis was known as 'The Sun King of France'?

q.e: Louis XIV, who reigned for 72 years (1643-1715), was "the Sun King." He built Versailles.

q: Who is attributed credit for recording the epic poem The Odyssey?

q.e: Homer is the ancient Greek poet traditionally credited with composing both The Iliad and The Odyssey around the eighth century BCE.

q: In the War of the Pacific (1879 - 1883), Bolivia lost its access to the Pacific Ocean after being defeated by which South American country?

q.e: Chile defeated Bolivia and Peru in the War of the Pacific (1879-83), and Bolivia lost its coast, becoming landlocked.

q: How many years did the Hundred Years' War last?

q.e: The Hundred Years' War lasted 116 years, from 1337 to 1453, with several truces.

q: Which of these founding fathers of the United States of America later became president?

q.e: James Monroe, a Founding Father, became the fifth US president (1817-25). The Monroe Doctrine is named after him.

q: On which day did the attempted coup d'etat of 1991 in the Soviet Union begin?

q.e: The coup attempt by hardliners against Gorbachev began on 19 August 1991 and collapsed in three days. It sped up the end of the USSR.

q: Which infamous European traitor was known as "the last person to enter Parliament with honest intentions"?

q.e: Guy Fawkes was arrested guarding 36 barrels of gunpowder beneath the House of Lords during the Gunpowder Plot of 1605. The cynical joke about him being the only honest man to enter Parliament is often attributed to playwright George Bernard Shaw.

q: Who was the last Roman emperor in the Year of Four Emperors (69 AD)?

q.e: Vespasian emerged victorious in the Year of the Four Emperors (69 AD) after Galba, Otho and Vitellius. He founded the Flavian dynasty.

q: Adolf Hitler was born on which date?

q.e: Adolf Hitler was born on 20 April 1889 in Braunau am Inn, Austria.

q: As poverty and racial tensions pushed African-Americans out of the southern US, many of them moved north in an event known as what?

q.e: Between roughly 1910 and 1970, about six million African Americans relocated from the rural American South to northern and western cities during the Great Migration.

q: Who crowned Charlemagne as Holy Roman Emperor on Christmas Day in 800?

q.e: Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne emperor on Christmas Day 800 in Rome. The title was later linked with the Holy Roman Empire.

q: Which of the following countries was the first to send an object into space?

q.e: Germany's V-2 rocket first reached space in 1944, becoming the first human-made object to do so. Sputnik 1 was the first satellite (1957).

q: When Christopher Columbus sailed to America, what was the first region he arrived in?

q.e: On October 12, 1492, Christopher Columbus made landfall on an island in the Bahamas that the indigenous Lucayan people called Guanahani, which Columbus renamed San Salvador.

q: Prior to his fame as a seer of the future, he treated plague victims in 16th-century France. Who was he?

q.e: Before publishing his famous prophetic work Les Prophéties in 1555, Michel de Nostredame worked as an apothecary and physician treating victims during outbreaks of bubonic plague across southern France.

q: In 1776, 23-year-old William & Mary grad Edmund Randolph became Attorney General of which state?

q.e: Edmund Randolph, aged 23, became Virginia's first Attorney General in 1776. He later became the first US Attorney General.

q: His oral polio vaccine was first tested on volunteer convicts, then in large-scale trials in the Soviet Union. Who was he?

q.e: Albert Sabin developed the oral polio vaccine and tested it in the USSR in the late 1950s. Jonas Salk had earlier made the injected one.

q: On May 7, 1915, a German U-boat sank which British ocean liner?

q.e: A German U-boat torpedoed RMS Lusitania off Ireland on 7 May 1915, killing 1,198 people, including 128 Americans.

q: Col. Paul Tibbets commanded which nicknamed B-29 bomber over Japan in August 1945?

q.e: Col. Paul Tibbets piloted the B-29 Enola Gay, named after his mother, which dropped the first atomic bomb on Hiroshima on August 6, 1945. Bockscar was the B-29 that bombed Nagasaki three days later.

q: After unsuccessful talks about oil production and debt repayment, Iraq occupied Kuwait. In January 1991 the US launched an air attack against military targets in Iraq and Kuwait in this operation.

q.e: Operation Desert Storm began on January 17, 1991, as the combat phase of the Gulf War. It followed Operation Desert Shield, which was the defensive buildup to protect Saudi Arabia.

q: This union, made up of European countries, was established by the Maastricht Treaty in 1992. Starting as a trade body it is now an economic and political partnership between its members.

q.e: The Maastricht Treaty (signed 1992, in force 1993) created the European Union. The euro and common foreign policy followed.

q: The Punic Wars were a series of three wars fought between these two powers.

q.e: The three Punic Wars (264-146 BC) were fought between Rome and Carthage. Rome destroyed Carthage in 146 BC.

q: Valeria Messalina was the third wife of this Roman emperor.

q.e: Valeria Messalina was the third wife of Emperor Claudius. She was executed in 48 AD for conspiracy.

q: Philip II of France, Richard I of England and Frederick I led this campaign.

q.e: The Third Crusade (1189-92) was led by Philip II of France, Richard I of England and Frederick I Barbarossa, who drowned en route.

q: Yu the Great was the legendary first Chinese monarch of this dynasty.

q.e: Yu the Great is the legendary founder of the Xia Dynasty, said to be the first Chinese dynasty. He is famed for flood control.

q: What was the name of the first jet-powered fighter used in World War II?

q.e: The Messerschmitt Me 262 was the first operational jet fighter in WWII, entering service in 1944.

q: Which US President delivered the following words: Ask not what your country can do for you, ask what you can do for your country.?

q.e: John F. Kennedy spoke these words during his inaugural address on January 20, 1961. The speech called for public service and civic responsibility from citizens and allies around the globe.

q: Which US President said these words: A democracy is nothing more than mob rule, where fifty-one percent of the people may take away the rights of the other forty-nine.?

q.e: This quote is widely attributed to Jefferson or Franklin, but no evidence links it to either. The quote's true origin is unknown.

q: How many Medal of Honor citations have been issued during the Vietnam War?

q.e: About 250 Medals of Honor were awarded for action in Vietnam, many posthumously. The count varies by source.

q: His saying, Veni Vidi Vici (I came I saw I conquered) is known all over the world. His war feats clothed him with glory giving him political power.

q.e: Julius Caesar wrote "Veni, vidi, vici" after beating Pharnaces II of Pontus at Zela in 47 BC. He became dictator, then was assassinated in 44 BC.

q: This island was Englands first overseas colony.

q.e: Newfoundland is often called England's oldest overseas colony: Sir Humphrey Gilbert claimed it for Elizabeth I in 1583.

q: Slavery was outlawed in all British colonies in this year.

q.e: The Slavery Abolition Act passed in 1833 and took effect on 1 August 1834 across most British colonies.

q: What was the nickname of Tom Cruises character in Top Gun?

q.e: Tom Cruise's Top Gun character was Lt. Pete "Maverick" Mitchell. The sequel Top Gun: Maverick came out in 2022.

q: What NBA team won their 16th NBA Championship title on June 8,1986?

q.e: The Boston Celtics won their 16th NBA title in June 1986, beating the Houston Rockets, with Larry Bird as MVP.

q: This was an attempt to establish the use of the metric system in the United States. However it was not accepted and the US never converted.

q.e: The US Metric Conversion Act of 1975 made metric measurement voluntary. The US still uses customary units for most everyday purposes.

q: This aircraft was proposed by Boeing in the 80s, but never entered production due to excessive noise from its unducted fan engines and high production costs.

q.e: The Boeing 7J7 was a 1980s design with propfan engines. Falling fuel prices and noise concerns led to its cancellation.

q: Three of these political events occurred in the 80s. Which one happened earlier?
The Winter of Discontent in the UK
The Collapse of the Soviet Union

q.e: The Winter of Discontent in the UK was in 1978-79, before the 1980s. Strikes then helped Margaret Thatcher win the 1979 election.

q: Mel Gibson starred in all of the following four movies. However, only one of them was produced during the 80s. Which one?

q.e: Lethal Weapon 2 was released in 1989. Mad Max (1979) and Braveheart (1995) were not 1980s films.

q: The TV-series Taxi was first released during this period.

q.e: Taxi aired on ABC and then NBC from 1978 to 1983, so it debuted in the 1970s.

q: In what year did the French Revolution begin?

q.e: The French Revolution began in 1789 with the storming of the Bastille on 14 July.

q: In what year was Napoleon Bonaparte crowned emperor of France?

q.e: Napoleon crowned himself Emperor of the French on 2 December 1804 at Notre-Dame, with Pope Pius VII watching.

q: In what year did the French pull out of Indochina?

q.e: France pulled out of Indochina after the Geneva Accords of 1954, following Dien Bien Phu. Vietnam was split at the 17th parallel.

q: What statesman became the first President, under the Fifth Republic of France, in 1959?

q.e: Charles de Gaulle helped draft the constitution of the French Fifth Republic in 1958 and took office as its first president on January 8, 1959.

q: In what year was Francois Mitterrand elected President of France?

q.e: François Mitterrand, a Socialist, won the French presidency in 1981 and served two terms until 1995.

q: What French monarch was known as the Sun King?

q.e: Louis XIV was "Le Roi Soleil," the Sun King. He chose the sun as his emblem.

q: The term Summer of Love, associated with the hippie counterculture movement, refers to the summer of what year?

q.e: During the summer of 1967, roughly 100,000 young people gathered in San Francisco's Haight-Ashbury neighborhood, creating a defining cultural moment for the hippie movement.

q: The Free Speech Movement was a student protest that began in 1964 on the campus of which university?

q.e: The Free Speech Movement began in autumn 1964 at the University of California, Berkeley, led by Mario Savio.

q: In 1969, John Lennon and Yoko Ono held two, week-long Bed-Ins for Peace. In which city was their first Bed-In?

q.e: John Lennon and Yoko Ono held their first Bed-In at the Amsterdam Hilton in March 1969, and the second in Montreal that May, where "Give Peace a Chance" was recorded.

q: This is the code name of the bombing operation in North Vietnam, carried out by the US armed forces, which lasted between 1965 and 1968.

q.e: Operation Rolling Thunder was the sustained US bombing of North Vietnam from March 1965 to November 1968.

q: This US President introduced his policy of 'vietnamization'- enabling the South Vietnamese to take more responsibility for fighting the war on their own.

q.e: Richard Nixon's "Vietnamization" policy (1969) shifted the fighting to South Vietnamese forces as US troops left.

q: During the American Civil War, in April 1862, Union Flag Officer David Farragut, who was in command of the West Gulf Blockading Squadron, took control of which vital port of the South?

q.e: In April 1862, Farragut's fleet ran past the forts and captured New Orleans, the Confederacy's biggest city and port.

q: Ulysses S. Grant and Robert E. Lee served together in which military conflict, regarded as a prelude to the American Civil War?

q.e: Grant and Lee both served in the Mexican-American War (1846-48), as did many other Civil War generals.

q: The Battle of Grunwald, the Battle of Chojnice, and the Battle of Swiecin are three battles fought during this war.

q.e: The Thirteen Years' War (1454-66) pitted Poland and the Prussian cities against the Teutonic Order. Grunwald (1410) was in the earlier Great War.

q: The Battle of Ludford Bridge, the First Battle of St Albans, and the Battle of Blore Heath are three battles fought during this war.

q.e: Ludford Bridge, St Albans and Blore Heath were Wars of the Roses battles (1455-1459) between Lancaster and York.

q: The Battle of Sandepu, the Battle of Mukden, and the Battle of Dairen are just three of the battles fought during this war.

q.e: Sandepu, Mukden and Dalny (Dairen) were battles of the Russo-Japanese War (1904-05). Japan's win surprised the world.

q: The Battle of Passchendaele, the Battle of Cer, and the Battle of the Frontiers were fought during this war.

q.e: Passchendaele (1917), Cer (1914) and the Frontiers (1914) were WWI battles.

q: The Battle of El Alamein, the Battle of Narvik, and the Battle of Crete were fought during this war.

q.e: El Alamein, Narvik and Crete were WWII battles (1940-42).

q: The Battle of the Nile, the Battle of Radzyn, and the Battle of Aspern-Essling.

q.e: The Nile (1798), Aspern-Essling (1809) and Radzyn were fought during the Napoleonic wars (and the French Revolutionary Wars before them).

q: A mob of French peasants stormed the Bastille and started the French Revolution
Japan opened ports to international shipping
Argentina gained independence from Spanish rule

q.e: On 14 July 1789, Parisians stormed the Bastille prison, a key event of the French Revolution. Bastille Day is France's national day.

q: Which of these events occurred on November 22, 1963?
John F. Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas
The United States bombed North Vietnam for the first time
Robert F. Kennedy was assassinated in Los Angeles
The Beatles performed first concert in the US

q.e: John F. Kennedy was fatally shot by Lee Harvey Oswald on November 22, 1963, while riding in a presidential motorcade through Dealey Plaza in Dallas. His brother Robert F. Kennedy was assassinated five years later, in June 1968.

q: What historical event took place on October 14, 1066 AD?
England was conquered by the Normans in the Battle of Hastings
The Chinese first used fireworks in battle

q.e: William of Normandy defeated King Harold at the Battle of Hastings on 14 October 1066, leading to the Norman conquest.

q: What historical event occurred on March 15, 44 BC?
Julius Caesar was assassinated by members of the Roman senate
The first calendar was started by the Mayans in Central America

q.e: Julius Caesar was stabbed 23 times in the Theatre of Pompey by a conspiracy of Roman senators led by Marcus Junius Brutus and Gaius Cassius Longinus. The date is commemorated as the infamous Ides of March.

q: Which of these events took place on June 18, 1815?
The noble gas Neon was discovered
Russia claimed the territory of Alaska
Andrew Jackson and his troops defeated the British at New Orleans

q.e: Napoleon was beaten at Waterloo on 18 June 1815 by Wellington and Blücher. He was exiled to St Helena.

q: The date July 2, 1937 is remembered with what event?
Amelia Earhart and her co-pilot disappeared flying across the Pacific Ocean
Japan bombed Shanghai, off the coast of China, killing over 2,000

q.e: Amelia Earhart and navigator Fred Noonan disappeared over the central Pacific on July 2, 1937, while en route to Howland Island during an attempt to circumnavigate the globe.

q: Which of these events occurred on December 29, 1170 AD?
Thomas Becket, Archbishop of Canterbury, was slain in his church
Mongols crossed the Danube river into Hungary
Danish ships landed at Greenland and claimed it as a province
Black Plague began in Genoa, Italy

q.e: Archbishop Thomas Becket was murdered in Canterbury Cathedral on 29 December 1170 by knights of Henry II.

q: Robert E. Lee commanded the Confederate army at Gettysburg. Who led the Union forces?

q.e: Major General George G. Meade led the Union Army of the Potomac at Gettysburg, taking command only three days before.

q: Which of these landmarks could not be found on the Gettysburg battlefield?

q.e: Hell's Half Acre is in Fort Worth, Texas. Gettysburg has Devil's Den, Little Round Top, Cemetery Ridge and Culp's Hill.

q: This twenty-year-old was the only civilian killed during the Battle of Gettysburg.

q.e: Jennie (Mary Virginia) Wade, aged 20, was killed in her sister's house by a stray bullet on 3 July 1863, the only civilian killed in the battle.

q: This 70-year-old citizen of Gettysburg grabbed his rifle during the first day of the battle and joined the Unions Iron Brigade. Not surprisingly, he was the only civilian to take part in the battle itself.

q.e: John Burns, a 69-70-year-old Gettysburg shoemaker and War of 1812 veteran, volunteered to fight on the first day.

q: This Union general was killed by a sniper on the first day of the Battle of Gettysburg.

q.e: Maj. Gen. John F. Reynolds, a Union corps commander, was killed by a sharpshooter on 1 July 1863.

q: This cavalry officer commanded the Union cavalry at Gettysburg.

q.e: Brig. Gen. John Buford's cavalry delayed the Confederates on the first day at Gettysburg, giving Union infantry time to take the high ground.

q: This operation, led by General Dwight Eisenhower, was launched on 8 November 1942 and it was aimed at gaining control over Morocco and Algeria.

q.e: Operation Torch (8 November 1942) was the Allied invasion of French North Africa (Morocco and Algeria) led by Eisenhower.

q: This May 1942 battle was the first one to be fought only by aircraft carriers.

q.e: The Battle of the Coral Sea (May 1942) was the first naval battle fought entirely by aircraft, with the ships never seeing each other.

q: Even though mainland Britain was not actually invaded in World War II, it had prepared a resistance movement, known under what name?

q.e: The British Auxiliary Units were secret resistance cells trained to operate behind German lines if Britain was invaded.

q: Who accepted the surrender of the German military forces in Northwest Germany, Holland and Denmark on May 4, 1945?

q.e: Field Marshal Montgomery accepted the German surrender at Lüneburg Heath on 4 May 1945. Germany surrendered fully on 7-8 May.

q: Even though Bertha was a formidable gun, this one was even bigger. Paris Gun was used to bombard Paris during World War I. What was its main purpose?
To attack the morale of enemy soldiers
To kill as many civilians as possible

q.e: The Paris Gun was a long-range German gun in WWI that shelled Paris from about 120 km in 1918. Its main effect was terror and psychological.

q: What year did the Holocaust begin?

q.e: Nazi persecution of Jews started in 1933 when Hitler took power, but the mass murder of the Holocaust came later, from 1941.

q: Which of the following was the first Roman emperor to convert to Christianity in 313 AD?

q.e: Constantine I, who issued the Edict of Milan in 313 with Licinius, favored Christianity. He was baptized on his deathbed in 337.

q: Which writer witnessed the eruption of Mt. Vesuvius in 79 AD?

q.e: Pliny the Younger provided the only surviving eyewitness account of Vesuvius's eruption in two letters sent to historian Tacitus. His uncle, Pliny the Elder, tragically died attempting to rescue victims across the Bay of Naples.

q: Which Roman Emperor wrote The Meditations that was actually a sort of personal diary?

q.e: Marcus Aurelius recorded his private reflections, known as Meditations, in Greek between roughly 170 and 180 AD while on military campaigns along the Danube frontier.

q: Who was the great Roman orator who created a Latin stylebook which is still used in Latin classes today?

q.e: Cicero (106-43 BC) was a Roman orator and statesman, and his prose style remains a model in Latin classes.

q: Which of these poets wrote many poems of love and manners widely read by Ancient Romans?

q.e: Ovid (43 BC-17 AD) wrote the Ars Amatoria and Metamorphoses. Augustus exiled him to the Black Sea.

q: The first military submarine (Turtle) could accommodate this number of people.

q.e: The Turtle (1775), built by David Bushnell, was operated by one person, who hand-cranked it. It tried to attach explosives to a British ship.

q: One man who made a fortune out of gold rushes was Levi Strauss. He developed the concept of this.

q.e: In 1873, Levi Strauss and tailor Jacob Davis received a patent to reinforce work pants with copper rivets, creating the first blue jeans made of sturdy denim. Strauss had originally moved to San Francisco in 1853 to open a dry goods wholesale business during the California Gold Rush.

q: Many people seeking an easy fortune emigrated to California, USA during the California Gold Rush (1848-1858). The gold rush was sparked by the discovery of gold near this city.

q.e: Gold was found at Sutter's Mill in Coloma, California, in January 1848, near Sacramento. About 300,000 people came.

q: One of the earliest gold rushes was probably the Spanish search for the mythical city of El Dorado. According to early legends, the King of the Muiscas would do this as part of a religious ceremony.
Turn whatever he touches into gold

q.e: In the El Dorado ("the gilded one") legend, the Muisca king covered himself in gold dust and dived into Lake Guatavita as an offering.

q: On October 19, 2006 Nissan Motor Company recalled 80,000 cars in U.S. due to what defects?

q.e: Nissan recalled vehicles in 2006 for defects, including a key-related problem. Recalls like this are issued if the defect poses a safety risk.

q: Which of these refers to the lower house of the Russian Parliament ?

q.e: The State Duma is the lower house of the Russian Federal Assembly. The Federation Council is the upper house.

q: On May 28, 2006 Barry Bonds hit his 715th career homerun against which National League team?

q.e: On 28 May 2006, Barry Bonds hit his 715th home run, passing Babe Ruth for second place all-time, against the Colorado Rockies.

q: The North and South (between Maryland and Pennsylvania) were separated by what famous line?

q.e: The line was surveyed between 1763 and 1767 by English astronomers Charles Mason and Jeremiah Dixon to resolve a border dispute between the colonies of Maryland and Pennsylvania. It later became the symbolic cultural divider between the northern and slaveholding southern states.

q: Who was President of the USA when the Korean War began?

q.e: Harry Truman was President when North Korea invaded South Korea on 25 June 1950.

q: Which battle, fought in Europe during WWII, started on December 16, 1944?

q.e: The Battle of the Bulge began on December 16, 1944, as Nazi Germany launched a massive counter-offensive through the densely forested Ardennes region of Belgium and Luxembourg.

q: North Vietnamese troops entered this South Vietnamese city, marking the unofficial end to the Vietnam War in 1975.

q.e: North Vietnamese tanks rolled into Saigon on 30 April 1975, which was renamed Ho Chi Minh City.

q: This politician was the British Prime Minister who declared war on Germany in 1939.

q.e: Neville Chamberlain declared war on Germany on 3 September 1939. He was replaced by Winston Churchill in May 1940.

q: Operation Torch was planned to bring Morocco and Algiers under the Allies' domination. Who was the general in charge of the operation?

q.e: General Dwight Eisenhower was Supreme Allied Commander for Operation Torch in 1942. He later became US President.

q: During World War II, this politician was the powerful leader of the Soviet Union, the country which suffered a record death toll in the war.

q.e: Joseph Stalin led the Soviet Union as General Secretary throughout World War II, during which the USSR suffered an estimated 27 million military and civilian deaths.

q: This man became U.S. Secretary of State after the Second World War. He developed a reconstruction plan, later named after him, to help the European countries recover after the war.

q.e: General George C. Marshall served as U.S. Secretary of State from 1947 to 1949 and crafted the European Recovery Program, commonly known as the Marshall Plan. His post-war reconstruction efforts earned him the Nobel Peace Prize in 1953.

q: In February 1992 this treaty was signed. It established the European Union.

q.e: The Maastricht Treaty was signed on 7 February 1992 and created the European Union.

q: The first book edition of the detective story, The Valley of Fear, was released in February 1915. This is its author.

q.e: Sir Arthur Conan Doyle wrote The Valley of Fear (1914-15), the fourth and last Sherlock Holmes novel. Professor Moriarty appears in it.

q: In February of this year, the last episode of M*A*S*H was broadcast.

q.e: The final episode of M*A*S*H aired on 28 February 1983 and drew over 100 million viewers.

q: In February 1924 President Woodrow Wilson died at this age.

q.e: Woodrow Wilson died on 3 February 1924, at 67.

q: Which one of these events did not happen in the same year as the others?
Barry Gordy, Jr. invested $700 in founding Motown Records
The novel Peyton Place was published
Allen Ginsberg publishes the book Howl and Other Poems
Elvis Presley recorded the song Hound Dog

q.e: Berry Gordy founded Motown (Tamla Records) in 1959 with an $800 family loan.

q: Who was the first person to be U.S. President of 50 states?

q.e: Dwight Eisenhower was President when Alaska and Hawaii became states in 1959, giving the US 50 states.

q: Which of these events did not occur in 1957?
Sputnik III was launched and circled the Earth eleven times.
Leave It to Beaver, a TV show about idyllic American life, first aired.
Charles Van Doren won $129,000 on the TV show Twenty-One.
The great Jackie Robinson retired from baseball

q.e: Sputnik 3 was launched in May 1958, not 1957. In 1957 the USSR launched Sputnik 1 (October) and Sputnik 2 (November, with Laika).

q: Who commanded the three B-52 Stratofortresses which made the first globe-circling nonstop flight in 1957?

q.e: Maj. Gen. Archie J. Old Jr. led three B-52s in a nonstop round-the-world flight in January 1957 (Operation Power Flite), taking about 45 hours.

q: Which list contains only countries which formed the European Economic Community?
France, West Germany, Italy, The Netherlands, Belgium, and Luxembourg
Spain, France, Austria, West Germany, Finland, and Portugal
Denmark, Sweden, The Netherlands, England, Belgium, and Luxembourg
Sweden, France, Italy, Austria, West Germany, and Spain

q.e: The Treaty of Rome (1957) created the European Economic Community with six members: France, West Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Belgium and Luxembourg.

q: Which Ohio-born singer was famous with the hits Music! Music! Music!, Molasses, Molasses, and Youll Never Get Away?

q.e: Teresa Brewer (born in Toledo, Ohio) had hits like "Music! Music! Music!" (1950).

q: Which of these events did not happen in 1950?
General Dwight D. Eisenhower is elected President.
CBS got an FCC license to broadcast in color nation-wide.
Both Pillsbury and general Mills begin selling cake mixes.

q.e: Eisenhower was elected President in 1952, not 1950, beating Adlai Stevenson.

q: A fictional case of poisoning is observed in Agatha Christies And Then There Were None. In the novel, this character dies of poisoning.

q.e: In Agatha Christie's And Then There Were None, Emily Brent dies of a cyanide injection. The poisoned victims also include Marston.

q: Arsenic became a popular murder weapon in the Middle Ages, because symptoms resembled those of this disease.

q.e: Arsenic poisoning has symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea, which looked like cholera, so murders could go undetected. A reliable test was developed in 1836 (the Marsh test).

q: There is a theory that Napoleon Bonaparte was poisoned with this substance.

q.e: Some theories say Napoleon was poisoned with arsenic on St Helena, though most historians think stomach cancer killed him in 1821.

q: Who was the faithful wife of Odysseus who waited 20 years for his return from the Trojan War?

q.e: In Homer's Odyssey, Penelope famously delayed her aggressive suitors by weaving a burial shroud by day and unravelling it each night while awaiting Odysseus. Telemachus is her and Odysseus's son.

q: This Victorian politician, best remembered as the originator of the modern police force, sought to repeal the Corn Laws as a measure to fight the Irish potato famine.

q.e: Sir Robert Peel established London's Metropolitan Police in 1829 (giving rise to the nicknames bobbies and peelers) and later pushed to repeal the protectionist Corn Laws in 1846 during the Great Famine.

q: The Great Exhibition, a symbol of the Victorian Age, was held in London in what year?

q.e: The Great Exhibition took place in London's Crystal Palace in 1851, and showcased industry and design from around the world.

q: This woman was a Victorian era feminist, especially concerned with the welfare of working girls.

q.e: Josephine Butler (1828-1906) campaigned for women's education and against the Contagious Diseases Acts and child prostitution.

q: Issued during the Victorian period, it is the name of the worlds first official adhesive postage stamp.

q.e: Issued in Great Britain in May 1840, the Penny Black featured the profile of Queen Victoria and became the world's first adhesive postage stamp used in a public postal system.

q: The Salvation Army, a world-wide charity organization, was established in what year?

q.e: William Booth founded the Salvation Army in London in 1865, originally as the Christian Mission.

q: Name the British socialist intellectual movement, among whose members was the famous Irish playwright Bernard Shaw.
The Fellowship of the New Life

q.e: The Fabian Society, founded in 1884, promotes gradual socialist reform. George Bernard Shaw, Sidney and Beatrice Webb and H. G. Wells were members.

q: Certainly one of the most famous sieges is the siege of Troy. Although archaeologists are not sue whether or not it really happened, there is evidence that the siege is not merely mythological. According to legends, who killed the Greek hero Achilles?

q.e: In Greek legend Paris shot Achilles in the heel with an arrow, which Apollo guided.

q: On February 28, 1983 a record 105.9 million viewers tuned in to watch the last show of this programs eleven-year run.

q.e: The series finale of MASH, titled Goodbye, Farewell and Amen, drew about 106 million viewers and held the record for the most-watched television broadcast in American history until Super Bowl XLIV in 2010.

q: How many people were murdered as a result of the Salem Witch Trials?

q.e: The Salem witch trials led to 20 executions: 19 hanged and Giles Corey pressed to death. Several more died in jail.

q: How old was Giles Cory when he was pressed to death?

q.e: Giles Corey was about 81 when he was pressed with stones for refusing to enter a plea in September 1692.

q: Dorothy Good, who was the youngest person to be accused of witchcraft, was how old?

q.e: Dorothy Good, around four years old, was accused and jailed for months. She was the daughter of Sarah Good.

q: Which well-known author changed his name as a result of the Salem Witch Trials?

q.e: Nathaniel Hawthorne added a "w" to the family name (Hathorne), distancing himself from his ancestor Judge John Hathorne of the Salem trials.

q: Who was the first man to be accused of witchcraft?

q.e: The first people accused in Salem were Tituba, Sarah Good and Sarah Osborne in February 1692. John Proctor was accused later and hanged.

q: The son of this famous singer was kidnapped on December 8, 1963 at Harrahs Lake Tahoe.

q.e: Frank Sinatra Jr., aged 19, was abducted from Harrah's Lake Tahoe on 8 December 1963. He was released after Sinatra paid a ransom.

q: On July 30, 1865 along the beaches of California, off Crescent City, a summer storm developed and this ship came across a submerged pinnacle known as The Dragons Teeth.

q.e: The side-wheel steamer Brother Jonathan struck a rock near Crescent City, California, on 30 July 1865 and sank, with about 225 deaths.

q: Which temperature scale came first, Fahrenheit or Celsius?
They were developed at the same time
They were developed so close together that no one knows

q.e: Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit proposed his temperature scale in 1724, while Swedish astronomer Anders Celsius developed his competing centigrade scale nearly two decades later in 1742.

q: In what year was slavery banned in the British colonies?
