q.e: The Slavery Abolition Act received royal assent in 1833 and took effect in 1834.

q: Samuel Colt patented his revolver in this year, and later built the first industrialized firearm factory.

q.e: Samuel Colt patented his revolver in 1835-36 and set up his factory in Paterson, New Jersey.

q: Although it had been around for a long time, it was not until this person used chloroform, that it became a popular anesthetic.

q.e: Queen Victoria used chloroform for the birth of Prince Leopold in 1853, boosting its acceptance. Dr John Snow administered it.

q: The first photograph is considered to be an image produced by the French inventor Nicéphore Niépce, in what year?

q.e: Nicéphore Niépce made "View from the Window at Le Gras" in 1826 or 1827, the oldest surviving photograph. It needed hours of exposure.

q: The first Balfour Declaration, UKs committment to the establishment of a Jewish national home was issued in what year?

q.e: The Balfour Declaration of 2 November 1917 stated British support for a "national home for the Jewish people" in Palestine.

q: This engineer, architect and industrialist invented the rotary lathe, used in plywood manufacturing.

q.e: Immanuel Nobel, Alfred Nobel's father, invented the rotary lathe for peeling plywood veneers.

q: This tool was originally made in Germany, but in 1896, after 5 years of hard work, Karl Elsener doubled its features.

q.e: Karl Elsener, founder of Victorinox, improved the Swiss army knife in 1896-97 by adding a second spring, which allowed tools on both sides.

q: This engineer, sometimes called The Father of Cool, invented the modern air conditioning system, soon after he graduated from Cornell University in 1901.

q.e: Willis Carrier submitted designs for the first modern electrical air conditioning system in 1902 to control humidity at a printing plant in Brooklyn, New York.

q: Which general gave Stonewall Jackson his nickname?

q.e: Brig. Gen. Barnard Bee called Jackson "a stone wall" at First Bull Run (21 July 1861), and Bee died in the battle.

q: During the early months of 1862, General Stonewall Jackson led a successful campaign in which region?

q.e: Jackson's 1862 Shenandoah Valley campaign was a masterpiece of speed. His small army beat three Union forces.

q: Where was Stonewall Jacksons body buried?

q.e: Jackson is buried in Lexington, Virginia, near the Virginia Military Institute, in what is now Stonewall Jackson Memorial Cemetery.

q: General Stonewall Jackson did not participate at which of these battles?

q.e: Jackson died in May 1863, and so was not at Gettysburg in July. Lee later said he missed him there.

q: The first evidence of human existence in Europe dates back to approximately how many years ago?

q.e: Early human traces in Europe go back far further than 35,000 years: tools and bones in Spain are over a million years old. Modern humans arrived about 45,000 years ago.

q: Under what ruler was Christianity officially acknowledged in the Roman Empire?

q.e: In 313 AD, Emperor Constantine I and Licinius issued the Edict of Milan, granting religious tolerance and legal rights to Christians across the Roman Empire.

q: In 1957 Jimmy Hoffa became president of which union?

q.e: Jimmy Hoffa became president of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters in 1957 and disappeared in 1975.

q: On which show did Elvis Presley make his first TV appearance?

q.e: Elvis Presley first appeared on national TV on the Dorsey Brothers' Stage Show on 28 January 1956.

q: Which one of these was not part of the Million Dollar Quartet, formed in 1956 by Sun Records?

q.e: The Million Dollar Quartet was Elvis Presley, Carl Perkins, Jerry Lee Lewis and Johnny Cash, jamming at Sun Records on 4 December 1956. Willie Nelson wasn't there.

q: On what Mediterranean island did the Minoan civilization arise?

q.e: The Bronze Age Minoan civilization flourished on the island of Crete from around 2000 BC to 1450 BC, centered at the palace complex of Knossos.

q: Which was the largest empire in pre-Columbian America?

q.e: At its peak in the early 16th century, the Inca Empire spanned roughly 2,500 miles (4,000 km) along the Andes, ruling an estimated 10 to 12 million people.

q: This civilization arose in Central Mexico and its members spoke the Nahuatl language .

q.e: The Aztecs founded their capital, Tenochtitlan, in the Valley of Mexico around 1325 and spoke Nahuatl, a language still spoken by over a million people today. While Toltecs also spoke Nahuatl, the Aztec civilization is the primary empire centered there before Spanish conquest.

q: The first underground metro in North America, the Boston subway, was opened on September 1 of this year.

q.e: The Tremont Street Subway in Boston opened on 1 September 1897, the first subway in North America.

q: The Fourth Crusade (1202–1204) was called upon by Pope Innocent II and was originally intended to retake Jerusalem by conquering this country.

q.e: The Fourth Crusade, called by Pope Innocent III, aimed to reach Jerusalem by first attacking Egypt, but it ended up sacking Constantinople in 1204.

q: The crusaders considered themselves sort of pilgrims and so, before joining a Crusade, they swore a vow to do this.
To preach Christianity to Muslim prisoners
To kill at least ten Muslims

q.e: Crusaders took a vow to reach Jerusalem and received indulgences. They wore a cross as a sign.

q: The military power of the Teutonic Order was broken after the Battle of Grunwald, after a defeat by these two countries.

q.e: At Grunwald (1410) the combined armies of Poland and Lithuania broke the Teutonic Knights' power.

q: This largest Christian military order was established in the aftermath of the First Crusade and is widely known as this.

q.e: Founded around 1119 by French nobleman Hugues de Payens, the Knights Templar were tasked with protecting Christian pilgrims traveling to Jerusalem. Officially recognized by the Catholic Church around 1129, they became one of the wealthiest and most influential military orders of the Middle Ages.

q: NASA was established in this year, on July 29.

q.e: NASA was created by the National Aeronautics and Space Act, signed 29 July 1958, and began operating on 1 October 1958.

q: One of these events did not take place on March 19.
Americas first recorded bank robbery took place
General Fromm was executed for plot against Hitler

q.e: Indira Gandhi was India's Prime Minister 1966-77 and 1980-84, so she wasn't PM on every date.

q: One of these events did not take place on a summer day.
Admiral Nelson was buried at St. Pauls Cathedral
President Adams settled in a new capital

q.e: Admiral Nelson was killed at Trafalgar in October 1805 and buried at St Paul's Cathedral in January 1806, in winter.

q: The English Navigation Acts were a series of laws which restricted foreign shipping. Resentment against the Navigation Acts was a cause for which war?

q.e: The Navigation Acts (1651 onwards) forced trade onto English ships and were a major cause of the Anglo-Dutch Wars. They later angered American colonists.

q: In the Battle of Gaugamela, 331 B.C. , Alexander the Great of Macedonia defeated which king?

q.e: At Gaugamela (331 BC) Alexander the Great beat Darius III of Persia, leading to the fall of the Persian Empire. Darius fled and was later killed by his own satraps.

q: F. D. Toussaint Louverture, a freed self-educated slave, was one of the leaders of which uprising?

q.e: Toussaint Louverture was a key general of the Haitian Revolution, which began in 1791 and led to Saint-Domingue gaining independence from France as Haiti in 1804.

q: This conflict, which lasted from 1839 to 1842, is regarded as a trade-inspired war between Great Britain and the Qing Empire in China.

q.e: The First Opium War (1839-42) was fought over Britain's opium trade with China. It ended with the Treaty of Nanking, which ceded Hong Kong to Britain.

q: In this film, the Vietnam War veteran, played by Roy Scheider experienced a war flashback, involving the execution of an enemy soldier.

q.e: In the 1983 helicopter thriller Blue Thunder, Roy Scheider plays Frank Murphy, a Vietnam veteran who suffers flashbacks.

q: Hornets Nest is associated with which battlefield?

q.e: The "Hornets' Nest" was a sunken road at Shiloh (April 1862) where Union troops held off repeated Confederate attacks for hours.

q: On which battlefield was Lookout Mountain a dominant feature?

q.e: Lookout Mountain overlooks Chattanooga, Tennessee. The "Battle Above the Clouds" was fought there in November 1863.

q: It is estimated that the crew of the Mayflower consisted of how many people?

q.e: The Mayflower's crew was about 25-30 men, besides the 102 passengers.

q: How many passengers were aboard the Mayflower when it crossed the Atlantic?

q.e: The Mayflower carried 102 passengers in 1620 (about 50 Pilgrims and others), plus a crew. One baby, Oceanus, was born on the way.

q: In 1596, navigator Cornelis de Houtman set foot on the shore of what future colonial possession?

q.e: Cornelis de Houtman led the first Dutch trading voyage to the East Indies in 1595-97, reaching Banten (Java). It set up Dutch colonialism there.

q: Dutch independence from Spain (1648) was recognized in this Treaty.

q.e: The Peace of Münster (1648) ended the Eighty Years' War, with Spain recognizing the independence of the Dutch Republic. It was part of the Peace of Westphalia.

q: The first Dutch railway opened in this year -- the same year Belgian independence was recognized by the Dutch.

q.e: The first Dutch railway (Amsterdam-Haarlem) opened in 1839, the same year the Treaty of London led the Netherlands to recognize Belgium.

q: Who was the second wife (1879) of King William the Third of Netherlands? Her only daughter, Wilhelmina ascended the throne on September 6th, 1898 at the age of eighteen.

q.e: Emma of Waldeck and Pyrmont married William III in 1879. She served as regent until her daughter Wilhelmina came of age in 1898.

q: What was the nickname of William, Prince of Orange, Count of Nassau (Willem, Prins van Oranje, Graaf van Nassau), killed in 1584 in the city of Delft?

q.e: William of Orange, "William the Silent," led the Dutch Revolt against Spain. He was assassinated in Delft in 1584.

q: The famous rhyme I had a little bird. Its name was Enza. I opened the window. And In-flew-Enza refers to what disaster?

q.e: The 1918 flu pandemic ("Spanish flu") killed an estimated 50 million people. The skipping-rope rhyme about "Enza" (influenza) was sung by children.

q: In the year 1770, the worst ever famine in history struck this region, considered to be one of the most densely populated areas on Earth.

q.e: The Great Bengal Famine of 1770 killed around ten million people, a third of the population, under East India Company rule.

q: In 1931 a big flood hit this country/area causing the deaths of approximately 850.000 - 4.000.000 people.
The flooding of the Volga - Russia
The flooding of the Nile - Egypt

q.e: The 1931 China floods, in the Yangtze, Huai and Yellow river basins, may have killed 1-4 million, one of the deadliest natural disasters ever recorded.

q: In 1991, a cyclone, unofficially known as Cyclone Gorky, struck this country leaving at least 138.000 people dead.

q.e: The 1991 Bangladesh cyclone made landfall on 29 April 1991 with a storm surge of up to 6 m and killed about 138,000 people.

q: General Dwight Eisenhower headed an operation whose aim was to gain control of Morocco and Algiers. What was the name of the operation?

q.e: Operation Torch was the Allied landing in French North Africa in November 1942, led by Eisenhower.

q: Hitler promoted General Friedrich Paulus in February 1943, in an attempt to lift his spirits. What was his promotion?

q.e: Hitler promoted Friedrich Paulus to Field Marshal on 30 January 1943, hinting he should die rather than surrender (no German field marshal had been captured). Paulus surrendered the next day at Stalingrad.

q: The following words belong to which famous World War II general: Crete was the grave of the German parachutists.�?

q.e: General Kurt Student commanded the German paratroopers who took Crete in 1941 at heavy cost. He reportedly called the island "the grave of the German paratroopers."

q: In 1943, General Friedrich Paulus was in charge of the German forces in which area?

q.e: In 1943 Paulus's Sixth Army was trapped at Stalingrad on the Volga, not in the Caucasus. He surrendered on 31 January 1943.

q: US General Patton, leader of the Third Army was famous for which of the following?

q.e: George S. Patton led the Third Army across France in 1944. He was famous for aggressive speed, ivory-handled pistols and profane speeches.

q: The first space tourist was this businessman.

q.e: American investment manager Dennis Tito paid an estimated 20 million dollars to fly aboard the Russian Soyuz TM-32 mission to the International Space Station in April 2001.

q: Pas dArmes was a tournament, in which knights were dared to fight. If knights refused to fight, they had to leave this behind as a sign of humiliation.

q.e: In a "pas d'armes" ("passage of arms"), a knight who refused a challenge had to leave his spurs hanging as a sign of shame.

q: Don Quixote de la Mancha is a fictional knight from the self-titled novel, written by this author.

q.e: Spanish author Miguel de Cervantes published the two volumes of 'Don Quixote' in 1605 and 1615. It is widely considered one of the earliest and most influential modern novels in history.

q: What was the French governmental structure until the French Revolution?

q.e: Before the Revolution, France was an absolute monarchy under the Ancien Régime, with the king holding supreme power.

q: In the Crimean War, France, the United Kingdom, the Kingdom of Sardinia, and the Ottoman Empire fought against what country?

q.e: In the Crimean War (1853-56), the UK, France, Sardinia and the Ottoman Empire fought against Imperial Russia.

q: Where was Napoleon finally defeated on June 18, 1815?

q.e: The Battle of Waterloo took place in present-day Belgium, where Anglo-allied forces led by the Duke of Wellington and a Prussian army commanded by Gebhard von Blucher decisively defeated Napoleon Bonaparte.

q: The tradition of engagement rings was started by Maximilian of Austria. He gave one such ring to her.

q.e: Archduke Maximilian of Austria gave Mary of Burgundy a diamond engagement ring in 1477, which is often cited as the first on record.

q: This type of pattern is common in traditional Chinese womens clothing.

q.e: The peony symbolizes wealth and honor in China and is a classic motif in women's clothing and embroidery.
Mary Quant helped popularize the miniskirt in 1960s London. She named it after her favorite car, the Mini.

q: He created Chanel No. 5 for Coco Chanel.

q.e: Ernest Beaux, a perfumer born in Russia, created Chanel No. 5 in 1921 for Coco Chanel.

q: In 1996 President Clinton was re-elected as the first two-term Democrat since what former US President?

q.e: Bill Clinton's 1996 win made him the first Democrat since Franklin D. Roosevelt (1936, 1940, 1944) to win a second full term.

q: In 1996, TWA Flight 800 exploded and crashed into the Atlantic Ocean shortly after take off, killing all 230 aboard. The flight was bound from New York to what popular European destination?

q.e: TWA Flight 800 exploded off Long Island on 17 July 1996 on a flight from New York's JFK to Paris, with a stop in Rome. All 230 aboard died.

q: The first cloned mammal, Dolly, was named after country singer Dolly Parton. Why?
Dolly Parton had just released a single named Dolly
Dolly Parton was an outspoken supporter of stem cell research
Dolly Parton was the embryologists favorite singer

q.e: Ian Wilmut and the Roslin Institute team cloned Dolly using a cell taken from an adult sheep's mammary gland, inspiring them to name the lamb after singer Dolly Parton.

q: Which church official commissioned Michelangelo, to paint the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel, the residence of the Pope in the Vatican city?

q.e: Pope Julius II, known as the 'Warrior Pope,' commissioned Michelangelo in 1508 to paint the Sistine Chapel ceiling, a monumental project finished four years later in 1512.

q: Jacques Cartier, a notable discoverer of the Renaissance period, was the first French explorer to reach Quebec in which year?

q.e: Jacques Cartier made the first of his three voyages to Canada in 1534 and claimed it for France, at Gaspé.

q: Who or what was a medieval fief?
A vassal who had his vassals

q.e: A fief was land granted by a lord to a vassal in return for loyalty and military service in feudal society.

q: Which medieval unit of volume is the largest?

q.e: A tun, about 252 gallons of wine, was the biggest of the old English liquid measures. It's bigger than a butt, hogshead or barrel.

q: At the battle of Hastings (1066) an army of Normans, led by William the Conqueror, defeated the Anglo-Saxon forces. Who actually were Normans?
Vikings who settled in Normandy and spoke French
A mixture of Dutch, French and Spanish

q.e: The Normans were descendants of Norse Vikings who settled in Normandy (hence "Northmen") and took on the French language and culture.

q: Who would typically own a 100-acre piece of land during medieval times?
A poor knight or a wealthy free peasant

q.e: A hundred acres was a substantial holding for a free peasant (yeoman) or a lesser knight. Most serfs held 15-30 acres.

q: Peace in our time were the famous words by Chamberlain when he returned to the UK from which meeting?

q.e: British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain uttered the phrase in London on September 30, 1938, after signing the Munich Agreement with Adolf Hitler, which permitted Germany to annex Czechoslovakia's Sudetenland.

q: On May 10th 1940, Germany invaded France, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg. Which country bore the main thrust?

q.e: The German offensive of 10 May 1940 broke through the Ardennes and across Luxembourg to reach Sedan and the Channel. France bore the main impact.

q: Where did the biggest amphibious operation during WW2 take place?

q.e: Normandy in 1944 was the largest amphibious assault in history. Okinawa (1945) was the largest in the Pacific.

q: What did rich Egyptian women place on top of their heads and kept it there all day?
A jewel made of serpents skin

q.e: Some tomb paintings show women wearing cones on their heads, which may have been scented fat that melted. Scholars still debate what they really were.

q: Roman women were jealous of the captive-women from the German tribes that their men captured. That is why they used to cut off the captives long blond braids and used them as this.

q.e: Roman women cut the blond hair of German captives to make wigs and hairpieces, as blond hair was fashionable.

q: Who was the first woman said to wear trousers?

q.e: Sarah Bernhardt was known for wearing trousers, including on stage. In France, women needed police permission to do so until 2013 (rarely enforced).
Coco Chanel brought jersey fabric and sporty sweaters into women's fashion in the 1910s-20s.

q: Who were first to wear something like mens underwear?

q.e: Ancient Egyptians wore a linen loincloth (shendyt), the earliest known form of underwear.

q: The Edsel was a terrible dud for Ford Motor Co. How was the name derived?
It was the name of one of Henry Fords sons
It was the name of Henry Fords first grandchild.
It was the maiden name of Henry Fords first wife.
It was the maiden name of Henry Fords second wife.

q.e: Ford's 1958 Edsel was named after Edsel Ford, Henry Ford's son. It flopped, losing hundreds of millions.

q: Funky Fries was a brand name of frozen French Fries developed by the Ore-Ida subsidy of Heinz Foods. Which of the following was not a flavor of Funky Fries?

q.e: Funky Fries came in odd flavors and colors, such as Cinnamon and Chocolate. Strawberry wasn't one of them.

q: Which of these is the most recognizable feature of Maya architecture?

q.e: Stepped pyramids, such as El Castillo at Chichen Itza and Temple I at Tikal, are the iconic centerpieces of Maya ceremonial centers, serving as monumental religious temples and tombs.

q: Which of the following was NOT a result of the failed attempt to rescue American hostages during the Iran hostage crisis of 1980?
The relocation of the US Embassy in Iran
The formation of U.S. Army's 160th Special Operations Aviation Regiment
The creation of US Special Operations Command (USSOCOM)
The plan for a second rescue mission, Operation Credible Sport

q.e: The April 1980 hostage rescue (Operation Eagle Claw) failed, killing 8 US servicemen. It led to Secretary of State Vance's resignation and hurt Carter, but the embassy stayed.

q: Who was shot and killed at Manila airport, the Phillippines in 1983?

q.e: Benigno Aquino Jr., a Philippine opposition leader, was assassinated at Manila airport on 21 August 1983 as he returned from exile. It fueled protests against Marcos.

q: 1982 saw the murders associated with this over-the-counter drug.

q.e: In 1982 seven people died in Chicago after taking Tylenol laced with cyanide. It led to tamper-resistant packaging.

q: "Sitzkrieg� is a term referring to the first period of WW II that lasted until May 1940. This period is also known as what?

q.e: The "Sitzkrieg" is the Phoney War, the lull between Germany's invasion of Poland in September 1939 and the attack in the west in May 1940.

q: Which Central European country fought alongside the Allies on all European and African fronts during WW II and was left on the eastern side of the curtain at the Yalta Conference?

q.e: Poland fought with the Allies from 1939 to 1945 on many fronts but ended up in the Soviet sphere after the Yalta Conference.

q: Which country was invaded by the Soviet Army in 1968?

q.e: In August 1968 Warsaw Pact forces, led by the Soviet Union, invaded Czechoslovakia to end the "Prague Spring" reforms.

q: Which nations catholic bishops issued the famous letter to their German counterparts, in which they forgave and asked for forgiveness?

q.e: In 1965 Polish bishops wrote to German bishops, "We forgive and ask for forgiveness." It was a step toward post-war reconciliation.

q: What was the name of the organization of Central and Eastern European communist states, established as a counterweight against NATO?

q.e: The Warsaw Pact (1955) was the Soviet-led military alliance of the Eastern Bloc, formed in response to West Germany's NATO membership. It dissolved in 1991.

q: When did the Berlin Wall fall, ending symbolically the Cold War?

q.e: The Berlin Wall fell on 9 November 1989. German reunification followed in October 1990.

q: Che Guevara was a Marxist revolutionary, who took part in the Cuban Revolution under the command of Fidel Castro. Where did Che Guevara die?

q.e: Che Guevara was captured and executed in Bolivia on 9 October 1967, while trying to start a guerrilla uprising.

q: This rebellion broke in 1857 in _____, fighting against the British colonial control over the country. It is sometimes referred to as the Sepoy Mutiny or the Sepoy Rebellion.

q.e: The Indian Rebellion of 1857 began with sepoys (Indian soldiers) in the East India Company's army. It led to the British Crown taking direct control in 1858.

q: Which Russian Empress brought Rasputin into the center of the Imperial court?

q.e: Empress Alexandra, wife of Nicholas II, trusted Rasputin because he seemed to ease their son Alexei's hemophilia. He gained influence at court.

q: The average income in the United States in 1952 was $3,515.00. What was the average price of a house at that time?

q.e: In 1952 the average new home cost about $17,000, while the average income was about $3,500, showing how prices have risen.

q: In what year was the first microwave oven manufactured by Tappan and offered in the USA for $1300.00?

q.e: Tappan introduced the first microwave oven for home use in 1955 for about $1,295. Raytheon's "Radarange" had come in 1947.

q: Which of these was NOT a Broadway flop?
Teaneck Tanzi: The Venus Fly Trap (1983)

q.e: Broadway flops are common, with a famous one being Moose Murders (1983). This question's answer is the only one not a flop.

q: This great 1949 movie was remade into a 2006 movie flop starring Sean Penn, James Gandolfini, Kate Winslet, Jude Law, and Anthony Hopkins.

q.e: All the King's Men (1949) won Best Picture. The 2006 remake with Sean Penn and Jude Law was a box-office failure.

q: Which ancient countries battled each other during the Punic Wars?

q.e: The three Punic Wars spanned from 264 BC to 146 BC, ending with the complete destruction of Carthage by the Roman Republic. The term Punic derives from the Latin word Poeni, which the Romans used for Phoenicians.

q: She was Miss Moneypenny in 14 of the James Bond films.

q.e: Lois Maxwell played Miss Moneypenny in 14 Bond films, from Dr. No (1962) to A View to a Kill (1985).

q: Who was the patron of Athens during its Golden Age?

q.e: Pericles led Athens (c. 461-429 BC) during its Golden Age and sponsored the Parthenon.

q: What was the name of the famous market place in Athens?

q.e: The Agora was Athens' public square and marketplace, and the center of political and social life.

q: Who was the Soviet General Secretary during the Cuban Missile Crisis in October 1962?

q.e: Nikita Khrushchev led the USSR as First Secretary of the Communist Party during the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis.

q: Which of these countries was not part of the Warsaw Pact of 1955 ?

q.e: Yugoslavia was non-aligned and was not part of the Warsaw Pact. The Pact included the USSR, Poland, East Germany, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria and Albania.

q: What was the name of the political liberalization in Czechoslovakia, which started on January 5 and lasted until August 20, 1968?

q.e: Led by Alexander Dubcek under the slogan 'socialism with a human face,' the Prague Spring ended abruptly in August 1968 when Warsaw Pact troops invaded Czechoslovakia.

q: The North African Campaign, also known as The Desert War, began in 1940. It included campaigns fought in several African countries. Which of the following was not one of the locations of the North African Campaign?

q.e: The North African Campaign was fought in Libya, Egypt, Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia, not South Africa.

q: When did the United States enter World War II?

q.e: The United States formally entered World War II on December 8, 1941, the day after Japan's surprise attack on the naval base at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii.

q: What term is generally used to describe the genocide of approximately six million European Jews during World War II?

q.e: The Holocaust refers to the systematic state-sponsored murder of roughly six million Jews and millions of others by the Nazi regime between 1941 and 1945.

q: What Chinese warrior and strategist wrote The Art of War?

q.e: Sun Tzu was an ancient Chinese military general from the Eastern Zhou period credited with writing The Art of War, an influential 13-chapter treatise on strategy and tactics.

q: Perhaps the greatest warrior-king in Roman history, what warrior summed up his victory in these three words, Veni, Vidi, Vici. ?

q.e: "Veni, vidi, vici" ("I came, I saw, I conquered") was Julius Caesar's report on his quick victory over Pharnaces in 47 BC.

q: The US, Britain and Germany were the main belligerents at Normandy during WWII, but three other nations had troops there who fought in their own organized national units. Which of the following was NOT one of those three nations?

q.e: At Normandy, Canada, Free France and Poland also fought in their own units, along with the US and the British. Japan was fighting in the Pacific.

q: During WWII, American troops assaulted two beaches at Normandy. Three other beaches with code names Gold, Sword and Juno were assaulted by troops who mostly came from these two nations.

q.e: The British (Gold and Sword) and Canadians (Juno) landed at three beaches on D-Day. The Americans landed on Utah and Omaha.

q: Which American Indian tribe was predominantly located in North Georgia?

q.e: The Cherokee were in the north of Georgia until the Indian Removal Act and the Trail of Tears (1838).

q: Which German-American physicist is credited for advising U.S. President Franklin Roosevelt to start the development of an atomic bomb?

q.e: In August 1939, Albert Einstein signed the famous Einstein-Szilard letter warning President Roosevelt that Nazi Germany might develop nuclear weapons, which eventually helped spur the Manhattan Project.

q: What U.S. President gave a speech beginning with the phrase Four score and seven years ago?

q.e: Abraham Lincoln delivered these famous opening words at the dedication of the Soldiers' National Cemetery in Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, on November 19, 1863.

q: Which of these is one of the reasons why the United States entered World War I?
Germany tried to persuade Mexico to enter the war.

q.e: In January 1917, British intelligence intercepted the Zimmermann Telegram, in which Germany secretly proposed a military alliance with Mexico if the United States entered the war, promising to help Mexico reclaim territory in Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona.

q: Under whose administration did the United States send large numbers of troops to Vietnam?

q.e: Lyndon Johnson sent large numbers of ground troops to Vietnam from 1965, after the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution (1964).

q: In 221 BC Zheng of the Qin Dynasty defeated the last independent Chinese state, the State of Qi, and thus unified China. The same year he named himself Shi Huangdi, which means this.

q.e: Qin Shi Huangdi means "First Emperor of Qin." He united China in 221 BC and began the Great Wall's connection and terracotta army.

q: Who gave the sermon at President Lincolns funeral?

q.e: Dr. Phineas D. Gurley, Lincoln's pastor, gave the sermon at the White House funeral on 19 April 1865.

q: How many civilians were killed in the Battle of Gettysburg?

q.e: Jennie Wade was the only civilian killed in the battle itself. Both armies lost thousands of soldiers there.

q: Steve Bochco had many successes on TV. However, this 1990 ABC police drama, that also featured the cast breaking out in song, was a failure.

q.e: Cop Rock (1990), Steven Bochco's musical police drama, was canceled after 11 episodes.

q: What was the most contested (captured, recaptured) town in the U.S. Civil War?

q.e: Winchester, Virginia, changed hands about 70 times during the Civil War, more than any other town.

q: Where did General Shermans March to the Sea begin and end?

q.e: Major General William Tecumseh Sherman began his March to the Sea after leaving captured Atlanta in November 1864 and ended by taking the port of Savannah that December.

q: In 1962 President Kennedy of the US and Chairman Khrushchev of the Soviet Union were able to peacefully end a confrontation which might have led to a nuclear war. Where was this crisis centered?

q.e: The Cuban Missile Crisis (October 1962) centered on Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba. A deal was made for the US to promise not to invade Cuba.

q: Early in his administration this US President survived being shot by an assassin and even showed a sense of humor when he told his wife, Honey, I forgot to duck.

q.e: After being shot by John Hinckley Jr. outside a Washington, D.C. hotel on March 30, 1981, Ronald Reagan famously quipped to his wife Nancy in the emergency room, 'Honey, I forgot to duck'—borrowing a line from boxer Jack Dempsey.

q: Children, and many adults too, were happy when the first Disneyland opened in California in this year.

q.e: Disneyland opened in Anaheim, California, on July 17, 1955, welcoming thousands of visitors on its famous opening day, often called Black Sunday.

q: When did the Allies capture Tobruk during World War II?

q.e: The Allies captured Tobruk in January 1941 and the Axis took it in June 1942. The Allies retook it in November 1942.

q: Where did the D-Day invasion occur?

q.e: Operation Overlord commenced on June 6, 1944, when Allied forces launched the amphibious invasion across five beachheads along the coast of Normandy, France. Cherbourg was an important deep-water port captured later in June to supply the campaign.

q: When did the Germans invade Yugoslavia and Greece during World War II?

q.e: Germany invaded Yugoslavia and Greece in April 1941. They were also joined by Italy, Bulgaria and Hungary.

q: Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin, who in 1961 became the first human to enter outer space, died in 1968. What was the cause of his death?
He was killed in a plane crash.
He developed AIDS and was not treated.
He was killed in an car accident.
A plane he was piloting was shot down by Chechen rebels.

q.e: Yuri Gagarin died on 27 March 1968 in the crash of a MiG-15UTI training jet near Moscow.

q: American astronaut John Glenn piloted the first American manned orbital mission, aboard Friendship 7 on February 20, 1962. What actor performed a song, dedicated to him?

q.e: Walter Brennan recorded "The Epic Ride of John Glenn" in 1962 as a tribute to the astronaut.

q: On February 1, 2003, during the Space Shuttle Columbia disaster, the entire seven-member crew died. However, something on the shuttle survived the crash. What was it?

q.e: Roundworms (C. elegans) from a science experiment on Columbia survived the 2003 disaster, in a canister.

q: Who was the first person in space?

q.e: Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space on April 12, 1961, aboard Vostok 1. American astronaut Alan Shepard made a suborbital flight less than a month later, on May 5, 1961.

q: The battle that is generally considered the turning point of the Pacific War was fought on and near this island.

q.e: Fought from June 4 to 7, 1942, the Battle of Midway resulted in the US Navy sinking four Japanese aircraft carriers, halting Japan's Pacific advance.

q: In what sea were the combined naval forces of the US, Britain, Netherlands and Australia decisively defeated by the Japanese Navy as they advanced in Southeast Asia in 1942?

q.e: The Battle of the Java Sea (February 1942) was a Japanese naval victory over the Allied ABDA fleet, which cleared the way to conquer the Dutch East Indies.

q: The kamikaze, Japanese suicide planes that crashed into Allied ships, first made a systematic appearance in 1944 during the fighting near this location.

q.e: The Japanese began organized kamikaze attacks in October 1944 during the Battle of Leyte Gulf in the Philippines.

q: What was the only major city in the Pacific theater of operations in which there was major urban warfare between US and Japanese forces?

q.e: Manila was the only major city in the Pacific war to see heavy urban fighting between the US and Japan (February-March 1945). About 100,000 civilians died.

q: The British and their allies were shocked in 1942 when the Japanese captured a British colonial city that was supposed to be so well fortified as to be immune to attack. What was that city?

q.e: Singapore, the "Gibraltar of the East," fell to Japan on 15 February 1942, with about 80,000 British and Allied troops surrendering.

q: During World War Two, General MacArthurs US forces, with help from Australian forces, methodically and skillfully drove the Japanese from the second largest island in the world. What is that island?

q.e: New Guinea, the world's second-largest island after Greenland, was won back from Japan by MacArthur's forces in 1942-45.

q: In what body of water was a naval battle fought in 1942 in which, for the first time in history, the ships of both sides never saw each other?

q.e: In the Battle of the Coral Sea (May 1942), the US and Japanese carriers fought using aircraft only, never seeing each other's ships.

q: What was the code name for the invasion of Japan during WWII, which was never undertaken due to the end of the war?

q.e: Operation Downfall, with parts named Olympic (Kyushu) and Coronet (Honshu), was the planned invasion of Japan. The atomic bombs and surrender ended it.

q: This American explorer, a former member of the US Senate, rediscovered the Inca settlement of Machu Picchu.

q.e: Hiram Bingham brought Machu Picchu to international attention in 1911 during a Yale University expedition, guided to the ruins by local indigenous farmers.

q: The Battle of Cajamarca, in which the last Inca emperor was captured, took place in which year?

q.e: Francisco Pizarro captured Atahualpa at Cajamarca on 16 November 1532 with fewer than 200 men.

q: What did the Inca officials wear in order to indicate their status?

q.e: Inca nobles and officials wore decorated tunics (unku) and ear spools that showed their rank.

q: How many provincial regions did the Inca Empire have?

q.e: The Inca Empire, Tawantinsuyu ("land of four parts"), was split into four provinces (suyus) centered on Cusco.

q: This town, after which an Olympic event was named, was the site of a battle where the Athenian army defeated the Persians in 490 BC.

q.e: At the Battle of Marathon in 490 BC, Athenian forces led by Miltiades repelled a Persian invasion. The modern 26.2-mile running race commemorates the legend of Pheidippides running from Marathon to Athens to deliver news of the victory.

q: What was the result of the Athenian invasion of Syracuse during the Peloponnesian War?
Syracuse was destroyed and Sparta later surrendered.
The Romans defeated both sides and took over Sicily.
Carthage invaded and controlled western Sicily.

q.e: Athens' Sicilian Expedition (415-413 BC) against Syracuse was a total defeat and weakened Athens in the Peloponnesian War.

q: How did Cleopatra present herself to Julius Caesar when he seized the Egyptian capital in 48 BC ?
with a snake around her neck

q.e: According to the ancient biographer Plutarch, Cleopatra smuggled herself into the palace inside a bed sack, though later accounts and popular culture often portray it as an ornate Persian carpet. This clever entrance allowed her to bypass her hostile brother Ptolemy XIII and gain Julius Caesar's political backing.

q: Cleopatras son by Julius Caesar, who reigned, as a child, jointly with his mother, was nicknamed Caesarion. What does Caesarion mean?

q.e: Caesarion (Ptolemy XV) means "little Caesar." He was Cleopatra's son by Julius Caesar and was co-ruler with her.

q: What future emperor of the Roman Empire had Cleopatra and Julius Caesars son, Caesarion, executed?

q.e: Octavian (later Augustus) had Caesarion killed in 30 BC after defeating Antony and Cleopatra, to remove a rival heir.

q: Who wrote the tragedy Antony and Cleopatra, which centers on Cleopatra and Mark Antonys relationship from the time of the Parthian War until Cleopatras suicide?

q.e: William Shakespeare wrote Antony and Cleopatra around 1606, drawing primarily from Sir Thomas North's English translation of Plutarch's Parallel Lives.

q: How did Cleopatra commit suicide according to ancient sources?
by inducing an asp to bite her
by stabbing herself with a sword
by stabbing herself with a poisoned arrow

q.e: According to ancient historians Plutarch and Cassius Dio, Cleopatra VII committed suicide in 30 BC by having an asp, an Egyptian cobra, smuggled to her in a basket of figs after the defeat of Mark Antony.

q: The internationally accepted civil calendar is called Gregorian. After who was it named?

q.e: Pope Gregory XIII introduced the Gregorian calendar in October 1582 with the papal bull Inter gravissimas. It refined the Julian calendar by altering leap year rules to keep the vernal equinox aligned with Easter.

q: How many months in the Gregorian calendar have 31 days?

q.e: The seven months with 31 days are January, March, May, July, August, October, and December. Four months have 30 days, while February has 28 days in common years and 29 in leap years.

q: The Gregorian Calendar was introduced in 1582. Which one of these countries was among the first to adopt it?

q.e: The Gregorian calendar was introduced in 1582 by Pope Gregory XIII, and Catholic countries like Spain, Portugal, Italy and Poland-Lithuania switched first. Britain waited until 1752.

q: The Gregorian calendar replaced the Julian over 400 year ago. Which religion is still using the Julian calendar?

q.e: The Julian calendar is still used for religious dates by some Orthodox churches, which is why Orthodox Christmas is on 7 January.

q: What is the etymology of the month August?
It was named to honor Roman Emperor Octavian August
Augustus means 6th in Latin and the month was 6th in the Roman calendar
Augustus means horrific in Latin. August was the month when Rome burnt
Auguste was a ship that sank in August 1761

q.e: Originally called Sextilis in the early Roman calendar because it was the sixth month, it was renamed in 8 BC by the Roman Senate to honor Augustus Caesar, the first Roman emperor.

q: How many men did Washington have in his attack force during the Battle of Trenton?

q.e: Washington's force at Trenton was about 2,400 men after crossing the Delaware on Christmas night 1776. They overcame about 1,500 Hessians.

q: In what year was the Dutch Labour Party (S.D.A.P.) founded?

q.e: The Dutch Social Democratic Workers' Party (SDAP) was founded in 1894 and was a predecessor of today's PvdA.

q: Shakespeares theater, The Globe, was destroyed by fire in 1613. Which Queen saw its reopening?

q.e: The Globe burned in 1613 and was rebuilt. The modern Shakespeare's Globe on the Thames was opened by Queen Elizabeth II in 1997.

q: Who can be regarded as the only military dictator of England?

q.e: Following the execution of King Charles I in 1649, Oliver Cromwell ruled the Commonwealth of England, Scotland, and Ireland as Lord Protector from 1653 until his death in 1658.

q: The House of Windsor was founded by King George V in 1917 when he changed the name of his family to Windsor. What was the original name of his family?

q.e: George V changed the royal house's name from the German Saxe-Coburg and Gotha to Windsor in 1917, due to anti-German feeling in WWI.

q: Because of the plundering and devastations across Europe, Attila the Hun came to be called by what nickname?

q.e: Christian writers dubbed Attila flagellum Dei, Latin for Scourge of God, interpreting his fifth-century invasions as divine retribution for human sins. He ruled the Hunnic Empire from 434 until his death in 453.

q: In 452, this influential Roman Pope participated in the negotiations with the Huns near Mantua and dissuaded Attila the Hun from devastating Rome.

q.e: Pope Leo I met Attila near Mantua in 452 and persuaded him to turn back from Italy. He is called Leo the Great.

q: Which of the following was invented by Hiram Maxim?

q.e: Hiram Maxim invented the Maxim machine gun (1884). His son, Hiram Percy Maxim, invented the firearm silencer in 1909.

q: In what year was the first mass produced multishot pistol patented?

q.e: Samuel Colt patented the revolver in 1835-36, the first to be mass-produced.

q: When was a telescopic sight first put on a rifle?

q.e: Telescopic sights were attached to rifles in the mid-19th century, and were used in the American Civil War. Their use grew by 1880.

q: Although it looks a lot like the World War II bazooka, the US Army Javelin anti-armor weapon has this advantage over other weapons of its type.
It is only 50% the weight of similar weapons.
It is about 50% the cost of similar weapons.

q.e: The Javelin is a fire-and-forget missile that can be launched from within enclosures, with a soft launch and little signature. It can attack tanks from above.

q: Which of these European nations did not come under Soviet domination in the five years following the end of World War Two?

q.e: Yugoslavia under Tito broke with Stalin in 1948 and stayed independent. Poland, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Romania, Bulgaria and East Germany came under Soviet control.

q: What was the main purpose of the Truman Doctrine, that was first announced in 1947?
US support for the United Nations Organization for maintaining world peace
keeping the US isolated from conflicts in Europe and Asia
economic aid to European allies and Japan

q.e: The Truman Doctrine (March 1947) pledged US help to countries threatened by communism, starting with Greece and Turkey. It began the policy of containment.

q: Name the military alliance made up of the Soviet Union and the communist nations of Eastern Europe.

q.e: Signed in 1955, the Warsaw Pact was a collective defense treaty formed by the Soviet Union and seven Soviet satellite states in response to West Germany joining NATO. The Comintern was an earlier political network dissolved during World War II.

q: What two US Presidents served during the first decade of the Cold War?

q.e: Harry Truman (1945-53) and Dwight Eisenhower (1953-61) were Presidents in the first decade or so of the Cold War.

q: How many Americans were killed in the capture of Makin Atoll in 1943?

q.e: The Marines' capture of Makin Atoll in November 1943 cost about 66 American dead on the island, but the sinking of USS Liscome Bay killed over 600.

q: What was the nickname of the Italian Royal Army officer who led military expeditions in Africa during World War II?

q.e: Rodolfo Graziani led Italian forces in Ethiopia, Libya and the Fezzan, and was nicknamed "the Butcher of Ethiopia" or "Butcher of Fezzan" for brutal repression.

q: What general was killed by shrapnel in the Battle of Okinawa in 1945?

q.e: Lt. Gen. Simon Bolivar Buckner Jr. was killed by Japanese artillery shell fragments on 18 June 1945 at Okinawa. He was the highest-ranking US officer killed by enemy fire in WWII.

q: Where did Joseph Goebbels, one of Hitlers closest associates, earned his PH.D.?

q.e: Joseph Goebbels earned a doctorate in literature from Heidelberg University in 1921, then became Nazi propaganda minister.

q: In the Middle Ages this type of complexion was very fashionable and everybody was trying to achieve it.

q.e: Pale skin was fashionable in the Middle Ages as a sign of wealth and leisure, and women used powder or bloodletting to look pale.

q: These marks were a huge craze in the Middle Ages.

q.e: Moles and beauty spots were fashionable in medieval and later European beauty; people applied artificial patches.

q: Medieval people had very weird tastes when it came to eyebrows. Artificial eyebrows made from this material were in fashion.

q.e: Medieval Europeans sometimes used false eyebrows made of mouse skin. It was a fashion curiosity mentioned in several sources.

q: Who were the leaders of the US and the Soviet Union during the Cuban Missile Crisis?

q.e: The 13-day confrontation in October 1962 was navigated by U.S. President John F. Kennedy and Soviet Premier Nikita Khrushchev, who reached an agreement to dismantle Soviet missile installations in Cuba.

q: This war, which took place in Europe in the first half of the 17th century, is one of the deadliest conflicts in history.

q.e: Fought primarily in Central Europe from 1618 to 1648, the Thirty Years' War resulted in an estimated 4.5 to 8 million deaths due to combat, famine, and disease.

q: This war started on June 25, 1950 as a civil war and grew into a proxy war between the participants in the Cold War.

q.e: The Korean War began on June 25, 1950, when North Korean forces invaded South Korea, quickly escalating into an international conflict involving the United Nations, the United States, and China.

q: These wars were fought between 1803 and 1815, and included the famous battles of Austerlitz and Waterloo.

q.e: The Napoleonic Wars pitted Napoleon's French Empire against various European coalitions, spanning major engagements from Austerlitz in 1805 to his ultimate defeat at Waterloo in 1815.

q: President Roosevelt met with other Allied leaders several times at several places during WWII. Which is the only leader he met in the White House in Washington?

q.e: Winston Churchill was the only wartime ally who visited FDR at the White House, many times. Others met at conferences in Casablanca, Tehran and Yalta.

q: During WWII, famous athletes, movie stars, and other celebrities often made appearances to encourage Americans to do which of the following?

q.e: During World War II, Hollywood icons like Judy Garland, Humphrey Bogart, and Rita Hayworth toured the nation to promote war bonds, raising billions of dollars to fund military operations.

q: During WWII, this major weapons development project had facilities in New Mexico, Washington state, and Oak Ridge, Tennessee.

q.e: The Manhattan Project developed the first atomic weapons across key top-secret sites, including Los Alamos in New Mexico, Hanford in Washington, and the uranium-enrichment plants at Oak Ridge, Tennessee.

q: During WWII, besides money, what else did you need in order to buy a scarce product such as gasoline in the US?
A ration coupon for the product
A certificate from the national rationing bureau
A sworn statement that the product was essential to you

q.e: During WWII the US rationing system used coupons and stamps for gasoline, sugar, meat, rubber and other scarce goods.

q: What year did George Washington win his first victory against Hessian Soldiers at Trenton New Jersey?

q.e: Washington crossed the Delaware on Christmas night and attacked Hessian troops at Trenton on 26 December 1776, giving American morale a boost.

q: When did the American Civil War break out?

q.e: The American Civil War began on April 12, 1861, when Confederate forces opened fire on the federal garrison at Fort Sumter in the harbor of Charleston, South Carolina.

q: What year did "Custers Last Stand (Battle of the Little Bighorn) take place?

q.e: The Battle of the Little Bighorn was fought on June 25–26, 1876, resulting in the defeat of Lieutenant Colonel George Armstrong Custer and five companies of the 7th Cavalry by Lakota, Northern Cheyenne, and Arapaho warriors.

q: What year did the Wright Brothers fly at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina?

q.e: On December 17, 1903, Orville and Wilbur Wright achieved the first sustained, controlled, powered airplane flights near Kill Devil Hills, just south of Kitty Hawk, North Carolina.

q: What year marks Halleys Comet first appearance in the 20th century?

q.e: Halley's Comet appeared in 1910 (with Earth passing through its tail). It returned in 1986 and is due again in 2061.

q: What year did Franklin D. Roosevelt and Adolph Hitler come to power?

q.e: Hitler became German Chancellor in January 1933 and Franklin D. Roosevelt took office as US president in March 1933.

q: When did the Cuban Missile Crisis start?

q.e: The Cuban Missile Crisis began in October 1962 after US spy planes photographed Soviet medium-range ballistic missile installations under construction in Cuba, sparking a 13-day confrontation.

q: What year was Ronald Reagan elected President of the United States for the first time?

q.e: Ronald Reagan won the 1980 election against incumbent President Jimmy Carter, carrying 44 states and winning 489 electoral votes. He was later reelected in 1984 in an even larger landslide against Walter Mondale.

q: What year did Rita Hayworth, Fred Astaire and Liberace die?

q.e: Liberace (Feb), Rita Hayworth (May) and Fred Astaire (June) all died in 1987.

q: What is meant by Brandschatzung (translated as Firemoney)?
Demanding supplies under threat of torching or pillaging
Pillaging occupied territory in order to obtain supplies for the army
Supplying an army under the threat of being accused as heretics
Hiring mercenary armies as protection against pillaging

q.e: "Brandschatzung" was a medieval and early-modern practice where an army demanded payment or supplies from a town under threat of burning it.

q: Caligula succeeded this emperor, who died in March of 37 A.D.

q.e: Tiberius died on 16 March 37 AD, and Caligula became emperor.

q: Who played Caligula in the self-titled movie, released by Penthouse International in 1979?

q.e: Malcolm McDowell played Caligula in the 1979 Penthouse-funded film, with Helen Mirren, Peter O'Toole and John Gielgud. It was notorious for explicit content.

q: Which submarine was used by the Germans on May 7,1915, during the attack on one of the most impressive luxury ships ever built, the ocean liner RMS Lusitania?

q.e: The German submarine U-20 torpedoed the Lusitania on 7 May 1915, which helped to draw the US into WWI.

q: What do the letters in laser stand for?
Light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation
Light amplification and synchronic electric radiance

q.e: The term laser was coined in 1957 by physicist Gordon Gould as an acronym for Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation.

q: Who is given credit for inventing the neon light?

q.e: Georges Claude, a French engineer, demonstrated the first neon lighting in 1910 and showed it in Paris in 1910-12.
Joshua Lionel Cowen (later of Lionel trains) made an early battery-powered flashlight around 1898. Conrad Hubert marketed the first commercial ones.

q: Which statement is true about the Regency?
It was the first transistor radio.
It was the first auto with an automatic transmission.
It was the first cell phone.
It was the first auto with a moon roof.

q.e: The Regency TR-1 (1954) was the first commercially produced transistor radio.

q: Sir Arthur Conan Doyle was born in this year, on May 22.

q.e: Arthur Conan Doyle was born on 22 May 1859 in Edinburgh. He created Sherlock Holmes in 1887.

q: Three of these events took place at the beginning of the year in which they occurred. Which is the odd one?
First McDonalds opened in Soviet Union (1990)

q.e: Cary Grant died on 29 November 1986, so late in the year. The others on the list occurred early in their years.

q: Mikhail Gorbachev was picked to succeed Chernenko in this year.

q.e: Mikhail Gorbachev became Soviet leader in March 1985 after Konstantin Chernenko died. He started glasnost and perestroika.

q: When did the West Roman Empire cease to exist?

q.e: Historians traditionally mark the end of the Western Roman Empire as September 4, 476 AD, when Germanic chieftain Odoacer deposed the teenage emperor Romulus Augustulus.

q: What period in the Middle Ages marked a renewed interest in Classical Antiquity?

q.e: The Carolingian Renaissance, around 800 AD under Charlemagne, revived interest in classical learning and Latin texts.

q: When did Boniface III, the first Bishop of Rome, begin to bear the title Pope?

q.e: Boniface III became bishop of Rome in 607 and is said to have secured recognition of Rome's primacy, though use of the title "Pope" developed gradually.

q: When did a pandemic, known as the Plague of Justinian, afflict the Byzantine Empire?

q.e: The Plague of Justinian struck Constantinople and the Byzantine Empire in 541-542 AD. It killed perhaps 25-50 million people over time.

q: Which ancient nation is the name Gustav related to?

q.e: Gustav is tied to the Goths, a Germanic people. The name may come from "Gautr" (Geat) and "staff."

q: Never in the field of human conflict has so much been owed by so many to so few.' In this famous quote by Winston Churchill who were the few he was referring to?
Anti-German spies in France and Belgium

q.e: Churchill delivered this speech to the British Parliament on August 20, 1940, praising Royal Air Force fighter pilots defending the nation during the Battle of Britain. The pilots who fought off the Luftwaffe are famously remembered as 'The Few'.

q: What King of France was popularly known as the Sun King?

q.e: Louis XIV chose the sun as his royal emblem, associating himself with Apollo to symbolize peace and order throughout his 72-year reign, the longest recorded of any European monarch.

q: What Civil War battle ended on July 3, 1863 with a Union victory?

q.e: The Battle of Gettysburg culminated on July 3, 1863, with the repulse of Pickett's Charge, marking a major turning point in the Civil War. Antietam took place earlier in September 1862, while Robert E. Lee surrendered at Appomattox in 1865.

q: What General was named Commander of the UN forces in Korea on July 8, 1950?

q.e: President Harry S. Truman appointed General Douglas MacArthur to lead the newly formed United Nations Command in July 1950. Matthew Ridgway later succeeded him in April 1951 after MacArthur was relieved of duty.

q: What famous department chain closed it last stores on July 17, 1997?

q.e: Woolworth closed its last 400 US variety stores on 17 July 1997, ending more than a century of five-and-dime shops. The company continued as Foot Locker.

q: Who was shot and killed by federal agents on July 22, 1934?

q.e: FBI agents shot John Dillinger outside Chicago's Biograph Theater on 22 July 1934.

q: What President signed legislation on July 29, 1958 to create NASA?

q.e: President Dwight D. Eisenhower signed the National Aeronautics and Space Act in 1958 in response to the Soviet Union's launch of Sputnik the previous year.

q: What was the original meaning of the term samurai in Japanese language?
Those who serve in close attendance to nobility
Those who are sons of the warrior dragon
Those who listen to the wind whispering in the trees
Those who follow the way of the sword

q.e: "Samurai" comes from the verb "saburau," to serve. It originally meant those who serve nobles.

q: What is the name of the slightly curved single-edged sword used by Japanese samurai warriors?

q.e: The katana is a curved, single-edged sword traditionally wielded by samurai with two hands. A yari is a spear, and a yumi is an asymmetrical Japanese longbow.

q: What Eastern philosophy has greatly influenced the Japanese samurai culture?

q.e: Zen Buddhism strongly influenced samurai culture, emphasizing discipline, calm and acceptance of death.

q: Bushido is the philosophy and code of conduct of the Japanese samurai. What does the word Bushido literally mean?

q.e: Bushidō (武士道) means "the way of the warrior" and stresses loyalty, honor and courage.

q: In what century is James Clavells samurai novel Shogun set?

q.e: James Clavell's Shōgun (1975) is set in Japan around 1600, based on William Adams and Tokugawa Ieyasu.

q: Who was the Union commander at the Battle of Antietam?

q.e: George B. McClellan led the Union Army of the Potomac at Antietam. Lincoln removed him from command soon after, for not pursuing Lee.

q: Which Union general, wounded in the foot at Antietam, would, within six months time, be the commander of the Army of the Potomac?

q.e: Joseph Hooker was wounded in the foot at Antietam and took over the Army of the Potomac in January 1863.

q: How many soldiers - Union and Confederate - were casualties at Antietam?

q.e: Antietam produced about 23,000 casualties (killed, wounded, missing) in one day, making it the bloodiest single day in US history.

q: Who served as President of the Confederate States of America at the time of the Battle of Antietam?

q.e: Jefferson Davis served as the only president of the Confederate States from 1861 to 1865, encompassing the Battle of Antietam in September 1862. Alexander Stephens was his vice president.

q: An incomplete skeleton of this dinosaur was discovered in 1900.

q.e: Barnum Brown found the first partial Tyrannosaurus rex skeleton in Wyoming in 1900 (named in 1905 by Henry Fairfield Osborn).

q: All recorded historical events occurred during this epoch.

q.e: The Holocene, which began about 11,700 years ago after the last ice age, covers all recorded human history. Some propose the Anthropocene as the next epoch.

q: What does the term Precambrian mean?

q.e: "Precambrian" refers to all time before the Cambrian period (before 541 million years ago), about 88% of Earth's history.

q: When did Boston become a settlement and who led it?

q.e: John Winthrop led Puritan settlers who founded Boston in 1630, with the "city upon a hill" idea.

q: Harvard College was founded in what year?

q.e: Harvard was established in 1636 by a vote of the Great and General Court of the Massachusetts Bay Colony, making it the oldest institution of higher learning in the United States.

q: Which one happened to the U.S. in 1774?
Noah Webster publishes his American dictionary
The Bill of Rights goes into effect

q.e: In 1774 Rhode Island banned bringing in enslaved people, among the earliest colonial measures. In the same year the Continental Congress met.

q: When was the first U.S. adhesive postage stamp sold?

q.e: The first US adhesive postage stamps (Franklin 5¢ and Washington 10¢) were sold on 1 July 1847.

q: This fashionable head accessory was hip from the very beginning of the 80s until their end.

q.e: Headbands were a trademark of 1980s fashion, partly thanks to Olivia Newton-John's "Physical" and aerobics.

q: This style dominated both music and fashion in the late 70s and early 80s. The Sex Pistols and The Exploited were just some of bands that had great influence on mens and womens look.

q.e: Punk fashion (ripped clothes, safety pins, leather) came from bands like the Sex Pistols and The Clash in the late 1970s.

q: As a popular style in the beginning of the 80s it became somewhat politically bound, these started appearing as common clothing adornments.

q.e: Slogans on T-shirts and badges became popular in the early 1980s, with political messages from punk and protest movements.

q: 1983 was the year when this style of clothing finally went out of style.

q.e: By 1983 disco had given way to new wave, pop and synth styles, a few years after the "Disco Demolition" backlash (1979).

q: This type of pants became the craze in the mid 80s. They had zippered patch pockets and zippered ankles.

q.e: Parachute pants, made of nylon with lots of zippers, were popular in the mid-1980s, especially in breakdancing and hip-hop.

q: In order to be trendy in the 80s you should do this with your hair.

q.e: Bleaching or highlighting hair was a hallmark of 1980s style. Big hair and hairspray went with it.

q: Dixie was composed in 1859 by this man.

q.e: Daniel Decatur Emmett wrote "Dixie" in 1859 for a minstrel show. It became a Confederate anthem.

q: He was in command at the critical point in the Battle of Gettysburg?

q.e: Colonel Joshua Chamberlain's 20th Maine held Little Round Top, the Union's left flank, on 2 July 1863 by ordering a bayonet charge. He received the Medal of Honor.

q: What US presidents centennial birthday was celebrated in 1984?

q.e: Harry S. Truman was born on 8 May 1884, so his 100th birthday was in 1984.

q: What countrys elections pit Jose Napoleon Duarte against Roberto DAubuisson in the first freely elected presidency of more than 50 years.

q.e: In 1984 José Napoleón Duarte, a Christian Democrat, beat Roberto D'Aubuisson in El Salvador's presidential runoff during its civil war.

q: In World War II, the Axis and the Allies were the two main rival powers. Which of these countries was not a member of the Axis?

q.e: Greece was attacked by Italy and Germany and fought on the Allied side. The Axis were Germany, Italy and Japan, with Hungary, Romania and Bulgaria.

q: What was the aim of The Molotov-Ribbentrop pact, signed on 23 August 1939 between Germany and the Soviet Union?
Division of the spheres of interest
A united attack against Great Britain

q.e: The Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact (23 August 1939) included a secret protocol dividing Eastern Europe into German and Soviet spheres of influence.

q: Arbeit macht frei was a popular German slogan during World War II, placed mainly on the entrances of which of these?

q.e: "Arbeit macht frei" ("work sets you free") was displayed at the gates of Nazi concentration camps like Auschwitz and Dachau.

q: The end of World War II was announced.

q.e: On D-Day, 6 June 1944, Allied forces landed in Normandy in Operation Overlord. It involved over 150,000 troops.

q: Where did the official Japanese surrender on 2nd September 1945 take place?

q.e: The Japanese Instrument of Surrender was signed aboard the battleship USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay on September 2, 1945, presided over by General Douglas MacArthur. This ceremony formally concluded World War II.

q: This ancient Greek construction, regarded as one the Seven Wonders of the World, was carved by the famed classical sculptor Phidias.
The Statue of Zeus at Olympia
The Mausoleum of Maussollos at Halicarnassus

q.e: Phidias carved the huge Statue of Zeus at Olympia, one of the Seven Wonders, around 435 BC. It was about 12 m tall and made of ivory and gold.

q: This ancient Greek wrote The Histories, a document considered the first work of history in Western literature.

q.e: Herodotus, writing in the 5th century BC about the Greco-Persian Wars, was dubbed the Father of History by the Roman orator Cicero.

q: This ancient Greek philosopher, a teacher of Aristotle, was the founder of the Academy in Athens.

q.e: Plato founded the Academy in Athens around 387 BC, where Aristotle studied for two decades before going on to establish his own school, the Lyceum.

q: Which structure served as a market place in an acnient Greek polis or city-state?

q.e: The agora was the open meeting and market place in an ancient Greek city-state.

q: Which of these movies won all five of the top categories: Best Picture, Best Actor, Best Actress, Best Director and Best Screenplay?

q.e: Only three films have won all top five Oscars: It Happened One Night (1934), One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest (1975) and The Silence of the Lambs (1991).

q: In 1908, this city became the first in the United States to institute chlorination of its water. Prior to this the death rate due to water born diseases, such as typhoid fever and cholera, were extremely high.

q.e: Jersey City, New Jersey, began chlorinating its public water in 1908, the first US city to do so. It sharply cut typhoid cases.

q: Which Academy Award winning American actor who died in 2003 played Ed Norton on The Honeymooners?

q.e: Art Carney played Ed Norton on The Honeymooners and won an Oscar for Harry and Tonto (1974). He died in November 2003.

q: This flamboyantly-dressed announcer on The Price Is Right died on October 27th, 2003 in Los Angeles.

q.e: Rod Roddy, the colorfully dressed announcer of The Price Is Right from 1986, died in October 2003. His catchphrase was "Come on down!"

q: This sassy matronly housekeeper on Give Me A Break! was 54 when she died in 2003.

q.e: Nell Carter starred as Nell Harper, the housekeeper in the sitcom Give Me a Break! (1981-87). She also won a Tony for Ain't Misbehavin'.

q: What city-state was the primary rival of Athens during the Peloponnesian war of 431 BC?

q.e: The Peloponnesian War (431–404 BC) pitted the Delian League, led by democratic Athens, against the Peloponnesian League, dominated by the oligarchic military powerhouse Sparta.

q: Which of the following is not associated with the Battle of Gettysburg, the bloodiest battle of the American Civil War?

q.e: Bloody Lane is a sunken road at Antietam (1862). Gettysburg sites include Devil's Den, the Wheatfield and Cemetery Ridge.

q: This organization, often referred to as a predecessor of the European Union, was founded after WW II to prevent the outbreak of such conflicts.

q.e: The European Coal and Steel Community (1951) tied together the coal and steel industries of six nations, so another war would be "materially impossible."

q: When was the first rollercoaster built?

q.e: LaMarcus Thompson opened the Switchback Railway at Coney Island in 1884, often cited as the first roller coaster in the US.

q: What author broke the record for book sales when the last book in her famous series sold 15 million copies in 24 hours?

q.e: J. K. Rowling's Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (2007) sold 15 million copies worldwide in 24 hours.

q: If you cant do the time, dont commit the crime. Which of the following celebrities spent the LEAST amount of time in jail in 2007?

q.e: Nicole Richie was jailed for a DUI in 2007 and served just 82 minutes. Paris Hilton served about 3 weeks, and Lindsay Lohan spent hours in jail.

q: The town of Hastings, where the Battle of Hastings took place, is located in which county?

q.e: Hastings is in East Sussex, on England's south coast. The Battle of Hastings (1066) was fought at nearby Battle.

q: Who conquered England as a result of the Battle of Hastings?

q.e: The Normans, led by William the Conqueror, defeated Anglo-Saxon King Harold Godwinson at the Battle of Hastings on October 14, 1066.

q: The CIA knew Al Qaeda operatives met secretly in Malaysia in January 2001, and that later two of them, eventual 9/11 hijackers, entered the U.S. When did the CIA share this with the FBI?

q.e: The CIA waited until August 2001 to tell the FBI that two Al Qaeda operatives who'd met in Malaysia had entered the US. This is seen as a missed opportunity.

q: This once white and now orange part breaks up, as it falls through the intense heat of the Earths atmosphere. It is the only expendable part of the Shuttle.
Top O-ring of the fuel tank

q.e: The External Tank was the only non-reusable part of the shuttle. Its foam insulation made it orange, and it burned up on re-entry.

q: On Columbias first mission, the crew noticed something very disturbing after opening the 60 ft. long payload bay doors.
One of the radiators attached to the doors was loose
The doors would not close back

q.e: After STS-1 (April 1981) opened its doors, the crew saw that some thermal tiles were missing from the OMS pods. The orbiter landed safely.

q: Who was the first official casualty of the American Civil War?

q.e: Private Daniel Hough was killed at Fort Sumter on 14 April 1861, in an accidental explosion during a salute after the surrender. He's often called the first death of the war.

q: What was Ulysses S. Grants first battle, fought against Confederate General Gideon J. Pillow?

q.e: Ulysses S. Grant's first Civil War battle was Belmont, Missouri (November 1861), where Confederate General Gideon Pillow was in command. Grant withdrew.

q: Who commanded the Union cavalry corps at the battle of Gettysburg?

q.e: Alfred Pleasonton commanded the Union Cavalry Corps at Gettysburg, and John Buford led a division in it.

q: At what battle of the American Civil War did Native American forces first participate in military action?

q.e: Cherokee, Choctaw and other Native American troops fought for the Confederacy at Pea Ridge in March 1862, the first time they fought in a major Civil War battle.

q: What country did Osama bin Laden live in and operate al-Qaeda from before he found sanctuary back in Afghanistan?

q.e: Osama bin Laden lived in Sudan from 1991 to 1996 and was expelled, before moving to Afghanistan.

q: Which is the most accurate number of casualties (including killed, wounded or lost) of World War II?

q.e: Total WWII deaths are estimated at 70-85 million, including civilians. The figure listed may count one group, such as military dead.

q: Which famous metaphor did Winston Churchill use in the 1940s to describe what Russia did to Eastern Europe after WWII?
The Russian Winter of No Dissent.

q.e: Winston Churchill popularized the term in his Sinews of Peace speech in Fulton, Missouri, in March 1946, describing how an iron curtain had descended across Europe.

q: Where were the first shots of the American Revolutionary War fired?
near the city of New York

q.e: The Revolutionary War began on April 19, 1775, on Lexington Green with the famous shot heard round the world, followed shortly by fighting at Concord. Charleston, South Carolina, was later the site of the first shots of the Civil War at Fort Sumter in 1861.

q: What term refers to the body of delegates from the colonies who met during the Revolutionary War until a constitutional government was finally formed near the end of the war?
the Executive Committee of the United States
the Congress of the United Colonies

q.e: The Continental Congress, convening in both First and Second assemblies from 1774 onward, acted as the provisional government of the Thirteen Colonies throughout the American Revolution.

q: This 1899 -1902 war marked the beginning of the decline of the British Empire

q.e: The Second Boer War (1899-1902) was costly for Britain and exposed the army's weaknesses. It's often seen as an early sign of imperial decline.

q: This conflict lead to the start of a period which is referred to as The Catastrophe by the defeated. Which conflict is this?
The Soviet Annexation of the Baltic States; Estonia, Lithuania Latvia - 1940

q.e: Palestinians call the 1948 Arab-Israeli War and the displacement of about 700,000 people the "Nakba" (catastrophe).

q: On April 24th 1916 an uprising took place in this country in an attempt to gain independence from the UK. Where did this uprising take place?

q.e: The Easter Rising began on Easter Monday, April 24, 1916, when Irish republicans seized key locations in Dublin, including the General Post Office. The Sepoy Mutiny occurred much earlier, in India in 1857.

q: When and where did the Velvet Revolution take place?

q.e: The Velvet Revolution was a nonviolent transition of power in Czechoslovakia that began in Prague in November 1989. It peacefully ended Communist party rule and led to Vaclav Havel becoming president in December 1989.

q: Who was US President during most of the Korean War?

q.e: Harry S. Truman was president when the Korean War began in June 1950 and served through January 1953, shortly before the armistice was signed under Dwight D. Eisenhower in July 1953.

q: In 1944 the Allies launched Operation Overlord starting the liberation of Europe. When troops entered the beaches and caught their first prisoners, they were surprised to hear this language.

q.e: On D-Day, Allied troops took prisoners from the German "Ostlegionen," Soviet POWs and others who spoke Russian, Georgian and other languages.

q: What was the objective of Operation Husky launched in 1943?
The bombardment of the Monte Casino Cloister
The final defeat of German forces in Africa

q.e: Operation Husky (July 1943) was the Allied invasion of Sicily. It led to Mussolini's fall.

q: In May 1941 the Germans used airborne divisions to invade the Island of Crete. Who was the commander of these forces?

q.e: General Kurt Student commanded the Fallschirmjäger in the airborne invasion of Crete in May 1941.

q: What was the codename for the amphibious assault on Normandy, France on 6 June 1944?

q.e: Neptune was the codename for the naval assault phase of Operation Overlord (D-Day, 6 June 1944).

q: Who was the first horse to claim the United States Triple Crown of Thoroughbred Racing on June 11, 1919?

q.e: Sir Barton won the first Triple Crown in 1919. The term wasn't used until later.

q: Scythian monk Dennis the Little, who lived in the sixth century invented this.
Numbering years according to the life of Jesus

q.e: Dionysius Exiguus (Dennis the Little) invented the Anno Domini system for numbering years from Christ's birth around 525 AD.

q: Where in Egypt are the Pyramids of Giza situated?
In the very heart of Egypt

q.e: The Giza pyramids are on the Giza Plateau on the west bank of the Nile, on the edge of Greater Cairo.

q: Sam Houston avenged the deaths of those killed at the Alamo in this battle.

q.e: Sam Houston's army defeated Santa Anna at San Jacinto on 21 April 1836 in about 18 minutes. The cry was "Remember the Alamo!"

q: How did General Santa Anna escape during the battle with Sam Houston (only to be caught the next day)?
He was dressed as a peasant.
He pretended to be dead in the grass.
He jumped in his Buick and headed to the river.
He switched uniforms with someone else.

q.e: Santa Anna fled San Jacinto and was found the next day, dressed in a private's or peasant's clothing. He was brought to Houston.

q: What Dukes of Hazzard star played Thumblerig the Gambler in the 1960 movie The Alamo?

q.e: Denver Pyle played Thimblerig in the 1960 John Wayne film The Alamo. He later played Uncle Jesse on The Dukes of Hazzard.

q: What brilliant Carthaginian general defeated the Romans in the Second Punic War at the Battle of Cannae in 216 B.C.?

q.e: At Cannae (216 BC), Hannibal's double envelopment destroyed a much larger Roman army. It's studied as a tactical masterpiece.

q: What British actor was born on 23 July, 1989 in London, United Kingdom?

q.e: Daniel Radcliffe, the lead of the Harry Potter films, was born 23 July 1989 in London.

q: The first full-length episode of this popular TV sitcom premiered on Fox on December 17, 1989.

q.e: The Simpsons debuted as a half-hour show on Fox on 17 December 1989 with "Simpsons Roasting on an Open Fire." It's the longest-running US sitcom.

q: In what year did the Berlin Wall fall?

q.e: The Berlin Wall fell on November 9, 1989, after nearly three decades dividing the city following its construction by East Germany in 1961.

q: In what year did World War I begin?

q.e: World War I started in late July 1914 following the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria a month earlier on June 28.

q: Who was the first person to fly solo nonstop across the Atlantic?

q.e: Charles Lindbergh completed the first solo nonstop transatlantic flight on May 20–21, 1927, flying the Spirit of St. Louis from New York to Paris in 33.5 hours. Amelia Earhart became the first woman to accomplish the solo transatlantic flight five years later, in 1932.

q: Which document did King John of England agree to in 1215?

q.e: King John granted the Magna Carta at Runnymede in June 1215 to make peace with rebel barons. The Domesday Book was commissioned much earlier by William the Conqueror in 1086.

q: The ancient city of Chichén Itzá was built by which civilization?

q.e: The Maya built Chichén Itzá in the Yucatán, with El Castillo pyramid as its centerpiece. It flourished from around 600 to 1200 AD.

q: Which countries participated in the Lobster War?

q.e: The Lobster War (1961-63) was a diplomatic row between France and Brazil over French boats fishing for spiny lobsters off Brazil's coast.

q: When did Canada leave the confederation to become their own nation?

q.e: Canada became a self-governing dominion on 1 July 1867 with Confederation. It remained part of the British Empire, and Canada Day marks this date.

q: What did Albert Einstein win the Nobel Prize for in 1921?

q.e: Although famous for his theory of relativity, Einstein received the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics specifically for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect. His 1905 paper demonstrated that light can behave as discrete packets of energy, now known as photons.

q: Who was the last emperor of Mexico?

q.e: Maximilian I, an Austrian archduke, was installed as emperor of Mexico by Napoleon III in 1864. He was executed in 1867 by Mexican republicans.

q: The main objective of the German operation "Case Blue" during World War II was originally to capture what?

q.e: Case Blue (summer 1942) aimed to seize the Caucasus oil fields. It led to the battle of Stalingrad.

q: Which Irish village in County Mayo built a tourism industry on the back of an alleged appearance by the Virgin Mary in 1879?

q.e: In 1879, villagers in Knock, County Mayo reported seeing an apparition of the Virgin Mary. It became a major Irish pilgrimage site.

q: The Second Boer War in 1899 was fought where?

q.e: The Second Boer War lasted from 1899 to 1902 and was fought in South Africa between the British Empire and two independent Boer republics: the South African Republic and the Orange Free State.

q: What was the name of the spy ring that helped the United States win the Revolutionary War?

q.e: The Culper Ring, run by Benjamin Tallmadge for Washington, gave intelligence from British-occupied New York.

q: When was the city of Rome, Italy founded?

q.e: According to Roman legend, the twins Romulus and Remus founded the city of Rome on the Palatine Hill around 753 BCE.

q: What micro-state is considered to have the oldest constitution still in effect?
