q.e: San Marino's governing framework relies on the Statutes of 1600, a series of six books written in Latin that form the oldest surviving constitutional documents still in operation.

q: When did Lithuania declare independence from the Soviet Union?

q.e: Lithuania declared the restoration of independence on 11 March 1990, the first Soviet republic to do so.

q: Which of the following Physicists aided Nazi Germany in their production of a nuclear weapon?

q.e: Werner Heisenberg led the German nuclear energy project in WWII. He never produced a bomb, and historians still debate why.

q: When did the French Revolution begin?

q.e: The French Revolution began in 1789, famously sparked by the convocation of the Estates-General in May and the storming of the Bastille on July 14.

q: In the 1960s, who was credited with the first recorded observations that chimps eat meat and make and use tools?

q.e: In 1960 at Gombe Stream National Park in Tanzania, Jane Goodall observed chimpanzees stripping leaves from twigs to fish for termites, disproving the belief that humans were the only tool-making animals. Dian Fossey and Birutė Galdikas, who also studied with Louis Leakey, focused on mountain gorillas and orangutans, respectively.

q: In 1986, Kerr-McGee agreed to pay $1.38 million to the estate of which nuclear-plant whistleblower?

q.e: Karen Silkwood, a worker at a Kerr-McGee plutonium plant, died in a mysterious car crash in 1974 while investigating safety violations. Her family later got a settlement.

q: A supposed Aug. 4, 1964 attack on the USS Maddox is known as which "Incident"?

q.e: The Gulf of Tonkin Incident prompted the US Congress to pass the Tonkin Gulf Resolution in August 1964, dramatically escalating American military involvement in the Vietnam War.

q: It is the process of producing identical copies of a DNA segment asexually. In 1996 the first successful one of an animal was made. The animals name was Dolly. Dolly later died, but Richard Seed announced that he intended try it on humans.

q.e: Cloning produces genetically identical copies. Dolly the sheep (born 1996) was the first mammal cloned from an adult cell.

q: This kind of music became largely popular in Europe and America in the 1990s. It is a melodic, free form combination between techno and house, having hypnotic qualities. The first distinctive track of this kind was Age Of Love, released in 1990.

q.e: Trance emerged in Europe in the early 1990s. "Age of Love" (1990) is often considered an early trance track.

q: This womans death was arguably the most shocking one of the decade. She died in 1997 in a car crash while evading paparazzi. The woman was taken to a hospital, but the two-hour efforts of surgeons to save her life were unsuccessful.

q.e: Diana, Princess of Wales, died following a crash in the Pont de l'Alma tunnel in Paris on August 31, 1997.

q: These became more advanced and more popular in the 1990, with some of the most influential ones being the Super Nintendo Entertainment System, the Sony Playstation, and the Sega Dreamcast.

q.e: The SNES (1990-91), PlayStation (1994) and Dreamcast (1998-99) were key video game consoles in the 1990s.

q: The 1938 incorporation of Austria in Greater Germany under the Nazi Regime is known as this.

q.e: On March 12, 1938, German Wehrmacht troops marched into Austria to enact the Anschluss, effectively annexing the country into the German Reich.

q: This German general was nicknamed The Desert Fox due to the skillful military campaigns he waged in North Africa, during World War II.

q.e: Field Marshal Erwin Rommel earned the nickname 'The Desert Fox' while commanding the German Afrika Korps during the North African campaign from 1941 to 1943.

q: Which member of the Nazi Party was known as Adolph Hitlers first architect of the Third Reich?

q.e: Albert Speer was Hitler's architect and later Minister of Armaments. He was sentenced to 20 years at Nuremberg.

q: The M1 Carbine is the most mass produced small arm weapon in the United States. Even though it was mainly produced by the Inland Division of General Motors, its design belongs to this famous company.

q.e: The M1 carbine, designed by Winchester (with David "Carbine" Williams), was made by several companies, including General Motors' Inland Division. About 6 million were produced.

q: One of the worlds greatest generals. By the age of 30 he ruled almost half of the world. This great leader died at the peak of his campaign at the age of 33. His was taught by Aristotle.

q.e: Alexander the Great studied under Aristotle starting at age 13 before conquering the Persian Empire and extending his realm as far east as the Punjab. He died in Babylon in 323 BC at just 32 years of age.

q: This Carthaginian general marched from Spain to Rome across the Alps. 14,000 of his 40,000 troops died because of the harsh climate. Later, he won the Battle of Cannae.

q.e: Hannibal Barca crossed the Alps in 218 BC during the Second Punic War and famously annihilated a much larger Roman army at the Battle of Cannae in 216 BC.

q: He was one of the best military officers of Russia during the World War II and involved in the taking of Berlin.

q.e: Marshal Georgy Zhukov led the Red Army to Berlin in 1945 and accepted Germany's surrender.

q: Along with the French general, this British general also led the campaign in Northern Africa during the World War II. He was accused of not fighting bravely enough, after his lack of success in Operation Lightfoot.

q.e: Bernard Montgomery commanded the British Eighth Army at El Alamein in 1942 (Operation Lightfoot).

q: Australia was officially settled in 1788 as the penal colony of New South Wales. Over the course of the 19th century this many new self-governing Crown Colonies were established on the continent.

q.e: After New South Wales, five other British colonies were set up: Van Diemen's Land (Tasmania), Western Australia, South Australia, Victoria and Queensland. They federated in 1901.

q: On July 1, 1997, the former British colony of Hong Kong reunified with the Peoples Republic of China. This man was the last governor of Hong Kong.

q.e: Chris Patten was the last British governor of Hong Kong (1992-97), before the handover to China on 1 July 1997.

q: On what album released in 1986 would I find the following lyrics: When I was 17 I did what people told me, Did what my father said and let my mother mold me

q.e: Janet Jackson's "What Have You Done for Me Lately" and "Control" are from her 1986 album Control. The lyric is from the title track.

q: In early 1985 the manufacturer of this drink changed the recipe of the product, but after months of complaints, it was forced by the consumers to restore the original formula.

q.e: Coca-Cola introduced 'New Coke' in April 1985 to counter Pepsi's rising popularity, but intense consumer backlash forced them to bring back the original formula as 'Coca-Cola Classic' just 79 days later.

q: At the time, this was the most complex ship, employing safety measures unseen before. She was double-bottomed and separated into 16 watertight compartments. Nevertheless, she sank on her maiden voyage.

q.e: The Titanic had a double bottom and 16 watertight compartments, which were meant to make it "practically unsinkable". The bulkheads didn't reach the top deck.

q: This tank was built during World War II, but had weight and speed issues. It never saw battle.

q.e: The Panzer VIII Maus was a German super-heavy tank, at 188 tons, built in 1944. Only two prototypes were completed.

q: This 15,000 ton, German-built ship maintained a route from Tallinn to Stockholm. In 1994, it sunk to the bottom of the Baltic Sea due to a badly designed bow door.

q.e: The MS Estonia sank in the Baltic on 28 September 1994 because its bow visor failed, killing 852 people.

q: All of these famous political leaders lost their power in the 80s, except one. Can you spot him?

q.e: François Mitterrand was President of France from 1981 to 1995, so he stayed in power throughout the 1980s.

q: What Celtic chieftain fought Julius Caesar in Gaul, in the first century B.C.?

q.e: Vercingetorix unified the Gaulish tribes in 52 BC against Roman conquest before being defeated and captured by Julius Caesar at the Siege of Alesia.

q: Although he spent 32 years as a criminal, this Wild West rogue killed only a single person. He was mainly engaged in robbing banks and became the first criminal to use an automobile for his escape.

q.e: Henry Starr (1873-1921), a Cherokee outlaw, was the first bank robber to use a getaway car. He was killed in 1921 in a bank robbery in Harrison, Arkansas.

q: His first crime was breaking into a store and taking a pair of pants, leaving a message that he would pay later. He went on to steal cattle from farmers, and later robbed the San Miguel Valley Bank robbery in Telluride, escaping with $20,000.

q.e: Butch Cassidy robbed the San Miguel Valley Bank in Telluride, Colorado, in 1889, his first major bank robbery.

q: After his father was killed, this man sought revenge. He joined Quantrills fighting force. It was reported that he often frothed at his mouth in his almost psychopathic rage in battles. Some sources say he had a silk string with knots for every shot Yankee.

q.e: "Bloody Bill" Anderson was a Confederate guerrilla leader who rode with Quantrill. He was killed in 1864.

q: This criminal was active during the Gold Rush. He was famous for leaving poems in the place of the gold that he had stolen. He never robbed valuables from the passengers of the stagecoaches, he preferred treasure boxes.

q.e: Black Bart (Charles Boles) robbed Wells Fargo stagecoaches between 1875 and 1883 and left poems at the scenes.

q: Jonestown, Guyana, home to the Peoples Temple religious cult, was virtually wiped off the map in November of 1978, when the cult leader induced 900 of his followers to drink cyanide laced Kool - Aid. What was this cult leaders name?

q.e: On 18 November 1978, Jim Jones led more than 900 members of the Peoples Temple to die in a mass murder-suicide at Jonestown, Guyana.

q: Which American novelist, held Acid Tests in the 1960s, together with his circle of friends, known as the Merry Pranksters?

q.e: Ken Kesey (One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest) and the Merry Pranksters held LSD "Acid Tests" in the mid-1960s, traveling on the bus "Furthur."

q: Name the route running from South Vietnam through Laos and Cambodia into North Vietnam, used by North Vietnamese for sending soldiers to the south and for supplying the NLF (National Liberation Front ).

q.e: The Ho Chi Minh Trail was a complex logistical network of paths and roads constructed starting in 1959 to transport personnel and material from North Vietnam through neighboring Laos and Cambodia into South Vietnam.

q: This American diplomat and statesman served as a National Security Advisor and later as a Secretary of State. He was awarded the 1973 Nobel Peace Prize for his role in negotiating a ceasefire and US withdrawal from the war in Vietnam.

q.e: Henry Kissinger shared the 1973 Nobel Peace Prize with Le Duc Tho of North Vietnam, who declined it. Kissinger's role remains disputed.

q: This American was sentenced to life in prison, because in 1968 he led the My Lai massacre of Vietnamese civilians, including women, children and elderly men.

q.e: Lt. William Calley was found guilty of the murders at My Lai (1968). He was sentenced to life, but served only 3½ years under house arrest.

q: What Union General in charge was defeated during the First Battle of Bull Run, the first major land battle of the American Civil War?

q.e: Union Brig. Gen. Irvin McDowell lost the First Battle of Bull Run (21 July 1861), and was replaced by McClellan.

q: This strategic meeting between the heads of the governments of the United Kingdom and the United States took place from December 22, 1941 to January 14, 1942.

q.e: The Arcadia Conference in Washington (22 December 1941 to 14 January 1942) set the "Germany first" strategy for the Allies.

q: The US mining of what nations harbors created a congressional frenzy in April of 1984 and was a case heard by the International Court of Justice?

q.e: In 1984 the CIA mined Nicaraguan harbors. Nicaragua took the US to the International Court of Justice, which ruled against the US in 1986.

q: General Lees three corps commanders at Gettysburg were Longstreet, A.P. Hill and who else?

q.e: Lee's three corps commanders at Gettysburg were James Longstreet, A. P. Hill and Richard Ewell, after Jackson's death.

q: At the beginning of WW II, The British and the French were so surprised by the swiftness of the German attack on its neighbor that for some time no response ensued. This period lasted till May, 1940 and is known by what name?

q.e: The Phoney War lasted from Germany's invasion of Poland in September 1939 until the invasion of France in May 1940.

q: Which plane was the first operational turbojet to take part in WW II?

q.e: The Messerschmitt Me 262 Schwalbe was the first operational jet fighter, in 1944.

q: Six gigantic guns were created during World War II, with the help of general Karl Baker. They were called Karl Monsers and were used in the Brest-Litovsk and Warsaw uprisings. What was their other deployment during the War?

q.e: Karl-Gerät mortars, 600 mm self-propelled siege guns, were used at Brest-Litovsk, Warsaw (1944), and in the Siege of Sevastopol in 1942.

q: Gerald Bull took part in another supergun program - project Babylon. He supplied the plans for a series of gigantic guns, but fortunately only one of them (the smallest one) was completed. This person commissioned the project.

q.e: Gerald Bull designed supergun "Project Babylon" for Saddam Hussein, then was assassinated in Brussels in 1990.

q: The Orient Express, a long-distance passenger train that has become a synonym with luxury travel, made its first run on October 4, 1883. This was the final destination of its first route.

q.e: The Orient Express started in Paris on 4 October 1883 and reached Constantinople (Istanbul) via Vienna and Budapest. The first service needed a ferry and train switch.

q: The optical telegraph (a collective term) preceded the electrical telegraph. It was much faster than riding couriers in to deliver messages over long distances. One of these is not an optical telegraph.

q.e: Optical telegraphs used semaphore signals, such as Chappe's system in France. Morse code is for the electric telegraph.

q: According to some theories, the parachute was invented in 1783 by Sebastien Lenormand in France. Two years later, Jean-Pierre Blanchard demonstrated it as a means of safely getting down on earth from this.

q.e: Sébastien Lenormand made a jump in 1783 with a parachute, and in 1785 Jean-Pierre Blanchard dropped a dog from a balloon with one.

q: Most gold rushes began with the discovery of placer gold by a single man or a party of people. Which one of these statements about placer mining is wrong?
Placer mining is not used any more
Placer gold is mined without tunneling
Hydrostatic pressure is used whenever possible
Placer gold deposits are usually found near big rivers and mountain streams

q.e: Placer mining, which separates gold from sand and gravel by panning or sluicing, is still used today, including by hobbyists.

q: This technique for extracting gold was discovered by chemist Carl Wilhelm Scheele in 1783, and was later developed in 1887 by John Seward MacArthur.

q.e: Gold cyanidation uses cyanide to dissolve gold from ore. It was developed in 1887 by John MacArthur and the Forrest brothers.

q: Which of the following was NOT an Egyptian pharaoh?

q.e: Imhotep was an architect and high official under Pharaoh Djoser, not a pharaoh. He was later worshipped as a god of medicine.

q: Who unified Upper and Lower Egypt?

q.e: Menes (often identified with Narmer) is credited with uniting Upper and Lower Egypt around 3100 BC, founding the First Dynasty.

q: Who was the first king in history to foster a belief in one God?

q.e: Pharaoh Akhenaten ruled Egypt in the 14th century BCE and replaced traditional polytheism with Atenism, the exclusive worship of the sun disc Aten. His successor, Tutankhamun, reversed these religious reforms and restored the traditional Egyptian pantheon.

q: The Allies and Axis were the two main opponent powers in the Second World War. Which of these leaders and his country were on the side of the Axis powers?

q.e: Benito Mussolini's Italy was part of the Axis with Germany and Japan. Italy switched sides in 1943.

q: The attack on Pearl Harbour was carried out on December 7, 1941, causing the United States to enter the war on the side of the Allies. Who was president of the USA at that time?

q.e: Franklin D. Roosevelt delivered his famous Infamy Speech to Congress the day after the attack, asking for a declaration of war. Winston Churchill was the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom at the time.

q: Which of the following leaders was not present at The Yalta Conference that took place in February 1945.

q.e: Yalta (February 1945) was attended by Churchill, Roosevelt and Stalin. Mao was leading communist forces in China.

q: This German military leader led the Sixth Army at the siege of Stalingrad. After months of siege, he was defeated and surrendered to the Russians.

q.e: Friedrich Paulus surrendered the German Sixth Army at Stalingrad on 31 January 1943. About 91,000 were taken prisoner.

q: In August 1944, the German forces in Paris surrendered to this French general who led a military unit from Normandy.

q.e: General Philippe Leclerc's 2nd Armored Division liberated Paris on 25 August 1944. The German commander Choltitz surrendered.

q: He made films from 1916 to 1939 and was married to Joan Crawford. His fathers name helped him launch his career, however Charlie Chaplin took a liking to him and the rest is history. What is the name of this actor who passed away in 2000?

q.e: Douglas Fairbanks Jr. (1909-2000) was the son of the silent film star. He was married to Joan Crawford from 1929 to 1933.

q: One of the most popular fictional cases of poisoning occurs in the movie Arsenic and Old Lace, based on a play by this playwright.

q.e: Arsenic and Old Lace (1944 film, Cary Grant) was based on Joseph Kesselring's 1939 play, about two aunts who poison lonely men with elderberry wine.

q: This torture device was used to rip the victim's flesh to shreds. Once this was accomplished, the victim would be left to dangle alive, with arms bound, left at the mercy of flies and other insects.

q.e: The cat's paw was an iron claw used to tear flesh. Scholars debate how often it was used.

q: He was one of the founders of the YIPPIES and helped announce the candidacy of Pigasus the Pig in Chicago during the 1968 Democratic National Convention. Who was the author of Steal This Book?

q.e: Abbie Hoffman co-founded the Yippies and wrote Steal This Book (1971). He and Jerry Rubin nominated a pig for president in 1968.

q: What woman became the third female to make the FBIs 10 Most Wanted List on August 18th 1970 when she went on the run after her alleged participation in the kidnapping and murder of Judge Harold Harley from the Marin County Hall of Justice?

q.e: Angela Davis was added to the FBI's Ten Most Wanted List in August 1970 for alleged involvement in the Marin County courthouse incident. She was acquitted in 1972.

q: Name the first great Greek tragic playwright who is now acknowledged as the Father of Drama?

q.e: Aeschylus (c. 525-456 BC) is called the "father of tragedy" for adding a second actor. His Oresteia trilogy survives.

q: Which Athenian politician and general led the disastrous attack on Spartan bases in Sicily?

q.e: Alcibiades pushed Athens to launch the Sicilian expedition (415 BC), then was recalled and defected to Sparta. Nicias led it, and it ended in disaster.

q: Who was the king of Sparta and leader of the 300 Spartans at the famous battle at Thermopylae?

q.e: King Leonidas I of Sparta led the 300 Spartans and allies against the Persians at Thermopylae in 480 BC.

q: Name Alexander the Greats favorite horse.

q.e: Alexander the Great tamed the spirited black stallion Bucephalus as a youth around 344 BC, and later named the city of Bucephala in modern Pakistan in the horse's honor.

q: Who was the statesman who re-codified the laws of Athens to make them more humane, and set the city on the road to democracy?

q.e: Solon, an Athenian statesman around 594 BC, canceled debts and reformed Athens's laws, laying the groundwork for democracy.

q: This British engineer is best known as the creator of the Great Western Railway, during the Victorian Age.

q.e: Isambard Kingdom Brunel designed the Great Western Railway (1833-41), the SS Great Western, the Great Eastern and many bridges.

q: Jeanne dArc was a 17-year old girl with no knowledge on military strategics. However, her self-sacrifice and strong belief in God inspired many French victories in the Hundred Years War. This siege was her first victory.

q.e: Joan of Arc arrived at the Siege of Orleans in April 1429, helping lift the English siege in just nine days and earning her the nickname the Maid of Orleans.

q: To what prominent religious group did the majority of people of Salem Village belong during the time of the notorious Salem witch trials in the 17th century?

q.e: The people of Salem Village were Puritans, who strongly believed in the Devil's presence.

q: Li Ka Shing, a Hong Kong businessman and one of the worlds richest men, paid an extremely large ransom for the safe return of his son, Victor Li Tzar. How much did he pay?

q.e: Billionaire Li Ka-shing's son Victor was kidnapped in 1996 by the gangster "Big Spender" Cheung Tze-keung. The ransom was reportedly about HK$1 billion.

q: Two years after Titanics tragic sinking - In the summer of 1914 - this ship started a journey from Quebec harbor to England. A heavy fog hid the horizon and she was hit by the Storstad, a Norwegian collier. Only 465 of the 1500 people onboard survived.

q.e: RMS Empress of Ireland sank in the St. Lawrence River on 29 May 1914 after a collision in fog with the Storstad. 1,012 died. It's Canada's worst peacetime maritime disaster.

q: On May 7th, 1915 this famous ship was hit by a torpedo near the shore of Queenstown, Ireland. It sank in 15 minutes.

q.e: RMS Lusitania was torpedoed by the German U-boat U-20 off the Old Head of Kinsale, Ireland, killing 1,198 passengers and crew. Its sister ship, the Britannic, sank in the Aegean Sea a year later in 1916.

q: During a hot night in August 1658, this ship was wrecked on Maamakunudhoo Atoll, while en route to Bengal. There was a small treasure onboard this ship: eight chests of silver and gold from West Africa.

q.e: The Persia Merchant was wrecked in 1658 at Maamakunudhoo Atoll, in the Maldives. It had been carrying silver and gold.

q: Said unsinkable, this ship started her maiden voyage with 2,220 passengers aboard in 1912. Unfortunately this was her first and her last voyage - she hit an iceberg and sank.

q.e: The RMS Titanic left Southampton on April 10, 1912, carrying an estimated 2,224 passengers and crew. It struck an iceberg late on April 14 and sank in the early morning of April 15, resulting in more than 1,500 deaths.

q: On July 19, 1545 King Henry VIII prepared to watch the new pride of his fleet sail out to engage the French. However, he ended up watching a disaster as this heavy ship heeled over and rapidly capsized when water poured into the lower gun ports.

q.e: The Mary Rose, Henry VIII's flagship, sank on 19 July 1545 in the Solent. Her wreck was raised in 1982.

q: Having been forgotten on the Treaty of Versailles and remaining legally at war, this country signed an official treaty with Germany, thus officially ending WW I .

q.e: There's a popular story that Andorra stayed technically at war with Germany for decades after WWI, but it's a myth with no real basis.

q: What object, often regarded as a symbol of American consumerism, was designed in 1957 by Don Featherstone, who was later awarded the Ig Nobel Prize, a parody of the Nobel Prize?

q.e: Don Featherstone designed the plastic pink flamingo in 1957 for Union Products. He won the Ig Nobel Prize for art in 1996.

q: This American woman, who worked as a physical therapist, invented a device that could be used by veteran soldiers, who had lost their arms. It was an electrical apparatus that could deliver food through a tube.

q.e: Bessie Blount Griffin (1914-2009) invented a feeding device for disabled veterans in the 1940s. She also worked as a nurse and physical therapist.

q: He was the inventor of condensed milk. In 1874 he died in Texas, in a county which was posthumously named after him.

q.e: Gail Borden patented condensed milk in 1856. Borden County, Texas, is named for him.

q: Homer set his epics in the last phase of the Bronze Age in ancient Greece. What is this phase called?

q.e: Homer's epics are set in Mycenaean Greece (about 1600-1100 BC), the Late Bronze Age. Troy and Agamemnon belong to that era.

q: The First Triumvirate was a secret pact in Ancient Rome aimed at controlling the Republic. It was formed in the mid-1st century BC by three great men - Pompey, Crassus, and who else?

q.e: The First Triumvirate (60 BC) was an informal alliance of Julius Caesar, Pompey and Crassus.

q: Which event did not occur in the same year as the other three?
Theodore Geisel writes Cat in the Hat.
UNIVAC becomes the first mass-produced computer.

q.e: Dr. Seuss (Theodor Geisel) wrote The Cat in the Hat in 1957 after a challenge to write a book using 236 simple words.

q: The Boston Celtics were the dominant professional basketball team in the 1950s. Which one of these never played for the Celtics in the 1950s?

q.e: Walter Dukes was a center who played for the Knicks, Pistons and Lakers, not the Celtics. Bill Russell, Bob Cousy and Bill Sharman were Celtics.

q: What society, that inhabited southern Mesopotamia, is widely regarded as the earliest civilization on Earth?

q.e: Sumer emerged in southern Mesopotamia around 4500 BC, creating some of the world's earliest cities, such as Uruk, along with the cuneiform writing system.

q: What was the predominating religion in the Achaemenid Empire, one of the first Persian empires?

q.e: Zoroastrianism was the religion of the Achaemenid Persian Empire (550-330 BC), under rulers such as Cyrus and Darius.

q: Harappan was the mature phase of this civilization that flourished in the river valleys in Sindh province of Pakistan, extending westward into Balochistan province, and in West India.

q.e: The Harappan civilization, better known as the Indus Valley Civilization, flourished from around 2600 to 1900 BCE across modern-day Pakistan and northwest India, named after its major type site of Harappa.

q: On September 1, 1957, this Grammy Award - winning singer was born. She began her career as lead singer for the Miami Sound Machine.

q.e: Gloria Estefan, born 1 September 1957 in Havana, was lead singer of the Miami Sound Machine.

q: The passenger pigeon was one of the most common birds in the world- it is estimated that there were about five billion in the United States alone. The last passenger pigeon died on September 1, 1914 in this zoo.

q.e: Martha, the last known passenger pigeon, died at the Cincinnati Zoo on September 1, 1914, at about 29 years of age. Unregulated commercial hunting and deforestation had driven the species from billions to extinction in mere decades.

q: On September 1, 1985, at a depth of 2 miles (3,8 km), south-east of Newfoundland, the wreck of the Titanic was discovered. Jean-Louis Michel was one of the two people who led the expedition. He was the other one.

q.e: The joint American-French expedition was led by Robert Ballard of the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution and Jean-Louis Michel of IFREMER, locating the wreck using the submersible camera system Argo.

q: The first Crusade was initiated by Emperor Alexius I, when he appealed to Pope Urban II for help in defending against the Muslims. Alexius I was the ruler of this great empire.

q.e: Alexios I Komnenos was Byzantine Emperor. His request for help against the Seljuk Turks led Pope Urban II to call the First Crusade in 1095.

q: The Kingdom of Jerusalem was established after the first Crusade. Godfrey of Bouillon was chosen to be King, but he refused the title and took this one instead.

q.e: After capturing Jerusalem in 1099, Godfrey of Bouillon declined the title of king and took "Advocatus Sancti Sepulchri" (Defender of the Holy Sepulchre).

q: The four events in this question took place on February 4. However, one of the pairs (event - the year in which it happened) is wrong.
First U.S. helicopter was shot down in Vietnam - 1962
Bank of the U.S. Shut Down - 1841

q.e: Patty Hearst was kidnapped by the Symbionese Liberation Army on 4 February 1974, not 1976.

q: In 1799, Napoleon began his campaign to conquer the Ottoman Empire, but was eventually defeated at this city.

q.e: Napoleon laid siege to Acre (Acco) in 1799 in his Syria campaign, but failed. This ended his Middle Eastern ambitions.

q: What conflict was initiated by a self-proclaimed mystic, named Hong Xiuquan, who claimed that he was the new Messiah?

q.e: Hong Xiuquan, who believed he was Jesus's younger brother, led the Taiping Rebellion (1850-64) in China, which killed 20 million or more.

q: In this 751 A.D. military conflict between Islamic forces and Chinese forces, the Chinese were completely defeated.

q.e: At the Battle of Talas in 751, the Abbasid Caliphate defeated the Tang Dynasty. It marked the limit of Chinese expansion to the west.

q: The Great Northern War was the war fought between a coalition of Russia, Denmark-Norway and Saxony-Poland one side and Sweden on the other side. The coalition attacked Sweden in what year?

q.e: In 1700 Russia, Denmark-Norway and Saxony-Poland attacked Sweden, starting the Great Northern War, which ended in 1721.

q: The Burnside Bridge is related to which Civil War battlefield?

q.e: Burnside's Bridge at Antietam was where Union troops under Ambrose Burnside crossed Antietam Creek on 17 September 1862, under fire from Georgian riflemen.

q: After the Romans left in 412-413 AD present-day Netherlands was populated by the Franks, Saxons and what other tribe?

q.e: After Rome withdrew, the Low Countries were home to Franks, Saxons and Frisians. The Frisians lived along the northern coast.

q: This was the second NASA space project. It helped develop the techniques, that made the famous Apollo missions possible. This spacecraft, the most sophisticated of its time, was launched by a converted Titan 2 rocket.

q.e: Project Gemini (1961-66) tested rendezvous, docking and spacewalks for Apollo. The two-man capsules were launched by Titan II rockets.

q: This was the first joint flight of the two rivals in the race to the Moon. It was also the first international manned spaceflight. A Soviet and an American spacecraft were joined to test the compatibility of their rendezvous and docking systems.

q.e: The Apollo-Soyuz Test Project in July 1975 linked American and Soviet spacecraft in orbit, a Cold War détente symbol.
Napoleon beat a larger Russian-Austrian army at Austerlitz on 2 December 1805, regarded as his tactical masterpiece.

q: Name the tax, which knights had to pay in order to avoid going to war.

q.e: Scutage ("shield money") was a payment in lieu of military service by feudal knights, which kings used to hire mercenaries.

q: In order to become a knight nowadays, you would have to be given the title in royal recognition, or to belong to an order. In the UK the knight is styled Sir and the female -- this.

q.e: The female equivalent of "Sir" for a knight is "Dame" (e.g., Dame Judi Dench). The Order of the British Empire makes both.

q: What term refers to the competition between Britain, France and Germany over African territory between the 1880s and the beginning of World War I in 1914?

q.e: The Scramble for Africa, formalized at the Berlin Conference of 1884 to 1885, saw European powers increase their control of the African continent from roughly 10 percent to around 90 percent by 1914.

q: Who was the first wife of Napoléon Bonaparte and the first Empress of the French?
Louise Catherine Eléonore Denuelle de la Plaigne

q.e: Joséphine married Napoléon in 1796 and was crowned Empress at Notre-Dame in 1804. After their marriage was dissolved because she produced no heir, Napoléon married Marie Louise of Austria in 1810.

q: This is a kind of body adornment that Indian women use. It became popular in many countries after Madonna adopted it.

q.e: The bindi is a dot worn on the forehead, traditionally marking the "third eye". It became a fashion fad in the West in the 1990s through Madonna and Gwen Stefani.

q: This English Renaissance musician was one of the first composers to write anthems set to English words?

q.e: Thomas Tallis (c. 1505-1585), a composer for Henry VIII, Edward VI, Mary and Elizabeth I, wrote early English-language anthems.

q: This Italian poet, considered one of the fathers of the Renaissance, is also regarded as the father of alpinism.

q.e: Petrarch's account of climbing Mont Ventoux in 1336 is often credited as the beginning of recreational mountaineering.

q: In ancient Japan geichas were famous for their fashion coiffures. However, it was difficult to preserve them during sleep. Still they managed to keep their complex hairdos. How?
Using pillows filled with buckwheat chaff

q.e: Geisha used a "takamakura," a raised pillow, to protect their hairstyles at night. Some were stuffed with buckwheat husk.

q: The first bodice was invented not to dress women, but to make them more attractive to men by pushing breast up and out. Where was it invented?

q.e: Women in Minoan Crete (c. 1600 BC) wore fitted bodices that left the breasts exposed, as seen in frescoes and the Snake Goddess figurines.

q: When did the term milliner appear for the first time?

q.e: "Milliner" derives from "Milaner", a dealer in goods from Milan, Italy, which is first recorded in the 1500s.

q: In order to get the Generation-X car buyers, this cross-over SUV was made by GM from 2001-2005. It was a financial failure.

q.e: The Pontiac Aztek (2001-05) was criticized for its styling. It's now remembered as a failure, but became cultured by Breaking Bad.

q: It was still the custom in the 1960s for many people to not eat meat on Fridays. McDonalds could not stand to lose these customers on Friday so this product was developed.

q.e: In 1962 McDonald's franchisee Lou Groen created the Filet-O-Fish for Catholic customers on Fridays. Ray Kroc's "Hula Burger" (grilled pineapple) lost to it in a taste test.

q: This movie featured two of the biggest stars of 1986. They were a married couple form 1985-1989. George Harrison also appeared in the movie. Although the movie was beautifully filmed, it was a critical and financial flop.

q.e: Shanghai Surprise (1986) starred then-married Madonna and Sean Penn. George Harrison produced its soundtrack and had a cameo. It flopped.

q: Water World and The Postman were two of the biggest flops in movie history. Who was the star of both of these films?

q.e: Kevin Costner starred in Waterworld (1995) and The Postman (1997), both expensive flops. He also directed The Postman.

q: Panasonic developed the VHS type of tape and Sony developed this type.

q.e: Sony's Betamax (1975) lost the home video format war to JVC's VHS. VHS offered longer recording times.

q: In Mesoamerican chronology, this period of time is dubbed Classic Era, and marks the peak of the cities of the Maya southern lowlands.

q.e: The Classic period of Maya civilization lasted from about 250 to 900 AD, with great cities like Tikal and Palenque.

q: Classic Maya kings carried this title, meaning supreme and sacred ruler.

q.e: Classic Maya rulers used the title k'uhul ajaw, "holy lord," with k'uhul meaning sacred or divine.

q: Mayas used a special kind of shorthand for easier counting, which consisted of these three main symbols.
Empty circle, filled circle and dot

q.e: The Maya used dots (1), bars (5) and a shell symbol (zero). The system was base-20.

q: What Turkish assassin shot and wounded Pope John Paul II in 1981?

q.e: Mehmet Ali Ağca shot Pope John Paul II in St. Peter's Square on 13 May 1981. The Pope survived and later forgave him.

q: Some academics consider World War I and II as two major parts of a single conflict. How many years apart were the two wars?

q.e: WWI ended in 1918 and WWII began in 1939, a gap of about 21 years. Some historians see them as one "Thirty Years' War of the 20th century."

q: The French Revolution began in 1789 with the storming of this building and ended in 1799 after succeeding to overthrow the absolute monarchy in France.

q.e: On July 14, 1789, Parisian revolutionaries stormed the medieval fortress and prison known as the Bastille to seize gunpowder and rebel against royal tyranny. The event is celebrated annually as France's National Day, commonly called Bastille Day in English.

q: Name the author of Slaughterhouse-Five who died April 11th 2007 at the age of 84.

q.e: Kurt Vonnegut, author of Slaughterhouse-Five (1969), drew on his experience as a POW during the Dresden bombing. He died on 11 April 2007.

q: He was 69 at the time of his death in April 2007. He sang Monster Mash. You remember, it was a graveyard smash.

q.e: Bobby "Boris" Pickett had a hit with "Monster Mash" (1962). He died in April 2007 aged 69.

q: Which playwright of Ancient Greece is generally regarded as the father of drama?

q.e: Aeschylus is "the father of tragedy." He wrote about 80 plays, of which seven survive.

q: This was a 1961 United States-planned and funded landing, which aimed at overthrowing the government of Fidel Castro, marked the climax of anti-Cuban US actions during the Cold War. What was the name of this invasion?

q.e: In April 1961, the CIA-sponsored Brigade 2506 of Cuban exiles landed at the Bay of Pigs (Playa Giron) in an unsuccessful attempt to topple Fidel Castro's government.

q: In 1945, Churchill, Stalin and Roosevelt made arrangements for post-war Europe. Where did the conference take place?

q.e: Churchill, Roosevelt and Stalin met at Yalta, in Crimea, in February 1945, and planned the post-war order of Europe.

q: What warrior king and his 300 Spartans held back the Persian army for two days in one of historys most heroic last stands?

q.e: King Leonidas I led the legendary Spartan defense against Xerxes I's invading Persian army at the Battle of Thermopylae in 480 BC.

q: What Soviet General and Hero of the Soviet Union led the Red Army during the Battle of Stalingrad and the Battle of Kursk?

q.e: Georgy Zhukov helped plan Soviet victories at Stalingrad, Kursk and Berlin. He was widely seen as the Soviet Union's top WWII commander.

q: He was the bravest and strongest Greek warrior in the Trojan War. He died when Apollo helped guide Pariss arrow to this warrior only vulnerable spot?

q.e: In Greek mythology, Achilles was held by his heel when his mother Thetis dipped him into the River Styx, leaving that single spot vulnerable to Paris's fatal arrow during the Trojan War.

q: The name of the first capital of the Empire, near which the tomb of the first Chinese emperor- Qin Shi Huang had been built.

q.e: Xianyang was the capital of Qin, and Emperor Qin Shi Huang's tomb with the terracotta army is near Xi'an, close to where Xianyang stood.

q: On 18 June 618, Gaozu took the throne, established the Tang Dynasty and opened a new age of prosperity. During the Tang Dynasty, this religion became predominant in China.

q.e: Buddhism flourished in Tang China (618-907) and became very influential, before being restricted by Emperor Wuzong around 845.

q: The Yuan Dynasty was the first foreign dynasty to rule over all of China. It was officially established by this Mongolian ruler in 1271 and ruled over China until 1368.

q.e: Kublai Khan, the grandson of Genghis Khan, proclaimed the Yuan Dynasty in 1271 and established his capital at Dadu, modern-day Beijing. His grandfather Genghis Khan had founded the broader Mongol Empire in 1206.

q: The Qing Dynasty was the last imperial dynasty of China. As a result of the 1911 revolution, a new Republic of China was established and this is what happened to the last Chinese emperor, Hsuan Tung.

q.e: Puyi, the last Qing emperor (Xuantong), abdicated on 12 February 1912 after the 1911 Xinhai Revolution. He was just six.

q: Ulysses S. Grants wife, Julia Dent Grant, had a cousin who was a CSA General. What was his name?

q.e: James Longstreet was Julia Dent Grant's cousin and was a friend of Ulysses S. Grant, even serving as best man at his wedding. He became a Confederate general.

q: In 1985 New Coke was introduced. For many reasons it was a great flop and the company went back to regular coke. How was New Coke different from regular coke?
It had more lime and less lemon.
It was enriched with vitamins A,C, and D.

q.e: New Coke (1985) tasted sweeter, closer to Pepsi, and was dropped after 79 days following backlash. "Coca-Cola Classic" returned.

q: It was a 1995 movie about a female pirate, played by Geena Davis, who races other pirates to find hidden gold. It starred Frank Langella, Mathew Modine, Maury Chaykin and Stan Shaw.

q.e: Cutthroat Island (1995), starring Geena Davis as pirate Morgan Adams, flopped so badly that it bankrupted Carolco Pictures.

q: Love Boat was a big TV hit, so a copy of it would be a big hit, too, right? This 1979 copy of Love Boat was to be based on the adventures, lives and loves of passengers on a train. What was the name of this nine-episode flop?

q.e: Supertrain (NBC, 1979) was a costly flop about a luxury nuclear-powered train, and ran for nine episodes.

q: In the 1960s, Humans finally achieved an age-old dream of landing on the Moon. Who was the first person to set foot on the Moon and in what year did this happen?

q.e: Apollo 11 Commander Neil Armstrong stepped onto the lunar surface on July 20, 1969, famously declaring it one small step for man. Lunar module pilot Buzz Aldrin joined him roughly 19 minutes later.

q: What astronaut almost drowned in 1961, when his Liberty Bell 7 capsule sank upon splashdown in the Pacific Ocean?

q.e: Gus Grissom's Liberty Bell 7 capsule sank after its hatch blew open on 21 July 1961. He nearly drowned, and the capsule was recovered in 1999.

q: On September 23, 1999, the Mars Climate Orbiter, whose mission was to study the Martian weather, climate, and water, crashed on the Martian surface, instead of starting to orbit around the planet. What was the reason for this accident?
Confusion in the system of units in the navigation of the spacecraft
The atmospheric stresses and friction were greater than expected.
A mechanical fault in the protective shield
Mars gravitation forces were greater than expected.

q.e: Lockheed Martin used Imperial units of pound-force-seconds, while NASA expected metric newton-seconds in the transfer of thruster data, causing the spacecraft to dip far too low into the Martian atmosphere and disintegrate.

q: This year was fatal for Russian space exploration, because after a normal re-entry of the capsule of the Soyuz 11 mission, the ground team opened the capsule to find the crew dead.

q.e: In June 1971, the three Soyuz 11 cosmonauts died when a valve opened and the capsule depressurized during re-entry. They had no spacesuits.

q: Where did the Japanese and Americans fight for about six months in 1942 before the Japanese were finally defeated and their advance in the Solomon Islands stopped?

q.e: The Guadalcanal Campaign lasted from August 1942 until February 1943. It marked the first major Allied land offensive in the Pacific theater, successfully stopping the Japanese advance toward Australia and securing Henderson Field airbase.

q: The last major battle of World War Two was also the one that caused the most casualties to the US and their allies (mostly British) in the Pacific War. Where was this battle fought?

q.e: The Battle of Okinawa (April-June 1945) was the bloodiest of the Pacific War. It cost about 12,000 US dead and over 100,000 Japanese and many Okinawan civilians.
Geli Raubal was Hitler's half-niece (daughter of his half-sister Angela). She died in 1931 in his Munich apartment, apparently by suicide.

q: What was the name of the airplane that dropped the a-bomb over Nagasaki on August 9, 1945?

q.e: The B-29 "Bockscar" dropped the "Fat Man" atomic bomb on Nagasaki on 9 August 1945. Charles Sweeney flew it.

q: Who led the Vichy regime in France during WWII?

q.e: Marshal Philippe Pétain, the WWI hero, headed the Vichy regime that collaborated with Germany from 1940 to 1944.

q: What is the name of the last Inca Emperor, who defeated his older half-brother in a civil war and took the throne?

q.e: Atahualpa won a civil war against his half-brother Huáscar in 1532. He was captured and executed by Pizarro in 1533.

q: What was the language of the Inca Empire, used by the Catholic Church to preach to Indians in the Andes area?

q.e: Quechua was the Inca language and is still spoken by millions in the Andes. The Church used it for evangelism.

q: This Spanish conquistador, the founder of the City of Lima, conquered the Inca Empire.

q.e: Francisco Pizarro captured Inca emperor Atahualpa at the Battle of Cajamarca in 1532 and founded Lima as Ciudad de los Reyes in 1535. Hernan Cortes, by contrast, conquered the Aztec Empire in Mexico a decade earlier.

q: This title, which in English means the only one, was used by the ruler of the Inca Empire.

q.e: "Sapa Inca" means "the only Inca" or "sole ruler" in Quechua. He was considered a descendant of the sun god Inti.

q: In early 6th century BC, the city states of Akragas, Gela, and Syracuse sent ships to the city of Himera in west Sicily, where they defeated an invading force coming from where?

q.e: In 480 BC, Greek cities of Sicily beat the Carthaginians at Himera. Tradition says it happened on the same day as Salamis.

q: To what dynasty did Cleopatra, the last Pharaoh of Ancient Egypt, belong?

q.e: Cleopatra VII belonged to the Ptolemaic dynasty, founded by Ptolemy I, a Macedonian general of Alexander the Great.

q: Cleopatra formed an alliance with Mark Anthony, one of the triumvirs who ruled Rome following Caesars death. How many children did Mark Anthony and Cleopatra have?

q.e: Mark Antony and Cleopatra had three children: the twins Alexander Helios and Cleopatra Selene II, and Ptolemy Philadelphus.

q: Who defeated Mark Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium, the last engagement in the Final War of the Roman Republic?

q.e: Octavian, who later became Augustus, the first Roman emperor, decisively defeated the joint naval forces of Mark Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium in 31 BC.

q: After Cleopatra and Anthonys death, who became guardian of their children?

q.e: After their parents' deaths in 30 BC, Octavia Minor, Antony's wife and Octavian's sister, raised the three children.

q: What was the name of the tough Colonel who commanded the Hessian Garrison during the Battle of Trenton?

q.e: Colonel Johann Rall commanded the Hessian garrison at Trenton and was mortally wounded in the battle of 26 December 1776.

q: The crossing of the Delaware, that preceded the Battle of Trenton, was aided by a regiment of boatmen from this Massachusetts town.

q.e: Colonel John Glover's Marblehead regiment of fishermen and mariners ferried Washington's troops across the Delaware.

q: At the time of the Battle of Trenton, the Hessian garrison numbered some 1500 men. Twenty soldiers were killed and eighty wounded. About how many soldiers were taken prisoner?

q.e: At Trenton, around 900 Hessians were captured, with about 20 killed and 80 wounded, in an American victory.

q: What Batavian led the ill-fated uprising against the Romans AD 69-70?

q.e: Gaius Julius Civilis, a Batavian noble, led the Batavian revolt against Rome (69-70 AD) during the Year of the Four Emperors.

q: What period of time during the Eighty Years War (1568- 1648) is referred to as the Twelve Years Truce?

q.e: The Twelve Years' Truce (1609-1621) was a pause in the Dutch fight against Spain during the Eighty Years' War.

q: In the Netherlands, who headed the famous postwar Cabinet of 1948 - 1958?

q.e: Willem Drees was Prime Minister of the Netherlands 1948-58, leading the postwar reconstruction and creating the old-age pension.

q: What was the connection between Mary Stuart (Queen of Scots) and Bloody Mary (Queen of England)?
Mary Stuarts grandmother, Margaret Tudor, was an aunt of the English Mary.
Bloody Mary had the Scottish Mary beheaded
They were both daughters of Henry VIII (but had different mothers).

q.e: Mary I of England (Bloody Mary) and Mary, Queen of Scots, were related through Margaret Tudor, Henry VIII's sister. Margaret was Mary Stuart's grandmother and Mary I's aunt.

q: When James, brother of king Charles II, married Mary of Modena, who was Catholic, the English Parliament wanted James to do what?
Abstain from having sex with his wife
Renounce his rights to the English throne
Force her to become Anglican or Presbyterian

q.e: James, Duke of York, was a Catholic, and his marriage to Catholic Mary of Modena in 1673 alarmed Parliament, which feared a Catholic succession. It led to the Test Act and later the Exclusion Crisis.

q: What decade witnessed the publishing of Charles Darwins The Origin of Species, and the first official game of baseball?

q.e: On the Origin of Species came out in 1859. The first recorded baseball game under Knickerbocker rules was in 1846, and baseball's early organized play was in the 1850s.

q: This decade saw the end of the Napoleonic Wars in Europe and the Year Without a Summer.

q.e: The Napoleonic Wars ended in 1815 at Waterloo. The Year Without a Summer, 1816, followed the 1815 eruption of Mount Tambora.

q: What decade was nicknamed the Mauve Decade, and saw the discovery of the X-rays by Wilhelm Rontgen?

q.e: The 1890s were called the "Mauve Decade" after the fashionable color. Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays in 1895.

q: During this decade the first modern railway opened, and Beethovens Ninth Symphony premiered in Vienna.

q.e: In the 1820s, the Stockton and Darlington Railway opened (1825), and Beethoven's Ninth Symphony premiered in Vienna in 1824.

q: What decade saw the the end of the Enlightenment, the invention of canned food, and the publishing of the atomic theory?

q.e: In the 1800s, Nicolas Appert invented canned food (1809), and John Dalton published his atomic theory (1808).

q: Mark Twain published Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, and Robert Louis Stevenson published Treasure Island and The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde during this decade.

q.e: The 1880s saw Huckleberry Finn (1884/85), Treasure Island (1883) and Jekyll and Hyde (1886).

q: To form an alliance against Attilas Huns, in 451 the Romans combined armies with which Visigoth leader?

q.e: Theodoric I, king of the Visigoths, joined the Roman general Aetius against Attila in 451 and died at the battle.

q: Honoria, sister of the Roman Emperor, broke the peaceful relations between Rome and Attila the Hun by trying to do what?

q.e: Honoria, Emperor Valentinian III's sister, sent her ring to Attila asking for his help to escape an arranged marriage. Attila took it as a marriage proposal and demanded half the Western Empire.

q: In 1946 George Kennan, a Russian specialist in the US embassy in Moscow, sent a long telegram to Washington. His telegram was very persuasive and is given much credit for the US adopting this kind of policy.

q.e: George Kennan's "Long Telegram" (February 1946) argued the US should contain Soviet expansion. It became the basis of Cold War US policy.

q: Which of the following is the best reason why the KMT (Nationalists) under Chiang Kai-shek were defeated by the communists in the civil war following World War Two and forced to flee to Taiwan in 1949?
There was much corruption and inefficiency in the KMT leadership.
The only support for the KMT was from Chinese peasants.
The US refused to give any aid to the KMT.
The communist forces greatly outnumbered the KTM and were better equipped.

q.e: The Kuomintang lost the Chinese Civil War largely because of corruption, runaway inflation and loss of popular support. The communists won peasant backing.

q: For a few years in the mid-1950s relations between the Soviet Union and the United States became less tense. What is this period of time called?

q.e: The "Thaw" after Stalin's death in 1953 saw easing of tensions, including Khrushchev's 1956 secret speech and the 1955 Geneva Summit.

q: Which of these were known as Stalins Organs?

q.e: Soviet Katyusha multiple-rocket launchers were nicknamed "Stalin's Organs" for the organ-pipe look and the howling sound of their rockets.

q: Who developed the deadly V-2 combat rocket during World War II and where was it built?

q.e: Wernher von Braun led the German team that developed the V-2 at Peenemünde. Mass production was at the Mittelwerk factory near Nordhausen, using slave labor.

q: It was believed in the Middle Ages that dilated pupils are infinitely enchanting. To dilate their pupils people used the juice of this plant as eye drops.

q.e: Atropa belladonna contains atropine, a chemical that blocks pupil constriction. Renaissance Italian women used drops from the plant for cosmetic dilation, which is how it earned the name belladonna, or beautiful lady.

q: This hair color was very fashionable in medieval times. Women applied special mixtures to their hair and stayed in the sunlight for hours to achieve it.

q.e: Venetian blonde, a golden hair color, was fashionable in the Renaissance. Women sat in the sun with bleaching mixtures on their hair.

q: What decade was nicknamed the Jazz Age in the United States, Canada and the United Kingdom?

q.e: Author F. Scott Fitzgerald popularized the term Jazz Age to describe the vibrant cultural and musical explosion of the 1920s. The era ended dramatically with the Wall Street crash of October 1929.

q: During this decade Soviet leader Joseph Stalin died, the European Common Market was established and the Korean War broke out and ended.

q.e: In the 1950s, Stalin died (1953), the Korean War ran 1950-53 and the Treaty of Rome (1957) created the European Economic Community.

q: During this decade the RMS Titanic sank on its debut voyage, World War I broke out, and Albert Einstein published his theory of general relativity.

q.e: The 1910s saw the sinking of the Titanic in April 1912, the outbreak of World War I in July 1914, and the publication of Albert Einstein's field equations for general relativity in late 1915.

q: During this decade World War II ended, India gained independence from Great Britain, and Israel was established.

q.e: The 1940s saw WWII end (1945), India's independence (1947), and the creation of Israel (1948).

q: During this decade there was an oil crisis, the Apollo 13 space mission was carried out, and the first modern computers were invented.

q.e: The 1970s saw the oil crises (1973, 1979) and Apollo 13 (1970), and personal computers appeared.

q: In this decade the Panama Canal was built, mass production of the automobile began, and the home phonograph became popular.

q.e: The 1900s saw the building of the Panama Canal (1904-14), Ford's Model T (1908) and the spread of the phonograph.

q: Martin Luther King, Jr., John F. Kennedy and Robert F. Kennedy were assassinated during this decade.

q.e: President John F. Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas in 1963, while civil rights leader Martin Luther King, Jr. and Senator Robert F. Kennedy were both fatally shot just two months apart in 1968.

q: These wars were fought in France between French Catholics and Protestants in the second half of the 16th century.

q.e: The French Wars of Religion (1562-98), sometimes called the Huguenot Wars, pitted Catholics against Protestant Huguenots. They ended with the Edict of Nantes.

q: Which of the Punic wars was fought between 264 and 241 BC in Sicily and Africa?

q.e: The First Punic War (264-241 BC) was fought over Sicily. Rome built its first big navy and won.

q: The Hindenburg Disaster in Lakehurst, New Jersey took place in the same year that the fabric Nylon was invented. What year was that?

q.e: The Hindenburg exploded at Lakehurst in May 1937. Nylon was invented by Wallace Carothers at DuPont in 1935, and patented in 1937.

q: On October 13th, 1971, Major League Baseball history was made when the first night game of a World Series was played between the Pittsburgh Pirates and this team.

q.e: The 1971 World Series Game 4 was the first World Series night game, played at Pittsburgh's Three Rivers Stadium. The Pirates beat the Orioles in seven games.

q: Name the French-language daily newspaper in Canada, whose first edition hit the streets of Montreal on October 13th, 1884.

q.e: La Presse was founded in Montreal in 1884. It was a daily that became Quebec's biggest French paper, and went digital-only in 2018.

q: Until 1494, wars were protracted and relatively bloodless, the sieges of towns slow and uncertain. However, war erupted in 1494 when the massive use of cannon made sieges last hours. To what event does this refer?
The French invasion of the English held counties of Normandy Aquitaine
The Dutch siege of s Hertogenbosch

q.e: In 1494 Charles VIII of France invaded Italy with powerful siege cannons, which made castle walls quickly outdated and began the Italian Wars.

q: In this year sprinter Jesse Owens was born, the Philadelphia Athletics won the World Series, and Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde came out as a silent film.

q.e: Jesse Owens was born 12 September 1913, and in 1936 he won four gold medals at the Berlin Olympics.

q: In this year George Martin, English producer of The Beatles, was born, Fox Film bought the Movietone system for recording sound onto tape, and Joe Paterno, longtime coach of Pennsylvania State Universitys college football team was born.

q.e: Sir George Martin (the "fifth Beatle") was born in 1926, as was Penn State's Joe Paterno.

q: In this year the Dow Jones Industrial Average reached its lowest level of the Great Depression, bottoming out at 41.22, Tarzan the Ape Man opened,and the Winter Olympics were held in Lake Placid, New York.

q.e: In 1932 the Dow Jones bottomed at 41.22 (July). Tarzan the Ape Man was released and the Winter Olympics were held at Lake Placid.

q: In this year Elvis Presley appeared on the Ed Sullivan show for the third time, the Brooklyn Dodgers moved to L.A., and The Bridge on the River Kwai was released.

q.e: In 1957, Elvis made his third and final Ed Sullivan appearance, The Bridge on the River Kwai was released, and the Dodgers announced the move to LA.

q: In this year the New York Jets of the American Football League beat the favored Baltimore Colts of the National Football League 16-7 in Super Bowl III, Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid came out, and Stevie Wonder came out with I Dont Know Why.

q.e: In Super Bowl III (January 1969), Joe Namath's Jets upset the Baltimore Colts 16-7, after "guaranteeing" a win.

q: In this year Notre Dame beat UCLA 71-70 in mens college basketball ending the Bruins 88-game winning streak, The Way We Were by Barbra Streisand was the number 1 song, and The Godfather II came out.

q.e: On 19 January 1974 Notre Dame ended UCLA's 88-game winning streak 71-70. The Godfather Part II premiered in December 1974.

q: In this year the U.S.A. upset the Soviet Union in Olympic hockey, Call Me by Blondie was the #1 song, and Star Wars: Episode V - The Empire Strikes Back came out.

q.e: The year 1980 saw the U.S. men's hockey team defeat the four-time defending champion USSR at the Lake Placid Winter Olympics, while The Empire Strikes Back topped the box office that same summer.

q: In this year the Green Bay Packers won the Super Bowl, Foolish Games/You Were Meant for Me by Jewel was the number 2 song, and the movie Titanic came out.

q.e: In 1997 the Packers won Super Bowl XXXI, and Titanic was released in December.

q: Which of these statements is true about the Battle of Artemisium?
It was the naval battle that took place at Thermopylae
It was the battle where king Darius was defeated
It was the final naval battle that destroyed the Greek fleet
It was the battle before the sacking of Athens

q.e: The naval Battle of Artemisium (480 BC) was fought at the same time as Thermopylae. After Thermopylae, the Greeks withdrew.

q: Who created the concept of the Dark Ages in the 1330s?

q.e: Petrarch coined the idea of a "dark age" in the 1330s, as a contrast to the classical light, and later writers named the Middle Ages that way.

q: What Renaissance humanist historian coined the term Middle Age?

q.e: Flavio Biondo, an Italian Renaissance historian, was the first to use "media tempestas" (Middle Age), in the 15th century.

q: Which of the following is not a period of the Paleozoic era?

q.e: The Paleogene belongs to the Cenozoic Era. The Paleozoic periods are the Cambrian, Ordovician, Silurian, Devonian, Carboniferous and Permian.

q: Gustav has been a common name for Swedish monarchs since the reign of Gustav Vasa or Gustav I. He became king in 1521, after leading the rebellion against King Christian II of this country who controlled most of the Sweden.

q.e: Gustav Vasa led a rebellion against Christian II of Denmark, who ruled Sweden, and became king in 1523 (his uprising began in 1521).

q: Most of the powers of the Swedish monarchy died with Gustaf VI Adolf who had two major interests in life besides his country: archeology and this science.

q.e: King Gustaf VI Adolf (1882-1973) was an archaeologist and also a keen botanist, with a famous rhododendron collection.

q: Frederick I Barbarossa, who was crowned Holy Roman Emperor in 1155, belonged to what royal dynasty?

q.e: Frederick Barbarossa was a Hohenstaufen, from the Swabian dynasty that held the Holy Roman throne in the 12th and 13th centuries.

q: Who was sworn in as the 13th President on July 10, 1850 following the death of President Zachary Taylor?

q.e: Millard Fillmore was Zachary Taylor's vice president and took the oath of office after Taylor died unexpectedly from a stomach ailment only 16 months into his term.

q: What is the term for the person who was usually the master of the Japanese samurai?

q.e: A daimyo was a powerful feudal lord who commanded samurai. The shogun was above the daimyo.

q: What marine reptiles evolved during the Triassic period and thrived during much of the Mesozoic era?

q.e: Ichthyosaurs ("fish lizards") were dolphin-shaped marine reptiles from the Triassic until the Cretaceous.

q: Which of the following was a large inland sea that covered much of central North America during the Late Cretaceous period?

q.e: The Western Interior Seaway split North America in two in the Late Cretaceous, from the Arctic to the Gulf of Mexico.

q: The Erie Canal is a canal in New York State, United States, that runs from the Hudson River to Lake Erie, connecting the Great Lakes with the Atlantic Ocean. The entire canal was opened in which year?

q.e: Construction on the 363-mile canal began in 1817 and was completed in October 1825, opening a vital trade route between Buffalo on Lake Erie and Albany on the Hudson River.

q: This significant battle on the WW II Eastern front is largely regarded as the largest armed conflict of all time.

q.e: Fought in July and August 1943, the Battle of Kursk involved roughly 2 million troops, over 6,000 tanks, and about 4,000 aircraft, making it the largest tank battle and single clash in military history.

q: What 1945 conference considered the final plans for the defeat of Germany and postwar Europe?

q.e: Held in February 1945 in Crimea, the Yalta Conference brought together Franklin D. Roosevelt, Winston Churchill, and Joseph Stalin to shape the post-World War II order. The Potsdam Conference followed later in July 1945 after Germany had surrendered.

q: What ancient Greek vessel was used to mix wine and water?

q.e: A krater was a large vessel used to mix wine with water at Greek symposia. The Greeks rarely drank wine undiluted.

q: What was the name of the ancient Greek wrestling school, which was later used for delivering lectures and conducting intellectual conversations?

q.e: The palaestra was an ancient Greek wrestling school and part of the gymnasium. Philosophers also taught there.

q: This ancient Greek, despite having a speech impediment, was one of the greatest orators in his time.

q.e: According to ancient accounts by Plutarch, Demosthenes overcame a speech impediment and weak voice by practicing speaking with pebbles in his mouth and shouting above crashing ocean waves.

q: This ancient Greek playwright was the earliest of the three classical Greek tragedians, the other two being Sophocles and Euripides.

q.e: Born around 525 BC, Aeschylus is often called the father of tragedy because he introduced a second actor, allowing for true dialogue rather than just exchanges with the chorus.

q: The 1998 film, Theres Something About Mary, helped make this model turned actress one of the highest paid actresses in Hollywood. Who said Is that ...is that hair gel?

q.e: In There's Something About Mary (1998), Cameron Diaz's Mary has the famous "hair gel" scene. It made her one of Hollywood's best-paid actresses.

q: This world famous haute couture designer moved to Miami when he was selected as the costume designer for Miami Vice. What designer was gunned down outside his house by spree killer Andrew Cunanan?

q.e: Gianni Versace was murdered outside his Miami Beach home in 1997 by serial killer Andrew Cunanan.

q: Always a bridesmaid and never a bride. No more! What daytime soap actress won an Emmy for her role as Erica Kane on her 19th try?

q.e: Susan Lucci, playing Erica Kane on All My Children, won her first Daytime Emmy in 1999 after 18 earlier losses.

q: The First Indochina War came to a dramatic and unexpected end when over 7,000 French soldiers were killed at which small Vietnamese village?

q.e: The French lost the battle at Dien Bien Phu in May 1954. This ended the First Indochina War, and the Geneva Accords split Vietnam.

q: The Cold war, which began in 1947 was a consequence of World War II. Who were the leaders of the two superpowers (The USA and the Soviet Union) at the beginning of the Cold War?

q.e: Harry S. Truman was US President and Joseph Stalin led the Soviet Union when geopolitical tensions solidified into the Cold War around 1947 with the announcement of the Truman Doctrine.

q: People Magazine named a 2007 Star of the Year. This star is the new face of Versace, plays around with a Grand-Am race car and became the father of two. Who is this Prince Charming?

q.e: Patrick Dempsey, of Grey's Anatomy ("McDreamy"), was People's "Star of the Year" in 2007. He also races cars.

q: What gentleman made the cover of Details Magazine and was ranked # 7 as a Good Father in Details Magazines 50 Most Influential Men Under 45?

q.e: Kevin Federline, Britney Spears's ex-husband, appeared on the cover of Details in 2007.

q: Time Magazine made a list of The Ten Best Buzzwords of 2007. The #1 Buzzword was a noun meaning an older woman who romantically pursues younger men. What was Time Magazines # 1 Buzzword in 2007?

q.e: "Cougar" was Time's top buzzword of 2007 in the sense of an older woman pursuing younger men. It was also a big word in TV and film.

q: Together at last! Late Show with David Letterman won the # 1 spot in The 10 Best TV Ads. Long thought to be estranged, what billionaire is Dave cuddling up with to cheer on their respective football teams.

q.e: David Letterman and Oprah Winfrey appeared together in a Super Bowl XLI commercial in 2007, ending their long feud.

q: Where did an FBI investigator argue futilely with his bosses a month before 9/11, by saying: Im trying to keep someone from taking a plane and crashing into the World Trade Center.?

q.e: In August 2001 a Minneapolis FBI agent warned headquarters about Zacarias Moussaoui, and said he feared he would crash a plane into the World Trade Center.

q: In the morning of September 17, 1976 the Shuttle manufacturer treated the world to a glimpse of the future; a test model of the orbiter, one not intended for space flight, rolled out of their Palmdale, CA plant. What name had the designers given this model?

q.e: Originally planned to be named Constitution, the orbiter was renamed Enterprise after a massive letter-writing campaign by Star Trek fans.

q: Space Shuttles are transported to the launch pad on this slow-moving 6,000,000 pound (approx. 2,725,000 kg) vehicle. Fully loaded, it moves at a rate of 1 mph.

q.e: The Crawler-Transporter moves the shuttle stack from the Vehicle Assembly Building to the pad at 1 mph. It was first built for Apollo.

q: During the days spent in orbit, the astronauts of Columbias last mission conducted dozens of experiments dedicated to improving life on Earth. Exactly how many days did the astronauts spend in orbit?

q.e: Columbia's final mission (STS-107) lasted about 16 days, from 16 January to 1 February 2003, and all seven crew died on re-entry.

q: On February 1, 2003 at 9:29am flight director Leroy Cain declared a contingency and asked Bill Foster, who was working ground control that day, to lock the doors. Contingency is a NASA term which meant this.
Personnel had to work overtime till communication was restored

q.e: When Flight Director Leroy Cain declared a "contingency," it meant the shuttle was lost, and the doors of Mission Control were locked to preserve data.

q: At what battle of the American Civil War did Generals U.S. Grant, William T. Sherman, George H. Thomas, and Joseph Hooker all fight at once?

q.e: Grant, Sherman, Thomas and Hooker all fought at the Battles for Chattanooga in November 1863, including Missionary Ridge and Lookout Mountain.

q: What Union naval ship sank Confederate raider CSS Alabama during the American Civil War?

q.e: USS Kearsarge sank the raider CSS Alabama off Cherbourg, France, on 19 June 1864.

q: In 1996, U.S. anti-terrorist investigators learned of an organization called al-Qaeda for the very first time from which one of the following?

q.e: In 1996 Jamal al-Fadl, a Sudanese defector and former al-Qaeda member, gave the US its first detailed insider information on al-Qaeda.

q: The first major act of terrorism attributed to bin Ladens al-Qaeda group was in 1998 when it blew up which of these?
U.S. embassies in Tanzania and Kenya
Khobar Towers housing complex in Dhahran, Saudi Arabia
a parking garage of the World Trade Center

q.e: In August 1998, al-Qaeda bombed the US embassies in Nairobi, Kenya and Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, killing more than 200 people.

q: How many al-Qaeda terrorists were involved in the near-destruction of the $1billion guided-missile destroyer USS Cole, which was protected by some 70 tons of armor shielding?

q.e: On 12 October 2000, two suicide bombers in a small boat blew a hole in USS Cole in Aden, Yemen, killing 17 US sailors.

q: Which of the following proved to be the greatest obstacle to saving lives in New York Citys 9/11 rescue efforts at the World Trade Center towers?

q.e: The FDNY's radios didn't work well in the Twin Towers on 9/11, so many firefighters didn't hear the evacuation orders.

q: In 1861 Italy was finally (largely) unified with Victor Emmanuel II assuming the title of King of Italy. Who became the first Prime Minister of Italy?

q.e: Camillo di Cavour, the architect of Italian unification, became Italy's first prime minister in March 1861. He died a few months later.

q: What happened at Prokhorovka on July 12th, 1943?
The biggest Tank batlle of WW II
The biggest infantry engagement of WW II

q.e: At Prokhorovka on 12 July 1943, during the Battle of Kursk, German and Soviet armor clashed in what is often called the largest tank battle of WWII, though some historians dispute the scale.

q: July 1969 will go into history as the month man first set foot on the Moon. However, in that same month and year another momentous event took place. Which event was that?
The Beatles give their last public performance
A coup in Libya brings to power Colonel Khadaffi

q.e: On 25 July 1969, Nixon announced the Nixon Doctrine in Guam: the US would help allies in Asia but expect them to handle their own defense.

q: In 1944 the Allies launched a very ambitious airborne and ground campaign into the Netherlands, codenamed Operation Market Garden. Who was in direct charge of the 1st British Airborne Division?

q.e: Major General Roy Urquhart commanded the 1st British Airborne Division at Arnhem in Operation Market Garden (September 1944).

q: What was the objective of Operation Hailstone that was launched in 1944 by the United States Navy?

q.e: Operation Hailstone (February 1944) was a US Navy carrier attack on Truk Lagoon, Japan's key Pacific base, sinking dozens of ships.

q: Who assassinated Robert F. Kennedy on June 5, 1968?

q.e: Sirhan Sirhan shot Robert F. Kennedy at the Ambassador Hotel in Los Angeles shortly after Kennedy's victory in the California primary. James Earl Ray assassinated Martin Luther King Jr. two months earlier in April 1968.

q: Who assassinated Austrian Archduke Franz Ferdinand and his wife on June 28, 1914?

q.e: Gavrilo Princip, a 19-year-old Bosnian Serb affiliated with the Black Hand movement, shot Archduke Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914, triggering the outbreak of World War I. Charles Guiteau assassinated U.S. President James A. Garfield in 1881.

q: In 1951 this famous actor was awarded a patent for the design of a blowout toy. He was very famous for his musical comedies.

q.e: Danny Kaye was granted a patent in 1951 for a blow-out toy. He was known for his musical comedies, like The Court Jester.

q: Which one of these people holds several patents for fishing lures?

q.e: Gary Burghoff, who played Radar in M*A*S*H, holds patents for fishing products and inventions.

q: Which musician holds a patent for an electronic device that helps a composer, a musician, or a conductor to interactively select parts of a musical score?

q.e: Harry Connick Jr. holds a patent for a system that lets musicians and conductors interact with digital scores.

q: Which one of the Pyramids of Giza has visibly retained its polished limestone casing at its apex?

q.e: The pyramid of Khafre still has some of its smooth Tura limestone casing at the top. Khufu's Great Pyramid lost almost all of it.

q: What American Idol winner was born on December 22, 1989 in Phoenix, Arizona?

q.e: Jordin Sparks, born 22 December 1989 in Phoenix, won American Idol season 6 (2007), the youngest winner at the time.

q: What ocean separated Laurentia from Baltica and Siberia during the Cambrian.

q.e: The Iapetus Ocean separated Laurentia from Baltica and Avalonia in the early Paleozoic. Its closure created the Appalachian-Caledonian mountains.

q: A historic site in Greeneville, Tennessee preserves the tailor shop and grave of which U.S. president?

q.e: The Andrew Johnson National Historic Site is in Greeneville, Tennessee, where Johnson ran a tailor shop. He is buried there.

q: In 1787, 1,100 farmers attacked an arsenal in Springfield, Massachusetts at the climax of which uprising?

q.e: Led by Revolutionary War veteran Daniel Shays, Shays' Rebellion was an armed uprising of indebted farmers protesting aggressive tax collection, which helped spur the drafting of the U.S. Constitution.

q: In 1990, this 5000 year old body was found in the Alps. Scientists discovered some tattoos on his leg which indicated that acupuncture was used as far back as the Copper-stone Age.

q.e: Ötzi the Iceman, found in 1991 in the Ötztal Alps, lived about 5,300 years ago. His 61 tattoos are on points used in acupuncture.

q: This man was known as the Mexican Robin Hood. He set up a band of 5 members, all with the same first name. His band is credited with stealing more than $100,000 in gold and over 100 horses.

q.e: Joaquín Murrieta was a legendary outlaw during the California Gold Rush. His gang was said to include several men named Joaquín.

q: On May 22, 1987, a multiple vortex tornado devastated this small Texas town.

q.e: The Saragosa, Texas, tornado of 22 May 1987 killed 30 people and destroyed about 85% of the town.

q: Which of these 1960s famous hippie gatherings did not take place in San Francisco?

q.e: Nambassa was a hippie festival held in New Zealand in the late 1970s and early 1980s, not in San Francisco.

q: The Battle of Uji, the Battle of Dan-no-ura, and the Battle of Muroyama were all fought during this war.
Wars of Sengoku Period in Japan

q.e: The Genpei War (1180-85) between the Taira and Minamoto clans in Japan featured the battles of Uji and Dan-no-ura. The Minamoto won, and Yoritomo became the first shogun.

q: Who is widely recognized as the leader of the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising during WW II?

q.e: Mordechai Anielewicz led the Jewish Combat Organization in the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising (April-May 1943) and died in the fighting.

q: His first film role was The Kentuckian. His Broadway appearance in Neil Simons Odd Couple launched his career, but many remember him as one of the Grumpy Old Men. Who was this great actor?

q.e: Walter Matthau starred in The Odd Couple on Broadway (1965) and Grumpy Old Men (1993). The question has the spelling "Mattheau".

q: On November 8, 1843 this ship left Lisbon, Portugal, with 84 convicts and headed for Goa, India. Near Cape of Good Hope the ship was taken by a strong current and was driven too close to the shore. She then struck the reef off Muli Island in Mulaku Atoll.

q.e: The Portuguese ship Prazer e Allegria wrecked in the Maldives in 1843 while carrying convicts.

q: What Dutch city was repeatedly plundered by the Vikings?

q.e: Dorestad was a major Carolingian trading town on the Rhine that the Vikings raided repeatedly in the 9th century.

q: This Mameluke was Napoleons constant attendant.

q.e: Roustam Raza, a Mameluke, served as Napoleon's bodyguard and valet from 1799 to 1814.

q: This Renaissance figure of Polish origin was the first rector of what is today the Vilnius State University.

q.e: Piotr Skarga, a Polish Jesuit, was the first rector of the Vilnius Jesuit Academy (1579), which is now Vilnius University.

q: As samurai warriors were supposed to set a good example to those beneath them - they were bound by Bushido, a strict ethic code. Bushido means way of the warrior and one of its central points states that a samurai must be completely loyal towards this person.

q.e: Bushido required a samurai to be absolutely loyal to his lord, the daimyo. Death was preferred to dishonor.

q: In the Middle Ages, the most commonly used monetary system was based on Livre, Sou and Dernier. Which relation between them is correct?

q.e: In the medieval system, 1 livre = 20 sous = 240 deniers. It was similar to Britain's pounds, shillings and pence.

q: This chocolate flavored milk drink, test-marketed by Nestle in 2002, was an utter failure.

q.e: Choglit was a chocolate-flavored milk drink that Nestlé test-marketed in 2002. It flopped.

q: What is the only tank battle fought during the so called Winter War (1939-1940)?

q.e: The Battle of Honkaniemi (February 1940) was the only large tank battle of the Winter War, and the Finns won.

q: What effective submachine gun was also known as the Schmeisser?

q.e: The MP40 is often wrongly called the "Schmeisser", after designer Hugo Schmeisser, but it was designed by Heinrich Vollmer.
Alice Ghostley played the Bewitched maid Esmeralda, who sneezed and lost her spells. She played the part for years.
