q: Which of the following was NOT an order of Greek column?

q.e: Ostrakon (ostracism) is a piece of broken pottery used for voting in Athens, and not a column. The Greek orders are Doric, Ionic and Corinthian.

q: This 2003 movie won seven Razzies. It had an all-star cast that included Al Pacino, Lainie Kazan, Christopher Walken and a very hot couple. What is the name of this flop directed and written by Martin Brest?

q.e: Gigli (2003), starring Ben Affleck and Jennifer Lopez, won multiple Razzies. Martin Brest directed it.

q: This Broadway show with a book and lyrics by Ira Levin opened in 1965 after 11 previews and much rewriting. It starred Lesley Ann warren, Elliot Gould, Beth Howland, and Charles Durning. What was the name of this Victorian melodrama?

q.e: Drat! The Cat! (1965), Ira Levin's musical, flopped on Broadway, ran only 8 performances. It's about a Victorian jewel thief.

q: It could not miss. It was directed by the great Elaine May. It featured Charles Grodin, Isabelle Adjani, Tess Harper, Carol Kane, Jack Weston, and, oh yes, Dustin Hoffman and Warren Beatty. It was a total flop. What was the name of this comedy?

q.e: Ishtar (1987), directed by Elaine May and starring Warren Beatty and Dustin Hoffman, became known as a major box-office flop.

q: This Russian cosmonaut was likely to have been the third or fourth person in space, but was dismissed from the cosmonaut corps in 1963, because of drunkenness and disorderly behavior at Chkalovskiy station.

q.e: Grigori Nelyubov, a Soviet cosmonaut, was expelled in 1963 for drunk behavior at a train station. He died in 1966.

q: This island, captured by US forces in 1944, was close enough for B29 bombers to fly round trip to Japan. A major air base was built there from which many B29 bombing attacks were launched and the planes carrying the atomic bombs took off.

q.e: Tinian, in the Mariana Islands, was captured by US forces in 1944. The atomic bombs were launched from its North Field airbase.

q: Adolf Hitlers father, Alois, changed his last name to Hitler. What was his original last name?

q.e: Alois Hitler was born Alois Schicklgruber (his mother's name) and took the name Hiedler/Hitler in 1877.

q: This kingdom, the largest in the Late Intermediate period of the cultural history of Peru, was eventually conquered by the Inca Empire in 1493.

q.e: Chimor, the Chimú Kingdom with its capital Chan Chan on Peru's north coast, fell to the Inca around 1470.

q: From what is the English word Friday derived?
Free, as Friday used to be the day of rest
Friesland, a region in the Netherlands

q.e: Friday originates from Old English Frigedag, meaning the day of Frige (associated with the Norse goddess Frigg). It was adopted as a Germanic calque of the Latin dies Veneris, the day of Venus.

q: In 5th century AD, a child hostage exchange was arranged, to keep peace between the Huns and the Romans. Attila, future king of the Huns was sent to the Roman court in exchange for which Roman hostage?

q.e: Aetius had been a hostage with the Huns as a youth, and Attila was said to have been in Rome as an exchange hostage.

q: In 451, Flavius Aëtius, in alliance with the Visigoths, finally defeated Attila the Hun. Where did the famous battle take place?

q.e: Aetius and Theodoric I beat Attila at the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains (also called Châlons) in 451 in Gaul.

q: Who was in charge of the 1st Polish Independent Parachute Brigade during operation Market Garden?

q.e: Major General Stanisław Sosabowski commanded the Polish brigade at Arnhem. Montgomery blamed him for the failure of Market Garden.

q: Galleys undoubtedly revolutionized the War at Sea, the main reason being the far superior fire power over any other sea-going ship at the time. On October 7th, 1571 for the first time galleys were in the forefront of a major sea battle. Which battle was this?

q.e: The Battle of Lepanto (7 October 1571), a Holy League victory over the Ottoman fleet, was the last major naval battle with galleys.

q: In 1598 the Imjin war in Asia ended with a devestating defeat of the Japanese Navy by the Allied Korean and Chinese Navies, ending the Japanese invasion of Korea. In what battle was the Japanese fleet decisively defeated?

q.e: In the Imjin War (1592-98), Admiral Yi Sun-sin won a final victory at Noryang (December 1598), though he was killed.

q: What was the name of Caligulas pet horse?

q.e: Caligula's favorite horse, Incitatus, was said to have a marble stable and he reportedly planned to make it consul.

q: Which of the following was introduced by the Western Union Compnay in 1933?
Sending money across the country by wire.

q.e: Western Union launched the singing telegram in 1933, when a singer delivered a message by song. It was first used for the birthday of a customer.

q: Which of these landmarks would NOT be found on the Antietam battlefield?

q.e: Antietam has Bloody Lane, Burnside's Bridge and the Cornfield. The Peach Orchard is at Gettysburg.

q: Several hundred specimens of this species of dinosaur were discovered at Ghost Ranch.

q.e: Hundreds of Coelophysis bauri skeletons were found at Ghost Ranch, New Mexico, in 1947. It's New Mexico's state fossil.

q: Multicellular organisms evolved during what period of the Mesoproterozoic era?

q.e: The Ectasian period (1.4-1.2 billion years ago) of the Mesoproterozoic era is when the first multicellular organisms (some red algae) may have evolved.

q: Who are the two ancient Greek architects who designed the Parthenon, a temple regarded as one of the worlds greatest cultural monuments.

q.e: Ictinus and Callicrates designed the Parthenon (447-432 BC) under Pericles. Phidias directed the sculpture.

q: In the ancient Greek society, these women were high-class entertainers, much like the Japanese geisha.

q.e: Hetaerae were educated courtesans in ancient Greece, who attended symposia and were well-known. Aspasia was the most famous.

q: Many in Hollywood were nervous when this lady was arraigned on charges of pandering and tax evasion on August 9, 1993. Who was known as the Hollywood Madam or Madam to the Stars?

q.e: Heidi Fleiss, the "Hollywood Madam," was arrested in 1993 for running a prostitution ring. She served 20 months in prison.

q: In 1895, this German physicist invented the use of electromagnetic radiation to take images of bones and organs inside the human body, which later led to the invention of the X-Ray Machine.

q.e: Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays in November 1895, famously producing an image of his wife Anna Bertha's hand that clearly revealed her bones and wedding ring.

q: This western character actor was in the role of Deputy Jake in Support Your Local Sheriff with James Garner. Before his death on 20 October 2003, he often played the villain in westerns and openly said it was because of his lazy eye.

q.e: Jack Elam, who was famous for villains in Westerns, had a blind left eye, which gave him a menacing look. He died on 20 October 2003.

q: The most famous battle of the Hundred Years War between England and France resulted in a massive French army being defeated by a much smaller English army, led by King Henry V. Where did this battle take place?

q.e: The Battle of Agincourt was fought on Saint Crispin's Day, October 25, 1415, in northern France, where English longbowmen devastated a numerically superior French knight force.

q: On 18 February 1943, Joseph Goebbels gave a speech, aiming to persuade the Germans not to give up Nazi idealism. The speech was delivered in front of which building, located near Potzdamer Platz?

q.e: Goebbels gave his "Total War" speech at the Berlin Sportpalast on 18 February 1943, after the defeat at Stalingrad.

q: Winston Churchill made the following statement about the battle that occurred between October 23 and November 3, 1942: Now this is not the end, it is not even the beginning of the end. But it is, perhaps, the end of the beginning. Name the battle.

q.e: Churchill delivered this famous line at London's Mansion House in November 1942, celebrating Bernard Montgomery's victory over Erwin Rommel's forces in Egypt. The Allied triumph marked a major turning point in the North African Campaign.

q: The 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology and Medicine went to three men from Oxford University who played a significant role in the discovery and development of penicillin and its use as an antibiotic. Which of these scientists did not share this prize?

q.e: Alexander Fleming, Howard Florey and Ernst Chain won the 1945 Nobel Prize for penicillin. Paul Winchell was an American ventriloquist.

q: Ever since the Napoleonic wars, conscript troops were blamed for a lack of professionalism and could not be trusted. However, this changed at the 1866 battle at...?

q.e: At Königgrätz (Sadowa) in 1866, Prussia, using conscripts and the needle gun, defeated Austria in the Austro-Prussian War.

q: Between 1639 and 1858 Japan was largely isolated from the outside world. The port of Nagasaki was only open to Dutch and Chinese ships. In 1858 Commander Perry forced the Japanese Shogun to stop preventing trade. What was one of the results of this event?
A rise to power of the Shogunate
The loss of Nagasaki to a foreign power

q.e: Commodore Perry's 1853-54 expedition forced Japan to open to the West, and led to the Meiji Restoration of 1868.

q: This animal, which lived during the early Cambrian period, is possibly one of the first fish to evolve.

q.e: Haikouichthys, a small Cambrian fish-like creature from China (about 518 million years ago), is considered one of the earliest known vertebrates.

q: Which holiday is celebrated on December 25?

q.e: Christmas has been traditionally observed on December 25 to celebrate the nativity of Jesus since at least 336 AD during the Roman Empire.

q: On which holiday do kids go trick-or-treating?

q.e: Halloween is celebrated annually on October 31, rooted in the ancient Celtic festival of Samhain. Trick-or-treating became widely popular across North America during the 1930s and 1940s.

q: What do people often hunt for at Easter?

q.e: Easter egg hunts are a traditional springtime activity where children search for hidden dyed hard-boiled eggs or chocolate eggs, which symbolize new life and resurrection.

q: On which date is Valentine's Day?

q.e: Valentine's Day is celebrated on February 14, originally honoring Christian martyrs named Valentine. March 17 is St. Patrick's Day, and October 31 is Halloween.

q: Which country celebrates Boxing Day on December 26?

q.e: Boxing Day, December 26, is a public holiday in the United Kingdom and many Commonwealth countries, such as Canada and Australia. The name probably comes from the old custom of giving boxes of gifts or money to servants and tradespeople.

q: The October holiday Mexicans call Día de la Raza is celebrated in the U.S. as what?

q.e: In the United States, October 12 was long celebrated as Columbus Day. In Mexico and other Latin American countries it was called Día de la Raza ("Day of the Race"), marking the arrival of Columbus in 1492.

q: Sleep in heavenly peace is a line from which carol?

q.e: Silent Night' was originally written in German as 'Stille Nacht, heilige Nacht' in 1818 by Joseph Mohr and Franz Xaver Gruber in Austria, containing the translated line 'Sleep in heavenly peace'.

q: Orange and this color are the colors of the holiday Halloween.

q.e: Halloween's signature colors stem from the ancient Celtic festival of Samhain: orange symbolizes the autumn harvest and turning leaves, while black represents the "death" of summer and the onset of winter.

q: What day marks the start of Easter fasting in Eastern Christianity?

q.e: Clean Monday, the first day of Great Lent in Eastern Orthodox churches, falls 48 days before Orthodox Easter. In Greece it's a public holiday where people often fly kites and eat seafood and flatbread.

q: Samhainophobia is the fear of this holiday.

q.e: Samhainophobia is the fear of Halloween. It's named after Samhain, the Celtic festival on October 31 and November 1 from which Halloween comes.

q: This is the World Blindness Awareness Month, and Halloween is celebrated on its last day. It is also called Red because of the Russian revolution of 1917.

q.e: October is World Blindness Awareness Month, and Halloween is the last day of it. The Russian Revolution of 1917 took place in October by the old calendar, so it's called the "October Revolution" and its color is red.

q: What holiday was first celebrated on June 19, 1910?

q.e: The first Father's Day was celebrated on June 19, 1910, in Spokane, Washington, inspired by Sonora Smart Dodd, who wanted to honor her father. It became an official US holiday in 1972.

q: Which US state hosts a carrot festival in the town that calls itself Carrot Capital of the World?

q.e: Holtville, California, calls itself the "Carrot Capital of the World" and holds an annual Carrot Festival. The area's warm desert climate is ideal for growing carrots in winter.

q: In what country is the popular tomato festival called La Tomatina celebrated annually?

q.e: La Tomatina is held annually on the last Wednesday of August in the town of Bunol, near Valencia, Spain. Participants throw roughly 150 metric tons of overripe tomatoes at each other purely for entertainment.

q: In what Eastern Orthodox country is the holiday The Protection of the Mother of God celebrated as one of the most important events in the Christian calendar?

q.e: The Feast of the Protection of the Mother of God (Pokrov) is celebrated on October 14 in the Russian Orthodox Church. It honors a vision in which the Virgin Mary spread her veil over the faithful to protect them.

q: Columbus Day, a holiday first observed by the Tammany Society, is officially celebrated in the USA in which month?

q.e: Columbus Day has been celebrated as a US federal holiday on the second Monday of October since 1971, marking Christopher Columbus's arrival in the Americas on October 12, 1492.

q: The 3rd Monday in April is Patriots Day - a legal holiday in this state.

q.e: Patriots' Day commemorates the opening battles of the American Revolutionary War at Lexington and Concord in 1775. In Massachusetts, the holiday is famously marked by the annual running of the Boston Marathon.

q: In the United Kingdom, what holiday is December 26th?

q.e: Boxing Day is celebrated on December 26 across the United Kingdom and many Commonwealth nations. Historically, it was the day servants and tradespeople received gift boxes and bonuses from their employers.

q: The origins of the widespread tradition of decorating a Christmas tree can be traced back to the 16th century, in this country.

q.e: The tradition of setting up decorated evergreen trees indoors originated in modern Germany and Alsace during the 16th century, often attributed to Protestant reformer Martin Luther. It became popular internationally in the 19th century after Queen Victoria and Prince Albert embraced it in Britain.

q: Halloween is celebrated the day before this Holy Catholic day.

q.e: Halloween is a contraction of All Hallows' Eve, referring to the evening before All Hallows' Day, better known as All Saints' Day on November 1. It kicks off the triduum of Allhallowtide, dedicated to remembering the dead and saints.

q: In some parts of this country, Halloween is called Pooky Night.

q.e: In parts of Ireland, Halloween is linked to the púca, a mischievous shape-shifting spirit of Irish folklore, and in some places it is called "Pooka Night". Halloween itself began as the Celtic festival of Samhain.

q: What does to Christmas tree a test mean for students?
To fill in the answer sheet randomly
To get a very high score on an exam that you havent studied for
To get a very low score on an exam that you have studied for

q.e: To "Christmas tree" a test means to fill in the answer sheet randomly, so the pattern of marked bubbles looks like a decorated tree. It's student slang for guessing without reading the questions.

q: In the US, Loyalty Day is celebrated on May 1st with parades and ceremonies. It was first observed in the 1930s and was designed as a counterweight to this holiday.

q.e: Loyalty Day, observed on May 1 in the United States, began in the early 20th century as a patriotic alternative to May Day, which is associated with labor movements and socialism. It became an official holiday in 1958.

q: The Chinese New Year is the most important of all traditional Chinese holidays and is celebrated on this date.

q.e: Chinese New Year follows the lunar calendar, so its date changes every year, falling between January 21 and February 20. It begins on the new moon and the celebrations last about 15 days, ending with the Lantern Festival.

q: ANZAC Day is a public holiday celebrated on April 25th, in this country.

q.e: ANZAC Day, April 25, commemorates Australian and New Zealand soldiers who landed at Gallipoli in 1915. It is a public holiday in both countries.

q: What does the word Christmas mean?

q.e: Christmas is derived from the Old English Cristes Maesse, which means the Mass of Christ. It was first recorded in 1038 to designate the church service celebrating Jesus's birth.

q: Macys Thanksgiving Day Parade is held annually, every Thanksgiving Day, in this US city.

q.e: First staged in 1924, Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade winds through Manhattan in New York City, ending outside Macy's flagship store in Herald Square.

q: The Thanksgiving Day Parade held in this city is regarded as the nations first.

q.e: Philadelphia's Thanksgiving Day parade, which started in 1920, is regarded as the first in the US. It predates the Macy's parade in New York, which began in 1924.

q: The day after Thanksgiving Day is called this in the United States.

q.e: The term 'Black Friday' was originally popularized by Philadelphia police in the 1960s to describe the heavy traffic and massive pedestrian crowds the day after Thanksgiving.

q: Тhe first Thanksgiving celebration is said to have taken place in the autumn of 1619 in this US state.

q.e: An English settlers' thanksgiving service was held at Berkeley Plantation in Virginia on December 4, 1619, years before the Pilgrims' feast in Plymouth in 1621. Virginia still claims the first Thanksgiving.

q: Which was the first US state to declare Christmas a legal holiday?

q.e: Alabama was the first state to make Christmas a legal holiday, in 1836. Oklahoma was the last state to do so, in 1907, and it became a federal holiday in 1870.

q: Which of these was a traditional Christmas dinner in early England?

q.e: In early England, a boar's head or pig's head was a traditional Christmas feast centerpiece. The "Boar's Head Carol" is one of the oldest English carols still sung.

q: Sending these items for Christmas is considered bad manners in Japan.

q.e: In Japan, writing names in red ink is associated with death notices, so red is considered unlucky for personal cards. That's why people avoid sending red Christmas cards.

q: It is customary in this country to put an artificial spider and a web on the Christmas tree.

q.e: The Ukrainian tradition stems from the folk tale of the Christmas Spider, where a poor widow finds webs spun over her tree turned magically into gold and silver, bringing good fortune.

q: In what major European city was the first commercial Christmas card introduced?

q.e: Sir Henry Cole commissioned the very first commercial Christmas card in London in 1843, featuring artwork designed by John Callcott Horsley.

q: At Christmas, Christians in the tropical areas of this country decorate banana or mango trees .

q.e: In India, Christians sometimes decorate banana or mango trees at Christmas, since the traditional fir tree doesn't grow in the tropics. They also decorate their houses with mango leaves and oil lamps.

q: Where does the earliest evidence of Christmas celebrations come from?

q.e: By around 200 AD, Christian writers in Egypt were discussing the date of Jesus's birth, which is the earliest evidence of Christmas being considered. The first recorded celebration on December 25 was in Rome in 336 AD.

q: How many times is the name of Santa Claus used in The Night Before Christmas?

q.e: The poem "A Visit from St. Nicholas" (1823) never uses the name "Santa Claus"; it calls him St. Nicholas and St. Nick. It's usually credited to Clement Clarke Moore and shaped the modern image of Santa.

q: Where is the United States' official national Christmas tree located?
Kings Canyon National Park in California
Big Bend National Park in Texas

q.e: The General Grant Tree, a giant sequoia in Kings Canyon National Park, California, was declared the "Nation's Christmas Tree" in 1926. Every year a ceremony takes place there.

q: In South Africa, what season does Christmas occur in?

q.e: South Africa is in the Southern Hemisphere, so December is in the middle of summer. Christmas is often celebrated outdoors with barbecues and trips to the beach.

q: In this country, the new year begins between January 21 and February 21, at new moon.

q.e: The Chinese New Year starts on the second new moon after the winter solstice, which falls between January 21 and February 20. The date changes each year because the Chinese calendar is based on the moon.

q: In what country can the remains of St. Valentine be viewed every February 14?

q.e: Remains said to be those of St. Valentine are kept in the Whitefriar Street Carmelite Church in Dublin, Ireland, and are displayed there on his feast day. Pope Gregory XVI gave them to the church in 1836.

q: Which popular flower, native to Japan, is a symbol of the Easter holiday?

q.e: The Easter lily is native to the southern islands of Japan and became a symbol of Easter because its white trumpet-shaped flowers suggest purity and new life. It was first brought to the US in 1880s.

q: In the past, mostly what color did Orthodox Christians paint their Easter eggs on Holy Thursday?

q.e: Orthodox Christians traditionally dye Easter eggs red on Holy Thursday, the color representing the blood of Christ and the joy of new life. The first egg dyed is often kept for protection.

q: Which PA county is known as the Christmas Tree Capitol of the World?

q.e: Indiana County, Pennsylvania, is known as the "Christmas Tree Capital of the World" because of the large number of Christmas trees grown there. It's also home to Jimmy Stewart's hometown, Indiana, PA.

q: In which language Frohliche Weihnachten is wished on Christmas?

q.e: "Fröhliche Weihnachten" means Merry Christmas in German. Germany gave the world many Christmas traditions, including the decorated tree and Advent calendars.

q: The Urn of Fate is part of the traditional Christmas celebrations in what country?

q.e: In Italy, the Urn of Fate (Urna del Destino) is a Christmas game where guests draw numbered gifts from a large bowl or urn. It adds an element of surprise to the family party.

q: In which country was the traditional Christmas mistletoe hung up for the first time?

q.e: Hanging mistletoe at Christmas is an old tradition in England and northern Europe. The plant was sacred to Celtic druids and appears in the Norse myth in which Baldr was killed by a mistletoe dart.

q: According to the tradition, on Christmas Eve, Christians in this country go to church wearing a completely new outfit.

q.e: In Egypt, many Coptic Christians dress in new clothes for church services at Christmas. The Coptic Church celebrates Christmas on January 7.

q: In which country was the first Christmas stamp released?

q.e: Canada issued the world's first Christmas stamp in 1898, a map of the British Empire that bore the words "XMAS 1898". It was designed to promote the Imperial Penny Postage rate.

q: In which of the following countries is Christmas not considered a day for the family?

q.e: In Japan, Christmas is not a traditional family holiday, but rather a romantic one, similar to Valentine's Day, where couples go on dates. Many families also enjoy fried chicken from KFC for the occasion.

q: In which language Próspero año nuevo is used to wish Happy New Year?

q.e: "Próspero año nuevo" is how you wish someone a Happy New Year in Spanish. Spanish speakers also eat twelve grapes at midnight, one for each stroke of the clock.

q: Where in the Americas could you wish Happy New Year by saying Bonne année?

q.e: "Bonne année" is French for Happy New Year, and is heard in Quebec, Canada, where French is the main language. The new year is often celebrated with family gatherings.

q: In which part of Africa could you most likely hear Gelukkige nuwe jaar when a New Year celebrations start?

q.e: "Gelukkige nuwe jaar" is Afrikaans for Happy New Year and is heard in South Africa. Afrikaans developed from Dutch and is one of the country's official languages.

q: The New Year greeting, Bliadhna mhath ùr, could be used in which part of the UK?

q.e: "Bliadhna mhath ùr" is Scottish Gaelic for Happy New Year, heard in the Scottish Highlands and Islands. New Year, called Hogmanay, is one of Scotland's biggest celebrations.

q: In America, horror films are often released in October, to cash in on the Halloween season. In Japan, horror films are a staple of which season?

q.e: In Japan, horror stories and ghost films are linked to summer, partly because of Obon, a festival when the spirits of ancestors are believed to return. A chilling scare was also thought to cool people down in the heat.

q: Everyone in Vietnam celebrates their birthdays during what holiday?

q.e: During Tết Nguyên Đán, the Vietnamese Lunar New Year, everyone traditionally turns a year older regardless of their actual date of birth.

q: Of what origin is Sinterklaas, the basis of the mythical holiday figure of Santa Claus?

q.e: Sinterklaas is the Dutch traditional figure based on Saint Nicholas, whose annual feast is celebrated on the eve of December 5 in the Netherlands.

q: Which was the first US state to recognize Memorial Day as an official holiday?

q.e: New York was the first state to officially recognize Memorial Day, in 1873. Waterloo, New York, was officially named the birthplace of the holiday in 1966.

q: The name Valentine, which was very popular in Late Antiquity, is derived from the Latin word valens. What does it mean?

q.e: The name Valentine comes from the Latin word "valens", meaning strong or healthy. There were several early Christian saints with that name.

q: What is the name of the popular harvest festival celebrated in China close to the autumnal equinox?

q.e: The Moon Festival, also known as the Mid-Autumn Festival, is celebrated on the 15th day of the eighth lunar month when the moon is believed to be at its fullest and brightest, traditionally marked by eating mooncakes.

q: As part of Easter celebrations, Easter Fires are traditionally lit in what location?
Indoors, in front of a crucifix
On the Easter table, in the form of candles

q.e: Easter fires are traditionally lit outdoors in many parts of Europe, such as Germany and the Netherlands, to welcome spring and drive away winter. Some are lit on Holy Saturday, and the fire is blessed.

q: Who is presented with a live domestic turkey at the annual ceremony known as National Thanksgiving Turkey Presentation?
the winners of the NFL Thanksgiving Classic
the best performer at the Macys Thanksgiving Day Parade

q.e: The National Turkey Federation has formally presented a live domestic turkey to the U.S. President at the White House every year since Harry S. Truman's administration in 1947.

q: What color is traditionally worn on Saint Patricks Day, celebrated annually on March 17 as a public holiday in the Republic of Ireland?

q.e: Wearing green on St. Patrick's Day became popular during the 1798 Irish Rebellion, associating the color with Irish nationalism and shamrocks. Saint Patrick's original symbolic color was actually blue, seen on the Order of St. Patrick insignia.

q: The Midsummer holiday is associated with which event in the Christian calendar?

q.e: Midsummer, around June 24, is linked to the feast of the Nativity of John the Baptist in the Christian calendar. Bonfires and flower garlands are common in northern Europe.

q: In this country Christmas is celebrated during the summer holiday season.

q.e: Because Australia lies in the Southern Hemisphere, December falls in early summer, leading to holiday traditions that often feature outdoor barbecues and trips to the beach. Austria, Holland, and Mexico are all located in the Northern Hemisphere, where December is winter.

q: On Christmas Eve, children from this country leave their shoes by the fireplace to be filled with gifts from Pere Noel.

q.e: In France, children put their shoes by the fireplace on Christmas Eve, hoping Père Noël (Father Christmas) will fill them with gifts. Some also leave a carrot for his donkey.

q: In which of these countries is Christmas celebrated on 7 January?

q.e: Christmas falls on January 7 in the Russian Orthodox Church because it follows the old Julian calendar, which runs 13 days behind the Gregorian calendar. Russia made Christmas a public holiday again in 1991 after the Soviet era.

q: In this country the Christmas period is generally referred to as Navidad.

q.e: "Navidad" is the Spanish word for Christmas. It comes from the Latin word for nativity, and the holiday season in Spain lasts until Epiphany on January 6.

q: The first Saint Patricks Festival was held on 17 March 1996 in this country.

q.e: The first St. Patrick's Festival in Dublin was held in 1996, and it has grown into a multi-day celebration. March 17 is the traditional feast day of Ireland's patron saint.

q: In what country is the New Year celebration known as Hogmanay?

q.e: Hogmanay is the traditional Scottish celebration of the New Year, famously involving traditions like first-footing, where the first guest across the threshold brings gifts of coal or shortbread for good luck.

q: What type of fish is traditionally consumed smoked at Christmas in France?

q.e: In France, smoked salmon is a traditional Christmas appetizer. The holiday meal also often includes oysters, foie gras and a Yule log cake, the bûche de Noël.

q: What meat is traditionally consumed at Christmas in Mexico?

q.e: Turkey is a traditional Christmas dish in Mexico, often served with other dishes like tamales and bacalao. Mexicans also eat it on the Christmas Eve feast, called Nochebuena.

q: When do the people of the Dominican republic celebrate New Year's Day?

q.e: Dominicans celebrate New Year's Day on January 1, like most of the world. The night before, they hold a big feast and many wear new clothes for good luck.

q: Carols are popular Christmas songs, performed on Christmas day. What was the original meaning of the word carol?

q.e: "Carol" originally meant a circle dance with singing, from the Old French "carole". Only later did the word come to mean a Christmas song.

q: What nationality were the immigrants that brought versions of the Halloween tradition to North America during the 1840s?

q.e: Millions of Irish immigrants fled to the United States and Canada during the Great Famine in the 1840s, popularizing Samhain-derived traditions like carving jack-o'-lanterns.

q: What holiday observed in the US coincides with Thanksgiving Day in Canada?

q.e: Canadian Thanksgiving falls on the second Monday of October, the same day as Columbus Day in the United States. Canada's celebration is a harvest festival and is earlier because of the cooler climate.

q: Which holiday is known as the Festival of Lights in India?

q.e: Diwali derives from the Sanskrit word 'deepavali', which means row of lights, and is marked by the lighting of clay lamps known as diyas. Holi is India's famous spring festival of colors.

q: How many nights does Hanukkah last?

q.e: Hanukkah lasts for eight nights and days to commemorate the miracle of a one-day supply of consecrated oil burning for eight days in the Second Temple in Jerusalem.

q: Which festival is famous for throwing colored powder?

q.e: Holi, the Hindu spring festival celebrated predominantly in India and Nepal, is known as the Festival of Colors because participants throw brightly tinted powders called gulal at one another.

q: Which saint's day is celebrated on March 17?

q.e: Saint Patrick's Day is celebrated on March 17, the traditional date of his death in the late 5th century. Saint Nicholas is celebrated on December 6, and Saint Valentine on February 14.

q: Which U.S. holiday falls on the fourth Thursday of November?

q.e: Thanksgiving was codified by President Franklin D. Roosevelt in 1941 to permanently fall on the fourth Thursday of November. Memorial Day occurs on the last Monday of May, while Labor Day is celebrated on the first Monday of September.

q: What is the Muslim holy month of fasting called?

q.e: Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic calendar, observed by Muslims worldwide with fasting from dawn to sunset to commemorate the revelation of the Quran.

q: In the Low Countries, St. Nicholas arrives by boat from which country?

q.e: In Dutch and Flemish folklore, Sinterklaas is traditionally said to travel by steamboat from Spain to the Netherlands each November, a tradition popularized by Jan Schenkman's 1850 book.

q: Which 2 countries mark Anzac Day for those who fought at Gallipoli in WWI?

q.e: Observed on April 25 each year, Anzac Day commemorates the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps landing at Gallipoli, Turkey, in 1915 during World War I. It remains one of the most solemn national occasions in both nations.

q: What four words end the first two lines of this famous Christmas poem ? Twas the night before Christmas, when all through the house Not a creature was stirring, ___ ___ __ _____.

q.e: The line 'not even a mouse' completes the opening rhyme in Clement Clarke Moore's 1823 poem originally titled 'A Visit from St. Nicholas.'

q: In the British Overseas Territory of Bermuda, kite flying is not just a hobby, but also an important part of which holiday?

q.e: In Bermuda, flying handmade kites is an Easter tradition, especially on Good Friday. It's said to have started when a teacher used a kite to explain the Ascension.

q: Which Chinese character is used in Chinese New Year decorations and is often placed upside-down on the front door of a house?
Fu - Blessing, Good Fortune, Good Luck

q.e: The character Fu (福), meaning blessing or good fortune, is often hung upside-down on doors at Chinese New Year. The word for "upside-down" sounds like the word for "arrived", so it means good fortune has arrived.

q: What was the original name of the US federal holiday known as Memorial Day?

q.e: Memorial Day was originally known as Decoration Day, established in 1868 by General John A. Logan to decorate the graves of Civil War soldiers with flowers. Congress officially declared it Memorial Day and a federal holiday under the Uniform Monday Holiday Act in 1968.

q: What event is celebrated on the Christian holiday called Pentecost?
Descent of the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles
The baptism of Jesus in the Jordan River

q.e: Pentecost, 50 days after Easter, celebrates the descent of the Holy Spirit on Jesus's apostles. It's often called the birthday of the Christian Church.

q: What is the name of the Christian holiday on which the revelation of God in human form (Jesus Christ) is celebrated?

q.e: Epiphany, celebrated on January 6, marks the revelation of Jesus to the world, especially the visit of the Magi (Three Kings). In Eastern churches the same idea is celebrated as Theophany.

q: What does the Christian holiday Corpus Christi commemorate?
Incarnation of Jesus Christ in human form

q.e: Corpus Christi, Latin for "Body of Christ", is a Catholic feast that honors the Eucharist, the bread and wine in the Mass. It's held on the Thursday after Trinity Sunday.

q: Which of the following does the Christian holiday Assumption of Mary commemorate?
Visiting of Virgin Mary by Gabriel

q.e: The Assumption of Mary, celebrated by Catholics and Orthodox on August 15, marks the belief that Mary was taken body and soul into heaven at the end of her life. It's a major feast day in many countries.

q: What meals are typically eaten during the celebrations of the Channukah holiday?

q.e: Foods fried in oil, such as potato latkes and jelly-filled doughnuts called sufganiyot, are traditionally eaten during Hanukkah to commemorate the miracle of the oil burning for eight days.

q: Christmas is the Christian holiday that celebrates the birth of Christ. Christ was born in this city, according to the Bible.

q.e: According to the Gospels of Matthew and Luke, Jesus was born in Bethlehem in Judea. Nazareth was where Mary and Joseph lived and where Jesus spent his childhood.

q: Finish the popular Christmas carol: Silent night Holy night All is calm all is bright Round yon virgin Mother and Child Holy infant ...

q.e: "Silent Night" was first performed on Christmas Eve 1818 in Oberndorf, Austria, with words by priest Joseph Mohr and music by Franz Xaver Gruber. It has been translated into hundreds of languages.

q: For Catholics, Protestants and most Orthodox Christians, the 25th of December is celebrated as Christmas. However, the Jerusalem, Russian, Coptic, Serbian and Georgian Orthodox churches celebrate the birth of Jesus on this date.

q.e: Several Orthodox churches still follow the old Julian calendar, so their December 25 falls on January 7 of the Gregorian calendar. Christmas is celebrated on that date in Russia, Serbia, Georgia and Egypt's Coptic Church.

q: The burning of the Yule Log is one of many Christmas traditions that come from the Yule festival. Do you know what this tradition symbolizes?

q.e: The Yule log tradition comes from ancient winter solstice festivals, and the fire symbolizes the return of light and warmth as the days begin to lengthen. The log was burned for the 12 days of Christmas.

q: On Halloween, children go door-to-door and yell trick-or-threat. However, in Scotland it is likely to hear children saying this.
The sky is blue, the grass is green, may we have our Halloween.
My eyes are blue, your house is too, my baskets green, may I have my Halloween.
I can smell something sweet around here.

q.e: In Scotland, children go "guising" on Halloween, performing a song, joke or poem in return for treats instead of just demanding them. This is an older version of trick-or-treating.

q: Many Protestant denominations celebrate this holiday on October 31 and some of them even meld it with Halloween.

q.e: Reformation Day, October 31, marks the day in 1517 when Martin Luther is said to have posted his 95 Theses in Wittenberg. Many Protestant churches celebrate it, sometimes together with Halloween.

q: Christian Nativity scenes are very popular during the Christmas holidays. However, a life-sized Nativity scene is on permanent display in Piazza San Pietro, in this city.

q.e: A life-sized Nativity scene is set up in St. Peter's Square in Vatican City every Christmas season, next to a giant Christmas tree. It's usually unveiled on Christmas Eve.

q: On Christmas Day in 1818, this famous carol which has since been translated in more than 300 languages, was performed for the first time, in Austria.
Angels We Have Heard On High

q.e: Silent Night (Stille Nacht) was composed by Franz Xaver Gruber with lyrics by Joseph Mohr and was first performed at St. Nicholas church in Oberndorf, Austria. Jingle Bells, by contrast, was written by James Lord Pierpont in the United States in the 1850s.

q: On what United States holiday are small versions of the flag placed by war memorials and next to graves of U.S. war dead?

q.e: Memorial Day is observed on the last Monday of May to honor fallen military service members, when volunteers place flags at graves in national cemeteries.

q: If you go to New York City, you might hear about Macys Day, another name for this Federal Holiday.

q.e: Thanksgiving is sometimes called "Macy's Day" in New York because of the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, held every year since 1924. It's known for its giant character balloons.

q: Every year on 14 July, France celebrates its national holiday, Fete Nationale, widely known as this.

q.e: English speakers know the holiday as Bastille Day, which commemorates the Storming of the Bastille on July 14, 1789, as well as the Fête de la Fédération held on the same date in 1790.

q: What is the origin of the tradition of putting Christmas presents in stockings?
St. Nicholas put some gold coins in stockings of three poor girls.
Santa Claus gives the dwarfs stockings every Christmas.
The Magi brought Jesus gifts in stockings.
The elves put fruit and candies in all childrens stockings.

q.e: The Christmas stocking tradition goes back to St. Nicholas, who is said to have secretly tossed gold coins through a window to save three poor sisters from hardship. The coins landed in stockings drying by the fire.

q: Every year, this country traditionally presents a Christmas tree to the London citizens to express appreciation for the British support during World War II.

q.e: Since 1947, the city of Oslo has gifted a large Norwegian spruce to London every year to stand in Trafalgar Square, thanking Britain for its alliance in World War II.

q: In 1970, a group labeled the United Native Americans of New England started a protest that is held annually on Thanksgiving Day and is called this.

q.e: Since 1970, the United American Indians of New England have held a National Day of Mourning on Thanksgiving Day at Plymouth, Massachusetts. It remembers the suffering of Native Americans after European settlement.

q: Turducken is sometimes served in place of the Thanksgiving turkey. Do you know what it is?
A turkey stuffed with a duck stuffed with a chicken
White cabbage fermented by Lactobacillus bacteria

q.e: Turducken is a portmanteau for a deboned chicken stuffed inside a deboned duck, which is then stuffed inside a deboned turkey, a dish popularized in Louisiana.

q: The roasted turkey is a traditional meal on Thanksgiving Day in the US and Canada. It is also a traditional meal on this holiday in the United Kingdom.

q.e: Roast turkey is a traditional Christmas dinner in the United Kingdom, and it became widespread in the Victorian era. Before that, goose and beef were more common.

q: People in which country used to decorate Christmas trees with artificial roses and set them on fire?

q.e: In Estonia, one of the earliest recorded Christmas trees was in Tallinn in 1441, set up by the Brotherhood of Blackheads. Legend says the tree was decorated with roses and burned at the end of the festivities.

q: Composed in 1857 by James Pierpont, this is the original name of the popular Christmas song, Jingle Bells.

q.e: James Lord Pierpont published the song in 1857 under the copyright title 'The One Horse Open Sleigh'. It was republished two years later in 1859 with the more familiar title 'Jingle Bells'.

q: Choose the correct words to complete the verse: He sprang to his sleigh, to his team gave a whistle, And away they all flew like the down of a thistle. But I heard him exclaim, ere he drove out of sight, Happy Christmas to all, ___ __ ___ _ ____ _____.!!
and to all a good night !!
hope I didnt give you a fright !!
may you sleep nice and tight !!
hope your clothes fit just right !!

q.e: "A Visit from St. Nicholas", written in 1823, is usually credited to Clement Clarke Moore. It is also known by its first line, "'Twas the Night Before Christmas", and it shaped the modern image of Santa.

q: According to The Twelve Days of Christmas, how many pipers piping did my true love give to me?

q.e: In the traditional carol, the eleventh day brings eleven pipers piping, followed by twelve drummers drumming on the final day.

q: If you received all of the gifts in the Twelve Days of Christmas, how many would you receive all together?

q.e: Because each gift is repeated on subsequent days, the total number of gifts corresponds to the 12th tetrahedral number, calculated by summing (13 - n) n for each day n, which equals exactly 364 items.

q: According to which calendar, decreed in 1582, does the new year begin on January 1?

q.e: Pope Gregory XIII introduced the Gregorian calendar via papal bull in October 1582 to correct inaccuracies in the older Julian calendar.

q: Each year, on January 1, a New Year concert takes place, presenting mostly music of the Strauss family, broadcast in over 40 countries. In which city does this concert take place?

q.e: The New Year's Concert is held every year in Vienna at the Musikverein by the Vienna Philharmonic Orchestra. It's known for the Strauss family's waltzes and polkas, and ends with the "Radetzky March".

q: This popular annual parade, which originated in 1890, takes place on New Year's Day in Pasadena, California.

q.e: The Tournament of Roses Parade was first staged in 1890 by Pasadena's Valley Hunt Club to showcase California's mild winter climate. It is traditionally followed by the Rose Bowl college football game.

q: In this country, New Year, called 'oshogatsu', is generally regarded as the most important public holiday. Homes and entrance gates are decorated with ornaments made of pine, bamboo and plum trees.

q.e: In Japan, oshōgatsu, the New Year, is the most important holiday of the year. Homes are decorated with kadomatsu (pine, bamboo and plum arrangements) to welcome the gods of the new year.

q: In the past St. Patricks Day was celebrated only as a strictly religious holiday. When did it become a public holiday?

q.e: St. Patrick's Day became an official public holiday in Ireland in 1903. Before that it was mainly a religious feast.

q: Easter is one of the most important religious holidays of the Christian liturgical year. What does Easter celebrate?
The revelation of God to humankind

q.e: In Christian tradition, Easter marks the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead on the third day following his crucifixion. The birth of Jesus is celebrated months earlier during Christmas.

q: In which language, spoken by native inhabitants of the US, does the following mean Merry Christmas and Happy New Year: Mele Kalikimaka me ka Hauʻoli Makahiki Hou?

q.e: Mele Kalikimaka me ka Hauʻoli Makahiki Hou is Hawaiian for "Merry Christmas and Happy New Year". Hawaiian is spoken by native Hawaiians and is one of Hawaii's two official languages.

q: The Julbukk, a small figure made of straw, is a common Christmas decoration in Sweden. What does the Julbukk resemble?

q.e: The Julbock (Yule goat) is a Scandinavian Christmas symbol, often made from straw and shaped like a goat. In Gävle, Sweden, a giant straw goat is erected each year and is often burned down by vandals.

q: In Greek folk tradition the malicious creatures called the Kallikantzaroi like to play bad pranks on people at Christmas time. Which of these is believed to be a way to drive them off?
Hanging a rabbits tail on the wall
Putting a lamb next to the Christmas tree

q.e: In Greek folklore, the Kallikantzaroi are goblins who emerge during the twelve days of Christmas. People drive them off by burning something that smells bad, like an old shoe, or by keeping a fire going.

q: How would you say Happy New Year during a party in Rio de Janeiro?

q.e: In Rio de Janeiro, Portuguese is spoken, so "Feliz Ano Novo" is the way to wish a Happy New Year. Many people wear white and watch fireworks on Copacabana Beach.

q: What Christmas song popularized the legend according to which Santa Claus categorizes children as naughty or nice?
Santa Claus Is Coming to Town
I Saw Mommy Kissing Santa Claus

q.e: Written by J. Fred Coots and Haven Gillespie in 1934, Santa Claus Is Comin' to Town introduced the famous lines about Santa making a list and checking it twice to find out who's naughty or nice.

q: The Flying Santa is a tradition that dates back to to Christmas Day of 1929. What does it involve?
dropping gifts from planes or helicopters
an air show featuring Santa Claus
a circus act featuring Santa Claus

q.e: The Flying Santa tradition began in 1929 in New England, when pilot Bill Wincapaw dropped gifts to lighthouse keepers and their families. It's still carried out by volunteers each year.

q: Halloween is typically linked to the ancient harvest festival of Samhain held on October 31–November 1. What is the origin of Samhain?

q.e: Samhain was an ancient Gaelic festival marking the end of the harvest season and the beginning of winter, observed across Celtic Ireland, Scotland, and the Isle of Man around November 1.

q: The Christian holiday Easter is linked to which big Jewish holiday?

q.e: According to the New Testament, the Last Supper was a Passover meal, which is why Easter's date is still tied to the lunar cycle and frequently coincides with the Jewish holiday.

q: The modern English word Easter is derived from which of the following?
The name of a pagan goddess
The name of a mythological beast

q.e: The word "Easter" probably comes from Eostre, an Old English name linked to a spring goddess mentioned by the monk Bede. The German word "Ostern" comes from the same root.

q: In Norway, there is a tradition of reading this type of books and watching this type of films around Easter.

q.e: In Norway, påskekrim, or "Easter crime", is a tradition of reading detective novels and watching crime shows during the Easter holiday. Publishers release new mysteries every spring, and TV schedules include them.

q: Who was the first European monarch to have turkey for Christmas according to popular history?

q.e: According to popular history, King Henry VIII was the first English monarch to enjoy turkey for Christmas dinner. Turkeys had been brought to Europe from the Americas in the 1500s.

q: What European city hosts the White Nights Festival, which culminates in the Scarlet Sails celebration?

q.e: St. Petersburg, Russia, hosts the White Nights Festival in summer, when the sky stays bright at night, and the Scarlet Sails celebration marks the end of the school year. Ships with red sails appear on the Neva river.

q: The first documented Thanksgiving ceremony in what was to become the USA took place in 1565 when a group of Spanish settlers held a mass for their safe delivery to the New World. What present day state did they land in?

q.e: The first recorded thanksgiving service in what's now the United States was held at St. Augustine, Florida, in 1565 by Spanish settlers under Pedro Menéndez de Avilés. It's about 56 years earlier than the Pilgrims' feast.

q: Joel Roberts Poinsett imported the popular decorative Christmas plants, poinsettias from this Central American country, where he worked as a US ambassador in the 19th century.

q.e: Joel Roberts Poinsett, the first US minister to Mexico, introduced the native Mexican plant Euphorbia pulcherrima to the United States in the late 1820s.

q: At Christmas, children usually put stockings or shoes by the fireplace, by the door or by the windowsill. In which country do children fill their shoes with hay and carrots for Santa's horse?

q.e: In the Netherlands, children leave shoes by the fireplace on St. Nicholas's Eve, filled with hay and carrots for Sinterklaas's horse. In the morning, they find treats or small gifts.

q: Which traditional Christmas plant is sometimes called the vampire plant?

q.e: Mistletoe is sometimes called the "vampire plant" because it's a parasite that attaches itself to a host tree and draws nutrients from it. Its berries are poisonous to humans.

q: According to ancient legends, the phrase Your Valentine, popular among lovers today, derived from St. Valentines expression of love for his sweetheart, shortly before he died. How did he express his love?

q.e: According to legend, St. Valentine wrote a note to the jailer's daughter, whom he had healed, and signed it "From your Valentine". That is thought to be the source of the Valentine's Day greeting.

q: In the United States, this holiday is the humorous and somewhat sarcastic alternative to St. Valentines Day, also celebrated on February 14, but by those without a significant other.

q.e: Singles Awareness Day, also called SAD, is a humorous alternative to Valentine's Day for people without a partner. It's celebrated on February 14.

q: This holiday is the Chinese equivalent of the Western, Saint Valentines Day.

q.e: The Qixi Festival, held on the seventh day of the seventh lunar month, is often called the Chinese Valentine's Day. It comes from the legend of the Cowherd and the Weaver Girl, two lovers who meet once a year.

q: In the USA, Black Friday, the day after Thanksgiving, is one of the busiest retail shopping days of the year. What neologism refers to the Monday immediately following Black Friday?

q.e: Cyber Monday was coined in 2005 by Ellen Davis and Scott Silverman of the National Retail Federation to encourage online shopping following Thanksgiving weekend. It quickly grew into one of the highest-grossing e-commerce days of the year.

q: The origins of Thanksgiving Day can be traced back to harvest festivals that have been celebrated since ancient times. What is the meaning of the Anglo-Saxon word from which the word 'harvest' is derived?

q.e: The word "harvest" comes from the Old English "hærfest", meaning autumn. Thanksgiving grew out of ancient autumn harvest festivals.

q: In which country did the Day of the Dead (Día de Muertos) begin?

q.e: Día de Muertos originated in Mexico, blending pre-Columbian Aztec traditions honoring Mictecacihuatl, queen of the underworld, with Catholic All Saints' and All Souls' Days.

q: What is the Jewish New Year called?

q.e: Rosh Hashanah, literally meaning head of the year, marks the Jewish civil New Year and occurs on the first day of Tishrei. Yom Kippur is the Day of Atonement, occurring nine days later.

q: Songkran, famous for water fights, is celebrated in which country?

q.e: Songkran marks the traditional New Year in Thailand, held every April, where water throwing symbolizes the washing away of sins and bad luck for the year ahead.

q: During the Christmas season in Newfoundland, homes are visited by a band of masked strangers. What are they called?

q.e: In Newfoundland and Labrador, mummers (also called "jannies") dress in disguises and visit homes during the Twelve Days of Christmas. Hosts try to guess who they are, and they get food and drink.

q: On the first day of which month do Jews celebrate New Year?

q.e: Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year, begins on the first day of Tishrei, usually in September or October. Tishrei is the seventh month of the Hebrew calendar, but it starts the year.

q: Jingle Bells, undoubtedly one of the most famous Christmas songs in the world, was written in 1857 by this person.

q.e: James Lord Pierpont composed and published the song in 1857 under its original title, One Horse Open Sleigh, originally intended for Thanksgiving rather than Christmas.

q: This city is the self-proclaimed Halloween Capital of the World.

q.e: Anoka, Minnesota, calls itself the "Halloween Capital of the World" and holds a big parade each year. It claims to have held the first Halloween celebration in the US in 1920.

q: In Celtic parts of western Brittany, the baking of kornigou is still used to proclaim the beginning of the winter season (which begins on the night of Halloween). Kornigou are cakes baked in the shape of this.

q.e: In Brittany, kornigou are cakes made in the shape of antlers or horns, baked to mark the start of winter. The word "kornigou" comes from the Breton for "little horn".

q: According to a popular Christmas story, the magical red nose of this flying reindeer provides light to guide Santa Clause through the darkness of Christmas Eve.

q.e: Rudolph was created in 1939 by Robert L. May for a booklet published by the Montgomery Ward department store. The character became a permanent fixture of Christmas culture after Johnny Marks adapted the tale into the hit 1949 song sung by Gene Autry.

q: According to some sources, the last one of the Twelve Days of Christmas falls on January 6. What major Christian holiday is celebrated on this date?

q.e: Epiphany commemorates the visit of the Magi, or Three Wise Men, to the baby Jesus and falls on January 6, officially concluding the traditional Twelve Days of Christmas.

q: Finish this popular Christmas song about Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer: All of the other reindeer Used to laugh and call him names They never let poor Rudolph ...

q.e: Written by Johnny Marks and popularized by Gene Autry in 1949, the song's lyric explains: 'They never let poor Rudolph / Join in any reindeer games.'

q: Christmas is believed to have originated from a pagan Roman festival. It lasted 7 days and included the winter solstice, which at that time fell on December 25. Which Roman god did this festival honor?

q.e: Saturnalia was an ancient Roman festival honoring Saturn, the god of agriculture, held in mid-December with banquets, gift-giving, and role reversals between masters and enslaved people.

q: It is obvious that vegetarians and vegans dont eat turkey on Thanksgiving day. This meal is a meatless imitation of turkey.

q.e: Tofurkey is a vegetarian "turkey" made from tofu and wheat protein, first sold in 1995. It's eaten at Thanksgiving by people who don't eat meat.

q: Complete these lyrics from the popular Easter song, Here Comes Peter Cottontail: Hes got jellybeans for Tommy, Colored eggs for sister Sue, Theres an orchid for your mommy And .........................................

q.e: "Here Comes Peter Cottontail" was a 1950 hit recorded by Gene Autry, and it became one of the best-known Easter songs. It was written by Steve Nelson and Jack Rollins.

q: How would you wish Merry Christmas to your French friend?

q.e: Joyeux Noel is the French phrase for Merry Christmas. Buon Natale is Italian, Frohliche Weihnachten is German, and Glaedelig Jul is Danish.

q: Which greeting means Happy New Year in Hebrew?

q.e: "Shanah Tovah" means "a good year" in Hebrew and is used to wish people a Happy New Year, especially on Rosh Hashanah. It is often said in full as "Shanah Tovah Umetukah", a good and sweet year.

q: What nocturnal omnivorous animal is an Australian alternative to the Easter Bunny?

q.e: The Easter Bilby campaign was launched in Australia during the 1990s to raise awareness and funds for the endangered native marsupial, as feral rabbits are considered an invasive pest.

q: The festival of San Fermín, which includes the famous running of the bulls event, is held in this Spanish city.

q.e: The festival takes place every July in Pamplona, Navarre, where participants run in front of a herd of fighting bulls along an 875-meter route to the bullring.

q: Which festival is NOT correctly matched with the country where it is held?
Día de los Muertos (Day of the Dead) - Mexico

q.e: La Tomatina, a giant tomato fight, takes place in Buñol, Spain, on the last Wednesday of August, not in Brazil. Thousands of people throw tomatoes at each other for about an hour.

q: Franksgiving is a portmanteau word coined by Atlantic City mayor Thomas Taggart to deride a Thanksgiving Holiday which was held a week earlier than usual. The term was derived from the name of what famous person?

q.e: "Franksgiving" refers to Franklin D. Roosevelt, who moved Thanksgiving a week earlier in 1939 to lengthen the Christmas shopping season. Many people were angry, and Congress fixed the date as the fourth Thursday in 1941.

q: Buy Nothing Day is an international day of protest against consumerism, typically observed on the Friday after American Thanksgiving in North America and on the following day internationally. Where was the first Buy Nothing Day organized?

q.e: Buy Nothing Day began in Vancouver, Canada, in 1992, started by artist Ted Dave and later promoted by the Adbusters magazine. It encourages people to avoid shopping for a day.

q: Which of these is another name for the cornucopia, the symbol of plenty that came to be associated with Thanksgiving and the harvest?

q.e: The cornucopia is also called the Horn of Amalthea, after the goat that nursed Zeus. According to myth, one of its horns broke off and became a horn of endless plenty.

q: Although St. Valentines Day was declared a Church holiday as early as 496, it was not until the 14th century, in medieval England and France, that it was associated with romantic love. What was believed to occur on February 14th, to cause this association?
Wild animals started their search for a mate.

q.e: By the 14th century, people in England and France believed that birds began choosing their mates on February 14, which linked the date with romantic love. The English poet Chaucer wrote about it in the 1380s.

q: Saint Valentine, a kind-hearted priest who according to legends lived in Rome during the third century AD, was sentenced to death, as he disobeyed the orders of which Roman emperor?

q.e: According to legend, St. Valentine disobeyed Emperor Claudius II by secretly marrying couples when the emperor had banned marriage for young soldiers. He was executed around 269 AD.

q: What Native American tribe is said to have celebrated with the colonists the 1621 harvest festival, known as the First Thanksgiving Day�?

q.e: Around 90 Wampanoag people, led by Ousamequin (Massasoit), joined the Pilgrims at Plymouth in autumn 1621 for a three-day feast marking a successful harvest.

q: Which holiday marks the end of Ramadan?

q.e: Eid al-Fitr translates to 'festival of breaking the fast' and marks the end of the dawn-to-sunset fasting month of Ramadan on the first day of Shawwal. Eid al-Adha, the 'festival of the sacrifice', occurs later during the annual Hajj pilgrimage.

q: Nowruz, the Persian New Year, begins on which kind of day?

q.e: Nowruz marks the first day of Farvardin in the Solar Hijri calendar and occurs at the exact astronomical moment of the vernal equinox, usually around March 20 or 21.

q: What traditional Scottish dish is served during a Burns Supper?

q.e: Haggis is the centerpiece of a Burns Supper, held annually around January 25 to celebrate Scottish poet Robert Burns. Burns famously addressed the dish as the Great chieftain o the puddin-race in a 1786 poem.

q: Christmas, a Christian holiday celebrated all over the world, is known under what name in the Netherlands?

q.e: In the Netherlands, Christmas is called "Kerstmis". The Dutch also celebrate Sinterklaas on December 5 as a big gift-giving holiday.

q: Which term refers to an Easter egg, decorated by the written-wax batik method?

q.e: A pysanka is a Ukrainian Easter egg decorated using the wax-resist, or batik, method, where designs are drawn in beeswax and then the egg is dyed. The word comes from the verb "to write".

q: How would you wish Merry Christmas in Scottish Gaelic?

q.e: "Nollaig Chridheil" is Merry Christmas in Scottish Gaelic. The Irish equivalent is "Nollaig Shona".

q: Samhain is one of the eight annual Sabbats (holidays) of Wiccans and is a celebration of darkness and death. Wiccans have a festival at the beginning of the Summer season to celebrate life and fertility, what is its name?

q.e: Beltane, celebrated around May 1, is the Celtic and Wiccan festival marking the start of summer, with fire, fertility and flowers. It's often paired with Samhain, which marks the start of winter.

q: Which of these greetings in different languages is more proper for Christmas than for New Year?

q.e: "Wesołych Świąt" is Polish for "Merry holidays" or Merry Christmas, and it's used at Christmas. To wish someone Happy New Year in Polish you say "Szczęśliwego Nowego Roku".

q: Which of these winter holiday gift-bringers is NOT a kid?

q.e: The Weihnachtsmann is the German version of Santa Claus, an old man with a beard. The Christkind, by contrast, is a child-like angel who brings gifts in parts of Germany and Austria.

q: Which organ pumps blood around the body?

q.e: The heart beats about 100,000 times a day, pumping around 2,000 gallons (about 7,500 liters) of blood through the body's circulatory network.
The lungs take in oxygen during inhalation and expel carbon dioxide during exhalation, processing roughly 2,000 gallons of air each day.

q: How many fingers are on two hands, counting thumbs?

q.e: In standard anatomical counting, a human hand has five digits consisting of four fingers and one thumb, yielding 10 total across two hands.

q: Which body part do you use to taste?

q.e: The tongue is covered with thousands of tiny bumps called papillae, which house the taste buds responsible for detecting sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami flavors.
The pancreas makes insulin, a hormone that helps cells take up sugar from the blood. When it doesn't work properly, diabetes can result.

q: Which sex chromosome is inherited only from the father?

q.e: Human mothers contribute an X chromosome through their egg cells, while sperm can carry either an X or a Y chromosome. Inheriting the father's Y chromosome typically determines male biological sex.

q: This heavy metal has the symbol Pb. It is a poisonous neurotoxin that can cause brain and blood disorders.

q.e: Lead takes its chemical symbol Pb from the Latin word 'plumbum', which is also the root for the English word 'plumbing'.

q: The pink ribbon is associated with raising awareness for what disease?

q.e: The pink ribbon was popularized by Charlotte Haley in the early 1990s (originally as peach-colored) and soon adopted in pink by Susan G. Komen and the Estée Lauder Companies. A red ribbon, by contrast, symbolizes HIV/AIDS awareness.

q: In the treatment of what serious disease is the isotope gold-198 used?

q.e: Gold-198 is a radioactive isotope that has been used in cancer treatment, for example as small implanted seeds that deliver radiation to a tumor. It decays quickly, so its effect is short-lived.

q: What bird can be associated with the infectious disease Varicella?

q.e: The varicella-zoster virus causes the highly contagious disease chickenpox, which typically produces an itchy, blister-like rash.

q: How often can a healthy adult donate blood?

q.e: In the United States, a healthy adult can donate whole blood about every 8 weeks (56 days). The wait gives the body time to replace the red blood cells and iron.

q: Of the 8 major blood types, which is the most common?

q.e: O-positive is the most common blood type worldwide, found in roughly 37% to 39% of the global population. AB-negative is generally the rarest of the eight major types.

q: The outbreak of what deadly disease is often referred to as Black Death?

q.e: The Black Death was a devastating bubonic plague pandemic caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis that swept through Eurasia and North Africa between 1346 and 1353. It wiped out an estimated 30% to 60% of the European population.

q: Which vitamin is the orange pigment beta-carotene converted to by the human body?

q.e: Beta-carotene is a provitamin A carotenoid that the human body cleaves into retinol, the active form of vitamin A, in the small intestine. This nutrient is essential for maintaining healthy vision and immune function.

q: According to some studies, lycopene, which is found in tomatoes, prevents this disease.

q.e: Lycopene, the red pigment in tomatoes, is an antioxidant that has been linked in some studies to a lower risk of certain cancers, particularly prostate cancer. The evidence is mixed, so it's not a proven preventive.

q: Animal liver is very rich in this health-beneficial mineral, as well as in vitamin A.

q.e: Liver is a very rich source of iron and vitamin A, which is why it has long been recommended for people with anemia. Too much vitamin A can be harmful, so it is best eaten in moderation.

q: What vitamin is the Garden strawberry a rich source of?

q.e: Strawberries are an excellent source of vitamin C, with a cup providing more than most people's daily needs. They also have fiber and antioxidants.

q: Paprika, and chili peppers in general, are very high in this essential vitamin.

q.e: Chili peppers and paprika are high in vitamin C, and a single red chili has more than an orange by weight. Vitamin C helps the body make collagen and fight infection.

q: What vitamin are lychee fruits rich in?

q.e: Lychees are rich in vitamin C, with a handful providing much of a day's needs. The fruit originated in southern China.

q: This is the vitamin that vegetarians should take, as it is not found in plants.

q.e: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) is produced almost exclusively by microorganisms and is not naturally found in plant foods, making fortified foods or supplements necessary for strict vegetarians and vegans. Vitamins A, C, and E are abundantly available from plant sources like carrots, citrus, and nuts.

q: Rose hips, the fruit of the rose plant, are rich in what vitamin?

q.e: Rose hips, the small red fruit of the rose plant, are one of the richest plant sources of vitamin C. In World War II, Britain made rose hip syrup to replace imported citrus fruit.

q: What essential vitamin is supplied through the consumption of carrots?

q.e: Carrots are rich in beta-carotene, an orange pigment and provitamin that the human body efficiently converts into active vitamin A (retinol), essential for vision and immune health.

q: What important vitamin does asparagus contain?

q.e: Asparagus is a good source of vitamin B9, or folate, which the body needs to make DNA and new cells. It is especially important during pregnancy.

q: Sigmund Freud, who was a heavy cigar smoker, developed this disease.

q.e: Sigmund Freud smoked about 20 cigars a day, and he developed cancer of the mouth and jaw, which led to dozens of operations before he died in 1939. He kept smoking despite the warnings of his doctors.

q: The medical term cardio, deriving from a Greek word, refers to which organ of the human body?

q.e: Cardio comes from the ancient Greek word kardia, meaning heart. Medical terms like cardiology (the study of heart diseases) and cardiovascular system rely on this root.

q: Erythrocytes are a type of blood cells, consisting mainly of hemoglobin. What does the word erythro mean?

q.e: The prefix erythro comes from the Ancient Greek word erythros, meaning red, while cyte comes from kytos, meaning hollow vessel or cell. In contrast, white blood cells are called leukocytes, derived from leukos, meaning white.

q: Your physician has ordered an electroencephalogram (EEG), the graphic recording of the electrical activity of what organ?

q.e: An electroencephalogram (EEG) measures electrical activity across the brain using small electrodes attached to the scalp. An electrocardiogram (ECG or EKG) measures heart activity, while an electromyogram (EMG) evaluates muscles.

q: The term encephalon, defined as the brain of a vertebrate, derives from a Greek word which means what?

q.e: "Encephalon" comes from a Greek phrase meaning "in the head", from en (in) and kephalē (head). It's another word for the brain, and it's why we have the word "encephalitis".

q: Because of the substance present in these structures of the human body, they can be preserved for centuries avoiding decomposition.

q.e: Teeth are covered with enamel, the hardest substance in the body, made mostly of the mineral hydroxyapatite. This is why teeth often survive for centuries after other tissues have decayed.
Arterial blood is bright red because it carries oxygen bound to hemoglobin away from the lungs. Venous blood, which has released much of its oxygen to body tissues, appears darker red or maroon.

q: Which of the following disease does Propecia (finasteride) treat?

q.e: Propecia (finasteride) is used to treat male pattern hair loss. It blocks the conversion of testosterone to DHT, a hormone that shrinks hair follicles.

q: Which blood type is called the universal recipient?

q.e: Individuals with type AB positive blood are universal recipients because their red blood cells have both A and B antigens and lack anti-A, anti-B, and anti-Rh antibodies. Type O negative, by contrast, is the universal red blood cell donor.

q: Extract from the Periwinkle plant is one of the worlds most powerful drugs, used to fight this disease.

q.e: The Madagascar periwinkle is the source of vincristine and vinblastine, drugs used to treat cancers such as leukemia and Hodgkin lymphoma. The discovery of their power helped to spark interest in plants as sources of medicine.

q: In 1993 the Scottish hotel-owner Campbell Aird received a bionic organ, which was the first of its kind. This is the organ.

q.e: In 1993, hotel owner Campbell Aird became the first person to be fitted with a bionic arm, a myoelectric prosthetic developed in Scotland. It's controlled by electrical signals from the wearer's muscles.

q: The Fallopian tubes are part of this system in the human body.

q.e: The Fallopian tubes are part of the female reproductive system, linking the ovaries to the uterus. Eggs travel through them, and fertilization usually happens there.

q: Nephrectomy is a surgical removal of which internal organ?

q.e: A nephrectomy is the surgical removal of a kidney, a procedure used for cancer, severe injury or donation. People can live a healthy life with one kidney.

q: One type of hair on the human body is called vellus hair. Where is it located?

q.e: Vellus hair is the fine, short, light "peach fuzz" that covers most of the body, except the palms and soles. It helps regulate body temperature.

q: Which of the following is true about the sources of vitamin B5?
It is found in a large variety of foods.
It is found only in plant products.
It is synthesized in the skin under the influence of the sun rays.
It is found only in animal products.

q.e: Vitamin B5 (pantothenic acid) is found in almost all foods, and its name comes from a Greek word meaning "from everywhere". Because of this, a true deficiency is rare.

q: Vitamin B12 is a set of complex chemical compounds synthesized in nature only by this group of organisms.

q.e: Only bacteria and archaea, a type of microbe, can make vitamin B12. Animals get it from eating other animals or from the bacteria in their food, which is why vegans often need supplements.

q: Which of the following is a water soluble vitamin also known as riboflavin?

q.e: Vitamin B2, also called riboflavin, is a water-soluble vitamin that helps the body use energy from food. It is found in milk, eggs and leafy greens.

q: The lack of this vitamin may cause seborrhea and dry skin.

q.e: A lack of vitamin B6 can cause skin problems like seborrheic dermatitis (an itchy, flaky rash) as well as irritability and anemia. It's found in fish, poultry, bananas and potatoes.

q: Brocas area is located in the human brain. What is it responsible for?

q.e: Located in the frontal lobe of the dominant hemisphere, Broca's area coordinates the motor functions necessary for speech production.

q: Synesthesia is a special condition of the brain which is characterized by which of the following unusual events?
Seeing colors when listening to music or reading letters/numbers
Seeing colors generated by the brain not based on reality

q.e: Synesthesia is a neurological phenomenon where the stimulation of one sensory pathway leads to involuntary experiences in a second pathway, such as experiencing specific colors when hearing musical notes or viewing printed numbers.

q: Which of these would not cause a muscle cramp?

q.e: Common triggers for muscle cramps include dehydration, low levels of electrolytes like potassium or magnesium, overexertion and poor circulation. Body weight by itself isn't a direct cause.

q: What is the approximate surface of the skin of an average adult human?

q.e: An adult's skin covers about 1.5 to 2 square meters, making it the body's largest organ. It protects against germs, regulates temperature and gives us the sense of touch.

q: The deficiency of what vitamin causes Rickets and Osteomalacia in humans?

q.e: Vitamin D regulates calcium and phosphate absorption in the body, and its deficiency leads to weak, soft bones, manifesting as rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.

q: An overdose of what vitamin can cause diarrhea, nausea and heartburn?

q.e: Very high doses of vitamin B5 (pantothenic acid) can cause diarrhea and an upset stomach. It's normally harmless at the levels found in food.

q: Niacin is the name of this B vitamin.

q.e: Niacin is another name for vitamin B3. A lack of it causes pellagra, a disease with skin, digestive and mental symptoms.

q: What is the largest organ of the human body?

q.e: The skin forms the integumentary system and accounts for about 16 percent of an adult's total body weight. The liver is the heaviest internal organ, weighing roughly 3 to 3.5 pounds (1.4 to 1.6 kg).

q: How many teeth does an adult usually have, including wisdom teeth?

q.e: A full set of permanent adult teeth includes 32 teeth: 8 incisors, 4 canines, 8 premolars, and 12 molars (which include the four wisdom teeth). Children have only 20 primary (baby) teeth.

q: Which organs clean your blood and make urine?

q.e: A pair of healthy kidneys filters about 120 to 150 quarts of blood every day, producing roughly 1 to 2 quarts of urine to remove waste products.

q: What do red blood cells carry around the body?

q.e: Red blood cells use an iron-rich protein called hemoglobin to bind oxygen in the lungs and transport it to tissues throughout the body.

q: What is the colored part of the eye called?

q.e: The iris is the thin, circular, pigmented muscle structure in the eye that controls how much light reaches the retina by adjusting the size of the pupil.

q: What is the shorter of the 2 forearm bones, which shares its name with a geometry term?

q.e: The radius runs along the thumb side of the forearm and is slightly shorter than the adjacent ulna. The humerus is the long bone located in the upper arm, not the forearm.

q: What is the main symptom of the uncommon blood disorder, known as methemoglobinemia?
Faster breathing because of lack of haemoglobin

q.e: In methemoglobinemia, the blood has too much methemoglobin, a form of hemoglobin that cannot carry oxygen well. The result is a bluish or grayish skin color.

q: Which scientist discovered that blood could be separated into blood plasma and red blood cells and the components frozen separately, thus lasting longer?

q.e: Dr. Charles Drew found that blood plasma could be separated from red cells and stored longer, which made large-scale blood banks possible. His work saved many lives during World War II.

q: In December of 1979 the World Health Organization announced the eradication of what infectious disease?

q.e: Following a worldwide vaccination campaign, the Global Commission certified smallpox eradicated in December 1979, and the WHO officially endorsed the finding in May 1980.

q: Scientists have proved that one of the health dangers, which ingesting sugar on a habitual basis involves, is the suppression of the activity of which system of the human body?

q.e: Diets high in sugar are linked to obesity, type 2 diabetes and inflammation, and some studies suggest they can weaken immune responses. Researchers are still working out the details.

q: What infectious disease can be transmitted by a mosquito bite?

q.e: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium parasites transmitted to humans through the bites of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes. The other options are made-up words.

q: Named after a 19th century British surgeon and anatomist, the Bowmans capsule is located in which organ/s of the human body?

q.e: Bowman's capsule is a cup-shaped structure in each of the kidney's filtering units (nephrons), where blood is first filtered. It was named after the English surgeon Sir William Bowman, who described it in the 1840s.

q: What chemical is added to table salt in some European countries to prevent tooth decay?
