q.e: Fluoride, usually in the form of sodium fluoride, is added to salt in some countries, including Switzerland, Germany and France. It strengthens tooth enamel and helps prevent cavities.

q: This term, denoting an internal organ, also refers to a color which is a mixture of dark brown and grey?

q.e: "Liver" is both the large organ that filters blood and makes bile, and the name of a brownish-gray color. The color is named after the organ's reddish-brown look.

q: What disease do the following famous people share: Menachem Begin, Halle Berry, Carol Channing, Miles Davis, Ella Fitzgerald, Ray Kroc, Arthur Ashe, and Ty Cobb?

q.e: All of these famous people had diabetes. The disease affects how the body handles blood sugar, and today it is far more common than in their time.

q: This medical term refers to a disease-causing protein agent that contains no genetic material.

q.e: A prion is an infectious protein that has no DNA or RNA. Prions cause diseases such as mad cow disease and Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, and Stanley Prusiner won a Nobel Prize in 1997 for discovering them.

q: Although natural, this food contains more calories than beet-sugar. It is used in a lot of skin-care products, but in the ancient Egyptians considered it --to be a cure for impotence and sterility.

q.e: Honey has been used as a food and medicine since ancient times, including in ancient Egypt. A tablespoon has more calories than a tablespoon of table sugar, but it contains small amounts of other compounds.

q: These fruits of the Family Musaceae are a valuable source of Vitamin A, Vitamin C, and potassium and are highly recommended by doctors to patients, whose potassium levels are low.

q.e: Bananas belong to the family Musaceae and are botanically classified as berries, with a medium banana providing around 420 milligrams of dietary potassium.

q: How does chocolate affect blood cholesterol levels?
It raises both LDL (bad cholesterol) and HDL(good cholesterol)

q.e: Research on chocolate and cholesterol is mixed: dark chocolate's flavanols may modestly improve some cholesterol markers, but chocolate also contains saturated fat and sugar. Moderation is the usual advice.

q: Besides containing vitamin E, this fruit also has many carotenoids, especially Beta-carotene, which helps you cope with harmful sun rays.

q.e: Mangoes contain vitamin E, vitamin C and carotenoids such as beta-carotene, which the body turns into vitamin A. They help keep skin and eyes healthy.

q: Bitter melon, or bitter gourd, has been traditionally used by Asians, Panamanians and Colombians in the prevention and treatment of this disease.

q.e: Bitter melon has been used in traditional medicine across Asia and Latin America to treat illnesses including malaria, and also diabetes. Scientific evidence for such uses is limited.

q: Stinging nettle has a large number of medicinal properties. What vitamin, essential for blood clotting, does fresh stinging nettle contain in large amounts?

q.e: Fresh stinging nettle is rich in vitamin K, which the body needs for blood to clot properly. Cooking removes the sting.

q: The consumption of blood oranges prevents this medical problem.

q.e: Blood oranges get their red color from anthocyanins, powerful antioxidants that may help protect the eyes. They also contain vitamin C, but no food can guarantee that you won't develop cataracts.

q: High consumption of meat protein deprives the body of calcium. Lack of calcium causes this disease.

q.e: Calcium is the main mineral in bones, and a lack of it over time, along with a lack of vitamin D, can lead to osteoporosis, a disease that makes bones brittle. Weight-bearing exercise also helps protect them.

q: Cranberries are known for preventing infections of this system in the human body.

q.e: Cranberries contain proanthocyanidins, compounds that help prevent Escherichia coli bacteria from adhering to the bladder wall. This makes them a traditional remedy for urinary tract infections (UTIs).

q: The word umbilicus refers to what part of the human body?

q.e: The umbilicus is the medical term for the belly button or navel, which marks the attachment site of the umbilical cord in placental mammals.

q: What disease is named after the main character of an epic poem by Italian physician and poet Girolamo Fracastoro?

q.e: Syphilis got its name from Syphilus, a shepherd in an epic poem published in 1530 by the Italian physician Girolamo Fracastoro. In the poem, Syphilus is cursed with the disease.

q: What dangerous disease did Queen Elizabeth I survive in 1562?

q.e: Queen Elizabeth I caught smallpox in October 1562 and nearly died, but she recovered. She was left with some scarring, and it is said that she wore heavy makeup afterward.

q: In preparation for a blood test, the lab slip says you have to be NPO for 8 hours prior to the test. What do you have to do?
Do not take anything by mouth
Lie flat in bed for 8 hours

q.e: NPO is short for the Latin "nil per os", meaning "nothing by mouth". It means no food or drink, often before surgery or certain blood tests.

q: After checking your blood pressure, the doctor says the diastolic pressure is elevated. To which number is he referring?

q.e: Diastolic pressure is the bottom number in a blood pressure reading, measuring the pressure in your arteries when the heart rests between beats. The top number represents systolic pressure.

q: Leukemia is a disease harming this bodily system.

q.e: Leukemia is a cancer of the blood-forming tissues, such as the bone marrow, and it affects the white blood cells that are a key part of the immune system. It is the most common childhood cancer.

q: This is the total number of bones in the adult human body.

q.e: Adults normally have 206 bones, down from roughly 270 at birth because several bones fuse together as a child grows. Over half of an adult's 206 bones are located in the hands, wrists, feet, and ankles.

q: Tee is a good anti-stress therapy. Flavonoids may prevent oxidation of bad cholesterol in the blood, which leads to accumulation of plaque in artery walls. It also prevents blood clot formation. Thus, tea is good for this too.

q.e: Tea contains flavonoids, antioxidants that may help protect the heart by keeping LDL cholesterol from oxidizing and by helping blood vessels to function well. Studies generally support a modest benefit.

q: Tea could reduce the risk for gastric, esophageal, and skin types of these.

q.e: Some studies suggest the polyphenols in tea may lower the risk of certain cancers, including gastric, esophageal and skin cancers. The evidence is not conclusive, so tea isn't a substitute for medical advice.

q: You can reduce contact with your teeth when drinking soda, by doing this.

q.e: Using a straw when drinking soda helps limit how long the sugary, acidic liquid is in contact with your teeth. Rinsing with water afterward also helps.

q: Which of these organs has no known function in the human body?

q.e: The appendix was once thought to be useless, but it contains immune tissue and may serve as a reserve of helpful gut bacteria. Some people live a normal life without it.

q: The main function of this organ of respiration is to transport oxygen from the atmosphere into the bloodstream.

q.e: Lungs contain hundreds of millions of tiny air sacs called alveoli, where gas exchange occurs across a surface area of about 50 to 75 square meters. The diaphragm is the muscle that drives this ventilation, while the trachea is the airway leading to them.

q: These organs are very sensitive and often fail in people with very high blood pressure or diabetes.

q.e: The kidneys contain millions of tiny blood vessels that are easily damaged by high blood pressure and diabetes, the two leading causes of kidney failure. Controlling these conditions protects them.

q: Which of these is best describes the cause of Parkinsons disease?
Changes in the myelin sheath of the neuron
Decreased blood flow to the brain

q.e: Parkinson's disease is caused by the loss of dopamine-producing nerve cells in a part of the brain called the substantia nigra. Dopamine is a neurotransmitter that helps control movement.

q: Déjà Vu is one of the curios brain phenomenon. Which of these most accurately describes the term?
A sensation of something seen or experienced before
A spontaneous involuntary creation of a false memory
A sudden flash of a long forgotten memory
The feeling that something familiar was never seen before

q.e: French for 'already seen', déjà vu describes the eerie sensation that a current experience has happened before. By contrast, jamais vu ('never seen') is the feeling of unfamiliarity with a situation that one logically knows is familiar.

q: This disease had 7 pandemics and is still causing epidemics.

q.e: Cholera has caused seven pandemics since 1817, and the current one began in 1961. It spreads through water contaminated with the bacterium Vibrio cholerae.

q: This terrible disease killed as much as 5% of the worlds population and affected almost 20% in just six months.

q.e: The 1918 influenza pandemic, often called the Spanish Flu, infected roughly 500 million people—about one-third of the world's population at the time. It is estimated to have killed between 20 million and 50 million people worldwide.

q: This organ contains many bacteria, which begin to digest surrounding organs immediately after death.

q.e: The intestines hold trillions of bacteria. After death, the bacteria begin to break down the tissue, starting the decomposition process.

q: What part of the human body does the science periodontics study?

q.e: Periodontics derives from Greek words meaning around the tooth, focusing on the structures supporting teeth, including the gums, cementum, and alveolar bone.

q: Three of the following four disorders are actually different names for the same disease. Which is the odd one?

q.e: "Manic depression", "bipolar disorder" and "manic-depressive illness" are all names for the same condition, which causes swings between high and low moods. "Maniac" is not the name of a disease.

q: Emphysema is a chronic disease affecting the organs of which system of the body?

q.e: Emphysema is a form of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) in which the alveoli, the tiny air sacs in the lungs, become damaged and rupture. This reduces oxygen absorption into the bloodstream, severely impairing the respiratory system.

q: This organ, which is the largest gland in the human body, plays a major role in metabolism and has a variety of functions, including glycogen storage, plasma protein synthesis, and drug detoxification.

q.e: The liver is the heaviest internal organ and largest gland in the body, typically weighing about 1.5 kilograms (3.3 pounds) in adults. The skin is the body's overall largest organ, but the liver holds the title among internal organs and glands.

q: What lobe in the brain is responsible for retaining verbal memory?

q.e: The left temporal lobe, especially the hippocampus, plays a key role in forming and retrieving verbal memories. Damage there can cause trouble remembering words and conversations.

q: This organ expands up to 500 times its normal size during the pregnancy.

q.e: During pregnancy, the uterus grows to about 500 times its normal size, from the size of a small pear to a large organ holding the baby. It returns to near its original size after birth.

q: What is the function of the thalamus, a part of the human brain with an egg-like shape?
It deals with the various types of sensory information.
It regulates the organisms automatic functions.
It helps humans to keep their balance.

q.e: The thalamus is an egg-shaped relay center deep in the brain that passes sensory information, such as touch, sight and hearing, to the cortex. Smell is the exception.

q: Which disease is treated by Synthroid (levothyroxine)?

q.e: Synthroid (levothyroxine) is a synthetic thyroid hormone used to treat hypothyroidism, a condition in which the thyroid gland doesn't make enough hormone. It is among the most commonly prescribed drugs.

q: What is the biggest artery in the human body?

q.e: The aorta carries oxygen-rich blood directly from the left ventricle of the heart into systemic circulation. In an adult, it measures over 1 foot (around 30 cm) long and roughly 1 inch (2.5 cm) in diameter.

q: A caries is formed as a result of food debris. Food remnants mix with saliva and bacteria, and result into this mixture that glues to the teeth.

q.e: Dental plaque is a soft, sticky biofilm of bacteria and food remnants that forms on teeth; if not brushed away, it hardens into tartar (calculus) and produces acids that cause cavities.

q: Despite its natural origins, this food is particularly bad for your teeth; it is sticky and contains concentrated fruit sugar.

q.e: Dried fruits are sticky and have concentrated sugars, so they cling to teeth and feed cavity-causing bacteria. Brushing or rinsing after eating them helps.

q: This substance is naturally present in water. It keeps the enamel strong and can stop or even reverse the process of tooth decay.

q.e: Fluoride helps prevent cavities by forming fluorapatite, which remineralizes tooth enamel and makes it more resistant to acid. Many public water systems add fluoride to keep concentrations around the recommended level of 0.7 milligrams per liter.

q: What marrow produces blood cells in the human body?

q.e: Red bone marrow, found in flat bones like the hip and breastbone, produces red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets. Yellow marrow, in the long bones, stores fat.

q: What is the building block of green plants that cant be broken down into sugar molecules and passes through the human body undigested?

q.e: Dietary fiber is the part of plant foods that humans cannot digest, so it passes through the body mostly intact. It helps digestion and heart health.

q: How much blood does the average adult human have?

q.e: Blood makes up roughly 7 to 8 percent of an adult human's total body weight, equating to about 1.2 to 1.5 gallons or 5 to 6 liters. The exact volume varies depending on body size and sex.

q: Approximately what percentage of humans have blood of the type Rh +?

q.e: About 85% of people have Rh-positive blood, meaning they have the Rh factor protein on their red blood cells. The remaining 15% are Rh-negative.

q: What percentage of humans have type O blood?
There is no way to tell.

q.e: Type O is the most common blood type in many countries, with about 45% of people in the US having it, including O-positive and O-negative. O-negative is the universal donor type for red cells.

q: Healthy people over 17 can donate what part of their blood every two weeks?

q.e: Platelet donors can give as often as every two weeks, much more often than whole-blood donors. Platelets help blood to clot and are in constant demand for cancer patients.

q: Who was the first physician to demonstrate that arteries carry blood throughout the body?

q.e: The Greek physician Galen showed in the 2nd century that arteries carry blood rather than air, which earlier doctors believed. His ideas remained influential until William Harvey described circulation in 1628.

q: In 1924 who was the German mathematician who developed a proof showing that blood types were genetic?

q.e: In 1924, the German mathematician Felix Bernstein showed that the ABO blood types are inherited through three versions of one gene. His work explained patterns that had puzzled scientists for years.

q: This person developed the first system to produce donatable blood plasma and was the first director of a Red Cross Blood Bank in the USA.

q.e: Charles Drew developed methods to process and store blood plasma and became the first director of the American Red Cross blood bank. He also resigned in protest when the Red Cross segregated blood by race.

q: Which of the following is high in Vitamin E?

q.e: Sunflower seeds are one of the best sources of vitamin E, an antioxidant that protects cells. Almonds and wheat germ are also rich in it.

q: What is the male reproductive organ which secretes an alkaline fluid?

q.e: The prostate gland makes a slightly alkaline fluid that is part of semen. It helps protect sperm in the acidic environment of the female reproductive tract.

q: What system of the human body provides a site for blood cell formation?

q.e: Hematopoiesis, the formation of cellular blood components, occurs in the red bone marrow found inside bones, making the skeletal system essential for blood cell production.

q: Which part of the brain, located inside the temporal lobe, is associated with memory formation?

q.e: The hippocampus, named for its resemblance to a seahorse, plays a critical role in converting short-term memories into long-term memories and supporting spatial navigation.

q: Identify the true statement regarding cardiac muscle.
It contracts moderately fast in response to stimulation of nerve impulses.
It is attached to the skeleton and moves its parts.
It contract quickly in response to stimulation of nerve impulses.

q.e: Cardiac muscle, found only in the heart, is striated like skeletal muscle but works involuntarily. It contracts rhythmically and does not tire.

q: Identify a true characteristic of the smooth muscle tissue.
It contracts slowly in response to nerve stimulation impulses.
It is a muscle only found in the stomach.
It contracts quickly in response to nerve stimulation impulses.

q.e: Smooth muscle, found in the walls of organs such as the stomach and blood vessels, contracts slowly and involuntarily. It moves things such as food through the digestive tract.

q: What term refers to wasting away or degeneration of a muscle?

q.e: Muscle atrophy is the decrease in muscle mass and tissue caused by disuse, aging, or neurological conditions. In contrast, hypertrophy refers to the increase and growth of muscle cells.

q: What word denotes the ability of the muscle to transmit impulses?

q.e: Conductivity is the ability of muscle to carry electrical impulses. Muscles also have excitability, contractility, extensibility and elasticity.

q: Identify a true characteristic of skeletal muscle.
It is striated, made up of long slender, striped cells.
It is found in the stomach and intestines.
It is non-striated, composed of spindle shaped cells.

q.e: Skeletal muscle is made of long, striped (striated) fibers and is under voluntary control. It attaches to bones with tendons and moves the skeleton.

q: Name the longest bone in the body.

q.e: The femur, or thigh bone, accounts for about a quarter of an adult's total height and is also the strongest bone in the human body. The tibia and fibula make up the lower leg, while the humerus is in the upper arm.

q: What disease took many lives in Russia, Poland and Romania during World War I ?

q.e: Typhus, spread by body lice, killed hundreds of thousands in Russia, Poland, Romania and Serbia during and after World War I. Crowded, unsanitary conditions helped it spread.

q: In 1952, this disease struck the U.S. and became the worst epidemic in the nations history at that time.

q.e: The 1952 polio epidemic in the United States infected around 58,000 people, causing more than 3,100 deaths and paralyzing over 21,000 victims. The outbreak spurred the rapid rollout of Jonas Salk's polio vaccine, declared safe and effective in 1955.

q: In what internal human organ are the islets of Langerhans located?

q.e: Named after German anatomist Paul Langerhans who discovered them in 1869, these pancreatic cells produce vital hormones including insulin and glucagon.

q: Electrooculography is a medical procedure which inspects the potential of which bodily organ?

q.e: Electrooculography (EOG) measures the electrical potential between the front and back of the eye, using electrodes placed around it. It is used to study eye movements and retina function.

q: Sigmoidoscopy is a medical examination of which internal organ?

q.e: A sigmoidoscopy examines the lower part of the large intestine, the rectum and the sigmoid colon, with a thin, flexible camera. It is used to screen for polyps and cancer.

q: Uncontrolled hypertension (high blood pressure) leads to all of the following EXCEPT this one.

q.e: Uncontrolled high blood pressure can damage the heart, brain and kidneys, causing heart attack, stroke and kidney disease. It doesn't cause thyroid disease.

q: Blood sugars are checked under 2 conditions: Fasting and Post-prandial. Fasting means after having not eaten (for example in the morning on rising). Post-prandial means after eating. When are post-prandial checks typically taken?

q.e: A post-prandial blood sugar test is done about two hours after a meal. It shows how well the body handles the sugar from food.

q: Which of the following is a normal fasting blood sugar?

q.e: A normal fasting blood glucose level is below 100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L). Readings between 100 and 125 suggest prediabetes, and 126 or above on two tests suggests diabetes.

q: Which of the following is a normal post-prandial blood sugar?

q.e: A normal blood sugar two hours after eating is less than 140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L). Higher readings suggest the body is not handling sugar well.

q: Which of the following is least likely to cause tooth decay according to The American Dental Association?

q.e: Tooth decay happens when bacteria in the mouth turn sugars and starches into acid that eats away at enamel. How often you eat sugary foods matters even more than how much.

q: What deadly and infectious disease that most often attacks the lungs used to be known as consumption?

q.e: Tuberculosis was historically called consumption because it appeared to consume patients from the inside as they experienced severe weight loss and wasting. It is caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

q: An important supplement for pregnant women, what is vitamin B9 more commonly known as?

q.e: Vitamin B9 is also called folate, and its supplement form is folic acid. Taking it before and during early pregnancy helps prevent neural tube defects.

q: The vitamins from the B complex have many functions but generally play most important role in which of these processes of the human body?

q.e: B vitamins help the body turn food into energy and are central to cell metabolism. They also help make red blood cells and support the nervous system.

q: Which of these is not among the systems of the human body that vitamins of the B group mainly benefit?

q.e: B vitamins mainly benefit the nervous system, the digestive system, the skin and the blood, but they aren't typically linked to the respiratory system. They are mostly water-soluble, so the body needs a regular supply.

q: Vitamin B2 has which of these interesting properties?
It is fluorescent under UV light.
It is can be absorbed only through the skin.
It can be found in all three physical conditions of matter.
It melts at more than 10 000 degrees C.

q.e: Vitamin B2 (riboflavin) glows yellow-green under UV light, which is why vitamin-rich urine can look bright yellow. Its name comes from the Latin "flavus", meaning yellow.

q: Niacin, also known as vitamin B3 or nicotinic acid, is a vitamin that can be synthesized by which organ?

q.e: The liver can make niacin from the amino acid tryptophan. That's why foods rich in tryptophan, like turkey and milk, help prevent niacin deficiency.

q: This vitamin of the B complex, popular also under the name vitamin H, is not included in the recommended daily intake by some health organizations.

q.e: Vitamin B7, biotin, is also called vitamin H, from the German words for "skin and hair". Some health organizations set no official daily value because deficiency is rare.

q: What kind of animal causes the parasitic Dracunculiasis disease that is endemic to Sub-Saharan Africa?
A worm whose eggs are ingested when drinking contaminated water
An insect that injects a plasmodium through its bite
A mite that is carried by poultry
A lizard that carries dangerous unicellular parasites

q.e: Dracunculiasis, or Guinea worm disease, is caused by a parasitic worm that people catch by drinking water containing tiny water fleas carrying its larvae. Cases have fallen from millions to only a handful per year thanks to eradication efforts.

q: The common name of the tendo calcaneus or calcaneal tendon of the human body was derived from the name of this Greek mythological hero.

q.e: According to myth, Thetis dipped her infant son Achilles into the River Styx to grant him invulnerability, but held him by the heel, leaving that spot unprotected.

q: Where in the human body is the Golgi organ located?

q.e: The Golgi tendon organ is a sensor located in tendons, near where they attach to muscles. It detects tension and helps prevent muscles from being overloaded.

q: The so-called McBurneys point is located in this part of the human body.

q.e: McBurney's point is a spot on the lower right side of the abdomen, about two-thirds of the way from the navel to the hip bone. Tenderness there is a classic sign of appendicitis.

q: Oxytocin is an important hormone for the human body especially for women. What is it responsible for?

q.e: Oxytocin causes the uterus to contract during labor and triggers milk letdown during breastfeeding. It's also called the "love hormone" because it's linked to bonding.

q: Which word refers to a sound caused by abnormal or pathological heart valves?

q.e: Heart murmurs are abnormal rushing or whooshing sounds made by turbulent blood flow across the heart valves. While wheezing occurs in the respiratory airways, an aneurysm is an abnormal bulge in a blood vessel wall.

q: The clavicle is the bone that connects your upper arm to the rest of your body via your shoulder. What is the clavicle more commonly known as?

q.e: The clavicle, commonly called the collarbone, runs horizontally between the sternum (breastbone) and the scapula (shoulder blade).

q: What are baby teeth scientifically called?

q.e: Primary teeth are called deciduous teeth, sharing a Latin root with deciduous trees that shed their leaves annually. Humans normally develop 20 deciduous teeth before they are replaced by 32 permanent teeth.

q: Vitamin A plays an important role in vision, growth, healthy skin and hair, immune function, and reproduction. Which of these is not a significant source of Vitamin A?

q.e: Good sources of vitamin A include liver, eggs, dairy, and orange and green vegetables like carrots and spinach. Nuts and grains are not significant sources.

q: Which of the following is not a heart valve?

q.e: The heart's four valves are the mitral, tricuspid, aortic and pulmonary valves. The carotid is an artery in the neck, not a heart valve.

q: How many types of blood vessels are there?

q.e: The main kinds of blood vessels are arteries, veins and capillaries, and smaller arterioles and venules are often counted separately, which makes four or five types. They would stretch about 60,000 miles if laid end to end.

q: On average, how much of a persons body weight is muscle?

q.e: Muscle makes up around 40% of an average person's body weight, though this varies with age, sex and fitness. Skeletal muscle is the main component.

q: How many muscles are in the human body?

q.e: The human body has roughly 600 to 650 skeletal muscles, depending on how they are counted. Together they make up a large part of body weight.

q: There are 3 types of muscle in the human body. What are they?

q.e: Human muscle tissue is classified into skeletal muscle which enables voluntary movement, smooth muscle found in hollow organs, and specialized cardiac muscle in the heart wall.

q: Which of these organs is responsible for the degradation of red blood cells?

q.e: The spleen acts as a blood filter where specialized macrophages engulf and break down old or damaged red blood cells, recycling their iron back into the body.

q: What is the name of the pigment that determines the color of human skin?

q.e: Melanin is produced by specialized cells called melanocytes and dictates the pigmentation of human skin, hair, and eyes. Melatonin, by contrast, is a hormone that regulates the sleep-wake cycle.

q: Skin consists of how many basic layers?

q.e: Human skin consists of three primary layers: the outermost epidermis, the underlying dermis containing blood vessels and nerves, and the deeper subcutaneous hypodermis.

q: The deficiency of vitamin C leads to this disease, which can be lethal.

q.e: Scurvy results from a severe lack of ascorbic acid (vitamin C), which is essential for collagen synthesis, leading to bleeding gums, opening wounds, and eventual heart failure.

q: Vitamin C is necessary for the production of this protein in the human body.

q.e: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is a vital cofactor for enzymes that synthesize collagen, the most abundant structural protein in human skin, bone, and connective tissue.

q: What chemical compound is commonly known as vitamin C?

q.e: Ascorbic acid derives its name from a- (not) and scorbutus (scurvy), referencing its ability to prevent and treat the vitamin C deficiency disease. Acetylsalicylic acid is the generic chemical name for aspirin.

q: Where is the smallest bone in the body?

q.e: The stapes, or stirrup bone, is located in the middle ear and measures only about 3 millimeters by 2.5 millimeters, transmitting sound vibrations to the inner ear.

q: The femur is in which part of the body?

q.e: The femur, or thigh bone, connects the pelvis to the knee and is both the longest and strongest bone in the human body.

q: Which vitamin does your skin make in sunlight?

q.e: When human skin is exposed to ultraviolet B (UVB) sunlight, it converts 7-dehydrocholesterol into previtamin D3, which then metabolizes into active vitamin D. Most other vitamins must be obtained directly through diet.

q: If which organ secretes too much insulin, hypoglycemia can occur?

q.e: The beta cells in the islets of Langerhans within the pancreas secrete insulin to lower blood glucose levels. If excess insulin is released, blood sugar drops abnormally low, leading to hypoglycemia.

q: Roughly how many watts of power does your brain run on?

q.e: The brain runs on about 12 to 20 watts, which is similar to a dim light bulb, even though it uses around 20% of the body's energy. It is more energy-efficient than any computer of comparable power.

q: According to a study published in the Annals of Neurology, people who regularly come into contact with pesticides are 70 % more likely to develop what disease?

q.e: Studies, including one reported in the Annals of Neurology, have found that people regularly exposed to certain pesticides have a higher risk of Parkinson's disease. Researchers think the chemicals may damage dopamine-producing neurons.

q: This medical term refers to a decrease in the number of circulating leukocytes (white blood cells) in the blood.

q.e: Leukopenia is a lower-than-normal number of white blood cells (leukocytes), which can make infections more likely. It can be caused by infections, certain drugs or bone marrow problems.

q: Although minimal, the risk of transmitting this disease through a tattoo needle exists. This disease can also be transmitted through the ink or dirty equipment and environment.

q.e: Unsterilized tattoo needles or equipment can spread blood-borne infections like hepatitis B and C. That's why a clean, licensed studio using single-use needles is important.

q: Which blood constituent is involved in the formation of blood clots but has a shelf-life of only 5 days?

q.e: Platelets, the blood cells that help form clots, can be stored for only about 5 to 7 days, so blood banks need regular donors. They're kept at room temperature and gently agitated.

q: What is the strongest muscle in the body in relation to its size?

q.e: The masseter is the primary chewing muscle of the jaw and can exert a bite force exceeding 200 pounds (about 90 kg) on the molars. The gluteus maximus is the largest muscle overall, but the masseter produces the most force relative to its size.

q: What is the name of the anvil-shaped bone in the middle ear that along with the malleus and stapes allow us to hear?

q.e: The incus, often called the anvil, transmits vibrations between the malleus (hammer) and stapes (stirrup). The stapes is the smallest bone in the entire human body.

q: There is no cure for this disease that is characterized by the death of muscle cells and tissue. Diagnosis is often based on the results of a muscle biopsy.

q.e: Muscular dystrophy is a group of inherited diseases that gradually weaken muscles, and there is no cure, though treatments can help manage symptoms. A muscle biopsy can show the characteristic changes.

q: The Framingham Heart Study concluded that moderate drinkers were 50 % less likely to die from coronary diseases than this group of people.

q.e: The Framingham Heart Study found lower coronary heart disease risk in moderate drinkers than in non-drinkers, but heavy drinking raises the risk of many other health problems. More recent research questions whether alcohol has any benefit.

q: This agent, present in the skin of grapes, is one of the most important beneficiary agents in wine. It has antioxidant, anticoagulant, anti-inflammatory and anti-cancer properties.

q.e: Resveratrol is a compound found in grape skins, especially red grapes, and in red wine. It has antioxidant properties, but its health benefits in humans are still being studied.

q: This oil is said to be the richest natural source of vitamin E. It is widely used in cosmetics as an anti-ageing substance.

q.e: Wheat germ oil is one of the richest natural sources of vitamin E, an antioxidant that is widely used in skincare products. It can also go rancid quickly.

q: This nut is also a source of folic acid, which diminishes the risk of birth defects and heart diseases. It is often combined with chocolate.

q.e: Hazelnuts contain folate (vitamin B9) as well as vitamin E and healthy fats. They are the nut famously paired with chocolate, as in Nutella.

q: Age-related macular degeneration, cancer, heart diseases and neural-tube defects are all diseases which this green leafy vegetable will help you with, as a preventive measure. It is also a good source of iron.

q.e: Spinach has folate, lutein, vitamin K and iron. Lutein is linked to a lower risk of age-related macular degeneration, and folate helps prevent neural tube defects.

q: This is one of the few non-fish oils that contains linolenic acid, an omega-3 fatty acid. This will lower your chances of having a heart disease. It also contains no cholesterol.

q.e: Soybean oil is a plant source of alpha-linolenic acid, an omega-3 fatty acid, and as a plant oil it contains no cholesterol. It is widely used in cooking and food products.

q: This ingredient is used in a lot of cosmetic products. It is rich in micro-elements and minerals because it comes from the depths of the sea. It has been said that this ingredient can activate the chemical process typical for youthful skin.

q.e: Pearl powder, made from ground cultured pearls, has been used in Asian cosmetics and traditional medicine for centuries. Claims that it keeps skin young are mostly traditional, not proven.

q: These substances are added to lotions and creams because they smooth and soften the skin. There are several hundred different kinds.

q.e: Emollients are moisturizing ingredients that soften and smooth the skin by filling gaps between skin cells. Examples are petroleum jelly, shea butter and glycerin.

q: The active ingredient of absinthe is thujone. It is chemically similar to this psychoactive substance. Scientists also believe that thujone and this substance affect the same brain receptors.

q.e: Thujone is a compound in wormwood, the herb in absinthe. Contrary to old claims, absinthe doesn't cause hallucinations, and its strong effects come mainly from its very high alcohol content.

q: Common sage, also known as Garden sage, was found to be beneficial in mild to moderate cases of this dangerous disease.

q.e: Some small studies suggest sage extract may help memory and thinking in mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease, but it's not an established treatment. People should check with a doctor before using herbal remedies.

q: This deciduous tree, popular as Maidenhair Tree, was first used in China as a stimulant. It is generally accepted that it increases blood flow to the brain, stimulating memory, mental alertness and reducing mental fatigue.

q.e: Ginkgo biloba, also called the maidenhair tree, is a "living fossil" that has existed for about 200 million years. Many people take it for memory, but studies haven't shown strong benefits.

q: This blood alcohol content level is generally accepted by all 50 U.S. states as the level consistent with being legally intoxicated.

q.e: All US states now use a blood alcohol content of 0.08% as the legal limit for drivers over 21, and the older 0.10% limit was gradually lowered. Lower limits apply to commercial drivers and drivers under 21.

q: Tsaritsa Alexandra of Russia called on Grigori Rasputin to cure her only son Alexei, who suffered from this disease.

q.e: Alexei, the son of Tsar Nicholas II and Tsarina Alexandra, had hemophilia, a disorder in which blood doesn't clot properly. The family turned to the mystic Rasputin, whose influence at court became a scandal.

q: What is the name of the American who patented the first artificial heart?

q.e: Paul Winchell, a ventriloquist and inventor best known as the voice of Tigger, patented an artificial heart in 1963. He later donated the patent to the University of Utah, where artificial heart research continued.

q: The earliest recorded vaccination in history was carried out during the 17th century against this disease.

q.e: People practiced inoculation against smallpox long before modern vaccines, using material from sufferers. Edward Jenner then developed the cowpox-based vaccine in 1796, which led to the eradication of smallpox in 1980.

q: The acronym we now use for this disease was first coined in 1982. Initially referred to as the gay plague, this infectious disease killed 853 people that same year.

q.e: AIDS, or acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, got that name in 1982, when it replaced the earlier label GRID. The cause, HIV, was identified in 1983.

q: During a physical exam, the doctor says he wants to auscultate your heart. What instrument will he use?

q.e: Auscultation is the medical term for listening to the internal sounds of the body, usually using a stethoscope. The instrument was invented in France in 1816 by physician René Laennec.

q: Which term means a noncontagious inflammation of the skin, characterized chiefly by redness, itching, and the outbreak of lesions that may discharge serous matter and become encrusted and scaly.

q.e: Eczema is derived from the Greek word "ekzema," which translates roughly to "boil out" or "break out." The correct spelling retains the initial "ec-" prefix.

q: Studies have found that coffee may reduce the risk of this disease.

q.e: Large studies have found that people who drink coffee regularly have a lower risk of Parkinson's disease. Researchers think caffeine may protect brain cells, but that doesn't prove cause and effect.

q: Fainting is a loss of consciousness due to temporary insufficient blood flow to the brain. What is he medical term for fainting?

q.e: Syncope is the medical term for fainting, a temporary loss of consciousness caused by too little blood flow to the brain. It's often harmless but can sometimes signal a heart problem.

q: This disease, commonly known as Lou Gehrigs disease, occurs when the nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord gradually deteriorate.

q.e: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease affecting upper and lower motor neurons. It became known as Lou Gehrig's disease after the New York Yankees legend was diagnosed in 1939.

q: One version of this rare brain disorder is better known as Mad Cow and can be contracted by eating contaminated beef. There is no known cure.

q.e: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) is a rare, fatal brain disease caused by prions. A variant form is linked to eating beef from cattle with "mad cow disease" (BSE).

q: Named after a river region in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the symptoms of this viral disease include: red eyes, bleeding from orifices, and organ failure. The disease causes a type of hemorrhagic fever and the fatality rate is often 90%.

q.e: Ebola virus disease was first identified in 1976 near the Ebola River in what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It causes severe viral hemorrhagic fever with case fatality rates historically ranging from roughly 50% to up to 90%.

q: People diagnosed with this disease have an insatiable urge to eat non-food substances like dirt, paper, glue and clay.

q.e: Pica is a condition in which people crave and eat things that aren't food, such as dirt, chalk, paper or clay. It can be linked to iron deficiency, pregnancy or mental health conditions.

q: This progressive generative disease of the brain results in loss of cognitive ability and uncontrolled movements, called chorea, the Greek word for dance.

q.e: Huntington's disease is an inherited brain disorder that causes uncontrolled movements called chorea, from the Greek word for "dance", as well as mental decline. It is caused by a faulty gene on chromosome 4.

q: This disorder is the abnormal accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid in the ventricles of the brain.

q.e: Hydrocephalus, meaning "water on the brain", is a buildup of cerebrospinal fluid in the brain's ventricles. A shunt is often placed to drain the extra fluid.

q: What medical term is synonym of jaundice, a condition characterized by yellowing of the skin, sclera and mucous membranes?

q.e: Icterus is the medical word for jaundice, from the Greek "ikteros". The yellow color comes from a buildup of bilirubin.

q: At this stage of the plague, one of the the symptoms is the presence of black patches on the skin.

q.e: In septicemic plague, the infection spreads in the blood and can turn skin black from tissue death. This is one reason the medieval pandemic was called the "Black Death".

q: Located in the upper anterior portion of the chest cavity, the thymus is an organ belonging to which system of the human body?

q.e: The thymus, located behind the breastbone, is part of the lymphatic and immune systems and is where T cells mature. It is large in children and shrinks after puberty.

q: This extremely vital nerve is responsible for such varied tasks as heart rate, gastrointestinal peristalsis and sweating. It also controls quite a few muscle movements in the mouth, including speech and keeping the larynx open for breathing.

q.e: The vagus nerve, the 10th cranial nerve, runs from the brainstem to the abdomen and controls the heart rate, digestion and parts of speech and swallowing. Its name comes from the Latin for "wandering".

q: The human facial skull consists of double as well as single bones. Which of the following bones is not a facial bone?

q.e: The calcaneus is the heel bone in the foot, not a bone of the face. The facial skeleton includes bones such as the maxilla, mandible, nasal bones and zygomatic (cheek) bones.

q: Which of these terms refers to a bone surgeon?

q.e: An orthopedist (or orthopedic surgeon) specializes in the diagnosis, surgical treatment, and rehabilitation of disorders of the bones, joints, and musculoskeletal system.

q: This physician has been trained in the diagnosis and management of kidney disease.

q.e: A nephrologist is a doctor who specializes in the kidneys and treats conditions such as kidney failure and kidney stones. The name comes from the Greek "nephros", meaning kidney.

q: Which one of the following medications treats Alzheimers Disease (dementia)?

q.e: Aricept (donepezil) is a drug used to treat symptoms of Alzheimer's disease. It slows the breakdown of acetylcholine in the brain but doesn't cure the disease.

q: Which of the following drugs thins the blood? (That is, it decreases the ability of the blood to clot.)

q.e: Coumadin (warfarin) is a blood thinner that makes it harder for blood to clot, which is used to prevent strokes and clots. It works by blocking vitamin K, so patients need to watch their intake of vitamin K foods.

q: Which of these terms refer to the chambers of the heart -- the two on top and the two on the bottom respectively?
Atria and Ventricle, Atria and Ventricle

q.e: The human heart has four chambers: the right and left atria collect incoming blood at the top, while the right and left ventricles pump blood out from the bottom.

q: Cavities are generally painless. However, if not treated, they enlarge and eventually become painful as they reach the internal structure of the tooth, especially this part.

q.e: Tooth decay starts in the enamel and then reaches the dentin, a softer layer containing tiny nerve channels. By the time it reaches the dentin, cavities often start to hurt.

q: Which type of blood cells can be stored the longest?

q.e: Red blood cells can be stored refrigerated for about 42 days, while platelets last only 5 to 7 days. Plasma can be frozen and stored for up to a year.

q: An ancient Chinese book called The Inner Canon of Huangdi recommends breathing exercises, massage of the skin and flesh, and exercises of hands and feet as a remedy for complete paralysis, chills, and fever. Who was the author of this ancient book?

q.e: The Huangdi Neijing, or Inner Canon of the Yellow Emperor, is attributed to the legendary Yellow Emperor, though it was probably compiled over several centuries around the 2nd century BC. It is a foundation of traditional Chinese medicine.

q: Which of the following types of brain cells amplify the neural signals and maintain homeostasis?

q.e: Glial cells, such as astrocytes, support and protect neurons, maintain the brain's chemical balance and help signals travel. There are about as many of them as neurons.

q: Which of the following is not part of the group of brain-supplying arteries, known as the circle of Willis?

q.e: The circle of Willis is a ring of arteries at the base of the brain that includes the anterior and posterior cerebral arteries and the communicating arteries. The basilar artery feeds into it but isn't part of the circle itself.

q: This scientist, winner of the 1908 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, was the first to notice the existence of blood-brain barrier.

q.e: Paul Ehrlich, who shared the 1908 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, noticed that dyes injected into the blood stained most organs but not the brain. This led to the idea of the blood-brain barrier.

q: During his famous voyage to the Galapagos Islands, Charles Darwin studied differences in a specific animal's anatomy, his observations setting the stage for his eventual theory of evolution. What animal's anatomy did Darwin study?

q.e: Darwin noted that finch species across different Galápagos islands possessed beaks uniquely adapted to their specific food sources, such as cracking hard seeds or probing flowers. These observations provided critical evidence for natural selection.

q: This pollutant causes inflammation of the lungs, impaired breathing, coughing, chest pain, nausea, and throat irritation and permanent damage to lung tissue in long term exposure.

q.e: Smog contains ground-level ozone and fine particles that irritate the lungs, causing coughing, chest pain and reduced lung function. Long-term exposure can permanently harm lung tissue.

q: This gas is produced mainly by automobiles. It hiders the bodys ability to carry oxygen in the blood, causing serious problems for people with cardiovascular diseases.

q.e: Carbon monoxide binds to hemoglobin with an affinity roughly 200 times greater than that of oxygen, forming carboxyhemoglobin and preventing vital oxygen delivery to tissues.

q: Substance vital for treating what hereditary blood defect that occurs almost exclusively in males, has been produced by cloning?

q.e: Hemophilia, which mostly affects males, is treated with clotting factors such as factor VIII, which are now made using genetic engineering. This is safer than using factors taken from donated blood.

q: Which skeletal muscle is used in blowing, whistling, and smiling?

q.e: The buccinator, a cheek muscle, is used for blowing, whistling and smiling. It's sometimes called the "trumpeter's muscle" because it helps trumpeters hold air.

q: Which skeletal muscle raises or throws back the shoulders, assists in moving the head to one side or another, and helps hold the head erect?

q.e: The trapezius is a large, triangular muscle across the upper back and neck that raises the shoulders and helps hold the head up. It's named for its trapezoid shape.

q: Which skeletal muscle extends the foot, and is used to stand on tiptoes?

q.e: The gastrocnemius, the main calf muscle, points the foot down and lets you stand on tiptoes. It works with the deeper soleus muscle.

q: In what part of the human body are the Wormian bones, named after Ole Worm, located?

q.e: Wormian bones are small extra bones found in the sutures, or joints, of the skull. They're named after Ole Worm, a Danish physician, and are common in some conditions.

q: What nervous system ailment, characterized by symptoms of severe lethargy and fatigue, is primarily caused by the lack of vitamin B1 (Thiamine) in the diet?

q.e: Beriberi is caused by a lack of vitamin B1 (thiamine), and it affects the nerves and heart. It was common where people lived mostly on polished white rice.

q: This mental illness, classified by Emil Kraepelin in 1887, is characterized by persistent disorders in the perception or expression of reality. A person who suffers from this disease may have delusions, hallucinations, disorganized or catatonic behavior.

q.e: Schizophrenia is a serious mental illness involving delusions, hallucinations and disorganized thinking. Emil Kraepelin described it in the 1880s as "dementia praecox", and Eugen Bleuler coined the name "schizophrenia" in 1908.

q: This medical condition is characterized by subsequent decay of body tissues, caused by infection or thrombosis or lack of blood flow.

q.e: Gangrene occurs when body tissue dies due to a critical loss of blood supply or severe bacterial infection, most commonly affecting the extremities. Impetigo and tinea are superficial bacterial and fungal infections of the skin that do not involve massive tissue necrosis.

q: Urticaria is a relatively common form of allergic reaction, that causes red skin welts. Which is the other term which refers to this skin ailment?

q.e: Urticaria, commonly called hives, involves swollen, intensely itchy wheals triggered by histamine release from mast cells during allergic or inflammatory reactions.

q: Which medical term refers to the crackling sound, produced when two rough surfaces in the human body come into contact?

q.e: Crepitus is the crackling or popping sound heard or felt when rough surfaces rub together, like bone ends or in a joint. Cracking knuckles is a common, usually harmless, example.

q: When you take a shower or bath for a long time, the skin on your fingertips shrivels. This happens because your body does this.
Absorbs water in the hypotonic solution
Loses water in the hypotonic solution
Loses water in the hypertonic solution
Absorbs water in the hypertonic solution

q.e: Wrinkled fingers in the bath aren't just from soaking up water; research suggests the nervous system causes blood vessels in the fingertips to narrow. Wet, wrinkled fingers may give a better grip on slippery objects.

q: This mineral, an important component of all living creatures cellular membranes, is one of the major minerals required in the structural composition of bones and teeth.

q.e: Phosphorus, mostly as calcium phosphate, makes up a major part of bones and teeth, and it's also found in cell membranes and DNA. It's found in dairy, meat and nuts.

q: Between the lungs, behind and slightly to the left of your breastbone.
On top of the lungs, behind and slightly to the left of your breastbone.
Beneath the lungs, behind and slightly to the left of your breastbone.
To the right of the lungs, behind and slightly to the left of your breastbone.

q.e: The heart rests in the central chest cavity known as the mediastinum, flanked by the lungs and sitting just behind the sternum with about two-thirds of its mass tilted toward the left.

q: Which tree, that grows on the Canary Islands, Cape Verde and Madeira, secretes a reddish juice, called Dragons blood?

q.e: The dragon tree (Dracaena draco) grows in the Canary Islands, Cape Verde and Madeira, and its red resin is known as "dragon's blood". It has been used as a dye and medicine since ancient times.

q: What fruit is believed to be the highest in vitamin C content?

q.e: The Kakadu plum, an Australian fruit also called gubinge, is believed to have the highest vitamin C content of any fruit, up to about 100 times that of oranges. Indigenous Australians have long used it as food and medicine.

q: Which part of the brain mainly controls balance?

q.e: The cerebellum, located at the base of the skull behind the brainstem, coordinates voluntary movements and integrates sensory input to maintain posture and balance.

q: What term means fear of skin diseases?

q.e: Dermatosiophobia is the fear of skin diseases. Phobias are named by combining a Greek word with "phobia", which means fear.

q: A wax sculpture at the London Madame Tussauds museum depicts Amy Winehouse lying in a pool of blood with an apple and a bullet hole in her head. The statue is a recreation of this American authors accidental manslaughter of his wife Joan Vollmer.

q.e: William S. Burroughs, author of Naked Lunch, accidentally shot and killed his wife, Joan Vollmer, in Mexico City in 1951 while playing a "William Tell" game. He was never tried for it and later said it shaped his writing.

q: It is the magical power of this herb: In the event of some kind of troublesome misfortune, gather the root with care during the descent of the lions cub and hang it around your neck. It will drive away cares and cause a merry heart. - Syrenius (1540 - 1611).

q.e: Angelica, the "herb of angels", was believed in medieval Europe to ward off evil and protect against plague. Its stalks are still used in cooking and candied.

q: When the arm is bent in the elbow joint humans use the biceps branchii musle and the triceps is used when it is extended. What is the name of the muscle that abducts the arm in the shoulder?

q.e: The deltoid is the thick, triangular muscle over the shoulder that raises the arm to the side (abducts it). It gives the shoulder its rounded shape.

q: Pathogenic microorganisms which get into the human body are called antigens because they cause the formation of antibodies. The antibodies are produced by what blood cells?

q.e: Antibodies are made by B lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell. When they recognize an antigen, they develop into plasma cells that produce large numbers of antibodies.

q: In 1658 he became the first person to describe and observe red blood cells (erythrocytes).

q.e: Dutch scientist Jan Swammerdam was the first to observe red blood cells with a microscope in 1658. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek later described them in more detail.

q: Bone surfaces are not featureless and smooth but are scarred with an array of bumps, holes, and ridges called bone markings. What is the name of a bone marking which is very large, blunt and irregularly shaped?

q.e: A trochanter is a large, blunt projection on a bone, like those at the top of the femur where muscles attach. The femur has a greater and a lesser trochanter.

q: This disease is characterized by the presence of the following symptoms: recurrent, episodic vertigo, hearing loss, a sensation of aural fullness and tinnitus. It is a balance disorder of the inner ear, first described by a French physician in 1861.

q.e: Ménière's disease is an inner-ear disorder causing vertigo attacks, hearing loss, ringing in the ears (tinnitus) and a feeling of fullness. It was named for the French physician Prosper Ménière, who described it in 1861.

q: For a few seconds after exposure to strong light we continue to see the shape of the light source even after we dont look at it any more. What are these fleeting images in our brain called?

q.e: Afterimages occur when the photoreceptors in your retina, such as rods and cones, become temporarily desensitized or fatigued after staring at a bright image, continuing to signal the brain briefly after the stimulus ends.

q: In which city is the Eiffel Tower?

q.e: Designed by Gustave Eiffel's engineering company, the 330-meter-tall iron tower was completed in Paris for the 1889 World's Fair. It stands on the Champ de Mars along the Seine River.

q: Which country is home to the Great Wall?

q.e: The Great Wall is a series of fortifications stretching thousands of miles across northern China, built over multiple dynasties to protect against nomadic invasions.

q: In which city is the Statue of Liberty?

q.e: Dedicated in 1886 as a gift from France, the Statue of Liberty stands on Liberty Island in New York Harbor, within the municipal boundaries of New York City.

q: Which country is home to the pyramids of Giza?

q.e: The Giza pyramid complex sits just outside Cairo, Egypt, and includes the Great Pyramid of Giza, built around 2560 BC for Pharaoh Khufu.

q: Which country is home to the Sydney Opera House?

q.e: Designed by Danish architect Jørn Utzon and opened in 1973, the Sydney Opera House is one of Australia's most recognizable landmarks situated on Sydney Harbour.

q: Which is the only Ancient Wonder still standing?

q.e: Built around 2560 BC as a tomb for Pharaoh Khufu, the Great Pyramid of Giza is both the oldest of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World and the only one that remains largely intact.

q: Which country gave the Statue of Liberty to the United States as a centennial gift?

q.e: France gifted the Statue of Liberty to celebrate the alliance formed during the American Revolution and the abolition of slavery. It was dedicated in New York Harbor in 1886.

q: The famous Statue of Liberty lies between New York and New Jersey. Another, much smaller Statue of Liberty of the same shape is located where?

q.e: A quarter-scale bronze replica, standing about 37 feet tall, was gifted to Paris by American expatriates in 1889 and sits on the Île aux Cygnes in the Seine.

q: What iconic world landmark, sometimes called the Crossroads of the World, was formerly named Longacre Square?

q.e: Times Square in New York City was called Longacre Square until 1904, when the New York Times moved its headquarters there and the area was renamed. It is nicknamed the "Crossroads of the World".

q: Which medieval monument is an essential part of the archaeological sites of the Greek island Rhodes?
The Palace of the Grand Master

q.e: The Palace of the Grand Master was built by the Knights Hospitaller, a medieval order of crusading knights who ruled Rhodes from 1309 to 1522. It sits inside the walled Old Town, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

q: Who commissioned the St. Basils Cathedral?

q.e: Ivan IV, known as Ivan the Terrible, ordered Saint Basil's Cathedral to be built on Red Square in Moscow between 1555 and 1561 to commemorate the capture of Kazan and Astrakhan.

q: Which was the first Egyptian pyramid?

q.e: Built around 2670 BC at Saqqara for Pharaoh Djoser, the Step Pyramid was designed by the architect Imhotep. It predated the smooth-sided Great Pyramid of Giza by roughly a century.

q: What was the original height of the Great Pyramid?

q.e: The Great Pyramid was originally about 481 feet (146.6 m) high, but it has lost its smooth outer casing stones, so it is now around 455 feet. It was the tallest man-made structure for nearly 4,000 years.

q: What is the estimated frame of time in which the Great Pyramid was constructed?

q.e: The Great Pyramid is believed to have been built in roughly 15 to 20 years, during the reign of Pharaoh Khufu around 2560 BC. That's an astonishing pace, given that it used more than 2 million stone blocks.

q: What is the length of the entire Great Wall, with all of its branches?

q.e: The "5,500 miles" figure is the commonly quoted length of the Great Wall of China including its branches. A later Chinese survey counted all wall sections from many dynasties and arrived at a much larger total of about 13,000 miles.

q: The name, Chargoggagoggmanchauggauggagoggchaubunagungamaugg, containing ten a-s, refers to what United States geographical landmark ?

q.e: That long name belongs to a lake in Webster, Massachusetts, often called Lake Webster. The name comes from a Native American word that is said to roughly mean a fishing place at the boundaries, a neutral meeting ground.

q: The cable cars of this city are the only mobile National Monument.

q.e: San Francisco's cable cars are the only moving National Historic Landmark in the United States. The system has operated since 1873 and still uses a cable running under the street.

q: The Great Pyramid of Giza, the oldest of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, was built approximately how long ago?

q.e: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built around 4,500 years ago and is the oldest of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. It's the only one of those wonders that still largely stands today.

q: Which big capital city is famous for being the site of the magnificent Saint Basils Cathedral?

q.e: Saint Basil's Cathedral, famous for its colorful onion-shaped domes, stands in Red Square in Moscow. It was commissioned by Ivan the Terrible in the 1550s to commemorate military victories.

q: The Statue of Liberty, is one of the most widely known statues in history. What country is it in?

q.e: The Statue of Liberty stands on Liberty Island in New York Harbor in the United States. It was a gift from France, dedicated in 1886, designed by Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi, and its iron framework was engineered by Gustave Eiffel.

q: Which tower, located in the Palace of Westminster in London, is usually referred to as Big Ben?

q.e: "Big Ben" is actually the nickname of the Great Bell inside the tower, not the tower itself. The tower, called the Clock Tower, was renamed the Elizabeth Tower in 2012 for Queen Elizabeth II's Diamond Jubilee.

q: Which is the tower located in Toronto, Canada, whose construction was started on February 6, 1973 by the Canadian National Railway?

q.e: The CN Tower, standing 1,815 feet (553 m) tall, was constructed by Canadian National Railway to demonstrate Canadian industrial strength and improve telecommunications in Toronto.

q: The design of which Japanese tower is based on the Eiffel Tower in Paris?

q.e: Tokyo Tower, completed in 1958, was modeled on the Eiffel Tower, but it's taller at 333 meters, compared with the Eiffel Tower's roughly 330 meters. It's painted white and international orange to meet aviation safety rules.

q: Which of the following is a tall tower in New Zealand, part of the SKYCITY Auckland casino complex.

q.e: The Sky Tower in Auckland, New Zealand, is 328 meters tall and opened in 1997. It's the tallest free-standing structure in the Southern Hemisphere and has a viewing deck and a bungee-like jump.

q: Which Australian tower was previously known as the AP Tower or The Centrepoint?

q.e: Sydney Tower, formerly called Centrepoint Tower, is 309 meters tall and opened in 1981. It is the tallest observation tower in Sydney and in the Southern Hemisphere's biggest city.

q: How old is the Great Wall of China?

q.e: Parts of the Great Wall date back more than 2,000 years, to the time of China's first emperor, Qin Shi Huang, around 221 BC. The best-known stone and brick sections were built much later, during the Ming dynasty.

q: In what direction does the Tower of Pisa lean?

q.e: The Leaning Tower of Pisa leans toward the southeast, and it began sinking soon after construction started because it was built on soft soil. Engineers reduced the tilt in the 1990s and 2000s, so it is now stable.

q: Approximately how high is the Tower of Pisa?

q.e: The Leaning Tower of Pisa is about 56 meters (183 feet) tall on its low side. Because it leans, the highest side is a bit taller than the lowest.

q: Which country is home to the huge and spectacular statue of Jesus Christ the Redeemer, constructed in 1931?

q.e: Christ the Redeemer stands on Corcovado mountain in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Completed in 1931, the 30-meter-tall statue is one of the New Seven Wonders of the World.

q: How many workers were recruited to build the Taj Mahal?

q.e: About 20,000 workers, including masons, carvers and craftsmen from across Asia, built the Taj Mahal over roughly two decades, from 1632 to 1653. Mughal emperor Shah Jahan commissioned it as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal.

q: In which city is the Colosseum?

q.e: The Colosseum, also known as the Flavian Amphitheatre, was commissioned around 70-72 CE under Emperor Vespasian in Rome, Italy. It could hold an estimated 50,000 to 80,000 spectators.

q: The Taj Mahal is in which country?

q.e: Commissioned in 1631 by Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan to house the tomb of his wife Mumtaz Mahal, the Taj Mahal is located in Agra, India.

q: Big Ben is in which city?

q.e: Big Ben is the nickname for the Great Bell inside Elizabeth Tower, which stands at the north end of the Houses of Parliament in London, England. The tower was renamed Elizabeth Tower in 2012 to honor Queen Elizabeth II's Diamond Jubilee.

q: Machu Picchu is in which country?

q.e: The 15th-century Inca citadel of Machu Picchu is located in Peru's Cusco Region, perched roughly 7,970 feet (2,430 meters) above sea level in the Andes.

q: Which Italian city has a famous leaning tower?

q.e: The Leaning Tower of Pisa is the freestanding bell tower of Pisa Cathedral, which began tilting during construction in the 12th century due to soft subsoil.

Stonehenge is a prehistoric monument located on Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire, England, constructed between roughly 3000 BC and 2000 BC. It consists of an outer ring of vertical sarsen standing stones topped by horizontal lintels.

q: In which European city can you visit the Parthenon?

q.e: The Parthenon is a former temple dedicated to Athena, built atop the Acropolis in Athens between 447 and 432 BCE during the height of the Athenian Empire.

q: More than 2 million stone blocks of 2.5 tons each make up which structure built for Khufu?

q.e: Built around 2560 BC for the Pharaoh Khufu (Cheops), the Great Pyramid of Giza contains roughly 2.3 million stone blocks and originally stood about 146.6 meters (481 feet) tall.

q: Which tunnel runs between Folkestone and Coquelles?

q.e: The Channel Tunnel stretches 31.3 miles (50.5 km) beneath the English Channel, linking Folkestone in Kent, England, to Coquelles in Pas-de-Calais, France. It opened for regular service in 1994.

q: Which huge statue of Helios was destroyed by an earthquake and later sold for scrap?

q.e: Erected around 280 BC on the Greek island of Rhodes, the roughly 108-foot (33-meter) bronze statue collapsed in a major earthquake in 226 BC. It remained in ruins until an Arab force captured the island in 654 AD and sold the metal to a merchant.

q: Nelsons Column, built to commemorate Admiral Horatio Nelsons death, is a monument in this famous London square.

q.e: Nelson's Column stands roughly 169 feet (51.6 m) tall in central London's Trafalgar Square. It honors Admiral Horatio Nelson, who died leading the Royal Navy to victory at the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805.

q: Attila the Huns palace and headquarters in Europe were situated on the territory of which modern country?

q.e: Attila the Hun's capital is believed to have been on the Great Hungarian Plain, between the Danube and Tisza rivers, in what is now Hungary. The exact site has never been found.

q: Which peculiarity of the Great Pyramid interior distinguishes it from the other pyramids?
The ascending passages and upper chambers
The larger number of its chambers

q.e: Unlike other pyramids, whose chambers are mostly underground or at ground level, the Great Pyramid has a Grand Gallery and upper chambers that sit high inside the structure. These ascending passages lead to the King's Chamber.

q: What year was the Eiffel Tower constructed?

q.e: The Eiffel Tower was constructed as the grand entrance arch for the 1889 Exposition Universelle, which celebrated the centennial of the French Revolution. Construction took just over two years, finishing in March 1889.

q: What is the other name of the Venus de Milo statue?

q.e: Discovered on the Greek island of Milos in 1820, the Venus de Milo is also called 'Aphrodite of Milos' because Venus is the Roman name for the Greek goddess of love, Aphrodite.

q: When Helen Keller passed away, in what cathedral were her ashes placed?

q.e: Helen Keller died in 1968, and her ashes were placed at the Washington National Cathedral, next to those of her teacher, Anne Sullivan. She was deaf and blind, and she became a famous author and activist.

q: Arc de Triomphe is a monument that stands in the centre of the Place de lÉtoile in this city.

q.e: Commissioned by Napoleon in 1806, the Arc de Triomphe stands at the center of the Place Charles de Gaulle (historically the Place de l'Étoile) in Paris, honoring those who fought for France.

q: What is the oldest cathedral in Germany?

q.e: Trier Cathedral, in Germany's oldest city, is the country's oldest cathedral, and it sits on a site first built in the 4th century. Emperor Constantine's mother, Helena, is linked to its early history.

q: This US state, known as the Equality State, is home of Devils Tower, featured in the movie Close Encounters of the Third Kind.

q.e: Wyoming earned the nickname Equality State after becoming the first territory to grant women the right to vote in 1869; it is also home to Devils Tower, which President Theodore Roosevelt declared the first US National Monument in 1906.

q: The Statue of Zeus, a Wonder of the Ancient World created in the ancient city of Olympia in 435 BC, was made primarily of what material?

q.e: The Statue of Zeus at Olympia was made of ivory plates and gold over a wooden frame, a style called chryselephantine. It was about 12 meters tall and showed Zeus seated on a throne.

q: This city is situated at the foot of the Alborz mountain range and one of its most famous landmarks is the Azadi Tower.

q.e: Tehran, Iran's capital, lies at the foot of the Alborz mountains, and the Azadi Tower, completed in 1971, is its best-known symbol. It was originally called the Shahyad Tower.

q: Where was the great Statue of Zeus located?

q.e: The Statue of Zeus was located in the Temple of Zeus at Olympia, Greece, the site of the ancient Olympic Games. The statue was lost, probably destroyed in a fire in late antiquity.

q: Where would you find the only royal palace to serve as an official residence in the USA?

q.e: Iolani Palace in Honolulu served as the official royal residence for King Kalakaua and Queen Liliuokalani until the overthrow of the Hawaiian monarchy in 1893. Completed in 1882, it even featured electric lights before the White House did.

q: Buckingham Palace, the official home of the Queen of England, was built in what year?

q.e: The original Buckingham House was built in 1703 for the Duke of Buckingham, and the British royal family later turned it into a palace. It's the monarch's official London residence, which since 2022 means King Charles III.

q: The design of this London monument, situated near Speakers Corner in Hyde Park, is based on the design of the triumphal arch of Constantine, located in Rome.

q.e: Marble Arch was designed by John Nash in the 1820s after the Arch of Constantine in Rome. It originally stood in front of Buckingham Palace before being moved to its current site near Speakers' Corner in 1851.

q: Brussels' famous comedic statue, Manneken Pis, has a female counterpart. Where will you find the Jeanneke Pis?

q.e: Jeanneke Pis is a small statue of a girl squatting, in Brussels, put up in 1987 as a counterpart to the Manneken Pis. Both are in the Belgian capital's old city.

q: The statue of the Little Mermaid is in this harbour.

q.e: Sculpted by Edvard Eriksen and unveiled in 1913, the bronze statue of the Little Mermaid sits along the Langelinie promenade in Copenhagen's harbor.

q: The Leaning Tower of Pisa is actually a campanile and has this number of bells.

q.e: The Leaning Tower of Pisa is the bell tower (campanile) of Pisa Cathedral, and it holds seven bells, one for each note of the musical major scale. Galileo is said to have used the tower for experiments with falling objects.

q: This TV tower in Shanghai, China, was designed around a Tang Dynasty poem.

q.e: The Oriental Pearl Tower, completed in 1994, has spheres inspired by a Tang dynasty poem about pearls falling onto a jade plate. It's 468 meters tall and a symbol of modern Shanghai.

q: Which 350-meter tower in Las Vegas, Nevada, is actually a famous hotel and casino?

q.e: The Stratosphere Tower, now called the STRAT, stands 350 meters (1,149 ft) tall on the Las Vegas Strip. It has thrill rides on top, and it's the tallest observation tower in the United States.

q: What is the name of the tower that was built in Kuwait before the Iraqi invasion on August 2, 1990?

q.e: Liberation Tower in Kuwait City began construction in 1987, and its work was interrupted by the Iraqi invasion in 1990. After Kuwait was liberated in 1991, it was renamed and later completed in 1996.

q: What was the main reason for constructing the Great Wall of China?
To keep citizens from immigrating to other countries

q.e: The Great Wall was built to defend against raids by nomadic groups from the north, and it also helped control borders and trade routes. It was built and rebuilt by many Chinese dynasties over centuries.

q: Which Chinese Dynasty is responsible for the construction of most of the Great Wall of China?

q.e: While Emperor Qin Shi Huang connected early earthen ramparts in the 3rd century BCE, the iconic stone and brick wall standing today was built mainly during the Ming Dynasty (1368–1644).

q: About how many years did the Tower of Pisa take to build?

q.e: The Leaning Tower of Pisa took almost 200 years to complete, from 1173 to 1372, because construction was interrupted by wars and by the building's sinking. Builders waited for the soil to settle, which may have kept it from falling.

q: This landmark built by Constantine the Great stands in the center of Bethlehem.

q.e: The Church of the Nativity in Bethlehem stands over the site traditionally believed to be Jesus's birthplace. The first church was commissioned by Constantine the Great and completed around 339 AD.

q: Where is the Taj Mahal located?

q.e: Commissioned by the Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan in 1631 as a mausoleum for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, the white marble monument sits on the banks of the Yamuna River in Agra, India.

q: This simple farm house at the seaside was transformed into a palace for King George IV.

q.e: The Royal Pavilion in Brighton, England, began as a modest farmhouse and was turned into a lavish palace by the architect John Nash for the Prince Regent, later George IV. Its design is Indian-inspired, with onion domes.

q: What is the name of the landmark office complex in downtown Detroit, where General Motors headquarters is located?

q.e: The Renaissance Center, with its cluster of towers on the Detroit riverfront, has served as General Motors' world headquarters since 1996. It was originally built in the 1970s as a revitalization project.

q: What landmark is known in the Egyptian language as ipet resyt, or the southern sanctuary?

q.e: Luxor Temple, on the east bank of the Nile in Egypt, was known to the ancient Egyptians as ipet resyt, "the southern sanctuary". It was linked to nearby Karnak by an avenue of sphinxes.

q: What landmark near Islamic Cairo was home to Egypts rulers for 700 years?

q.e: The Citadel of Saladin in Cairo, begun in 1176 by Saladin, was the seat of Egypt's rulers for about 700 years. It stands on a hill overlooking Cairo's Islamic district.

q: In what palace is the famous Sistine Chapel located?

q.e: The Sistine Chapel is in the Apostolic Palace in Vatican City, the pope's official residence. Michelangelo painted its famous ceiling between 1508 and 1512.

q: Which landmark in Greece is also known as Cecropia?

q.e: The Acropolis of Athens was once known as Cecropia, after the legendary first king of Athens, Cecrops. The Parthenon, built in the 5th century BC, is its most famous building.

q: Upon completion, the Washington Monument, built to commemorate the first US President, became the worlds tallest structure. What is the name of the architect who designed it?

q.e: Robert Mills designed the Washington Monument, a 555-foot obelisk completed in 1884. It was the tallest structure in the world until the Eiffel Tower surpassed it in 1889.

q: The Great Pyramid of Giza claimed to be the worlds tallest man-made structure for around four millennia. Along which river is the monument located?

q.e: The Great Pyramid stands on the Giza plateau, on the west bank of the Nile near Cairo. It remained the world's tallest man-made structure until the 14th century, when Lincoln Cathedral in England surpassed it.

q: What large Art Deco statue has become an icon of Rio de Janeiro and Brazil?

q.e: Christ the Redeemer, an Art Deco statue completed in 1931, towers above Rio de Janeiro from the top of Corcovado mountain. It was designed by French sculptor Paul Landowski and Brazilian engineer Heitor da Silva Costa.

q: In what Spanish city is the Alhambra Palace located?

q.e: The Alhambra is a hilltop palace-fortress in Granada, in southern Spain. It was built mostly in the 13th and 14th centuries by the Nasrid rulers, the last Muslim dynasty in Spain.

q: The monument called The Egg, located in Saint Antonio, Ibiza, was erected in honor of which great explorer?

q.e: The "Egg of Columbus" monument in Sant Antoni de Portmany, Ibiza, honors Christopher Columbus. Its egg shape refers to the story of Columbus standing an egg on its end to prove a point.

q: He was, arguably, the greatest architect in British history. He designed St. Pauls Cathedral in London.

q.e: Sir Christopher Wren was commissioned to rebuild 52 parish churches across London after the Great Fire of 1666, culminating in his masterpiece, St. Paul's Cathedral, which was completed in 1710.

q: The Christ the Redeemer statue overlooks which city?

q.e: The 98-foot (30-meter) Art Deco statue stands atop Mount Corcovado, looking over Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, since its completion in 1931.

q: Petra, the city carved into rock, is in which country?

q.e: Petra, established around the 4th century BCE as the capital of the Nabataean Kingdom, is located in southwestern Jordan and is famed for its rock-cut architecture like Al-Khazneh (The Treasury).

q: Angkor Wat is in which country?

q.e: Angkor Wat is a massive temple complex located in northwest Cambodia, originally constructed in the early 12th century by King Suryavarman II as a Hindu temple dedicated to Vishnu.

q: What is the tallest building in the world?

q.e: The Burj Khalifa in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, stands at 828 meters (2,717 feet) tall and has held the record for the world's tallest building since its completion in 2010. Shanghai Tower is the second-tallest at 632 meters (2,073 feet).

q: The prehistoric monument Stonehenge is located in which English county?
