q.e: Stonehenge stands on Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire, England, with its earliest earthworks dating back to around 3000 BCE. Its iconic central ring of sarsen stones and inner bluestones were erected around 2500 BCE.

q: The Itaipu on the Brazil–Paraguay border is one of the world's largest what?

q.e: Completed in 1984 on the Paraná River between Brazil and Paraguay, the Itaipu Dam is a massive hydroelectric power plant that regularly rivals China's Three Gorges Dam in total annual electricity production.

q: Built as a Roman Catholic mission, which site did Santa Anna besiege in 1836?

q.e: Originally established in the 18th century as Mission San Antonio de Valero, the Alamo fell to Mexican General Santa Anna in March 1836 after a 13-day siege.

q: How tall is Chicago's Sears Tower?

q.e: Chicago's Sears Tower, now the Willis Tower, is 1,451 feet (442 meters) tall to its roof, and about 1,729 feet with its antennas. It was the world's tallest building from 1974 to 1998.

q: Who built the famous monument Taj Mahal?

q.e: Mughal emperor Shah Jahan commissioned the white marble mausoleum in Agra in 1631 to honor his favorite wife, Mumtaz Mahal. The complex took around two decades and thousands of artisans to complete.

q: The Great Pyramid of Giza is believed to have been built as the tomb of this Egyptian pharaoh.

q.e: Built during the Fourth Dynasty around 2560 BC, the Great Pyramid of Giza was constructed as a monumental tomb for Pharaoh Khufu, known to the ancient Greeks as Cheops.

q: Who built the Statue of Liberty, which was a gift from France to the US?

q.e: French sculptor Frédéric-Auguste Bartholdi designed the copper statue, while civil engineer Gustave Eiffel created its internal structural framework. It was dedicated in New York Harbor on October 28, 1886.

q: Why was the Taj Mahal built by Mughal emperor Shah Jahan?
It was built in memory of his wife, Mumtaz Mahal
It was built as a palace for the emperor.
It was built as a temple for the alter of eternal sanctity.
It was built as an amusement park attraction.

q.e: Shah Jahan commissioned the ivory-white marble mausoleum in 1631 to house the tomb of his favorite wife, Mumtaz Mahal, who died during childbirth. Located in Agra, India, construction of the complex took over twenty years.

q: The wedding ceremony of Charles, Prince of Wales and Lady Diana Spencer took place at this famous landmark, which is also the seat of the Bishop of London.

q.e: Prince Charles and Lady Diana Spencer married at St Paul's Cathedral in London on July 29, 1981, in front of a TV audience of millions. The cathedral, designed by Christopher Wren, is the seat of the Bishop of London.

q: This large, half-human statue is situated at the west bank of the Nile River.

q.e: Carved from a single ridge of limestone, the Great Sphinx stands roughly 66 feet (20 meters) high on the west bank of the Nile at Giza. It features the body of a lion and the head of an Egyptian pharaoh, typically thought to represent Khafre.

q: The Colossus of Rhodes was a giant statue, erected at the Greek island Rhodes harbor in 3rd century BC. Which ancient Greek god did the statue depict?

q.e: Constructed around 280 BC, the roughly 108-foot (33-meter) bronze statue represented Helios, the sun god and patron deity of the island of Rhodes.

q: Which classical Greek sculptor designed the magnificent Statue of Zeus?

q.e: The Greek sculptor Phidias created the Statue of Zeus at Olympia, and he also oversaw the sculptures of the Parthenon in Athens. His statues are among the most admired works of ancient Greece.

q: In this four-mile area know as the strip one can find a replica of the Statue of Liberty, gondolas floating on canals, the castles of Camelot, and a replica of the Eiffel Tower. Best of all what happens in this city stays in this city.

q.e: The Las Vegas Strip features famous themed resorts including New York-New York, The Venetian, Excalibur, and Paris Las Vegas. The iconic marketing slogan What Happens Here, Stays Here was introduced by the Las Vegas Convention and Visitors Authority in 2003.

q: This cathedral, situated on Ludgate Hill, dates back to the 17th century and is the seat of the Bishop of London.

q.e: Designed by architect Sir Christopher Wren in the English Baroque style, the present cathedral was built between 1675 and 1710 following the Great Fire of London.

q: Following his idea of strong Italy, this Italian ruler wanted to fix the Leaning Tower of Pisa, so cement was poured into its foundation.

q.e: In the 1930s, Benito Mussolini's government poured concrete into the foundations of the Leaning Tower of Pisa in an effort to straighten it, but this actually made the tilt worse. Engineers solved the problem only decades later.

q: Which tall tower in Malaysia, built in 1995, is a place for annual races up the stairs to the top?

q.e: Menara Kuala Lumpur (KL Tower), completed in 1995, stands 421 meters tall and hosts the annual "Tower Run", a race up its 2,058 steps. It is used for telecommunications as well as sightseeing.

q: Which famous Moscow TV and radio tower was designed by Nikolai Nikitin?

q.e: The Ostankino Tower, designed by Nikolai Nikitin and completed in 1967, is a 540-meter TV and radio tower in Moscow. It was the tallest free-standing structure in the world until 1975.

q: Whose statue is at the top of Philadelphias City Hall?

q.e: Alexander Milne Calder sculpted the 37-foot-tall bronze statue of Pennsylvania founder William Penn, which was hoisted atop Philadelphia City Hall's tower in 1894.

q: What palace is known as the official residence of the President of Brazil?

q.e: The Palácio da Alvorada, designed by Oscar Niemeyer, is the official residence of Brazil's president in the capital, Brasília. It was completed in 1958 and is known for its elegant curved columns.

q: Which architectural landmark is considered the epitome of Byzantine architecture in Constantinople?

q.e: Commissioned by Byzantine Emperor Justinian I and completed in 537 AD, the Hagia Sophia was famed for its massive pendentive dome that revolutionized medieval architecture.

q: What is the official name of the Statue of Liberty, which commemorates the centennial of the signing of the US Declaration of Independence?
Lady Liberty Entering the New World

q.e: Sculptor Frédéric-Auguste Bartholdi originally titled the monument 'Liberty Enlightening the World' ('La Liberté éclairant le monde') when it was dedicated in 1886.

q: The former Winter Palace in Saint Petersburg, Russia now contains one of the worlds greatest museums of art and culture. What is it called?

q.e: Catherine the Great founded the State Hermitage Museum in 1764 when she acquired a collection of 255 paintings from Berlin merchant Johann Ernst Gotzkowsky. The Winter Palace served as the official winter residence of Russian tsars until 1917.

q: Where in St Petersburg can you find the famous statue of Peter the Great on horseback, sometimes called The Bronze Horseman?
In Decembrists Square, near the Admiralty
In front of the Finland Railway Station

q.e: The Bronze Horseman, a statue of Peter the Great on a rearing horse, stands in Senate Square (also called Decembrists' Square) in Saint Petersburg, near the Admiralty. Catherine the Great commissioned it, and Pushkin wrote a famous poem about it.

q: This statue, which was enshrined in 2005, is 108-metre (354 ft) tall.
Buddhist statue of Guanyin, Sanya, China
Yellow Chinese emperors Huangdi and Yandi, China
Statue of Peter I, Moscow, Russia

q.e: The Guanyin of the South Sea of Sanya stands about 108 meters tall on Hainan Island, China, and was consecrated in 2005. It depicts the Buddhist goddess of mercy.

q: Chichén Itzá was built by which civilization?

q.e: Chichén Itzá was a major pre-Columbian city built by the Maya civilization in Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula between roughly the 6th and 10th centuries CE. The Aztecs flourished much later in central Mexico.

q: The Alhambra palace is in which country?

q.e: The Alhambra is a medieval palace and fortress complex built in Granada, Spain, primarily during the Nasrid dynasty in the 13th and 14th centuries.

q: Finished under Ptolemy II, which Ancient Wonder stood over 400 feet tall?

q.e: Built on the island of Pharos around 280 BC during the reign of Ptolemy II Philadelphus, the Lighthouse of Alexandria stood roughly 330 to 380 feet tall. The Colossus of Rhodes was much shorter, standing about 108 feet high.

q: The Great Pyramid is one of the pyramids of the Giza pyramid complex. Which monument is NOT a part of that complex?

q.e: The Giza complex has the pyramids of Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure, plus the Great Sphinx. The Pyramid of Amenemhat I is at Lisht, far to the south, and isn't part of it.

q: Who ordered the construction of Dolmabahçe Palace?

q.e: Sultan Abdülmecid I ordered the Dolmabahçe Palace, built between 1843 and 1856 on the Bosphorus in Istanbul. It's a blend of Ottoman and European architecture and replaced the Topkapı Palace as the sultans' main residence.

q: This massive step pyramid (about 210 by 150 feet in size) is the most well-preserved monument from the age of the Sumerians. In the 4th century BC the river Euphrates changed its course and the city, in which this pyramid was built, was abandoned.

q.e: The Ziggurat of Ur, in what is now Iraq, was built around 2100 BC by King Ur-Nammu. It's the best preserved ziggurat, a stepped temple-tower, from ancient Sumer.

q: This building inspired the Biblical myth of the Tower of Babel. It was a gigantic seven-stage multicolored pyramidal tower, over 300 feet high. However, only the ground plan and traces of the three stairs leading up to it have been preserved.

q.e: The Etemenanki, a ziggurat dedicated to Marduk in ancient Babylon, is widely believed to have inspired the Biblical story of the Tower of Babel. Little of it survives today.

q: What is the name of the tall tower in Rotterdam, built specially for the 1960 Floriade in the Netherlands?

q.e: The Euromast in Rotterdam was built in 1960 for the Floriade garden festival and is about 185 meters tall including a later extension. It's among the best-known landmarks of the Dutch port city.

q: This building, designed by Louis H. Sullivan, is one of the most famous early skyscrapers housing a flagship department store. This store appears in Theodore Dreisers novel Sister Carrie. It was named a National Historic Landmark in 1975. Name the store.

q.e: The Carson Pirie Scott building in Chicago, designed by Louis Sullivan, is famous for its ornate iron decoration at the entrance. It appears in Theodore Dreiser's 1900 novel Sister Carrie and is now known as the Sullivan Center.

q: Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, the first president of the Republic of Turkey, used this palace as a presidential residence.

q.e: Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, founder of modern Turkey, used Dolmabahçe Palace as his presidential residence in Istanbul and died there in 1938. The palace clocks are set to the time of his death, 9:05.

q: I dont speak, I cannot hear, but I always tell the truth.

q.e: A mirror shows exactly what is in front of it, so it "tells the truth" without a voice or ears. This is a classic riddle, and its answer comes from taking the description literally.

q: How does this proverb continue: The squeaking wheel gets ...

q.e: The traditional American proverb 'The squeaking wheel gets the grease' means that the most vocal or insistent complaints are the ones that receive immediate attention and resources.

q: If you were running a race and passed the person in second place, what place would you be in?

q.e: Passing the runner in second place means you take their position, placing you in 2nd place. To take 1st place, you would have to overtake the person leading the race.

q: A row consists of 10 letters. The first six are - Z, O, T, T, F, F. Which is the tenth letter?

q.e: The sequence represents the first letters of numbers starting at zero: Zero, One, Two, Three, Four, Five, Six, Seven, Eight, Nine. The tenth number is Nine, making the letter N.

q: I always go up and down the stairs without moving.

q.e: This classic riddle describes a stair runner or carpet, which spans the full flight of stairs from top to bottom while remaining stationary.

q: If the mother of a boy spanks him and then his father comes and does the same, who hurts the most?

q.e: The boy is the one being spanked, so he is hurting the most. Riddles like this tempt you to focus on the parents and overthink.

q: Three cats can eat 3 mice in 1.5 hours. How long will it take 10 cats to eat 20 mice?

q.e: Three cats eating 3 mice in 1.5 hours means each cat takes 1.5 hours to eat 1 mouse. Therefore, 10 cats can eat 10 mice in 1.5 hours, and 20 mice in 3 hours.

q: Which letter comes next in this series: W-L-C-N-I-T-?

q.e: The letters are the first letters of the words in the sentence "Which Letter Comes Next In This Series", so the next letter is S. Always check whether a letter sequence spells out a hidden phrase.

q: Take two apples from three apples and what do you have?

q.e: This classic riddle hinges on reading carefully: if you literally take two apples into your hands from a group of three, you are holding those two apples.

q: I have four legs in the morning, two legs in the afternoon and three legs in the evening. What am I?

q.e: This is the famous Riddle of the Sphinx solved by Oedipus: a human crawls on all fours as a baby, walks on two legs in adulthood, and uses a cane in old age.

q: Why do Chinese people eat more rice than Japanese people?
Because Chinese people are more than Japanese people
Because Chinese rice ripens more quickly than Japanese rice
Because Japanese people export rice for other countries and the Chinese dont
Because Chinese rice is more delicious than Japanese rice

q.e: It is a pun on "more": there are simply more Chinese people than Japanese people. China's population is more than ten times Japan's.
It is a pun: the letter Y sounds like the word "why", and a smart person is always asking why. Word-play riddles often depend on how letters sound.

q: What is the number of men born last year in USA?

q.e: This is a wordplay riddle: human beings are born as babies or infants, not as grown men. Therefore, no 'men' were born anywhere last year.

q: This is what you can see once in a minute, twice in a moment, but never in a thousand years.

q.e: This classic word puzzle plays on spelling rather than units of time: the letter M appears once in the word 'minute', twice in 'moment', and not at all in the phrase 'a thousand years'.

q: What is heavier a pound of bricks or a pound of feathers?
There is no way to tell

q.e: Both items weigh exactly one pound regardless of material. While a pound of feathers occupies vastly more volume due to lower density, mass and gravitational pull remain identical.

q: If I had $654,987, how much change is that?

q.e: One dollar equals 100 cents, so multiply 654,987 by 100 to get 65,498,700 cents. Converting to a smaller unit always means multiplying.

q: A woman once said about a man, I am not his wife but this mans mother is the mother-in-law of my mother. What were the man and the woman?

q.e: If the man's mother is the mother-in-law of the woman's mother, she is the mother of the woman's father. That makes the man her father, and the woman his daughter. Work riddles like this out one family link at a time.

q: The name of what is coded in the following: 86,smopuim?
the name of a software product

q.e: This is a coded-name puzzle whose solution is a software product's name. Cipher puzzles often replace letters with numbers or symbols, or reverse and shift the characters.

q: What on earth could dance, and live and die? Without legs, or lungs, or being alive?

q.e: Fire dances as flickering flames, feeds on oxygen like breath, and dies when its fuel is exhausted, fitting all the clues in the classic riddle.

q: Im one of five, and Im not alive. The one who sent me forth became king, the one who got me died. What am I?

q.e: It's one of the five smooth stones that David took when he faced Goliath. David, who later became king of Israel, slung one stone that killed the giant.

q: I have eight to spare, in case I lose my one. Im not a number. What am I?

q.e: This riddle plays on the popular folklore that cats have nine lives, meaning they have eight spare lives if they lose one.

q: A farmer had 12 sheep and 3 cows. All of the animals except 9 sheep died. How many animals did he have left in his farm?

q.e: The phrasing states that all animals died except nine sheep, which means exactly nine sheep survived and all the cows perished.

q: An old man was looking at a photograph of a young man. Somebody asked him who it was. The mans answer was the following: Brothers and sisters, I have none. But that mans father is my fathers son. Who was in the photograph?

q.e: "My father's son" must be the speaker himself, since he has no brothers. So the man in the photograph has the speaker as his father, which makes him the speaker's son.

q: What number comes next in the row - 31, 28, 31, 30, ?

q.e: This sequence lists the number of days in each month starting from January (31, 28, 31, 30), meaning the next month is May, which has 31 days.
This is the "look-and-say" sequence: each term describes the one before it. 13112221 is read as "one 1, one 3, two 1s, three 2s, one 1", which gives 1113213211.

q: What is the largest number you can write out with numbers 1, 2, and 3?

q.e: Using exponents, 3 to the power of 21 gives 10,460,353,203, far bigger than 123 or 321. Raising a big number to a big power grows faster than any other arrangement.

q: You have a square and a circle and the perimeter of the square is equal to the circumference of the circle. Which of the two figures covers a bigger area?
No conclusion can be drawn from the given information.

q.e: By the isoperimetric inequality, among all two-dimensional shapes with a fixed perimeter, a circle encloses the maximum possible area. For a perimeter P, a circle covers about 0.0796 times P squared, while a square covers only 0.0625 times P squared.

q: At the beginning of the day, I was behind a car at a stoplight, whose vanity plate read: 4SBWIU. What is the driver of this car most likely a fan of?

q.e: The plate reads 4S BWIU, a pun on "Force be with you", the famous line from Star Wars. Vanity plates often use numbers and letters to stand for sounds.

q: I went to my favorite restaurant to pick up some carry out for an early dinner. I saw the owners car parked out front. The vanity plate asked a question. What do you suppose the plate read?

q.e: The plate reads E10YET, which sounds like "Eaten yet?". Say the plate aloud to hear it, since "E10" sounds like "eaten".
This is a classic pun based on the phrase two lips. Tulips are perennial spring-blooming geophytes in the lily family.

q: 12 candles were alight. The wind blew out 5 of them. How many candles were left?

q.e: All 12 candles are still there initially, though riddles often play on the fact that the 7 burning ones will eventually melt away while the 5 blown out remain intact.

q: A team of two horses ran for 3 miles. How many miles did each of the horses run?

q.e: Because the two horses were hitched together as a team, each individual horse covered the full 3-mile distance simultaneously.

q: How many times does the digit 3 occur in the numbers from 1 to 50?

q.e: The digit 3 appears in the units place 5 times (3, 13, 23, 33, 43) and in the tens place 10 times (30 through 39). Because 33 contains two 3s, the total count is 5 + 10 = 15 occurrences.

q: A lion can eat a sheep in 2 hours, a wolf - in 3 hours, and a dog - in 6 hours. How long will it take the three animals to eat a sheep if they eat together?

q.e: In one hour, the lion eats 1/2 of the sheep, the wolf eats 1/3, and the dog eats 1/6. Adding those fractions gives 3/6 plus 2/6 plus 1/6, which equals exactly 1 whole sheep eaten in 1 hour.

q: Suppose youre taking a multiple-choice quiz. One question has three choices - A, B, C. You do not know the answer and guess A. The instructor then announces that C is incorrect. Should you switch to B before turning in your paper?
It depends on when the announcement was made

q.e: This works like the Monty Hall problem: your first guess has a 1 in 3 chance, so the chance that the right answer is among the others is 2 in 3. Once C is ruled out, switching to B gives you a 2 in 3 chance, as long as the instructor knew the answer and picked a wrong option.

q: The train leaves in 2 minutes and the distance to the train station is 2 miles. If you drive the first mile at 30 miles/h, at what speed should you drive the second mile?

q.e: To arrive in 2 minutes you needed an average of 60 mph over 2 miles. Driving the first mile at 30 mph already used the full 2 minutes, so no speed can save you.

q: One watermelon weighs 10kg (22 lbs) plus the half of its own weight. How much does it weigh?

q.e: If a watermelon weighs 10 kg plus half its weight, the 10 kg must represent the other half. Doubling 10 kg gives the total weight of 20 kg (44 lbs).
The differences between consecutive numbers increase by two each step: +3, +5, +7, +9, and +11. Adding the next difference of 13 to 39 gives 52.

q: Joe had 29 pairs of socks. How many socks did he have?

q.e: Since one pair contains 2 individual items, 29 pairs equals 29 multiplied by 2, which gives 58 socks.

q: One camera could take 350 pictures and Bob bought 3 cameras of the same type. How many pictures could he take?

q.e: Three cameras can each take 350 pictures, so 3 × 350 = 1,050. The question just needs a simple multiplication.

q: In an office building, there are 350 windows and half as many doors. How many doors are there in 3 office buildings?

q.e: Half of 350 windows gives 175 doors per building, so three buildings have 3 × 175 = 525 doors. Read each step carefully to avoid mixing up the window and door counts.

q: After a long walk, two sons and two fathers find three apples. Each of them has an apple and they all go their way. How is that possible?
they were a boy, his father and his grandfather
one of them had a hidden apple

q.e: The group consists of three generations: a grandfather, his son, and his grandson. The middle man is both a son to the grandfather and a father to the boy, making two fathers and two sons.

q: What number multiplied by 10 equals the square of the same number, times 5?

q.e: Set up the equation 10x = 5x². Divide both sides by 5x to get 2 = x, so the number is 2. (Zero also works, but it's the trivial answer.)

q: Bob has a book of 100 pages and in 10 seconds he can count out 10 pages. What is the shortest time in which Bob can define where the 60th page is?

q.e: Bob counts back from the end: page 60 is 40 pages from the last page of 100. At one page per second, counting 40 pages takes 40 seconds, faster than counting 60 from the front.

q: A fish costs a dollar and half a fish. How much do 5 fish cost?

q.e: If a fish costs $1 plus half a fish (F = 1 + 0.5F), subtracting 0.5F shows that half a fish equals $1, making one whole fish $2. Therefore, five fish cost $10.

q: A father has seven sons, and each son has one sister. How many children does the father have?

q.e: All seven brothers share the same single sister, meaning there are seven boys and one girl, totaling eight children.

q: Its quarter past three. Of how many degrees is the angle formed by the hands of the clock at this moment?

q.e: At 3:15, the minute hand points directly at the 3, but the hour hand has moved a quarter of the way toward the 4. Since each hour span is 30 degrees, one-quarter of 30 degrees equals 7.5 degrees.

q: This food is one of the most versatile and convenient. You can boil it, fry it, poach it, scramble it, use it in baking. What is it?

q.e: Eggs can be prepared through numerous methods such as boiling, poaching, and frying, while also serving as crucial binders and leaveners in baking.

q: What letter should be added the group of letters P, N, N, E, S, O, R, H, E, T, and I to form a twelve-letter word that is related to blood?

q.e: The letters plus Y spell "hypertension", a medical term for high blood pressure. When a puzzle lets you add one letter, try common word endings or beginnings.

q: Each morning I appear To lie at your feet, All day I follow you No matter how fast you run, Yet I nearly die In the midday sun. What am I?

q.e: Your shadow stretches long across the ground during the early morning and late afternoon due to low sun angles, but shrinks to almost nothing beneath you around midday when the sun is directly overhead.

q: I am related to the water but I am not wet. I am related to a shadow but I am multicolored. I create an illusion but show what is real. What am I?

q.e: A mirror shows a reflection: it relates to water (reflective surfaces), has no wetness, and gives an illusion of space while showing what is truly in front of it. The riddle's contradictions all describe it.

q: A contestant on a TV show had to answer 26 questions. For each correct answer he received 8 points, while a wrong answer penalized him 5 points. How many answers did the man answer correctly, bearing in mind that he eventually had 0 points?

q.e: If he got c right and 26 minus c wrong, then 8c = 5(26 − c). That gives 13c = 130, so he got 10 correct and 16 wrong.

q: My first stop was the supermarket. When I had completed my shopping and was in the parking lot, I spied this snazzy auto with the following vanity plate: 10S42. What sport is the driver of this vehicle most likely a fan of?

q.e: The plate 10S42 reads "Tennis, too", since "10" sounds like "ten" and "42" sounds like "for two". Say the characters out loud.

q: On the on-ramp to the freeway, I was behind an auto with the following plate: 4IS. What is the likely profession of the driver of this car?

q.e: The plate 4IS sounds like "for eyes", so the driver is likely an eye doctor, an optometrist. Vanity plates are often puns on how characters sound.

q: Nine passengers carried with them enough food for five days. Several other passengers joined the first group and they all shared the same food, which was now enough for three days. How many passengers joined the first group?

q.e: Nine passengers had food for 5 days, which is 45 passenger-days. For the same food to last 3 days, 45 ÷ 3 = 15 people must share it, so 6 more people joined.

q: A pole is 20 m high. An ant is climbing it as follows - every day she ascends 5 m and every night she descends 4 m. In how many days will the ant be on the top of the post?

q.e: The ant gains a net of 1 meter every 24 hours, reaching 15 meters by the end of night 15. On day 16, she climbs 5 meters to reach the full 20-meter top before sliding down.

q: In a basket there are three sorts of apples. How many apples do you have to take from the basket to make sure you have at least 2 apples of the same sort?

q.e: By the Pigeonhole Principle, if you take 3 apples, each could potentially be a different sort. Taking a 4th apple guarantees that at least two must belong to the same variety.

q: An old potter was selling pots. Once, a woman came and bought a pot for its sticker price. She had to pay $1 plus half its price. What was the price?

q.e: Let the price be p. She paid $1 plus half of p, so p = 1 + p/2. That means p/2 = 1, so p = $2.

q: Four glasses and a jug weigh as mush as 17 iron balls do. The jug weighs as much as a glass and 7 balls. How many balls does the jug weigh?

q.e: Call the jug weight j and a glass weight j − 7. Then 4(j − 7) + j = 17, so 5j = 45 and j = 9 balls.

q: Somewhere, there is a very interesting village. And whats so interesting about it? Well, in this village there is a barber, a very special barber. He cuts the hair of everybody in the village that doesnt cut his own hair. Who then cuts the barbers hair?
Such village cannot exist, it is a paradox

q.e: This is the barber paradox, a version of Russell's paradox. If the barber cuts his own hair, he shouldn't, and if he doesn't, he should, so no such barber can exist.

q: There is a branch with 10 birds on it. I shot 2 of them and then 1 more. How many birds are left on the branch?

q.e: In this classic riddle, the loud sound of the first gunshot frightens away all the remaining live birds, leaving zero birds on the branch.

q: If you have in your suitcase 6 white socks, 4 red socks, 8 green socks, and 2 brown socks, how many socks would you have to pull out (without looking at them) to be sure you have a matching pair?

q.e: Because there are four distinct colors of socks, the pigeonhole principle guarantees that drawing five socks ensures at least two will share the same color. Drawing only four could leave you with one sock of each color.

q: One iPod can hold 950 songs and 3 movies. How many iPods of this model would one person have to buy to have 27 movies and 8550 songs?

q.e: Each iPod holds 3 movies, so 27 movies need 9 iPods. Eight thousand five hundred fifty songs at 950 per iPod is also 9, so the answers agree.

q: A monster had double the amount of eyes he had ears, triple the amount of ears he had legs, and had six legs. How many eyes did he have?

q.e: With six legs, the monster has 3 × 6 = 18 ears, and double that is 36 eyes. Just work forward from the legs.

q: Five years ago the sum of the age of a sister and a brother was 8. What will be the same sum in 5 years?

q.e: Five years ago the two ages added up to 8, so now they add up to 8 + 5 + 5 = 18. Five years from now, add another 10 to get 28.

q: A cowboy was looking after 100 animals (oxen, cows and calves). For his job he was paid $100 (for every ox he received $10, for every cow $5 and for every calf $0.5). How many were the oxen, the cows and the calves?

q.e: Solve with trial and error: 1 ox ($10) + 9 cows ($45) + 90 calves ($45) is 100 animals and exactly $100. Calves are cheap enough to make up most of the herd.

q: In a lake there were lilies. The strange thing about them was that they doubled their number once per day. If on the 15th day half of the lake was covered with lilies, on which day will the whole lake be covered with them?

q.e: The lilies double daily, so if they cover half the lake on day 15, they cover the whole thing a day later, on day 16. Doubling problems work backward: halve the amount to go back one day.

q: Five girls are sitting next to each other on a train. Ann and Betty are as close to each other as Ann and Kate are. Dana and Ann are sitting as close to each other as Dana and Kate are. Between which two of her friends is the fifth girl, Jane, sitting?

q.e: Arrange the girls so the distances match: Betty, Jane, Ann, Dana, Kate. Ann is two seats from both Betty and Kate, and Dana is one seat from both Ann and Kate, so Jane is between Betty and Ann.

q: Two people get to a river and find a boat capable of accommodating only one person. Using this boat, both of them manage to cross the river. If they crossed without any of the them swiming the river which of the following is true?
They were on different banks of the river.

There was a bridge on the river.

q.e: Because the two people started on opposite sides of the river, one could row the boat across to the other, who then simply rowed it back.

q: A man walked by an old fisherman and asked him how many fish he had caught. The fisherman replied: The half of the eight, the nine without its tail, and the six without its head. How many fish did the fisherman caught?

q.e: Each phrase is a pun on the shape of the number: half of an 8 is a 0 or 3, a 9 without its tail is a 0, and a 6 without its head is a 0. The sum of 0 + 0 + 0 gives no fish.

q: A bar of soap is placed on one of the sides of a pair of scales. On the other side there is 3/4 of a bar of the same soap and а 3/4 kg metal weight. The scales are in balance. How much does a bar of soap weigh?

q.e: Let a bar of soap weigh x. Then x = 3/4 x + 3/4 kg, so the remaining 1/4 of a bar weighs 3/4 kg, and the whole bar weighs 3 kg.

q: A boy and a pig weigh as much as 5 crates. The pig weighs as much as 4 cats. 2 cats and the pig weigh as much as 3 crates. How many cats weigh as much as the boy?

q.e: A pig equals 4 cats, and 2 cats plus a pig make 3 crates, so 6 cats make 3 crates, and one crate equals 2 cats. The boy and pig are 5 crates (10 cats), so the boy is 10 − 4 = 6 cats.

q: Several rabbits and hens are placed together in a cage. How many rabbits and hens are there, if the total number of their heads is 35, and the combined number of their legs is 94?

q.e: If all 35 animals were hens, there would be 70 legs, so the extra 24 legs come from rabbits having 2 more each. That makes 12 rabbits and 23 hens.

q: 10% of all the people living in a certain town in Georgia have unlisted phone numbers. If you selected 100 names at random from the towns phone book, on average, how many of these people would have unlisted phone numbers?

q.e: Because the sample is drawn entirely from the phone book, none of them will have unlisted numbers, as unlisted numbers are deliberately excluded from published directories.

q: My grandson is about as many days as my son is weeks, and my grandson is as many months as I am in years. My grandson, my son and I together are 120 years. Can you tell me my age in years?

q.e: In days and weeks, the son is about 7 times older than the grandson. In months and years, the narrator is 12 times older. Then g + 7g + 12g = 120 means g = 6, so the narrator is 72.

q: The stubs obtained by burning ten candles will yield one extra candle if you melt them all together. If you burned 100 candles, how many extra candles could you make?

q.e: Burning the first 100 candles yields 100 stubs, which melt into 10 new candles. Burning those 10 produces 10 more stubs, making 1 final candle, for a total of 11 extra candles.

q: Charlie asked Margaret how old she was and she answered him: In two years I will be twice as old as I was five years ago. How old is she?

q.e: If her current age is x, the equation is x + 2 = 2(x - 5). Solving this gives x + 2 = 2x - 10, which means x = 12 years old.

His poem did not have a name.

q.e: Key wrote the poem in September 1814 after witnessing the British bombardment of Fort McHenry in Baltimore. It was set to the tune of a British drinking song, To Anacreon in Heaven, before Congress adopted it as the national anthem in 1931.

Which musical is about the life of Alexander Hamilton?

q.e: Created by Lin-Manuel Miranda and debuting off-Broadway in 2015, Hamilton blends hip-hop with musical theater to tell the story of the first U.S. Secretary of the Treasury. The production earned a record-setting 16 Tony nominations, winning 11.

q: Which Broadway musical features the iconic song "The Circle of Life"?

q.e: The musical The Lion King, featuring music by Elton John and lyrics by Tim Rice, opened on Broadway in 1997 and famously begins with the grand performance of Circle of Life.

q: Sammy Davis Jr. starred on Broadway more than once, but which of these was his first show there?
Stop the World - I want to Get off

q.e: Sammy Davis Jr.'s Broadway debut was Mr. Wonderful in 1956, a musical built around his talents as a singer, dancer and comedian. It ran for over 380 performances.

q: Lisa Minnelli starred in this 1976 musical movie directed by her father, Vincente Minnelli.
Tell Me That You Love Me, Junie Moon

q.e: A Matter of Time (1976) was directed by Vincente Minnelli, Liza's father, and also starred Ingrid Bergman. It was his last film as director.

q: This Broadway musical, produced by David Merrick, featured Jerry Orbach in the role of musical director, Julian Marsh.

q.e: 42nd Street opened on Broadway in 1980, produced by David Merrick, with Jerry Orbach as director Julian Marsh. Its director, Gower Champion, died on the day of the opening night.

q: The Wind in the Willows was published in 1908 without much notice. What famous author and playwright, best known for Winnie the Pooh, adapted part of the book for the stage in 1929, thus making the book famous?

q.e: A. A. Milne, creator of Winnie-the-Pooh, adapted The Wind in the Willows for the stage as Toad of Toad Hall in 1929. The play helped to make Kenneth Grahame's 1908 book widely loved.

q: What was the first name of the character Masterson in the musical comedy Guys and Dolls?

q.e: Sky Masterson is the high-rolling gambler in Guys and Dolls (1950), who bets he can take any girl to Havana. The musical was based on stories by Damon Runyon, with music and lyrics by Frank Loesser.

q: What was the original name of the melodramatic musical, West Side Story?

q.e: Originally conceived in 1949 as East Side Story, the musical focused on a Catholic boy and a Jewish girl in Manhattan's Lower East Side. By the mid-1950s, the creators shifted the setting to the Upper West Side and updated the conflict to Puerto Rican and white gangs.

q: Who wrote the book The Color Purple that was adapted into a Broadway play?

q.e: Alice Walker wrote The Color Purple (1982), which won the Pulitzer Prize and was made into a film in 1985 and a Broadway musical in 2005. It tells the story of Celie, a Black woman in the American South.

q: This musical comedy, directed by Nancy Walker, is a pseudo autobiography of 1970s disco group, Village People.

q.e: Can't Stop the Music (1980), directed by Nancy Walker, is a loosely fictionalized story of the Village People's formation. It was a box-office flop but became a cult favorite.

q: This became the longest running Broadway play on 9 January, 2006 .

q.e: On January 9, 2006, Andrew Lloyd Webber's musical The Phantom of the Opera played its 7,486th performance on Broadway, surpassing Cats to become the longest-running show in Broadway history.

q: Daddy Warbucks is a character in this popular musical that opened in April 21, 1977.

q.e: Annie, a musical based on the comic strip Little Orphan Annie, opened on Broadway on April 21, 1977, and ran for nearly six years. Daddy Warbucks is the billionaire who adopts Annie.

q: All That Jazz is the opening number of which 1975 Bob Fosse musical?

q.e: "All That Jazz" is the opening number of Chicago (1975), directed and choreographed by Bob Fosse. Its music is by John Kander and its lyrics are by Fred Ebb.

q: Which musical of the 50s featured the song Some Enchanted Evening?

q.e: "Some Enchanted Evening" is from South Pacific, which opened on Broadway in 1949 and won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama in 1950. The film version was released in 1958.

q: Which Rogers and Hammerstein musical features the comic character Ado Annie?

q.e: Ado Annie is the girl who "cain't say no" in Rodgers and Hammerstein's Oklahoma! (1943). She provides the show's comic relief.

q: The character of Professor Harold Hill was created by composer Meredith Willson for which musical about Mid-West small town life in the turn of the 20th century?

q.e: Meredith Willson's The Music Man (1957) is about con man Harold Hill, who arrives in River City, Iowa, in 1912, selling band instruments to the townspeople. It won the Tony for Best Musical.

q: The beautiful Belle changes everyones fate in which Broadway musical?

q.e: Based on the 1991 Disney animated film, Beauty and the Beast premiered on Broadway in 1994, running for over 5,400 performances until 2007.

q: Nicely-Nicely Johnson is a second banana character in which Frank Lessor musical?

q.e: Nicely-Nicely Johnson is a gambler in Guys and Dolls, composed by Frank Loesser, who leads the show-stopping song about rocking the boat. The musical premiered in 1950.

q: Which musician(s) created the rock opera Tommy?

q.e: Tommy, the first major rock opera, was created by The Who, mostly written by Pete Townshend, and released in 1969. It tells the story of a "deaf, dumb and blind" boy who becomes a pinball champion.

q: I Enjoy Being a Girl is from what Broadway musical?

q.e: "I Enjoy Being a Girl" is from Rodgers and Hammerstein's Flower Drum Song (1958), a musical about Chinese Americans in San Francisco. It was one of the first major Broadway musicals with a mostly Asian American cast.

q: The musical Miss Saigon is based on what classical opera?

q.e: Claude-Michel Schönberg and Alain Boublil based Miss Saigon on Giacomo Puccini's 1904 opera Madama Butterfly, transposing the tragic romance to the Vietnam War in the 1970s.

q: Which of these songs from the movie Cabaret originated in the Broadway version?

q.e: "Tomorrow Belongs to Me" was written for the stage version of Cabaret (1966) by composer John Kander and lyricist Fred Ebb. It is performed at an ominous beer garden scene.

q: According to a popular song from the 2003 puppet musical Avenue Q, what is the Internet for?

q.e: Avenue Q (2003) is a musical for adults, with puppets in the style of Sesame Street, that won the Tony for Best Musical. Its songs poke fun at the troubles of young adulthood.

q: Which movie adaptation of a Broadway musical won eleven Academy Awards?

q.e: West Side Story won 10 competitive Academy Awards in 1962, including Best Picture, plus an honorary award for choreographer Jerome Robbins, for a total of 11. It still holds the record for most Oscars won by a musical.

q: Which musical, directed by Robert Wise, is ranked # 41 on the AFI Top 100 list?
Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs

q.e: West Side Story (1961), directed by Robert Wise and Jerome Robbins, ranks #41 on the American Film Institute's list of the 100 greatest American films (1998 list). It transplants Romeo and Juliet to New York's gang-ridden streets.

q: In 1982 Julie Andrews, James Garner and Lesley Ann Warren starred in this musical about a female impersonator.

q.e: Victor/Victoria (1982), directed by Blake Edwards, stars Julie Andrews as a singer who pretends to be a male female impersonator in 1930s Paris. It earned seven Oscar nominations.

q: In the movie The Phantom of the Opera, Raoul remembers Christine, while listening to which song?

q.e: In the 2004 film, Raoul hears "Think of Me" at an auction in the opening and remembers Christine. The song is first sung by Christine when she steps in for the diva Carlotta.

q: Ernest Borgnine debuted on Broadway playing a male nurse in what production?

q.e: Ernest Borgnine made his Broadway debut in Harvey (1947), playing the male nurse Marvin Wilson. He later won an Oscar for Marty in 1955.

q: What is Ryan and Sharpays last name in the film High School Musical?

q.e: Sharpay and Ryan Evans are the twins in High School Musical (2006), who run the drama club at East High. Their family name suits their wealthy, spotlight-loving image.

q: When Stella Adler returned to the USA she began teaching with this famous theater group.

q.e: Stella Adler, a leading acting teacher, was a member of the Group Theatre in the 1930s and later taught the "Method" in her own studio. Her students included Marlon Brando.

q: What High School Musical character was the head of the science club?

q.e: Taylor McKessie is Gabriella's smart friend in High School Musical and a leader of the school's academic clubs. She sings in "Stick to the Status Quo".

q: Where do Troy Bolton and Gabriella Montez meet in the film High School Musical?
at a New Years Eve party

q.e: Troy and Gabriella first meet at a New Year's Eve party at a ski lodge, where they sing karaoke together. They are surprised to find that they are classmates after the holidays.

q: This Irish-born Grammy Award-winning actor played King Arthur in the1967 film Camelot, based on the 1960 Broadway musical.

q.e: Richard Harris, born in Limerick, Ireland, played King Arthur in the 1967 film Camelot, which was based on the 1960 Broadway hit. He was also known as the first Dumbledore in the Harry Potter films.

q: William Friedkin directed several art films after Good Times, including the Golden Globe-nominated film version of this off-Broadway play written by Mart Crowley.

q.e: William Friedkin directed the 1970 film version of Mart Crowley's play The Boys in the Band, which was one of the first films to portray gay characters frankly. He later directed The French Connection and The Exorcist.

q: What song does the movie High School Musical 3 start out with?

q.e: High School Musical 3: Senior Year (2008) opens with "Now or Never", a song performed during a basketball game daydream. The cast includes Zac Efron and Vanessa Hudgens.

q: What is the name of the play the students preform in High School Musical 3?

q.e: In High School Musical 3, the students put on a spring musical called "Senior Year" about their own experiences. It's a show within the movie.

q: This British rock band, known for smashing their instruments at the end of their concerts, recorded the rock opera Tommy in 1969.

q.e: Composed primarily by guitarist Pete Townshend, Tommy was released in May 1969 as a double album telling the story of a deaf, mute, and blind boy.

q: This musical tells the story of a con-man salesman and a librarian from Iowa.

q.e: Meredith Willson's 1957 hit musical The Music Man follows slick con artist Harold Hill as he tries to scam the residents of River City, Iowa, but falls in love with Marian the librarian instead. It won five Tony Awards, beating West Side Story for Best Musical.

q: This musical centers on the feud between farmers and sheep herders in the Mid West.

q.e: Oklahoma! (1943) is built around the rivalry between farmers and cowmen in the Oklahoma Territory, not sheep herders, as in the "Farmer and the Cowman" song. It was Rodgers and Hammerstein's first collaboration.

q: This musical, set on the Mississippi River, tells the story of a riverboat gambler and the young innocent girl.

q.e: Show Boat (1927), by Jerome Kern and Oscar Hammerstein II, follows life on the Cotton Blossom, a Mississippi River showboat, including the romance of gambler Gaylord Ravenal and Magnolia. It was one of the first musicals to deal with serious themes like racism.

q: This musical is set in the Alphabet City section of Manhattan and centers on people coping with AIDS.

q.e: Jonathan Larson's rock musical Rent premiered off-Broadway in 1996 and was loosely based on Puccini's 1896 opera La Boheme. It won both the Tony Award for Best Musical and the Pulitzer Prize for Drama.

q: This Broadway musical, set in pre-Nazi Austria, relates the exploits of an ex-nun who is sent out to be a governess to seven motherless children.

q.e: The Sound of Music (1959) is set in Austria in 1938, and centers on Maria, a postulant who becomes governess to the seven von Trapp children. It's based on a true story and the real Maria von Trapp's memoir.

q: Which musical is based on Mark Twains novel The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn?

q.e: Big River (1985) is a musical version of Mark Twain's Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, with music and lyrics by country star Roger Miller. It won the Tony Award for Best Musical.

q: Which musical traces the life of American composer/actor George Cohan?

q.e: George M! (1968) is a musical biography of the entertainer George M. Cohan, starring Joel Grey. It features Cohan's songs, such as "Give My Regards to Broadway".

q: Bali Hai is the forbidden mystical island in which musical of the 50's?

q.e: Bali Ha'i is the mysterious island in South Pacific that calls to the sailors. It was inspired by islands in the Pacific theater, where James Michener's stories were set.

q: Hot Honey Rag is the closing song of which popular musical based on a play by Maurine Dallas Watkins?

q.e: "Hot Honey Rag" is the final number of Chicago, danced by Roxie Hart and Velma Kelly. The musical is based on a 1926 play by Maurine Dallas Watkins, a reporter who covered real murder trials.

q: Leaning on a Lamp Post was sung in which popular musical of the 80s?

q.e: "Leaning on a Lamp-Post" is a cheerful song from Me and My Girl, a British musical that was a hit in the 1930s and again when revived in the 1980s. The show is set in the world of an aristocratic family and a Cockney hero.

q: Which musical showcased the hauntingly beautiful song Angel of Music?

q.e: "Angel of Music" is a duet from Andrew Lloyd Webber's The Phantom of the Opera (1986), sung by Christine and Meg Giry. It is how Christine explains her mysterious teacher.

q: The song Whatever Happened to Class? was cut from the movie version of which Bob Fosse musical?

q.e: "Class" is a song from the stage version of Chicago that was cut from the 2002 film, where it was sung by Velma and Mama Morton. The movie also cut other songs to speed up the story.

q: Which long running Broadway show opens with the song I Hope I Get It?

q.e: A Chorus Line (1975) opens with "I Hope I Get It", in which dancers audition for a Broadway show. It ran for 6,137 performances, once the longest-running show in Broadway history.

q: The babershop tune Lida Rose was sung in which Meredith Wilson musical?

q.e: "Lida Rose" is a barbershop-style number sung by a quartet in Meredith Willson's The Music Man (1957), in which the Buffalo Bills sang. It's paired with "Will I Ever Tell You?".

q: Which Fosse musical features a lawyer singing "Razzle Dazzle in order to con a jury?

q.e: "Razzle Dazzle" is sung by lawyer Billy Flynn in Chicago, where he explains that the way to win a case is to give the jury a show. The musical is about celebrity and the legal system.

q: Which Rogers and Hammerstein musical featured the comic lament Pore Jud is Daid?

q.e: "Pore Jud Is Daid" is a darkly comic song in Oklahoma!, sung by Curly to the hired hand Jud, as he tries to convince him to hang himself. It shows the tension between the two men.

q: Which Wilson musical features the song Gary, Indiana?

q.e: "Gary, Indiana" is sung by young Winthrop in The Music Man, which was Meredith Willson's tribute to his home state. The town was Willson's real hometown in a way, as he was from Iowa.

q: What musical showcases the song One throughout the entire play?

q.e: The song One serves as a recurring motif in the 1975 Broadway musical A Chorus Line, culminating in the show's famous gold-costumed finale.

q: The great opera about Spain, Carmen, was written in which language?

q.e: Although set in Seville, Spain, Carmen was composed by French composer Georges Bizet with a French libretto by Henri Meilhac and Ludovic Halevy. It premiered in Paris at the Opera-Comique in March 1875.

q: In 1972, this song from the Broadway rock musical Godspell made it all the way to #13.

q.e: "Day by Day" from Godspell (1971) was a Top 20 hit in 1972, reaching #13 on the US charts. The musical, by Stephen Schwartz, is based on the Gospel of Matthew.

q: Professor Henry Higgins is the haughty language expert from which musical adaptation of a Shaw play?

q.e: My Fair Lady, written by Alan Jay Lerner and Frederick Loewe, debuted on Broadway in 1956 as an adaptation of George Bernard Shaw's 1913 play Pygmalion.

q: Simba is the lead character in which movie musical later made into an award-winning Broadway play?

q.e: Simba is the protagonist of Disney's 1994 animated musical 'The Lion King', which was adapted for Broadway in 1997 and won six Tony Awards, including Best Musical.

q: Huckleberry Finn, one of the Mark Twain characters, appears in which Broadway show by Roger Miller?

q.e: Big River (1985) has music and lyrics by country singer Roger Miller, who won seven Tony awards for the show's score. Miller was also famous for "King of the Road".

q: Which Irving Berlin musical is based on the life Annie Oakley?

q.e: Annie Get Your Gun (1946), by Irving Berlin, is a musical based on the sharpshooter Annie Oakley and her romance with Frank Butler. It starred Ethel Merman and includes "There's No Business Like Show Business".

q: In which long-running musical does Christine Daaé appear?

q.e: Christine Daaé is the young soprano at the center of The Phantom of the Opera. The musical opened in London in 1986 and on Broadway in 1988, and it's the longest-running show in Broadway history.

q: Daddy Warbucks is the leading male character in which Broadway show suitable for children?

q.e: Oliver 'Daddy' Warbucks is the billionaire who takes in the orphan Annie in the 1977 Broadway musical, which is based on Harold Gray's comic strip 'Little Orphan Annie'.

q: The song Bidin My Time is from what musical?

q.e: "Bidin' My Time" is from Girl Crazy (1930), with music by George Gershwin and lyrics by Ira Gershwin. The show launched the career of Ethel Merman.

q: This 50s Broadway musical starring Rosalind Russell was based on the play My Sister Eileen.

q.e: Wonderful Town (1953), with music by Leonard Bernstein, is based on the play My Sister Eileen, and Rosalind Russell starred. It's about two sisters from Ohio who move to Greenwich Village.

q: Which song, featured in the play The Phantom of the Opera was taken out from the movie?

q.e: Some songs and musical passages from the stage version of The Phantom of the Opera were shortened or cut in the 2004 film adaptation to keep the running time down. Film versions of musicals often trim material.

q: Anita is the best friend of the female lead in which musical that was later transformed into an award-winning movie musical?

q.e: In West Side Story, Anita is a friend and confidante of Maria and the girlfriend of Bernardo. The role was played by Rita Moreno in the 1961 film, for which she won an Oscar.

q: Which musical, featuring the songs Youre the Topand I Get a Kick Out of You, was written by Cole Porter?

q.e: Anything Goes debuted on Broadway in 1934 starring Ethel Merman and featured a score filled with Cole Porter standards. My Fair Lady, which features songs like I Could Have Danced All Night, was composed decades later by Lerner and Loewe.

q: Who wrote the lyrics and music for the Tony Award-winning musical Kiss Me, Kate?

q.e: Cole Porter wrote the music and lyrics for Kiss Me, Kate (1948), a musical about a troubled acting couple staging a version of The Taming of the Shrew. It won the first Tony Award for Best Musical.

q: Hans Zimmer wrote the beautiful love theme Can You Feel the Love Tonight? for which Broadway/Hollywood musical?

q.e: "Can You Feel the Love Tonight" was written by Elton John (music) and Tim Rice (lyrics) for The Lion King (1994), and it won an Oscar for Best Original Song. Hans Zimmer composed the film's score.

q: Tony senses that Something's Coming to change his life in which Bernstein, Sohdheim, and Robbins musical collaboration?

q.e: "Something's Coming" is sung by Tony in West Side Story (1957), with music by Leonard Bernstein and lyrics by Stephen Sondheim. The show was conceived and choreographed by Jerome Robbins.

q: What was the name of Rogers girlfriend, who committed suicide in the Broadway musical Rent?

q.e: April was Roger's girlfriend in Rent, who died by suicide after learning she had AIDS. Her death is the reason Roger shuts himself off from love.

q: In the Broadway musical Rent, Mark, played by Anothony Rapp, starts working at which news company?

q.e: In Rent, Mark Cohen is a filmmaker who takes a job with the TV tabloid show "Buzzline". Anthony Rapp played him in the original cast.

q: In the musical Rent, who was Maureen dating, before she started dating Joanne?

q.e: In Rent, Maureen was dating Mark before she left him for Joanne. Mark documents the breakup with his camera.

q: In what musical does rouged knee Velma Kelly brag, I know a whoopee spot, where the gin is cold and the pianos hot .?

q.e: Velma Kelly sings "All That Jazz" in Chicago, welcoming the audience to the world of 1920s jazz and crime. The song opens the musical.

q: Which Frank Sinatra musical also starred Bing Crosby and Grace Kelly?

q.e: High Society (1956) is a musical remake of The Philadelphia Story and stars Frank Sinatra, Bing Crosby and Grace Kelly, with songs by Cole Porter. It was Grace Kelly's last film before she became Princess of Monaco.

q: Which Frank Sinatra musical was the first MGM film to be shot on location in 1949?
Take me Out to the Ballgame

q.e: On the Town (1949), starring Frank Sinatra and Gene Kelly, was one of the first Hollywood musicals to shoot on location, in New York City. It follows three sailors on 24 hours of shore leave.

q: Which are the authors of the Tony-winning musical Spamalot?

q.e: Spamalot (2005), based on Monty Python and the Holy Grail, was written by Eric Idle, with music by Idle and John Du Prez. It won the Tony for Best Musical; Tim Rice was not involved.

q: In which country do the events of the opera Aida take place?

q.e: Verdi's opera Aida is set in ancient Egypt and tells the story of an Ethiopian princess enslaved in Egypt and the Egyptian general Radamès. It's famous for its grand "Triumphal March".

q: In terms of acts, how long is the opera Aida?

q.e: Aida is an opera in four acts, with music by Giuseppe Verdi and a libretto by Antonio Ghislanzoni. It premiered in Cairo in 1871.

q: In what 2009 musical film does Fergie from the Black Eyed Peas play a character named Saraghina?

q.e: In the 2009 film Nine, Fergie played Saraghina, the beach prostitute from the main character's childhood. She performed the number "Be Italian".

q: Which of these does the following quote belong to: Hell is full of musical amateurs.?

q.e: The quote "Hell is full of musical amateurs" comes from George Bernard Shaw's play Man and Superman (1903). It is spoken by the Devil in the dream sequence.

q: What is the occupation of Floria Tosca in Giacomo Puccinis world-famous opera Tosca?

q.e: Floria Tosca is a famous opera singer in Puccini's Tosca (1900), set in Rome. She is in love with the painter Cavaradossi.

q: What character did Kylie Minogue portray in the 2001 musical movie Moulin Rouge!?

q.e: Kylie Minogue played the Green Fairy, the absinthe-induced spirit that appears to Christian in Moulin Rouge! (2001). The film was directed by Baz Luhrmann.

q: What is the meaning of the Greek word théatron from which the word theatre is derived?

q.e: The ancient Greek noun 'théatron' literally translates to 'a place for viewing', derived from the verb 'theasthai', meaning 'to behold' or 'to view'.

q: Samuel Beckett and Harold Pinter are typically associated with what style of theatre?

q.e: Samuel Beckett and Harold Pinter are associated with the Theatre of the Absurd, a style that shows the meaninglessness of life through odd dialogue and situations. Beckett's Waiting for Godot is a famous example.

q: What is the name of Sharpays twin brother in the movie High School Musical?

q.e: Ryan Evans is Sharpay's twin brother in High School Musical, played by Lucas Grabeel. He is the less ambitious but equally talented twin.

q: Where do Troy and Gabriela first meet in the movie High School Musical?

q.e: Troy and Gabriella first meet at a ski lodge during a New Year's Eve party in High School Musical. They are forced to sing karaoke together.

q: What 2002 musical film, directed by Rob Marshall, centers on two criminals-of-passion?

q.e: Chicago centers on murderesses Roxie Hart (Renée Zellweger) and Velma Kelly (Catherine Zeta-Jones). It won six Academy Awards, including Best Picture, making it the first musical to win the top prize since Oliver! in 1968.

q: Name the 1956 movie musical directed by Walter Lang and based on the book Anna and the King of Siam by Margaret Landon.

q.e: The King and I starred Deborah Kerr as Anna Leonowens and Yul Brynner as King Mongkut of Siam, earning five Academy Awards out of nine nominations.
William Shakespeare wrote Hamlet around 1599 to 1601. It stands as his longest play, comprising roughly 4,000 lines and nearly 30,000 words.

q: Which musical features a masked man living under the Paris Opera?

q.e: Composed by Andrew Lloyd Webber and based on Gaston Leroux's 1910 novel, The Phantom of the Opera debuted in London's West End in 1986. It became the longest-running show in Broadway history, closing in 2023 after nearly 14,000 performances.

q: In "Wicked", what is the given name of the Wicked Witch of the West?

q.e: Author Gregory Maguire created the name Elphaba for his 1995 novel by phoneticizing the initials of L. Frank Baum (L-F-B), the creator of 'The Wonderful Wizard of Oz'. Nessarose is her younger sister, the Wicked Witch of the East.

q: The musical revue "Five Guys Named ___" was inspired by jazzman Louis Jordan. Fill in the name.

q.e: Five Guys Named Moe (1990) is a musical revue built on the music of Louis Jordan, the jazz and jump-blues star of the 1940s. It came to Broadway in 1992.

q: In 2001, Reba McEntire starred on Broadway as Annie Oakley in which musical?

q.e: Reba McEntire starred as Annie Oakley in a Broadway revival of Annie Get Your Gun in 2001. The country star was praised for the role.

q: Which was the first Broadway play written by a Black woman, about a family moving to the suburbs?

q.e: Lorraine Hansberry's play opened on Broadway in 1959, taking its title from Langston Hughes's poem Harlem. At age 29, Hansberry also became the youngest American playwright to win the New York Drama Critics' Circle Award.

q: Marilyn Monroes first movie appearance was in this 1947 musical comedy movie.

q.e: Marilyn Monroe had tiny roles in 1947, in Dangerous Years and The Shocking Miss Pilgrim, which starred Betty Grable. Her first major role came a few years later.

q: In the 1930s, Will Lee was a member of this famous theater group.

q.e: Will Lee, who later played Mr. Hooper on Sesame Street, was a member of the Group Theatre in the 1930s. He was later blacklisted during the McCarthy era.

q: What legendary actress starred alongside Fred Astaire in the 1957 musical movie Funny Face?

q.e: Audrey Hepburn starred with Fred Astaire in Funny Face (1957), which has music by George and Ira Gershwin. She plays a bookshop clerk who becomes a fashion model in Paris.

q: In 1981 Richard Dreyfuss starred in Whose Life Is It Anyway?. Which actress was famous for starring in the Broadway version?

q.e: In 1980, Mary Tyler Moore starred in the Broadway production of Whose Life Is It Anyway?, a play about a paralyzed man's right to die. She took over the role created in the original by a male lead, adapted for a woman.

q: Jerry Orbach starred with Anna Maria Alberghetti in which Tony-award winning Broadway musical?

q.e: Carnival! (1961), a musical based on the film Lili, starred Anna Maria Alberghetti and Jerry Orbach. Orbach was also in the original cast of The Fantasticks.

q: Jerry Orbach received his first Tony Award nomination for his portrayal of Sky Masterson, in which Broadway show?

q.e: Jerry Orbach played Sky Masterson in a 1965 Broadway revival of Guys and Dolls. He later became famous as Detective Lennie Briscoe on Law & Order.

q: Jerry Orbach won the Tony Award for Best Actor for his role in which 1968 musical?

q.e: Jerry Orbach won the 1969 Tony Award for Best Actor in a Musical for Promises, Promises (1968), with music by Burt Bacharach and lyrics by Hal David. The musical is based on the Billy Wilder film The Apartment.

q: Actor John Cazale won an Obie for his performance in which off-Broadway play, written by Israel Horovitz?

q.e: John Cazale won an Obie Award for the Israel Horovitz play The Indian Wants the Bronx (1968), in which he acted with Al Pacino. He later played Fredo in The Godfather.

q: What production did Broderick Crawfords Broadway acting career began on?

q.e: Broderick Crawford began his Broadway career in Of Mice and Men (1937), playing Lennie Small, and later won an Oscar for All the King's Men. His parents were also in show business.

q: Which was the Marx Brothers first feature length movie that was not based on a Broadway show?

q.e: Monkey Business (1931) was the first Marx Brothers film not based on a Broadway show; it was written directly for the screen. They had been in The Cocoanuts and Animal Crackers, which were stage hits.

q: How old was Cio-Cio-San, a character in Giacomo Puccinis opera, Madame Butterfly ?

q.e: Cio-Cio-San, the title character of Puccini's Madama Butterfly, is a 15-year-old geisha in Nagasaki. The opera premiered in Milan in 1904.

q: Having won 6 Tony Awards, including Best Musical, this 1950s production is a modern retelling of the Faust legend. Its main characters are Mr. Applegate, Joe Boyd and Lola.

q.e: Damn Yankees (1955) is a baseball musical that retells the Faust legend, in which a fan sells his soul to the devil, Mr. Applegate, to help the Washington Senators beat the New York Yankees. It won the 1956 Tony Award for Best Musical.

q: Which Broadway play is based on Christopher Isherwoods book, I am a camera?

q.e: Cabaret is based on Christopher Isherwood's Berlin stories, which were also adapted into the play I Am a Camera. Isherwood lived in Berlin in the early 1930s as the Nazis were coming to power.

q: At what event was the opera Aida premiered?
The opening of the Suez Canal
The opening of La Scala in Milan
The opening of the Panama Canal
The opening of the National Opera House in Rome

q.e: Verdi's Aida was commissioned by the Khedive of Egypt and premiered at the Cairo Opera House in December 1871. It's often said to have opened the Suez Canal in 1869, but it did not.

q: This Massachusetts born musical composer wrote Sleigh Ride, Holiday for Strings, The Typewriter and Plink, Plank, Plunk.

q.e: Leroy Anderson, born in Cambridge, Massachusetts, wrote light orchestral pieces like "Sleigh Ride", "The Typewriter" and "Plink, Plank, Plunk!". "The Typewriter" uses an actual typewriter as an instrument.

q: Which 1951 Tony winner for Best Musical had its music and lyrics written by Frank Loesser and included such characters as Nathan Detroit, Miss Adelaide, and Sky Masterson?

q.e: Guys and Dolls, with music and lyrics by Frank Loesser, won the Tony Award for Best Musical in 1951. It features gamblers Nathan Detroit and Sky Masterson and their sweethearts.

q: Jonathan Larson based his rock musical on the opera La Boheme. What rock musical about young artists and musicians and their struggle, hopes and fears made it to # 2 on Entertainment Weeklys New Classics List?

q.e: Rent (1996) was written by Jonathan Larson, who loosely based it on Puccini's opera La Bohème. Larson died just before the show's first preview, and it won the Pulitzer Prize and the Tony for Best Musical.

q: What was the name of the sleazy lawyer in the musical and movie Chicago?

q.e: Billy Flynn is the showy lawyer in Chicago who represents Roxie Hart. He charges $5,000 and is known for his "razzle dazzle" strategy.

q: What is the full name of Charity, the leading character from the popular Broadway musical Sweet Charity?

q.e: Charity Hope Valentine is the dance-hall hostess with a hopeful heart in Sweet Charity (1966), directed and choreographed by Bob Fosse. Gwen Verdon starred in the original.

q: What was the first Broadway comedy to run for over 5500 performances?

q.e: Oh! Calcutta!, a revue, ran for years on Broadway after a 1976 revival, totaling over 5,900 performances. It was known for its nudity.

q: The famous Leporello Catalogue Aria is from which Mozart opera?

q.e: The "Catalogue Aria" is sung by Leporello in Mozart's opera Don Giovanni (1787), where he lists his master's many conquests. It's a famous comic piece.

q: In what city was the first permanent drama theater in Europe opened?

q.e: The Roman Theatre of Málaga, built in the 1st century BC, is one of the oldest theaters in Spain. Older theaters, such as the Theatre of Dionysus in Athens, are found in Greece, so which one is "first" depends on the definition.

q: What Shakespearean comedy inspired Cole Porters musical Kiss Me, Kate?

q.e: Kiss Me, Kate' revolves around actors staging a musical version of Shakespeare's 'The Taming of the Shrew', paralleling their backstage drama with Petruchio and Katherine.

q: This Irish playwright, novelist and poet wrote the following line in his famous play Waiting for Godot: We are all born mad. Some remain so.

q.e: Samuel Beckett, the Irish author of Waiting for Godot (1953), won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1969. The play is a landmark of the Theatre of the Absurd.

q: In which musical does Curly sing Surrey With the Fringe on Top to entice his girlfriend to accompany him to a party?

q.e: In Oklahoma!, Curly sings "The Surrey with the Fringe on Top" to Laurey, describing the horse-drawn carriage he plans to take her to the box social. It's one of the show's best-known songs.

q: Which Broadway show features the character of Billy Bigelow as the male lead?

q.e: Billy Bigelow is the carousel barker in Rodgers and Hammerstein's Carousel (1945), a musical about love and redemption. The song "Soliloquy" is his big moment.

q: Shoeless Joe Hardy sold his soul to the devil in which 50s musical revised in the 1990s?

q.e: Shoeless Joe Hardy sells his soul to the devil in Damn Yankees (1955), which was revived on Broadway in 1994. The show is based on the novel The Year the Yankees Lost the Pennant.

q: Charlemange of the Holy Roman Empire was a character in which Fosse musical?

q.e: Charlemagne is a character in Pippin (1972), a musical by Stephen Schwartz and Bob Fosse about the king's son. The real Pippin was Charlemagne's son.

q: Who originated the role of Deena Jones in the Broadway play Dreamgirls?

q.e: Sheryl Lee Ralph originated the role of Deena Jones in Dreamgirls (1981), the Supremes-inspired musical about a girl group. She later starred in the TV series Abbott Elementary.

q: Who originated the role of Effie on the Broadway production Dreamgirls?

q.e: Jennifer Holliday originated Effie White in Dreamgirls and won the Tony Award in 1982. Her showstopper is "And I Am Telling You I'm Not Going".

q: The original Broadway play Dreamgirls was designed to feature which actress/singer?

q.e: Dreamgirls (1981), directed by Michael Bennett, is loosely based on the story of The Supremes. Nell Carter was a Broadway star at the time, and she performed in the musical Ain't Misbehavin'.

q: Which were the two authors of the 1955 Broadway play Inherit the Wind?
Jerome Lawrence and Robert E. Lee
Jerome Robbins and Robert E. Lee

q.e: Jerome Lawrence and Robert E. Lee wrote Inherit the Wind (1955), a fictionalized version of the 1925 Scopes "Monkey" Trial. It's a play about the teaching of evolution.

q: What was the name of the riverboat in the Kern/Hammerstein musical, Showboat?

q.e: The Cotton Blossom is the showboat in Kern and Hammerstein's Show Boat (1927), which travels up and down the Mississippi River. The musical is based on Edna Ferber's novel.

q: Which of the following actors was not a performer in the original Broadway production of Hair?

q.e: Hair, a "tribal love-rock musical" about the hippie counterculture, opened on Broadway in 1968. Matthew Broderick, who was only a child then, was not in it.

q: Where do Christine and Raoul sing their love duet, All I Ask of You in The Phantom of the Opera?
On the roof of the Paris Opera House
On stage during a performance of Il Muto
In box 5 during a performance of Il Muto
On the grand staircase of the Paris Opera House

q.e: Christine and Raoul sing "All I Ask of You" on the roof of the Paris Opera House, unaware that the Phantom is listening. It's a love duet that infuriates him.

q: Which of these movie musical numbers was NOT nominated for a Best Original Song Oscar?
Blame Canada, South Park: Bigger, Longer and Uncut
Under the Sea, The Little Mermaid
Somewhere Over the Rainbow, The Wizard of Oz

q.e: "Come What May" from Moulin Rouge! was ruled ineligible for an Oscar, because it had been written earlier for another project. The film still earned several other nominations.

q: The song A Little Priest, from Stephen Sondheims 1979 musical Sweeney Todd, is about what?

q.e: "A Little Priest" in Sweeney Todd (1979) is a dark comic duet in which Sweeney and Mrs. Lovett decide to use his victims' bodies as meat for her pies. Stephen Sondheim wrote the music and lyrics.

q: This 1972 musical won 8 Academy Awards but not the Best Picture Award.

q.e: Cabaret (1972) won eight Academy Awards, including Best Director for Bob Fosse and Best Actress for Liza Minnelli, but lost Best Picture to The Godfather. It still holds the record for most Oscars won without winning Best Picture.

q: Stallone studied drama at this University, but dropped out and returned to New York, where he made appearances in a few small off-Broadway plays.

q.e: Sylvester Stallone attended the American College of Switzerland and later the University of Miami, where he studied drama. He then moved to New York to act before finding fame with Rocky.

q: This 1944 Oscar-winning musical, starring Judy Garland under the direction of Vincente Minnelle, tells the story of four sisters living in St. Louis during the Louisiana Purchase Exposition Worlds Fair.

q.e: Meet Me in St. Louis (1944) stars Judy Garland and was directed by Vincente Minnelli, who later married her. It introduced "The Trolley Song" and "Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas".

q: In the movie The Phantom of the Opera, Christines dad called her by what name?

q.e: In The Phantom of the Opera, Christine's father called her "Little Lotte", and tells her that he'll send the Angel of Music. The name is a Swedish fairy tale reference.

q: What Hollywood actor and singer performed the song Singin in the Rain in the 1952 musical film Singin in the Rain?

q.e: Gene Kelly starred as Don Lockwood and performed the iconic street dance while battling a real-life fever of over 101 degrees Fahrenheit during shooting. Kelly also co-directed and choreographed the classic musical.

q: What disease takes the life of Nicole Kidmans character, Satine, in the 2001 musical Moulin Rouge!?

q.e: Satine succumbs to tuberculosis, historically known as consumption, reflecting the plot of Alexandre Dumas fils's novel The Lady of the Camellias and Puccini's opera La Bohème.

q: How many Mel Brooks films, released in the period 1968-1995, were recast into Broadway musicals?

q.e: Two Mel Brooks movies became Broadway musicals: The Producers (2001) and Young Frankenstein (2007). The Producers won a record 12 Tonys.

q: This 1967 Roman Polanski film has been produced as a musical called Dance of the Vampires.

q.e: The 1967 film The Fearless Vampire Killers by Roman Polanski was adapted as the musical Tanz der Vampire in Vienna in 1997 and as Dance of the Vampires on Broadway in 2002. Polanski directed the original film and acted in it.

q: In the song On My Own from the musical. Les Miserables, Eponine sings that the trees are full of what?

q.e: "On My Own" is sung by Éponine in Les Misérables when she is in love with Marius, who loves someone else. It is one of the show's best-known songs.

q: In the 1978 musical, Grease, Betty Rizzo sings a song called There Are Worse Things I Could Do. What does she consider to be the worst thing she could do?

q.e: In Grease, Rizzo's song "There Are Worse Things I Could Do" shows a vulnerable side, as she hides a pregnancy scare from her friends. It's the character's emotional high point.

q: In the musical Wicked, which premiered on Broadway in October 2003, Elphaba sings in all of the following numbers except one. Which one is it?

q.e: In Wicked (2003), "Thank Goodness" is Glinda's song after the Wizard's rule is revealed, so Elphaba doesn't sing it. Elphaba sings on songs like "The Wizard and I" and "Defying Gravity".

q: This musical follows the life of a poor Russian milkman and his family.

q.e: Fiddler on the Roof (1964) follows Tevye, a poor Jewish milkman in the Russian village of Anatevka, and his five daughters. It's based on stories by Sholem Aleichem.

q: This musical is set in Germany in 1930 and is based on the play I Am a Camera.

q.e: Cabaret is set in Berlin around 1930, as the Nazis rise to power, and it's based on Christopher Isherwood's stories and the play I Am a Camera. Its main setting is the Kit Kat Klub.

q: Which Rogers and Hammerstein hit musical features the song Kansas City sung by a cowboy who returns from the big city?

q.e: "Kansas City" is sung by Will Parker in Oklahoma!, who has just returned from a trip to the big city and is amazed at its tall buildings. It is one of the show's comic numbers.

q: In which musical does the lovely Sunrise/Sunset number represent the parents' hopes for their daughters?

q.e: "Sunrise, Sunset" in Fiddler on the Roof is sung by Tevye and Golde at their daughter Tzeitel's wedding, as they reflect on how quickly children grow up. It's one of the show's best-known songs.

q: The tune The Music of the Night a major theme in which Weber musical?

q.e: The Music of the Night is sung by the titular Phantom in Andrew Lloyd Webber's 1986 musical adaptation, which became the longest-running show in Broadway history.

q: Soliloquy", sometimes called My Boy Bill," is the longest song in which Rogers and Hammerstein musical?

q.e: "Soliloquy" is a long song in Carousel, nearly eight minutes, in which Billy Bigelow imagines the life of his unborn child. It's also known by the line "My Boy Bill".

q: The first Opera House was built in Italy, in this year.

q.e: The first public opera house, the Teatro San Cassiano, opened in Venice in 1637. Before then, operas were performed for royal courts.

q: This singer of the title song from the rock opera Jesus Christ Superstar (1971) didnt have another hit until 1985.

q.e: Murray Head sang the title song of Jesus Christ Superstar (1970-71), then had another hit with "One Night in Bangkok" from the musical Chess in 1985. His career was mostly in theater and acting.

q: Which musical features Mabel Norman, a character based on a real-life silent screen actress?

q.e: Mack and Mabel (1974), a musical by Jerry Herman, is about the silent film director Mack Sennett and the actress Mabel Normand. It was a flop that gained a cult following.

q: Which song from the musical The Music Man is performed by an ensemble?

q.e: "Iowa Stubborn" is an ensemble number in The Music Man, in which the townspeople of River City explain how stubborn they are. It was written by Meredith Willson.

q: The song Aint Misbehavin, written by Fats Waller, is credited to the show of the same name, but actually had its Broadway debut in what revue?

q.e: "Ain't Misbehavin'" by Fats Waller was introduced in the 1929 Broadway revue Hot Chocolates, where Louis Armstrong performed it. The 1978 show Ain't Misbehavin' later honored Waller's music.

q: In this musical later made into a movie, Sandy is a major character with very few lines.

q.e: Sandy is the dog in Annie, who only barks. Annie finds him as a stray and brings him to the orphanage.

q: Seymour is the leading man in which Broadway hit show based on a movie?

q.e: Seymour Krelborn is the nerdy florist's assistant who raises the man-eating plant Audrey II in Little Shop of Horrors. The 1982 off-Broadway musical by Howard Ashman and Alan Menken was based on Roger Corman's 1960 B-movie.

q: What song does the wind-up monkey box play in the movie The Phantom of the Opera?

q.e: "Masquerade" is the music played by the wind-up monkey music box in Phantom of the Opera. It also becomes the big ensemble number at the Opera Populaire's New Year's ball.

q: Anything You Can Do I Can Do Better is a comic duet from which Broadway/Hollywood musical?

q.e: The show tune was written by Irving Berlin for the 1946 musical Annie Get Your Gun, staged as a competitive singing duel between sharpshooters Annie Oakley and Frank Butler.

q: Ill Know When My Love Comes Along is a love theme from which musical of the 40's and 50's?

q.e: "I'll Know" is the duet sung by Sarah Brown and Sky Masterson in Guys and Dolls (1950). Frank Loesser wrote it, and the two characters are an unlikely couple.

q: Before the Parade Passes By is a song from which Broadway show later made into a movie starring Barbra Streisand?
