q.e: "Before the Parade Passes By" is sung by Dolly Levi in Jerry Herman's Hello, Dolly!, when she decides to rejoin life after mourning her husband. Barbra Streisand starred in the 1969 film.

q: This musical, set in Berlin in 1929, was written by Fred Ebb and John Kander.

q.e: Cabaret premiered on Broadway in 1966, featuring music by John Kander and lyrics by Fred Ebb. The story was adapted from Christopher Isherwood's 1939 novel Goodbye to Berlin and focuses on the decadent Kit Kat Klub during the rise of the Nazi party.

q: Who wrote the music for the world famous musical West Side Story that debuted on Broadway in 1957?

q.e: Leonard Bernstein composed the score for West Side Story, which features classics like Tonight and Maria. Stephen Sondheim contributed the lyrics rather than the music.

q: Who wrote the musical La Cage aux Folles which focuses on a gay couple?

q.e: Jerry Herman wrote the music and lyrics for La Cage aux Folles (1983), with a book by Harvey Fierstein. Its anthem "I Am What I Am" became an enduring pride song.

q: In the Broadway musical Rent, which two characters meet for the first time, while singing the song, Light My Candle?

q.e: Mimi and Roger meet when she knocks on his door asking for a light for her candle in "Light My Candle" in Rent. The scene mirrors Mimi's meeting with Rodolfo in La Bohème.

q: In the musical Paint Your Wagon the rain is Tess and the fire is Jo. What do they call the wind?

q.e: In Paint Your Wagon (1951), by Lerner and Loewe, the song "They Call the Wind Maria" is a lonely miner's song. Wind, rain and fire are given names in the song.

q: Ado Annie in the musical Oklahoma has a bit of a problem. According to her song, what is Ado Annies major problem?
How Can I Get Him to Notice Me?

q.e: In Oklahoma!, Ado Annie sings "I Cain't Say No", explaining she can't say no to any man who asks. It's the comic highlight of the musical.

q: Don Giovanni is an opera in two acts by what popular composer?

q.e: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart composed 'Don Giovanni' with librettist Lorenzo Da Ponte, and it premiered in Prague in 1787. Falstaff is the title character of an opera by Giuseppe Verdi.

q: Which musical show did Stephen Sondheim write in 1979?

q.e: Sweeney Todd: The Demon Barber of Fleet Street opened on Broadway in 1979, with music and lyrics by Stephen Sondheim. It won the Tony for Best Musical.

q: Which famous ballet by Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky was first performed at the Bolshoi Theatre in Moscow in 1877?

q.e: Tchaikovsky's 'Swan Lake' premiered at the Bolshoi Theatre in March 1877. 'The Nutcracker' premiered 15 years later in 1892, while 'The Firebird' was composed by Igor Stravinsky.

q: The building at 1619 Broadway in New York City is also known by this name.

q.e: The Brill Building at 1619 Broadway was the home of music publishers and songwriters, such as Carole King and Neil Sedaka. The term "Brill Building sound" refers to the pop songs written there in the late 1950s and early 1960s.

q: In a Puccini opera, what is the name of the tragic lady who falls in love with the callous Lieutenant Pinkerton?

q.e: Giacomo Puccini's 1904 opera centers on the young geisha Cio-Cio-San, known as Madame Butterfly, who marries US Naval Lieutenant B.F. Pinkerton. Suzuki is the name of her loyal maid.

q: Burt Bacharach was the musical accompanist for this famous lady.

q.e: Burt Bacharach worked as Marlene Dietrich's musical director and accompanist from 1958 to 1961. He toured the world with her before his big hits.

q: Who commissioned composing of the opera Aida?

q.e: Ismail Pasha, the Khedive of Egypt, commissioned Aida from Verdi, which premiered in Cairo in 1871. Verdi was reluctant at first, but accepted.

q: How many operas did Italian opera composer Giuseppe Verdi compose?

q.e: Verdi composed about 28 operas, depending on how revised versions are counted. His last works were Otello (1887) and Falstaff (1893).

q: Which statement is untrue about the main character of the opera Aida?
In the opera, Aida is a Roman Empress.
In the opera, Aida has royal blood.
The 1987 movie version of Aida is performed topless.
In the opera, Aida is a slave girl.

q.e: Aida is not a Roman empress; she's an Ethiopian princess held as a slave in Egypt. The story is set in the time of the pharaohs.

q: What character did Marni Nixon voice in the 1964 musical film Mary Poppins?

q.e: Marni Nixon, the "ghost singer" for Natalie Wood and Audrey Hepburn, appeared in Mary Poppins as the voice of the geese in the "Jolly Holiday" scene. She also had a small role in The Sound of Music.

q: In the musical Legally Blonde, what are Elle and Emmett doing together during the song Take It Like a Man?

q.e: In "Take It Like a Man" in Legally Blonde, Elle and Emmett go shopping for his new suit. The song is about being tough and getting a "chip on your shoulder".

q: What does Emmett say that Elle needs in order to work hard and do well in law school in Legally Blonde: The Musical?

q.e: Emmett tells Elle she needs to find a chip on her shoulder, meaning a determination to prove herself. It's a reference to the underdog spirit.

q: In what popular musical film did Barbra Streisand star in 1969?

q.e: Hello, Dolly! (1969) was Barbra Streisand's third film, after Funny Girl (1968) and was directed by Gene Kelly. Walter Matthau co-starred as Horace Vandergelder.

q: Which pianist's music does the musical Aint Misbehaving feature?

q.e: Ain't Misbehavin' (1978) is a revue of music by Thomas "Fats" Waller, the Harlem stride pianist, composer and entertainer. It won the 1978 Tony Award for Best Musical.

q: Who played Mame Dennis on Broadway in the musical Mame?

q.e: Angela Lansbury originated Mame Dennis in the 1966 Broadway musical Mame by Jerry Herman and won a Tony. Rosalind Russell had played her in the 1958 film Auntie Mame.

q: How many daughters did Tevye have in the musical Fiddler on the Roof?

q.e: Tevye and his wife Golde have five daughters: Tzeitel, Hodel, Chava, Shprintze, and Bielke. The musical's plot primarily revolves around the marriage arrangements of the three oldest daughters.

q: What Southerner penned the lyrics for the musical Lil Abner?

q.e: Johnny Mercer, a Savannah, Georgia songwriter, wrote the lyrics for Li'l Abner (1956), a musical based on Al Capp's comic strip. Gene de Paul composed the music.

q: What Broadway star appearing in Sondheims Company also played a character on the TV sitcom, Alice?

q.e: Beth Howland played Amy in the original 1970 Broadway cast of Sondheim's Company and later played the dim-witted waitress Vera on the TV sitcom Alice. Amy sings the patter song "Getting Married Today".

q: In the musical version of Grey Gardens, Act 1 centers around the fictitious engagement of Little Edie Beale to what political figure?

q.e: In Act 1 of Grey Gardens (2006), set in 1941, Little Edie Beale is engaged to Joseph Kennedy Jr., the elder brother of JFK. The engagement is fictional.

q: What is the title of the popular song from the 1953 musical Kismet that has been covered by many musicians?

q.e: "Stranger in Paradise" from Kismet (1953) was based on a theme from Borodin's Polovtsian Dances. Tony Bennett had a hit with it in 1953.

q: In which Italian opera is the famous aria Casta Diva sung?

q.e: "Casta diva" is a famous aria from Bellini's opera Norma (1831), sung by the Druid priestess Norma. It's known as a very demanding bel canto piece.

q: What is the Japanese name of Madame Butterfly in Puccinis self-titled opera?

q.e: In Puccini's Madama Butterfly, the heroine's Japanese name is Cio-Cio-San, which means "butterfly". American Lieutenant Pinkerton calls her Butterfly.

q: In this opera by Giuseppe Verdi an Ethiopian princess, is captured and brought into slavery in Egypt.

q.e: Giuseppe Verdi's four-act opera Aida premiered in Cairo in 1871. Tosca and Norma are also famous Italian operas, but they were composed by Giacomo Puccini and Vincenzo Bellini, respectively.

q: What is the final song of the musical The Light in the Piazza?

q.e: "Fable" is the final song of The Light in the Piazza (2005), with music and lyrics by Adam Guettel. The musical won six Tony Awards.

q: What character did Stephen Gately play in the stage musical Chitty Chitty Bang Bang?

q.e: Stephen Gately of the Irish band Boyzone played the Child Catcher in Chitty Chitty Bang Bang in the West End in 2002. The musical is based on Ian Fleming's children's novel.

q: The soundtrack of this Broadway musical includes the popular song Tomorrow with the famous chorus: Tomorrow, tomorrow, I love ya, tomorrow, youre always a day away..

q.e: Tomorrow was written by Charles Strouse and Martin Charnin for the 1977 musical Annie, based on the classic comic strip Little Orphan Annie.

q: The King of Egypt, Amneris and Amonasro are three characters from this opera.

q.e: Amneris, the King of Egypt and Amonasro are all characters in Verdi's Aida. Amonasro is Aida's father, the king of Ethiopia.

q: One of the pairs (composer - an opera of his) is wrong.

q.e: William Tell is an opera by Rossini (1829), not Dvořák. Dvořák wrote Rusalka.

q: Who wrote the first opera entitled Madame Butterfly?

q.e: Giacomo Puccini wrote Madama Butterfly, which premiered at La Scala in 1904 and failed at first. He revised it, and it became a success.

q: The second act of the opera Madame Butterfly closes with what famous chorus?

q.e: The Humming Chorus (Coro a bocca chiusa) closes Act 2 of Madama Butterfly, as Cio-Cio-San waits all night for Pinkerton to return. The singers hum, with no words.

q: #5 on the list of highest-grossing films is a musical which takes place in Austria. It was made in 1965 and grossed $2,269,800,000. Sing the scales for me on a hill top.

q.e: Directed by Robert Wise, The Sound of Music stars Julie Andrews as Maria von Trapp and won five Academy Awards, including Best Picture.

q: The 2012 Academy Award-winning musical drama Les Misérables was based on a novel by this French author.

q.e: Victor Hugo published his monumental historical novel Les Misérables in 1862. Alexandre Dumas, another famous 19th-century French novelist, is best known for The Three Musketeers and The Count of Monte Cristo.

q: This Irish playwright and a co-founder of the London School of Economics wrote more than 60 plays during his lifetime, which earned him a Nobel Prize in Literature in 1925.

q.e: George Bernard Shaw (1856-1950), a co-founder of the London School of Economics, won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1925. He also won an Oscar for Pygmalion in 1938.

q: This Irish playwright, who was awarded a Nobel Prize in Literature and an Oscar, harboured a lifelong animosity toward schools and teachers.

q.e: Shaw hated his schooling, which he thought was about memorizing and being punished. He wrote that schools were like prisons, and his play Pygmalion is about teaching.

q: This playwright, director and actor, born Allan Stewart Konigsberg, was thrown out of New York University after one semester for poor grades.

q.e: Woody Allen was born Allan Stewart Konigsberg in New York City in 1935 and was dismissed from NYU in 1953 after failing a course in motion picture production.

q: This redhead playwright became the first person in history to be awarded both a Nobel Prize and an Oscar, for his contributions to literature and for his work on the film Pygmalion.

q.e: George Bernard Shaw was awarded the 1925 Nobel Prize in Literature and later won the Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay in 1938 for the film version of his play Pygmalion.

q: Who composed the famous musical Cats?

q.e: Andrew Lloyd Webber composed 'Cats', which premiered in London's West End in 1981 and was based on T.S. Eliot's 1939 poetry collection 'Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats'.

q: This romantic musical film, which featured the songs Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas and The Boy Next Door, is set at the time of the Louisiana Purchase Exposition.

q.e: Meet Me in St. Louis (1944) was set around the 1904 World's Fair, also known as the Louisiana Purchase Exposition. It starred Judy Garland and Margaret O'Brien.

q: What musical film directed by Gene Kelly starred Barbra Streisand?

q.e: Gene Kelly directed Hello, Dolly! (1969), with Barbra Streisand as Dolly. Kelly was best known as a dancer in Singin' in the Rain.

q: What celebrated movie star portrayed Vicki Lester in the 1954 movie musical A Star Is Born?

q.e: Judy Garland played Vicki Lester in the 1954 musical version of A Star Is Born, a role that earned her an Oscar nomination. James Mason played Norman Maine.

q: The 1961 movie musical West Side Story was loosely based on which famous play by William Shakespeare?

q.e: West Side Story reimagines Romeo and Juliet by replacing the feuding Montagues and Capulets with rival 1950s New York street gangs, the Jets and the Sharks.

q: What actor portrayed Nick Arnstein in the 1968 musical movie Funny Girl?

q.e: Omar Sharif played the gambler Nick Arnstein in Funny Girl (1968), opposite Barbra Streisand as Fanny Brice. She won the Oscar for Best Actress.

q: What Academy Award-winning actress portrayed Angelique in Bob Fosses 1979 musical movie All That Jazz?

q.e: Jessica Lange played Angelique, the Angel of Death, in All That Jazz (1979), her film debut after King Kong. Roy Scheider played the lead.

q: Who played Dr. Frank N. Furter in the comedy-horror musical film The Rocky Horror Picture Show?

q.e: Tim Curry originated the role of Dr. Frank N. Furter in the 1973 London stage production of 'The Rocky Horror Show' before reprising it in the 1975 film adaptation.

q: What prominent playwright wrote the plays A Glass Menagerie, A Streetcar Named Desire, The Rose Tattoo, The Night of the Iguana?

q.e: Tennessee Williams became one of the leading American dramatists of the 20th century, winning Pulitzer Prizes for both A Streetcar Named Desire and Cat on a Hot Tin Roof.

q: What were the names of the lovers in the musical West Side Story?

q.e: The lovers in West Side Story are Tony and Maria. Their names suggest an update of Romeo and Juliet.

q: What playwright wrote Tambourlaine, Dido and Edward II?

q.e: Christopher Marlowe wrote Tamburlaine, Dido, Queen of Carthage and Edward II. He was a contemporary of Shakespeare and was killed in 1593.

q: What Irish playwright and author said, I can resist everything except temptation.?

q.e: The famous quip comes from Lord Darlington in Oscar Wilde's 1892 comedy play, Lady Windermere's Fan. Wilde was renowned for his biting wit and paradoxes across plays, essays, and his novel The Picture of Dorian Gray.

q: This Irish playwright became a vegetarian at the age of twenty-five, after hearing a lecture by H. F. Lester.

q.e: George Bernard Shaw became a vegetarian in 1881, at 25, after hearing a lecture by H. F. Lester. He stayed vegetarian for the rest of his life.

q: What famous playwright, born in Dublin, stated, If there is nothing wrong with the world, there wouldnt be anything for us to do.?

q.e: This is a quote attributed to George Bernard Shaw, the Dublin-born playwright. He was known for his wit and social criticism.

q: What Nobel Prize-winning Irish poet and dramatist contributed greatly to the Theatre of the Absurd?

q.e: Samuel Beckett, an Irish writer who lived mostly in France, won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1969. His Waiting for Godot is a key work of the Theatre of the Absurd.

q: "The 100% American is 99% an idiot.� was a remark made by this non-American playwright.

q.e: This quip is credited to George Bernard Shaw, who was Irish and often made fun of American culture. He visited the US in 1933.

q: What famous playwright wrote: "Life is a tale told by an idiot -- full of sound and fury, signifying nothing.�?

q.e: "Life's but a walking shadow... a tale told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, signifying nothing" is from Shakespeare's Macbeth (Act 5, Scene 5). Macbeth says it after hearing his wife has died.

q: This actor, who won a Tony Award for leading role in Jerome Robbins Broadway, is the son of Ruth and Alex Greenspan.

q.e: Jason Alexander won the 1989 Tony Award for Best Leading Actor in a Musical for Jerome Robbins' Broadway. He's best known as George Costanza on Seinfeld.

q: In the 80s, Andrew Lloyd Webber dominated the musical theatre. Which of the following is not a show of his?

q.e: The 1975 musical Chicago was composed by John Kander with lyrics by Fred Ebb, who also created Cabaret. Andrew Lloyd Webber dominated the West End and Broadway with hits like Cats, Evita, and The Phantom of the Opera.

q: The search for The Holy Grail is one of the central themes in the opera Persifal by this German composer.

q.e: Richard Wagner's Parsifal (1882) is about the knight who seeks the Holy Grail. It was his final opera.

q: Which musical features the song "Defying Gravity"?

q.e: Defying Gravity is the climactic act-one finale of Wicked, originally belted out by Idina Menzel as Elphaba in 2003. The musical is based on Gregory Maguire's 1995 novel exploring the backstory of the witches of Oz.

Composed by Andrew Lloyd Webber for Cats, Memory is sung by the aging glamour cat Grizabella, famously introduced by Elaine Paige. Its lyrics were adapted by Trevor Nunn from T. S. Eliot's poem Rhapsody on a Windy Night.

q: Which musical is built around ABBA songs?

q.e: Mamma Mia! is a jukebox musical written by Catherine Johnson featuring hits by the Swedish pop group ABBA, including Dancing Queen and the title track. Jersey Boys, by comparison, is a biographical musical centered on the catalogue of Frankie Valli and The Four Seasons.

q: In "Hello, Dolly!", Horace Vandergelder lives in which New York city?

q.e: Horace Vandergelder is a rich merchant from Yonkers, New York, in Hello, Dolly! He's the "half-a-millionaire" whom matchmaker Dolly Levi plans to marry.

q: This famous actress and singer starred opposite Robert De Niro in the 1977 musical movie New York, New York.

q.e: Liza Minnelli starred opposite Robert De Niro in New York, New York (1977), directed by Martin Scorsese. The film introduced the title song, later recorded by Frank Sinatra.

q: In 1947 Gregory Peck founded this important theater with the help of Mel Ferrer and Dorothy McGuire.

q.e: Gregory Peck, with Mel Ferrer and Dorothy McGuire, founded the La Jolla Playhouse in California in 1947. It reopened in 1983 and has since sent shows like Jersey Boys to Broadway.

q: What actor starred alongside Liza Minnelli as her characters lover and music partner in Martin Scorseses 1977 musical movie New York, New York?

q.e: Robert De Niro played saxophonist Jimmy Doyle opposite Liza Minnelli in New York, New York (1977). Scorsese directed the film, which pays homage to old Hollywood musicals.

q: Al Pacino won a Tony Award, a Drama Desk Award and a Theater World Award for his role in which play?
Does the Tiger Wear a Necktie?

q.e: Al Pacino won his first Tony Award in 1969 for Does the Tiger Wear a Necktie?, a play about drug addicts in a reform school. It was early in his career, before The Godfather.

q: Actor Edward Norton joined a theater group called The Signature Players that produced plays written by which great playwright?

q.e: Edward Norton was part of the Signature Theatre Company in New York, which devotes each season to a single playwright. Edward Albee was the playwright in the 1993-94 season.

q: In 2002, rapper and actor Mos Def starred in what Pulitzer Prize-Winning Broadway play?

q.e: Mos Def starred in Suzan-Lori Parks's Topdog/Underdog (2002), a play about two brothers called Lincoln and Booth. It won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama.

q: She was born in May of 1929 and was famous for her coloratura soprano roles in opera.

q.e: Beverly Sills (born May 25, 1929) was an American coloratura soprano who later led the New York City Opera and the Metropolitan Opera. She was nicknamed "Bubbles".

q: In his first major role, actor Jerry Orbach played El Galo, in which 1960 musical comedy?

q.e: Jerry Orbach played El Gallo in the original 1960 off-Broadway production of The Fantasticks, introducing "Try to Remember". The show ran for 42 years.

q: Although his claims to be related to former Vice President Al Gore remain dubious, this fiery American author, playwright and social critic is definitely the stepbrother of Jacqueline Onassis.

q.e: Gore Vidal was the stepbrother of Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis, as their parents' marriages were to Hugh D. Auchincloss. He was a writer of novels, essays and plays.

q: Richard Benjamin, an alumnae of Northwestern University, began as a fine actor and then did fine work behind the camera. His wife also attended NWUs Theatre Program. What is her name?

q.e: Paula Prentiss, who was married to Richard Benjamin, studied at Northwestern University's theatre program. They starred together in the film Catch-22 and the TV show He & She.

q: Born in Vladivostok, Russia in 1920, this Academy Award-winning actor is best know for playing King Mongkut of Siam 4,626 times onstage. He also reprised the role in the film version of the musical.

q.e: Yul Brynner won an Academy Award in 1956 for reprising his role as King Mongkut in the film adaptation of Rodgers and Hammerstein's The King and I.

q: This Shakespearean play is referred to as The Scottish Play or The Scottish King by most actors and theater people since it is considered bad luck to mention the name of the play.

q.e: A long-standing theatrical superstition holds that speaking the name 'Macbeth' inside a theatre brings disaster, leading actors to refer to the tragedy simply as 'The Scottish Play.'

q: Who wrote the opera Mozart et Salieri?

q.e: Mozart and Salieri (1898) is a one-act opera by Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov, based on a play by Pushkin. It dramatizes a false rumor that Salieri poisoned Mozart.

q: This Spanish playwright and poet, author of The Dog in the Manger and The Widow from Valencia, maintained that a writers business is to write so as to make himself understood.

q.e: Lope de Vega (1562-1635) was a Spanish Golden Age dramatist who wrote hundreds of plays. His El perro del hortelano is The Dog in the Manger.

q: In his works, this Greek playwright, whose contribution to the theater was the addition of a second actor to the scenes, focused on mans position in the cosmos, in relation to the gods.

q.e: Aeschylus is said to have added a second actor to Greek tragedy, making dialogue and conflict possible. His works include the Oresteia trilogy.

q: This very popular opera singer from Australia lived 1861-1931. She had two foods named after her.

q.e: Renowned Australian soprano Dame Nellie Melba inspired chef Auguste Escoffier to create Peach Melba around 1892, as well as Melba toast.

q: What is the name for a vocal musical composition for between two and eight singers, written in the Renaissance and early Baroque eras and often performed without musical accompaniment?

q.e: A madrigal is a vocal piece for several voices, usually without instruments, that was popular in the Renaissance and early Baroque. Composers include Monteverdi and Thomas Morley.

q: The hit song If I Were a Rich Man, which reflected the dreams of a poor milkman, came from which musical of the 60s?

q.e: If I Were a Rich Man is sung by the milkman Tevye in the 1964 Broadway hit Fiddler on the Roof, with music by Jerry Bock and lyrics by Sheldon Harnick. The other musicals listed debuted later, with Chicago in 1975, 42nd Street in 1980, and Cats in 1981.

q: For which opera did Gershwin become posthumously famous?

q.e: Porgy and Bess premiered in 1935, and George Gershwin died in 1937, aged 38. The opera was not hugely successful at first, but its songs, like "Summertime", became jazz standards.

q: This star from Boston Public is the only actress from the original Broadway cast of Dreamgirls who appeared (and sang) in the 2006 movie adaptation.

q.e: Loretta Devine was in the original 1981 Broadway cast of Dreamgirls (as Lorrell Robinson) and in the 2006 film. She also appeared in Boston Public.

q: The story in the 1955 Broadway play Inherit the Wind is a fictionalized version of what famous event in US history?

q.e: Jerome Lawrence and Robert E. Lee wrote Inherit the Wind based on the 1925 Scopes 'Monkey' Trial, in which high school teacher John T. Scopes was tried for teaching human evolution in Tennessee.

q: In the real-life events on which the 1960 Broadway play Inherit the Wind was based, the defense lawyer was able to take the case pro bono because he made his money defending another client. Who was this rich client?

q.e: The real-life Scopes trial of 1925 had Clarence Darrow as defense lawyer, who volunteered to help John Scopes. Inherit the Wind (1955) is a fictionalized account, so details differ.

q: Who starred as the defense lawyer in the premiere of the 1955 Broadway play Inherit the Wind?

q.e: Paul Muni played Henry Drummond, the defense lawyer based on Clarence Darrow, in the 1955 Broadway premiere of Inherit the Wind. Melvyn Douglas also appeared.

q: In the premiere of the 1955 Broadway play Inherit the Wind, who played the role of the prosecutor?

q.e: Ed Begley played Matthew Harrison Brady, the character based on William Jennings Bryan, in the original Broadway Inherit the Wind. He later won an Oscar for Sweet Bird of Youth.

q: Which cat sings Memory in the Andrew Lloyd Weber hit musical, Cats?

q.e: Grizabella the Glamour Cat sings the emotional showstopper Memory; Elaine Paige originated the role in London in 1981, and Betty Buckley won a Tony for it on Broadway.

q: The song Send in the Clowns from the musical A Little Night Music was specifically written for which actress?

q.e: Stephen Sondheim wrote "Send in the Clowns" for Glynis Johns in A Little Night Music (1973). He crafted it to suit her limited vocal range.

q: This fabulous woman was the first actor to qualify for the category of the winners of an Oscar, an Emmy, a Tony, and a Grammy. She won her Oscar in 1961 for best Supporting Actress for her role in a musical, set in New York City.

q.e: Rita Moreno won the Oscar for Best Supporting Actress for West Side Story (1961). She is one of the few people to win an Emmy, a Grammy, an Oscar and a Tony.

q: Which actress played young soprano Christine in the movie The Phantom of the Opera?

q.e: Emmy Rossum played Christine Daaé in Joel Schumacher's 2004 film The Phantom of the Opera. She was 17 when she was cast.

q: What 1996 musical movie co-written by Oliver Stone set a Guinness World Record for Most costume changes in a film?

q.e: Evita (1996) holds the Guinness record for most costume changes in a film, with Madonna wearing 85 outfits. Alan Parker directed; Oliver Stone wrote an earlier draft.

q: Summertime is the best-known song from what popular musical by George Gershwin?

q.e: Summertime is an aria composed in 1934 by George Gershwin for the 1935 opera Porgy and Bess, with lyrics by DuBose Heyward. It has gone on to become one of the most recorded songs in music history, with thousands of recorded versions.

q: This music became popular in the mid 1900s. It was characterized by the use of very little musical material and repetition of patterns.

q.e: Minimalism uses few musical ideas, repeated and gradually changed. Composers include Steve Reich, Philip Glass and Terry Riley.

q: In the musical Les Miserables, which character sings the solo I Dreamed a Dream?

q.e: Fantine sings 'I Dreamed a Dream' in Act I after being fired from Jean Valjean's factory and forced into poverty.

q: Miss Gooch is a character in which award-winning Jerry Herman musical based on an earlier play?

q.e: Agnes Gooch is Mame Dennis's secretary in Mame, a musical by Jerry Herman based on the play Auntie Mame. She sings "That's How Young I Feel" during a hilarious scene.

q: In this musical the song I Won't Send Roses is performed when the male lead is trying to convince his girl that he is not right for her?

q.e: "I Won't Send Roses" is sung by director Mack Sennett to Mabel Normand in Jerry Herman's Mack and Mabel (1974). The song shows he is unromantic.

q: Which movie musical featured Anne Blythe singing Baubles, Bangles and Beads?

q.e: Anne Blyth sang "Baubles, Bangles and Beads" in the 1955 film Kismet. The song is based on a theme by Borodin.

q: Who wrote the music for Girl Crazy which opened at the Alvin Theatre on October 14, 1930?

q.e: George Gershwin composed the music for Girl Crazy (1930), with lyrics by Ira Gershwin. The show included "I Got Rhythm" and made Ethel Merman a star.

q: Stranger in Paradise is the love theme sung by a young prince in which musical?

q.e: In Kismet (1953), "Stranger in Paradise" is sung by the Caliph, a young ruler who falls in love with Marsinah. The music is adapted from Borodin.

q: The Russian Five, considered the great musical intellectuals of the 19th century included Balakirev, Cui, Mussorgsky, Borodin and this composer who wrote the opera The Tale of Tsar Saltan.

q.e: Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov was one of the "Mighty Handful", also known as "The Five". The group included Balakirev, Cui, Mussorgsky and Borodin.

q: Cyndi Lauper made her 2006 Broadway debut in the revival of what opera?

q.e: Cyndi Lauper made her Broadway debut in 2006 in The Threepenny Opera, in the role of Jenny. She later won a Tony for composing the score for Kinky Boots.

q: Solomon Linda, an African Zulu, wrote and recorded this song in 1939 that The Tokens took to the top of the Billboard Hot 100 in 1961. Can you name the African lullaby and Broadway tune that begins A-Wimoweh, a-wimoweh?

q.e: Solomon Linda originally recorded the song as 'Mbube' in 1939 with The Evening Birds, which was later adapted into the chart-topping 1961 pop hit 'The Lion Sleeps Tonight'.

q: The 1972 song Day By Day was a huge hit from this musical.

q.e: "Day by Day" from Godspell (1971), written by Stephen Schwartz, reached #13 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1972. The lyrics were adapted from a prayer by St. Richard of Chichester.

q: A fine singer and a great comedic actress, this jazz vocalist would often interrupt a song by asking a member of the audience Are you O.K., honey? She starred in Hello Dolly on Broadway but was not in the original cast.

q.e: Pearl Bailey took over from Carol Channing as Dolly in the Broadway production of Hello, Dolly! in 1967 in an all-Black cast. She won a special Tony for her performance.

q: Who wrote the music and lyrics for the groundbreaking Broadway musical Hair?

q.e: The lyrics for Hair (1967) were written by Gerome Ragni and James Rado, with music by Galt MacDermot. The musical was a hit for its hippie spirit.

q: Who wrote the musical The Man of La Mancha which had its world premier at the Goodspeed Opera House in Connecticut?

q.e: Man of La Mancha (1965) premiered at the Goodspeed Opera House in Connecticut. It has music by Mitch Leigh, lyrics by Joe Darion and a book by Dale Wasserman.

q: Which is the author of the musical Kiss of the Spider Woman which opened on Broadway in 1993?

q.e: Kiss of the Spider Woman (1993) has music by John Kander and lyrics by Fred Ebb, with a book by Terrence McNally. It's based on Manuel Puig's novel.

q: Who wrote the musical The Unsinkable Molly Brown in the 1960s?

q.e: Meredith Willson wrote the music and lyrics for The Unsinkable Molly Brown (1960), after The Music Man. The title role was played by Tammy Grimes on Broadway.

q: What is Elphabas nickname in the musical Wicked?

q.e: In Wicked, Elphaba is nicknamed "Elphie" by her friends, a name she gets from Glinda. The name is derived from L. Frank Baum.

q: What kind of prince is Fiyero in the musical Wicked?

q.e: Fiyero is a prince of the Vinkus (Winkie Country) in Wicked. In the original book, his name is Fiyero Tigelaar.

q: What actress originally played Glinda on the Broadway musical Wicked?

q.e: Kristin Chenoweth originated the role of Glinda the Good Witch when Wicked premiered on Broadway in October 2003. Her performance earned her a Tony Award nomination for Best Actress in a Musical alongside her co-star Idina Menzel, who played Elphaba.

q: In 1968 Burt Bacharach and Hal David had a hit with Ill Never Fall in Love Again, sung by Dionne Warwick. The song was written for this very popular musical that originally starred Jerry Orbach, Edward Winter, and Jill OHara.

q.e: "I'll Never Fall in Love Again" is from the 1968 musical Promises, Promises, with a book by Neil Simon, based on the movie The Apartment. Dionne Warwick's version was a hit.

q: Who wrote the libretto for the opera Aida?

q.e: The libretto for Aida was written by Antonio Ghislanzoni, in Italian. Camille du Locle helped develop the story from an outline from Egyptologist Auguste Mariette.

q: What is the first song in the musical Legally Blonde?

q.e: "Omigod You Guys" opens Legally Blonde: The Musical (2007), as Elle's sorority sisters celebrate before Warner proposes. The musical is based on the 2001 film.

q: Which of these works by Adam de la Halle is considered to be a forerunner of comic opera?
Le jeu de Robin et Marion
La Chanson du roi de Sicile
La chanson du Henri de la Halle

q.e: Adam de la Halle wrote Le Jeu de Robin et Marion in c. 1280, a pastoral play with music, often seen as an early comic opera. He was nicknamed "the Hunchback of Arras".

q: This opera character is a Persian Princess. Any man who desires to wed her must first answer her three riddles. If he fails, he will be beheaded.

q.e: Princess Turandot is a Chinese princess in Puccini's last opera, Turandot, who beheads suitors who fail to answer three riddles. The opera was unfinished when he died in 1924.

q: Libiamo nelieti calici (Drinking Song) is a famous duet with chorus from this popular opera by Verdi.

q.e: "Libiamo ne' lieti calici" is the drinking song in Verdi's La traviata (1853), sung by Alfredo and Violetta. It's one of the best-known opera duets.

q: What Italian opera follows the plight of the Jews as they are assaulted and subsequently exiled from their homeland by a Babylonian King?

q.e: Verdi's Nabucco (1842) is about the Hebrews exiled in Babylon by King Nebuchadnezzar. Its chorus "Va, pensiero" became an unofficial Italian anthem.

q: Nessun Dorma (None shall sleep), one of the best-known tenor arias, is sung by Calaf, the unknown prince in this famous opera.

q.e: Nessun Dorma appears in the final act of Giacomo Puccini's opera Turandot, which premiered posthumously in 1926. The aria gained massive global popularity in 1990 when Luciano Pavarotti sang it for the FIFA World Cup.

q: Who composed the opera Lelisir damore (The Elixir of Love) in which a peasant boy falls in love named Nemorino falls in love with Adina, a wealthy landowner?

q.e: Gaetano Donizetti composed L'elisir d'amore (1832), a comic opera. In it, Nemorino buys a fake love potion to win Adina.

q: This is the first Italian city Clara and Margaret visit in the musical The Light in the Piazza. Here they meet Fabrizio and Clara falls in love.

q.e: Clara and her mother Margaret first visit Florence (Firenze) in The Light in the Piazza. There Clara's hat blows away and she meets Fabrizio.

q: What is the name of the song in the musical The Light in the Piazza during which Clara becomes lost and goes crazy, until Margaret finds her and takes her to the hotel room?

q.e: "Hysteria" is the song in The Light in the Piazza in which Clara has an episode. Her mother Margaret has to protect her and her secret.

q: This opera was composed in 1786 and was based on a stage comedy by Beaumarchais. Cherubino and Marcellina are just two of the characters in it.

q.e: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart composed The Marriage of Figaro (Le nozze di Figaro) with librettist Lorenzo Da Ponte, premiering it at Vienna's Burgtheater in 1786. It is based on Pierre Beaumarchais's 1778 play, the second installment in his Figaro trilogy.

q: Prince Igor is a famous opera by this composer.

q.e: Alexander Borodin composed Prince Igor, which is best known for the Polovtsian Dances. It was unfinished when he died in 1887 and was completed by Rimsky-Korsakov and Glazunov.

q: The use of Japan as a location for a love story in the opera Madame Butterfly was partially in response to the writings of which European Japanophile?

q.e: Lafcadio Hearn, a Greek-born writer who moved to Japan, wrote about Japanese life and folklore for Western readers. His books inspired the Western view of Japan in the early 1900s.

q: The composer of the opera Madame Butterfly also wrote the opera on which the play Rent is based. What is the name of that opera?

q.e: Giacomo Puccini's 1896 opera La Boheme inspired Jonathan Larson's 1996 musical Rent, updating the 19th-century tuberculosis epidemic among Paris bohemians to the late 20th-century HIV/AIDS crisis in New York City.

q: This poet and playwright was the first Irishman honored with the Nobel Prize in Literature. In his later years he served as an Irish Senator for two terms.

q.e: William Butler Yeats won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1923, the first Irishman to do so. He also served as a senator in the Irish Free State from 1922 to 1928.

q: What classic musical comedy, directed by Howard Hawks, features Marilyn Monroes signature rendition of the song "Diamonds Are a Girl's Best Friend"?

q.e: Gentlemen Prefer Blondes (1953) paired Marilyn Monroe with Jane Russell and produced Monroe's iconic performance in a hot pink gown. The Seven Year Itch, another famous Monroe comedy, was directed by Billy Wilder instead of Howard Hawks.

q: Uncommon Women and Others, The Heidi Chronicles, Isnt It Romantic, and The Sisters Rosensweig are written by this playwright.

q.e: Wendy Wasserstein won the Pulitzer Prize and a Tony for The Heidi Chronicles (1988). Her plays are about the lives of professional women.

q: Lysistrata, The Birds, The Wasps, The Frogs are plays by this ancient Greek playwright.

q.e: Aristophanes (c. 446-386 BC) was an Athenian comic playwright. Lysistrata is about women who withhold sex to end a war.

q: This playwright is the author of Our Town, The Skin of Our Teeth, Bernice, and The Merchant of Yonkers.

q.e: Thornton Wilder won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama for both Our Town (1938) and The Skin of Our Teeth (1942); his farce The Merchant of Yonkers later became the musical Hello, Dolly!.

q: What playwright is the author of The Way of the World, The Mourning Bride and Love for Love?

q.e: William Congreve, the Restoration comedy writer, wrote The Way of the World (1700). It features the witty couple Mirabell and Millamant.

q: Hedda Gabler, The Wild Duck, An Enemy of the People and Ghosts are plays written by this playwright.

q.e: Henrik Ibsen, a Norwegian dramatist, wrote Hedda Gabler, The Wild Duck, An Enemy of the People and Ghosts. He is called the "father of modern drama".

q: What playwright penned Waiting for Lefty, Golden Boy, Till the Day I Die and Awake and Sing?

q.e: Clifford Odets, a playwright of the Group Theatre, wrote Waiting for Lefty, Golden Boy and Awake and Sing! in the 1930s. His plays often focused on the working class in the Great Depression.

q: This Academy Award-winning actress starred opposite Judy Garland in the 1944 romantic musical film Meet Me in St. Louis.

q.e: Margaret O'Brien played Tootie in Meet Me in St. Louis (1944) and received a special Juvenile Academy Award for her work. Judy Garland was her co-star.

q: Lakeboat, Glengarry Glen Ross, Speed-the Plow, American Buffalo, The Duck Variation are plays by this playwright.

q.e: David Mamet, a Chicago playwright, wrote Glengarry Glen Ross, which won the 1984 Pulitzer Prize for Drama. American Buffalo and Speed-the-Plow are other plays.

q: Name the playwright who wrote The Second Man, End of Summer, No Time for Comedy.

q.e: S. N. Behrman wrote high comedies like The Second Man (1927) and No Time for Comedy (1939). He also wrote screenplays.

q: Line, The Indian Wants the Bronx and Park Your Car in Harvard Yard were written by this playwright.

q.e: Israel Horovitz wrote Line, The Indian Wants the Bronx and Park Your Car in Harvard Yard. He also founded the Gloucester Stage Company.

q: Which playwright wrote Riders to the Sea, The Tinkers Wedding, The Playboy of the Western World?

q.e: John Millington Synge wrote Riders to the Sea, The Tinker's Wedding and The Playboy of the Western World. The last caused riots when it opened at the Abbey Theatre in Dublin in 1907.

q: Name the Austrian journalist, writer, satirist, essayist, aphorist, playwright and poet who said, "Education is a crutch with which the foolish attack the wise to prove that they are not idiots.�

q.e: Karl Kraus (1874-1936) was an Austrian satirist who published the magazine Die Fackel. His play The Last Days of Mankind portrays World War I.

q: "Half the world is composed of idiots, the other half of people clever enough to take indecent advantage of them� was uttered by this writer and Broadway critic.

q.e: This is a quip about human folly. The source is uncertain, though Walter Kerr was a Broadway critic for the Herald Tribune and New York Times.

q: Which American lyrical poet, playwright and feminist wrote "April comes like an idiot, babbling and stewing flowers.�

q.e: Edna St. Vincent Millay's poem "Spring" includes the line "April comes like an idiot, babbling and strewing flowers". She won the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry in 1923.

q: Aristotle Onassis had a notorious affair with this opera diva.

q.e: Aristotle Onassis, the Greek shipping tycoon, had a long affair with the soprano Maria Callas, before marrying Jacqueline Kennedy in 1968. Callas was born in New York.

q: Eye of newt and toe of frog Wool of bat and tongue of dog is one of the most famous spells in English literature. In what Shakespeare play do the three witches cast their evil spells?

q.e: The famous incantation is chanted by the Three Witches around their cauldron in Act 4, Scene 1 of Shakespeare's tragedy Macbeth.

q: Who composed the music for the Broadway rock opera "Jesus Christ Superstar"?

q.e: Andrew Lloyd Webber composed the music for the 1970 rock opera 'Jesus Christ Superstar', collaborating with lyricist Tim Rice before the show opened on Broadway in 1971.

q: Fragments of the "Ode to Joy" appear in the libretto of which 1805 opera, Beethoven's only one?

q.e: Beethoven's only opera, Fidelio (1805), tells the story of Leonore, who disguises herself as a man to save her husband from prison. It was revised twice before 1814.

q: Hedwig Lachmann translated an Oscar Wilde play into German for which Richard Strauss opera?

q.e: Richard Strauss's opera Salome (1905) is based on Oscar Wilde's play, in Hedwig Lachmann's German translation. The "Dance of the Seven Veils" is its best-known scene.

q: This German-born cellist came to the USA to play with the Metropolitan Opera and then began writing his own operettas. He wrote The Naughty Marietta in 1910.

q.e: Victor Herbert, born in Dublin in 1859 and raised in Germany, was a cellist in the Metropolitan Opera orchestra. He wrote the operettas Naughty Marietta (1910) and Babes in Toyland.

q: It was one of the longest running off-Broadway plays. Its orchestra consisted of a harp and a piano. It was written by Tom Jones and Harvey Schmidt. It originally starred Rita Gardner, Thomas Bruce and Kenneth Nelson.

q.e: The Fantasticks (1960), by Tom Jones and Harvey Schmidt, ran for 42 years off-Broadway, the longest-running musical in the world at that time. It was played by a small cast with a harp and piano.

q: This form of traditional Japanese theater, which aims to make the audience laugh, is characterised by brief plays, stock characters and exaggerated dialogue.

q.e: Kyōgen is a comic form of traditional Japanese theater, usually performed between Noh plays. It uses ordinary speech and simple stories.

q: A playwright is someone who writes for the theatre. One of the following famous Greeks was not a playwright.

q.e: Tyrtaeus was a Spartan poet who wrote war elegies, not plays. Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides and Aristophanes were Athenian playwrights.

q: This ensemble song was removed just prior to the opening of the musical Show Boat, but its music remained as part of the overture.
Til Good Luck Comes My Way

q.e: "Misery's Comin' Around" was cut from Show Boat before its 1927 opening, but the music stayed in the Overture. Jerome Kern composed the score.

q: Dear Elle:hes a lucky guy-- Im, like, gonna cry-- I got tears coming out of my nose! Mad props!.... are the first lines of lyrics in this song sung by Margot in the musical Legally Blonde.

q.e: "Omigod You Guys" opens Legally Blonde: The Musical. It's sung by Elle's sorority sisters, including Margot, Serena and Pilar.

q: Four Emmys! Four Grammys! Three Oscars! But most people know him best for his one Tony - the 1976's Tony for Best Musical Score for A Chorus Line. Who is this American composer?

q.e: Marvin Hamlisch won a Tony Award for A Chorus Line in 1976 and also won Oscars for The Way We Were and The Sting. He also won a Pulitzer Prize, and was one of the few EGOT winners.

q: Who is the Drama Club teacher, portrayed by Alyson Reed in the movie High School Musical?

q.e: Ms. Darbus is the drama teacher at East High in High School Musical. Alyson Reed played the role.

q: Who is the author of the musical The Most Happy Fella, telling the story of an Italian vineyard owner who falls in love at first sight with a much younger woman?

q.e: Frank Loesser wrote The Most Happy Fella (1956), based on Sidney Howard's play They Knew What They Wanted. It features about 30 songs and is nearly an opera.

q: What Broadway dancer/singer made a miraculous comeback to the stage in Kiss of the Spider Woman after being involved in a car accident four years earlier and subsequently being told she would never dance again?

q.e: Chita Rivera was in a car accident in 1986, which broke her leg badly. She returned in Kiss of the Spider Woman in 1993 and won a Tony Award.

q: Which character from the book Les Miserables was left out of the musical?

q.e: Azelma is Éponine's younger sister in the novel Les Misérables. She is left out of the musical, which focuses on Éponine.

q: What is the name of the Italian maker of musical instruments who is considered the inventor of the piano?

q.e: Bartolomeo Cristofori of Padua, Italy, invented the piano around the year 1700 while working as the keeper of instruments for Prince Ferdinando de' Medici.

q: What is the name of the Israeli National Theater?

q.e: Habima Theatre in Tel Aviv is Israel's national theater. It was founded in Moscow in 1917 and performs in Hebrew.

q: Who is the king of the Greek gods?

q.e: Zeus became king of the gods on Mount Olympus after leading the overthrow of his father, Cronus, and the Titans. Poseidon and Hades are his brothers who took control of the sea and underworld respectively.

q: Who is the Greek god of the sea?

q.e: Poseidon is the Olympian god of the sea, storms, and earthquakes, often depicted holding a trident. His brother Zeus rules the sky, while Hades rules the underworld.

q: In Greek mythology, who is the god of the underworld?

q.e: Hades, the eldest male child of Cronus and Rhea, ruled the underworld after drawing lots with his brothers Zeus and Poseidon. Ares was the god of war, while Hermes served as the herald of the gods.

q: Who was the King of Gods in Ancient Greek mythology?

q.e: Zeus was the king of the gods in Greek mythology, ruling from Mount Olympus as god of the sky and thunder. The Romans called him Jupiter.

q: What mythology did the god "Apollo" come from?

q.e: Apollo was originally a Greek god, and the Romans adopted him under the same name rather than giving him a new one. That's unusual, as most Greek gods had a different Roman name.

q: In most traditions, who was the wife of Zeus?

q.e: Hera was the wife of Zeus and the queen of the Greek gods, as well as the goddess of marriage. The Romans knew her as Juno.

q: This Greek goddess's name was chosen for the dwarf planet responsible for discord on Pluto's classification amongst astronomers.

q.e: Discovered in 2005, Eris was named after the Greek goddess of discord because its discovery sparked the astronomical debate that led to Pluto's reclassification as a dwarf planet in 2006.

q: In Greek mythology, who is the god of wine?

q.e: Dionysus was the Greek god of grape cultivation, wine, and ritual madness, known as Bacchus to the Romans. Hephaestus was the blacksmith god of fire and forge, and Apollo governed prophecy, music, and light.

q: Which of the following is not true about the life of Tiresias?
Sailed with the Argonauts to find the golden fleece
Athena turned him into a woman, and then years later back into a man
Hera blinded him after he agreed with Zeus in an argument
Revealed to Oedipus that Oedipus had married his own mother

q.e: Tiresias was a blind prophet of Thebes who, according to myth, spent several years living as a woman. He did not sail with the Argonauts; he appears in stories like Oedipus and the Odyssey.

q: Which figure from Greek mythology traveled to the underworld to return his wife Eurydice to the land of the living?

q.e: The legendary musician Orpheus charmed Hades and Persephone with his lyre, but lost Eurydice forever when he violated the condition not to look back at her before reaching the surface.

q: Who was the only god from Greece who did not get a name change in Rome?

q.e: While major Greek deities like Zeus, Hera, and Athena were equated with Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva, the god of music, prophecy, and healing was adopted into the Roman pantheon directly as Apollo.

q: What mytological creatures have women's faces and vultures' bodies?

q.e: Harpies were winged monsters of Greek myth, usually shown with women's faces and the bodies of vultures. They were associated with storm winds and snatching things away.

q: An Ankh is the Egyptian Hieroglyph for what?

q.e: The ankh, often shaped like a cross with a looped top, is the ancient Egyptian hieroglyphic symbol representing eternal life.

q: The greek god Poseidon was the god of what?

q.e: Poseidon was the Greek god of the sea, and also of earthquakes and horses. He carried a three-pronged trident and was a brother of Zeus.

q: Which Greek & Roman god was known as the god of music, truth and prophecy, healing, the sun and light, plague, poetry, and more?

q.e: Apollo was the Greek (and Roman) god of music, prophecy, healing, poetry and the sun. His oracle at Delphi was the most famous in the ancient world.

q: How many heads does Cerberus have?

q.e: Cerberus, the monstrous hound guarding the gates of the Greek underworld, is traditionally depicted with three heads representing the past, present, and future.

q: Which of these mythological creatures is said to be half-man and half-horse?

q.e: In Greek mythology, centaurs possess the upper body of a human and the lower body and legs of a horse. The Minotaur, by contrast, has the body of a man and the head of a bull.

q: What weakpoint of Achilles was expoited by the Trojan prince, Paris?

q.e: Achilles' heel was his one weak spot. According to the legend, his mother held him by the heel while dipping him in the river Styx, and Paris's arrow, guided by Apollo, struck that spot.

q: Who in Greek mythology, who led the Argonauts in search of the Golden Fleece?

q.e: Jason assembled the Argonauts and sailed aboard the Argo to Colchis to retrieve the Golden Fleece, a quest demanded by King Pelias so Jason could claim his rightful throne.

q: The Nike apparel and footwear brand takes it's name from the Greek goddess of what?

q.e: Nike is the winged goddess of victory in Greek mythology, often depicted alongside Athena and Zeus. Phil Knight and Bill Bowerman rebranded their company from Blue Ribbon Sports to Nike in 1971, adopting the iconic swoosh logo.

q: In the "Argonautica", Eros' arrow makes Medea fall in love with whom?

q.e: In the Argonautica, an epic poem by Apollonius of Rhodes, the goddess Aphrodite sends Eros to make Medea fall in love with Jason. Medea then helps Jason win the Golden Fleece.

q: Abducted as a child by Theseus, she was later carried off by Paris. Who is she?

q.e: Helen, later known as Helen of Troy, was said to have been kidnapped as a girl by Theseus. Her later abduction by Paris, prince of Troy, set off the Trojan War.

q: Who killed Achilles according to Greek mythology?

q.e: Paris killed Achilles with an arrow to the heel, guided by the god Apollo. This is how the "Achilles heel" idiom came about.

q: According to legend, each leaflet of a 4-leaf clover has a meaning. What does the 1st leaf mean?

q.e: A four-leaf clover is considered lucky, and each leaf is said to stand for something: hope, faith, love and luck. The first leaf is usually hope.

q: We get this very popular word from one of Athenas aliases in Greek mythology.

q.e: In Homer's Odyssey, Athena disguises herself as Odysseus' trusted friend Mentor to advise his young son Telemachus, giving rise to our modern word for a wise guide.

q: The word berserk referring to Norse warriors, means what in Old Norse?

q.e: The Old Norse 'berserkr' likely combines 'ber-' (bear) and 'serkr' (shirt), describing fierce warriors who wore pelts into battle and fought with uncontrollable fury.

q: Where does the ghost of Bloody Mary appear when summoned according to a popular urban legend?

q.e: The classic folklore ritual requires participants to chant her name repeatedly into a bathroom mirror in a darkened room, usually while holding a candle, to reveal her reflection.

q: What is the favorite victim of The Hook according to the popular urban legend?

q.e: In the urban legend of "The Hook", a young couple parked in a lovers' lane hear about an escaped killer with a hook for a hand, and later find a hook hanging from their car door. It's a classic campfire story.

q: What is the Choking Doberman from the popular urban legend choking on?

q.e: In the "Choking Doberman" legend, a dog is rushed to the vet and the vet finds that it is choking on human fingers, and the owner discovers a burglar nearby. It's an urban legend, not a real event.

q: The legends of King Arthur and the Round Table are some of the most famous tales about knights. Who was the head of the table?

q.e: King Arthur's Round Table was round so that no one could sit at the head of it, meaning all the knights were equal. It's a symbol of fairness and unity.

q: During what century is the King Arthur believed to have lived?

q.e: The legendary King Arthur is usually placed in the late 5th or early 6th century, after the Romans left Britain and the Saxons were invading. Historians still argue about whether he was a real person.

q: According to legend, what year is the luckiest year to be born in?

q.e: In Chinese astrology the dragon is the most auspicious of the 12 zodiac animals, and it stands for power, luck and success. Many parents hope to have a child in a Dragon year.

q: The amarok, which is typical for the mythology of the Eskimos, is what kind of an animal?

q.e: The amarok is a giant wolf from Inuit mythology that hunts people who hunt alone at night. Stories about it served as warnings to children.

q: Anubis was the jackal-headed judge of the dead from what mythology?

q.e: Anubis was the jackal-headed Egyptian god of embalming and the afterlife. He guided souls and weighed their hearts against a feather to judge them.

q: He was the first man, according to Norse mythology.

q.e: In Norse mythology, Ask was the first man, and Embla was the first woman. The gods Odin, Vili and Vé created them from trees on a seashore.

q: What kind of creature is the leprechaun in Irish mythology?

q.e: The leprechaun is a mischievous fairy in Irish folklore, usually shown as a small shoemaker who guards a pot of gold. If you catch one, legend says he must grant you wishes.

q: What is the traditional craft practiced by leprechauns according to Irish mythology?

q.e: In Irish folklore, leprechauns are solitary cobblers who mend shoes for the fairies, earning gold that they secretly hoard in hidden pots.

q: In Greek mythology, a minotaur was made up of what two creatures?

q.e: The Minotaur had the head of a bull and the body of a man, born to Queen Pasiphae of Crete. He was imprisoned inside the Daedalian labyrinth at Knossos until slain by Theseus.

q: It is believed that the goblin legend began in what European country?

q.e: The word "goblin" comes from the Old French "gobelin", and stories of these mischievous creatures spread through medieval Europe. Goblins appear in the folklore of many countries.

q: Where does the British mythological creature Afanc live according to legend?

q.e: The Afanc is a monster of Welsh legend that lives in lakes and rivers. It is often described as a giant beaver- or crocodile-like creature.

q: What is the Banshee spirit from Irish mythology associated with?

q.e: In Irish folklore, the banshee is a female spirit whose wailing foretells the death of someone in the family. Her name comes from the Irish "bean sí", or "woman of the fairy mound".

q: In what form was the nymph who suckled Zeus in the cave?

q.e: Zeus was nursed in a cave on Crete by the goat Amalthea (or, in some versions, by a nymph who owned the goat). It kept him safe from his father, Kronos.

q: According to Greek myths, when Zeus grew up, what did he use to retrieve his brothers and sisters?

q.e: With the help of a potion, probably made by the Titaness Metis, Zeus made his father Kronos vomit up the siblings he had swallowed. The bitter drink freed Hestia, Demeter, Hera, Hades and Poseidon.

q: In Roman mythology, Spes was the goddess of which of the following?

q.e: Spes was the Roman goddess of hope, often shown holding a flower. Her Greek counterpart is Elpis.

q: In Roman mythology, the god Volturnus was associated with which of the following?

q.e: Volturnus was a Roman god of waters, linked to the river Tiber and the river Volturno. He had his own festival, the Volturnalia, in August.

q: What material did goddess Cura use to create humans according to Roman mythology?

q.e: In the Roman legend, the goddess Cura (Care) shaped the first human out of clay, and Jupiter gave it a spirit. They then argued about who should name it, and Saturn judged that it be named "homo" from "humus", or earth.

q: The Roman god Uranus is associated with which of the following?

q.e: Uranus was the Greek personification of the sky, and the Romans called him Caelus. Uranus is the only planet named after a Greek god rather than a Roman one.

q: What is the name of the Roman God of war?

q.e: Mars is the Roman god of war and an agricultural guardian. Ares is his Greek mythological counterpart, while Jupiter is the king of the Roman gods.

q: Which Egyptian creature has a lion's body and a human head?

q.e: The Great Sphinx of Giza depicts the recumbent body of a lion with the head of an Egyptian pharaoh. In contrast, a centaur is half-human and half-horse, while a Minotaur has the body of a man and the head of a bull.

q: Which hero had only one weak spot: his heel?

q.e: According to legend, Achilles' mother Thetis dipped him into the River Styx to grant him invulnerability, holding him by his heel. He was ultimately killed during the Trojan War when Paris struck that unprotected heel with an arrow.

q: Which legendary king pulled the sword from the stone?

q.e: In Arthurian legend, Arthur proves his rightful claim to the throne of Britain by extracting the enchanted sword from an anvil mounted on a stone, a feat prophesied by Merlin.

q: Which of these Roman gods doesn't have a counterpart in Greek mythology?

q.e: Janus, the two-faced Roman god of beginnings, gates, transitions, and time, is uniquely Roman with no direct Greek equivalent. Mars corresponds to Ares and Juno corresponds to Hera.

q: Who is the God Loki's son?

q.e: Fenrir is the monstrous wolf fathered by Loki with the giantess Angrboda. Hel is Loki's daughter, while Sigyn is his loyal wife.

q: In Norse Mythology, what is the name of the symbol commonly referred to as the "Tree of Life"?

q.e: Yggdrasil is the great ash tree in Norse myth that connects the nine worlds. It is often called the World Tree or Tree of Life.
Hera was the Greek goddess of marriage and women, and also queen of the gods as the wife of Zeus. She was known for her jealousy of Zeus's many lovers.

q: Who is the father of Icarus, who flew too close to the sun?

q.e: In Greek myth, the master craftsman Daedalus built the Labyrinth for King Minos and later crafted wings of feathers and wax for himself and his son Icarus to escape Crete.

q: Hel was the daughter of which Norse Mythological figure?

q.e: In Norse mythology, Hel rules over the realm of the dead and is the child of the trickster god Loki and the giantess Angrboda. Her siblings are the monstrous wolf Fenrir and the sea serpent Jormungandr.

q: What animal did Queen Pasipahe sleep with before she gave birth to the Minotaur in Greek Mythology?

q.e: Pasiphaë, queen of Crete, fell in love with a magnificent white bull sent by Poseidon, and the Minotaur, part man and part bull, was her child. It was later imprisoned in the Labyrinth.

q: In Greek mythology, Persephone must return to the underworld because she had eaten what kind of seeds?

q.e: Persephone consumed pomegranate seeds while in the underworld, which bound her to Hades under divine law. Because she swallowed them, she had to return to the underworld for a portion of each year, creating the seasons.

q: What is the name of the first human being in Norse mythology?

q.e: According to Norse mythology, the gods Odin, Vili, and Ve created the first two humans from trees found on a beach: Ask from an ash tree and Embla from an elm.

q: The Hippogriff, not to be confused with the Griffon, is a magical creature with the front half of an eagle, and the back half of what?

q.e: In mythology, a griffin has the front half of an eagle and the hindquarters of a lion, whereas a hippogriff is the legendary offspring of a griffin and a mare, giving it the rear body and legs of a horse.

q: Who was the Roman god of fire?

q.e: Vulcan was the Roman god of fire and the forge, and the counterpart of the Greek god Hephaestus. The word "volcano" comes from his name.

q: In Greek Mythology, who killed Achilles?

q.e: The Trojan prince Paris killed Achilles by shooting an arrow into his vulnerable heel, guided by the god Apollo. Achilles had earlier slain Paris's brother Hector outside the walls of Troy.

q: The Norse god Odin has two pet crows named "Huginn" and "Muninn". What do their names mean?

q.e: Huginn and Muninn are two ravens (often mistaken for crows) that fly across Midgard every day to bring news back to Odin. In Old Norse, Huginn translates to thought and Muninn translates to memory or mind.

q: According to Japanese folklore, what is the favorite food of the Kappa.

q.e: In Japanese folklore, the river-dwelling Kappa are said to adore cucumbers so much that people historically threw cucumbers inscribed with family names into rivers to appease them. This connection lives on in sushi culture, where cucumber rolls are known as 'kappa maki'.

q: Which greek god/goddess tossed a golden apple with the words "for the fairest" into the middle of the feast of the gods?

q.e: Eris, the goddess of discord, threw the golden apple after being excluded from the wedding of Peleus and Thetis. The resulting dispute among Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite sparked the Judgement of Paris and ultimately the Trojan War.
The Roman god Neptune was identified with the Greek god Poseidon, ruler of the sea. The planet Neptune is named after him.

q: Who is the god of war in Polynesian mythology?

q.e: Oro was the Polynesian god of war, especially important in Tahiti. He was also associated with peace and fertility.

q: According to the Egyptian Myth of Osiris, who murdered Osiris?

q.e: In ancient Egyptian myth, the god of chaos and storms, Set, plotted against and murdered his brother Osiris, cutting his body into pieces before Osiris was resurrected by his wife Isis.

q: What is the name of the Greek god of blacksmiths?

q.e: Hephaestus is the Greek god of forges, metallurgy, fire, and craftsmen. Vulcan is his Roman mythological equivalent.

q: What is the name of the Greek god of peaceful deaths?

q.e: Thanatos was the personification of non-violent, peaceful death, often depicted with his twin brother Hypnos (Sleep). Violent death was instead personified by the Keres, while Hades ruled the underworld.

q: After slaying which monster did Theseus follow a thread out of the labyrinth?

q.e: Ariadne gave Theseus a sword and a ball of red thread, which he unrolled as he ventured into the Labyrinth to ensure he could find his way out after slaying the half-man, half-bull Minotaur.
Medusa is the best-known Gorgon, and her name comes from a Greek word meaning "guardian" or "ruler". Her gaze turned people to stone until Perseus beheaded her.

q: What is the name of a famous guarding monster in Greek Mythology?

q.e: In Greek mythology, Cerberus is the multi-headed hound of Hades who guards the entrance to the Underworld to prevent the dead from escaping. The Golem originates instead from Jewish folklore.

q: This Greek goddess, daughter of Zeus and Metis, is the virgin patron of Athens. The Parthenon was built as her temple.

q.e: The Parthenon on the Acropolis of Athens was dedicated to Athena Parthenos ('Athena the Virgin') and completed in 438 BC to honor the city's patron deity.

q: This town, closely linked to the legend of the Loch Ness monster, lies at the mouth of the river Ness.

q.e: Inverness is situated in the Scottish Highlands where the River Ness flows into the Moray Firth, just north of Loch Ness. The name Inverness comes from Scottish Gaelic meaning 'mouth of the River Ness'.

q: In Scandinavian mythology this is the equivalent of the apocalypse.

q.e: Ragnarök is the end of the world in Norse mythology: a great battle in which gods such as Odin and Thor are killed, and the world is destroyed and reborn.

q: Who was the god of mountains in the Inca mythology?

q.e: The Apus are mountain spirits in Inca (Quechua) beliefs that protect people and are honored with offerings. Many Andean communities still respect them.

q: Vampires are common to the folklore of many countries. The Civatateo is an Aztec vampire, created when a noblewoman died at childbirth. In aboriginal mythology, vampires had suckers on their fingers. What are the Yakshis (sort of Indian vampires) like?

q.e: In Indian folklore, Yakshis are spirits who often appear as beautiful women to lure men, and then drain their life. They are especially known from stories in Kerala.

q: The banshee, a female spirit in Irish mythology, is known for doing what?

q.e: In Irish folklore, the banshee's mournful wailing, also known as keening, was considered an omen heralding the imminent death of a family member.

q: A dwarf is a little humanoid creature with a large head and a long beard, typical for what mythology?

q.e: Dwarves appear in Norse mythology as skilled craftsmen who live underground and forged items like Thor's hammer. Later Scandinavian and Germanic folklore made them familiar fantasy characters.

q: Osiris had an equivalent in Greek mythology. Who was this counterpart of his?

q.e: Osiris, the Egyptian god of the dead and resurrection, is often compared with the Greek god Hades, who ruled the underworld. Their roles are not identical, as Osiris also stood for rebirth.

q: These creatures ruled the world until they were overthrown by the Twelve Olympians, led by Zeus.

q.e: The Titans were twelve children of Uranus and Gaea who were toppled by Zeus and his siblings in the ten-year war known as the Titanomachy.

q: Norse mythology associates the aurora with this beautiful goddess.

q.e: Freya is the Norse goddess of love, beauty and war, and in some Scandinavian folk traditions the northern lights are linked to her. She rode a chariot pulled by cats.

q: Zeus was married to this goddess.

q.e: Hera was married to Zeus, the king of the Greek gods. She was the goddess of marriage, which made Zeus's many affairs especially painful for her.

q: Hephaestus is the Greek God of fire and the patron of blacksmiths. Who is the Roman god of fire and craftsmanship?

q.e: Vulcan is the Roman god of fire and the blacksmith's craft, equal to the Greek Hephaestus. He was said to work in a forge beneath volcanoes.

q: According to Greek mythology, this god is responsible for lust, love and sex.

q.e: Eros is the Greek god of love, desire, and sexual passion. Cupid is his counterpart in Roman mythology, while Kama is the god of love in Hindu tradition.

q: According to Greek mythology, who was Adonia?
The name of a festival to celebrate Adonis and Aphrodite

q.e: The Adonia was a festival in ancient Greece honoring Adonis, the lover of Aphrodite. Women planted quick-growing "gardens of Adonis" on rooftops that wilted fast, to mourn his early death.

q: What is the name of the dwelling place of the Norse gods?

q.e: Asgard is the realm and stronghold of the Aesir gods in Norse mythology, connected to the earthly realm Midgard by the rainbow bridge Bifrost. Valhalla is merely a majestic hall located within Asgard.

q: In Norse mythology, what kind of animals are Odins two companions that kept him informed of various events?

q.e: Odin's two ravens, Huginn ("thought") and Muninn ("memory"), fly around the world each day and report back to him what they see. Odin is called the "raven god".

q: What is Bifrost in North mythology?
the rainbow bridge that leads to Asgard
the serpent that kills Thor at Ragnarok
Odins great hall for fallen warriors
the wolf that kills Odin at Ragnarok

q.e: Bifröst is the rainbow bridge connecting Midgard, the world of humans, to Asgard, home of the Norse gods. The god Heimdall guards it.

q: Which of these statements about goblins is NOT true according to legend?
Goblins are almost an entirely male race.

q.e: Goblins appear in many folktales as greedy, mischievous creatures that live in caves or houses. The details differ from story to story, and no legend gives goblins a special taste for horse meat.

q: Who was the mother of Zeus?

q.e: The Titaness Rhea bore Zeus along with his siblings Hestia, Demeter, Hera, Hades, and Poseidon, hiding baby Zeus on Crete so his father Cronus would not swallow him.

q: Who is the mother of the Greek god Hephaestus?

q.e: In Greek myth, Hephaestus was the son of Hera, and in some versions she bore him without a father. He was thrown from Olympus because he was lame, and he became the god of blacksmiths.

q: In Egyptian mythology this is known as the soul/personality of a person. It is sometimes depicted as a human-headed bird.

q.e: In Egyptian belief, the ba was a person's soul or personality, shown as a human-headed bird. It could leave the body after death and travel between the tomb and the world of the living.

q: Camulatz is the bird that ate the heads of the first men according to this mythology.

q.e: Camazotz is a bat-like death god in the Maya Popol Vuh who cuts off the head of the hero Hunahpu. His name means "death bat".

q: In Greek mythology, the Harpies were beautiful winged women best known for doing this to Phineas (a King of Thrace, son of Agenor who had the gift of prophecy).

q.e: The Harpies tormented the blind prophet Phineas by snatching or fouling his food each time he tried to eat. The Argonauts rescued him by chasing them away.

q: Hugin and Munin are Odins two companion birds in Norse mythology. They are these bird species.

q.e: In Norse mythology, Hugin (thought) and Munin (memory or mind) are two ravens that fly across the entire world, Midgard, and return to perch on Odin's shoulders to report everything they see.

q: Which Greek god is known as the Earth-shaker?

q.e: Poseidon is called the "Earth-shaker" because the Greeks thought he caused earthquakes by striking the ground with his trident. He was also the god of the sea and of horses.

q: William Tell, who, according to legend shot an apple off the head of his son, is a folk hero of this country.

q.e: According to 15th-century legends, the Austrian bailiff Albrecht Gessler forced William Tell to shoot an apple off his son's head with a crossbow in the central Swiss canton of Uri. Tell's defiance became a central symbol of Swiss independence.

q: According to a mythological story, Zeus was cheating on his wife Hera with a nymph called Io. Just before Hera caught them, Zeus transformed Io into what animal to hide her true identity?

q.e: Zeus turned Io into a white heifer (a young cow) to hide her from Hera, but Hera got suspicious and asked for the cow as a gift. She then set the hundred-eyed Argus to guard her.

q: According to Greek mythology, what did Cronus do to Zeuss five siblings when they were born?
He hid them from the other titans.

q.e: Warned by a prophecy that one of his children would overthrow him, Cronus swallowed Hestia, Demeter, Hera, Hades, and Poseidon as infants. Their mother Rhea saved Zeus by replacing him with a swaddled stone, and Zeus later returned to force Cronus to disgorge his siblings.

q: Name the Titan who stole fire from Zeus and gave it to mortals.

q.e: The Titan Prometheus stole fire from the gods and gave it to humans, and for that Zeus chained him to a rock where an eagle ate his liver every day. The liver grew back each night.

q: Sailors prayed to this Greek god for a safe voyage, sometimes drowning horses as a sacrifice.

q.e: Greek sailors prayed to Poseidon for safe journeys and sometimes sacrificed horses to him by drowning them. He was both feared and honored as the god of the sea.

q: According to Arthurian legend, the Round Table stands in a mighty castle located in this mythical city.

q.e: Camelot first appeared in 12th-century French romances by Chrétien de Troyes as the primary castle and court of King Arthur. Avalon is a different mythical location in the lore, known as the legendary island where Arthur's sword Excalibur was forged and where he was taken to heal.

q: To what ethnic group did legendary King Arthur belong?

q.e: King Arthur is a legendary leader of the Britons, the Celtic-speaking people of Britain, who fought against Saxon invaders. The earliest stories of him come from Welsh and British traditions.

q: Who did Merlin reserve the Perilous Seat for according to Arthurian legend?
the knight who would be successful in the quest of the Holy Grail
the knight who would kill Mordred
the knight who would become a traitor

q.e: The Siege Perilous was a seat at the Round Table that Merlin reserved for the knight who would achieve the Holy Grail. Anyone else who sat in it would be harmed, and Sir Galahad finally took the seat.

q: How many fates are there according to Greek mythology?

q.e: In Greek mythology, the three Moirai are Clotho, who spins the thread of life, Lachesis, who measures its length, and Atropos, who cuts the thread to choose the manner of death.

q: What do Demeter, Hades, Hera, Zeus, Poseidon, and Hestia have in common?
They are all children of Kronos and Rhea.
They all have thrones on Olympus.

q.e: Demeter, Hades, Hera, Zeus, Poseidon and Hestia were the first generation of Olympians, born to the Titans Kronos and Rhea. Kronos swallowed them at birth, except for Zeus, who later freed his siblings.

q: In Roman mythology, the god Orcus was regarded as the punisher of which of the following?

q.e: Orcus was a Roman god of the underworld who punished those who broke their oaths. His name was also used for the underworld itself, and is the origin of the word "ogre".

q: In Roman mythology, the goddess Carmenta is a protector of which of these?

q.e: Carmenta was a Roman goddess of childbirth and prophecy. She is also said to have invented the Latin alphabet.

q: Who is the Roman god of fire and volcanoes?

q.e: Vulcan is the ancient Roman god of fire, metalworking, and volcanoes, closely equated with the Greek god Hephaestus.

q: Who was the long-suffering wife of the Greek god Zeus?

q.e: Hera was both the sister and wife of Zeus, as well as the goddess of marriage and family. Juno is her direct Roman mythological counterpart.

q: What sports legend has as his epitaph: 61/61 Against All Odds 1935-1985

q.e: Roger Maris of the New York Yankees hit 61 home runs in 1961, breaking Babe Ruth's single-season record of 60. He died in 1985, and his grave marker commemorates the record.

q: This New Yorker is best known for his short stories The Legend of Sleepy Hollow and Rip Van Winkle.

q.e: Washington Irving wrote "The Legend of Sleepy Hollow" and "Rip Van Winkle", both published in 1819 and 1820 in his collection The Sketch Book. He was one of the first American writers to be famous in Europe.

q: Mae is the first name of what American film legend and sex symbol?

q.e: Mae West was a Hollywood star and writer known for her witty, bold style in the 1930s, in films such as She Done Him Wrong. She was often in trouble with censors.

q: This Greek god is the son of Zeus and Leto, and Artemiss twin.

q.e: In Greek mythology, Apollo and Artemis were twin archers born to Leto on the island of Delos after she fled the wrath of Zeus's jealous wife, Hera.

q: In the comedy Monty Python and the Holy Grail, King Arthur and his Knights decide not to go to Camelot for what reason?
Because it is a silly place
Because it is a far away place
Because it is a boring place
Because it is a smelly place

q.e: In Monty Python and the Holy Grail (1975), King Arthur's knights skip Camelot, saying "'tis a silly place", after watching a musical number there. It's one of the film's best-known jokes.

q: One of Zeus lovers was Io. What kind of animal did Io turn into, when she tried to avoid detection?

q.e: According to Greek myth, Zeus transformed Io into a white heifer to hide her from his jealous wife Hera. Hera was not fooled and sent a gadfly to endlessly pursue and sting Io across the world.

q: Which animal became sacred in Chinese mythology after saving a man who was trapped in a ditch?

q.e: The tiger is one of the most powerful symbols in Chinese culture, standing for strength and protection against evil. It is also one of the 12 animals of the Chinese zodiac.

q: The Holy Grail is sometimes associated with which magical object in Celtic mythology?

q.e: In Welsh legend, the cauldron of Bran the Blessed could revive dead warriors, and many scholars compare it to the Holy Grail. The story is told in the Mabinogion.

q: The hippocampus, a mythical monster with the head of a horse and body of a fish, pulled the chariot of which god?

q.e: The hippocampus, with a horse's head and fish's tail, drew the chariot of the sea god Poseidon (Neptune to the Romans). The name also inspired the brain's "hippocampus", which looks like a seahorse.

q: Which of the following is an evil mythological hybrid of a woman and a bird?

q.e: In Greek mythology, harpies were wind spirits often depicted as winged women or birds with women's heads who snatched victims and food. Titans were an elder race of deities, and an ogress is a female giant.

q: This animal was considered an important spirit among most of the Northern tribes. It was responsible for sorrow and death, and was an omen of impending evil.

q.e: The coyote appears in many Native American stories, often as a trickster, and its meaning varies by tribe. In some northern traditions it was seen as an omen of trouble.

q: What is the Roman name for Zeus?

q.e: In ancient Roman religion and mythology, Jupiter was the king of the gods and ruler of the sky, equivalent to the Greek god Zeus. Mars corresponds to Ares, and Neptune corresponds to Poseidon.

q: Who stole fire from the gods to give to humans?
