q.e: In Greek mythology, the Titan Prometheus stole fire from Mount Olympus hidden in a hollow fennel stalk to aid humanity, which led Zeus to bind him to a rock as punishment.

q: Who defeated Medusa by looking at her reflection?

q.e: In Greek mythology, Perseus used a polished bronze shield given to him by the goddess Athena to view Medusa's reflection safely, beheading her without turning to stone.

q: In Egyptian myth, which jackal-headed god guards the dead?

q.e: Anubis was the ancient Egyptian canine god of mummification and the protector of tombs, often depicted as a jackal or a man with a jackal head.

q: Which Norse God has a horse named Sleipnir?

q.e: Sleipnir is the eight-legged steed ridden by the Allfather, Odin, described in the Poetic Edda as the best of all horses. The mythical beast was fathered by the stallion Svadilfari and birthed by Loki after shapeshifting into a mare.

q: In Norse mythology, what is the name of the serpent which eats the roots of the ash tree Yggdrasil?

q.e: Nidhogg is a dragon in Norse myth that gnaws at the roots of Yggdrasil, the World Tree. A squirrel named Ratatoskr carries insults between him and the eagle at the top.

q: In Greek Mythology, who was the daughter of King Minos?

q.e: Ariadne, the daughter of King Minos of Crete, gave Theseus a sword and a ball of red thread to navigate the Labyrinth and defeat the Minotaur. Athena was an Olympian goddess, not a mortal Cretan princess.

q: According to Algonquian folklore, how does one transform into a Wendigo?
Drinking the blood of many slain animals.

q.e: In traditional Algonquian folklore, the Wendigo is a malevolent spirit associated with winter and famine that can possess humans who resort to cannibalism, condemning them to an insatiable hunger for human flesh.

q: What was the punishment for Sysiphus's craftiness?
Cursed to roll a boulder up a hill for eternity.
Tied to a boulder for eternity, being pecked by birds.
Standing in a lake filled with water he could not drink.
To fell a tree that regenerated after every axe swing.

q.e: King Sisyphus was condemned to Hades to repeatedly push a massive boulder up a steep hill, only for it to roll back down just before reaching the top. The punishment of being tied down while birds pecked at his liver was suffered by Prometheus, not Sisyphus.

q: Talos, the mythical giant bronze man, was the protector of which island?

q.e: In Greek mythology, Talos was forged by Hephaestus to guard Europa on Crete, patrolling the island's shores three times each day to ward off invaders.

q: Who is the Egyptian god of reproduction and lettuce?

q.e: Min was the Egyptian god of fertility and reproduction, and lettuce was sacred to him. Egyptians believed lettuce boosted fertility.

q: Which of the following is NOT a god in Norse Mythology.

q.e: Norse gods include Odin, Thor, Loki, Freya, Baldr and Tyr. "Jens" isn't a Norse god's name, although it's a common Scandinavian name.

q: Nidhogg is a mythical creature from what mythology?

q.e: Nidhogg is a dragon-like creature from Norse mythology that lives beneath the World Tree, Yggdrasil. Its name roughly means "malice striker".

q: What immense structure is referred to in Norse Mythology as the Yggdrasil.

q.e: Yggdrasil is an enormous ash tree in Norse mythology that links the nine worlds. Its roots and branches stretch through all of them.

q: Who is a minor god that is protector and creator of various arts, such as cheese making and bee keeping.

q.e: Aristaeus was a minor Greek god, a son of Apollo, who taught people beekeeping, cheese-making and olive growing. He was said to have lost his bees after Eurydice died.

q: This folk singing legend, who was a member of the group Peter, Paul and Mary, died in September of 2009.

q.e: Mary Travers, of the folk trio Peter, Paul and Mary, died on September 16, 2009. The group is known for songs like "Puff, the Magic Dragon" and "If I Had a Hammer".

q: According to Arthurian legend, Queen Guineveres love affair with this knight of the Round Table led to the downfall of Camelot.

q.e: Sir Lancelot was King Arthur's closest companion and greatest knight, but his secret romance with Queen Guinevere divided the Round Table and sparked a civil war that culminated in the fall of Camelot and Arthur's death at the Battle of Camlann.

q: According to an urban legend, in Geneva in 2002 an intoxicated groom was suffocated at his bachelor party by which of the following?
Passing out face down on the shag carpet

q.e: This is an urban legend: a story that's retold as if it were true but has no reliable source. Such tales spread by word of mouth and online, and they're usually unverifiable.

q: According to Greek mythology, he was the best friend of Pythias.

q.e: Damon and Pythias are a famous pair of friends in Greek legend. When Pythias was sentenced to death, Damon offered to take his place so he could settle his affairs, and the tyrant was so moved by their loyalty that he freed them both.

q: North Americans believed these were poisonous until 1820, when Colonel Robert Gibbon Johnson disproved that myth during a public demonstration on the courthouse steps in Salem, NJ. They were imported from Mexico to Europe in the middle of 16th century.

q.e: Because tomatoes belong to the nightshade family Solanaceae, many Westerners long feared they were poisonous until public demonstrations and growing popularity in the 19th century disproved the myth.

q: According to a legend, when Confucius died, twelve animals rushed to his bedside. The order of the Chinese Horoscope is the order in which they arrived. What was the first animal to arrive at Confucius bedside?

q.e: In the most common Chinese zodiac legend, the Jade Emperor held a race to decide the order of the animals. The rat hitched a ride on the ox and jumped off at the end to finish first.

q: What is the name of the monstrous creature from Greek Mythology, that is the offspring of Typhon and Echidna?

q.e: The Chimera was a fire-breathing hybrid creature composed of a lion, a goat, and a serpent, eventually slain by Bellerophon. Pegasus was fathered by Poseidon and foaled by Medusa, while Chiron was a wise centaur born of Cronus.

q: What is the name of the legendary half-man and half-goat (or half-horse) creature often associated with male sexuality in Greek mythology?

q.e: Satyrs were nature spirits and companions of Dionysus depicted with horse or goat features. Pan was a specific god with goat legs and horns, rather than the name of the mythological creature type itself.

q: Hermes is the Greek god of shepards, land travel, weights and measures, oratory, literature, merchants and athletics. His Roman equivalent however, is usually considered to be just the god of trade, profit and travel. Who is the Roman god in question?

q.e: The Romans equated Hermes with Mercury, who was depicted with winged sandals and a herald's staff called the caduceus. Mars corresponds to Ares, and Saturn corresponds to Cronus.

q: Poseidon, the Greek god of the sea, was very popular and powerful among Greek sailors. His Roman equivalent was inferior in power and popularity. Who was the Roman god of the sea?

q.e: Neptune was the Roman god of the sea, equated with the Greek Poseidon. The Romans honored him at the Neptunalia festival in July.

q: Which word refers to the ancient Greek songs, performed by a chorus in honor of the Greek god, Dionysus?

q.e: The dithyramb was a wild choral song, sung and danced in honor of Dionysus, the Greek god of wine. Ancient Greek drama is thought to have grown out of this tradition.

q: Within the Olympian tradition, Dionysos was said to be the son of Zeus and which mortal woman?

q.e: Dionysus was the son of Zeus and the mortal princess Semele. She was killed when she saw Zeus in his full glory, and Zeus sewed the baby into his thigh until he was born.

q: According to Scandinavian mythology, the chaos will defeat the guardians of good and this catastrophe will bring the world to an end. What is the name of this final battle between evil and good, in which the gods will be outnumbered?

q.e: In Norse mythology, Ragnarok is the cataclysmic series of events and final battle where gods like Odin and Thor die, resulting in the world being submerged in water before resurfacing anew.

q: This is the goddess of eternal youth, the guardian of the golden apples of youth in the Scandinavian mythology.

q.e: Iðunn is the Norse goddess of youth who keeps the apples that keep the gods young. When the giant Thjazi kidnapped her, the gods began to age.

q: According to a Polish legend, which city in Poland was named after a hero who defeated a fearful dragon?

q.e: According to Polish legend, Krakow is named after Prince Krak, who defeated the Wawel Dragon that lived in a cave under Wawel Hill. In some versions, a clever shoemaker kills it with a poisoned sheep.

q: The phrase Herculean task, meaning a difficult task that requires great effort, originates from the stories of the Twelve Labors of the divine hero Hercules. Which of these is not one of the labors Hercules had to perform?
Clean the Augean stables in a single day

q.e: The Twelve Labors of Hercules include killing the Nemean Lion, capturing Cerberus and cleaning the Augean stables. Stealing fire is not one of them; that was Prometheus.

q: Which Greek god guides the dead to the river Styx to pay their toll to Charon so that they can get into the underworld?

q.e: Hermes was the messenger of the gods and also the guide of souls, leading the dead to the underworld. Charon the ferryman then took them across the river Styx for a coin.

q: Who is the mother of the nine muses in Greek mythology?

q.e: Mnemosyne, the Titaness of memory, gave birth to the nine Muses after mating with Zeus for nine consecutive nights. Clio, Melpomene, and Urania are three of her daughters.

q: Name the creature from British and European mythology which is shaped like a serpent or dragon and swallows its own tail.

q.e: The Ouroboros is an ancient emblem depicting a snake or serpent-like dragon eating its own tail, symbolizing eternity and the cycle of destruction and rebirth.

q: Which of the following actors has NOT played King Arthur?

q.e: Many actors have played King Arthur, including Richard Harris in Camelot, Nigel Terry in Excalibur, Sean Connery in First Knight and Clive Owen in King Arthur (2004). Arthur is one of the most filmed legendary figures.

q: Aegina was one of the many nymphs seduced by Zeus, but unlike some others, this nymph didnt get away with it. Which king caught Aegina and Zeus?

q.e: Sisyphus, king of Corinth, told the river god Asopus where his daughter Aegina had been taken by Zeus. Zeus punished him, and in the underworld, Sisyphus has to push a boulder up a hill forever.

q: Who thought that Atlantis was a naval power lying in front of the Pillars of Hercules and that it sank into the ocean in a single day and night of misfortune.

q.e: Plato introduced the legend of Atlantis around 360 BCE in his dialogues Timaeus and Critias, using it as an allegorical example of imperial hubris falling out of divine favor.

q: Which one-handed knight of the Round Table returns Excalibur to the Lady of the Lake according to Arthurian legend?

q.e: Sir Bedivere is the knight who returns Excalibur to the Lady of the Lake after Arthur's final battle. In many versions he is described as missing a hand.

q: What is the name of the traitor who, according to Arturian legend, fought Arthur at the Battle of Camlann?

q.e: In Arthurian legend, Mordred seizes the throne while King Arthur is away and fatally wounds him at the Battle of Camlann, where Mordred is also slain.

q: After Queen Guinevere is found in an adulterous love affair, King Arthur is forced to condemn her to burn at the stake. Who arrives to save Queen Guinevere?

q.e: In the medieval romances, Lancelot rescues Guinevere from being burned at the stake, which helps lead to the breakup of the Round Table. His love for the queen is central to the legend.

q: Gordium, the city where according to legend Alexander the Great undid the intricate Gordian Knot, was the capital of this ancient kingdom.

q.e: Gordium was the capital of Phrygia, the kingdom of King Midas, in what is now Turkey. Alexander the Great cut the Gordian Knot with his sword in 333 BC, which an oracle said would make him ruler of Asia.

q: With which two figures from Greek/Roman mythology is Gemini associated?

q.e: In Greek mythology, Castor and Pollux are twin brothers known together as the Dioscuri. Zeus placed their stars in the heavens as the constellation Gemini so they would never be separated after Castor died.

q: Blow winds, and crack your cheeks! Rage! Blow! The tragedy, this line was extracted from is based on a legend, that had been mentioned in numerous chronicles, poems, and sermons, before Shakespeare created his interpretation of it.

q.e: The line is from King Lear, in the storm scene. Shakespeare based the play on the old legend of King Leir of Britain, told in chronicles such as Geoffrey of Monmouth's.

q: This acting legend starred with legendary Jimmy Stewart in the Cheyenne Social Club.

q.e: Henry Fonda co-starred with James Stewart in the 1970 Western comedy The Cheyenne Social Club. The two were close friends in real life.

q: Hercules is the Roman name of the greatest Greek hero:

q.e: Heracles, whose name means 'glory of Hera', is the original Greek hero famed for completing the Twelve Labors. The Romans later adapted his name as Hercules.

q: Who is considered to be the most beautiful goddess in Norse mythology?

q.e: Freya is the Norse goddess associated with love, beauty, fertility, and gold, famous for her unmatched beauty and her carriage pulled by two cats.

q: In the 1991 movie The Fisher King, Robin Williams' character is obsessed with the legend of the Fisher King and tries to get the Holy Grail. He believes that this object is actually the Grail.

q.e: In The Fisher King (1991), directed by Terry Gilliam, Robin Williams plays Parry, a man who becomes convinced that a trophy in a mansion is the Holy Grail. The story draws on the Arthurian Fisher King legend.

q: In Norse myth, what is the giant tree that connects the worlds?

q.e: Yggdrasil is the sacred ash tree that connects the nine realms of Norse cosmology, including Asgard and Midgard. Bifröst is the burning rainbow bridge leading to Asgard, while Valhalla is the majestic hall ruled by Odin.

q: Which Greek figure flew too close to the sun on wax wings?

q.e: Icarus ignored warnings from his master craftsman father, Daedalus, flying too close to the sun until the beeswax holding his feathered wings together melted, plunging him into the sea.

q: In Norse mythology, what is the rainbow bridge connecting Midgard to Asgard called?

q.e: Bifröst is the glowing rainbow bridge guarded by the god Heimdall that links Midgard, the world of mortals, to Asgard, the realm of the gods. Yggdrasil is the great world tree supporting the cosmos, while Gjallarbrú is the bridge to the underworld realm of Hel.

q: What is the staff carried by Mercury, now an emblem of medicine, called?

q.e: The caduceus features two snakes entwined around a winged staff and was carried by the Roman god Mercury (Hermes in Greek mythology). It is often confused with the Rod of Asclepius, which has only one snake and is the true historical symbol of healing.

q: This well known plant derives its scientific name from Atropos, one of the Fates in Greek mythology, who held the shears to cut the thread of human life. The plant grows shiny black berries that are sweet to the taste but very toxic.

q.e: Belladonna, or deadly nightshade, has the scientific name Atropa belladonna, named after Atropos, the Fate who cuts the thread of life. Its sweet black berries are highly poisonous.

q: What is H₂O more commonly called?

q.e: The chemical formula H2O indicates that every water molecule consists of two hydrogen atoms covalently bonded to a single oxygen atom. Table salt is sodium chloride, with the formula NaCl.

q: What force pulls things down toward the Earth?

q.e: Gravity is the fundamental attractive force between masses, accelerating objects on Earth's surface downward at approximately 9.8 meters per second squared. Friction opposes relative motion, while magnetism only attracts or repels magnetic materials.

q: Which part of a plant takes in water from the soil?

q.e: Plant roots absorb water and dissolved minerals from the soil through microscopic root hairs, transporting them upward through vascular tissues called xylem.

q: What do plants need from the Sun to make food?

q.e: During photosynthesis, plant cells use green chlorophyll pigments to absorb sunlight, converting water and carbon dioxide into glucose and oxygen.

q: How many laws of thermodynamics are there?

q.e: There are four laws of thermodynamics, numbered zeroth through third. The zeroth defines temperature, the first conserves energy, the second says entropy increases, and the third says absolute zero is unreachable.

q: Which element has the highest melting point?

q.e: Carbon has the highest melting/sublimation point of any element, about 3,600 °C (at normal pressure graphite sublimes rather than melts). Tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal, at 3,422 °C.

q: What lies at the center of our galaxy?

q.e: At the gravitational center of the Milky Way sits Sagittarius A, a supermassive black hole with an estimated mass about 4 million times that of our Sun.

q: What is the hottest planet in the solar system

q.e: Venus is the hottest planet, at about 465 °C (870 °F), thanks to a thick carbon dioxide atmosphere that creates a runaway greenhouse effect. Mercury is closer to the Sun but cools at night.

q: What animal takes part in Schrödinger's most famous thought experiment?

q.e: Physicist Erwin Schrödinger proposed the paradox in 1935 to illustrate the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics, where an unobserved cat could theoretically be both alive and dead simultaneously.

q: What is the powerhouse of the cell?

q.e: Mitochondria generate most of a cell's ATP, the molecule that stores energy. They have their own DNA, passed down from the mother.

q: Which type of rock is created by intense heat AND pressure?

q.e: Metamorphic rocks form when existing igneous, sedimentary, or older metamorphic rocks are altered by intense heat and pressure deep within the Earth. Igneous rocks form from cooling molten rock, while sedimentary rocks form from compacted sediments.

q: What is the first element on the periodic table?

q.e: Hydrogen, atomic number 1, is the lightest and most abundant element in the universe. The periodic table is ordered by atomic number.

q: Dry ice is the solid form of what substance?

q.e: Dry ice is solid carbon dioxide (CO2), which does not melt into a liquid under normal atmospheric conditions. Instead, it sublimates directly into gas at about minus 109.3 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 78.5 degrees Celsius).

q: How many chromosomes are in your body cells?

q.e: Human body cells (somatic cells) have 46 chromosomes, or 23 pairs. Egg and sperm cells have 23 chromosomes.

q: About what percentage of the Earth's surface is water?

q.e: About 71% of Earth's surface is covered by water, and most of it is in the oceans. That's why the planet looks blue from space.

q: How many planets make up our Solar System?

q.e: The Solar System has eight planets, since Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006. They are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

q: Which of the following blood vessels carries deoxygenated blood?

q.e: While most arteries carry oxygen-rich blood away from the heart, the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle into the lungs to receive oxygen.

q: 99.95% of an atom's mass is in which part?

q.e: Almost all of an atom's mass is in the nucleus, made of protons and neutrons. Electrons are about 1,800 times lighter.

q: What yellow powder is carried from flower to flower by wind, birds and insects?

q.e: Pollen is the fine, powdery substance produced by seed plants containing male gametes. Nectar is a sugary fluid produced by flowers to attract pollinators, while spores are reproductive cells of non-flowering organisms like ferns and fungi.

q: Which scientist gave his name to the unit of electrical current?

q.e: The ampere, the unit of electric current, is named after the French physicist André-Marie Ampère. He founded electrodynamics in the 1820s.

q: This is one of the first signs of pregnancy.

q.e: A missed period is commonly the first sign of pregnancy, but it can have other causes. A pregnancy test confirms it.

q: How far along are you approximately, when you feel the baby move for the first time?

q.e: Most women feel the baby's first movements ("quickening") between 16 and 25 weeks, often around 18-20. First-time mothers feel it later.

q: The surface of this planet is unique, it is the only one which has water in large quantities.

q.e: Earth is the only known planet with large amounts of liquid water on its surface. Other worlds may have subsurface oceans, such as Europa.

q: The term arthro is of Greek origin. It refers to which part of the body?

q.e: "Arthro-" comes from the Greek "arthron", meaning joint. Arthritis means joint inflammation.

q: Gastro is a common medical prefix, derived from the Greek word gastros which means what?

q.e: The root appears in terms like gastritis (inflammation of the stomach) and gastroenterology, which studies the stomach and intestines.

q: Onco, coming from the Greek word onkos refers to what?

q.e: "Onco-" comes from the Greek "onkos", meaning mass or tumor. An oncologist treats cancer.

q: If your physician tells you that you have Presbycusis due to the normal process of aging, he may suggest that you need which of these?

q.e: Presbycusis is age-related hearing loss, usually affecting high-pitched sounds. Hearing aids are a common treatment.

q: Which of these most accurately describes the medical term, necrosis?

q.e: Necrosis is the premature, unprogrammed death of cells and living tissue caused by external factors such as infection, toxins, or severe trauma, distinguishing it from programmed cell death (apoptosis).

q: Which side effect is not related to the use of marijuana?

q.e: Marijuana can cause dry mouth, red eyes, slower reaction time and anxiety in some people. It is not reliably linked to violent behavior.

q: The sphygmomanometer is a device invented by Samuel Siegfried Karl Ritter von Basch, used to measure what?

q.e: A sphygmomanometer uses an inflatable cuff paired with a mercury or aneroid manometer to measure arterial blood pressure in millimeters of mercury (mmHg).

q: Pre-eclampsia, thought to be caused by inflammatory mediators, is a medical condition associated with which of these?

q.e: Pre-eclampsia is a pregnancy complication of high blood pressure and organ stress, usually after 20 weeks. It needs medical monitoring.

q: The medical prefix bucco refers to which part of the head?

q.e: "Bucco-" refers to the cheek, from the Latin "bucca". The buccal cavity is the mouth cavity.

q: The prefix of Greek origin, oto is used in medical terminology to refer to what body part?

q.e: "Oto-" comes from the Greek for ear. An otolaryngologist treats ear, nose and throat.

q: Procedural Memory, a category of the long-term memory, refers to which of these basic human abilities?
The ability to acquire and develop skills
The ability to gain and store general knowledge and information
The ability to consciously retrieve stored facts and information

q.e: Procedural memory is the long-term memory of how to do things, such as riding a bike or typing. It operates without conscious thought.

q: In the study of memory, what does the term mnemonist refer to?
Individual who tends to create false memories
Individual who has recovered from amnesia

q.e: A mnemonist is a person with an exceptional memory, who often uses techniques such as memory palaces. Solomon Shereshevsky is a famous case.

q: This is one of the most common health problems that comes from being overweight.

q.e: Being overweight raises the risk of high blood pressure (hypertension), as well as diabetes and heart disease. Weight loss can help lower blood pressure.

q: In the USA, obesity is the second leading cause of preventable death after this one.

q.e: In the US, obesity has been described as the second leading cause of preventable death, after smoking. Both affect heart disease and cancer risk.

q: Which of the following has the most fat?

q.e: Blue cheese is high in fat, with about 30% of its weight as fat. Compare labels, since fat varies among cheeses.

q: This is the most recommended activity that helps prevent or fight obesity.

q.e: Regular exercise, along with a healthy diet, is a main recommendation to prevent and fight obesity. It improves metabolism and heart health.

q: At what time in a womans life is she most likely to gain the most weight?

q.e: Pregnancy is the period in which a woman is most likely to gain the most weight. Doctors recommend a recommended range based on BMI.

q: Laughter is one of the first expressions of emotions babies learn to convey. At about what age do babies start to laugh?

q.e: Babies start laughing at around three to four months of age. It's one of the first social expressions.

q: Which part of the body is decomposed last, but before the bones?

q.e: Hair and nails are some of the slowest parts of a body to decompose, since they're made of tough keratin. Bones last longer.

q: Due to this, there is almost no atmosphere on the Moon.

q.e: The Moon's gravity is about one-sixth of Earth's, too weak to hold a substantial atmosphere. Any gases escape into space.

q: The side of the Moon that we see is this.

q.e: Due to tidal locking, the Moon takes the exact same amount of time to rotate once on its axis as it does to orbit Earth (about 27.3 days), showing us the same near side every night.

q: The Moon is changing its position it relation to the Earth. In what way?
Moving along the Earths Y axis
Moving along the Earths X axis

q.e: Because of tidal friction transferring angular momentum from Earth's rotation to lunar orbit, the Moon is slowly drifting away from Earth at a rate of roughly 3.8 centimeters (1.5 inches) per year.

q: Which factor ensures that many of the craters on the Moons surface remain well preserved in comparison to those on Earth?

q.e: The Moon lacks a substantial atmosphere, meaning there is virtually no weather, wind, or liquid water to erode craters over billions of years, unlike on Earth.
The Moon formed about 4.5 billion years ago, probably when a Mars-sized body (Theia) hit the early Earth. The debris combined into the Moon.

q: Moons shape is not quite round. What does it resemble?

q.e: The Moon is slightly egg-shaped, not a perfect sphere, because of Earth's tidal forces. Its surface is also covered with craters.

q: This astral body, known as Earths only natural satellite, is the subject of study selenology.

q.e: The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite, and selenology is the study of the Moon. The word comes from Selene, the Greek moon goddess.

q: This contractile tissue of the body is the subject of study of myology.

q.e: Myology is the study of muscles. The Greek "mys" means muscle.

q: What term is used to designate a hurricanes calm, low-pressure center around which winds of high velocity spin?

q.e: The eye of a tropical cyclone is a roughly circular, calm region of sinking air typically 20 to 40 miles wide. It is surrounded by the eyewall, where the most severe winds and rains occur.

q: Poisoning by this substance is often referred to as painters colic.

q.e: Painter's colic is lead poisoning, as lead was used in paint. Symptoms include abdominal pain.

q: If the doctor writes, CNs 2-12 intact, which of the following would be true?
The patient is able to close and open the eyes.
The cervical nerves are all functioning normally.
All of the lymph nodes in the cervical chain are normal.

q.e: "CN 2-12 intact" means cranial nerves 2 through 12 are working. Cranial nerves control senses and facial muscles, including eye movement.

q: In medical parlance, what is an AKA?

q.e: AKA in medical shorthand means an above-knee amputation. BKA means below-knee amputation.

q: If the doctor orders an EKG, what part of the body is going to be examined?

q.e: An EKG (or ECG, short for electrocardiogram) records the electrical activity of the heart over time to detect arrhythmias and other cardiac conditions. Brain activity is instead measured using an EEG (electroencephalogram).

q: In medical terms, what is a CVA?

q.e: CVA means cerebrovascular accident, which is a stroke. It occurs when blood flow to the brain is blocked or a vessel bursts.

q: If you were taking a course in entomology, what would you be studying?

q.e: Entomology is the study of insects. The Greek "entomon" means insect.

q: People with this disorder have difficulty engaging in everyday human interaction.

q.e: Autism spectrum disorder affects communication and social interaction, in varying degrees. It is a spectrum.

q: In humans, which of these organs belongs to the integumentary system?

q.e: The integumentary system includes the skin, hair and nails. The skin is the body's largest organ.

q: Which of these is a popular database name?

q.e: Oracle is a major database system, from Oracle Corporation. Others include MySQL and PostgreSQL.

q: Which commercial building can also store data?

q.e: A data warehouse is a system for storing large amounts of data. Warehouses can also store physical goods.

q: Which hat is a distribution of the Linux operating system?

q.e: Red Hat is a Linux distribution, which became Red Hat Enterprise Linux. IBM bought the company in 2019.

q: If a doctor prescibes a medicine and the prescription reads, Instill 2 - 3 gtts in OD bid. What does OD mean?

q.e: "OD" stands for the Latin "oculus dexter", meaning the right eye. "OS" is the left eye and "OU" is both. "Gtts" means drops, and "bid" means twice a day.

q: Gold carats measure purity, whereas diamond carats measure this quality.

q.e: In gemstones, one carat is a unit of mass strictly defined as exactly 200 milligrams (0.2 grams), completely separate from the karat scale used for gold alloy purity.

q: We all know what acute angles, obtuse angles, right angles, and straight angles are, but what is a reflex angle?
An angle greater than 180 degrees but less than 360 degrees.
The angle a telescope makes with the Earth
The angle you need to look a fish in the eye.

q.e: In geometry, an angle smaller than 90 degrees is acute, 90 to 180 degrees is obtuse, exactly 180 degrees is straight, and anything between 180 and 360 degrees is a reflex angle.

q: During this month of the pregnancy women go through a lot of mood swings like being easily irritated or start crying when they hear a song on the radio.

q.e: Hormonal changes in early pregnancy can cause mood swings. They often peak in the first trimester.

q: In astrophysics, which theorem defines what parameters black holes are characterized by?

q.e: The "no-hair theorem" says black holes can be described by just mass, charge and angular momentum. John Wheeler popularized the phrase.

q: What do mathematicians call any rectangular table of numbers?

q.e: In mathematics, a matrix is a rectangular array of numbers, symbols, or expressions arranged in rows and columns, widely used to solve systems of linear equations.

q: In a list of numbers what, is the mode?
The number of items in the list
The biggest number minus the smallest number

q.e: In statistics, the mode is the value that appears most often in a data set. By contrast, the middle number is the median, and the biggest minus the smallest is the range.

q: ICQ is a type of what?

q.e: ICQ ("I seek you") was an early instant messaging program, released in 1996. It was popular before MSN Messenger and others.
WWW stands for World Wide Web, a system of linked pages invented by Tim Berners-Lee in 1989. It isn't the same as the internet.

q: In the web address http://www.microsoft.com, the com at the end means what?

q.e: ".com" stands for "commercial". It was one of the original top-level domains.

q: What is the speed of light in free space?

q.e: Light travels at about 299,792 km/s (186,282 miles per second) in a vacuum. Nothing with mass can reach this speed.

q: What is the main purpose of pulleys?
They decrease the force needed to lift something.

q.e: Pulleys change the direction of a force and, in combinations, reduce the effort needed to lift a load. The trade-off is that you pull more rope.

q: Who came up with the laws of gravity?

q.e: Sir Isaac Newton formulated the law of universal gravitation, publishing it in his 1687 work 'Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica'. Albert Einstein later expanded upon gravity with his theory of general relativity in 1915.

q: Which planet has been described as a sister planet to Earth?

q.e: Venus is often called Earth's twin or sister planet due to its similar size, mass, and composition, with a diameter of about 12,104 km compared to Earth's 12,742 km.

q: Which planet was named after the Roman god of war?

q.e: Mars is named after the Roman god of war, because of its red color, like blood. Its moons, Phobos and Deimos, mean fear and dread.

q: Approximately how many years ago did the formation of the Earth take place?

q.e: Earth formed about 4.54 billion years ago. Scientists date it using radioactive decay in meteorites and rocks.

q: Which medical specialty largely replaced the old general practice specialty?

q.e: Family medicine (family practice) gradually replaced general practice in the US, requiring formal residency training. It was recognized as a specialty in 1969.

q: Which of the following doctors is least likely to ever be on call?

q.e: Emergency physicians work in shifts, so they are not typically "on call" at home. Many other specialists take call.

q: What do we call the ratio of a circles circumference to its diameter?

q.e: Pi (π) is the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, approximately 3.14159. It's an irrational number.

q: What do we call these numbers: 0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, etc?

q.e: Square numbers are formed by multiplying an integer by itself, such as 0x0=0, 1x1=1, 2x2=4, and so on. Cubic numbers involve multiplying an integer by itself twice, yielding values like 1, 8, and 27.

q: What do we call the square root of negative one?

q.e: The symbol i represents the imaginary unit, defined such that i squared equals -1. Mathematician Leonhard Euler introduced this notation in 1777.

q: What do we call the base for natural logarithms ?

q.e: The number e (≈ 2.71828) is the base of natural logarithms. It's named after Leonhard Euler.

q: Which of these three sets is the largest: the set of all whole numbers, the set of all even numbers, the set of all odd numbers?
The set of all even numbers
The set of all whole numbers
The set of all odd numbers

q.e: In set theory, all three infinite sets have the same cardinality (aleph-null) because they can each be put into a one-to-one correspondence with the natural numbers.

q: If you flip a fair coin three times what is the probability you will get three heads ?

q.e: Each fair coin flip has two equally likely outcomes (heads or tails). For three independent flips, the total number of possible combinations is 2 2 2 = 8, and getting three consecutive heads represents only 1 of those 8 outcomes (a probability of 1/8).

q: Botox (botulinum toxin) is used to treat which one of the following diseases?

q.e: Botox is approved to treat chronic migraine, as well as muscle spasms, excessive sweating and more. It was originally studied for eye muscle disorders.

q: Where is the femoral artery located?

q.e: The femoral artery is a major systemic blood vessel that originates in the groin and runs down the upper thigh, named after the femur (thigh bone). It is the main blood supply for the lower body.

q: How long on average does it take for the suns rays to reach earth?

q.e: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth. The Sun is about 150 million km away.

q: How much does human hair grow in a year?

q.e: Human hair grows about 1.25 cm (half an inch) per month, or around 15 cm (6 inches) a year. Growth varies from person to person.

q: This term refers to a division of the psyche dominated by the pleasure principle.

q.e: The id is the part of the psyche in Freud's theory that runs on the pleasure principle. The ego and superego are the other parts.

q: What is the name for a unit of DNA usually consisting of regulatory regions and a protein-encoding region?

q.e: A gene is the basic physical and functional unit of heredity, composed of DNA sequences that encode instructions for synthesizing molecules like proteins or functional RNAs.

q: You might not be successful at exterminating microbes - they have been around this long.

q.e: Microbes have existed for at least 3.5-3.8 billion years, long before plants and animals. They're everywhere, including inside us.

q: People use a kind of microbe to make this.

q.e: Microbes such as yeast are used to make bread, beer, wine, cheese and yogurt. Fermentation is the process.

q: There are billions of these microscopic creatures in your bed and they feed on this.

q.e: Microscopic house dust mites thrive in mattresses and bedding, feeding primarily on the dead skin flakes shed by humans and household pets.

q: There is proof that microbes existed on this planet.

q.e: No microbes have been confirmed on Mars. Scientists are searching for signs of past life, using rovers like Perseverance.

q: What is called a capitated plan in the medical fields?
An insurance plan, which pays the doctor a certain amount per month
A treatment plan which relates to the patients head.
An insurance plan, which only covers up to a certain amount per visit
A treatment plan which has a definite endpoint.

q.e: A capitated plan pays a doctor or group a fixed amount per patient, usually monthly, whatever services are used. It differs from fee-for-service.

q: If the nurse writes NKDA on your chart, what does it mean?
You told the nurse you are not allergic to any medications.
Your vital signs are WNL (within normal limits).
You did not pay your bill.

q.e: NKDA means "no known drug allergies". It's noted on charts to alert staff.

q: What is the smallest basic particle of matter?

q.e: An atom is the smallest unit of an element that keeps its chemical properties, but subatomic particles like quarks and electrons are smaller. The question refers to the basic unit.

q: The construction of this famous building was completed on November 1st, 1800. It was designed by Irish-born architect James Hoban, who was inspired by the Leinster House in Dublin.

q.e: The White House, designed by James Hoban, was completed in 1800 and John Adams moved in that November. Hoban was inspired by Leinster House in Dublin.

q: In which movie does Bud Abbott "prove to Lou Costello that 13 x 7 = 28?

q.e: The 13 × 7 = 28 routine is in Abbott and Costello's In the Navy (1941). It is a classic math gag.

q: Which of these is a movie about a mathematician who develops a formula that predicts the prices of stock markets?

q.e: The Bank (2001) is an Australian thriller about a mathematician who finds a formula to predict markets. Pi (1998) is a different film about a number theorist.

q: What does the term bolts from the blue mean?
Horizontal lightning that seems to come from no where
Lighting strikes on a clear day

q.e: A "bolt from the blue" is lightning from a clear sky, striking away from a storm. The idiom means a sudden surprise.

q: According to the U.S. National Weather Service, after you see and hear the last flash of lightning and roar of thunder, you should wait how long before presuming outdoor activities?

q.e: The National Weather Service advises waiting 30 minutes after the last thunder before resuming outdoor activity. "When thunder roars, go indoors."

q: Which statement concerning whales is true?
Some whales have one blow hole and some have two.
All whales have two blow holes.
Every whale has exactly one blow hole.
Only some whales have blow holes.

q.e: Toothed whales have one blowhole, while baleen whales have two. Whales breathe through them.

q: Which of these statements is true?
Humans and elephants are the only mammals that cry.
Humans are the only mammals that cry.

q.e: Humans produce emotional tears, which is rare among animals. Other animals produce tears to lubricate their eyes.

q: the laser used in eye surgery

q.e: A single bolt of lightning can reach temperatures of around 53,500 degrees Fahrenheit (roughly 30,000 kelvins). This is about five times hotter than the surface of the sun, which is roughly 10,000 degrees Fahrenheit (about 5,500 degrees Celsius).

q: All telephones in the USA were shut down on August 2, 1922. Why?
It was the day when Alexander Graham Bell died.
The International Brotherhod of Communications Workers went on strike.
The electrical workers in New York, Chicago, and Washington went on strike.
It was the day for the Orson Welles War of the Worlds radio telecast.

q.e: Phone service in the US was silenced for one minute at Alexander Graham Bell's funeral on August 4, 1922. Bell died on August 2.

q: In which US city did Einstein live out his last years?

q.e: Albert Einstein joined the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, New Jersey, in 1933 after fleeing Nazi Germany, and lived there until his death in 1955.

q: What important thing did Einstein do on August 2nd, 1939?
He proved the Theory of Special Relativity
He found the speed of light

q.e: On August 2, 1939, Einstein signed a letter, written with Leo Szilard, to President Roosevelt about the potential for nuclear weapons. It helped lead to the Manhattan Project.

q: In 1948 Albert Einstein was offered this new job.
Head of the Institute for Advanced Study
Chief of the Atomic Energy Commission

q.e: Einstein was offered the presidency of Israel in 1952, after Chaim Weizmann died. He declined.

q: Only youre not sore to the touch
Never as it might damage the muscle
It depends which muscle it is
Always as it helps heal the soreness

q.e: Sore muscles (delayed onset muscle soreness) usually improve with light activity and rest. Avoid intense exercise on very sore muscles.

q: Which of these statements about Petroleum, sometimes called 'black gold', is not true?
It is used for the production of solvents, fertilizers and plastics.
It is found in formations in he Earth.

q.e: Petroleum is a non-renewable resource because it takes millions of years to form from ancient organic matter buried under heat and pressure.

q: The study of the effect of light on chemicals

q.e: Actinology is the study of the chemical effects of light and radiation. "Actinic" means relating to radiation.
Psephology is the study of elections and voting. The word comes from the Greek "psephos", pebble, used for voting.
Ludology is the study of games, especially video games. It comes from the Latin "ludus", game.

q: What is the exact value of the mathematical constant pi, a real number which is in common use in mathematics, physics, and engineering?

q.e: Pi is irrational, so its decimal expansion never ends or repeats, and it has no exact decimal value. 3.14159 is just an approximation.

q: Whose was the proposal to use the 16th letter of the Greek alphabet, π, as a symbol for Archimedes constant, also known as Ludolphs number?

q.e: Welsh mathematician William Jones first used the symbol π for the circle constant in 1706. Euler popularized it.

q: Pi Day is celebrated by many lovers of the mathematical constant, π, on what date?

q.e: Pi Day is celebrated on March 14 because the calendar date in month/day format (3/14) matches the first three significant digits of the constant pi (3.14).

q: 123facts.com is a great site, isnt it? But do you know what the .com part stands for?

q.e: Introduced in 1985 as one of the original top-level domains, .com stands for commercial, intended primarily for for-profit business entities.

q: Which domain is used by European Union institutions?

q.e: The ".eu" domain is used by the European Union and its institutions. It launched in 2005.

q: Governments of any country (payment goes to UN funds)

q.e: Only US federal agencies and other government entities may use ".gov". It's a restricted domain.

q: If 123facts.de existed, in which language would the quizzes most likely be written?

q.e: ".de" is Germany's country domain, so the quizzes would most likely be in German. Domains show country, not always language.

q: What is the most likely suffix of a web page established by a Scottish company or individual?

q.e: A Scottish company would normally use ".uk" (or ".scot"). The ".scot" domain was added in 2014.

q: Which domain name is owned by Spain?
Spain is the only country without a national domain

q.e: ".es" is Spain's country-code top-level domain. España is the Spanish name.

q: What is the chemical symbol of Einsteinium, a rare earth metal named after Albert Einstein.

q.e: Einsteinium (Es), atomic number 99, is a synthetic element named after Albert Einstein. It's an actinide, not a rare earth.

q: What is the chemical symbol for Uranium?

q.e: Uranium's symbol is U, atomic number 92. It's used in nuclear power.

q: What is the chemical symbol for Vanadium?

q.e: Vanadium's symbol is V, atomic number 23. It's used in steel alloys.

q: The lightest baby weighed this much.

q.e: Premature babies weighing under 300 g have survived. The record changes, so check recent sources.

q: This is the length of the worlds longest documented hair.

q.e: The longest documented hair is 5.63 m (18 ft 5 in), belonging to Xie Qiuping of China. It was measured in 2004.

q: This is the length of the longest fingernails.

q.e: Record fingernails have been measured at several meters in total. Records vary by hand and measurement method.

q: This chemical element is the final element produced by stellar nucleosynthesis and the heaviest element which does not require a supernova for its formation.

q.e: Iron is the end of the chain of nuclear fusion in stars, because fusing iron uses energy rather than releasing it. Heavier elements form in supernovae.

q: Convective rain occurs in regions with what daytime whether?

q.e: Convective rain comes from warm, moist air rising after a hot day, forming cumulus clouds and showers. It's common in the tropics and summer afternoons.
RAM stands for Random Access Memory, a computer's short-term working memory. Its data is lost when power is off.

q: What does the ROM part of a CD-ROM stand for?

q.e: CD-ROM stands for Compact Disc Read-Only Memory. Data stamped onto the disc during manufacturing can be read optically by lasers, but it cannot be modified or rewritten.

q: How are CDs and DVDs read?

q.e: Optical drives use semiconductor lasers to scan microscopic pits and lands stamped onto the disc's reflective surface, converting reflected light into digital binary code. CDs utilize an infrared 780 nm laser, whereas DVDs use a red 650 nm laser.

q: Why is Blue Ray better than Red Ray/Laser?

q.e: Blu-ray uses a blue-violet laser with a shorter wavelength than red lasers, so it can read smaller pits and store more data. A DVD uses red.

q: What does the Greek prefix anthro refer to?

q.e: "Anthro-" comes from the Greek "anthropos", meaning human or mankind. Anthropology is the study of humans.

q: What does the Latin prefix homo refer to?

q.e: "Homo" is Latin for "man" or "human", as in Homo sapiens. It is different from the Greek prefix "homo-", meaning same.

The prefix 'australo-' comes from the Latin word 'australis', which means 'southern'. This root appears in geographical names like Australia as well as the hominid genus Australopithecus, meaning 'southern ape'.

q: What does the suffix lith refer to (as in Neolithic Age)?

q.e: The element -lith comes from the ancient Greek word lithos, meaning stone. It is used in historical periods like Paleolithic and Neolithic, as well as geological terms like monolith.

q: What is the meaning of the prefix paleo (as in the Paleolithic Age)?

q.e: Paleo- comes from the ancient Greek word palaios, meaning ancient or old. In contrast, meso- means middle (as in Mesolithic) and neo- means new (as in Neolithic).

q: What does the term Homo erectus mean?
a man who is able to stand upright
a creature that has the ability to reason
a man who can make tools

q.e: In Latin, Homo means human and erectus means upright. First discovered in Java in 1891 by Eugène Dubois, this species walked on two legs in a fully upright posture.

q: What day is internationally recognised and annually observed as World AIDS Day?

q.e: World AIDS Day is on December 1 each year. It was first held in 1988.

q: The Earths atmosphere comprises of which two main elements?

q.e: Nitrogen accounts for roughly 78% of dry air by volume, while oxygen makes up about 21%, leaving all other gases to share the remaining 1%.

q: How long is one day on planet Earth?

q.e: One solar day on Earth lasts exactly 24 hours, which is the time it takes the Sun to return to the same position in the sky. Earth's sidereal day—one rotation relative to distant stars—is slightly shorter at about 23 hours and 56 minutes.

q: What percentage of the Earths surface is covered by water?

q.e: About 71% of Earth's surface is covered by water, with oceans holding around 96.5% of all that planetary water.

q: A pair of fair dice are rolled and the numbers on the dice are added. What is the probability that you will roll a seven?

q.e: With two dice, 6 of the 36 outcomes sum to seven, so the probability is 1/6. Seven is the most likely sum.

q: What function is equal to its derivative?

q.e: The function e^x is its own derivative. It is the only function (apart from constant multiples) with this property.

q: Which mathematician proved that every angle can be trisected?

q.e: It's impossible to trisect an arbitrary angle with only a compass and straightedge, as proven by Pierre Wantzel in 1837. It can be done with other tools.

q: What is the symbol for Vanadium?

q.e: Vanadium's symbol is V. It's named after Vanadis, a Norse goddess.

q: What is the symbol for Polonium?

q.e: Polonium's symbol is Po. Marie Curie discovered it and named it after her native Poland.

q: What is the symbol for Magnesium?

q.e: Magnesium's symbol is Mg. It's the lightest structural metal.

q: What is the symbol for Gold?

q.e: Gold's symbol is Au, from the Latin "aurum". Silver's symbol Ag comes from "argentum".

q: What is the symbol for Cobalt?

q.e: Cobalt's symbol is Co. It gives a deep blue color to glass.

q: What is the symbol for Iron?

q.e: Iron's symbol is Fe, from the Latin "ferrum". It's the most common element on Earth by mass.

q: What is the symbol for Thallium?

q.e: Thallium's symbol is Tl. It's a toxic metal that was once used as rat poison.

q: What is the symbol for Helium?

q.e: Helium is represented by He and has an atomic number of 2, making it the second most abundant element in the universe. A single 'H' is the chemical symbol for hydrogen.

q: Grasslands cover this part of land on Earth.

q.e: Grasslands cover about a fifth of the Earth's land (some estimates are higher, up to 40% including savannas). They include prairies, steppes and pampas.

q: Deserts are advancing and taking over the land. For instance, in Mali the desert is advancing at this speed.

q.e: Deserts are expanding in the Sahel and other regions due to drought, overgrazing and climate change. The rate varies by place.

q: Many credit this book by Rachel Carson with launching the environmentalist movement.

q.e: Published in 1962, Rachel Carson's 'Silent Spring' detailed the adverse environmental effects of synthetic pesticides like DDT. The book led to a nationwide ban on DDT for agricultural uses and catalyzed the modern environmental movement.

q: In the winter of 1998-1999 this U.S. state broke the record of Mt. Ranier from 1971-1972 for the largest amount of cumulative snowfall in history.

q.e: Washington State's Mount Baker Ski Area received 1,140 inches (95 ft) of snow in 1998-99, a record. It beat Mount Rainier's 1971-72 record.

q: What term is used by skiers to describe wet granular snow?

q.e: Skiers call wet, granular snow "corn snow". It forms from repeated melting and refreezing.

q: What is the known top speed that a snow avalanche can reach?

q.e: Avalanches can reach 130 km/h (80 mph), and powder avalanches even faster, at 300 km/h. Slab avalanches often start at 60-90 km/h.

q: Which of these is classified on the Hamilton-Norwood scale?

q.e: The Hamilton-Norwood scale classifies stages of male pattern baldness. It was developed in the 1950s-70s.

q: Anemometers, from the Greek word anemos meaning wind, can be used to measure this.

q.e: An anemometer measures wind speed (and some types, pressure). The word comes from the Greek "anemos" for wind.

q: How long can a total lunar eclipse last?

q.e: A total lunar eclipse can last up to around 1 hour 47 minutes in totality. The whole process takes hours.

q: The implementation of MPAs is one way to protect the coral reefs from destruction. What does MPA stand for in this context?

q.e: MPA stands for Marine Protected Area, a section of ocean with restrictions on fishing or other activities. They help coral reefs and marine life recover.

q: This country is the worlds largest exporter of corals.

q.e: Indonesia is the world's largest exporter of corals, for the aquarium and decor trade. Collection can damage reefs.

q: What is the most common reason for getting a massage?

q.e: Relaxation is the most common reason people get a massage. Others are pain relief and injury recovery.

q: Smooth strokes are enhanced by this substance, which is often used during a massage.

q.e: Massage oils reduce friction so the therapist can use smooth strokes. Common oils include almond and jojoba.

q: As massage relaxes the body, relieves pain and reduces stress, it contributes to this.

q.e: Massage is linked to reduced stress and muscle tension, which can improve sleep. Studies have shown some benefit.

q: What is the predominant mood of a person with anxiety?

q.e: Anxiety is mainly characterized by fear and worry. It's a common condition that can be treated.

q: Which of the following people is generally at the highest risk of suicide?
A divorced, unemployed man living alone
A depressed housewife with a disabled child
A single mother with 4 children who is on welfare

q.e: Risk factors for suicide include isolation, loss and mental illness. If you or someone you know is struggling, call or text 988 in the US, or contact local emergency services.

q: Which one of these is an operating system?

q.e: Windows Vista is a Microsoft operating system, released in 2007. Others are Windows 11, macOS and Linux.

q: This animals evolutionary lineage is the best documented and the most clearly understood.

q.e: The horse has one of the best-documented evolutionary histories, from Hyracotherium (Eohippus) to modern Equus. The fossil record shows gradual changes.

q: Which of these is an output device that produces audible sound?

q.e: A speaker is an output device that produces sound. Input devices include the keyboard and mouse.

q: In geometry, which angles are called opposite?

q.e: Opposite (vertical) angles are formed by two intersecting lines and are equal. They are across from each other.

q: What does the equation y = mx + b represent?

q.e: The equation y = mx + b is the slope-intercept form of a straight line, where m is the slope and b is the y-intercept.

q: What is the symbol for Hydrogen?

q.e: Hydrogen is designated by the single letter H and has an atomic number of 1, being the simplest and lightest element. Its name comes from the Greek words meaning 'water-former'.

q: What is the symbol for Nickel?

q.e: Nickel's symbol is Ni, atomic number 28. It is used in coins and stainless steel.

q: What is the symbol for Boron?

q.e: Boron's symbol is B, atomic number 5. Borax contains boron.

q: What is the symbol for Neon?

q.e: Neon's symbol is Ne, atomic number 10. It glows reddish-orange in signs.

q: What is the symbol for Sulfur?

q.e: Sulfur's symbol is S, atomic number 16. It's yellow and smells when burned.

q: What is the symbol for Bismuth?

q.e: Bismuth's symbol is Bi, atomic number 83. Pepto-Bismol contains a bismuth compound.

q: What is the symbol for Platinum?

q.e: Platinum's symbol is Pt, atomic number 78. It's a rare, dense metal used in jewelry and catalytic converters.

q: What is the symbol for Cadmium?

q.e: Cadmium's symbol is Cd, atomic number 48. It is toxic and used in batteries.

q: The botanical term bonsai, deriving from Japanese, refers to which of these?
A technique for miniature growing trees
A type of fertilizer that reduces the size of trees
A region in Japan where miniature trees grow

q.e: Bonsai is an art form using pruning, root reduction, and potting techniques to cultivate normal tree species into miniature, stylized versions.

q: The halting problem computability theory was solved in what year?
It cannot be solved for all possible cases.

q.e: Alan Turing proved in 1936 that no general algorithm can solve the halting problem for all programs. It is undecidable.

q: Which of effect of these is the main reason for the existence of the water cycle on Earth?
Thermal energy in the Earths core

q.e: The Sun's energy drives the water cycle, evaporating water from oceans and land. Gravity brings it back as precipitation.

q: Water can be found in three main states on Earth. Which of the following is not one of them?

q.e: Water exists as a solid (ice), liquid and gas (vapor). "Crystal" is not a state of matter for water, although ice forms crystals.

q: Which of these is not one of the state-changing processes through which water goes in nature?

q.e: Water changes state by evaporation, condensation, freezing, melting, sublimation and deposition. "Concentration" is not one of them.

q: Evapotranspiration is a term connected to which of these groups?

q.e: Evapotranspiration is the movement of water from soil and plants into the air. It combines evaporation and transpiration from plants.

q: This type of pollutant causes acidification of rivers, lakes and also damages tree foliage and degrades soil quality.

q.e: Acid rain is caused by sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from burning fossil fuels. It acidifies lakes and damages trees and buildings.

q: Osteology is an important part of physical and forensic anthropology. What does an osteologist study?

q.e: An osteologist studies bones. Osteology is key in anthropology and forensic science.
A philologist studies language in written historical sources, including its structure and development. The word means "love of words".
A cetologist studies whales, dolphins and porpoises (cetaceans). The Greek "ketos" means whale.

q: If you studied petrology, where would your interests lie?

q.e: Petrology is the study of rocks, their origin and composition. The Greek "petra" means rock.
Auxology is the study of growth, especially in humans. It looks at height and weight over time.

q: During first quarter moon, what time does the moon rise?

q.e: A first quarter moon rises around noon and sets around midnight. It's half lit, as seen from Earth.

q: This construction in the United States is struck by lightning around 500 times a year.

q.e: The Empire State Building is struck by lightning about 20-25 times a year. Its lightning rod helps conduct the charge safely.

q: Silver and gold are in the same group on the periodic table. What group are they in and what are their atomic symbols, respectively?

q.e: Copper (Cu), silver (Ag) and gold (Au) are in Group 11 of the periodic table, the coinage metals. They conduct electricity well.

q: What is the derivative of y in this function related to the exponential constant e: If y=e^x?

q.e: The derivative of e^x is e^x, so the function's slope equals its value at every point. This property makes it unique.

q: In Roman numerals, what is the symbol for 1000?

q.e: In Roman numerals, M represents 1000, derived from the Latin word 'mille'. Among the other options, L represents 50, C represents 100 (from 'centum'), and D represents 500.

q: What is the name of the property used in this addition equation: 12 + 0 = 12?

q.e: Zero is the additive identity, so adding zero leaves a number unchanged. That's the identity property of addition.

q: What prevents scientists from fulfilling one of science fiction writers dreams - to clone a dinosaur?
The need for a mother from a closely related species
The lack of knowledge about their embryonal development
The difference in environmental conditions now and then

q.e: We can't clone a dinosaur because DNA breaks down over time, and no intact dinosaur DNA has been found. A cloned embryo would also need a surrogate mother.

q: What was the name of the first monkey to go in outer space?

q.e: Albert I, a rhesus monkey, was launched in a V-2 rocket in 1948 but did not survive. Albert II reached space in 1949.

q: Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), the molecule of heredity, is doubled in what stage of cell division?

q.e: DNA is replicated during the S (synthesis) phase of the cell cycle, between G1 and G2. This ensures each daughter cell gets a full copy.

q: A card is selected at random from a regular poker deck of cards. The jokers have been eliminated. What is the probability that the selected card is a diamond?

q.e: A standard 52-card deck has four suits of 13 cards each: hearts, diamonds, clubs, and spades. The probability of drawing a diamond is 13 out of 52, which simplifies to 1 in 4 (25%).

q: A regular fair pair of dice is rolled. What is the probability that the role will be a 7?

q.e: There are 36 possible outcomes when rolling two six-sided dice, and 6 combinations yield a sum of 7: (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), and (6,1). Reducing 6 out of 36 gives a 1 in 6 probability.

q: In the southern part of the United States, what months are peak season for tornadoes?

q.e: In the southern US, tornado season peaks in spring, March to May. Another smaller peak occurs in the fall.

q: According to the electromagnetic spectrum, which region is the most energetic?

q.e: Gamma rays are the most energetic part of the electromagnetic spectrum, with the shortest wavelengths. They come from nuclear processes and cosmic events.

q: What computational device was designed by Charles Babbage?

q.e: Charles Babbage designed the Difference Engine in the 1820s, a mechanical calculator, and later the Analytical Engine. The latter is considered a forerunner of computers.

q: What continent are tigers native to?

q.e: Tigers are native exclusively to Asia, with historical ranges extending from Turkey to eastern Russia and southeast Asian islands like Sumatra. Lions are the large wild cats primarily found in Africa.

q: What continent is the aardvark native to?

q.e: Aardvarks are burrowing, nocturnal mammals native to sub-Saharan Africa, where they feed almost exclusively on ants and termites. Their name translates to earth pig in Afrikaans.

q: Which of these is represented by the chemical formula C12 H22 O11?

q.e: C12H22O11 is the formula for sucrose (table sugar). Lactose and maltose have the same formula.

q: The name of which country is derived from the Latin word for silver?

q.e: Argentina is derived from argentum, the Latin word for silver, which also gives silver its chemical symbol Ag. Early Spanish and Portuguese explorers named the region after stories of vast silver deposits along the Rio de la Plata (Silver River).

q: What is the maximum angle of field of vision compound eyes can have?

q.e: Compound eyes can have a very wide field of view, up to nearly 360° in some insects, such as dragonflies. They detect motion well.

q: Stereopsis is a process in visual perception giving the organism a sensation of what?

q.e: Stereopsis is the perception of depth and three-dimensional structure derived from binocular vision. Because our two eyes are horizontally separated, each retina receives a slightly different image, which the brain fuses into a single 3D view.

q: Which was the first nation to adopt a metric system?

q.e: France officially adopted the metric system in 1795 following the French Revolution to replace a chaotic patchwork of thousands of traditional regional units.

q: What unit is used in the metric system for measuring time?

q.e: The second is the base unit of time in the International System of Units (SI), defined since 1967 by transitions of the cesium-133 atom.

q: There is a unit called a Yottagram. How many grams are in one Yottagram?

q.e: A yottagram is 10^24 grams. Yotta is the largest SI prefix, together with ronna and quetta.

q: Which nation issued the first metric currency - a unit that was divided in 100 parts?

q.e: The US introduced a decimal currency with the Coinage Act of 1792 (a dollar of 100 cents). Russia had a decimal ruble earlier, under Peter the Great.

q: Which two of these are produced when an acid and a base are mixed together?

q.e: When an acid reacts with a base in a neutralization reaction, hydrogen ions (H+) combine with hydroxide ions (OH-) to form water (H2O), while the remaining ions form an ionic salt.

q: What happens to an indicator when touched by an acid or a base?

q.e: Indicators such as litmus change color when they touch an acid or base. Litmus turns red in acid and blue in base.

q: A ionic compound with H (hydrogen) in the front is most likely to be which of the following?

q.e: Compounds that start with H, such as HCl, are usually acids because they release hydrogen ions in water. Water itself is an exception.

q: a base with a bitter taste
an acid with a sour taste
an acid with a bitter taste
a base with a sour taste

q.e: Soap is made from fats and a strong base, and is slightly basic. It feels slippery and tastes bitter.

q: What is the range of the pH scale?

q.e: The pH scale ranges from 0 to 14, with 7 neutral. Lower is acidic and higher is basic.

q: Approximately how long is one astronomical unit (1 a.u.)?

q.e: One astronomical unit is the average distance from Earth to the Sun, about 149.6 million km (93 million miles). It is used for distances in the Solar System.

q: Their barrels are open at both ends.
They are loaded with missiles not cannon balls.
They are made of very heavy metals.
They are not placed on wheels.

q.e: Recoilless guns vent part of the propellant gas out the rear (their barrels are open at both ends), balancing the forward thrust of the shell. That cancels most of the recoil, so they can be light.

q: What is an endothermic chemical reaction?
A chemical reaction in which energy is used up
A chemical reaction in which energy is released
A chemical reaction in which oxides are produced
A chemical reaction in which carbon compounds are involved

q.e: An endothermic reaction absorbs energy (usually heat) from its surroundings, so the surroundings get colder. Instant cold packs use this.

q: The Metal Storm weapons, that can fire tens of thousands of rounds a minute, were developed where?

q.e: Metal Storm was an Australian company based in Brisbane, which developed electronically fired stacked-projectile guns. It filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
Heterodonts have teeth of different shapes (incisors, canines, molars), as humans do. Most reptiles are homodonts, with all teeth alike.

q: Which of the following is not true about the egg yolk?
It contains 75% of the protein of the egg.
It is placed in a yolk sac.
Its usual color varies from pale yellow to deep orange.
It contains almost 100% of total amount of fat and cholesterol in the egg.

q.e: Egg yolk holds most of an egg's fat, vitamins and minerals, but only about 40% of its protein. The white contains most of the rest.

q: Which was the first version of Microsoft Windows to support Plug and Play?

q.e: Windows 95 was the first version of Windows to support Plug and Play, which lets the system detect new hardware automatically. It was released in August 1995.

q: The main purpose of the observatory located on the north shore of Big Bear Lake in the San Bernardino Mountains, California is studying what?

q.e: The Big Bear Solar Observatory in California studies the Sun. Lake Big Bear's air is steady and clear, ideal for sun observations.

q: Which of these islands is known as the location of numerous important world observatories?

q.e: Hawaii's Mauna Kea hosts some of the world's major observatories, thanks to its altitude, dry air and dark skies. It's about 4,200 m high.

q: The largest semilunar cartilages, also called the menisci, are located in this part of the body.

q.e: The menisci are C-shaped cartilage pads in the knee that cushion the joint. Tears are a common sports injury.

q: Which of these can help produce pencils, without cutting down trees?

q.e: Recycled denim (jeans) has been used to make pencils without cutting trees. Other pencils use recycled newspaper or plastic.

q: Which of the following is not a common symptom of fibromyalgia?

q.e: Fibromyalgia mostly causes widespread pain, fatigue and sleep problems. A low red blood count points to anemia, which is a different condition.

q: The USA leads� the world in per capita consumption of water. Which country is second?

q.e: The US has among the highest water use per person in the world, with Canada close behind. Much of it goes to irrigation and household use.

q: What does the scientific term virga mean?
The effect on Mars that makes it appear as if water was on Mars
The salt that remains after sea water has been desalinated

q.e: Virga is rain that evaporates before it reaches the ground. It looks like streaks hanging from clouds.

q: It has been proved that drinking only bottled water can have this effect on your health.

q.e: Bottled water usually lacks fluoride, so people who drink only bottled water may miss the protective effect against cavities. Many tap supplies add it.

q: Venus is named after the Roman Goddess of what?

q.e: Venus is named after the Roman goddess of love and beauty (Aphrodite to the Greeks). It's the brightest planet in our sky.

q: Venus is the third brightest object in the sky after the Sun and what other object?

q.e: Because its dense cloud deck reflects roughly 70% of incoming sunlight, Venus reaches an apparent magnitude of up to -4.92, outshining all celestial objects except the Sun and Moon.
Mach 1, the speed of sound, is about 1,225 km/h (761 mph) at sea level at 15 °C. It varies with temperature and altitude.

q: Who was the first actor to attain the rank of Brigadier General in the US Air Force?

q.e: James Stewart, the actor, became a brigadier general in the US Air Force Reserve in 1959. He flew bombers in World War II.

q: Which of these particles has a negative charge?

q.e: Electrons carry a negative elementary charge, while protons have a positive charge and neutrons are electrically neutral. A positron is the antimatter counterpart of an electron, carrying a positive charge.

q: In math and science a double tilda is often used as a symbol. Which is symbolized by a double tilde?
Has the same atomic number as
Has the same first derivative as
Has the same atomic weight as

q.e: The double tilde (≈) means "is approximately equal to". A single tilde (~) usually means "similar" or "about".

q: Which of these waves have the highest wave length?

q.e: Radio waves have the longest wavelengths of the electromagnetic spectrum, from millimeters to hundreds of kilometers. Gamma rays have the shortest.

q: Which of these living creatures appearred on Earth first?

q.e: The earliest jawless fish evolved roughly 500 million years ago during the Cambrian and Ordovician periods. Seed plants did not emerge until about 360 million years ago, followed by reptiles around 315 million years ago.

q: What was the name of the command module of Apollo 11?

q.e: The Apollo 11 command module was named Columbia, and the lunar module was Eagle. Michael Collins stayed in Columbia while Armstrong and Aldrin landed.

q: How did Edwin Eugene Buzz Aldrin, Jr. get his nickname Buzz?
His sister gave it to him.
He was given that nickname because he was an engineer.
He was extremely talkative as a child, to the point of being annoying.
His beloved grandfather called him Buzz.

q.e: Aldrin's older sister Fay Ann mispronounced the word 'brother' as 'buzzer', which was soon shortened to 'Buzz'. The family adopted it as his lifelong nickname, and he made it his legal first name in 1988.

q: How much time did the astronauts from Apollo 11 spend on the lunar surface?

q.e: Armstrong and Aldrin spent about 21½ hours on the Moon, of which about 2½ hours were outside. They stepped out on July 20, 1969.

q: On which part of the body is the surgical procedure osteotomy performed?

q.e: An osteotomy is a surgical cut in a bone, to shorten, lengthen or realign it. It's used to correct deformities.

q: This place, popular as the center of the Whiskey rebellion, is the worlds first nuclear powered city.

q.e: Pittsburgh was the center of the Whiskey Rebellion (1791-94). Nearby Shippingport, Pennsylvania, had the first full-scale US nuclear power plant for civilians, opening in 1957.

q: What large and obvious summer asterism do Vega, Deneb, and Altair form?

q.e: The Summer Triangle connects three prominent first-magnitude stars in the Northern Hemisphere's night sky: Vega in Lyra, Deneb in Cygnus, and Altair in Aquila.

q: Spectroscopic analysis revealed that Plutos surface is composed mainly of this element.

q.e: Spectroscopy shows Pluto's surface is mostly nitrogen ice, with methane and carbon monoxide ice. It also has a thin atmosphere.

q: The reclassification of Pluto as a dwarf planet in 2006 caused the emerging of what?
Risings among astronomy teaches in the USA
New ethnical conflicts in the Middle East
A sect of violent Pluto followers

q.e: When Pluto was reclassified in 2006, the word "plutoed" came into use, meaning to demote. It was the American Dialect Society's 2006 word of the year.

q: By forcing other cells to produce copies of them
By transforming other cells into viruses

q.e: Because viruses lack the cellular machinery required for independent metabolism and division, they must hijack a host cell's molecular machinery to replicate their genetic material and build new virions.

q: Which of the following is not one of the defense mechanisms against viruses in humans?
Acid nature of the stomach contents

q.e: R (resistance) genes are part of the immune system of plants, not humans. Human antiviral defenses include interferons, antibodies and T cells.

q: Which of these companies recycled old sneakers to make tennis courts?

q.e: Nike's Reuse-A-Shoe program grinds old sneakers into "Nike Grind", used for surfaces such as tennis courts and playgrounds.

q: The first facial hair appears in this area during puberty.

q.e: In puberty, boys' first facial hair usually appears at the corners of the upper lip, then spreads to the cheeks and chin. It takes years to fill in.

q: Only three groups of land creatures get cavities - humans, pets kept by humans, and this group.

q.e: Few animals get cavities, and those that do eat sugary or starchy foods. Bears with access to human food and honey have been reported with dental decay.

q: How many genes does the human DNA contain?

q.e: Humans have about 20,000-25,000 protein-coding genes. Older estimates, before the Human Genome Project, were as high as 100,000.

q: Where exactly is the retina of the eye positioned?
Its lining the inner surface of the eye.
Retina is a synonym of pupil.

q.e: The retina lines the inner back surface of the eyeball. It holds the light-sensitive rods and cones.

q: Which of these is not a type of conic section?

q.e: The conic sections are the circle, ellipse, parabola and hyperbola, formed by slicing a cone. A ray is not a conic section.

q: In mathematics, what type of conic section would this equation show: x^2+y^2=9?

q.e: x² + y² = 9 is a circle centered at the origin with radius 3. The general form is x² + y² = r².

q: Which of the following is not a level 4 (Transport Layer) network protocol?

q.e: RIP (Routing Information Protocol) is a routing protocol that works at the application layer, not the transport layer. TCP and UDP are transport layer protocols.

q: What is the most abundant element in Mercurys atmosphere?

q.e: Mercury has a thin exosphere, with oxygen as the most abundant element, followed by sodium, hydrogen and helium. It is too weak to count as a real atmosphere.

q: What element comprises more than half of Mercurys mass?

q.e: Iron makes up about two-thirds of Mercury's mass, mostly in its large metallic core. It is the densest planet relative to its size.

q: In what part of the apple are the toxic compounds cyanogenic glycosides found?

q.e: Apple seeds contain amygdalin, a cyanogenic glycoside that releases toxic hydrogen cyanide when chewed and digested. However, accidental ingestion of a few whole seeds poses virtually no danger because their outer coating protects them.

q: Which of these is said to be helpful in reducing swelling from bee stings?

q.e: Folk remedies include onion, baking soda paste or a cold compress for stings. Cold packs and antihistamines reduce swelling; see a doctor if you are allergic.

q: Which of the following vitamins is known as Folic Acid?

q.e: Vitamin B9 is folate, and folic acid is its synthetic form. It's important in pregnancy to prevent neural tube defects.

q: What is the symbol for the speed of light?

q.e: The symbol 'c' represents the speed of light in a vacuum, roughly 299,792 kilometers per second (about 186,282 miles per second). It comes from the Latin word 'celeritas', which means swiftness or speed.

q: What does a concave mirror do with the object that is reflected?
Depends on the on the distance between the object and the mirror.
It widens the size of the object.
It increases the size of the object.
It decreases the size of the object.

q.e: A concave mirror can produce enlarged, upright images up close, or inverted, real images when the object is farther away. It depends on the distance from the focal point.

q: Light slows down in this object and causes it to look bent.

q.e: Light slows down in water, glass and other media, and that causes refraction. A straw looks bent in a glass of water.

q: Saturns largest moon is known by what name?

q.e: Titan is Saturn's largest moon and the second-largest in the Solar System. It has a thick atmosphere and lakes of liquid methane.

q: On what date was the planet Neptune discovered?

q.e: Neptune was discovered on September 23, 1846, by Johann Galle, using calculations by Urbain Le Verrier. It was the first planet found by mathematical prediction.

q: What part of the microscope holds the draw tube in place?

q.e: In a microscope, the body tube holds the lenses and connects the eyepiece to the objective lenses. The draw tube fits inside it.

q: This microscope part supports the glass slide and the specimen.

q.e: The stage supports the slide, and stage clips hold it in place. Light passes up through an opening.

q: What was the occupation of the person after whom the human sideburns were named?

q.e: Sideburns were originally called 'burnsides' after Union Army general Ambrose Burnside, who was famous for his thick facial hair connecting his mustache to his temples.

q: According to the properties it exhibits, light is defined as what?
