q.e: Einstein helped popularize tensor calculus in general relativity, using the work of Ricci and Levi-Civita and help from Marcel Grossmann.

q: A "combination lock" has three integers. Each integer is a member of this set: {0, 1, 2, 3, 4,}. How many such locks with different combinations can be made?

q.e: Each of the 3 dials has 5 choices, so 5 × 5 × 5 = 125 combinations.

q: What do mathematicians call a quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides?

q.e: In North American geometry, a trapezoid is defined as a quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides (or at least one pair in the inclusive definition). In British English, this shape is called a trapezium.

q: Both Newton and Leibnitz claimed credit for inventing� calculus. Which statement about calculus is true?
Whoever invented it, we use Leibnitz notation.
Whoever invented it, we use Newton's notation.

q.e: We use Leibniz's notation (dy/dx and ∫) in calculus today, as it's more flexible than Newton's dot notation. Both men developed calculus independently.

q: What scale is used only to describe hurricanes forming in the Atlantic Ocean and northern Pacific Ocean?

q.e: The Saffir-Simpson scale rates hurricanes from Category 1 to 5 by sustained wind speed. It only applies to the Atlantic and northeast Pacific.

q: Who proposed a general method of classifying how technologically advanced a civilization is?

q.e: Soviet astronomer Nikolai Kardashev proposed the scale in 1964: Type I uses a planet's energy, Type II a star's, Type III a galaxy's.

q: The Fujita scale rates a tornados intensity by the damage it inflicts on human-built structures, this scale classifies hurricanes by the intensity of their sustained winds.

q.e: Developed in 1971 by civil engineer Herbert Saffir and meteorologist Robert Simpson, the Saffir-Simpson scale categorizes hurricanes from 1 to 5 based on 1-minute maximum sustained wind speeds. The Beaufort scale, by contrast, is a broader empirical scale for wind speed at sea and on land.

q: In a tropical cyclone, this area is characterized with the strongest winds, the tallest clouds, and the heaviest rain.

q.e: The eyewall surrounds the calm, low-pressure eye and contains the storm's most violent convective energy, generating the highest surface winds and deepest storm clouds.

q: This is a natural healing method that uses the reflex points of the feet, which correspond to different organs and areas of the body.

q.e: Reflexology is based on the idea that points on the feet and hands correspond to organs. There's little scientific evidence for it beyond relaxation.

q: This technique is used to relax soft tissue. It is done using both hands, exercising light pressure.

q.e: Effleurage is a light, gliding stroke in Swedish massage, often used to begin and end a session. The word is French for "to skim".

q: Which of the following medications is effective for both depression and anxiety?

q.e: Paxil (paroxetine) is an SSRI approved for depression and several anxiety disorders, including panic and social anxiety.

q: Which of the following disorders is NOT a form of anxiety?

q.e: Cyclothymia is a mild form of bipolar disorder (a mood disorder), not an anxiety disorder. Panic disorder, GAD and phobias are anxiety disorders.

q: Of the following medications for anxiety, which is potentially addictive?

q.e: Ativan (lorazepam) is a benzodiazepine, so it can cause dependence and is generally used short-term. SSRIs aren't addictive.

q: A cells life cycle is the series of changes the cell goes through from the time it is formed until it reproduces itself. It includes two stages. What are these two stages?

q.e: The cell cycle has interphase (growth and DNA replication) and cell division (mitosis, then cytokinesis). Most of a cell's life is spent in interphase.

q: The meninges, a system of membranes that envelop the central nervous system, consist of three layers. Which of the following is not a name of a layer?

q.e: The three meninges are the dura mater, arachnoid mater and pia mater. Gray matter is brain tissue, not a membrane.

q: This evolutionary theory, proposed by the inimitable Stephen J. Gould and Niles Eldridge, argues that evolution occurs not gradually but rapidly after periods of stasis and in isolated, localized areas.

q.e: Niles Eldredge and Stephen Jay Gould proposed punctuated equilibrium in 1972. Fossils often show long stability and then sudden changes.

q: This monastic egghead pioneered the study of genetics, which eventually explained the mechanisms of speciation through genetic mutation. Who is the "father of modern genetics?�

q.e: Gregor Mendel was an Augustinian friar who crossbred roughly 28,000 pea plants between 1856 and 1863 to discover the fundamental laws of genetic inheritance. James Watson and Francis Crick co-discovered the double-helix structure of DNA nearly a century later in 1953.

q: Which of these represents the locus of points, the sum of whose distances from two given points is equal?

q.e: An ellipse is the set of points whose distances to two foci sum to a constant. A circle is the special case with the foci together.

q: What is the path taken by a bullet fired from a rifle into the air (ignoring friction)?

q.e: Ignoring air resistance, a projectile follows a parabola. Real bullets deviate with drag.

q: Which of the following statements about quadrilaterals (4-sided figures) is true?
A square is a type of parallelogram.
A parallelogram is a type of trapezoid.
A rhombus is a type of rectangle.
A rectangle is a type of square.

q.e: A parallelogram is defined as a quadrilateral with two pairs of parallel sides, which fits the definition of a square. In contrast, rectangles require four right angles, meaning rhombuses are not necessarily rectangles.

q: There have been numerous debates over whether this moon, discovered in 1978, should be considered a satellite or a separate planet.

q.e: Charon was discovered in 1978 by James Christy. It is so large compared with Pluto that the two orbit a point between them.

q: Which branch of botany is concerned with the study of trees and woody plants?

q.e: Dendrology (Greek "dendron", tree) is the study of trees and shrubs. Botany covers all plants.

q: The earliest trees on the planet were a type of ferns and are considered to have appeared in which period of Earths geological history?

q.e: The first trees (Archaeopteris, and earlier Wattieza) appeared in the Devonian period of the Paleozoic Era, about 385 million years ago.

q: Mark the incorrect statement about sequoias, which are among the largest and oldest trees on the planet.
Sequoias can reach up to 150 m (490 ft) in height.
Sequoias can live for more than 2000 years.

q.e: Giant sequoias reach about 95 m, and coast redwoods up to roughly 116 m. So 150 m is too high. Sequoias can live over 3,000 years.

q: Who was first to prove that beside an irrational number, pi is also transcendental number (i.e. is not a root to any polynomial equation with rational coefficients)?

q.e: Ferdinand von Lindemann proved in 1882 that pi is transcendental. This showed that squaring the circle with compass and straightedge is impossible.

q: Which programming language is based on Horn clauses?

q.e: Prolog (Programming in Logic), from 1972, is built around logic and Horn clauses, and is used in AI and computational linguistics.

q: The water cycle is the continuous movement of water above and below the surface of the planet. What is this process also known as?

q.e: The hydrologic cycle describes the continuous movement of Earth's water through evaporation, transpiration, condensation, and precipitation.

q: Which line contains only types of precipitation?

q.e: Precipitation includes graupel, sleet, snow and hail. Fog, dew, frost and clouds are condensation, not precipitation.

q: Ice caps and glaciers are the second largest water reservoirs on Earth after oceans. What percent of the planet's water do they hold?

q.e: About 97% of Earth's water is salty. Glaciers and ice caps hold roughly 2% of all water, or about 69% of fresh water.

q: Which of these is the study of cells?

q.e: Cytology is the study of cells ("cyto" means cell). Histology studies tissues.

q: Because of introducing a classification scheme for distinguishing living organisms, Carolus Linnaeus is known as the father of what field of science?

q.e: Swedish naturalist Carl Linnaeus published Systema Naturae in 1735, introducing binomial nomenclature to give every species a standardized two-part Latin name. His system earned him the title of the father of modern taxonomy.

q: What unit in the metric system do astronomers use to measure the wavelength of light?

q.e: Astronomers measure light in nanometers (a billionth of a meter), or sometimes in ångströms. Visible light is about 400-700 nm.

q: Inert gases are found in Group 18 of the Periodic Table. Which is the inert gas with atomic number 54?

q.e: Xenon (Xe) has atomic number 54. Noble gases are very unreactive because their outer shells are full.

q: Lanthanoids and actinoids are not included with the rest of the periodic table for convenience. Which series of elements are found in these two series, respectively?

q.e: The lanthanoids run from lanthanum (La) to ytterbium (Yb) or lutetium, and the actinoids from actinium (Ac) to nobelium (No) or lawrencium.

q: The constant e is present in countless fields of mathematics but its most significant function is related to its use in what?
The limiting value of the sum of the squares of the odd numbers

q.e: e ≈ 2.718 is the base of natural logarithms. It appears in exponential growth, compound interest and probability.

q: Identify the property used in this addition equation: 678 + 45 = 45 + 678.

q.e: The commutative property of addition states that changing the order of the addends does not change the sum (a + b = b + a). In contrast, the associative property involves regrouping terms using parentheses without changing their order.

q: Which is the mathematical property used in this addition equation: (57 + 63) + 14 = 57 + (63 + 14)?

q.e: (a + b) + c = a + (b + c) is the associative property: the grouping doesn't change the sum.

q: Which of these are considered the two developers of the modern calculus?

q.e: Isaac Newton and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz independently developed the foundational concepts of calculus during the late 17th century, sparking a famous dispute over priority.

q: In 2005, this famous Russian cosmonaut set a record for total time, spent in space.

q.e: Sergei Krikalev had logged about 803 days in space by 2005. The record has since been broken by Gennady Padalka and Oleg Kononenko.

q: Along with Neil Armstrong and Michael Collins, who was the third member of the Apollo 11 crew?

q.e: Buzz Aldrin was the lunar module pilot of Apollo 11 (1969) and the second person to walk on the Moon.

q: Who was the pilot of SpaceShipOne, the spaceplane that completed the first privately funded human spaceflight?

q.e: Mike Melvill piloted SpaceShipOne in June 2004 and became the first commercial astronaut. Brian Binnie flew the Ansari X Prize flights later.

q: What was nationality of Vladimir Remek - the first cosmonaut from a country other than the Soviet Union or the United States?

q.e: Vladimír Remek of Czechoslovakia flew on Soyuz 28 in 1978 as part of the Soviet Intercosmos program.

q: In 1905, this British scientist suggested the word genetics to describe the study of inheritance.

q.e: William Bateson coined "genetics" in 1905-06 and championed Mendel's work in Britain.

q: This genetic disorder is characterized by the premature fusion of the bones of the skull, which affects the shape of the head and face.

q.e: Pfeiffer syndrome is a rare genetic disorder with premature fusion of the skull bones (craniosynostosis) and abnormal hands and feet.

q: Genes are the units of heredity in living organisms. Variants of the same gene are known under what name?

q.e: Alleles are different versions of the same gene. For example, there are alleles for blue or brown eyes.

q: This cell structure exists only when the long pieces of Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), called chromosomes, replicate themselves.

q.e: A chromatid is one of the two identical copies of a replicated chromosome, joined at the centromere. They separate during cell division.

q: This chemical element has a smell similar to garlic and is part of the structure of Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), the molecule that carries genes.

q.e: Phosphorus is part of the DNA backbone (the phosphate groups). White phosphorus has a garlic-like smell.

q: What time of the day do tornadoes most often strike?

q.e: Tornadoes most often form in late afternoon and evening, between about 3 and 9 p.m., when the ground is hottest.

q: Who developed a punch card that was used with mechanical tabulating machines in the 1890 U.S. Census?

q.e: Herman Hollerith's punch card system processed the 1890 US census much faster. His company later became part of IBM.

q: When a patient presents with a sore throat, which of the following diagnoses may indicate immediate intubation?

q.e: Epiglottitis, swelling of the flap over the windpipe, can block the airway, so it's an emergency. Drooling and a muffled voice are warning signs.

q: All of the following medications are contraindicated during pregnancy, EXCEPT which one?

q.e: Nitrofurantoin is generally considered safe for UTIs in early pregnancy. Many other drugs are not.

q: If a patient has chest pain and ST elevation in nearly all leads of the EKG, what is the likely diagnosis?

q.e: Pericarditis causes widespread ST elevation on the EKG, unlike a heart attack, which affects specific areas. Chest pain eases when leaning forward.

q: All of the following are treatments for rheumatoid arthritis EXCEPT which one?

q.e: Carbamazepine is an anticonvulsant, and doesn't treat rheumatoid arthritis. Methotrexate and TNF inhibitors do.

q: Elmali Kilise, a rock sanctuary built in Byzantine style, dates back to the Comnenan period and is located in which district?

q.e: Elmalı Kilise, the "Church with the Apple", is a rock-cut church in the Göreme Open Air Museum in Cappadocia, Turkey.

q: Almost all organisms on Earth have a vision restricted to small range of the electromagnetic spectrum (between 320 and 800 nm). This is considered to be a consequence of which of these evolutionary facts?
The atmosphere had different composition when life emerged
At the time when life emerged, the electromagnetic spectrum was different

q.e: Life began in the water, which filters out most wavelengths. The light that gets through is mostly in the visible range, so vision evolved for it.

q: Who was the first person to propose the idea of a metric system?

q.e: Flemish mathematician Simon Stevin proposed decimal fractions and a decimal system of measures in the 1580s. The metric system itself was created in France in the 1790s.

q: What does the prefix milli mean?

q.e: Derived from the Latin mille, meaning thousand, the SI prefix milli- denotes a factor of one thousandth (10 to the power of -3), as seen in millimeters and milligrams.

q: What is the reaction called when an acid and a base are mixed together?

q.e: An acid and a base react in a neutralization reaction, forming water and a salt.

q: Taxonomy of vertebrates divides fishes into what two basic groups?

q.e: Fishes are split into jawed (e.g. sharks, bony fish) and jawless (e.g. lampreys and hagfish).

q: If a wireless network is set up in a home, yet the signal is weak in certain areas, you may buy one of these to increase the existing signal strength.

q.e: A Wi-Fi repeater (extender) picks up the router's signal and rebroadcasts it, which extends the range but often halves speed.

q: Windows Vista commercials have boasted of the Record Live Television capability of the operating system. What is necessary to use this function?

q.e: Windows Vista Media Center needs a TV tuner card to receive and record live TV.

q: The carbon atom in amino acids has four elements/groups attached to it in all amino acids (except for proline). Which of the following is not among these four?

q.e: An amino acid's central carbon has an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen and a variable R group. A methyl group is only one possible R group (alanine).

q: Which of these animals only has molars?

q.e: Adult aardvarks have only molar-type cheek teeth, with no incisors or canines. Their teeth lack enamel and keep growing.

q: Eggs have a very high nutrition value. Which of the following substances is not present within an egg?

q.e: An egg has protein, fat, vitamins and minerals, but no chlorophyll, which is the green pigment found in plants.

q: What is the main protein found in the egg white?

q.e: Ovalbumin is the main protein in egg white, about 54% of the total. It's used in labs as a model protein.

q: Which of the following primates is the closest related to humans? (That is, this primate has more DNA in common with humans than any other living creature does.)

q.e: Chimpanzees and their close relatives, bonobos, share about 98.8% of their DNA with humans, making them our closest living evolutionary relatives. Gorillas follow next, sharing around 98.4% of human DNA.

q: Name the ligament that attaches to the head of the femur and the acetabulum.

q.e: The ligamentum teres connects the femoral head to the acetabulum and carries a small artery.

q: What is the most distant object you can see unaided under the best possible conditions?

q.e: Under dark skies, the Triangulum Galaxy (M33) at ~2.7 million light-years is often named as the most distant naked-eye object. The Andromeda galaxy is a bit closer.

q: What type of glands are the Glands of Montgomery?

q.e: Montgomery glands are sebaceous glands around the nipple (areola), which lubricate and protect it, especially while breastfeeding.

q: About 95% of fresh water in the USA is underground. What is the name of the biggest source of fresh water in the USA?

q.e: The Ogallala Aquifer underlies parts of eight Great Plains states and irrigates much of US farmland. It is being depleted faster than it refills.

q: What is the term for the points in the lunar cycle when the tides range is minimal?

q.e: Neap tides occur twice a month during the first and third quarter moons when the gravitational forces of the Sun and Moon pull at right angles, minimizing tidal range. Conversely, spring tides produce the greatest tidal range when the Sun and Moon align.

q: It is amazing but true that sometimes hot water can freeze faster than cold water. What is this effect called?

q.e: Named after Tanzanian student Erasto Mpemba who noticed it while making ice cream in 1963, the Mpemba effect describes the counterintuitive observation that warm water can freeze faster than cold under certain conditions.

q: Which scientist discovered the atmosphere of Venus?

q.e: Mikhail Lomonosov noticed a ring of light around Venus during its 1761 transit and concluded it had an atmosphere.

q: What was the first privately financed craft to go into outer space?

q.e: SpaceShipOne, designed by Burt Rutan and funded by Paul Allen, was the first privately funded craft to reach space, in 2004.

q: What was the name of the first space station?

q.e: Salyut 1 was launched by the Soviet Union on April 19, 1971, making it humanity's first orbital space station. Skylab was the first American station, launched two years later in 1973.

q: The Earths atmosphere is about 78.8 % nitrogen and almost 21 % oxygen. This element is the third most abundant comprising about 0.93 % of the atmosphere.

q.e: Argon is a noble gas that makes up roughly 0.934% of dry atmospheric air, far exceeding carbon dioxide, which is present at about 0.04%.

q: Which is the highest layer of the Earth's atmosphere?

q.e: The exosphere begins at about 310 to 620 miles (500 to 1,000 km) above Earth's surface and gradually fades into the vacuum of space, with gas molecules so sparse they rarely collide.

q: Which of the following terms describes a dark layer of clouds that bring rain or snow?

q.e: Nimbostratus clouds form dark, thick, featureless layers that bring steady rain or snow ('nimbus' is Latin for rain). Cirrus clouds are high, wispy clouds made of ice crystals that do not produce ground precipitation.

q: Tympanoplasty is a type of reconstructive surgery performed on which part of the body?

q.e: Tympanoplasty repairs a damaged eardrum (tympanic membrane) and sometimes the tiny middle-ear bones.

q: The first successful experiment with nuclear fission, the process in which the nucleus of an atom splits into two or more smaller nuclei, was conducted in which year?

q.e: Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann discovered nuclear fission in December 1938. Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch explained it.

q: These two physicists received the 1951 Nobel Prize for Physics for their pioneering work popularly known as splitting the atom.
Lise Meitner and Otto Robert Frisch

q.e: John Cockcroft and Ernest Walton "split the atom" in 1932 by firing accelerated protons at lithium. They shared the 1951 Nobel Prize.

q: This is the year in which the worlds first nuclear power plant generating electricity for commercial use was officially connected to the Soviet power grid.

q.e: The Obninsk Nuclear Power Plant in the USSR was connected to the grid in 1954, the first to supply a power grid.

q: This 1903 Nobel Prize laureate discovered radioactivity in 1896.

q.e: Henri Becquerel discovered spontaneous radioactivity while investigating phosphorescent uranium salts in 1896, later sharing the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with Marie and Pierre Curie.

q: What is the name of the red supergiant that marks Orions right shoulder?

q.e: Betelgeuse marks the right shoulder of Orion from the constellation's perspective, though it appears in the upper left to observers on Earth. Bellatrix marks the opposite shoulder.

q: What is the name of the star cluster that is also known as "The Seven Sisters�?

q.e: The Pleiades (M45), the Seven Sisters, is an open star cluster in Taurus. Six or seven stars are visible to the naked eye.

q: Lipitor and Zocor are two popular brand names which fall under what class of cholesterol lowering drugs?

q.e: Lipitor (atorvastatin) and Zocor (simvastatin) belong to statins, which lower blood cholesterol by inhibiting the HMG-CoA reductase enzyme in the liver.

q: What famous scientist discovered Jupiters four largest satellites?

q.e: Galileo found Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto in 1610, now the Galilean moons. This helped support the Sun-centered model.

q: Which of these is a medical term that refers to crying?

q.e: Lacrimation is the production of tears. Lacrimal glands make tears.

q: In baseball, when a quarterback throws a pass, the ball follows what type of path?

q.e: The ball thrown by a quarterback in American football (not baseball) follows a roughly parabolic arc, ignoring drag.

q: What conic section is used to describe electromagnetic waves?

q.e: In this quiz's scheme, EM waves are tied to parabolas (such as a parabolic antenna's reflector). In reality, EM waves are sinusoidal.

q: When you ping a network node, which protocol is being utilized?

q.e: The ping command uses ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) echo requests and replies to test whether a host is reachable.

q: We watch TV thanks to which of these processes forming light?

q.e: CRT televisions make light by cathodoluminescence: electrons strike phosphors on the screen, which glow.

q: In chemistry and physics, what do we call free radicals?
Atoms with at least one unpaired electron
Atoms not part of a molecule

q.e: Free radicals are atoms or molecules with at least one unpaired electron, which makes them highly reactive. They can damage cells.

q: How is an atom having the valance of 1 called?

q.e: A monovalent atom, with a valence of one, is also called a monad. Dyad, triad and tetrad follow.

q: What is the name of the scale that is used to rate the intensity of tornadoes?

q.e: Developed by meteorologist Tetsuya Theodore Fujita in 1971, the Fujita scale rates tornado intensity based on damage caused. The Richter scale measures earthquake magnitude.

q: Weve all heard about the importance of insulin, but where does its name come from?
It comes from the Latin insula, which means island.
It means that it is produced inside the body.
Its name means reduces sugar in Greek.

q.e: Sir Edward Albert Sharpey-Schafer coined the term insulin in 1916 from the Latin word insula (island), referencing the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas where the hormone is produced.

q: Which of the following groups of animals does nematology study?

q.e: Nematology studies nematodes (roundworms), including soil worms and parasites like hookworm. C. elegans is a lab favorite.

q: In which part of the digestive system are the so-called Brunners glands located?

q.e: Brunner's glands lie in the duodenum and release alkaline mucus to neutralize stomach acid.

q: How is the discipline of biology dedicated to the study of fungi called?

q.e: Mycology comes from the Greek word 'mykes', meaning mushroom or fungus. By contrast, myology is the anatomical study of the muscular system.

q: What part of a ducks body is recommended for treating coughs in traditional Chinese medicine?

q.e: In traditional Chinese medicine, the dried inner lining of a duck's gizzard is used for coughs and digestion. Evidence for this is thin.

q: This medical term refers to a condition, characterized by enlargement of the thyroid gland.

q.e: A goiter is an enlarged thyroid, often caused by iodine deficiency or thyroid disease. It can cause a visible swelling in the neck.

q: Human toes and fingers go by what common name?

q.e: Each human hand and foot typically has 14 phalanges: three in each finger and toe, and two in each thumb and big toe. Carpals form the wrist, while tarsals make up the ankle and heel.

q: What does the Davson-Danielli cell model look like?
Two layers of proteins sandwich a phospholipid bilayer
There are no proteins, only a phospholipid bilayer
Proteins and phospholipids are structured in a checkerboard pattern
Proteins are embedded in a phospholipid bilayer

q.e: The Davson-Danielli model of 1935 described a lipid bilayer sandwiched between two protein layers. It's been replaced by the fluid mosaic model.

q: Chemistry is defined as the natural science of matter, dealing with the composition of substances and their properties, reactions and interactions. Which of the following would NOT be an example of a chemical reaction?
converting liquid water to gaseous steam
mixing vinegar and baking soda together
the burning of a piece of wood

q.e: Boiling liquid water into steam is a physical change of state, because the chemical formula remains H2O throughout. The other options involve chemical reactions where new substances are formed.

q: What term describes the concentration of a solution in moles per liter?

q.e: Molarity is moles of solute per liter of solution, written as M. A 1 M solution has one mole per liter.

q: pH, or the negative log of the H3O+ (hydronium ion) concentration, is the measure of acidity or basicity of an aqueous solution. Which solution would have the lowest pH at room temperature?
a strong acid such as sulfuric acid
a weak base such as ammonium hydroxide
a weak acid such as acetic acid
a strong base such as sodium hydroxide solution

q.e: Because pH is calculated as the negative logarithm of hydronium concentration, stronger acids produce higher hydronium concentrations and thus lower pH values. A standard 1 molar solution of sulfuric acid has a pH around 0, whereas bases have pH values above 7.

q: What do we call a triangle that has three unequal sides?

q.e: A scalene triangle has three sides of completely different lengths and three unequal angles. In contrast, an equilateral triangle has three equal sides, and an isosceles triangle has two.

q: You have a string that is 120 inches. You must use this to enclose a shape of maximum area. What shape should you form?
A square of 60 inches on each side
A square of 30 inches on each side
A triangle of 30 inches on each side

q.e: The isoperimetric theorem proves that a circle encloses the greatest area of any shape with a fixed boundary length. A circle of circumference 120 inches yields an area of roughly 1,146 square inches, compared to 900 square inches for a 30-inch square.

q: Fats are a highly concentrated source of energy. It is estimated that one gram of fat provides how many calories?

q.e: Dietary fats provide 9 kilocalories per gram, more than double the energy density of carbohydrates and proteins, which each supply about 4 kcal per gram.

q: Carbohydrates can be found in breads, cereals, fruits, and vegetables. Which of these compounds is not a carbohydrate?

q.e: Carbohydrates are sugars, starches and fibers. Glycerol is an alcohol (polyol), though it has a sweet taste and relates to fats.

q: These compounds are emitted by plants and form gasses, which can be smelled.

q.e: Aromatic compounds from plants evaporate and are smelled as fragrance. They are a main part of essential oils.

q: These substances, present in some essential oils, slow down the development of bacteria.

q.e: Bacteriostatic substances stop bacteria from multiplying without necessarily killing them. Bactericidal ones kill them.

q: More than 2000 years ago this famous philosopher and founder of medicine stated that The way to health is an aromatic bath and scented oils massage every day.

q.e: Hippocrates (c. 460-370 BC) is the "father of medicine". The saying about aromatic baths is traditionally attributed to him.

q: These are often used as weather indicators. Before the weather gets dry, they open up. If it will be wet, they return to their normal shape.

q.e: Pine cone scales contain cells that absorb moisture from humid air and swell, closing the cone to protect the seeds from damp conditions, and reopen when the air is dry.

q: This flower opens up in sunny weather. When rain is expected, it closes tightly.

q.e: The scarlet pimpernel closes its flowers before rain and in cloudy weather, so it's the "poor man's weatherglass."

q: If at noon on the 2nd of February you see this animals shadow, be sure the weather will be cold.

q.e: Groundhog Day is celebrated each year on February 2 in North America, with the famous Punxsutawney Phil supposedly predicting six more weeks of winter if he sees his shadow. The tradition evolved from the Christian holiday of Candlemas and European badger or hedgehog weather lore.

q: Once a tropical cyclone reaches wind speeds of at least 39 mph, it is classified as a tropical storm. At what minimum wind speed is a tropical storm classified as a hurricane or typhoon?

q.e: Under the Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale, a system becomes a Category 1 hurricane when sustained winds reach at least 74 mph (roughly 119 km/h). Tropical storms span sustained winds from 39 to 73 mph.

q: This plant, native to the shallow waters of the Amazon River basin, is the largest representative of waterlilies.

q.e: The giant Victoria water lily (genus Victoria) produces floating leaves that can reach up to about 10 feet (3 meters) in diameter in the Amazon basin.

q: This moon, bearing the name of the ferryman of the dead in Greek mythology, is the largest satellite of Pluto.

q.e: Charon was discovered in 1978 by astronomer James Christy and is more than half the diameter of Pluto itself. Because Charon is so large relative to Pluto, the two bodies orbit a common center of mass located outside Pluto.

q: This mathematician was the first to develop an algebraic method of solving any cubic equation.

q.e: Niccolò Fontana Tartaglia found a method for solving the cubic around 1535, which Cardano later published in Ars Magna (1545).

q: Who was the first mathematician to use the term group?

q.e: Évariste Galois, before dying at age 20 in a duel in 1832, first used "group" for the algebraic structure and laid the groundwork for group theory.

q: The subject that studies the solution of a system of linear inequalities is called Linear Programming. Which of these men was most instrumental in its development?

q.e: George Dantzig developed the simplex method in 1947, which made linear programming practical.

q: Different colors derive form the different wavelengths of the spectrum of light. What part of it do we call visible light, i.e. we can perceive with our eyes?

q.e: Visible light is roughly 380-740 nm, from violet to red. Infrared and ultraviolet lie outside this range.

q: What is the science of colors called?

q.e: Chromatics is the science of color. It's closely related to optics and color theory.

q: Which of these processes does the cactus perform only at night?

q.e: Cacti open their stomata at night (CAM photosynthesis) to cut water loss, taking in CO₂ then and using it by day.

q: Roughly how fast does light travel?

q.e: The speed of light in a vacuum is defined as exactly 299,792,458 meters per second, which rounds to approximately 300,000 kilometers per second (or roughly 186,000 miles per second).

q: What is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature?

q.e: Mercury has a melting point of about -38.8 degrees Celsius (-37.9 degrees Fahrenheit), making it the only metal that is liquid at standard room temperature. Gallium melts just above room temperature at about 29.8 degrees Celsius.

q: What is the most abundant element in the Earth's crust by mass?

q.e: Oxygen makes up about 46% of the Earth's crust by mass, primarily bound in silicate minerals and oxides. Silicon is the second most abundant element, accounting for roughly 28%.

q: What is the process of decorating metal by using acid to bite patterns into the surface?

q.e: Etching uses an acid or mordant to cut into unprotected parts of a metal surface to create a design. Engraving, by contrast, relies on a sharp tool called a burin to physically carve directly into the metal.

q: At a party, a doctor asked a nurse: Are you an RN or an LPN? The nurse replied: Im an RN. I got my BSN at Georgetown. Are you an MD or a DO? The doctor replied: Im a DO. Which of the following statements can be concluded from this conversation?
The doctor was trained in osteopathic manipulation.
The doctor is going to get lucky tonight.
The doctor is not really a doctor at all.

q.e: An MD and a DO are both fully licensed physicians. DOs receive extra training in osteopathic manipulative treatment.

q: What scientists study recent or fossilized skeletal remains in order to find traces of ancient diseases?

q.e: Paleopathologists examine ancient bones and mummies for evidence of disease. Tuberculosis and arthritis can be found.

q: Diarthrosis joints permit a variety of movement and can be divided into six classes. The femur and hip connection would be considered which joint class?

q.e: The hip joint is a classic ball-and-socket synovial joint formed by the spherical head of the femur fitting into the cup-shaped acetabulum of the pelvis. Hinge joints, like the knee or elbow, allow movement in primarily one plane.

q: Earthquakes that occur at the boundaries of tectonic plates are called interplate. The less frequent type of earthquakes, called this, occur in the interior of the lithospheric plates.

q.e: Most earthquakes happen at plate boundaries (interplate). Rarer intraplate earthquakes occur far from boundaries, such as New Madrid, Missouri, in 1811-12.

q: It is said that twins develop their own language, called this.

q.e: Idioglossia refers to a private language developed between two or very few people, most frequently observed between young twins. Sindarin and Quenya, by contrast, are fictional Elvish tongues invented by J.R.R. Tolkien.

q: In 1938, Edward Kasner wrote a 1 followed by 100 zeros and showed it to his baby nephew. What the baby said became the name of that written number. What did the kid say?

q.e: Edward Kasner's nine-year-old nephew Milton Sirotta coined "googol" (10^100) in 1938. It inspired Google's name.

q: Referred to as the father of integral calculus, he initiated the sciences of hydrostatics, static mechanics and pycnometry (the measurement of the volume or density of an object). He was killed by a Roman soldier who did not know who he was.

q.e: Archimedes of Syracuse was killed in 212 BCE during the Roman siege of Syracuse by a soldier whom he famously told not to disturb his geometric circles drawn in the sand.

q: Which of the following models of double-stranded DNA replication proved to be correct?

q.e: In 1958 Meselson and Stahl showed DNA replicates semiconservatively: each new double helix has one old and one new strand.

q: The term 'petrodollar', a dollar earned by a country through the sale of oil, was invented in 1973 by this Egyptian-born American professor and economist.

q.e: Ibrahim Oweiss coined "petrodollar" in 1973, around the oil crisis. It refers to oil revenues recycled in dollars.

q: This is the study of winds.

q.e: Anemology is the study of winds. The Greek "anemos" means wind, and an anemometer measures wind speed.

q: Which term refers to the study of atmospheric dust and its effect on life on Earth?

q.e: Coniology (koniology) studies atmospheric dust and its effects. The Greek "konis" means dust.

q: What is the study of whales called?

q.e: Cetology is the study of whales, dolphins and porpoises (cetaceans).

q: Which word means the study of dogs?

q.e: Cynology is the study of dogs. The Greek "kyon" means dog.

q: Free-fall is defined as a condition in which a falling object experiences acceleration due only to gravity. Therefore, in this case, the only weight acting on an object is its own weight. Which of the following is not an example of an object in free-fall?
A skydiver with an open parachute
A feather falling through a vacuum tube
The Earths orbit around the Sun
A space shuttle with the rockets off

q.e: A skydiver with an open parachute isn't in free fall, since air drag balances weight. An object only under gravity is in free fall.

q: Although Newtons and Einsteins theories are generally widely accepted and used in many fields of science, there are some researchers who have developed alternative theories of gravity. Which of the following is one of these theories?

q.e: The Brans-Dicke theory (1961) is a scalar-tensor alternative to general relativity. It adds a scalar field with a variable gravitational constant.

q: This intricate name, given to water, is a common hoax to misleadingly present water as a dangerous and harmful compound.

q.e: The dihydrogen monoxide hoax uses the systematic chemical name for water (two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen atom) to list real properties, such as causing burns as steam or rust on iron, to create parody petitions.

q: The source of the Amazon, the widest river in the world, is located in this area of Peru.

q.e: The Amazon's most distant source is traced to the Peruvian Andes (the Apacheta/Mismi area in Arequipa). The Amazon is the largest river by volume.

q: On a plane, a map is drawn so that the border of any two intersecting areas is more than just one point. You wish to color the map so that two intersecting area have different colors. What is the minimal number of colors you will need to color any such map?

q.e: The Four Color Theorem, proven by Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken in 1976, demonstrates that no more than four colors are required to color the regions of any planar map so that no two adjacent regions share a color.

q: What is the nearest star to the Sun?

q.e: Proxima Centauri, about 4.24 light-years away, is the nearest star to the Sun. It is a faint red dwarf with an Earth-sized planet candidate.

q: Which of the following is part of the frontal lobe, an area at the front of each cerebral hemisphere?

q.e: The precentral gyrus in the frontal lobe holds the primary motor cortex, which controls voluntary movement.

q: In 1912, a jawbone and fragments of a skull were discovered and originally named "dawn-man�. It wasn't until 41 years later that it was exposed as a hoax. This darling of creationist skepticism is known as what?

q.e: The Piltdown Man fossils presented by Charles Dawson in 1912 were proven in 1953 to be a forgery consisting of a modern human cranium combined with an altered orangutan jawbone.

q: This celestial body is the darkest of Uranus larger moons and its most distinctive feature is a large equatorial ring of bright material (supposedly a crater) named Wunda, which contrasts with the rest of the planet's dark surface.

q.e: Umbriel is the darkest of Uranus's large moons. Its bright ring-like feature, Wunda, is possibly a crater.

q: Which of these is the study of knowledge?

q.e: Epistemology is the branch of philosophy that studies knowledge: what it is and how we get it.

q: The endocrine system is made up of glands. Aden(o) means glands; adren(o) means the adrenal glands. What term means enlargement of the adrenal glands?

q.e: The suffix "-megaly" means enlargement, so adrenomegaly is enlarged adrenal glands. Splenomegaly is an enlarged spleen.

q: e^(pi*i) +1 = 0 is an important formula, involving the key mathematical constant e, which is popularly known as what?

q.e: The formula e^(ipi) + 1 = 0 is widely known as Euler's identity (a special case of Euler's formula), named after Swiss mathematician Leonhard Euler. It famously links five fundamental mathematical constants: e, i, pi, 1, and 0.

q: Chromatin, found in the nucleus of a cell, consists of a complex of Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), the gene-carrying molecule. Which of the following types of chromatin is rich in genes?

q.e: Euchromatin is loosely packed and gene-rich, so it's active in transcription. Heterochromatin is tightly packed and mostly inactive.

q: What computational device was invented in 1617?

q.e: John Napier invented Napier's bones in 1617: rods used to multiply and divide. He also invented logarithms.

q: Which of the following tests would be appropriate to confirm the diagnosis of B12 deficiency in a patient whose B12 level is at the low end of the normal range?

q.e: A raised methylmalonic acid level confirms B12 deficiency when serum B12 is borderline, as B12 is needed to process MMA. Homocysteine also rises.

q: What is the chemical formula for baking soda?

q.e: Baking soda is pure sodium bicarbonate, which consists of one sodium, one hydrogen, one carbon, and three oxygen atoms (NaHCO3). C3H8 is propane, and C12H22O11 is table sugar (sucrose).

q: What does the metric prefix nano mean?

q.e: Nano- is an SI prefix derived from the Greek word nanos, meaning dwarf. It represents a factor of 10 to the negative ninth power, or one billionth.

q: Which one of the following is indicative of Direct Disc Labeling capabilities?

q.e: LightScribe lets a disc drive burn labels onto the top of a special CD or DVD using the same laser used for data.

q: This group of alloys, which is a combination of at least one metal and one or more other elements, is used to clad fuel rods in nuclear plants.

q.e: Zircaloy, a zirconium alloy, is used for fuel-rod cladding in nuclear reactors because it absorbs few neutrons and resists corrosion.

q: Which of these is not one of the methods used by viruses to make the host cell release the newly produced viruses?

q.e: Viruses leave cells by budding, lysis or exocytosis. "Virosis" is not a release mechanism; it simply means a viral disease.

q: Who thought of the name iPod?

q.e: Vinnie Chieco, a freelance copywriter, suggested the name "iPod" for Apple's 2001 music player, inspired by the pod bay in 2001: A Space Odyssey.

q: Which of these commands will return a Windows® computers node IP address, Subnet mask and information on whether it was assigned via DHCP and how long the lease is?

q.e: In Windows, "ipconfig /all" shows IP address, subnet mask, DHCP status and lease times, plus the MAC address and DNS servers.

q: The largest known impact crater on Mercury is named what?

q.e: The Caloris Basin, about 1,550 km across, is the largest known impact crater on Mercury. It was formed by an impact more than 3.8 billion years ago.

q: Who is the author of the 1988 book 'The Alchemist'?

q.e: Paulo Coelho (Brazilian) wrote The Alchemist, published in Portuguese in 1988. It is one of the best-selling books ever.

q: What is the name of an Easter egg made for the Russian Tsars between 1885 and 1917.

q.e: Peter Carl Fabergé made jeweled Easter eggs for the Russian imperial family from 1885 to 1917. 50 imperial eggs were made.

q: A tropical cyclone is a storm with a closed circulation around a center of low pressure. Based on strength and location a tropical cyclone can be referred to by different names. Which of the following is not a possible name for a tropical cyclone?

q.e: A mesocyclone is a rotating updraft within a thunderstorm and not a tropical cyclone. Tropical cyclones are called hurricanes, typhoons or cyclones.

q: What is the name of this famous theorem? If x, y, and z are non-zero positive integers, then x^n+y^n=z^n has no solution if n is an integer greater than two.

q.e: Pierre de Fermat wrote this statement in the margin of a book in 1637, claiming he had a proof that could not fit. Known as Fermat's Last Theorem, it remained unproven until British mathematician Andrew Wiles solved it in 1994.

q: Compared to men, women are much more likely to fall into this group in regards to their color vision.

q.e: Tetrachromats have four types of cone cells in their eyes instead of three, allowing them to see a wider spectrum of color. Because the extra photopigment gene is carried on the X chromosome, this condition appears almost exclusively in women.

q: Which is the most bitter substance known to taste researchers?

q.e: Denatonium, commonly sold as Denatonium benzoate (Bitrex), can be detected by humans at concentrations as low as 10 parts per billion. It is routinely added to toxic household products and antifreeze to prevent accidental swallowing.

q: What planet do we live on?

q.e: Earth is the third planet from the Sun and the only astronomical object known to harbor life.

q: What is the closest star to Earth?

q.e: The Sun is an average of roughly 93 million miles (150 million km) away, making it our nearest star. The closest star system beyond the Sun is Alpha Centauri, about 4.2 light-years away.

q: Which planet is known as the Red Planet?

q.e: Mars appears reddish in the night sky because its surface contains abundant iron oxide, commonly known as rust.

q: Which planet is famous for its big rings?

q.e: While all four giant planets possess rings, Saturn features the most extensive and visually dramatic ring system, composed mostly of water ice and rock particles spanning hundreds of thousands of kilometers.

q: What do we call the Moon when it looks like a whole circle?

q.e: A full moon occurs when the Moon sits opposite the Sun relative to Earth, completely illuminating the side facing us. A new moon occurs when the illuminated side faces entirely away.

q: Which planet is known for having a prominent Great Red Spot?

q.e: Jupiter's Great Red Spot is an enormous anticyclonic storm wider than the entire planet Earth that astronomers have tracked continuously for well over a century.

q: On August 6, 2012, the Curiosity rover, which is part of a NASA mission, successfully landed on this planet.

q.e: Curiosity touched down inside Gale Crater on Mars using a pioneering sky crane maneuver. It was sent to determine whether Mars could ever have supported microbial life.

q: In what war had Neil Armstrong served before becoming an astronaut?

q.e: Neil Armstrong flew combat missions as a Navy pilot in the Korean War before becoming a test pilot and then an astronaut. In 1969 he became the first person to walk on the Moon.

q: The International Space Station is a joint project of five space agencies, including NASA. Which Space Agency is not part of the project?

q.e: The International Space Station involves five space agencies: NASA (USA), Roscosmos (Russia), JAXA (Japan), ESA (Europe), and CSA (Canada). China was excluded primarily due to US legislation passed in 2011 prohibiting bilateral cooperation with NASA.

q: Which planet of the Solar System is nicknamed the Blue Planet?

q.e: Earth is nicknamed the Blue Planet because liquid water covers roughly 71% of its surface, giving it a distinctive blue appearance from space.

q: Which of the following planets is closest to the Sun?

q.e: Mercury orbits closest to the Sun at an average distance of about 36 million miles (58 million kilometers). Venus is the second planet from the Sun, averaging about 67 million miles away.

q: Which planet of the Solar System is also known as The Evening Star?

q.e: Venus is the third-brightest natural object in Earth's sky after the Sun and Moon; because its orbit lies inside Earth's, it is visible only around sunrise as the Morning Star or sunset as the Evening Star.

q: Which of the following Solar System planets was not named after a Greek or Roman God?

q.e: Earth is the only planet in the Solar System not named after a mythological deity; its name derives from Old English 'eorðe' and Proto-Germanic 'ertho', meaning ground or soil. Uranus is named after a Greek deity, while the rest are named after Roman gods.

q: Which is the largest of the so-called terrestrial planets of the Solar System?

q.e: The terrestrial (rocky) planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars, and Earth is the largest, at about 12,742 km across. Venus is only slightly smaller.

q: How long does it take for the planet Earth to orbit the Sun once?

q.e: Earth takes roughly 365.25 days to complete one orbital revolution around the Sun. To account for the extra quarter of a day each year, an extra leap day is added to the calendar every four years.

q: Scientists estimate that the Earth and the Solar System were formed how long ago?

q.e: Radiometric dating of the oldest known moon rocks and meteorites dates the formation of the Solar System to roughly 4.54 billion years ago, coalescing from a giant rotating cloud of gas and dust.

q: Fill in the missing letter in this chain that has to do with the Solar System we live in: M, V, E, M, J, _, U, N.

q.e: The letters represent the planets ordered by distance from the Sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune, making S the missing letter.

q: The planet Mars is named after which of the following?

q.e: Because of its reddish appearance in the night sky, reminiscent of blood, ancient Romans named the fourth planet after Mars, their god of war. The Greeks called it Ares for the same reason.

q: What type of weather pattern on Mars can obscure the surface from view?

q.e: Martian dust storms can swell to encompass the entire planet, as seen by NASA's Opportunity rover in 2018 when a massive global storm blocked sunlight and ended its mission.

q: How long is one day on the planet Jupiter?

q.e: Despite being the largest planet in our solar system, Jupiter rotates faster than any other, completing one full rotation on its axis in about 9 hours and 55 minutes.

q: What element is the atmosphere of Jupiter mostly comprised of?

q.e: Jupiter is a gas giant made up mostly of hydrogen, with helium as the next most common gas. Its composition is much closer to the Sun's than to Earth's.

q: How long does it take for the planet Mercury to orbit the Sun once?

q.e: As the closest planet to the Sun, Mercury travels at an average orbital speed of about 47 kilometers per second (29 miles per second), completing a full orbit in just under 88 Earth days.

q: What is the size of Mars compared to the size of Earth.
The two planets can not be compared.

q.e: Mars has an equatorial diameter of about 4,212 miles (6,779 km), roughly half the size of Earth's diameter of about 7,918 miles (12,742 km). In total volume, about six planets the size of Mars could fit inside Earth.

q: How long does it take Saturn to complete one orbit around the Sun?

q.e: Saturn takes about 29.5 years to circle the Sun once, so a year on Saturn lasts nearly three decades. Its slow trip is why it moves so gradually across our night sky.

q: The atmosphere of Saturn consists mainly of what element?

q.e: Saturn's atmosphere is mostly hydrogen, with helium making up most of the rest. Like Jupiter, it is a gas giant with no solid surface.

q: How long does it take Neptune to orbit the Sun once?

q.e: Neptune takes about 165 Earth years to orbit the Sun. It was discovered in 1846, and it completed its first full orbit since that discovery in 2011.

q: Which of these orders the terrestrial planets from smallest to largest by diameter?

q.e: Mercury is the smallest rocky planet, followed by Mars, Venus and Earth. Venus is almost the same size as Earth, but Mars is only about half as wide as Earth.

q: Which is the hottest planet of the Solar System?

q.e: Despite Mercury being closest to the Sun, Venus is hotter due to an intense runaway greenhouse effect created by its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere, which traps heat at roughly 867 degrees Fahrenheit (464 degrees Celsius).

q: Which is the largest planet in our solar system?

q.e: Jupiter has an equatorial diameter of about 88,846 miles (142,984 km) and is more than twice as massive as all other planets in the solar system combined.

q: How many planets are in our solar system?

q.e: The solar system has eight official planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. Pluto was considered the ninth planet until 2006, when the International Astronomical Union reclassified it as a dwarf planet.

q: What is the name of our galaxy?

q.e: Our solar system resides in the Milky Way, a barred spiral galaxy containing an estimated 100 to 400 billion stars. Andromeda is our nearest large galactic neighbor, roughly 2.5 million light-years away.

q: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?

q.e: Neil Armstrong made history on July 20, 1969, by becoming the first person to set foot on the Moon during NASA's Apollo 11 mission. Buzz Aldrin joined him shortly after, while Michael Collins remained in lunar orbit piloting the command module.

A shooting star is a meteor: the visible streak of light created when a meteoroid burns up upon entering Earth's atmosphere. If any piece survives the journey and strikes the ground, it is called a meteorite.

q: Since Pluto's demotion, which is the smallest planet?

q.e: After the International Astronomical Union reclassified Pluto as a dwarf planet in 2006, Mercury became the smallest planet, with a diameter of about 4,879 kilometers (roughly 3,032 miles).

q: This satellite, launched from Cape Canaveral on January 31, 1958, by the Jupiter-C vehicle, was the first United States Earth satellite.

q.e: Explorer 1 carried a cosmic ray detector designed by James Van Allen, leading to the groundbreaking discovery of the Earth's surrounding Van Allen radiation belts.

q: Extraterrestrial life may be closer than we think. Which of these natural satellites of Saturn is believed to have suitable conditions for existence of life?

q.e: Titan, Saturn's biggest moon, has a thick atmosphere and lakes of liquid methane and ethane. Scientists also think it has a hidden water ocean, which is why it is a target in the search for life. Saturn's moon Enceladus is another candidate.

q: The plot of the 1968 Stanley Kubrick movie 2001: A Space Odyssey involves a space mission to which planet of the Solar system?

q.e: In the 1968 film 2001: A Space Odyssey, the spaceship Discovery One travels to Jupiter. The film was based on Arthur C. Clarke's writing, and in his novel the destination is Saturn.

q: The Roman god of war Mars corresponds to which god from the Greek mythology?

q.e: Ares was the Greek god of war, whose Roman counterpart was Mars. Zeus corresponds to Jupiter, Hades to Pluto, and Hermes to Mercury.

q: Which of the following planets is not named after a Roman god?

q.e: Uranus is named after the Greek personification of the sky, Ouranos. Most other planets in the solar system bear names from Roman mythology, such as Mars (god of war) and Neptune (god of the sea).

q: This scientist, called the father of modern physics, improved the telescope and discovered the four largest satellites of Jupiter.

q.e: In January 1610, Galileo Galilei turned his improved telescope toward Jupiter and discovered its four largest moons: Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto, now called the Galilean satellites.

q: From what country was the first astronaut who was not Russian or American?

q.e: Vladimir Remek became the first non-American and non-Soviet citizen in space when he launched aboard Soyuz 28 in March 1978 as part of the Soviet Interkosmos program.

q: In what country was the first reported working telescope created?

q.e: The earliest known working telescope was patented in the Netherlands in 1608 by German-Dutch eyeglass maker Hans Lippershey. Galileo Galilei heard about the Dutch invention the following year and improved the design for astronomical use.

q: These small bodies are considered left overs from the formation of the Solar system some 4.6 billion years ago.

q.e: Asteroids are rocky and metallic leftovers from the formation of the Solar System about 4.6 billion years ago. Most of them orbit in the belt between Mars and Jupiter.

q: This moon is the most volcanic object in the solar system. Its volcanoes erupt sulfur, sulfur dioxide and silicate rock, constantly resurfacing it.

q.e: Io's intense volcanic activity is caused by tidal heating, where gravitational pulling from Jupiter and neighboring moons generates immense internal friction. With over 400 active volcanoes, its surface is continuously renewed by sulfurous lava.

q: Where can an asteroid belt, a region of greatest concentration of orbiting asteroids, be found nearest to Earth?

q.e: The main asteroid belt lies roughly 2.2 to 3.2 astronomical units from the Sun, situated entirely between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter.

q: On May 5, 1961, this man became the first U.S. astronaut in space.

q.e: Shepard completed a suborbital flight aboard Freedom 7 on May 5, 1961, reaching an altitude of roughly 116 miles (187 km). John Glenn became the first American to orbit Earth the following year, in 1962.

q: In 2001, NASA sent this unmanned spacecraft to orbit Mars in search of signs of water and volcanic activity on the surface.

q.e: NASA launched Mars Odyssey in 2001, and it has been mapping the planet from orbit ever since. Its instruments found evidence of large amounts of water ice just below the surface.

q: Io and Europa are two of the larger satellites of which Solar System planet?

q.e: Io and Europa are two of Jupiter's four large Galilean moons, along with Ganymede and Callisto. Galileo discovered them in 1610, and Io is the most volcanically active body in the Solar System.

q: What is the distinctive feature of the sixth planet of the Solar System (counted from the Sun)?

q.e: The sixth planet from the Sun is Saturn, famous for its bright rings made of billions of pieces of ice and rock. Jupiter, Uranus and Neptune have rings too, but theirs are much fainter.

q: When was the Hubble Space Telescope put into orbit by the Space Shuttle?

q.e: The Hubble Space Telescope was carried into orbit aboard Space Shuttle Discovery during mission STS-31 in April 1990.

q: Who was the first person to orbit the Earth?

q.e: Yuri Gagarin completed a single 108-minute orbit around Earth aboard Vostok 1 on April 12, 1961. John Glenn became the first American to orbit the Earth the following year, in February 1962.

q: Name the first four planets of the Solar System in order of their distance from the Sun?

q.e: The four inner terrestrial planets closest to the Sun are Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars, followed outward by the gas giants Jupiter and Saturn.

q: What was the name of the first spacecraft to study Mars?

q.e: Mariner 4 flew past Mars in July 1965 and sent back the first close-up photos of another planet. They showed a cratered, dry world rather than the canals people had imagined.

q: Mars has the tallest known mountain in the Solar System. What is its name?

q.e: Olympus Mons is a massive shield volcano standing roughly 13.6 miles (about 22 km) tall, which makes it nearly two and a half times the height of Mount Everest above sea level. It spans about 370 miles (roughly 600 km) across.

q: The North Star, Polaris, is located within which constellation?

q.e: Polaris serves as the tail tip of Ursa Minor (the Little Bear), also known as the Little Dipper. Ursa Major contains the Big Dipper, whose two outer pointer stars (Merak and Dubhe) can be followed directly to Polaris.

q: Which of the following is NOT a constellation of the Zodiac (the ring of constellations that the sun passes through each year)?

q.e: The Winged Horse represents the constellation Pegasus, which sits north of the ecliptic. The twelve traditional zodiac constellations include Pisces (The Fish), Cancer (The Crab), and Sagittarius (The Archer).

q: German astronomer Johannes Kepler showed that the planets circle the Sun in this type of path.

q.e: Kepler's first law of planetary motion, published in 1609, overturned the ancient belief in circular orbits by demonstrating that planets orbit the Sun along elliptical paths.

q: What was the star at the center of the Solar System called by the Romans?

q.e: The ancient Romans named the Sun 'Sol', personified by the solar deities Sol Indiges and later Sol Invictus. 'Helios' was the equivalent sun deity in ancient Greek mythology.

q: What is the name of the major gap in the ring system around Saturn?

q.e: Discovered by astronomer Giovanni Domenico Cassini in 1675, the Cassini Division is a gap about 4,800 kilometers (3,000 miles) wide separating Saturn's A and B rings.

q: How many years does it take for the planet Uranus to orbit the Sun once?

q.e: Uranus orbits at an average distance of roughly 1.8 billion miles (2.9 billion km) from the Sun, requiring about 84 Earth years to complete a single revolution. Because of this, each of its seasons lasts around 21 Earth years.

q: According to the distance between the planets and the Sun, Jupiter is situated between which two planets in the Solar system?

q.e: Moving outward from the Sun, the inner terrestrial planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars. Jupiter sits fifth, between Mars and Saturn, separated from Mars by the main asteroid belt.

q: How many moons, revolving around Jupiter, did Galileo Galilei discover in the 17th century?

q.e: In 1610, Galileo Galilei discovered Jupiter's four largest moons: Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto. Today, these are collectively known as the Galilean moons.

q: Which one is not a name of a Galilean moon revolving around Jupiter?

q.e: The four Galilean moons of Jupiter are Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto, named after figures from Greek myth linked to Zeus. Athena is a Greek goddess but not one of these moons.

q: The first directly-observed collision between two solar system bodies was between Jupiter and which comet?

q.e: Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 broke apart and struck Jupiter in July 1994, giving astronomers their first direct view of a collision between two Solar System bodies.

q: The four Jovian planets in the Solar system are Jupiter, Saturn, Neptune and which other planet?

q.e: The four giant planets are Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants, while Uranus and Neptune are often called ice giants.

q: Which two planets of the Solar System, characterized by a low magnetic field, have no moons at all?

q.e: Mercury and Venus are the only two planets in the solar system without natural satellites. Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos, while Earth has one.

q: Which planet spins on its side?

q.e: Uranus has an extreme axial tilt of about 98 degrees, meaning its rotational axis points almost directly at the Sun, causing it to roll on its side as it orbits.

q: Roughly how long does sunlight take to reach Earth?

q.e: At an average distance of about 93 million miles (150 million km) between the Sun and Earth, light traveling at roughly 300,000 km per second takes approximately 8 minutes and 20 seconds to make the trip.

q: What is the name of the brightest star in the night sky as seen from Earth?

q.e: Sirius, located in the constellation Canis Major roughly 8.6 light-years away, has an apparent visual magnitude of -1.46, making it nearly twice as bright as Canopus, the next brightest star. Polaris is famous for pointing north, but it ranks only around 48th in nighttime brightness.

q: This ancient thinker, who was the first person to propose a heliocentric model of the Solar system, considered that the Earth revolves around the Sun.

q.e: Aristarchus of Samos proposed a heliocentric model around the 3rd century BCE, placing the Sun at the center of the known universe roughly 1,800 years before Nicolaus Copernicus. Hipparchus, who lived later, favored the traditional geocentric model.

q: What astronaut or cosmonaut performed the first space walk on March 18, 1965?

q.e: Soviet cosmonaut Alexei Leonov conducted the first spacewalk during the Voskhod 2 mission on March 18, 1965, spending about 12 minutes outside the spacecraft. American astronaut Ed White made the first US spacewalk nearly three months later.

q: What NASA astronauts made the first untethered space walk in history in 1984?
Bruce McCandless II and Robert L. Stewart
Terence T. Henricks and Bruce E. Melnick
Anna Lee Fisher and Frederick D. Gregory

q.e: In February 1984, Bruce McCandless II and Robert Stewart made the first untethered spacewalks, using a jet-powered backpack called the Manned Maneuvering Unit. It let them float freely away from the Space Shuttle Challenger.

q: Neil Armstrong was the first man to walk on the moon on July 20th, 1969. Who was the astronaut that followed him?

q.e: Buzz Aldrin stepped onto the lunar surface about 19 minutes after Neil Armstrong during the Apollo 11 mission on July 20, 1969. Pete Conrad was the third man on the Moon during Apollo 12 in November 1969.

q: This constellation was named after a Greek hero who bragged to be the greatest hunter. Goddess Hera heard that and sent a scorpion after him to test his skills. The hero was stung to death by the scorpion. Zeus felt sorry and sent him to the sky.

q.e: Orion represents the mythical hunter in Greek lore, placed opposite the constellation Scorpius so the two never appear in the night sky at the same time. Sirius is the brightest star in the night sky and belongs to Canis Major, Orion's hunting dog.

q: What is the name of the first solar-powered spacecraft on a mission to Jupiter that was launched from Cape Canaveral Air Force Station in August 2011?

q.e: NASA's Juno spacecraft launched in August 2011 and reached Jupiter in 2016. It is powered by giant solar panels, even though Jupiter is far from the Sun, and it studies the planet's atmosphere and interior.

q: What was the name given by Neil Armstrong to the landing site on the moon where the Apollo 11 Lunar Module made the first moon landing?

q.e: After guiding the Lunar Module Eagle to a touchdown in the Moon's Mare Tranquillitatis on July 20, 1969, Neil Armstrong announced, Houston, Tranquility Base here. The Eagle has landed.

q: Name the first artificial satellite, put in orbit on October 4 in 1957, which marked the beginning of the space race.

q.e: Sputnik 1 was launched by the Soviet Union into low Earth orbit in October 1957, transmitting radio beeps for about 21 days until its batteries died.

q: Which famous person was both born and died in years, when Halleys Comet was visible?

q.e: Samuel Clemens, better known as Mark Twain, was born on November 30, 1835, two weeks after Halley's Comet reached perihelion, and died of a heart attack on April 21, 1910, one day after its next perihelion.

q: This open cluster can be found in the constellation of Taurus, and is known as M45. According to Greek mythology, seven of its brightest stars are sisters.

q.e: The Pleiades, or Seven Sisters, is an open star cluster roughly 440 light-years away from Earth in the Taurus constellation. In Charles Messier's astronomical catalog of deep-sky objects, it is cataloged as M45.

q: This dog was the first living being to orbit planet Earth. She went into space aboard the Soviet Unions Sputnik 2 on November 3, 1957.

q.e: Laika, a stray dog found on the streets of Moscow, became the first animal to orbit the Earth aboard Sputnik 2. She paved the way for human spaceflight, proving that living organisms could survive the launch into microgravity.

q: The Lunar seas are actually plains of gabbro and this rock. The same rock is also a main component of the surface of Mars.

q.e: The dark "seas" on the Moon are huge plains of hardened basaltic lava. Basalt also makes up much of the surface of Mars.

q: Larger than Pluto and Mercury, this natural satellite is the largest moon of the entire solar system.

q.e: With a diameter of about 3,273 miles (5,268 km), Jupiter's moon Ganymede is roughly 8% larger than the planet Mercury and about 2% larger than Saturn's largest moon, Titan.

q: Named after the leading sylph in Alexander Popes poem Rape of the Lock, the moon Ariel is the natural satellite of which planet of the solar system?

q.e: Ariel is a moon of Uranus, discovered in 1851. Many Uranian moons take their names from characters in the plays of Shakespeare and the poems of Alexander Pope.

q: Mars has two natural satellites. What are their names?

q.e: Discovered by astronomer Asaph Hall in 1877, Phobos and Deimos are named after the twin mythological sons of the Greek war god Ares (the equivalent of the Roman Mars), representing fear and dread.

q: What is the name of the six-wheeled robotic vehicle of the Pathfinder Mission on Mars?

q.e: Sojourner was NASA's first Mars rover, landing with the Mars Pathfinder spacecraft on July 4, 1997, and operating for about three months.

q: The first moons of Jupiter discovered belong to this group.

q.e: Italian astronomer Galileo Galilei discovered Jupiter's four largest moons—Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto—in January 1610 using a homemade telescope.

q: What is the fifth largest moon of Jupiter, named after the nymph of Greek Mythology, who nursed young Zeus (Jupiter) with goat milk.

q.e: Amalthea is a small, reddish moon of Jupiter, discovered in 1892. It is named for the nymph who, in Greek myth, nursed the infant Zeus with goat's milk.

q: Cupid, named after a character in a Shakespearean play and discovered in 2003 with the help of the Hubble telescope, is a small natural satellite of which planet?

q.e: Cupid is a tiny moon of Uranus, spotted in 2003 in Hubble Space Telescope images. It is named after a character in Shakespeare's play Timon of Athens.

q: This space object, named after the mythological son of Ares (Mars), is the larger and innermost of Mars two moons, orbiting closer to its major planet than any other satellite in the Solar System.

q.e: Phobos, whose name means "fear" in Greek, is the larger of Mars's two moons and orbits closer to its planet than any other moon in the Solar System. It is slowly spiraling inward, and it may break apart in tens of millions of years.

q: What is the name of the largest moon of Saturn and the second largest moon in the Solar System, which was the first satellite to be discovered after the discovery of the four Galilean moons?

q.e: Dutch astronomer Christiaan Huygens discovered Titan in 1655. It is larger than the planet Mercury and the only moon in the solar system known to have a dense atmosphere.

q: This moon of Saturn looks somewhat like a bulls eye if viewed from a certain angle because of the huge Herschel crater on its surface.

q.e: Mimas's Herschel crater measures about 86 miles (139 km) across, covering nearly one-third of the moon's entire diameter. This massive impact feature gives the moon a striking resemblance to the Death Star from Star Wars.

q: A joint NASA/ESA/ASI robotic spacecraft mission to Saturn and its moons was launched in 1997. What is the spacecraft known as?

q.e: Launched in October 1997, Cassini entered orbit around Saturn in 2004, while the Huygens probe detached to make a historic landing on Titan in January 2005.

q: In 1919, the Smithsonian published "A Method of Reaching Extreme Altitudes" by which rocket pioneer?

q.e: Robert Goddard's 1919 classic paper 'A Method of Reaching Extreme Altitudes' outlined the mathematical theory of rocket propulsion and anticipated reaching the Moon, pioneering modern liquid-fueled rocketry.

q: This constellation is often associated with Ganymede, who was a beautiful Phrygian youngster. Jupiter once saw him, fell in love with the lad and came to the earth as a bird, which took him to the skies. Since then he has served as the cup bearer of the gods.

q.e: Aquarius, the water-bearer, is linked to Ganymede, a Trojan prince Zeus carried off to serve as cupbearer to the gods. Jupiter's largest moon is named after him too.

q: The Andromeda Galaxy, also known as M31, is visible to the naked eye, but only when the sky is very dark. The Persian astronomer Abd-al-Rahman Al Sufi described it as a small cloud in 964, but years later it became clear that it was a galaxy of this kind.

q.e: The Andromeda Galaxy is a barred spiral galaxy, similar in structure to our own Milky Way, located roughly 2.5 million light-years away from Earth.

q: Which of these is the study of Mars?

q.e: Areology is the study of Mars, from Ares, the Greek god of war and the counterpart of the Roman Mars. Geology is the study of Earth.

q: Which Russian astronaut became the first person to be married in space, while he was on the International Space Station?

q.e: Russian cosmonaut Yuri Malenchenko married Ekaterina Dmitriev in 2003 while he was aboard the International Space Station. She was on Earth, in Texas, and took part by video link.

q: This asteroid, orbiting around the sun, is sometimes called the second moon of the Earth but it is not a real satellite.

q.e: Cruithne is an asteroid that loops around the Sun on a path that keeps it near Earth, which earned it the nickname "Earth's second moon". It is not a true satellite because it does not orbit Earth.

q: How many players does a soccer team have on the field?

q.e: A soccer team has 11 players on the field at once, including the goalkeeper. A match can be played with as few as seven per side before it must be abandoned.

q: How many rings are on the Olympic flag?

q.e: The five interlocking rings represent the five inhabited continents of the world: Africa, the Americas, Asia, Europe, and Oceania. The symbol was designed in 1913 by Pierre de Coubertin, the co-founder of the modern Olympic Games.

q: In which sport do you score a "home run"?

q.e: A home run in baseball is when the batter hits the ball out of play, usually over the outfield fence, and gets to run all the bases and score. It's the most exciting hit in the sport.

q: How many points is a standard free throw worth in basketball?

q.e: A successful free throw in basketball awards exactly one point. Field goals made from inside the three-point arc are worth two points, while shots made from beyond the arc are worth three.

q: Which player holds the NHL record of 2,857 points?

q.e: Wayne Gretzky, nicknamed "The Great One", holds the NHL record of 2,857 career points, made up of 894 goals and 1,963 assists. No other player has reached even 2,000.

q: Which African American is in part responsible for integrating Major League baseball?

q.e: Jackie Robinson broke Major League Baseball's modern color barrier on April 15, 1947, when he started at first base for the Brooklyn Dodgers. His jersey number, 42, was retired across all major league teams in 1997.

q: Which of these NHL teams originally played in Atlanta?

q.e: The Calgary Flames began as the Atlanta Flames in 1972 and moved to Canada in 1980. Atlanta later got a new team, the Thrashers, who moved to Winnipeg in 2011.

q: Who won the UEFA Champions League in 2017?

q.e: Real Madrid won the 2017 Champions League final, beating Juventus 4-1 in Cardiff. They became the first team to win the title in back-to-back seasons since the competition was renamed in 1992.

q: In what sport is a "shuttlecock" used?

q.e: A shuttlecock, or "birdie", is the feathered or plastic projectile that players hit in badminton. It's shaped to fly in a stable way, with the heavy cork end first.

q: In the 2014 FIFA World Cup, what was the final score in the match Brazil - Germany?

q.e: Germany beat Brazil 7-1 in the 2014 World Cup semifinal in Belo Horizonte. It is one of the most shocking results in World Cup history, and Germany went on to win the title.

q: What is the name of the "tool" used to hit the white ball in snooker or billiards?

q.e: A cue stick is typically made of tapered wood, such as ash or maple, with a leather tip designed to strike the cue ball. Players apply chalk to the tip to increase friction and prevent miscues.

q: Which team has won the most Stanley Cups in the NHL?

q.e: The Montreal Canadiens hold the NHL record with 24 Stanley Cup championships, their most recent win coming in 1993, while the Toronto Maple Leafs rank second with 13 titles.

q: The Los Angeles Dodgers were originally from what U.S. city?

q.e: The Dodgers began in Brooklyn and moved to Los Angeles after the 1957 season. The name comes from Brooklyn residents who had to "dodge" the trolleys.

q: What was the year of estabilishment of the Bari Italian Football Club?

q.e: Bari, a football club from southern Italy, was founded in 1908. It has spent most of its history moving between Serie A and the lower divisions.

q: How many players are there in an association football/soccer team?

q.e: A soccer (association football) team has 11 players on the field, including the goalkeeper. Each side may also name substitutes on the bench.

q: What national team won the first UEFA Nations League?

q.e: Portugal won the first UEFA Nations League in 2019 by beating the Netherlands 1-0 in the final in Porto. The tournament was created to make international friendlies more meaningful.

q: What team did England beat to win in the 1966 World Cup final?

q.e: England defeated West Germany 4-2 after extra time at Wembley Stadium to win the 1966 FIFA World Cup, with Geoff Hurst scoring a famous hat-trick.

q: Who did Steven Gerrard win the Champions League with?

q.e: Steven Gerrard won the Champions League with Liverpool in 2005, captaining a team that came back from 3-0 down at halftime to beat AC Milan on penalties in Istanbul. It's called the "Miracle of Istanbul".

q: Which NFL team plays for New England?

q.e: The New England Patriots play their home games at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, representing the six-state New England region. Founded as the Boston Patriots in 1959, they changed their name to New England when moving to Foxborough in 1971.

q: "Stadium of Light" is the home stadium for which soccer team?

q.e: The Stadium of Light is Sunderland's ground in northeast England and opened in 1997. Its name honors the region's mining history and the miners' lamps.

q: In baseball, how many fouls are an out?

q.e: A foul ball counts as a strike but cannot count as the third strike, except for a bunt. So a batter generally cannot strike out by hitting foul balls, no matter how many.

q: Which of these NHL teams have never moved since their inception?

q.e: The St. Louis Blues joined the NHL in 1967 as part of its first expansion and have stayed in the same city ever since. They won their first Stanley Cup in 2019.
